Each day between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., the public was invited to view 15 tulip-centric floral arrangements created by professional florists, local garden clubs, and college floral design classes. Attendees were also encouraged to enjoy the thousands of tulips in bloom around the cemetery grounds, planted during December in time for them to bloom at the In the hour before the exhibit opened ,florists scurried across the chapel floor, adjusting their design pieces with meticulous focus. Because each artist is working with tulips, which wilt throughout the day, each exhibit requires a small amount of maintenance each morning to remain fresh. “Tulips tend to drink a lot of water,” said florist Suzy Skram as she changed the water in her exhibit’s pot. “They need a lot of encouragement to keep looking beautiful. Adding fresh water daily and even cutting the stems will encourage the tulips to last throughout the show.” Florist Susan Cohn said that although creating art with tulips was difficult, she liked the meaning it brought to each piece. “Just like life, the tulips are transitory. They’re not here forever,” she explained. A few florists also took time to speculate why the event has so much staying power with audiences year after year. “Flowers tell a story,” said florist Francesca Ricci. “You can ask women what flowers they had for a graduation corsage or something specific that they wanted in a wedding bouquet or something incredibly beautiful that someone gave them at some time. That could be a grand bouquet or just a single stem. Piedmont Real Estate Update March 2024 Generational Trends in Real Estate We often hear about the impact Millennials have had on the world since they came of age decades ago. From dominating the workplace and shaping social media to being environmentally conscious and native to the world of technology, they have undeniably altered the landscape. Their effect on real estate has also had an impact. From 2014 - 2022, Millennials formed the biggest share of buyers. However, in 2023, many home buyers of that generation put off a purchase due to the high cost of borrowing and unique buying habits. As a result, Gen Xers and younger Baby Boomers stepped up and took the lead. 2023 Profile of Home Buyers Since 2013, the National Association of Realtors has produced an annual report on the habits and trends of Buyers and Sellers. In 2023, we saw a few interesting data points in their research that we wanted to share. “Seventy-eight percent of home buyers financed their home purchase—a share that decreases as the age of the buyer increases. Younger buyers continue to depend on savings for their downpayment, while older buyers use proceeds from the sale of their previous residence. Twentytwo percent of younger Millennials received downpayment help in the form of a gift or a loan from a friend or relative. Older Millennial and Gen X buyers’ purchases were delayed the longest due to debt at a median of five years. Buyers overall were delayed primarily by student loan debt and high rental costs holding back saving. In fact, 35 percent of younger Millennials reported having student loan debt with a median loan balance of $30,000, compared to 30 percent of older Millennials with a median of $40,000. While only three percent of older Boomers had student loan debt with a median balance of $9,000. This may be due to not only their personal educational loans but accumulating debt from their children’s education. * AGE OF HOME BUYERS & SELLERS* Silent Generation 1925 - 1945 Younger Boomers 1955 - 1964 Older Gen Y/ Millennials 1980 - 1989 Gen Z 1999 - 2004 Older Boomers 1946 - 1954 Gen X 1965 - 1979 Younger Gen Y/ Millennnials 1990 - 1998 Characteristics of Home Buyers in 2023* First-time buyers made up 26 percent of all home buyers, a decrease from 34 percent last year. Seventy percent of younger Millennials and 46 percent of older Millennials were first-time home buyers. Behind these groups, 21 percent of Gen Xers were also first-time home buyers. Baby Boomers, both younger Boomers and older Boomers, made up the largest generation of home buyers at 39 percent. At a meeting on Monday, March 18, Piedmont City Council directed the Moraga Canyon housing project team to begin developing a specific plan for the project after narrowing the project’s options from four to two. The project’s “Option One” would keep all existing city facilities at the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue and place 130 housing units in Blair Park across the road. “Option Three” would place 130 housing units north of the skate park adjacent to the Corporation Yard and relocate the city’s corporation yard to Blair Park. Options two and four were eliminated based on the Council’s decision to prioritize the possibility of expanding the existing youth sports field to a full-size soccer field. Elements of the two preferred project options will be incorporated into the new specific plan, which will be drafted by JZMK Partners, a consulting firm hired by the city. “Certainly, as we know, housing in Piedmont is really expensive,” said Piedmont Planning Witter plaque.......................1 Letters...............................2 3rd annual Food Fest. .............3 Question Man. ......................4 Tulip Exhibition....................5 Schools. .............................6 Mock Trial team. ...................6 Laramie Project–PHS ............9 Mother-Daughter Tea . .......... 10 PPD Blue ......................... 11 Sports. ............................. 12 Museums. ......................... 16 Music, Theater................... 17 Movies. ............................ 18 PCA events. ....................... 20 Walking Piedmont............... 21 Wed. So, the addition of market-rate and affordable homes will help alleviate that to some extent,” he said. During public comment, several members of the community expressed strong support for option one, while others questioned the financial implications of these projects for the city. “I’m asking [City Council] to vote for option one mainly because of fiscal responsibility,” said Jill Lindenbaum. “I think we should be prudent about our resources and realistic. Is now really the time to be building a deluxe, new soccer field?” Some residents were also concerned about the lack of integration between market rate and low-income housing units, which they believe will isolate future residents from the community. “Please distribute the income groups throughout the city so as not to create a poor neighborhood in one corner [of the city],” said community member Karen Harley. “Historically, in other parts of our country, creating a ghetto is a situation ripe for strife and contention,” she added. The discussion was spirited as community member Julie Collins took the podium for a rebuttal. “This idea of a ghetto [...] I don’t believe that’s going to happen. And we desperately need more residents. I mean, our population has almost dropped by 1,000 since 2020,” said Collins. At this meeting, the City also announced that it would seek up to 199 new housing units rather than the previously planned 132 units. The project’s initial goal was to build 60 low-income housing units and 72 market-rate units. All new housing units added to the plan would be market rate, with 60 low-income units and up to 139 potential market-rate units in total.

articles.text: In November of 2023, shortly before the beginning of Advent, my daughter called to say that she had decided to seek confirmation in the Catholic Church and that she needed a letter to the priest of the church she was joining certifying that she had been baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. I responded as follows. December 2, 2023 This letter is written to confirm that Kristen Anne Phillips (Hopkins) was baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit by me on Easter Sunday (April 3) 1994 in a service of public worship at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. I am happy that Kristen (my beloved daughter) is continuing her spiritual journey by becoming part of the Roman Catholic tradition. It is truly the mother church to which she is turning. I commend her to your care. May the Peace of Advent guide us all this season. The Reverend Dr. H. James Hopkins Now, as Easter approaches, she will be confirmed on Holy Saturday, March 30, 2024. Last week we were talking about this and I told her I wanted to write about her decision and asked her to summarize the main reasons for her decision. Her answers are important. At least to me, they represent not a repudiation of religious tradition in which she was raised, but rather a testimony to the human longing for a spiritual home, a community, a tradition, a place, in which our souls can thrive. articles.text: In true community fashion, the third annual Piedmont Food Fest represents the convergence of talent, creativity, and dedication from an array of contributors, planners, partners, and sponsors motivated to deliver the most memorable festival experience on April 20 in Piedmont Park. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who have enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, and boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discoverPhotos by Meghan Bennett Last year’s attendees at the Piedmont Food Fest had a chance to meet local retailers. Emeryville Taiko performed traditional Japanese taiko drumming at last year’s Piedmont Food Fest. ing something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year’s lineup of food vendors will include fan favorites such as Robert Dorsey Catering, The Chairman, La Santa Torta, Arthur Mac’s, Satay by the Bay, and Kiss My Boba, as well as newcomers MOMOlicious, Lahore Di Khushboo, Sunrise Deli, Hila Gelato, and Annie’s T Cakes. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrant No Spices will be reprising their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. The event is free to attend and Early Bird discounts on Beer & Wine tastings as well as KidZone passes are available through March. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org for more information on this can’t-miss community experience. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: Tulip enthusiasts have plenty to be excited about this month. Mountain View Cemetery’s 16th Annual Tulip Exhibition will soon open for three days of spectacular tulip floral designs created by Bay Area florists, local garden clubs, and college floral design classes. The exhibit will be held in the Tower Chapel from Friday, March 22 through Sunday, March 24, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Community members are invited to view the extravagant exhibits as well as enjoy the thousands of tulips planted around the cemetery grounds this Spring. Additionally, event organizers will hold special demonstrations each day at 2 p.m. where audiences can learn basic floral arrangement skills. Agnes Kang created this piece called “Tantalizing Tulips” on behalf of the Piedmont Garden Club in 2018. The Organization of Floral Art Designers contributed this design with bright orange and yellow tulips and orange wire ribbon in 2018. The exhibit is free and no reservations are required. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s tulip exhibition has become a cherished community tradition. “Our family puts this event on the calendar months in advance,” said community member Barbara Turtle. “The exhibits are fabulous, and it gives us the perfect reason to come and enjoy all the beautiful tulips in bloom throughout the cemetery grounds.” Every year, Mountain View Cemetery celebrates spring by displaying thousands of tulips in bloom. Imported directly from Holland, the tulips are delivered in December and planted in early January so that they mature close to Easter. Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, the tulip exhibition returned to Mountain View Cemetery last year after a three-year absence due to COVID-19. Mountain View Cemetery, located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue, is an historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont that has served the community since 1863. For more information on the cemetery or its annual tulip exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery.org or call 510-658-2588. Using four life-sized urns, floral designer Lyal Nickals of San Leandro created a dramatic entry to the Tower Chapel for the annual Tulip Show at Mountain View Cemetery in 2018.
articles.title: 16th Annual Tulip Exhibit opens this Friday

articles.text: The Piedmont Public Works Department has announced the opening of a new ADA-compliant access ramp in Dracena Park. Completed on March 7, the ramp provides a low-incline pathway connecting Dracena Avenue to the main body of the off-leash dog area in the park. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that the ramp is “for all intents and purposes, very usable at this point.” Community members have responded positively to the development so far. “I think this park is special,” said community member Jeff Hamm, who visits the Dracena Park off-leash dog area once a week. “I like all the trees, and my dogs really like to run around here.” Hamm mentioned that he noticed the new ramp but did not consider it an eyesore. “I think it’s a good thing that more people can access the park,” he said. Public rights-of-way and facilities are required to be accessible to persons with disabilities under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990. The city first received a request for ADA access to an offleash dog park in mid-2023. After a review of all parks in Piedmont and consulting with the city attorney, Public Works identified Dracena Park as the best site for a possible ADA ramp. Construction for this project began on February 5. For questions about the project contact Gonzales at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov. Staff photos An ADA-compliant ramp at the entry to Dracena Park finished installation on March 7.
articles.title: ADA ramp installed at Dracena Park

articles.text: When Maryann Phelps tripped on the recently constructed bulbout on the corner of Oakland Avenue and El Cerrito Avenue, she didn’t remember falling. “It all happened so fast. I just went down,” she recalls. Phelps credits her fall to a small, threeinch raised curb on the northeastern bulb-out at that intersection which caught her foot as she tried to cross the street. A longtime resident of El Cerrito Avenue, she was at about 7:30 p.m. and barely noticed it in the evening darkness. After her fall, two strangers passing by helped her to her feet and walked her home, where her husband drove her to the fire station to be checked out. Phelps is currently recovering from an unrelated concussion and wanted to rule out the possibility of complications. “We were hoping the fire department would give us the okay to go home, but they didn’t,” said Phelps. Phelps spent Wednesday night, March 13, bouncing between hospital rooms in Alta Bates Summit Medical Center before her X-rays and CAT scans came back normal, and she left the hospital. The ordeal left her with scraped heel palms, a black eye and lingering pain in her jaw. Phelps said the current design of the bulb-outs poses a hazard and she would like to see more safety measures taken by the City to prevent trip-and-falls. “I’d just like to see something placed there before it happens to somebody else,” she said. Staff Photos The northeastern bulb out recently constructed on the corner of Oakland and El Cerrito Avenues caused a community member to trip and fall last week due to poor visibility of its curb.

Mountain View Cemetery’s 16th Annual Tulip Exhibition will soon open for three days of spectacular tulip floral designs created by Bay Area florists, local garden clubs, and college floral design classes. The exhibit will be held in the Tower Chapel from Friday, March 22 through Sunday, March 24, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Community members are invited to view the extravagant exhibits as well as enjoy the thousands of tulips planted around the cemetery grounds this Spring. Additionally, event organizers will hold special demonstrations each day at 2 p.m. where audiences can learn basic floral arrangement skills. Agnes Kang created this piece called “Tantalizing Tulips” on behalf of the Piedmont Garden Club in 2018. The Organization of Floral Art Designers contributed this design with bright orange and yellow tulips and orange wire ribbon in 2018. The exhibit is free and no reservations are required. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s tulip exhibition has become a cherished community tradition. “Our family puts this event on the calendar months in advance,” said community member Barbara Turtle. “The exhibits are fabulous, and it gives us the perfect reason to come and enjoy all the beautiful tulips in bloom throughout the cemetery grounds.” Every year, Mountain View Cemetery celebrates spring by displaying thousands of tulips in bloom. Imported directly from Holland, the tulips are delivered in December and planted in early January so that they mature close to Easter. Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, the tulip exhibition returned to Mountain View Cemetery last year after a three-year absence due to COVID-19. Mountain View Cemetery, located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue, is an historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont that has served the community since 1863. For more information on the cemetery or its annual tulip exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery.org or call 510-658-2588. Using four life-sized urns, floral designer Lyal Nickals of San Leandro created a dramatic entry to the Tower Chapel for the annual Tulip Show at Mountain View Cemetery in 2018. ADA ramp installed at Dracena Park By Matt Simons The Piedmont Public Works Department has announced the opening of a new ADA-compliant access ramp in Dracena Park. Completed on March 7, the ramp provides a low-incline pathway connecting Dracena Avenue to the main body of the off-leash dog area in the park. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that the ramp is “for all intents and purposes, very usable at this point.” Community members have responded positively to the development so far. “I think this park is special,” said community member Jeff Hamm, who visits the Dracena Park off-leash dog area once a week. “I like all the trees, and my dogs really like to run around here.” Hamm mentioned that he noticed the new ramp but did not consider it an eyesore. “I think it’s a good thing that more people can access the park,” he said. Public rights-of-way and facilities are required to be accessible to persons with disabilities under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990. The city first received a request for ADA access to an offleash dog park in mid-2023. After a review of all parks in Piedmont and consulting with the city attorney, Public Works identified Dracena Park as the best site for a possible ADA ramp. Construction for this project began on February 5. For questions about the project contact Gonzales at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov. Staff photos An ADA-compliant ramp at the entry to Dracena Park finished installation on March 7. Resident trips, injured by bulb-outs By Matt Simons When Maryann Phelps tripped on the recently constructed bulbout on the corner of Oakland Avenue and El Cerrito Avenue, she didn’t remember falling. “It all happened so fast. I just went down,” she recalls. Phelps credits her fall to a small, threeinch raised curb on the northeastern bulb-out at that intersection which caught her foot as she tried to cross the street. A longtime resident of El Cerrito Avenue, she was at about 7:30 p.m. and barely noticed it in the evening darkness. After her fall, two strangers passing by helped her to her feet and walked her home, where her husband drove her to the fire station to be checked out. Phelps is currently recovering from an unrelated concussion and wanted to rule out the possibility of complications. “We were hoping the fire department would give us the okay to go home, but they didn’t,” said Phelps. Phelps spent Wednesday night, March 13, bouncing between hospital rooms in Alta Bates Summit Medical Center before her X-rays and CAT scans came back normal, and she left the hospital. The ordeal left her with scraped heel palms, a black eye and lingering pain in her jaw. Phelps said the current design of the bulb-outs poses a hazard and she would like to see more safety measures taken by the City to prevent trip-and-falls. “I’d just like to see something placed there before it happens to somebody else,” she said. See Bulb-out Injury on page 29 Staff Photos The northeastern bulb out recently constructed on the corner of Oakland and El Cerrito Avenues caused a community member to trip and fall last week due to poor visibility of its curb.

articles.text: Sports, games and camp crafts will be offered to pre-teens and young teens by Julian and Quincy Scherman, sons of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman, at the fourth annual Scherman Summer Camp. Campers will learn new games, get some fresh air, practice new skills, make friends and be themselves. Campers will have fun playing kickball, capture the flag, soccer, basketball, poker, and dominos. Julian, aided by brother Quincy, will teach the art of wood-burning and how to make paracord survival bracelets. Scherman Summer Camp is a screen-free old-fashioned camp. It is open to students entering grades 5-10 and will be held at the Havens School playground. One-week sessions begin the weeks of June 3, June 10, and June 17. The camp will run daily from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. For more information and to register, call the Recreation Department at 420-3070.

Piedmont’s primary defense attorney team for much of the year has included Gus Von Metzsch, Mary Schickedanz, and Jacques Saldhana with closing defense summations by Hempeck. Piedmont’s prosecuting attorneys will urge for a 1st degree murder charge and include Lizzy Long, Ellie Bleharski, and Hannah Sullivan, with Elena Stevens making the closing arguments for the prosecution. Team members playing other roles crucial to a case like bailiff, trial characters and witnesses include Anna Caputo, Arianna Kortum, Ayaan Jajodia, Chloe Graham, Claire Warner, Ellie Schleuning, Emily Williamson, Hallie Burden, Heiko Sexton-Boer, Ella Hughes, Kira Pan, Luisa Cole, Maddy Hill, Ryo Woltag, Sasha Jerez, and Sophie Santander. PHS History teacher Hillary Freeman is the faculty advisor and will accompany the students to the finals in Los Angeles. “Ms. Freeman has been really great in supporting us and letting us stand on our own when we can,” said Hempeck. “She’s given me a lot of opportunities to lead and instruct the team as president, which makes the role feel really meaningful.” The Mock Trial Team solidified its skill during February in competition with 15 other schools in the county twice a week in the Renee C. Davidson Superior Courthouse in Oakland. According to senior Elena Stevens, the work started well before February, however. “Since August, I’ve found that the preparation our team does for the competition is like no other activity I’ve participated in in high school. Just the sheer number of hours everyone is willing to put in truly makes the team what it is, and has contributed to the tight knit bond the team has formed.” said Stevens. If Piedmont can round up the rest of the state with a victory on Sunday they would move on to the National competition in July with a new case packet. Whether they win or not, the season has taught many life lessons to team members. As the leader, Hempeck has worked on how to give constructive criticism this year, to create a positive environment. “In an activity like Mock Trial, it’s easy to get competitive or feel shame when you mess up, and that is definitely a culture I worked to change throughout the season,” said Hempeck. articles.text: A formidable flock of bird calling contestants are fine tuning their calls for Friday, March 29, when the 55th annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will be held in the Alan Harvey Theater. The event was founded more than half a century ago by former Piedmont High School biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck. Tickets are still available for the 7:00 p.m. event. This year’s celebrity judge is Alex Hirsch, a former contest winner and creator of the hit Disney animation series Gravity Falls. This year’s expert ornithology judge is PHS Alum Yossi Fendel, with PHS senior Daniel Banin serving as master of ceremonies. Math teacher Auban Willats will also be on the judging panel. Fifteen entries will try to impress the judges and the audience. The entries include several large groups with several English classes performing en masse. Ornithology students should have a wing up on the competition in memorizing the scientific names and showing off bird behavior. Well over 100 students will perform bird calls. Tickets are available at Showtix4u.com/event-details/81154. Prices are $25 for general admission, and $15 for students. The Bird Calling Steering Committee includes outgoing Assistant Principal Erin Igoe, ornithology teacher Andy Willats, and PHS dance teacher Amy Moorhead. The show is produced by outgoing librarian Kathryn Levenson. For decades the bird calling winners appeared on national television as Piedmont’s public face to the world performing their bird calls on the Johnny Carson Show, and David Letterman Show among others. For questions contact Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12. ca.us or call 594 2781. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: 55th Piedmont Bird Calling Contest on March 29

articles.text: March is Women’s History Month, a time to celebrate and recognize the remarkable achievements and contributions of women throughout the past and present, and the role they play in inspiring future generations. Sally Ride made history on June 18, 1983, when she became the first American woman to travel to space. She was born in 1951 in Encino, California, and from a young age was fascinated by science. Her journey toward becoming an astronaut began at Stanford University, where she earned a Bachelor of Science in Physics and a Bachelor of Arts in English. She continued her education at Stanford, earning a Master of Science and a Doctorate in Physics. Towards the end of her academic career, she came across an advertisement for NASA’s astronaut program and decided to apply. In 1978 Ride joined the astronaut program. Out of 8,000 applicants, she was one of 35 individuals chosen and one of only six women selected. After years of training, she was assigned to the historic STS-7 mission. On June 18, 1983, Sally Ride embarked on the STS-7 mission aboard the space shuttle Challenger, making her the first American woman to travel to space and only the third woman in history to achieve this incredible milestone. The crew of five returned after a 147-hour mission. After this groundbreaking achievement, Sally Ride embarked on a second mission where she journeyed back into space in 1984 for an 8-day voyage. After leaving NASA in 1989, Sally Ride founded Sally Ride Science in 2001 to pursue her long-time “passion of motivating girls and young women to pursue careers in science, math, and technology” as explained by Sally Ride. Her remarkable accomplishments broke gender barriers and paved the way for future generations of women. She is an inspiration to many, encouraging them to believe in themselves and pursue careers in STEM. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a nonprofit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Sally Ride: Journey to Outer Space

articles.text: Dedicated on September 24, 1948 in honor of Jean C. Witter, Jr., beloved son, star quarterback, respected team captain, Optimo Award winner and honor student at Piedmont High School from 1935-1938. Jean took his athletic talents to U.C. Berkeley where his blocked punt led the Bears to a 16-0 upset win over Stanford in the 1941 Big Game. He also played rugby all four years and captained the 1942 National Championship Cal rugby team. Upon graduation from Cal, Jean was commissioned as an Ensign, United States Naval Reserve, and assigned to the USS San Francisco. He courageously gave his life for freedom on November 13, 1942 during the Battle of Guadalcanal, one of the fiercest naval battles of WWII. His ship took forty-five major hits while inflicting severe damage to a Japanese task force with vastly superior firepower. The destroyer escort, USS Witter, was named in his honor.
articles.title: WITTER FIELD

articles.text: Dress rehearsal of The Laramie Project by the PHS Advanced Acting class. Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform The Laramie Project at Alan Harvey Theater Thursday through Saturday this week. The performance comes 25 years after of the death of Matthew Shepard, a young gay man living in LaraThe cast includes: Breah Bell, Logan Faucher, Ella Fleischer, Jacob Hanke, Sophie Hess, Miranda Long, Charlotte Mascola, Alexis Montero Castro, Phoenix Nwokedi, Ella Puckett, Macy Puckett, Benjamin Sachs, Dahlia Saffouri, Clio Salzer, Friedie Schickedanz, Martha Schickedanz, Xander Schulte Sasse, Sadie Shoop, Louisa Symkowick, Eve Tellegen, and Isabella Wire. The Laramie Project is a true story that presents a deeply Rehearsal photos by Sophie Hess complex portrait of homophobia, justice, and acceptance. The narrative follows a community’s response to the 1998 murder of Shepard. The play, written by members of the Tectonic Theater Project, is drawn from over 200 recorded interviews with the citizens of Laramie after Shepard’s death. The resulting play -- a portrait of an American town forced to confront itself -- helped to change the way hate and love and acceptance are discussed in this country. articles.text: The Mother-Daughter Team of Girl Scout Troop 30713: (front) Min Kim (left), Emma Chan, Cortney Allen; (back): Skye Prata Baack, Lucy Allen, Maya Chan, Michele Kwok, Sally Baack, Jeannie Choi, and Kate Tong. On Sunday, March 17, Piedmont 9th grade Girl Scout Troop 30713 hosted the annual Piedmont Tea. It was the first time the Troop hosted the event. More than 100 guests, comprised of Girl Scouts, non-Girl Scouts, mothers, daughters, grandmothers, sisters, and friends, enjoyed the traditional afternoon tea at Veterans Hall. The tea service was followed by teacup painting for a take-home memento of the afternoon. Begun in 2010, the Annual Tea has become a beloved Piedmont tradition, and Troop 30713 is looking forward to hosting it again next Spring. Troop 30713 Girl Scouts pull out prizes for the 10 raffle winners at the annual Mother-Daughter Tea. Guests enjoy the afternoon Tea and Teacup Painting.

articles.text: Piedmont Adult School is offering a new class in its Spring session, “Learn to Draw Songbirds with Colored Pencil.” The class will be held on Mondays, from 6:30- 8:30 p.m. from April 15 to May 20. In this introductory course, students will learn a wide variety of techniques such as layering, blending, and adding texture, to help bring their birds to life. Instructor Jennifer Linderman will demonstrate how to simplify each bird using shapes, light, and shadow, capturing their form and proportions. Students will be provided with a printed reference photo of the bird and other relevant handouts as guides. A list of materials to purchase will be provided in advance of the class. This class offers a unique opportunity for students to explore their creativity and learn new artistic skills in a supportive The instructor for the songbird art class is Jennifer Linderman, a mixed media artist with more than 13 years of experience as a teacher. and inspiring environment. For more information and to register, please visit piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655

pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 20, 2024 Mother-Daughter Tea a big success Learn to draw songbirds at Adult School art class Piedmont Adult School is offering a new class in its Spring session, “Learn to Draw Songbirds with Colored Pencil.” The class will be held on Mondays, from 6:30- 8:30 p.m. from April 15 to May 20. In this introductory course, students will learn a wide variety of techniques such as layering, blending, and adding texture, to help bring their birds to life. Instructor Jennifer Linderman will demonstrate how to simplify each bird using shapes, light, and shadow, capturing their form and proportions. Students will be provided with a printed reference photo of the bird and other relevant handouts as guides. A list of materials to purchase will be provided in advance of the class. This class offers a unique opportunity for students to explore their creativity and learn new artistic skills in a supportive The instructor for the songbird art class is Jennifer Linderman, a mixed media artist with more than 13 years of experience as a teacher. and inspiring environment. For more information and to register, please visit piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655 The Mother-Daughter Team of Girl Scout Troop 30713: (front) Min Kim (left), Emma Chan, Cortney Allen; (back): Skye Prata Baack, Lucy Allen, Maya Chan, Michele Kwok, Sally Baack, Jeannie Choi, and Kate Tong. On Sunday, March 17, Piedmont 9th grade Girl Scout Troop 30713 hosted the annual Piedmont Tea. It was the first time the Troop hosted the event. More than 100 guests, comprised of Girl Scouts, non-Girl Scouts, mothers, daughters, grandmothers, sisters, and friends, enjoyed the traditional afternoon tea at Veterans Hall. The tea service was followed by teacup painting for a take-home memento of the afternoon. Begun in 2010, the Annual Tea has become a beloved Piedmont tradition, and Troop 30713 is looking forward to hosting it again next Spring. articles.text: Minor damage inflicted on home, no injuries Tom Phelps woke up around 10 a.m. on Wednesday, March 13, and saw orange cones lined up on the street from his bedroom window. “I thought they must be fixing the curb,’” he recalled. “After my morning routine, I sat on the bed, looked out the window, and realized, holy vow, there’s a tree down there!” A significant portion of a cityowned tree on the sidewalk in front of his home had split off and fallen onto his front lawn and on his roof and rain gutter. The tree just narrowly missed the front room window. Workers from the Public Works Department were called to dispose of the tree. The tree was cut up, processed, and removed within half an hour of the workers’ arrival, and their lawn was once again empty by 1 p.m. Public Works attributes the tree’s fall to high winds in the area. “Anytime you have an urban forest, you’re always concerned A fallen tree lands on the Phelps roof and rain gutter, narrowly missing the window. about the health of your trees,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “I think Piedmont does a very good job of maintaining its trees. We trim around a thousand trees every year, and we just completed our tree survey. We’ve been having strong wind events recently, which caused this tree to fail unexpectedly.” Public Works attributes the city-owned tree’s fall to high winds in the area. articles.text: 5-game winning streak ends with 1-run loss to Archie Williams Piedmont’s baseball team beat both Hayward and St. Patrick before having a five-game winning streak interrupted by a 5-4 loss to Archie Williams in San Anselmo on Friday, December 15. The pair of victories were over Hayward, 15-7 at Humphries Diamond, and 8-6 against St. Patrick on Tuesday, December 12 in Vallejo. Piedmont put on a strong hitting display with home runs in each of the games. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos hit a two-run shot against St. Patrick, and Markos Lagios cracked homers against both Hayward and the Peregrine Falcons. “Batting leadoff, I usually try to get deeper in the count, but I’m trying to hit the ball. too. He threw a fastball and left it right over the plate,” Lagios said following the win over Hayward. It’s been a strong start to the season for Piedmont, giving coach Eric Olson one of the best starts in his years with the team, “We’re certainly happy with where we are,” said Olson. “The bats were alive, I’m super proud of the guys. We don’t have a huge team like last year, so everyone’s been playing,” The Highlander bats have been a major part of the team’s hot start, with 18 hits against Hayward, eight against St. Patrick, and five against Archie Williams. “We’re proving we’re one of the best teams in NCS, so we just have to keep swinging and producing,” Will Parker said. “Every win we’ve had just pushes us to our final goal, which is to win the North Coast Section,” added Diego Delventhal. The Highlanders have an exciting week ahead, They will play at Oracle Park in San Francisco, home of the Giants on Saturday, March 23, in the Dante Benedetti Invitational. Their game with University will be at 11 a.m. and three runs scored. Papahadjopoulos was 3-for-3 with a double, two RBIs, and three runs scored. Dando was 3-for-3 with a double, four RBIs and two runs scored. Dicke was 3-for-4 with three RBIs and two runs scored. Vo was 2-for-4 with a double, two RBIs and a run scored. Fresh man pitcher Sam Ragones got the win, throwing three innings with five strikeouts, and allowing one earned run and one hit. 15-7 win over Hayward After allowing three runs in the top of the first inning, Piedmont stormed back to lead 4-3 in the bottom half. The Farmers tacked on two more in the top of the second, 5-4, but Piedmont rallied to add six runs in the bottom of the third, four more in the next inning, and one more in the fifth. The third inning started with a double by Parker off the deep right-center field fence, followed by Papahadjopoulos going opposite field for a double of his own off the right field fence—scoring Parker. Dando put PHS ahead with a single, while Brandon Dicke had an RBI single to make it 7-5. After Vo then smashed a double over the left fielder’s head, Lagios smacked a one-out, threerun homer over the left field fence and into Wildwood Elementary park—10-5. Final stats: Lagios was 3-for-5 with a double, homer, three RBIs, and two runs scored. Delventhal was 2-for-5 with a run. Parker was 2-for-3 with a double, RBI, 8-6 victory over St. Patrick St. Patrick opened with a 2-0 lead, but PHS got to the front with a three-run bottom of the second and added one more the following inning. The Bruins tacked on two more in the top of the fifth, but Piedmont rallied to add four runs in the bottom of the fifth. St. Patrick added two more in the top of the sixth Piedmont’s four-run bottom of the fifth started with Krumins getting hit by a pitch, while Parker brought him all the way around from first on a double to center field. Next up was Papahadjopoulos, cracking a tworun homer to left field. Dando singled, then scored after Jack Meyjes reached first on an error, then advanced to second. Final stats: Parker was 1-for-4 with a double, RBI and run scored. Papahadjopoulos was 2-for-2 with a homer, two RBIs, and three runs scored. Dando was 3-for-3 with a double, RBI and two runs scored. Ellis Moss got the win with 4.1 innings pitched and six strikeouts. 5-4 loss to Archie Williams Both teams were tied 1-1 after the first inning, while Archie Williams piled on four runs in the bottom of the fourth. PHS fought valiantly in the top of the seventh and scored three runs to close the score to 5-4 deficit, but couldn’t put the tying run across. Trailing 5-1 entering the final inning, Shafer Dando reached first base on a dropped third strike, while Jordan Vo drew a walk. With two outs and two runners on, Lagios cracked a threerun homer in a 1-2 count over the left field fence. But that was it, with Archie Williams striking out the last batter. Final stats: Lagios went 1-for-4 with a home run, three RBIs, and a run scored. Parker went 2-for-3, Krumins was 1-for-3 with an RBI. articles.text: Staff Photos Lucas Smolko defeated Lick-Wilmerding’s top singles starter, but lost in a match with Alameda. King and Tenney lost in three sets, 6-1, 2-6, 10-8. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team wrapped up a productivity week by winning three matches in three days. They shut out Hayward 7-0 on Thursday, March 14 on the road, edged past North Coast Section rival Lick-Wilmerding 4-3 in San Francisco the previous day, and beat league opponent Alameda 5-2 on Tuesday, March 12 at home. “We are playing well, which is important as the season is getting into full swing,” coach Jim Landes said. 7-0 over Hayward Hayward only had six players available and forfeited No. 2 and No. 3 doubles. At singles, Brahma won by a clean 6-0, 6-0 sweep, while Tenney also won 6-0, 6-0 at No. 2. Siddharth won 6-1, 6-0 at No. 3 and Olsen won 6-1, 6-4 at No. 4. In the only doubles match, Fasteau and Maximo Miller won easily 6-0, 6-0. 5-2 over Alameda At singles, Ben Breber won at No. 2 in double-bagel shutout fashion, 6-0, 6-0. Nate Welch had an impressive 6-2, 7-6 (7-2) win at No. 3. Lucas Smolko lost 6-1, 6-1 at No. 1 to Mason Conlin, while Graham Alban fell 6-2, 6-4. “The highlight of the singles was Nate Welch win at # 3 against an opponent who became stronger as the match wore on. Nate hit some big serves and forehands and pulled out the match in straight sets,” Landes said. In doubles, Nick King and Monte Imburg paired at No. 1 for a 6-2, 6-3 win. At No. 2 Hunter Fasteau and Will Tenney won a close match in straight sets, 7-5, 7-6 (7-2), while Torsten Olsen and Kasper Jansson won 6-1, 6-4 at No. 3. 4-3 over Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont split its singles matches but won two of three doubles to win a close match with a North Coast Section rival. At singles, Smolko defeated Soahil Michra in straight sets, 6-1, 7-6 (7-3) at No. 1. Breber also won 6-1, 6-3 at No. 2, while Welch suffered a 6-2, 6-2 loss at No. 3 and Alban dropped No. 4, 6-2, 6-4. “Lucas and Ben both won their singles matches in straight sets. Lucas had a tight second set but clinched his match and the team’s victory by playing a great second set tiebreak. It might have been best match Lucas has played this season thus far,” Landes said. At doubles, Arun Brahma and Imburg won 6-1, 7-5 at No. 1. Fasteau and Jansson won at No. 3 in three sets, 5-7, 6-3, 10-8. At No. 2 was another close battle, where Arun Brahma won in tennis against Lick and Hayward.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in two events over the weekend, the Dublin Distance Fiesta on Friday and Saturday, March 15-16 at Dublin HS, and the San Leandro Invitational on Saturday, March 16 at Burrell Field. They also opened their Western Alameda County Conference season at Castro Valley against CV and Bishop O’Dowd. Dublin Distance Fiesta It was an impressive day for freshman runner Sebastien Swain, finishing the 800 in 24th with a time of 1:59.14 in a loaded field of 985 runners. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team made a splash at the recent De La Salle invitational on Friday and Saturday, March 15-16, showcasing their talent against some of the area’s most skilled teams. Out of the 25 high school teams entered, the PHS boys’ team won 6th place and the girls’ team placed 8th overall. The high school team, still competing without a home pool, had 23 swimmers at the prelims and 11 reached the finals the next day. “There were a lot of new personal bests during Friday’s prelims. The energy from day one really showed how proud the swimmers were of what they accomplished,” coach Colby Price said. The team’s success was fueled by strong relay performances and standout individual swims. Taylor Rolefson and Josie Oesterer led the charge for the girls’ team, while Owen Blanford and Asher Takazawa had the most individual points for the boys. The boys’ squad clocked four North Coast Section automatic qualifying times and gained 12 NCS consideration times. Rolefson gained an automatic North Coast Section bid with a qualifying time in the 200 freestyle in 1:58.13. She also gained a pair of NCS consideration times, clocking a 59.99 in the 100 butterfly and a 55.28 in the 100 freestyle while competing in the 400 freestyle relay. Oesterer gained an NCS consideration time in 100 Back, clocking a 1:01.22. The girls’ 200 Medley relay team of Oesterer on the backstroke, Abigail Jacoby on breaststroke, Rolefson on fly and Sydney Olson swimming freestyle earned an NCS consideration time of 1:54.08. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team increased its winning streak to six matches with a 13-1 drubbing of Alhambra on Monday, March 18 in Martinez, 14-2 over Dougherty Valley on Friday, March 15 at Witter Field, and a surprising 11-4 beatdown of NCS power Novato on Tuesday, March 12. Of the group, Dougherty Valley is a Division 1 North Coast Section opponent, while Alhambra and Novato compete in Div. 2 which Piedmont was promoted to after last season. The Highlanders now look ahead to the start of their Western Alameda County Conference schedule, getting things started with a pivotal game with rival Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland. Piedmont has won six straight WACC titles over the Dragons. “We’re coming for Bishop O’Dowd, that’s all I’m going to say,” said senior Rylan Nelson confidently. 13-1 over Alhambra Piedmont only led 1-0 by the end of the first quarter, then exploded to lead 5-1 entering halftime. PHS piled on three more goals in the third and another five more in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s Rylan Nelson scored the game’s first goal at the 8:19 mark of the first quarter. The match waged on with neither team scoring in the remaining time of the opening quarter. In the second, Alhambra scored to tie the match at 1-1 with 8:42 to go, but it marked the only time the Bulldogs got on the Staff Photos Piedmont’s new coach Jeff Lamb and the Highlanders are on a hot streak with six wins in a row. scoreboard. From there, Connor Fredericks scored with 6:46 remaining, Oliver Shafroth sent one in nearly two minutes later, then Curtis Hohener assisted Nelson on a goal with 1:09 left in the half, making it 5-1. Piedmont sent in three more goals in the third quarter, all coming by way of assists. Shaforth tossed one to Cairo Osman at 7:52, Osman then assisted Hohener on the very next possession 30 seconds later, then Nelson flicked a pass to Hohener to put the Highlanders ahead comfortably 8-1 with 5:26 left in the third. In the fourth, Fredericks won the faceoff and turned up field, leading to Hohener assisting Nelson just 24 seconds in at 11:36, Fredericks then scored 25 seconds later. Hohener assisted Nelson for another goal at 9:34 left, then Fredericks assisted Nelson 50 seconds later, while Nelson closed the game with another goal at 7:36 on an assist from Shafroth. Final stats: Nelson had six goals, one assist, and recovered two ground balls. Hohener had two goals, three assists, and scooped two ground balls. Osman had a goal and assist. Shafroth had two goals, two assists, won six faceoffs, and gathered eight ground balls. Fredericks had two goals, two assists, five ground balls, and won six faceoffs. Ethan Alering had seven ground balls. 14-2 over Dougherty Valley Piedmont led 4-1 by the end of the first quarter and 5-2 by halftime. The Highlanders then exploded for four goals in the third quarter and five more in the fourth without allowing another goal to DVHS. PHS had three players with 3-goal hat tricks. Rylan Nelson had six goals on Alhambra, three goals on Dougherty Valley, and four on Novato.

articles.text: Piedmont plays University at Oracle Park this Saturday. Saturday, March 23 marks an exciting day for the Piedmont baseball team and parents of the players. The Highlanders will play a game in the 2024 Dante Benedetti Classic against University at 11:30 a.m. in Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. It represents a rare opportunity to step onto the pro field at Oracle Park likely for the only time in their sporting careers. “It’s going to be a thrill for me, too,” said coach Eric Olson. I’ve played on some big league fields before but as a Giants fan, it’s going to be an amazing time. We’re really humbled to be asked to participate,” Unlike his young players, Olson remembers fondly the years at Candlestick with players like Will Clark. “I was a Will Clark guy. Growing up in the 80s, we had Will Clark. Those were the Candlestick years. It’s going to be a thrill, I’m going to be just as excited running out to be third-base coach as these guys are running out to the field,” Olson said. Will Parker, the Highlanders’ catcher, grew up as a Giants’ fan and goes to games with his teammate Markos Lagios, a Dodgers fan. “I grew up a Giants fan and am a big Buster Posey fan. I’m going to be able to catch that game where he played, so it’s going to be really fun. It’s tough going to games with Markos as a Giants fan, Everyone is always asking me why I’m hanging out with him, so I’ll pretend I don’t know him sometimes,” Parker said. “It’s like a dream. I’m going to try and soak it in as much as I can. I always go when they play the Dodgers. Growing up on this side of the Bay and playing a San Francisco team, it’s sort of like our Battle of the Bay. Will and I have gone to almost every Giants-Dodgers game when it’s here,” Lagios mentioned. Senior infielder Peter Krumins is also a Giants fan. San Francisco winning the World Series in 2010, 2012, and 2014 helped spur his fandom as a youngster. “I’ve been a Giants fan my whole life. They had the dynasty from 2010 to 2014, and I would go to Opening Day with my grandpa for six years in a row. My favorite memory was sometime in the playoffs when it was pouring rain, I remember sitting there in the stands when Marco Scutaro had a big hit, then raised his hands to the sky in the middle of the rain. That moment just stuck with me,” Krumins said. Sophomore second baseman Diego Delventhal is another Giants fan, but his favorite player Brandon Crawford is now with the St. Louis Cardinals. “I have pictured being on the field when I was four or five. Just being out there is going to be a lot of fun,” Delventhal said. Tickets to the event can be purchased on GoFan.co. Scan the QR code provided with your phone. articles.text: Piedmont proved its lacrosse team can compete with the best. On Thursday, March 14, they stayed within striking distance of Div. 1 power Monte Vista before falling 9-6 at Witter Field “We understood Monte Vista’s offense and were working on it all day. They do a switch, and initially the girls couldn’t quite figure it out/ Then they settled down. We practiced really well for this team,” PHS coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont also lost to Div. 2 opponent Acalanes 10-9 in sudden-death overtime two weeks ago. The team feels like both matches prepare them for the rest of the way. “We were shutting them down, we played such good defense and we were really patient on attack. We’re matching these top teams. Last year, this would’ve been a much more difficult match for us. I’m so proud of how we’ve grown,” midfielder Hailey Marshburn said. “There’s so much to be said about this group as a whole. There’s not one major star-player on the team. We have a ton of talent and we all work together,” added Friedie Schickedanz. PHS was without one of their best attackers, Ruby Guzdar, forcing their attack to get creative. “If we had Ruby, it would have been a different game. We’re almost all righties and it forced us to go one direction, Ruby sends it in the other direction,” Chan said. Piedmont starts their Western Alameda County Conference portion of its season this week with a critical rivalry match, hosting Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, March 22. 9-6 loss to Monte Vista Monte Vista carried a 2-1 lead through the first quarter but Piedmont fought to a 5-4 lead in the second quarter. However, the Mustangs went up 7-5 in the third quarter and added two more unanswered goals in the fourth quarter before Piedmont’s last goal, 9-6. In the first quarter, Monte Vista opened with a goal on their first possession just 36 seconds into the game. The Mustangs then scored again at the 7:41 mark. Schickedanz then scored two and a half minutes later. Monte Vista scored again to start the second quarter with 10:55 left. From there, the HighFriedie Schickedanz takes a shot against Monte Vista. Staff Photos Laurel Bentley fires a shot in traffic against Monte Vista. landers came back to tie when Luisa Cole scored three minutes later by way of a shooting space opportunity near the net. Piedmont had a couple of shots from Chloe Graham and Peyton Watson, but they were blocked and went wide respectively. At the 4:21 mark, Piedmont tied when Hallie Burden drew a foul in shooting space, sending one past the goalie to tie it at 3-3. articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade. They highlight the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period was when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of Japan’s feudal military rule. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art, notably printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked both before and after the Meiji era. A museum member preview takes place on Thursday and Friday, April 4-5. A donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at the Legion of Honor through August 18. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints. Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849), Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
articles.title: Exhibit of Japanese Prints opens in April at Legion of Honor

articles.text: Installation view of Zanele Muholi: Eye Me at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) first major exhibition on the West Coast of South African artist Zanele Muholi is now on view through August 11. The multimedia exhibition, entitled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, features over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present alongside paintings, sculpture and video. Eye Me celebrates the artist’s Black queer community in post-Apartheid South Africa and showcases issues of gender identity, representation and race. Muholi was born in Durban and currently lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. The museum has featured works by Muholi in the past, including Faces and Phases in the 2011 exhibition Face of Our Time. Their work was also featured in Public Intimacy: Art and Other Ordinary Acts in South Africa, co-organized by SFMOMA and the Yerba Buena Center for Arts in 2014. To learn more and to purchase passes to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/zanele-muholi-eye-me/.
articles.title: SF MOMA features South African artist Zanele Muholi in new exhibit

articles.text: Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside will be open on select evenings this Spring beginning Saturday, March 16. Filoli is home to 16 acres of formal gardening grounds and a vast collection of native and exotic flowers. In 2021, a record 80,000 bulbs bloomed. In March, Orchids, magnolias, and citrus blossoms are beginning to unfold, and visitors will also catch a glimpse of vibrant Tulips, Irises, Wisteria, Peonies, and wildflowers. Filoli is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and evening tickets allow guests to visit the house and gardens from 5 p.m. through closing at 8 p.m., an ideal time to witness the “golden hour.” Evening tickets are released weekly for four weeks of availability. Food and drinks are available on-site through the evening at the Quail Cafe and Vegetable Garden Bar. To plan your visit, click www. filoli.org/. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside; they are available by phone at (650) 364-8300. Tulips are blooming beginning this month at Filoli House and Garden in Woodside.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will conclude its Schwabacher Recital Series with an evening performance on Wednesday, April 3, featuring mezzo-soprano Samantha Hankey accompanied by pianist Carrie-Ann Matheson. The recital series offers audiences an opportunity to hear upcoming gifted singers in an intimate setting. Now in its 40th year, the series features renowned artists and has been instrumental in launching international careers. Hankey’s current season marks her debuts at the Royal Opera Covent Garden in London, where she performs as Dorabella in Così fan tutte; at Semperoper in Dresden as Cherubino in Le Nozze di Figaro; Detroit Opera as the Fox in The Cunning Little Vixen; and at Lyric Opera of Kansas City in the role of Santuzza in Cavalleria Rusticana. Hankey will be accompanied by pianist Matheson who currently serves as San Francisco Opera Center Program’s artistic director. The recital includes songs by Claudie Debussy, Manuel de Falla, Alexander Zemlinsky, Cole Porter and Kurt Weill. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. and takes place at the Taube Atrium Theater at 401 Van Ness Avenue next to the War Memorial Opera House. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/schwabacher-recital-series/. Mezzo-soprano Samantha Hankey
articles.title: SF Opera’s Schwabacher Recital Series set for April 3

articles.text: Pulitzer prize finalist Lloyd Suh’s critically acclaimed new play The Far Country is now in performance at Berkeley Repertory Theatre with shows through Sunday, April 14. The Far Country follows Moon Gyet as he arrives at San Francisco’s Angel Island Immigration Station in the wake of the Chinese Exclusion Act with an invented biography and a new name. Moon, played by Tommy Bo, soon finds that passage to San Francisco, and the dream of a better life, comes with a price. “I’m incredibly proud to bring Lloyd’s beautiful play home to the Bay Area,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “It is an honor to share this story with our community, in this magical, complicated place that has inspired and compelled people from all over the world to leave their countries of origin to seek opportunity, safety, and home.” The cast includes Bo, Feodor Chin, John Keabler, Whit K. Lee, Tess Lina, Sharon Shao, and Aaron Wilton. A post-show discussion with Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation members and other panelists will be held on April 3 in Michael’s Second Act bar. The show is being performed at Berkeley Rep’s Peet’s Theatre, 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley. Purchase tickets by calling the box office at (510) 647-2949 or by visiting www.berkeleyrep.org.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep presents The Far Country on stage through April 14

Berkeley Playhouse presents Rent, directed by Kimberly Dooley, playing onstage now through Sunday, March 31. Based loosely on Puccini’s opera, La Boheme, but set in the East Village of New York City, Rent is a story about love, finding your voice and living for today. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, Jonathan Larson’s 1996 Broadway musical quickly became a pop cultural phenomenon. It was adapted into a musical drama film directed by Chris Columbus in 2005 to widespread acclaim. Larson’s Rent follows a year in the life of a group of impoverished young artists and musicians struggling to survive and create in New York City during the HIV/AIDS epidemic. The Berkeley Playhouse production is co-directed by Peet Cocke with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Mel Martinez. articles.text: A scene from the Academy Award winning film The Zone of Interest The Zone of Interest, based on the 2014 book written by Martin Amis and directed by Jonathan Glazer, was the 2024 Oscar winner in the category of Best International Feature Film. The narrative opens with a silent, dark screen. Three minutes go by as if the audience is asked to abandon all extraneous thoughts and give themselves over to what will follow. And then the screen reveals an idyllic scene, a family, husband, wife, and children, seated on a blanket near a wide river, surrounded by tall summer grass. A sense of tranquility suffuses the day. Soon they all walk back to their car and drive home to a lovely manor house. Their day is ending, the children go to their rooms, and the parents crawl into twin beds, their conversation wanders before saying good night and turning out the bedside light. The next day, with the same sense of normalcy, the mother, Hedwig (Sandra Huller), with a toddler in her arms, walks out into the back yard, pausing to look at the blossoming flowers, the grass underfoot seems newly mowed, stone pavers lead to a small pool. The mother chats with the little one, smiling, encouraging the child to look at the surrounding plants. And it’s in this moment, a static, bucolic photograph, that the camera pulls back, allowing the audience to see more of what is a large and manicured garden awash in sunshine. And for the first time a massive concrete wall, topped with barbed wire, is revealed, and just beyond are brick buildings, several with rising smokestacks. The wall, stark, unexpected, forbidding, begs the question: why is it there? The answer is that this is the family home of Rudolf Hoss (Christian Friedel), the commandant of the concentration camp Auschwitch. And therein is the challenge inherent in watching this remarkable film. We are absorbed by all that we see, and simultaneously revolted by a dark, unfolding truth. It is that feeling which haunts every scene of The Zone of Interest thereafter. We watch in almost disbelief at the family’s quotidian, seemingly benign, normal life. Hedwig has other wives over for coffee and gossip. The dinner table is set. The kids are ever-present, often in the yard. Doors open and close. They pause for brief conversations. In one scene, Hedwig walks into her bedroom holding a mink coat, tries it on, and stands before a full-length mirror, happy, luxuriating in its warmth and richness. There is no hint that she ever wonders at its origin. Yet, if she listens, if she ever were to listen, screams and gunshots can be heard in the distance. Rudolf meets with a number of Nazi officers who look over architectural plans for an extermination building. They speak casually about meeting certain production quotas, comparing their Teutonic efficiency to other camps. It is evident that theirs is a congenial corporation of death offered up as business as usual. The family, to include a mother on a visit to see Hedwig, gushing with praise and pride, is surrounded by an unimaginable horror. But to the filmmakers, the impact of the film resides in the Barbara Riccardi and Dana Myers, violins; Jonna Hervig, viola; Nancy Bien, cello; Explore the development of the fugue form in classical music over a 300-year span, including the Beethoven Grosse Fuge , Op. 133, then enjoy the Brahms Piano Quintet, Op. 34.

articles.text: If you’re a fan of Woody Allen and have found delight in his ability to write and direct films set in Manhattan, framed by the central character’s existential plight (What purpose? What meaning?) and seasoned by his chronic hypochondria, then you will not be disappointed by Whatever Works. The film opens with an aging Boris Yellnikoff (Larry David), lapsed physics professor at Colombia, an almost winner of the Nobel Prize. He is a self-absorbed misanthrope, standing on a New York street reminding anyone who will listen that he’s surrounded by mental pygmies and inchworms. He also reminds all who will listen that his genius is unequaled and he is surrounded by the dimmest of bulbs. Having divorced his wife some years back (she was too wealthy and too smart), he attempted suicide in a moment of hopelessness and despair and was left with a limp. He now lives alone in a walk up in Chinatown. Unexpectedly, a young waif, Melody St. Ann Celestine (Evan Rachel Wood), appears at the foot of his stairs in need of shelter and a meal. Against all of his more selfish instincts, Boris agrees to let her stay one night. And so Melody, the quintessential inchworm, a mental pygmy personified, a retired beauty pageant winner from a small Southern town, always cheery and definitely clueless, gradually inserts herself into Boris’ life. Not surprisingly, they begin a relationship and Boris grows accustomed to having company, inchworm or no. The theme of older men and younger women, ripe with Pygmalion-Henry Higgins implications, threads itself through some of Allen’s work and it’s hard not to be reminded of Soon-Yi and the ensuing scandal when Allen married her (she was Mia Farrow’s adopted daughter that Farrow and Allen, for a time, raised together). Of course, though Larry David delivers a solid portrayal of Boris, it’s impossible not to see Woody Allen doing Boris’ standup rants while wondering why Allen didn’t play the role himself. The character is pure Woody to include moments when Boris wakes in the dead of night with a panic attack, screaming “the horror, the horror,” Boris being an unyielding fan of Conrad’s Kurtz in The Heart of Darkness. While Whatever Works may seem to be a flip title, akin to that insouciant, adolescent rejoinder, “whatever,” Boris’ explanation of those two words is poignant and then some. There are also laugh out loud moments to be sure, though the film lacks the complexity and subtlety of, say, Hannah and Her Sisters, Manhattan, or, more recently, Vicky, Cristina, Barcelona. The fact is that even when Woody is not quite at the peak of his game, he can still deliver a smart and funny film. Whatever Works. Directed by Woody Allen. Starring Larry David, Evan Rachel Wood, Patricia Clarkson and Ed Begley. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Streaming on VUDU/prime/apple tv. The Zone of Interest – Academy Award winner Evan Rachel Wood and Larry David in Whatever Works A scene from the Academy Award winning film The Zone of Interest By Chris Honoré The Zone of Interest, based on the 2014 book written by Martin Amis and directed by Jonathan Glazer, was the 2024 Oscar winner in the category of Best International Feature Film. The narrative opens with a silent, dark screen. Three minutes go by as if the audience is asked to abandon all extraneous thoughts and give themselves over to what will follow. And then the screen reveals an idyllic scene, a family, husband, wife, and children, seated on a blanket near a wide river, surrounded by tall summer grass. A sense of tranquility suffuses the day. Soon they all walk back to their car and drive home to a lovely manor house. Their day is ending, the children go to their rooms, and the parents crawl into twin beds, their conversation wanders before saying good night and turning out the bedside light. The next day, with the same sense of normalcy, the mother, Hedwig (Sandra Huller), with a toddler in her arms, walks out into the back yard, pausing to look at the blossoming flowers, the grass underfoot seems newly mowed, stone pavers lead to a small pool. The mother chats with the little one, smiling, encouraging the child to look at the surrounding plants. And it’s in this moment, a static, bucolic photograph, that the camera pulls back, allowing the audience to see more of what is a large and manicured garden awash in sunshine. And for the first time a massive concrete wall, topped with barbed wire, is revealed, and just beyond are brick buildings, several with rising smokestacks. The wall, stark, unexpected, forbidding, begs the question: why is it there? The answer is that this is the family home of Rudolf Hoss (Christian Friedel), the commandant of the concentration camp Auschwitch. And therein is the challenge inherent in watching this remarkable film. We are absorbed by all that we see, and simultaneously revolted by a dark, unfolding truth. It is that feeling which haunts every scene of The Zone of Interest thereafter. We watch in almost disbelief at the family’s quotidian, seemingly benign, normal life. Hedwig has other wives over for coffee and gossip. The dinner table is set. The kids are ever-present, often in the yard. Doors open and close. They pause for brief conversations. In one scene, Hedwig walks into her bedroom holding a mink coat, tries it on, and stands before a full-length mirror, happy, luxuriating in its warmth and richness. There is no hint that she ever wonders at its origin. Yet, if she listens, if she ever were to listen, screams and gunshots can be heard in the distance. Rudolf meets with a number of Nazi officers who look over architectural plans for an extermination building. They speak casually about meeting certain production quotas, comparing their Teutonic efficiency to other camps. It is evident that theirs is a congenial corporation of death offered up as business as usual. The family, to include a mother on a visit to see Hedwig, gushing with praise and pride, is surrounded by an unimaginable horror. articles.text: A scene from Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs First things first: the kids will enjoy Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs, especially the return of Sid the Sloth, Manny and Ellie the wooly mammoths, Diego the saber-toothed tiger and, of course, Scrat the sort of squirrel. What is Scrat, really? It’s like asking if Goofy is a dog. Pluto yes, but Goofy? The movie opens with the irresistible Scrat in pursuit of that ever-elusive acorn. This time, the long-nosed sort of squirrel runs into a serious diversion in the form of Scratte, a foxy looking sort of squirrel. Their antics are inserted throughout the movie and eventually the acorn is forgotten – but that’s act three. Truth be told, for all of the attention given to Manny and company, Scrat has always had the most comic potential. The critter is funny. Sort of Road Runner funny. Anyway, as it turns out, Sid the sloth, wanting to start a family like Manny and Ellie (she’s pregnant and Manny is nervous) finds three large eggs, down in an ice cave. He wrestles them to the surface, the eggs hatch and surprise! The wee ones are three small T-rexes. That’s right, dinosaurs in the ice age (isn’t this the Pleistocene era?). And their mother is not happy when she discovers they’re gone. She grabs the three little guys plus Sid and heads home, which is a Mesozoic era jungle beneath the ice. Yep. Hot and humid below, frozen and cold above. The Ice Age gang goes looking for Sid, journeying into the land of the dinosaurs. The story may seem to unfold at a glacial pace but remember the designated audience is kids, and they love these characters There are the rascal twin possums; the aging Diego; Sid, Manny, and Ellie; and the new guy, Buck, a weasel who has lived in dinosaur land for too long. So, if time hangs heavy, days start to grow long, grab the kids and go. Or find it on streaming. Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs. Animation. Directed by Carlos Saldanha. With the voices of: Denis Leary, Ray Romano, Queen Latifah and John Leguizamo. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated: PG. Released in 2009. articles.text: A number of events came together this week. The result is titled “the joy of music”. On Saturday, pianist Mikhail Voskresensky presented a monumental concert in Mountain View. The unfortunate thing is that so few on the West Coast have even heard of him. First and foremost, he is an outstanding representative of the Classic Russian school of piano playing. The second thing to keep in mind is that he is 89 years old, and still plays magnificently. I’d like to add that he is a man of great moral principle. Risking well-deserved peace in old age, he took a stand against Russian aggression and came to the United States at the ripe age of 87. An entire chapter could be written about his This column has noted many salubrious changes in music in recent years. Unfortunately, despite the positive trend, we have also seen a degradation of music education. And with this degradation of music education, there is a general degradation in education as a whole. Outstanding musicians like conductor David Morales are actively involved in rectifying these wayward trends. He is the founder and Artistic Director of Cantare, where he conducts Conductor Leo Eylar the 100-voice Cantare Chorale. Maestro Morales inspires as he goes. When I was a teacher in San Francisco public schools, I sometimes had as many as 1200 students a week. All of my students learned to read music and recognize every instrument of the orchestra by sight and by sound. In addition, they sang a large repertoire of songs, and became proficient playing the recorder. Please understand that these were the minimum things that we enjoyed. We also learned how to participate in music by being team players, and at the same time retaining our individual philosophies. These are very important aspects of music. When we participate in music, A story of generosity, inclusivity and excellence.
