articles.text: Come celebrate the 30th Anniversary Edition of Random Kindness and Senseless Acts of Beauty at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, March 22, at 7 p.m. Register in advance: https:// eventbrite.com/e/854973166757. Join in an evening of education and inspiration with Dr. Paloma Pavel and friends. This book, with a foreword by Nobel laureate Desmond Tutu (South Africa), received a gold medal and was awarded “Peacemaker Book of the Year.” This evening will share historical roots of the remarkable phrase which began on a napkin, became a bumper sticker, a book, and then launched a global movement. This history will provide context for the current impact of the phrase including school curriculum, a congressional designation of National Random Kindness Day and Week, and chapters on numerous campuses in the USA. The annual Desmond Tutu Random Kindness Leadership award also honors this legacy. Doors will open for gallery viewing at 6:30 p.m. accompanied by peaceful sounds by pianist Arthur Kloian. Dr. Pavel will be joined later by a musical performance of members of the World Harmony Chorus under the direction of Betsy Blakeslee. Ms. Blakeslee conducts “refugee choruses” in global hotspots in the summer and brings the music of cultural bridgebuilding to the Bay Area through her selections this evening from Kenya and Ukraine. Her ensemble will be joined by surprise guests. When Japanese-American artist Mayumi Oda chose the 12th-century animals of the Choju-giga (playful animals) for her visual vocabulary to illustrate the Random Kindness book of wisdom, she was inspired by one of the earliest uses of art to encourage community action (manga). Annie Hallatt, the beloved Bay Area Bread and Puppet masque maker and animator will appear as “Raven” and bring the illustrations in the book to life with puppets and costumes. Annie and Paloma will lead eco-artists from the cohort of Laney College’s Eco-Art Matters class. Students have been learning about endangered species for this class under the direction of Sharon Siskin, Minoosh Zomorodinia, and Andree Singer Thompson (Emerita). This “council of all beings” will include animal characters that have been researched by the class, including endangered species (tule elk) as well as restoration successes such as the coho salmon. The gallery will feature the work of eco-artist Leslie Plato Smith in a series called “Vulnerability”, pairing humans and their animal allies in oil and watercolor visual works. Learn more about Dr. Pavel as a Fulbright scholar, an educator and eco-psychologist, and delegate to the UN Egypt Climate Summit after working for climate justice on several continents. The event will include a reception with light snacks.
articles.title: Random Kindness book anniversary event at PCA this Friday

articles.text: Friday, March 22, 7 p.m. Earth House Book Launch Event To celebrate the 30th Anniversary edition of the book Random Kindness and Senseless Acts of Beauty, Earth House, Inc. will have an Eco-Art party, with readings by co-author Paloma Pavel, along with a discussion of the book’s history. Betsy Blakeslee’s World Harmony Chorus will entertain and pre-publication copies of the hardback edition will be available for purchase. This event will also include an exhibition of paintings by Eco-artist Leslie Plato Smith, and a reception. To attend please register in advance at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/854973166757. Sunday, March 24. 11 a.m.- 2 p.m. Leslie Plato Smith Eco-Art Exhibit Local eco-artist Leslie Plato Smith will display a collection of works representing the vulnerability of all life on Earth as it continues to sustain attacks from careless human development. The gallery will be open for viewing on Sundays, March 24 and 31, and on Saturday, March 30, from 11 am – 2 pm, with light refreshments available. Sunday, March 24, 3 p.m. Kodaly Foundation Scholarship Auction Kodály Foundation for Music Education will celebrate its third anniversary birthday with soprano Kate Offer performing comic songs, accompanied by pianist/singer Eric Howe. The program Includes performance by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s Ensemble, led by Artistic Director Eric Tuan. A reception and scholarship benefit auction will follow to raise funds for students to attend the 2024 Kodály Summer Institute in San Anselmo. Auction items will include unique musical instruments, embroidered linens, and exquisite rugs. To learn more, visit kodalyfoundation.org/events. Suggested donation at the door (single $25; duo $40; student $10). Saturday, March 30, 7:30 p.m. Temescal String Quartet A concert titled “Taking Flight” explores the fugue form over a 300-year span and includes Beethoven’s Grosse Fugue, Op. 133. The Temescal Quartet will be joined by pianist Carl Blake in the second half of the concert for Brahms’ Piano Quintet, Op. 34. Suggested donation at the door is $25; children & students free. Refreshments served after the concert. Register at https://www.eventbrite. com/e/861920235627. Saturday, April 6, 11 a.m.– 2 p.m. Carolyn Lord Art Exhibit Reception A solo show of paintings by Carolyn Lord will feature paintings inspired by Googie architecture, flower gardens, and the California landscape. There will also be a grouping of landscapes from a painting trip to Colorado. Carolyn Lord is best known for her watercolors with sophisticated color and bold compositions, influenced by the California Watercolor Style. Lord has been active in the Oakland arts community for many years: The show will be open for viewing Saturdays and Sundays, 11 a.m.– 2 p.m. from April 6-21. Sunday, April 7, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio PCA Classic Jazz Club: Please join us for some late afternoon relaxation enlivened by In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Anthony Pegram. Celebrating the arrival of Spring with all your favorite songs and classic jazz and blues. This event is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing its magnificent Steinway grand piano. Enjoy the intimate clublike environment with snacks and complimentary wine. Bring a friend and plan to meet some new ones. Tickets are $25 in advance at https://bpt.me/6214927, or $30 at the door, cash or check only. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up-to-date vaccinations.

articles.text: Gail Anderson Needleman (1949-2022) was a beloved member of the music faculty at Holy Names University, and was co-creator of the online American Folk Song Collection before her untmely passing two years ago. Her translations of selected Lajos Bárdos choral works have recently been published by Edito Musica Budapest. To launch a scholarship fund in her memory, a third Birthday Celebration will be held at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, March 24 from 3:00- 5:30 pm and will feature a silent auction with items from Gail’s personal estate. The collection includes unique instruments, fine textiles, and exquisite rugs. The net proceeds from the silent auction go directly towards the Kodály Foundation for Music Education scholarship fund in Gail’s honor. Gail Anderson Needleman
articles.title: Kodaly Foundation Scholarship Auction at PCA on March 24

articles.text: The Temescal String Quartet with pianist Carl Blake will perform a chamber music concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, March 30 at 7:00 p.m. The concert will include Beethoven’s Grosse Fuge, Op. 133, as the quartet explores the fugue form over a 300-year span. The quartet will be joined in the second half by internationally-acclaimed pianist Carl Blake for the Brahms Piano Quintet, Op. 34. Temescal String Quartet is an active Oakland-based classical music ensemble consisting of four women who are frequent performers in various professional musical organizations in the Bay Area: Barbara Riccardi and Dana Myers, violist Jonna Hervig, and cellist Nancy Bien. Pianist Carl Blake Temescal String Quartet: Barbara Riccardi and Dana Myers, violins; Jonna Hervig, viola; Nancy Bien, cello Carl Blake is a Bay Area classical pianist who has performed recitals to international acclaim in Carnegie Recital Hall in New York, Wigmore Hall in London, and the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia. He is a two-time recipient of Fulbright Scholar Awards and toured as Artistic Ambassador for the U.S. State Department to Brazil, Peru, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Honduras, Barbados and Jamaica. Of the quartet and Blake, music critic Joseph Gold wrote in a review in June 2018, “The quintet performed with an ideal melding of ensemble. Ego was never an issue, and all were of a single purpose. As they played, the listeners were drawn in, and by doing so we encountered the glory of the music as if we were members of a transcendental partnership. They solved all problems of balance. The strings spoke as an ensemble and for themselves. Dr. Blake was ever so sensitive. He has a velvet touch and an artist’s soul. It takes really special talent to express the innermost feelings of introspection and warmth of emotion.” The suggested donation at the door is $25 per person. Children and students are admitted free. Refreshments will be served following the concert.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, March 20, 2024 Random Kindness book anniversary event at PCA this Friday Come celebrate the 30th Anniversary Edition of Random Kindness and Senseless Acts of Beauty at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, March 22, at 7 p.m. Register in advance: https:// eventbrite.com/e/854973166757. Join in an evening of education and inspiration with Dr. Paloma Pavel and friends. This book, with a foreword by Nobel laureate Desmond Tutu (South Africa), received a gold medal and was awarded “Peacemaker Book of the Year.” This evening will share historical roots of the remarkable phrase which began on a napkin, became a bumper sticker, a book, and then launched a global movement. This history will provide context for the current impact of the phrase including school curriculum, a congressional designation of National Random Kindness Day and Week, and chapters on numerous campuses in the USA. The annual Desmond Tutu Random Kindness Leadership award also honors this legacy. Doors will open for gallery viewing at 6:30 p.m. accompanied by peaceful sounds by pianist Arthur Kloian. Dr. Pavel will be joined later by a musical performance of members of the World Harmony Chorus under the direction of Betsy Blakeslee. Ms. Blakeslee conducts “refugee choruses” in global hotspots in the summer and brings the music of cultural bridgebuilding to the Bay Area through her selections this evening from Kenya and Ukraine. Her ensemble will be joined by surprise guests. When Japanese-American artist Mayumi Oda chose the 12th-century animals of the Choju-giga (playful animals) for her visual vocabulary to illustrate the Random Kindness book of wisdom, she was inspired by one of the earliest uses of art to encourage community action (manga). Annie Hallatt, the beloved Bay Area Bread and Puppet masque maker and animator will appear as “Raven” and bring the illustrations in the book to life with puppets and costumes. Annie and Paloma will lead eco-artists from the cohort of Laney College’s Eco-Art Matters class. Students have been learning about endangered species for this class under the direction of Sharon Siskin, Minoosh Zomorodinia, and Andree Singer Thompson (Emerita). This “council of all beings” will include animal characters that have been researched by the class, including endangered species (tule elk) as well as restoration successes such as the coho salmon. The gallery will feature the work of eco-artist Leslie Plato Smith in a series called “Vulnerability”, pairing humans and their animal allies in oil and watercolor visual works. Learn more about Dr. Pavel as a Fulbright scholar, an educator and eco-psychologist, and delegate to the UN Egypt Climate Summit after working for climate justice on several continents. It developed as an alternative to the ornate and opulent style of the Victorian age and indeed resulted in simpler, cleaner and what the architects of the time thought of as a more honest design. Valued and expressed in this architecture was the hand crafting of the building components both on the exterior and interior of the buildings. Even though it may have been largely developed because of nostalgia for the handworked aesthetic of the pre-industrial era, Craftsman buildings were thoughtful and very well constructed by craftspeople who took pride in the quality of their work. The development of the Craftsman Prairie style, attributed mainly to Frank Lloyd Wright, is considered by many historians to be the first truly American architectural style! It shares many of the Craftsman characteristics but is generally distinguished and recognizable by a very strong Two examples (above) of fine Craftsman homes of different materials in town that illustrate the main characteristics of the style: sheltering roofs with broad overhangs and exposed rafters, knee braces, prominent covered porches supported by often tapering pilasters (wide columns), and well proportioned windows with artistically divided lites (panes). horizontal feeling created by low slope hipped or even flat roofs with even larger overhangs than normal. articles.text: Dear Abby: I’m wondering about Eggcellent activities for our little one that might be happening in Piedmont to celebrate Spring. Is there anything nearby that we might take our almost 2-year old and our beloved, sweet dog, Buster Posey to before nap time? My mom used to take my sister and me to an egg hunt long ago. Ready to hop, –Andy, Di and baby Eva Dear Andy, Di and baby Eva: The Piedmont Rec Department is having a Bunny Blast on Saturday, March 23 from 9:30 to 11 a.m. in Piedmont Park. The egg hunt will start rain or shine at 9:45 a.m. Right now they are stuffing thousands of eggs for all hunters. Spring-themed activities will be set up around the Park. There’s even an opportunity to have photos taken with the Springtime Bunny. Register online before the event. There is a $10 fee for age 3 and older. As for Buster, you can bring him, but keep him on his leash or maybe with all the egg mayhem, leave him napping at home. For older egg hunters who still love a good chase, an Eggstravaganza is happening at Piedmont Community Church this Saturday, March 23, from 5-7 p.m. There’ll be an egg hunt, face painting, crazy fun games and all free. –Abby Dear Abby: What are the healthiest dog breeds? My dear dog-friend Turk just passed and I would like to avoid that feeling for a while. He lived to be nine – 63 in dog years. Far too short. –Silvia Dear Silvia: I’m so sorry to hear about Turk. Getting a new puppy (or a new older dog) is definitely worth thinking through the health concerns that affect certain breeds. I’m not sure if you prefer a big or small dog, but here are the top three breeds to get you started. 1. Australian Cattle Dog – are seen occasionally around Piedmont. The Guiness Book of Records says the World’s Oldest Dog was an ACD named Bluey, who lived to the ripe age of 29 – that’s 203 in dog years. 2. Poodles – are not only hypoallergenic but they also tend to have long, healthy lifespans of up to 18 years, regardless of whether they are Standard, Miniature or Toy. Eye and joint issues tend to affect them in their older years. 3. Border Collies – tend to be lovable and vigorous and tend to be healthy for most of their lives which can go on average from 12-18 years. However deafness and epilepsy can affect them when they get long in the paw. Certain breeds like bulldogs are known to develop respiratory issues. Pugs can commonly suffer from eye infections. Frenchies, which were named the top US Dog Breed last year, can suffer from excessive itching and licking as well as respiratory issues. Mutts and Crossbreeds (like Queen E’s Corgi/Dachshund mix) are commonly thought to be healthier dogs than some Purebreds. But there is no guarantee that the dog you pick won’t develop something which turns into a hefty vet bill. Lots for you to chew on. –Abby If you have dog news, please send it to Melandogs@gmail. com. articles.text: Another large turnout of 42 walkers and one K-9 best friend showed up last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk on a lovely, clear morning. It was noted that the unofficial start of the home buying season was Presidents Day weekend. The previous week there were only six Piedmont homes listed for sale. The group walked to three of them, as well as four others that were sold recently. The group decided to see two of the remaining homes for sale on the north and west sides of Piedmont. The first house was on Monte at the corner of Moraga Avenue. A 2800 square foot house, it was built in 1925 was currently listed at $2,457,000. The home’s front steps provided a good location for a group photo. Next, it was over a few blocks to 20 Langdon Court, an 1,800 square foot house built in 1952 and was listed at $1,650,000. The group walked back on Hardwick to Oakland Avenue for a long walk down to Jerome Avenue. On the way they saw a PG&E crew with eight trucks replacing poles and a transformer at San Carlos Avenue. The walkers also checked out the progress on two bulb-out/sidewalk extenders at El Cerrito and Jerome Avenues now expected to be completed by the end of the month. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales expects they will make the area safer by increasing pedestrian visibility, shortening street crossings, and reducing vehicle speeds. Nearby was 420 Jerome, the lowest priced home on the market, a 955 square foot home built in 1935 and listed for $925,000. The group got another look at the new surface at Witter Field, less than one block away. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Author and journalist Bill Wong, a Piedmont resident, will celebrate the release of his new book “Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America” on March 24. At the book release, Wong will read selections from his memoir and discuss some life experiences with his perspectives as a journalist, a son, an Oakland native, and as an Asian-American. Wong will read primarily from the first chapter to set up the contrast between the eras, and locales in the book. The book launch will take place this Sunday, March 24 from 1:00-2:00 p.m. in the Oakland Asian Cultural Center, 388 Ninth Street in Oakland. This release of the memoir is the culmination of 13 years of work in which he discusses his roots and his identity. “Many Americans are curious about ancestral roots, whether they begin in Europe, Africa, Asia or Latin America,” said Wong. “I think the book should have appeal to people of many ethnicities. It’s my optimistic and cautionary ‘Thank you America’ tale,” he added. Wong was born in Oakland’s Chinatown to Chinese immigrants. The language spoken at home was Cantonese with his father’s dialect of Hoisan or Toisan. When Wong attended Lincoln Elementary School, he began his own journey with the English language. Although raised first with the language of his father, he only knew his father for 20 years of life. The book explicates how Wong grew out of Chinatown, psychologically, linguistically and physically, to become part of the American culture. “Wong’s memoir is more than a personal recounting; it is a bridge between past and present, offering insights into the challenges and triumphs of the Chinese-American community,” said the Breaking News Network (BNN). Wong graduated from Oakland High School and as a student at UC Berkeley he wrote for The Daily Californian. After his undergraduate studies he was with the Peace Corp in the Philippines and later graduated from the Columbia School of Journalism in New York in 1970. Wong’s first professional experience was with the San Francisco Chronicle as a general assignment reporter in the summer of 1962. He went on to Author and Piedmont resident Bill Wong. become a staff writer with the Wall Street Journal, from 1970- 1979, and joined the Oakland Tribune in 1979 where he spent 17 years on staff and then as a syndicated columnist. He was highly respected and well read, and became a regular contributor on The News Hour with Jim Lehrer on PBS in 1995 and 1996. Wong’s book features photos from a trip he and his sisters took to his father’s village in 1994. For Bill’s older sisters who grew up in China, the trip was a homecoming. But for Bill it marked a journey of complicated emotions and part of his search for identify. Seeing his father’s worn home in China proved to be an emotional experience. Bill describes his book as an immigrant success story. “But our society has deep issues; we are still deciding what kind of democracy we want to be,” Wong qualified. To RSVP for the free book launch on Sunday, March 24, visit Oacc.cc/event/sonsofchinatown. For more on Bill Wong visit Williamgeewong.com. “Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America” by William (Bill) Gee Wong. Bill Wong and family members visiting Bill’s father’s home in China in 1994. Flo Oy Wong (left), Bill Wong, Felicia Wong, Li Keng Wong and Lai Wah Chop Webster.

articles.text: There was a good turnout of 17 readers for the First Mondays Reading Group on Monday, March 4 at the Community Hall. The group was there to discuss Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis. This debut novel was first published in 1954 and won the 1955 Somerset Maugham Award for fiction. The story follows the academic and romantic pursuits of Jim Dixon, a history lecturer at an English university. The book is regarded by many as the finest, and funniest, comic novel of the twentieth century, but it scandalized readers in 1954. Time magazine included Lucky Jim in its 100 Best English-language Novels from 1923 to 2005. Dixon has had a rocky start at the university and is concerned about losing his position. He tries to maintain a good relationship with his absent-minded department head, Professor Welch, in order to be awarded a permanent post. Dixon also has a difficult relationship with a sometimes girlfriend who also teaches at the university. He meets Christine Callaghan, who is the latest girlfriend of Welch’s son. Dixon becomes attracted to her and they navigate their relationships. The story reaches its climax during an important lecture that Dixon is to give. However, he drinks too much in an attempt to calm his nerves, mocks the university’s culture, and passes out. Welch lets Dixon know his position at the university will not be extended, but all turns out well and he becomes Lucky Jim. The book generated strong feelings among the group. Some readers really enjoyed it, while others had a strong dislike. Some members had read the book years before, and their current reactions were different. They didn’t appreciate Amis’ satire, and they found Dixon to be unlikable. For that matter, they didn’t like or were interested in any of the characters. They weren’t funny. They were flawed, selfish and petty. Some readers couldn’t believe the book is considered one of the best of the 20th Century. The humor was juvenile, and they found the happy ending to be unrealistic. On the other side of the discussion were those who liked Lucky Jim and felt it was a brilliant satire of British society and academic life of the 1950s. It provided a picture of the post-World War II in England. The cigarette smoking and treatment of women seem to be artifacts. It was noted that England in 1954 was still recovering from the war, but ten years later the Beatles and mini-skirts appeared. Times change and this story presents a time and place that Amis satirizes and even mocks. Some readers marveled at Amis’ command of the English language and a vocabulary that required constant dictionary use Maya Angelou’s I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is the group’s April book. by the readers. Others would have preferred language that regular people could more easily understand. Some readers didn’t feel Dixon was a “jerk.” Rather, they saw him as a sometimes misbehaving, girlfriend-loyal, job-insecure young man, trying to keep his cushy academic job, and sort out his romantic life. Possibly the presentation of Amis’ Lucky Jim in a London West End theater with all his flawed characters and satire would be more universally appealing today. However, the book did provide another lively, fun First Mondays Reading Group discussion. The group had previously selected I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou for April and Perestroika in Paris by Jane Smiley for May. Three new, non-fiction candidates for June were considered and Prequel by Rachel Maddow was selected. pages.text: Wednesday, March 20, 2024 23 First Monday book group explores Lucky Jim By Dick Carter There was a good turnout of 17 readers for the First Mondays Reading Group on Monday, March 4 at the Community Hall. The group was there to discuss Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis. This debut novel was first published in 1954 and won the 1955 Somerset Maugham Award for fiction. The story follows the academic and romantic pursuits of Jim Dixon, a history lecturer at an English university. The book is regarded by many as the finest, and funniest, comic novel of the twentieth century, but it scandalized readers in 1954. Time magazine included Lucky Jim in its 100 Best English-language Novels from 1923 to 2005. Dixon has had a rocky start at the university and is concerned about losing his position. He tries to maintain a good relationship with his absent-minded department head, Professor Welch, in order to be awarded a permanent post. Dixon also has a difficult relationship with a sometimes girlfriend who also teaches at the university. He meets Christine Callaghan, who is the latest girlfriend of Welch’s son. Dixon becomes attracted to her and they navigate their relationships. The story reaches its climax during an important lecture that Dixon is to give. However, he drinks too much in an attempt to calm his nerves, mocks the university’s culture, and passes out. Welch lets Dixon know his position at the university will not be extended, but all turns out well and he becomes Lucky Jim. The book generated strong feelings among the group. Author-journalist Bill Wong publishes memoir 13 years in the making By Jay Russell Author and journalist Bill Wong, a Piedmont resident, will celebrate the release of his new book “Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America” on March 24. At the book release, Wong will read selections from his memoir and discuss some life experiences with his perspectives as a journalist, a son, an Oakland native, and as an Asian-American. Wong will read primarily from the first chapter to set up the contrast between the eras, and locales in the book. The book launch will take place this Sunday, March 24 from 1:00-2:00 p.m. in the Oakland Asian Cultural Center, 388 Ninth Street in Oakland. This release of the memoir is the culmination of 13 years of work in which he discusses his roots and his identity. “Many Americans are curious about ancestral roots, whether they begin in Europe, Africa, Asia or Latin America,” said Wong. “I think the book should have appeal to people of many ethnicities. It’s my optimistic and cautionary ‘Thank you America’ tale,” he added. Wong was born in Oakland’s Chinatown to Chinese immigrants. The language spoken at home was Cantonese with his father’s dialect of Hoisan or Toisan. When Wong attended Lincoln Elementary School, he began his own journey with the English language. Although raised first with the language of his father, he only knew his father for 20 years of life. The book explicates how Wong grew out of Chinatown, psychologically, linguistically and physically, to become part of the American culture. “Wong’s memoir is more than a personal recounting; it is a bridge between past and present, offering insights into the challenges and triumphs of the Chinese-American community,” said the Breaking News Network (BNN). Wong graduated from Oakland High School and as a student at UC Berkeley he wrote for The Daily Californian. After his undergraduate studies he was with the Peace Corp in the Philippines and later graduated from the Columbia School of Journalism in New York in 1970. Wong’s first professional experience was with the San Francisco Chronicle as a general assignment reporter in the summer of 1962. He went on to Author and Piedmont resident Bill Wong. become a staff writer with the Wall Street Journal, from 1970- 1979, and joined the Oakland Tribune in 1979 where he spent 17 years on staff and then as a syndicated columnist. He was highly respected and well read, and became a regular contributor on The News Hour with Jim Lehrer on PBS in 1995 and 1996. Wong’s book features photos from a trip he and his sisters took to his father’s village in 1994. For Bill’s older sisters who grew up in China, the trip was a homecoming. But for Bill it marked a journey of complicated emotions and part of his search for identify. Seeing his father’s worn home in China proved to be an emotional experience. Bill describes his book as an immigrant success story. “But our society has deep issues; we are still deciding what kind of democracy we want to be,” Wong qualified. To RSVP for the free book launch on Sunday, March 24, visit Oacc.cc/event/sonsofchinatown. For more on Bill Wong visit Williamgeewong.com. “Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America” by William (Bill) Gee Wong. articles.text: In February Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 went on a backpacking and overnight camping trip to Point Reyes in West Marin. Before starting the hike, the Scouts had an opportunity to look through the Point Reyes Museum showing the diversity of the area and its many native species. After seeing the displays, the Scouts watched a short documentary film about the wildlife in Pt. Reyes National Seashore. The weather was beautiful and so was the hike. Many different thriving green plants could be found along the trail. A storm prior to the trip caused a number of trees to fall, blocking parts of the trail. Although it slowed the hiking, the trees proved to be a fun challenge to add to the approximately four-mile hike. After arriving at the campsite, everyone went to work setting up their tents and arranging their sleeping gear. There was not a After setting up camp, the Scouts hiked to the top of Point Reyes where they saw the elevation marker. Group photo of Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 at Pt. Reyes National Seashore. cloud in the sky, so it was a good time for taking a break and eat lunch. Then it was time to walk to the peak of Point Reyes. Some weren’t sure what to expect from the “peak” and it definitely wasn’t what some Scouts were imagining. Instead of scaling a mountain like at least one Scout had envisioned, they learned that the peak was a medium sized rock slightly raised above the ground. At least they could say they stood exactly on the peak of Point Reyes before walking back, hanging out for a while and making dinner at the campsite before it got dark. One of the patrols made some delicious penne pasta. In a short time, the sky which was crystal clear, was full of blinking, brilliant stars. Star gazing is something you can only truly experience away from cities. The Scouts eventually fell asleep in their tents and woke up around 6:30 a.m. to make breakfast and pack all their gear for the journey home. But to the Scouts’ surprise, the entire camp had become overrun with banana slugs during the night. At least one Scout had to scrape as many as 10 of the slimy critters off her tent. The Scouts made sure to warn one another if they were about to step on one because they seemed to be everywhere. A thick morning fog over the camp made it pretty cold. After packing up for the return hike, the Scouts did a trash sweep of the campsite to leave it as they found it when they arrived. The hike back to the parking lot was on a different trail and was much shorter – and downhill. This trail also had many more fallen trees partially blocking the trail and the trees were much larger than on the trail on Saturday. We helped each other over the ginormous trees and arrived safely back at the parking lot. Point Reyes was a beautiful spot to camp and was near the ocean which provided everyone with gorgeous views. The Scouts seemed to have a lot of fun on the trip and can hardly wait for a return trip. Beautiful views can be found at Point Reyes, from the glistening blue ocean to the luscious green landscape. Scouts encountered many obstacles including fallen trees on the trek to Point Reyes. Members of the Husky Patrol made a delicious pasta dinner before it got dark. The return trail from Point Reyes.

articles.text: It is with a profound sense of loss that the Goddard and DeVries families announce the passing of Bruce William Goddard at the age of 76. Bruce lost his battle with pulmonary fibrosis at his home in San Leandro, CA on March 10, 2024, while surrounded by his children and his dog, Geez. Bruce lived a remarkable life. Born Bruce William Goddard on May 6, 1947 at Merritt Hospital in Oakland, he was the son of Merle Goddard and Beverly Burger. He was a force of nature from the very start. Many of the eye-popping stories of hijinks from his childhood involved his siblings – Bob, Brian, and Brenda – who were sometimes collaborators and, at other times, victims. Bruce’s siblings Bob and Brenda preceded Bruce in death. Bruce is survived by his brother Brian, who is still owed from Bruce’s unfortunate losing position on their most recent bet. Bruce’s childhood formed his lifelong passion for politics, baseball, Americana music, and “Goddard humor.” He attended Oakland public schools, graduating from Skyline High School in 1964. He spent the next two years at Laney College in Oakland, where he was student body president and played wide receiver on Laney’s first-ever football team. Memorably, Bruce played a hard-fought game against a team of inmates inside San Quentin prison. Bruce then matriculated to UC Berkeley, earning a political science degree in 1969. Lifted by the spirit of the time and his determination to do good for the world, Bruce put his new degree to work with teaching jobs at “street academy” schools in New York and then Washington, DC. When his school folded, Bruce found himself in DC hard up for cash and a very long way from home. The circumstances led him to a taxicab career. He spent the next seven years driving a DC taxi, tending bar at DC clubs, traveling the world, and making lifelong friendships. The stories from his time in the nation’s capital have achieved legendary status. In retelling these stories, Bruce reminded us that “everyone who ever had a gun in my cab was mad at someone else, not me.” He became Dan Rather’s regular cabbie, a relationship that afforded Bruce a first-hand account of the unfolding Watergate scandal from one of the nation’s top newsmen. Later, a then-unknown singer named Emmylou Harris sang to Bruce backstage while he was tending bar at the DC club Reading Gaol. This is all not to be outdone, however, by one very strange and long night ending with a cup of coffee in, of all places, President Gerald Ford’s living room. As Bruce stared down the fast-approaching age of 30, he realized it was time to get back to his true love: politics. He moved back to the Bay Area, ran local political campaigns and moonlighted as a department store Santa Claus (“Sanity Clause”, a term he preferred.) In 1978, Bruce connected with Tom Bates, another Berkeley grad and ex-football player, on a mission to do some good. For the next decade, Bruce worked for the State Legislature as Assemblyman Tom Bates’ chief political lieutenant. Bruce was a fixture in the East Bay political scene for decades. Even when he wasn’t running a campaign, he was sought out for his sage political advice and candid observations. Those calls and requests for advice continued up until the week of his death. Most importantly, this was the time in which he met a fellow legislative staffer named Judy DeVries, whom he married in 1989. Judy brought her two children, Cisco and Will, into the blended family. Shortly thereafter, Caroline Goddard was born to Bruce and Judy. After a stint with AC Transit and earning a master’s degree in public administration from Cal State East Bay, Bruce joined the newly formed Alameda County Waste Management Authority, now known as StopWaste. Bruce’s political acumen, communication skills, and creativity were put to use in all manner of advertisements and campaigns focused on recycling and other environmental goals. The result was a significant increase in recycling and the emergence of one of the most influential environmental agencies in the State. His young daughter, Caroline, was often an uncredited star in the Authority’s TV spots. pages.text: Wednesday, March 20, 2024 27 Obituary Former PHS coach Bruce Goddard dies on March 10 It is with a profound sense of loss that the Goddard and DeVries families announce the passing of Bruce William Goddard at the age of 76. Bruce lost his battle with pulmonary fibrosis at his home in San Leandro, CA on March 10, 2024, while surrounded by his children and his dog, Geez. Bruce lived a remarkable life. Born Bruce William Goddard on May 6, 1947 at Merritt Hospital in Oakland, he was the son of Merle Goddard and Beverly Burger. He was a force of nature from the very start. Many of the eye-popping stories of hijinks from his childhood involved his siblings – Bob, Brian, and Brenda – who were sometimes collaborators and, at other times, victims. Bruce’s siblings Bob and Brenda preceded Bruce in death. Bruce is survived by his brother Brian, who is still owed from Bruce’s unfortunate losing position on their most recent bet. Bruce’s childhood formed his lifelong passion for politics, baseball, Americana music, and “Goddard humor.” He attended Oakland public schools, graduating from Skyline High School in 1964. He spent the next two years at Laney College in Oakland, where he was student body president and played wide receiver on Laney’s first-ever football team. Memorably, Bruce played a hard-fought game against a team of inmates inside San Quentin prison. Bruce then matriculated to UC Berkeley, earning a political science degree in 1969. Lifted by the spirit of the time and his determination to do good for the world, Bruce put his new degree to work with teaching jobs at “street academy” schools in New York and then Washington, DC. When his school folded, Bruce found himself in DC hard up for cash and a very long way from home. The circumstances led him to a taxicab career. He spent the next seven years driving a DC taxi, tending bar at DC clubs, traveling the world, and making lifelong friendships. The stories from his time in the nation’s capital have achieved legendary status. In retelling these stories, Bruce reminded us that “everyone who ever had a gun in my cab was mad at someone else, not me.” He became Dan Rather’s regular cabbie, a relationship that afforded Bruce a first-hand account of the unfolding Watergate scandal from one of the nation’s top newsmen. Later, a then-unknown singer named Emmylou Harris sang to Bruce backstage while he was tending bar at the DC club Reading Gaol. This is all not to be outdone, however, by one very strange and long night ending with a cup of coffee in, of all places, President Gerald Ford’s living room. As Bruce stared down the fast-approaching age of 30, he realized it was time to get back to his true love: politics. He moved back to the Bay Area, ran local political campaigns and moonlighted as a department store Santa Claus (“Sanity Clause”, a term he preferred.) In 1978, Bruce connected with Tom Bates, another Berkeley grad and ex-football player, on a mission to do some good. For the next decade, Bruce worked for the State Legislature as Assemblyman Tom Bates’ chief political lieutenant. Bruce was a fixture in the East Bay political scene for decades. Even when he wasn’t running a campaign, he was sought out for his sage political advice and candid observations. Those calls and requests for advice continued up until the week of his death. Most importantly, this was the time in which he met a fellow legislative staffer named Judy DeVries, whom he married in 1989. Judy brought her two children, Cisco and Will, into the blended family. Shortly thereafter, Caroline Goddard was born to Bruce and Judy. After a stint with AC Transit and earning a master’s degree in public administration from Cal State East Bay, Bruce joined the newly formed Alameda County Waste Management Authority, now known as StopWaste. Bruce’s political acumen, communication skills, and creativity were put to use in all manner of advertisements and campaigns focused on recycling and other environmental goals. articles.text: On their latest excursion, the Piedmont Seniors explored the world from the heart of Golden Gate Park at the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Among the areas they visited were a self-guided tour of the Osher Rainforest, the Kimball Natural History Museum, and Steinhart Aquarium followed by a tantalizing lunch at the Terrace Cafe and then a visit to the Morrison Planetarium. It had been several years since the Seniors’ last visit and they were eager to return. Upon arrival, the Seniors were met at the entrance by a courteous employee, who helped the group escape from the copious amounts of school children. She directed the Seniors to the Osher Rainforest, where the Seniors began their day’s exploration. Inside the dome of the Osher Rainforest, they were treated to a magnificent neotropical rainforest stretching 90 feet above, a lush, four-story rainforest that’s teeming with life, including live plants and. animals – everything from free-flying butterflies to exotic reptiles, amphibians, birds, and even a slithering Amazonian tree boa. The rainforest’s living plants include trees like the Brazilian beauty leaf and West Indies mahogany, dozens of shrubs, and hundreds of flowering plants from begonias and philodendrons to orchids, bromeliads, and even a rare corpse flower. The past, present, and future of life on Earth came alive for the Seniors through hands-on exhibits at the Kimball Natural History Museum, which features fascinating specimens, and a peek into the latest research conducted by the Academy’s scientists. The highlight was that of a towering T. rex in the main lobby. Another favorite was an albino Alligator mississippiensis that’s become one of the Academy’s most famous residents. The alligator, known as “Claude,” is part of an exhibit known as “The Swamp”, highlighting ecosystems of the Southeastern United States. The Piedmont Seniors then explored the world’s most vibrant, virtual ecosystems at the Steinhart Aquarium, one of the most biologically diverse and interactive aquariums in the world. Home of nearly 60,000 live animals, representing more than 1,000 unique species, Steinhart Aquarium offers an unprecedented view of underwater and terrestrial habitats, from species displayed nowhere else in the world to exhibits about cutting-edge research in little-known ocean ecosystems. The visit was definitely filled with discovery. At lunchtime, the group headed to the Terrace Café, where the food was delicious, the service impeccable, and the ambiance couldn’t be better. The seniors were seated indoors with all glass walls to offer a panoramic view of the luscious outdoor gardens. The “sous chef” came out to introduce herself and to meet and greet the Piedmont Seniors. The next visit at the Academy of Sciences was to the Morrison Planetarium for a half-hour production. The 75-foot dome immerses the audience inside cutting-edge visualizations and hyper-realistic virtual environments. From faraway galaxies to the workings of our own planet, the Piedmont Seniors experienced the cosmos like never before. But that wasn’t all. After their visit the Seniors boarded a bus to come home. On the way they were given a brief tour of parts of San Francisco, including seeing the home where Charles Manson once lived and the famous Painted Ladies, sometimes referred to as the “Seven Sisters,” a series of Pictured at the entrance of the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco are (front) Madeline Moore (left), Gloria Wilmer, Mona Jamieson, Elene Manolis, Patti Singer, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska; (back) Greg Jurin, Carole Jones, Nancy Hinsch, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Barbara Friede, Larry Singer, and Lois Horwitz. Not pictured: Jim Ayotte. Lunch at the Terrace Café was superb as Piedmont Seniors got to choose from a myriad of tasty options. fabulously painted Victorian and Edwardian houses near Alamo Square, built in the 1890s. The colors were added in the 1960s by a local artist. In all, it was a truly relaxing and very informative day. Everyone arrived back in Piedmont with smiles on their faces. If you would like more information the Piedmont Seniors, including future excursions, contact Janet Epstein, Seniors Coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov. Meetings are held on the fourth Wednesday of each month at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue at 10 a.m. Monthly excursions are scheduled year-round throughout the greater Bay Area. articles.text: More than 2.2 million Americans have what is often called “the sneak thief of sight.” It’s a condition that can take away nearly half of a person’s vision before they even notice and experts believe that half of the people who have glaucoma don’t even know it. Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that causes blindness through damage to the optic nerve. The nerve is like a cable that sends images from the eye to the brain. There is no cure for glaucoma, but medication and/or surgery can slow or prevent further vision loss. A person already suffering from glaucoma or blindness has to cope with living with this new disability, but it does not mean they have to lose their independence. Studies show that older adults with glaucoma are more likely to suffer falls that results in an injury requiring hospitalization. But with the assistance of a professionally-trained or family caregiver, a person with glaucoma can continue living in their home while still staying safe. Glaucoma and In-Home safety A fall-risk assessment can be helpful in determining the risks in the home for someone living with impaired vision. They should make sure no cords stick out, get rid of any loose or frayed rugs, and arrange the furniture so it is not an obstacle course. There are several additional steps that experts recommend to make the home safer for a person with glaucoma. The BrightFocus Foundation (www.brightfocus. org) says one of the biggest ways to help a person with vision loss is to improve lighting inside the home. This includes using overhead lights, under-cabinet lighting, and adding extra lighting in hallways and on any stairs. Additionally, a caregiver can help a person with glaucoma control glare inside the home. Glare can create different shadows that can be disorienting. The use of blinds and curtains makes a big difference with glare. The BrightFocus Foundation also recommends installing grab bars in bathrooms, putting handrails of both sides of any stairs, and mark the edge of each step with brightly-colored tape. It’s also a good idea to put tape around the edge of a bathtub, use nonskid, brightly-colored mats on the bathroom floor. Bright colors can help all around the bathroom, from towels to the toilet seat. The Mayo Clinic also recommends that people with glaucoma eat a healthy diet, because some vitamins and nutrients can help improve vision. While a healthy diet won’t prevent glaucoma from worsening, there are some foods to avoid. High amounts of caffeine can increase eye pressure and so can drinking too much of any liquid at one time – it’s best to space fluids out frequently over the day. Exercise may also reduce eye pressure for some forms of glaucoma. Perhaps most importantly, people with developing glaucoma should not ignore it. The Glaucoma Research Foundation (www.glaucoma.org) encourages everyone to talk about it. The gradual effects of the “sneak thief of sight” often go untreated because they go unspoken. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. So, for example, sitting in an airport on the public Wi-Fi is not a good time to log into your bank, or to log into a retail site and use your credit card to buy something. If you must do work or have access to a site where you need to put in sensitive information, it’s vital that you subscribe to a VPN, which is a Virtual Private Network. This type of service encrypts your activity on the web and keeps your identity hidden while surfing. Some of the top reviewed VPNs are CyberGhost, Private Internet Access, NordVPN, and there are several more. Also, make sure your device is not set to automatically connect to available Wi-Fi networks. If you don’t need it, turn Bluetooth off also. Change your passwords to sites you may visit online before you travel, and then change them again when you get home. When you are on the website, make sure it says “https” instead of just “http” (the “s” stands for “secure”). And, of course, when you get back home, check your credit card statements for any unrecognized charges. Enjoy your trip – but be careful out there. articles.text: Dear MacMama: I am going to be traveling, and my neighbor just came back from being overseas, and her phone was hacked. What kind of precautions can I take to prevent that from happening to me? Bert C., Oakland Dear Bert: Your timing on that question is excellent because the FBI just put out a statement last week for travelers and the public to avoid using free charging stations in airports, hotels, restaurants and shopping centers. They said in their announcement that hackers have found a way to use public USB ports to introduce malware, and even monitoring software onto devices. Devices like iPhones, and iPads, with compromised USB cables can be hijacked through software that can access usernames and passwords. When most of us travel by air, it seems like a welcome convenience that we can just plug our phones and iPads into USB ports that are often in the waiting area at the gate. It’s nice not to have to carry the charger, and just carry the USB cable. And, of course, more and more airlines, have these ports available right at your seat, even in economy. pages.text: Wednesday, March 20, 2024 29 Overcoming the ‘Sneak Thief of Sight’ By Ben Bloom More than 2.2 million Americans have what is often called “the sneak thief of sight.” It’s a condition that can take away nearly half of a person’s vision before they even notice and experts believe that half of the people who have glaucoma don’t even know it. Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that causes blindness through damage to the optic nerve. The nerve is like a cable that sends images from the eye to the brain. There is no cure for glaucoma, but medication and/or surgery can slow or prevent further vision loss. A person already suffering from glaucoma or blindness has to cope with living with this new disability, but it does not mean they have to lose their independence. Studies show that older adults with glaucoma are more likely to suffer falls that results in an injury requiring hospitalization. But with the assistance of a professionally-trained or family caregiver, a person with glaucoma can continue living in their home while still staying safe. Glaucoma and In-Home safety A fall-risk assessment can be helpful in determining the risks in the home for someone living with impaired vision. They should make sure no cords stick out, get rid of any loose or frayed rugs, and arrange the furniture so it is not an obstacle course. There are several additional steps that experts recommend to make the home safer for a person with glaucoma. The BrightFocus Foundation (www.brightfocus. org) says one of the biggest ways to help a person with vision loss is to improve lighting inside the home. This includes using overhead lights, under-cabinet lighting, and adding extra lighting in hallways and on any stairs. Additionally, a caregiver can help a person with glaucoma control glare inside the home. Glare can create different shadows that can be disorienting. The use of blinds and curtains makes a big difference with glare. The BrightFocus Foundation also recommends installing grab bars in bathrooms, putting handrails of both sides of any stairs, and mark the edge of each step with brightly-colored tape. It’s also a good idea to put tape around the edge of a bathtub, use nonskid, brightly-colored mats on the bathroom floor. Bright colors can help all around the bathroom, from towels to the toilet seat. The Mayo Clinic also recommends that people with glaucoma eat a healthy diet, because some vitamins and nutrients can help improve vision. While a healthy diet won’t prevent glaucoma from worsening, there are some foods to avoid. High amounts of caffeine can increase eye pressure and so can drinking too much of any liquid at one time – it’s best to space fluids out frequently over the day. Exercise may also reduce eye pressure for some forms of glaucoma. Perhaps most importantly, people with developing glaucoma should not ignore it. The Glaucoma Research Foundation (www.glaucoma.org) encourages everyone to talk about it. The gradual effects of the “sneak thief of sight” often go untreated because they go unspoken. How to avoid cell phone being hacked while traveling By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I am going to be traveling, and my neighbor just came back from being overseas, and her phone was hacked. What kind of precautions can I take to prevent that from happening to me? Bert C., Oakland Dear Bert: Your timing on that question is excellent because the FBI just put out a statement last week for travelers and the public to avoid using free charging stations in airports, hotels, restaurants and shopping centers. They said in their announcement that hackers have found a way to use public USB ports to introduce malware, and even monitoring software onto devices. Devices like iPhones, and iPads, with compromised USB cables can be hijacked through software that can access usernames and passwords. When most of us travel by air, it seems like a welcome convenience that we can just plug our phones and iPads into USB ports that are often in the waiting area at the gate. It’s nice not to have to carry the charger, and just carry the USB cable. And, of course, more and more airlines, have these ports available right at your seat, even in economy. But according to the FBI and cyber security experts, this is not safe. So, what are you to do when you must travel for many hours and your devices run out of juice? Just carry your own charger and plug it into an available electrical outlet instead. Yes, it’s bulkier, but it’s nothing compared to the nightmare of having your device hacked and even in some cases your identity stolen. This warning by the FBI is not new. The FCC has warned about “juice jacking” (as the malware and hacking scheme is called) since 2021. More and more, bad actors are finding a way to get into our devices. So, as we load more sensitive information onto our devices, we have to be more vigilant. The same caution applies to using public Wi-Fi, whether it’s in a hotel or airport, or coffee shop. If you must use public Wi-Fi, make sure you do not log into any sites that require a password, because hackers could be using software to capture sensitive information, like credit card numbers, and of course usernames and passwords. So, for example, sitting in an airport on the public Wi-Fi is not a good time to log into your bank, or to log into a retail site and use your credit card to buy something. If you must do work or have access to a site where you need to put in sensitive information, it’s vital that you subscribe to a VPN, which is a Virtual Private Network. This type of service encrypts your activity on the web and keeps your identity hidden while surfing. Some of the top reviewed VPNs are CyberGhost, Private Internet Access, NordVPN, and there are several more. Also, make sure your device is not set to automatically connect to available Wi-Fi networks. If you don’t need it, turn Bluetooth off also. Change your passwords to sites you may visit online before you travel, and then change them again when you get home. When you are on the website, make sure it says “https” instead of just “http” (the “s” stands for “secure”). And, of course, when you get back home, check your credit card statements for any unrecognized charges. Enjoy your trip – but be careful out there. On Thursday, March 15 ten volunteers — including five members of the Park Commission — gathered with Public Works staff to plant 40 riparian plants along Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park. Volunteers planted saplings of five different species, including Buttonwillow, California Box Elder, California Wild Rose, Oregon Ash, and White Alde. All are expected to thrive according to Park ComPark Commission Chair Tom Smegal and Tom Gandesbery planting saplings by Bushy Dell Volunteers Sara Gaucher and Tom Kelly planting saplings by the creek. mission Vice-Chair Kimberly Moses and Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent. “We had the opportunity because Watershed Nursery in Richmond had overstock from a project that had been delayed and they didn’t want the plants to go to waste,” explained Moses. “I thought of our ivyladen Bushy Dell Creek and on the off-chance that I could get permission from the City, I took Watershed up on the offer. Lucky for us Nancy [Kent] and the city maintenance crew accommodated our volunteer effort.” Moses added that the offer came at an opportune time in the season. Riparian plants usually thrive near streams or river banks. A little later and the summer drought would have made such a planting “impossible.” Volunteers at the event included commissioners Kimberly Moses, Tom Smegal, Arden Hall, Jack Fishrup, Barbara Giuffre, and Dave Johnson, as well as community members Tom Gandesbery, Sara Gaucher, and Tom and Jane Kelly. “This was a very small project, a sort of ‘proof of concept’ for volunteers to be allowed to plant riparian native plants in the park,” said Moses. “If we could work on educating dog owners about managing their pets near urban creeks, we could even clear ivy, acacia and privet from the creek and replace the invasive species that dominate it with beautiful native sycamore, alder and big leaf maples. Maybe even bring in some native California azalea!” For more information about the project or how to get involved with similar volunteering opportunities, contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting tonight, March 13, at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall. The primary action and review item is a financial report by Chief Business Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The school district has had a busy month, amidst negotiations over teacher salaries and plans to downsize staff to reflect decreased enrollment. In the February 28 meeting the board directed the Superintendent to pursue bringing an increase to the Measure H parcel tax to Piedmont ballots in November. There was not a formal vote about Measure H on February 28, it was a report for information and discussion only, “The Board gave direction, not a vote, to request that staff explore a parcel tax increase,” explained Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Alahydoian’s report is a second interim report with an update of actual expenditures and revenues through January 31. It will also have a projection of the budget adjustments necessary to close out the fiscal year. The Second Interim also includes a multiyear projection (MYP) that shapes the budget development process for 2024- 25. The Board must certify the District’s financial condition as Positive, Qualified or Negative, a background document states. The report will show that the district is on track to meet the 3% reserve requirement this year and in the next two fiscal years. The agenda for the meeting initially was going to announce a new tentative agreement with CSEA classified staff, however the announcement of the agreement has been pulled, as negotiations continue. Also on the board agenda is the personnel action report which includes the resignations at the end of the school year of PHS English Teacher Matthew Klein, Behavior Analyst Austin Lambe, and PHS Math Teacher Diana Miller. articles.text: According to preliminary results from the California primary election on March 5, Piedmont’s Measure F passed with more than 75% of the vote. Measure F will increase the existing city parcel tax, also known as the City Services Tax, by 20% (an additional $11-$19 per month for most households). It also change the tax’s renewal period from four to 12 years. As of 4:44 p.m. on Monday, March 11, the Alameda County Registrar of Voters reported 2,901 votes in favor and 924 votes against. The preliminary results are based on the most recent ballot counts and may change as additional mail-in ballots are counted. “Elections give the community the chance to express what’s important to them,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore of the measure’s approval. “We’re gratified both by the strong turnout among our voters and their overwhelming support for Measure F. High-quality services matter to Piedmont, as does investment in quality-of-life measures to ensure public safety. We take this message to heart and are committed to serving as responsible stewards.” The City Services Tax accounts for approximately 7% of the city’s General Fund budget. It supports services including police, fire, paramedics, parks, recreation, greenspaces, stormwater infrastructure, streets, and public facilities. Piedmont voters first approved the tax in 1981, and it has been renewed 11 times since then. Reports from the Registrar of Voters published as of Tuesday, March 12 show a total of 4,675 vote-by-mail ballots by Piedmont voters. The Registrar’s office will continue to update results as more ballots are counted. They have until April 4 to certify the results.

articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to the City Administrator and Chief of Police on March 8. I have noticed a significant increase in the number of vehicles driving on Piedmont streets with excessive window tinting. Just this week, while trying to cross Grand Avenue at the crosswalk, several cars which had excessive tinting passed me without stopping. The tinting was on all windows, including the front windshield, making it impossible for me to see the driver’s eyes and determine if he planned to stop and allow me to cross safely. When I was a reserve police officer in the 1990’s we always stopped and cited these vehicles. articles.text: Mark 1:7 He (John the Baptist) proclaimed, “The one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the thong of his sandals.” It is likely that Mark wrote his gospel primarily for the benefit of the gentile followers of Jesus living in Rome during the emperorship of Nero. Mark’s audience knew harassment, disparagement and persecution. Nero blamed them for a 64 CE fire that nearly destroyed the city. One of the messages Mark wanted to share with them was. “Jesus too knew what it was to be misunderstood and persecuted. But hold on. God is with you as God was with Jesus. The best is yet to come.” The beginning verses of Mark’s gospel are representative of the message that the best is yet to come. In them he tells of John the Baptist, whom the followers of Jesus in Rome likely had heard of, maybe even remembered, as popular, courageous, charismatic and odd, saying that though he, John, had important work to do, it was really work that was primarily to prepare the way for Jesus. John pointed beyond himself to Jesus. He was clear. The best was yet to come. The concluding verse of the passage emphasizes this theme. “I have baptized you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” John tells his audience, and through him, Mark, his hearers, that though John baptized with water, the essence of life, Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit, the essence of God. Again, the message: the best is yet to come. Children, especially as Christmas approaches, generally do not need any convincing that the best is yet to come.
articles.title: The best is yet to come

Perhaps one might say it’s a nuisance violation and hardly a priority. However, these codes allow police intervention with citizens sending the message that Piedmont does not tolerate code and crime violations. Sending the signal that Piedmont is unfriendly to scoff-laws and criminals will have an effect to move these types elsewhere. These “little things” are some of the best tools law enforcement has to thwart and prevent bigger crimes. –Mark Herrick A message for Consumer Affairs columnist Dear Wiley: I just read your Consumer Affairs article in The Piedmont Post, dated March 6, 2024 about license plates. The best is yet to come By Pastor Jim Hopins Mark 1:7 He (John the Baptist) proclaimed, “The one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the thong of his sandals.” It is likely that Mark wrote his gospel primarily for the benefit of the gentile followers of Jesus living in Rome during the emperorship of Nero. Mark’s audience knew harassment, disparagement and persecution. Nero blamed them for a 64 CE fire that nearly destroyed the city. One of the messages Mark wanted to share with them was. “Jesus too knew what it was to be misunderstood and persecuted. But hold on. God is with you as God was with Jesus. The best is yet to come.” The beginning verses of Mark’s gospel are representative of the message that the best is yet to come. In them he tells of John the Baptist, whom the followers of Jesus in Rome likely had heard of, maybe even remembered, as popular, courageous, charismatic and odd, saying that though he, John, had important work to do, it was really work that was primarily to prepare the way for Jesus. John pointed beyond himself to Jesus. He was clear. The best was yet to come. The concluding verse of the passage emphasizes this theme. “I have baptized you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” John tells his audience, and through him, Mark, his hearers, that though John baptized with water, the essence of life, Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit, the essence of God. Again, the message: the best is yet to come. They seem better suited to accepting the message of hope. We adults are likely to be much more skeptical. We have heard it all before. We are worn down by the onslaught of glimmering promises from advertisers, politicians and preachers that if we would just buy the right product, vote the right way, or believe the right things, heaven on earth will be ours. We are on guard against getting fooled again. Mark gets it. His people knew all about false promises. The promise of Pax Romana. The promise of an emperor who was sent by the gods. articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery displays a flower arrangement at a previous year’s tulip exhibition. The event’s exhibits are well-known in the community for their creativity. Tulip enthusiasts will have plenty to be excited about this month. Mountain View Cemetery’s 16th Annual Tulip Exhibition will open for three days of creative flower arrangements and displays in the cemetery’s Tower Chapel from Friday through Sunday, March 22-24, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Community members are invited to view the extravagant art exhibit inside the Tower Chapel at the cemetery, as well as enjoy the thousands In one creative display, lampshades are fashioned out of freshly cut tulips at the Tower Chapel. Some of the arrangements at the tulip exhibition are more minimalistic than others, like this solo arrangement. of tulips planted on the cemetery grounds. This is a free event, and no reservations or tickets are required. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s tulip exhibition has become a cherished community tradition. “Our family puts this event on the calendar months in advance,” said Barbara Turtle, a local community member. “The exhibits are fabulous, and it gives us the perfect reason to come and enjoy all the beautiful tulips in bloom throughout the cemetery grounds.” Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, the tulip exhibition returned to Mountain View Cemetery in March 2023 after a three-year absence due to the impact of Covid. Mountain View Cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue. For more information on the tulip exhibition, visit www. mountainviewcemetery.org. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has extended the deadline for its disaster preparedness survey through Sunday, April 7. Among other questions, the survey asks what type of disasters community members are concerned about, what steps they have taken to prepare for a disaster, and what barriers keep community members from becoming better prepared. Survey responses will help City officials better understand the levels of preparedness within the community, where gaps exist, and how they can best support more residents taking important steps to be ready for a disaster. Results will help the City plan outreach efforts and programs for emergency preparedness. The survey is available online at www.piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. For more information visit piedmont.ca.gov/disaster. For residents questions, contact Fire Chief Dave Brannigan at dbrannigan@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City disaster preparedness survey underway

articles.text: The Piedmont Fourth of July Parade Committee has announced that the theme for this year’s parade is “Small town, Big spirit” according to Committee Chair Kathy Kelleher. The principal planner of the parade was intentionally mum on the finer details of the parade, so as not to spoil any surprises. “It’s what we are,” laughed Kelleher, when asked what this year’s theme meant. “We are a small town with great spirit.” However, Kelleher did say that this year’s parade would be a vibrant display of the town’s spirit. “We’re really excited and planning is well underway. It’s going to be a great year, so stay in town,” she joked. The Fourth of July Parade is the largest city event of the year, with up to 6,000 people coming to Highland Avenue to view the parade entries. Planning for the event begins in February each year. In 2020, the parade was canceled because of COVID-19 concerns. It returned to full form last year. This will be the parade’s second year back since it was canceled. The parade will be on Highland Avenue on Thursday, July 4 starting at 11 a.m.
articles.title: July 4th parade committee announces theme

articles.text: “Do you have a favorite tree in town?” could be an odd question any other time of the year. But as Arbor Day nears it become relevant. The Piedmont Park Commission announced it is now accepting nominations for Piedmont’s annual Heritage Tree program. Community members may nominate a tree or group of trees to receive special recognition from the city. Winners will be announced at the next Park Commission meeting on Wednesday, April 3, and at the Arbor Day celebration on Friday, April 26 at Community Hall from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. Piedmont’s Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 to raise awareness and appreciation for the city’s local flora. Each year, the Park Commission selects up to five trees from the community’s nominations to receive a heritage tree designation from the City. The Park Commission will consider trees for the title based A Coast Live Oak in Piedmont Park, commonly known as “the climbing tree,” was nominated by the Brumfield family in 2019. on aesthetic, educational, or historical qualities. Any tree in Piedmont’s parks or public spaces is eligible for consideration. Trees on private property will not be considered. Community members whose nominees are selected will be recognized as part of the City’s annual Arbor Day celebration and receive a limited-edition Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. To nominate a tree or group of trees, community members can complete the online nomination form at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ HeritageTrees. Submissions are due by Friday, March 22. The dogwoods in front of City Hall were nominated for the Heritage Tree designation by Bobbe Stehr and Mark Enea in 2019.
articles.title: Heritage Tree nominations now open

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, March 13, 2024 SchOOLs Millennium students, parents defend counselor job By Jay Russell During the February 28 Piedmont School Board meeting, parents, staff, and students of Millennium High paraded to the microphone in numbers to defend the counseling position at their school that was under threat of being cut from the school district budget. The part-time counseling position (0.4 FTE) has since been spared by the district from cuts announced at the March 4 special board meeting. The position was identified as the job of the school’s only counselor, Stefanie Manalo-LeClair, who is known widely as “Ms. M.L.” “I can confirm that Ms. M. L. is not receiving a March 15 notice.” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. “We value her tremendously and recognize the incredible relationships she has with students, parents and guardians.” When parents and staff saw the position listed on the first list of potential budget cuts on February 14, they sprang into action. “We can’t afford to lose a Ms. M.L.,” said parent Jay Momet. The district agreed, as Manalo-LeClair’s counselor job, which includes helping student navigate course and prepare for college, is safe for now. The tight knit Millennium community strongly defended the importance of a school counselor. “Millennium is a gem, it should be protected, there is no place like it in this city. It is so different it is so unique it could be a case study on thriving,” said parent Monica Garcia. “Millennium is that place where kids can be themselves completely,” said parent Claudine Woo. The position may be safe from the receiving a March 15 pink slip, but it seems to have taken a community effort to humanize the situation. “The idea of losing this is so impactful, what we are talking about here is people, we are not talking about positions,” said Momet. articles.text: The Piedmont High School and Middle School Jazz Bands, directed by Trevor Meseroll, will present two shows at Yoshi’s in Jack London Square on Monday, April 1. A variety of selections from the Latin, pop, rock, and funk genres will be performed throughout the evening, with many featured student soloists. Selected soloists will appear on many of the pieces including PHS Jazz Band vocalist Clare Weiss, who represented Piedmont in the 2023 California State Jazz Choir. Several PHS and PMS Jazz Band Combos will also make special appearances at the concerts. This wonderful evening of jazz music is a fundraiser for the school district’s Jazz Band program. The 6:30 pm show will feature the 7th grade Jazz Band and PHS Jazz Band, followed by an 8:30 p.m. show with the 8th grade Jazz Band and PHS Jazz Band. These performances will raise funds to purchase instruments and supplies for the PHS and PMS Jazz Bands. In past years, proceeds from this annual fundraiser have enabled the Jazz Band program to purchase 3 new trumpets, 1 new trombone, two tenor saxophones, two baritone saxophones, two alto saxophones, alto, baritone and tenor saxophone cases, 20 new music stands, a guitar amp and bass amp, speakers, concert snare drum, baritone sax mouthpieces, and a variety of percussion accessories, including percussion hardware and jazz cymbals. This year’s proceeds will include money to purchase a new keyboard and several amplifiers. Tickets for both performances may be purchased at www.yoshis. com or by contacting the music program at jd’annunzio@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Tickets are $25 for each show. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ®

articles.text: There have been a recent slew of books and articles written about connection and conversation. It appears that everyone has finally realized that the damage from this combination of the massive rise of social media and our isolation because of a global pandemic might have affected our ability to talk to each other. We are, as a species, designed to be in community with each other, which does require “the gift of the gab,” to quote the Irish. When looking at the advice on connecting and speaking with others, the first thing that you will often read is that you must ask questions. “Get deeply curious about the other person’s experience,” the books will tell you. Well, that’s great, but how do you get curious if curiosity doesn’t come to you naturally? I have spent a lot of time thinking about curiosity, because it is so directly linked to the creative process. Without curiosity, there is no reason to explore a new idea or attempt a new invention. Similarly, if it never occurs to you that the person sitting across from you might have an interesting story to tell, you won’t think to ask about it. Step One: The first step to cultivating curiosity is realizing what you already know. Name it. If you are speaking with a colleague, remind yourself that you know that this person has three kids and once lived in Buenos Curiosity helps enrich conversations. Aires. Step Two: The second step to cultivating curiosity is recognizing what you don’t know. You might know that they lived in Buenos Aires, but you don’t know why. Or perhaps you realize that you don’t know if this person has a pet in addition to their three children? Step Three: Now that you know what you do and don’t know, ask yourself which of the elements that you do not know do you actually care about? You need to truly want to know the information in order for the curiosity to be authentic. If you can’t find anything that you care about, go back to step two, and this time look for things that you don’t know that connect with your life. For example, you might not have much experience with travel or have a pet, but it’s possible that you do not know why this colleague came to work at the same company as you. Step Four: Now that you have something that you don’t know that you genuinely want to understand, go after that information. Ask the question. Be ready to listen to the answer. Do the research. Observe with the intention of understanding. This process works for curiosity about other people and it also works for curiosity about things or situations: What do I know? What do I not know? What do I care about? Go after the information. Congratulations. Welcome to a world of curiosity. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in the 3Cs: Creativity, Communication and Connection. ninameehan.com
