articles.text: Piedmont’s school board adopted a student representative to the board in 2022 at the behest of a student, Gianna Yan. In the first year of the position Yan, Cleo Tahawi and Siddharth Bhatia took turns as the student voice during board meetings. After serving on the board last spring as the school’s representative, Bhatia won re-election in May 2023 on a vote of his classmates. Bhatia finished his second term in January this year, along with Millennium High representative Orla Cohen. Bhatia and Cohen have since relinquished their seats to Elena Stevens of PHS and Shakila Zuberi of MHS. Bhatia took the time to chat with the Post about his experience, and the future of the student representative seat on the board. He is the first two-term representative. Bhatia confirmed that the volunteer position wasn’t a small time commitment. “I met with the Superintendent before every board meeting, for around an hour, and I am always talking with students, talking to teachers and talking with administrators,” Bhatia said. “As a kid, you are in a different world. [The school board] is a world of adults and is hugely different from high school. It was a good introduction to the adult world,” he said. He expressed gratitude for his own growth and talked about the bigger picture, getting student voices heard. “Having the position is extraordinarily impor tant. School board members Ruchi Medhekar (left), student representative Siddharth Bhatia, and board members Hilary Cooper and Lindsay Thomasson. PHS senior Siddharth Bhatia (right) sitting on the school board as the Piedmont High student representative, alongside MHS representative Orla Cohen. Before, students did not feel like their voices would be heard even if they did speak up, so they didn’t,” Bhatia said. The big issue during his first term last school year was how students were graded, when questions arose about grading systems focused on “mastery” and offered a different grading scale. “I feel proud that we were able to share the students’ perspective on the standards-based grading program, which is going a lot better this year in part due to student feedback,” he said Bhatia is also proud of expanding and solidifying the student representative to the board with an official selection process for subsequent years. “I’m happy that I could get an election system in place for future student board members to get elected.” Bhatia said. Last year, he learned the ropes under the tutelage of Interim Superintendent Dr. Donald. “For someone who was only there for a year, Dr. Evans was super invested.” Bhatia said. In his second term, as an elected representative by classmates, Bhatia and the board dealt with new challenges and the big issue at hand – teacher compensation. With some changes afoot in the school district, Bhatia’s opinions have become more important as he works with new Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn. “The board has been super welcoming to us. It’s a new voice and I definitely felt listened to,” Bhatia said. Hawn has publicly praised the student board members calling their commentary refreshing. Bhatia has offered some advice to the new student members of the school board. “Keep your ears and eyes open, and don’t be afraid to say what you think,” he said. Now that his official obligations with the school board are over Bhatia has resumed his normal high school life for his last semester in Piedmont. He is currently taking an online math class and enjoying hanging out with his brother, Romi, who is also a graduating senior.
articles.title: Siddharth Bhatia describes work on School Board

articles.text: Come see the beautiful drama The Laramie Project by Moisés Kaufman and the members of the Tectonic Theater Project on Thursday, March 21, Friday, March 22, and Saturday, March 23. All shows start at 7:00 pm. The Laramie Project is a true story that presents a deeply complex portrait of homophobia, justice, and acceptance following a community’s response to the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard, a young gay man living in Laramie, Wyoming. In a series of personal reflections, the residents of Laramie react to the hate crime and surrounding media storm. The play encourages us to consider how we can work towards creating more compassionate communities. The cast includes Breah Bell, Logan Faucher, Ella Fleischer, Jacob Hanke, Sophie Hess, Miranda Long, Charlotte Mascola, Alexis Montero Castro, Phoenix Nwokedi, Ella Puckett, Macy Puckett, Benjamin Sachs, Dahlia Saffouri, Clio Salzer, Friedie Schickedanz, Martha Schickedanz, Xander Schulte Sasse, Sadie Shoop, Louisa Symkowick, Eve Tellegen, and Isabella Wire. The Laramie Project is a groundbreaking piece of theater. It has been seen by more than 10 million people in many countries. The Laramie Project was the 10th-most-frequently produced non-musical play on high school stages in 2011-12, according to the Educational Theatre Association. With all of the social and political division in the country, it is more important than ever to gather and think about our contributions to the communities in which we live. The Laramie Project includes strong language and mature content, including descriptions of homophobia, violence, and death. Contact director Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us with any questions. Student tickets are $12. General admission is $18. Buy tickets online at https://www.showtix4u. com/event-details/81701. All shows are in the Alan Harvey Theater at PHS at 800 Magnolia Avenue. Not pictured: Phoenix Nwokedi, Friedie Schickedanz, Dahlia Saffouri

articles.text: Last weekend members of Highlander Robotics arrived with their new robot, “Banshee,” for the FIRST Robotics Competition San Francisco Regional. After finishing third of 43 in qualification rounds with a 9-1 record, they went 4-1 during the double elimination playoffs to challenge the first seed alliance Eagle Strike from Los Altos. articles.text: Extensive damage; possible 1 year for repairs A home on Seaview Avenue sustained extensive damage following a house fire on Wednesday, March 6. The Piedmont Fire Department (PFD) responded to a 911 call at 9:36 a.m. when neighbors reported seeing smoke coming from the second floor. Firefighters arrived within minutes and saw fire burning from multiple second-story windows. Fire Captain Jon Fitzpatrick, the lead firefighter, immediately called for support from the Oakland Fire Department whose units arrived a few minutes later. After confirming no one was inside, the combined firefighters ventilated the attic and roof. They cut holes in the roof and fought through thick smoke to reach the origin of the fire. The fire was extinguished in less than 30 minutes, but firefighters remained on site for several hours to make sure there were no hot spots – bits of smoldering material that could reignite. PFD Fire Chief Dave Brannigan praised the successful operation in a press release. “Any firefight is a complicated and dangerous operation. This fire was advanced upon our arrival. Piedmont Fire’s aggressive attack, supported by Oakland Fire’s rapid response allowed our crews to contain the fire effectively and safely. It’s always a win when everyone walks away from a fire without injuries.” “We were out of town at the time of the fire,” said homeowners Steve Roland. “Most importantly, no one was injured as a result of the fire.” The Rolands are currently staying in a hotel with plans to lease a property for a year while their house is repaired. Although interior damage to their home is “severe,” the Rolands plan to return as soon as possible to Piedmont, where they have resided since 1996. “The support of our friends and the community has been heartening and endearing,” said Roland. “We would like to provide a special thank you to our dear neighbors, Joe and Beth Hurwich, [who] went into our house at the first signs of distress and called 911 when the fire became evident.” The Rolands also thanked the Piedmont and Oakland Fire Departments for their swift response and professionalism. “The Fire Department saved our house at personal risk and we are deeply indebted. We wish to call special attention to Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, who personally returned to meet with us at the site upon our return later in the day after the fire had been put out. He showed compassion and professionalism that we found particularly noteworthy.” Fire investigators are still working to determine the likely origin and cause of the fire. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team wrapped up a successful week with a pair of victories, defeating non-league San Leandro by the 10-run rule, 13-2, on Thursday, March 7, and shut out Division 4 North Coast Section opponent Justin-Siena 1-0 on Saturday, March 9 at Humphries Diamond. Saturday’s win over the Braves was a rematch of last year’s North Coast Section Semifinals, which Justin-Siena won 11-10. “I thought this was a great team win,” coach Eric Olson said after the win over San Leandro. “When the runs come early and often, we know its not going to be that way for the whole season, our league looks extremely strong. But I’m excited to see all nine guys contribute and get their at bats.” It was an impressive pitching display on both days. Peter Krumins threw six innings with six strikeouts and allowed only one hit in Saturday’s win over the Braves. Ellis Moss threw four innings with five strikeouts and two hits allowed against San Leandro. “We don’t have a lot of players in the dugout; we only had 12 people today. Coming into today, I was just telling myself to throw strikes and stay confident,” Moss said. Recording the team’s first home run of the season was senior Dimitri Papahadjopoulos with a grand slam against the Pirates. With a 3-0 lead in the top of the second, he turned on a first-pitch fastball to blast the ball over left-centerfield. “The approach was to just look for a pitch that I could hit. I was just waiting for a fastball down the middle, and I connected on it,” Papahadjopoulos said. 1-0 over Justin-Siena Piedmont started the game in a big way by turning a double play in the top of the first to end things for the Braves. Then in the bottom half of the first, Piedmont got itself on the board with leadoff hitter Diego Delventhal hitting a single, followed by Krumins drawing a walk and Will Parker smacking a double to left field to score Delventhal with no outs. However, that would be the only Staff Photos Peter Krumins pitched six innings of 1-hit ball with six strikeouts in Piedmont’s 1-0 win over JustinSiena. Ellis Moss threw four innings and had five strikeouts against San Leandro. scoring of the game with Justin Siena turning a double play, stranding Krumins at third. From there, Krumins dominated on the mound. After allowing a hit to the Braves first hitter of the game, he never allowed another hit through the next five innings before making his exit for John Olsen to close the game. Olsen struck out the No. 5 hitter, but the following batter hit a double to center. Staying composed, Olsen forced a popup then tossed a four-pitch strikeout for the game’s final out. Final stats: Delventhal went 2-for-3 with a double and a run scored. Parker was 1-for-3 with a double and an RBI. Krumins threw six innings, allowed one hit, and struck out five. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team reeled in its first two wins of the 2024 season in big fashion. After drubbing league foe Washington a 16-3 in Fremont on Thursday, March 7, Piedmont claimed a dominant 7-0 shutout against on Division 1 North Coast Section opponent California High at Witter Field the following night. “We put a full game together for the first time, which was great,” said first year head coach Jeff Lamb following the big win over the Cal High. “We’ve been playing good defense and finally put enough goals on the board. When your goalie and defense have a great game, it means you’re going to do well. Logan [Huh] shut down their best player and we got a shutout.” It was a statement win over California, a longtime D1 program. The last time PHS faced Cal High was 2022, when the Grizzles won 20-7. “This was a big win, I’m hyped. We had no idea what to expect with California, we saw they lost to O’Dowd by one, and we wanted to see how this game went. We’re coming for O’Dowd, again,” senior attacker Rylan Nelson. “We got to lock down the D and didn’t allow a single goal. The plan was to help each other out,” added senior defender Keita Clear. On Friday night, Cal struggled to find clear shooting lanes. Goalie Gus Von Metszch jad a big game with nine saves and the defense forcing difficult looks. 7-0 over California Piedmont led narrowly 1-0 by the end of the first quarter and extended the gap to 3-0 by halftime. Both teams went scoreless in the third quarter before the Highlanders piled on four goals in the final quarter. After back-and-forth possessions for over seven minutes of action in the first quarter, Oliver Shafroth broke the deadlock at the 4:47 mark. Cal High started the second quarter with a man-advantage, but did nothing with it. Shafroth then scored again with 4:37 left in the half, while Connor Fredericks scored with a man-advantage at the 3:32 mark—making it 3-0. With solid defense in the third quarter, Cal had five shots go wide of the net and another two saved by Von Metzsch. In the fourth, Fredericks scored nearly 30 seconds into the quarter, while Nelson added the fifth about three minutes later at 8:37 with a nifty backhanded shot after wrapping around the net. Shafroth scored Piedmont’s sixth at 4:55, while Curtis Hohener assisted Nelson for the final goal of the game at 2:01. Final stats: Shafroth had three goals, Fredericks scored twice and won six faceoffs, Nelson scored twice, Hohener had two assists, while Von Metzsch had nine saves. 16-3 over Washington Piedmont led 7-1 by the end of the first quarter and extended the gap to 10-2 by halftime. They added three goals in the third to lead 13-3 and scored three more in the fourth. Final stats: Hohener scored four goals, Nelson and FredGoalie Gus Von Metzsch made nine saves against California.

articles.text: Oliver Greenebaum, a PHS junior, competed at the 2024 Junior Olympics in Charlotte, North Carolina. The Piedmont Fencing Team has competed in several marquee events over the last month, including the South Coast RYC/ RJC in Pasadena on Friday through Sunday March 8-10, the RYC of the Rockies in Denver on February 23-25, while they also competed in the prestigious Junior Olympics in Charlotte from February 16-19. It’s been an impressive showing for former Piedmont resident and San Ramon Valley student Sophie Choi. She won the RYC of the Rockies’ Y-14 Women’s Foil category against a field of 14 fencers. “Sophie Choi dominated the Youth Under 14 category and won gold an impressive win, only losing once the entire day. It was a great achievement for her; she basically dominated everyone, and crushed some difficult competition along the way,” coach David Sinkkonen. Choi recently was also 15th of 40 at the South Coast RYC’s Junior Women’s Foil category and was 20th of 64 in the Youth 14 Women’s Foil. At the Junior Olympics, she was 138th of 248 in the Junior Women’s Foil. It’s also been a big month for Piedmont High junior Teresa McKay. At the South Coast RYC, she placed seventh of 40 in the Junior Women’s Foil category. She earned her D24 rating in the process, which is given to fencers on the ascent. “She made the podium with an impressive performance against tough competition packed with highly ranked fencers, including several National Team members,” Sinkkonen said. McKay competed in two events at the Junior Olympics. She was 140th of 239 in the Cadet Women’s Foil event and 189th of 239 in the Junior Women’s Foil. Also at the prestigious Junior Olympics was teammate Oliver Greenbaum, a Piedmont High junior. He competed in two events, the Cadet Men’s Foil and the Junior Men’s Foil. Sophie Choi of the Piedmont Fencing Team won the Y-14 Women’s Foil category at the RYC Of the Rockies in February. Teresa McKay, a PHS junior, placed seventh at the South Coast RYC in Pasadena.

articles.text: Staff Photos Ruby Guzdar had three goals in Piemdont’s narrow 10-9 loss to Acalanes. Piedmont battled Acalanes to overtime before losing 10-9 overtime at Witter Field on Wednesday, March 6. It was the girls’ team’s first loss of the season. With the Dons carrying a 5-1 overall record and looking like Division 2 North Coast Section contenders, the result was one that pleased Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. “We knew this was going to be our first challenge and one of the things we wanted to see was how well we could play defense. I felt our defense really stepped up. This was a game that showed how connected we were,” coach Chan said. Wednesday’s game had the energy of an NCS post=season game with both teams screaming between timeouts to generate energy. “I think these girls know what they are capable of. They know they can play and this was a game we really wanted to prove that,” Chan said. Wednesday’s game was a big response to last year’s 15-3 loss to Acalanes. “I’m really proud of all of us. Last year, we lost to this team 15-3. We know we’re much stronger this year, I feel we got goals right off of the bat and that made us a lot more confident,” said senior Ruby Guzdar. 10-9 loss to Acalanes Piedmont led 2-1 by the end of the first quarter but fell behind 4-3 by halftime. Acalanes maintained a one-goal, 6-5 lead through the third quarter, while the two sides finished regulation time in a 9-9 deadlock. Acalanes scored the game-winning Sudden Death goal nearly midway into the 3-minute overtime period. PHs went up 2-0 in the first with goals by Guzdar from a shot atop the circle at 10:40, while Friedie Schickendanz assisted Chloe Graham on a goal at 9:29. Acalanes got one back about three minutes later. In the second, Guzdar put Piedmont ahead 3-1 with 9:45 to play, but Acalanes went on a three-goal scoring run to end the first half up 4-3. In the third, Hallie Burden scored after a minute, 45 seconds to tie the match at 4-4, but Acalanes scored a pair of goals to lead 6-4 with 5:34 left in the quarter. But Schickendanz assisted Peyton Watson for a goal with just 3.3 seconds left to end the third down 6-5. Watson scored again to knot things up at 6-6 at the 10:18 mark, Friedie Schickendanz had two goals against Acalanes. Peyton Watson also scored twice against the Dons.

articles.text: Piedmont proved it is mighty team despite being undersized. In a stunning display of skill and determination, the Piedmont High School Swim Team emerged triumphant in their season opener against Castro Valley on Friday, March 8 at the Trojans’ home pool. Under the guidance of coach Colby Price, Piedmont’s 31 swimmers took on 91 swimmers from Castro Valley. “The meet was really exciting. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s production of The 39 Steps, made famous by the film by Alfred Hitchcock, is now on stage with performances through April 20. Based on Hitchcock’s 1935 British spy thriller film and adapted for the stage by Patrick Barlow, the play features a high-speed chase from a London music hall to Scotland’s highlands following a mysterious murder. Protagonist Richard Hanney aims to reveal the secrets of The 39 Steps, an international spy ring, while dodging devious spies and wooing beautiful bombshells. Performed by four actors who play more than 100 characters, the spoof is equal parts comedy and film noir thriller. The 39 Steps is directed by Susi Damilano with a cast that includes Greg Ayers, Maggie Mason, Renee Rogoff and Phil Wong. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/2023-2024-season/the-39- steps/. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Balanchine’s choreographic take on the classic tale by William Shakespeare, is being performed now through March 23. The San Francisco Ballet premiere of Midsummer occurred nearly 40 years ago, on March 12, 1985. The classic Shakespearian tale is a story of complicated love, where the famous playwright explores how people tend to fall in love with those who appear beautiful to them. In Balanchine’s ballet version, Titania and Oberon, queen and king of the fairies, celebrate their control over the mismatched human lovers in ecstatic dance. Fairy Puck spreads magic and mischief, encountering four Athenians who run away to the forest. The mischievous Puck casts a spell causing two men to fall in love with the same girl. The ballet concludes with an extended, lavish wedding dance featuring a large cast amid opulent sets. The upcoming performance includes updated costume and set designs by celebrated French designer Christian Lacroix. A conversation between San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo and author Jennifer Homans about the book Mr. B: George Balanchine’s 20th Century will be video recorded and available on www.sfballet. org throughout the run of performances. On Saturday, March 23 the Ballet will present “A Midsummer Night’s Dream Tea” in the Green Room of the Veterans Building at War Memorial Opera House. Guests are invited to partake in family-friendly activities, enjoy savory and sweet treats, and view a matinee performance of the ballet. Visit www.sfballet.org to purchase tickets. San Francisco Ballet dancers in A Midsummer Night’s Dream Photo by Chris Hardy
articles.title: SF Ballet now performing A Midsummer Night’s Dream

articles.text: Oakland Ballet will present its third annual Dancing Moons Festival March 14 through April 6 at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland and ODC Theater in San Francisco. The program is choreographed by all-Asian American Pacific Islander talent and will include a preview of the dance company’s Angel Island Project with choreography by Natasha Adorlee and Feng Ye. The project took inspiration from poetry carved by detainees held at the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station held thousands of immigrants through 1910 and 1940, mainly from China, Japan, India and the Philippines. “With captured imaginations, we take on a flight of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese Photo by John Hefti, courtesy of the Oakland Ballet Lawrence Chen (left) and Karina Eimon in Ballet des Porcelaines American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved in the walls by detainees,” Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig said. “The Angel Island Project helps us to trace who we are today by remembering from where we came.” Several selections will also be presented at the festival as works in progress, including Layer Upon Layer by Caili Quan (2022), Ballet des Porcelaines or The Teapot Prince by Phil Chan (original 1739; reimagined 2021), and highlights of Exquisite Corpse by Elaine Kudo, Seyong Kim, and Phil Chan (2023). For the first time since the festival’s inception, an exhibition of visual artists will be displayed at the cultural center. Artists include Asian Americans Sanjay Vora, Mark Shigenga and JaYing Wang. March 14 through 16 performances will take place at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland, and April 5 and 6 performances take place at the ODC Theatre in San Francisco. Showtimes vary. To purchase tickets, visit https://oaklandballet.org/ dancing-moons-festival/.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet Dancing Moons Festival begins tomorrow

articles.text: The art of Mary Lovelace O’Neal will be exhibited at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. An exhibition featuring new work by UC Berkeley Professor Emeritus of Arts Mary Lovelace O’Neal opens this Saturday. March 16, at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA). O’Neal, whose work spans more than six decades, focuses on abstracted mixed-media and minimalism using black as a backdrop. Her earliest works used “lampblack pigment,” or powdered soot created from burning oil. The strong, dark background provides a foundation for vibrant hues of paint, glitter and other materials she uses over it. “Painting with color was always a surprise. [It was] like dancing with the paint,” she said. O’Neal often explores themes of social justice, social movements, music and literature in her paintings. She was hired at the University of California, Berkeley in 1979, where she became the first African American professor awarded tenure in the Department of Art Practice in 1985, chair of the department in 1999, and professor emerita in 2006. On Thursday, March 21 at 6 p.m, she will discuss her recent paintings in a conversation with Eungie Joo, curator and head of contemporary art at the museum. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/new-work-mary-lovelaceoneal/.
articles.title: Mary Lovelace O’Neal exhibition opens Sat. at SFMOMA

articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade. They highlight the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period was when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of Japan’s feudal military rule. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art, notably printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked both before and after the Meiji era. A museum member preview takes place on Thursday and Friday, April 4-5. A donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at the Legion of Honor through August 18. pages.text: Wednesday, March 13, 2024 17 Mary Lovelace O’Neal exhibition opens Sat. at SFMOMA The art of Mary Lovelace O’Neal will be exhibited at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. By Allyson Aleksey An exhibition featuring new work by UC Berkeley Professor Emeritus of Arts Mary Lovelace O’Neal opens this Saturday. March 16, at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA). O’Neal, whose work spans more than six decades, focuses on abstracted mixed-media and minimalism using black as a backdrop. Her earliest works used “lampblack pigment,” or powdered soot created from burning oil. The strong, dark background provides a foundation for vibrant hues of paint, glitter and other materials she uses over it. “Painting with color was always a surprise. [It was] like dancing with the paint,” she said. O’Neal often explores themes of social justice, social movements, music and literature in her paintings. She was hired at the University of California, Berkeley in 1979, where she became the first African American professor awarded tenure in the Department of Art Practice in 1985, chair of the department in 1999, and professor emerita in 2006. On Thursday, March 21 at 6 p.m, she will discuss her recent paintings in a conversation with Eungie Joo, curator and head of contemporary art at the museum. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/new-work-mary-lovelaceoneal/. Exhibit of Japanese Prints opens in April at Legion of Honor By Allyson Aleksey The Legion of Honor in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade. They highlight the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period was when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of Japan’s feudal military rule. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art, notably printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked both before and after the Meiji era. A museum member preview takes place on Thursday and Friday, April 4-5. A donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at the Legion of Honor through August 18. articles.text: Jorge Lendeborg Jr., Nick Robinson, Alexandra Shipp, and Katherine Langford in Love, Simon Simon Spier (Nick Robinson) is 17-year-old, a senior in high school who has a close circle of friends, loving parents, to include a younger sister. He lives in a home in the affluent burbs, and is living with a secret that has nudged him since he was 13: he is gay. As is made clear in the set up, he is faced with a dilemma, one that causes him daily anguish and uncertainty – how to disclose his truth to his family (Jennifer Garner and Josh Duhamel), his friends, and ultimately all of his high school peers. We learn of his personal struggle as Simon discovers online a fellow traveller who calls himself “Blue.” Simon assumes he is a student at his high school, a kindred spirit who is uncertain about how to reveal his own sexual identity. With Blue, Simon can share the emotional cul-de-sac that he finds himself in – for both Blue and Simon, crossing a line that is fraught with risk. It would mean confronting a cultural taboo. This is precarious territory, most especially for adolescents who are ever vigilant to all the cues that society delineates when it comes to what is “normal” and “acceptable.” Simon realizes that to remain in the closet is to live his life as a lie, pretending to be one person while knowing he is someone else. He wants to push open that door, to step out as himself, yet he feels the terrifying weight that he will be judged and rejected for the person he knows himself to be. It is a weight that can seem unbearable, something he shares with Blue but no one else. And then there is the question of Blue’s identity, as their rapport increases in proportion to their online honesty. The template that the writers use for Simon’s journey is of a high school romance Embedded in the narrative is the fact that heterosexuality is a powerful norm and is what’s expected. In a perfect world, there would be no need to “come out” to parents or peers, no need to face that reveal with heart-stopping trepidation. But, we don’t live in a perfect world. Hence, Simon must constantly remind himself to just breathe as he carries his secret forward, day after day, one that torments him. Love, Simon is tenderly done and it offers Simon a most gentle way to solve and then resolve his inner struggle. His parents and his close circle of friends are remarkably decent, kind and caring. His peers astonishingly are nonplussed. Love, Simon could have been a much harsher film regarding the reactions of those he deeply cares about, as well as the kids in the hall. And the outcome of his reveal might have gone in a far more painful direction. There is a moment in the film that shows overt bullying and profound insensitivity in the high school cafeteria, however it is quickly quashed by a rescuing teacher. Adolescence can be a precarious, cruel place, often rigidly judgmental and at times deeply hurtful. Love, Simon is a wonderful film, nicely told, with a fine ensemble, led by Nick Robinson. It’s no small thing to find actors who can sustain a youthful naturalness while delivering superb portrayals, each scene ripe with verisimilitude. For many reasons, this is a film worth finding, if only to encourage Hollywood to explore further this very human landscape. Love, Simon. Directed by Greg Berlanti. Starring Nick Robinson, Josh Duhamel, Jennifer Garner. 1 hr. 49 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2018. Streaming on VUDU/prime/apple tv.

articles.text: No matter what the critics may say, Nicholas Sparks is a master at what he does, though there are those who will argue that he’s a shameless manipulator of the easily accessible emotions of tweenteen girls who embrace his movies and may even read his novels. Or not. Hard to dispute that Sparks has nailed this adolescent demographic by developing a winning formula that he can superimpose on just about any love story. Recall the Dear John movie; same difference. Granted, sometimes his characters grow up, meaning they’ve grown taller. Examples would be The Notebook, Message in a Bottle and Night in Rodanthe. So, judging The Last Song from the point of view of 16-year-old girls it’s impossible to say anything other than they will love this movie and will sniffle and sigh and feel their eyes welling with tears as Sparks and director Julie Ann Robinson take them through the formulaic, rollercoaster paces. In a nutshell: Ronnie Miller (Miley Cyrus) and her brother Jonah (Bobby Coleman) are driven by their mom, Kim (Kelly Preston), to spend the summer with their dad, Steve, who lives in a spacious and chic-worn beach house on Tybee Island, off the coast of Georgia. Mom and dad are divorced. Ronnie, feeling hurt and abandoned by her dad, is perpetually angry and hostile and not happy to be spending a weekend let alone a summer on the island. These are emotions that she shares at every opportunity. She pouts and snarls and stalks off in all directions. Until she meets Will (Liam Hensworth), an island resident, beach volleyball player, summer mechanic, who, like Ronnie, has just graduated from high school and is waiting to go to Vanderbilt University in the fall. Ronnie, a piano prodigy, has been accepted to Julliard for a full ride but refuses to go and, for good measure, refuses to play. She’s too angry and believes she will hurt her father, a composer, by walking away from her scholarship and her talent. Sparks is a master of girl meets boy girl on the beach, followed by boy pursues girl hoping to ignite a nascent spark. In this case, Ronnie practices complete indifference to Will’s attention (you can almost hear that quintessentially terrible teen word, “whatever,” trailing Ronnie from house to beach and back), while keeping her nose buried in Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina. When Ronnie discovers endangered sea turtle eggs in front of the beach house, she sets about trying to protect them from raccoons. Will, volunteering for a marine sanctuary, shows up to stand vigil with her. Romance takes hold and angry, indifferent Ronnie gets less angry and way less indifferent with everyone, her dad included. And so Sparks sets the hook, and, just to be sure, includes engaging montages of Will and Ronnie swimming, playing tag, getting in a mud fight, talking intensely, meeting his parents (he’s hugely wealthy) and, indeed, kissing. Lots of kissing. All chaste and lovely and very emotive. Of course, Sparks loves to pump up the volume regarding unfinished issues, pre-fab subplots and misunderstandings, willing to throw in, predictably, a terminal illness or an unsettling speed bump just to keep things interesting. And just when you thought it was safe to put away the tissue. Now remember who’s sitting in the audience, all those teen girls identifying with Ronnie and loving every moment. By that measure, The Last Song succeeds and then some, making Nicholas Sparks happy and rich and very good at what he does: gently and not so gently squeezing the hearts of tween-teen girls who love every minute. One last thing: The Last Song is a transition film for Miley who has paid her dues as Hannah Montana, a long-running tween-teen television show of the same name, one that became a cultural event for young girls. She’s been a phenom who has grown up on television. She can sing. But can she act and so carry a feature film? Perhaps a better question is: Is she credible to young people in the role of a girl with issues who finds herself on the cusp of becoming a woman? Answer: indeed. The Last Song. Directed by Julie Ann Robinson. Starring Miley Cyrus, Liam Hensworth, Greg Kinnear, Bobby Coleman and Kelly Preston. Released in 2010. Rated PG. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Disney+/Apple tv. articles.text: Jude Law as Watson and Robert Downey Jr. as Holmes in Sherlock Holmes Recall the image of Sherlock Holmes, made famous by Basil Rathbone who starred in some 14 movies featuring the English detective, always accompanied by Dr. John Watson, portrayed by Nigel Bruce. Rathbone was long-faced, inscrutable, an ever-present Mahogany Calabash pipe with a meerschaum bowl, and, of course, his signature deerstalker cap, a checked twill, double-brimmed lid that was soon identified as a detective’s hat. The first films, shot from 1939 to 1946, were inspired by the works of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle who preceded English mystery writers such as Agatha Christie, P.D. James and Ngalo Marsh, who created a panoply of studied whodunits involving the butler in the library with the candlestick, so to speak. Rathbone’s Holmes – always careful and deliberative, never given to emotional outbursts or physical confrontations – has likely shaped the expectations of many moviegoers who turned out to see the more contemporaneous Sherlock Holmes. Audiences are now in for a treat. The newly reconstructed Holmes is no longer a detective of the ilk of Agatha Christie’s Miss Marple or Hercule Poirot. Robert Downey’s Holmes is a rogue, dissolute, a master of martial arts, athletic and courageous, given to dark rooms, extreme experiments, harrowing tight spots, a 30th Anniversary Edition Publication Celebration An evening of inspiration and activation! articles.text: Performance at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall Internationally renowned pianist Mitsuko Uchida, a UC Berkeley Artist in Residence, will lead the Mahler Chamber Orchestra on Sunday afternoon, March 24 at 3 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall in a program presented by Cal Performances. Uchida and the Orchestra return to Zellerbach Hall following their March 2022 performance. The program features the latest installment in their continuing series of Mozart’s piano concertos, as well as the U.S premiere of a chamber orchestra arrangement of Jorg Widmann’s String Quartet No. 2. “What an extraordinary honor it is to have Mitsuko Uchida as our Artist in Residence,” said Cal Performances Executive and Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen. “Those who were in the audience for her recital back in 2014, as well as her performance with the Mahler Chamber Orchesa peerless interpreter of classic composers including Mozart, Beethoven, Schuber t and Schumann, and was awarded Artist of the Year in 2022 by Musical America. She has led the world’s finest orchestras over her decades-long career, including the Cleveland Orchestra, English Chamber Orchestra and Berlin Philharmonic. “Uchida has been on a lifelong search for truth and beauty – one that has enriched audiences around the world,” said Geffen. “This cherished artist’s extensive experience and abundant artistic vision will undoubtedly catalyze moments of profound learning, understanding, and enjoyment on our campus and throughout our community.” Tickets are available at www. calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall Tuesday through Friday, 12 to 5:30 p.m. and Saturday through Sunday, 1 to 5 p.m. Photo by Aram Boghosian Pianist Mitsuko Uchida tra in 2022, will be thrilled at this return, as will those of our patrons who have yet to experience her artistry.” Uchida, a Japanese native, is half. This was a program which showed just about every aspect of cello playing and musicianship. The wonder of it all was that she made everything look so easy. There are some who don’t like to hear kids perform. I am not one of them. Sometimes an opulent vocabulary is insufficient to describe a bounty of glories. I was very lucky to have known some of the greatest cellists of the 20th century. Young Miss Lam at 15 years of age seems destined to continue that lineage. She has a honeyed, singing tone which she combines with fluid motions, and an ease of tone production. Every note is vibrated – even the little notes. Nuance is ever- present. Her musicianship is always intelligent and completely put at the service of the music that she is playing. If I have left anything out, please fill in the blanks. For the pieces that had piano accompaniment, the well-known accompanist, Miles Graber, supported her with sensitivity. If I had to single out one piece to serve as an example, it would be three movements by the Italian baroque composer Pietro Locatelli. Every aspect of cello art was demonstrated here. There were numerous examples of what we refer to as “flying staccato” and they were absolutely spectacular. I didn’t know whether to close my eyes or watch the virtuosity. I was reminded of one of my coaches from my student days, the great Russian cellist. Gregor Piatigorsky. Bu, that is only part of the story. Melissa Lam was joined by three young colleagues to perform a movement of Beethoven’s 14th String Quartet. Violinists Anthony Chukhlov and Amanda Lam plus violist Samuel Seetapun were the other members of the quartet. Is it possible to play the quartet any better? I don’t think so. Whether you listen with your eyes open or closed, you should catch these kids the next time they play. You’re in for a treat.

articles.text: Melissa Lam’s concert Sunday afternoon in the Piedmont Center for the Arts could be summed up with one word: “Bravo!” But that doesn’t even begin to tell the whole story. Her program was a lesson in how to play the cello, and the program itself was a monumental one. There were concert pieces by Bach, Locatelli and Schumann in the first half and then a movement of one of Beethoven’s late string quartets, and cello concertos by Haydn and Dvorak in the second Young cellist Melissa Lam performed a spectacular concert accompanied by pianist Miles Graber on Sunday, March 10, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.

articles.text: Celebrating its second year, Piedmont’s Second Thursday Flix Fest will show the 1998 American comic mystery, Zero Effect, this Thursday, March 14. Written and directed by Jake Kasdan in his feature directional debut, it stars Bill Pullman as Daryl Zero, “the world’s most private detective”, and Ben Stiller as his assistant, Steve Arlo The far-out adventure is loosely based on Arthur Conan Doyle’s short story, A Scandal in Bohemia. Daryl Zero may be the world’s greatest detective, but he’s also a socially maladroit misanthrope. Among his quirks is that he never meets or has direct contact with his clients, instead conducting business through his assistant, Steve Arlo. As the movie begins, Zero and Arlo are hired by a Portland area millionaire, who has lost the key to a safe deposit box and is also being harassed by a blackmailer who forces him to follow elaborate instructions to deliver cash payments. The mystery takes off from there, enlivened by the presence of actors Kim Dickens, Angela Featherstone and Ryan O’Neal. Attendees are encouraged to hang out after the film to discuss what they’ve seen. The Film Fest takes place in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m. with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Register with the Rec. Department at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Guests are invited to bring snacks or lunch. The Flix Fest’s next movie will be the James Bond film, From Russia with Love, starring Sean Connery on April 11th.
articles.title: Piedmont Flix Fest to screen comedy-mystery tomorrow

articles.text: Piedmont resident Bill Wong, a consummate journalist in the Bay Area throughout the second half of the 20th Century, and a frequent guest on PBS on the MacNeil-Lehrer News Hour has announced the release of his second book “Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America.” The book launch will be on Sunday, March 24 from 1:00- 2:00 p.m. at the Oakland Asian Cultural Center, 388 Ninth Street, Oakland. The gathering will feature a reading, an engaging discussion with Harvey Dong from Eastwind Books, and a signing ceremony. The event will offer an intimate glimpse into the lives shaped by the Chinese Exclusion Act in the United States. Visit Oacc.cc/event/sonsofchinatown to rsvp for the free event. Wong’s book deals with issues of belonging, and assimilation as it directly affected Wong and his father, affectionately known as Pop. As Pop grappled with the systemic racism towards Asians, Wong wistfully describes his father’s efforts to establish a family business and build a life for them in segregated Oakland. Writing for the Wall Street Journal, Oakland Tribune, and Asian American periodicals, Wong chronicled Asian American experiences while honoring Chinese American history and identity, but he too faced discrimination. Sons of Chinatown poignantly weaves these father and son stories together with admiration and righteous anger. Through the mirrored lens of his father, Wong reflects on the hardships Asian Americans endured – and continue to face. Kirkus Reviews described Wong’s book as an “ultimately uplifting narrative,” one in which Wong “displays a deeper understanding of his sometimes obdurate, yet determined, perseverant parents.” “As William ‘Bill’ Gee Wong shares ‘Sons of Chinatown’ with the world, readers and attendees alike are afforded a rare opportunity to journey through the complexities of living between two cultures,” said the Breaking News Network (BNN). Bill Wong will release his much anticipated book on March 24, which he has been working on for the last 13 years.
articles.title: Journalist Bill Wong celebrates release of new book “Sons of Chinatown” on March 24

articles.text: If you have student loans, you likely received a “payment vacation” over the past few years, due to legislation related to COVID-19. But if you’re like millions of other borrowers, you may have recently been required to resume your payments. How will this affect your overall financial situation? Of course, the first thing that comes to mind is the effect on your monthly cash flow. But the amount of pressure you feel will depend on your income and the size of the required payments. If these payments do represent a real challenge, you may need to adjust your budget and spending habits as best you can. However, there might be other steps you can take to help ease the burden or possibly reduce the repayment time. Here are a few suggestions to consider: • Sign up for autopay Falling behind on your student loan payments can lead to late fees, and if you were to become truly delinquent, you could face even bigger troubles, such as wage garnishment. To avoid these problems, you can enroll in autopay, in which you move money automatically from a checking or savings account to your student loan provider. In addition to staying current on your loan, you might earn a .25 percent rate reduction, which is offered by many lenders and loan services to those who enroll in autopay. • Refinance your loan With a steady income, a reasonably good credit score and a manageable number of other debts, you might be able to refinance your student loan and reduce your interest rate, which will enable more of your monthly payments to go toward the principal. • Look for employer benefits Some employers – typically the larger ones – offer student loan repayment help to employees, so check with your human resources department. • Make extra payment If you feel strapped just making your regular student loan payments, you may not be able to make extra ones. But if you can afford to add to your payments consistently, you could pay off your loan earlier than you had thought. But just because you make an extra payment, the money doesn’t necessarily go toward reducing your principal – student loan services generally apply payments first to late fees and then to accrued interest. If you pay online, you should have an option to apply extra payments to the principal. Your loan servicer could also provide you with other ways of paying more toward principal. • Choose a payoff strategy If you have multiple student loans, and you can make more than the minimum payments, you may want to be strategic in how you pay off your loans. You could choose the “snowball” method by getting rid of the smallest loans first, a technique that can give you feelings of momentum and satisfaction. Or you could take the “avalanche” approach by first going after the loans with the highest interest rates. Either route could save you more money in the long run. It can certainly be challenging to deal with student loan debt. But with patience and diligence, and by exploring all your repayment options, you may be able to help yourself make progress toward putting these loans to rest. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a financial advisor in the Piedmont office at 370 Highland Avenue in Piedmont Tel 547-4589.
articles.title: How can you manage student loan payments?

articles.text: 36 walkers were on hand last week for the Walking on Wednesdays stroll about town. Those participating included Martin Levy, Matt Gerhardt, Priscilla Wanerus, Brenda Ferrero, Kat Lang, Mark Davis, Irene Thompson, Sharona Fischrup, Jack Fischrup, Mari Negron, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Ken Moy, Nadine Guffanti, Edith Lee, Noemi Alvarado, Sarah Johnson, Bill Ahern, Alissa Quan, Dana Shultz, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Marianne Jakus, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Peggy Shultz, Phil Witte, Jim Kuo, Will Adams, Lisa Euphrat, Rick Eigenbrode, Rob Smith, Pat Keller, Jim Kellogg, Sherry Jacobs, Chuck Oraftik, and Dick Carter. There was a large turnout of 36 walkers and two K-9 best friends last Wednesday at the Exedra for the Walking on Wednesday weekly stroll. The walkers admitted they find the local real estate market pretty interesting and it was going to be the morning’s subject. The unofficial start of the home buying season was the Presidents Day holiday weekend. A lack of homes for sale is a common factor throughout most markets, and that’s true in Piedmont. Zillow had only five Piedmont homes listed for sale. The prices ranged from $925K to $14,500K. The group could see three of the listed homes, along with five sold recently by going to the south side of the city. To add to the fun, the walkers were given $14,500K in “Piedmont Real Estate Fantasy Dollars” to make imaginary offers. The group started off for Wildwood Avenue. The parade of walkers stopped traffic when they crossed Highland Avenue to go up to 49 Sierra Avenue. It’s a 1914 Julia Morgan-designed three bedroom/three bath, 3,223 square foot home that sold last July for $3.2 million. Next, it was down to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. On the corner is a four bedroom/four bath, 4,792 square foot Monterey Colonial that sold in February for $4.5 million. It’s on a lot surrounded by terrific gardens that the walkers have enjoyed many times. The group went 500 Wildwood at the corner with Crocker. The For Sale sign had just gone up this week. This six bedroom/3.5 bath, 3,367 square foot home was built in 1920. It’s a beautiful Craftsman home with over 1/3 of an acre of gardens and a pool, and is listed at $3,095K. Architect and regular weekly walker Jim Kellogg said it was designed by John Hudson Thomas who was a contemporary and competitor of Julia Morgan. The walkers continued on Crocker to Lafayette Avenue and Muir Avenue for three more homes. The first is 7 Muir. According to Zillow you can “experience timeless elegance in this stately Georgian masterpiece. Designed by Albert Farr in 1930 it is beautifully sited on over 1/3 of an acre and offers breathtaking San Francisco Bay views.” It’s got six bedrooms and eight baths in 6,423 square feet. It was the most expensive home of the walk at $6,495K. Down the street is a classic 5 bedroom/5 bath home of 3,940 square feet built in 1925 that sold in February last year for $4,925K, $60K less than the asking price. At the end of the block was a five bedroom/3.5 bath home built in 1932 at 35 Muir. It was listed for $4,595K, but there was a Sale Pending sign on it. The group turned up LaSalle Avenue to make its return to the Exedra, but there was one last home at 345 LaSalle to see. It’s 3,619 square feet with four bedrooms and six baths and was built in 1979. It was bought in February 2023 for $2,500K and had been listed for $3,995, but sold this week for $4,150K, The walkers had enjoyed the tour to these beautiful homes, but it was time to get back to the Exedra. They decided next week they would check out the three other homes for sale on the north side of town. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 13, 2024 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers do the real estate tour 36 walkers were on hand last week for the Walking on Wednesdays stroll about town. Those participating included Martin Levy, Matt Gerhardt, Priscilla Wanerus, Brenda Ferrero, Kat Lang, Mark Davis, Irene Thompson, Sharona Fischrup, Jack Fischrup, Mari Negron, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Ken Moy, Nadine Guffanti, Edith Lee, Noemi Alvarado, Sarah Johnson, Bill Ahern, Alissa Quan, Dana Shultz, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Marianne Jakus, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Peggy Shultz, Phil Witte, Jim Kuo, Will Adams, Lisa Euphrat, Rick Eigenbrode, Rob Smith, Pat Keller, Jim Kellogg, Sherry Jacobs, Chuck Oraftik, and Dick Carter. By Dick Carter There was a large turnout of 36 walkers and two K-9 best friends last Wednesday at the Exedra for the Walking on Wednesday weekly stroll. The walkers admitted they find the local real estate market pretty interesting and it was going to be the morning’s subject. The unofficial start of the home buying season was the Presidents Day holiday weekend. A lack of homes for sale is a common factor throughout most markets, and that’s true in Piedmont. Zillow had only five Piedmont homes listed for sale. The prices ranged from $925K to $14,500K. The group could see three of the listed homes, along with five sold recently by going to the south side of the city. To add to the fun, the walkers were given $14,500K in “Piedmont Real Estate Fantasy Dollars” to make imaginary offers. The group started off for Wildwood Avenue. The parade of walkers stopped traffic when they crossed Highland Avenue to go up to 49 Sierra Avenue. It’s a 1914 Julia Morgan-designed three bedroom/three bath, 3,223 square foot home that sold last July for $3.2 million. Next, it was down to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. On the corner is a four bedroom/four bath, 4,792 square foot Monterey Colonial that sold in February for $4.5 million. It’s on a lot surrounded by terrific gardens that the walkers have enjoyed many times. The group went 500 Wildwood at the corner with Crocker. The For Sale sign had just gone up this week. This six bedroom/3.5 bath, 3,367 square foot home was built in 1920. It’s a beautiful Craftsman home with over 1/3 of an acre of gardens and a pool, and is listed at $3,095K. Architect and regular weekly walker Jim Kellogg said it was designed by John Hudson Thomas who was a contemporary and competitor of Julia Morgan. The walkers continued on Crocker to Lafayette Avenue and Muir Avenue for three more homes. The first is 7 Muir. According to Zillow you can “experience timeless elegance in this stately Georgian masterpiece. Designed by Albert Farr in 1930 it is beautifully sited on over 1/3 of an acre and offers breathtaking San Francisco Bay views.” It’s got six bedrooms and eight baths in 6,423 square feet. It was the most expensive home of the walk at $6,495K. Down the street is a classic 5 bedroom/5 bath home of 3,940 square feet built in 1925 that sold in February last year for $4,925K, $60K less than the asking price. At the end of the block was a five bedroom/3.5 bath home built in 1932 at 35 Muir. It was listed for $4,595K, but there was a Sale Pending sign on it. The group turned up LaSalle Avenue to make its return to the Exedra, but there was one last home at 345 LaSalle to see. It’s 3,619 square feet with four bedrooms and six baths and was built in 1979. It was bought in February 2023 for $2,500K and had been listed for $3,995, but sold this week for $4,150K, The walkers had enjoyed the tour to these beautiful homes, but it was time to get back to the Exedra. They decided next week they would check out the three other homes for sale on the north side of town. If you have student loans, you likely received a “payment vacation” over the past few years, due to legislation related to COVID-19. But if you’re like millions of other borrowers, you may have recently been required to resume your payments. How will this affect your overall financial situation? Of course, the first thing that comes to mind is the effect on your monthly cash flow. But the amount of pressure you feel will depend on your income and the size of the required payments. If these payments do represent a real challenge, you may need to adjust your budget and spending habits as best you can. However, there might be other steps you can take to help ease the burden or possibly reduce the repayment time. Here are a few suggestions to consider: • Sign up for autopay Falling behind on your student loan payments can lead to late fees, and if you were to become truly delinquent, you could face even bigger troubles, such as wage garnishment. To avoid these problems, you can enroll in autopay, in which you move money automatically from a checking or savings account to your student loan provider. In addition to staying current on your loan, you might earn a .25 percent rate reduction, which is offered by many lenders and loan services to those who enroll in autopay. • Refinance your loan With a steady income, a reasonably good credit score and a manageable number of other debts, you might be able to refinance your student loan and reduce your interest rate, which will enable more of your monthly payments to go toward the principal. • Look for employer benefits Some employers – typically the larger ones – offer student loan repayment help to employees, so check with your human resources department. • Make extra payment If you feel strapped just making your regular student loan payments, you may not be able to make extra ones. But if you can afford to add to your payments consistently, you could pay off your loan earlier than you had thought. But just because you make an extra payment, the money doesn’t necessarily go toward reducing your principal – student loan services generally apply payments first to late fees and then to accrued interest. If you pay online, you should have an option to apply extra payments to the principal. Your loan servicer could also provide you with other ways of paying more toward principal. • Choose a payoff strategy If you have multiple student loans, and you can make more than the minimum payments, you may want to be strategic in how you pay off your loans. You could choose the “snowball” method by getting rid of the smallest loans first, a technique that can give you feelings of momentum and satisfaction. Or you could take the “avalanche” approach by first going after the loans with the highest interest rates. Either route could save you more money in the long run. It can certainly be challenging to deal with student loan debt. But with patience and diligence, and by exploring all your repayment options, you may be able to help yourself make progress toward putting these loans to rest. articles.text: Change is all around us and Azucena Rasilla is there to chronicle it. Azucena Rasilla, a bilingual journalist from East Oakland who has reported on the rich cultural heritage and artistic landscape that surrounds us, will speak at the Pardee Home Museum on Sunday, March 17 at 4:00 p.m. The cost is $30 per person. Her work has appeared in the SF Chronicle, KQED, Eater, Curbed and the East Bay Express where she started her career. She is currently the arts & community reporter for Oaklandside (https://oaklandside. org/author/azucena-rasilla/). She serves as the host of Culture Makers (https://oaklandside.org/ culture-makers/), a live quarterly event focusing on creative people and artists in Oakland. It provides her with a platform to reflect on how reporting, entertainment and food service have changed since the pandemic four years ago. Her recent piece on movie theaters encapsulates some of these changes. Azucena will share her recommendations of amazing places to eat and listen to music, and about all the things that make Oakland exceptional, including the renown Pardee Home Museum. A champagne reception will follow the lecture with sweets and savories and a nod to the wearing of the green on St. Patrick’s Day. Visit Eventbrite to reserve your place or call Richelle Lieberman at 510-381-1973. Pardee Home Museum is located at 672 11th Street in Oakland. Enter through the white gate on Castro Street. articles.text: My wife comes from a family of smugglers. They smuggled gold into India and roses out of India. Nobody will exactly admit to it, but there have been whispers. The family passed through the Mumbai Airport decades ago. Something was discovered. An uncle paid a bribe. It is rude in India to count money in front of somebody; it took a minute for the customs agent to realize the bribe was too small. “Run!” the uncle said. They slipped away before the agent could catch them. My father-in-law, a botanist who emigrated to the United States in the 1970s, couldn’t bear to leave his roses behind. No other flower, except perhaps the lotus, has a deeper association with Indian identity. In Hindu mythology there was a discussion between Brahma, the creator, and Vishnu, the A kombucha made in India with sun-dried Damask rose petals protector, about which flower was more beautiful. After seeing an arbor laden with fragrant roses in Vishnu’s celestial garden, Brahma acknowledged the supremacy of the rose. Roses can be transported and planted with bare roots. It’s still not too late to get them in the ground this season, but, ideally, you would want to do it between January and February so they have more time to establish themselves before they bloom. If you’re planting a bare-root rose, first let it hydrate in a bucket of water for 24 to 48 hours. Dig a two-by-two-foot hole and mix in some manure or mushroom compost. Create a cone of soil below the plant so that the roots can fan out. Bury it up to the bud union— the place where the green stalks come out of the brown understalk. Don’t pack the soil too tightly and do give it a good watering and a top layer of mulch. If you already have roses, March is a good time to fertilize them. Once new growth is two to four inches long, apply a slow-release fertilizer and water well. Make sure you follow the instructions on the package as too much fertilizer can burn the roses and leach into groundwater. My father-in-law grew Damask roses, a variety that gets its name from Damascus, Syria. The Damask is believed to have been brought to India via Persia long ago by the ethnic group now known as Gujaratis. It’s famous not only for its pretty pink blooms but also for its amazing aroma and taste. The Damask rose has a wide range of culinary uses. My Gujarati mother-in-law uses sun-dried Damask rose petals to make a jam known as gulkand – a word derived from the Persian gul (rose) and quand (sweet). The Damask also goes into rose water and rose powder for use in many Indian and Middle Eastern dishes. At home, I’ve infused dried Damask rose petals in kombucha with great results. Damask roses have a long history in Europe and the United States. They were documented in England by 1540, and in 1791 Thomas Jefferson was growing a variety of Damask roses at his garden in Monticello. Locally, you’ll find them thriving in the Morcom Rose Garden on the Piedmont-Oakland border one block from Grand Avenue. Given the wide availability of Damask roses, you might wonder why my father-in-law bothered to put his on an airplane. I don’t fully understand the world of botanists, but I suspect from all the cuttings once growing in plastic buckets in his backyard that he was working on perfecting their taste and aroma. You can legally import bareroot Damask roses straight from India. All you need is a government-issued phytosanitary certificate. On second thought, however, maybe just go to Berkeley Hort. articles.text: The Leap Year kid celebrates another milestone by close friends, co-workers, and various alumni from the past 26 years of publishing the Piedmont Post. Drinks were served as well as various hors d’oeuvres before guests were seated for dinner. “Many, many thanks to Alan Carlson Parsons and the staff at Italian Colors for allowing a bunch of renegades to come in for a little while,” said Cathrall to the crowd of guests during dinner. “We’ll have a live mic throughout the evening, so I’ll let you all start eating. And then, the insults can begin,” he joked. Many were aware that his preference for such banquets was for it to become a roast rather than an evening filled with gushing sentiment. Friends old and new Wes and Jill with Gray stepped up to the microphone to tell stories of how they met Cathrall and his influence on their lives. “I’m blowing off one of my biggest fundraisers of the year to be here,” said Todd Kerr, publisher of the Berkeley Times, and a protegee of Cathrall as well as a former Piedmont Post staffer. With Cathrall’s encouragement, Kerr founded the Berkeley Times and modeled it in part after the Post. “I have immense respect for this guy. I mean, I do half the number of pages he does every week,” said Kerr, who grew up in Piedmont. Brian Kelly, the Editorial Cartoonist for the Post now living near Boston, flew in for the event. He recounted meeting Cathrall in the copy room of the San Leandro Times in 1998 when they both worked there. “I didn’t even really know him, but then he came up to me [in the copy room] and said ‘I’m founding my own paper, and I want you to do cartoons for it.’” Nearly 26 years later, Kelly still does cartoons for the Piedmont Post, despite living several states away. The last speaker of the night was reporter Matt Simons, who ended with an impromptu toast. “Let’s all raise a glass to Gray,” he said. “The guy who made all our lives just a little bit better by being in it.” Applause followed, accompanied by the raising of glasses to the Post’s editor and publisher. Mary Geong, a longtime friend, even found time to pull Cathrall aside and ask: “Do you know what it means to be 88? In my culture eight is a number that brings luck, and 88 makes you double lucky,” she said. Vosges is a significant factor in the Marais’ survival: its predecessor. Place Royale, built in 1612, was the first of the Royal parks of Paris. Its centuries of stability have attracted consistently high rents. The park is an historical anchor for this Marais neighborhood. Vosges was the earliest Parisian park-square, and it benefitted from city-planning, not helter-skelter. Fame, popularity, and beauty combine, and it drew imitation in other European cities. Its symmetry is pleasing – a perfect square framed on four sides with identical building facades, shops on the ground level, and classically styled stone archways inset with red brick. Historically, the Vosges tract of land was always owned by French kings dating back to the 14th century. Hôtel des Tournelles was a warren of buildings occupying the land tract and controlled by French kings, partly a royal business investment but seldom used as a royal residence. In 1559, Henry II died at Tournelles after being fatally injured in a joust. His widow Catherine de Médici took control and fled the derelict estate, moving to the Louvre, where she began constructing her new palace, the Tuileries in the Italianate style that the princess had grown up with. Following her death, the Grande Galerie was completed connecting the Tuileries to the Louvre that was in medieval condition. Though the Louvre existed in 1190 as a fortress, it was French King Louis XIV reigning for 72 years who envisioned the palace’s grandeur in the 17th century. Victor Hugo Museum at Vosges Writer and dramatist Victor Hugo published The Hunchback of Notre Dame in 1831 to immediate rave reviews, and he promptly moved to Nº 6 Place des Vosges in 1832. In his youth, Hugo was a conservative royalNapoleon was First Consul in charge of the revolutionary government when a naming contest was devised to propel the departments (akin to counties) to hastily collect taxes as troops were in the heat of battling the crown. The winner was the Department of Vosges of northeastern France’s Alsace region at the German border, and Place Royale was officially declared Place des Vosges in 1800. Hôtel Salé was built in 1659 and fully renovated in the 1970s when it was selected as the site for the museum. Picasso’s heirs generously endowed the city of Paris with the artist’s vast art portfolio in lieu of tax payments, not an infrequent occurrence with significant inheritance. Many Paris museums offer free admission on the first Sunday of the month. Due to Covid-19 museum openings are not yet permitted. Looking through the glass Browsing at Vosges through the art gallery is a treat. I confess that I find the gallery art so much more amusing than a visit to the Pompidou Center, though certain special exhibitions get high marks. A perfect sunny day relaxation is a stroll beneath the Vosges arches with gallery interludes, and then a café beverage or the Amaretto’s gelato around the corner. I’ve stopped in my tracks many a time to gawk through the gallery windows. Though typically an agent is occupied working the phones to rev up client demand, one should not hesitate in life’s enjoyment to marvel at artistic creations – and walk through the door. Represented artists are often at the top of their craft. The gallery agents are well-imbued in the art; they speak fluent English: and one’s curiosity gets satisfied, despite how impractical a purchase might be. Days of Our Lives There’s nothing like a pandemic to keep outings to a minimum. Paris is still in crisis due to new Covid-19 cases. One undeniably key factor is Intensive Care Units’ capacity; and over the weekend these are filling up so rapidly that specialized medical planes dispatched Covid and other patients from Paris hospitals to less-saturated regions. Paris has had a strict curfew from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. every day, along with restaurant closures in effect for three and a half months. But the strategy is having too little effect, and a third lockdown is under threat for the Ile-deFrance region that includes the capital city Paris. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest is shaping up to be a most memorable experience. The day-long event comes to town on Saturday, April 20th from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. in Piedmont Park. This year, the planning team focused on creating even more novel moments during this third incarnation of the annual multicultural festival that showcases the wide array of culinary and cultural talent resident in the Bay Area. With the event taking now taking place on a Saturday, the team hopes Food Festers will come early and stay late to take full advantage of the event. The team recently announced via its website this year’s lineup of 19 distinctive food trucks & vendors, which will feature fan favorites such as pork belly buns from The Chairman, quesabirrias from La Santa Torta, and burnt brown sugar milk tea from Kiss My Boba as well as treats from newcomers such as Nepalese momos from MOMOlicious, Lahori Charga hot chicken sandwiches from Lahore di khushboo, falafel balls from Sunrise Deli, and almond cookies from Annie’s T Cakes. Additionally, the day’s entertainment lineup will feature Chinese music from the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, a Japanese taiko demonstration from Oakland Taiko, gravity-defying feats from Beloved Little Circus, Tahitian dance from O Hina’aro Nui, a masterclass performance from the Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator Showcase, and a straight-from-Carnaval samba show from Amor do Samba. The event is free to attend and Early Bird discounts on beer and wine tastings as well as KidZone passes are available through March. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org for more information.

No longer is he the bumbling foil; rather, he’s as capable intellectually and physically as Holmes. When together they bicker and disagree and yet have been friends for years. So much does Holmes need Watson’s assistance that he is willing to undermine Watson’s impending marriage. This new Holmes is a surprise and far more interesting than any of Holmes’ antecedents, making this an engaging film. However, at the center of every Holmes narrative is a mystery: the essential whodunit. And here the screenwriters stumble. Rather than writing a tale that will keep the audience guessing, the villain, Lord Blackwood (Mark Strong), is revealed at the outset. It’s never a question of who but how, hence this Holmes becomes a howdunit which is never as compelling. Still, the film is rich with close calls for Holmes and Watson as well as Irene Adler (Rachel McAdams), the one woman in Holmes’ life who continues to interest him with her courage, intelligence and insouciance. Suffice it to say that Holmes, in this incarnation, is a man of action as well as a man of incisive deductive reasoning, making for a solidly entertaining movie. Sherlock Holmes. The board voted in favor of moving forward with a proposed increase to one of the city’s two parcel taxes, Measure H, with a plan of putting the proposal on the ballot in November this year. Measure H is applied to all land parcels in the city but varies by home size. It requires a twothirds approval by voters for any change. The measure can only be presented to voters in a regularly scheduled election. The funds Measure H plans to generate would be earmarked for the next fiscal year. Funds would be made available for the 2025-26 school year. Piedmont has had parcel taxes since 1985. The current Measure H parcel tax was approved by voters in November 2019 for eight years of revenue, from 2020 to 2028. The school board proposes to use Measure H taxes to generate more funds for school salaries in the short term. Current parcel taxes in Piedmont Measure G: Ongoing base parcel tax cost $2,932 per parcel and it generates $11.5 million per year. Measure H: In 2019 Measure H added a $0.25 per square foot and it generates $2.8 million per year specifically to recruit and retain high quality educators. Taxes for a resident with a 2500 square foot house are $625 per year. “This is not something we take lightly as a board,” said board member Cory Smegal. “It’s hard to go out to the community and ask for a tax increase, let’s be honest. We are all going to need to be all in. I appreciate APT and CSEA coming forward and saying ‘we are all in.’” Elise Marks, President of the Teachers Union, offered her support, saying teachers and students would mobilize to campaign for Measure H. “I recognize that this community is already so generous. articles.text: Recent high drama in the Piedmont School District fittingly culminated with a special meeting of the school board in the Drama classroom at Alan Harvey Theater on Monday, March 4. While the number of cuts was dialed back, the school board voted in favor of a host of cuts to save on next year’s budget. Seven full-time and four parttime teaching “certificated” jobs have been approved to be eliminated from next year’s budget totaling 8.7 FTE or Full Time Equivalent. Due to a requirement in the teachers’ contracts with the district, a list of cuts was first presented to the public at the board meeting on February 14. articles.text: Piedmont’s biannual street resurfacing project will include the repair of portions of 17 of the city’s streets, but some residents have expressed concern that the project will not be enough to restore the city’s roads to an acceptable state. The Public Works Department said they plan to begin street resurfacing this summer. “I’ve started noticing that there are more potholes on different streets, and even more common streets like Blair Avenue,” said resident Lilly Guardia-Labar. She wrote a letter to the editor, published in the Piedmont Post on February 28, expressing concern over the poor condition of city streets. She cited potholes as a safety issue. “There are children riding bicycles on these surfaces, people who walk on these surfaces, and who drive on these surfaces. These potholes could puncture our tires,” she said. The Public Works Department said it recognizes the safety concerns. “I think there’s a reasonable expectation when people drive down the roadway that they’re not going to pop a tire, break an axle, or hit something that’s going to make them lose control,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. articles.text: Editor: As I have been reading a lot of viewpoints in the Post regarding teachers’ salaries, APT negotiations, and potential striking, I thought it might be good to remind the Piedmont public that they can find related information on Transparent California (https://transparentcalifornia. com). Transparent California shows public position salaries and benefits, which can be compared among school districts. I was surprised to see the range in Piedmont teaching salaries, with some reaching as high as $124,000 per year (not including benefits). All tenured teachers are making well above the average annual pay in the Bay Area, especially when counterpoised with the fact that they have four months off a year. Interpret this information as you may. It sure is interesting. –Alex Guidici REVIEWERS

articles.text: Lent is a season for discernment, reflection, introspection, confession and repentance. One of the lectionary readings for the middle of this season is John 2:13- 23, an account of Jesus cleansing the Temple in Jerusalem. Unfortunately, much preaching and teaching about this text focuses solely on the reasons for Jesus’ forceful critique of the temple practices of his time without bringing that critique into our time. The result is that this dramatic story becomes a source of anti-Jewishness rather than an invitation for us to review our own religious practices through the lens of Jesus’ way. For Jesus and his contemporaries, the Temple was central to their religious experience. It was an enduring symbol of their desire to experience heaven on earth. Admittedly, in the ancient world, temples were religious, economic and political centers. However, their highest call was to serve as places where humans could connect with God, where mortals could meet the eternal. For many well-intentioned reasons, primarily to meet the needs of religious pilgrims, animals were sold and currency was exchanged on the temple grounds. It seems that sale of the animals and the exchange of money had become very exploitative. Pilgrims who simply wanted to fulfill the mandates of their religion were being ripped off. They came to the temple to experience heaven. Instead, they were met with a hell of noise, confusion, manipulation and fraud. His own shock at what he observed, coupled with the experience of his friends, caused Jesus to take precipitous action. Fashioning a handmade whip, he chased the livestock salesmen and the money changers from the Temple. It is important that our consideration of this act not stop with condemnation of the practices Jesus found so problematic.
