articles.text: Public Works estimates completion date of April 5 Piedmont’s Public Works Department says that construction is “over halfway done” at its three bulb-out projects at the intersections of Oakland Avenue and El Cerrito Avenue, Oakland Avenue and Jerome Avenue, and Nova Avenue and Magnolia Avenue. The estimated completion date for all three is April 5. Two of the four bulb-outs at both intersections on Oakland Avenue are done and work has begun on a third at both sites. “They are currently forming their third ramp locations, and I believe they anticipate pouring those next week if weather allows,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. Meanwhile, the construction site at Nova Avenue and Magnolia Avenue has started to take its final shape. “The flat work has been completed down there, so the island has been formed and poured. The sidewalk and curb bulb-out extension have also been formed and poured,” said Gonzales. “There are still some components that need to be completed, but all of the heavy construction has been completed at this point.” Public Works hopes these bulb-outs (sidewalk extensions) will make the area safer by increasing pedestrian visibility, shortening street-crossing distances, and reducing vehicle turn speeds by narrowing the street. The total construction cost for this project is $773,885. The funding includes a $50,000 contribution from Piedmont Beautification and approximately $600,000 of State Gas Tax funding. The intersection of Oakland Avenue and Jerome Avenue Staff Photos The intersection of Oakland Avenue and El Cerrito Avenue
articles.title: Oakland Ave. bulb-outs halfway done

articles.text: Editor: As PUSD continues to troubleshoot the budget shortfall, a parcel tax increase is one of the scenarios worth exploring. While any tax increase should rightfully be met with scrutiny, this tax is a logical investment in our homes. I live on the border of Piedmont. The homes on our side of the street are in Piedmont and the homes on the other side - just 30 feet away - are in Oakland. A simple Redfin or Zillow search shows that the pricing for the homes on our side are valued an average of 41% higher than the homes on the Oakland side of the street. Like many families who live in Piedmont, we moved here for the great community, and the usual reasons of good weather and proximity to jobs. All good reasons, but not good enough to explain why we would pay 40%+ more for our home when we could live 30 feet away and still meet those same criteria. For us and many Piedmonters, we moved to Piedmont for its schools. When looking at comparable neighborhoods, the main cause of significant swings in home pricing is always the quality of the public schools. PUSD provides high-quality public education to our children and enviable student-to-teacher ratios compared with immediately adjacent communities. Everyone is aware of the Piedmont school budget crises, and one of the solutions being discussed is to raise our property taxes to help cover the shortfall. This is not just a tax, it is an investment in the single asset that, for most households, is their largest – their home. The math is very simple. There are est. 4,000 homes in Piedmont. PUSD needs to cover a $2.3 million budget shortfall. If we were to simply increase property taxes to cover this, it would work out to $575 per house per year. Currently all homeowners pay $2,932 per year through Measure G, and $0.25/ft. (on their home square footage) through Measure H. This means an average 2,500 square foot home in Piedmont pays $3,557/year in taxes to support our schools. Add in the $575 increase and this would become $4,132/year. Run that math out 30 years with the mandatory annual increases and these taxes would total approximately $155,000 over 30 years, or $62/ft. on the average 2,500 square foot home. The average home price in Oakland is $608/ft. and in Piedmont it is $946/ft., so for an investment in our schools of $62/ft. you get a return of $338/ft., or about 540% on your money. On an annualized basis over 30 years, this is 11% per year, and if you live in your home less than 30 years the returns are even higher! To put that in context: 30-year U.S. treasuries are yielding around 4.5% per year, so an investment in our schools that helps your community, your neighbors, our teachers and students, would actually give you a return that is almost three times higher. This is what you call a “no-brainer” investment.
articles.title: Investing in our schools is a “no-brainer” investment in our homes

A simple Redfin or Zillow search shows that the pricing for the homes on our side are valued an average of 41% higher than the homes on the Oakland side of the street. Like many families who live in Piedmont, we moved here for the great community, and the usual reasons of good weather and proximity to jobs. All good reasons, but not good enough to explain why we would pay 40%+ more for our home when we could live 30 feet away and still meet those same criteria. For us and many Piedmonters, we moved to Piedmont for its schools. When looking at comparable neighborhoods, the main cause of significant swings in home pricing is always the quality of the public schools. PUSD provides high-quality public education to our children and enviable student-to-teacher ratios compared with immediately adjacent communities. Everyone is aware of the Piedmont school budget crises, and one of the solutions being discussed is to raise our property taxes to help cover the shortfall. This is not just a tax, it is an investment in the single asset that, for most households, is their largest – their home. The math is very simple. There are est. 4,000 homes in Piedmont. PUSD needs to cover a $2.3 million budget shortfall. If we were to simply increase property taxes to cover this, it would work out to $575 per house per year. Currently all homeowners pay $2,932 per year through Measure G, and $0.25/ft. (on their home square footage) through Measure H. This means an average 2,500 square foot home in Piedmont pays $3,557/year in taxes to support our schools. Add in the $575 increase and this would become $4,132/year. Run that math out 30 years with the mandatory annual increases and these taxes would total approximately $155,000 over 30 years, or $62/ft. on the average 2,500 square foot home. The average home price in Oakland is $608/ft. and in Piedmont it is $946/ft., so for an investment in our schools of $62/ft. you get a return of $338/ft., or about 540% on your money. On an annualized basis over 30 years, this is 11% per year, and if you live in your home less than 30 years the returns are even higher! To put that in context: 30-year U.S. treasuries are yielding around 4.5% per year, so an investment in our schools that helps your community, your neighbors, our teachers and students, would actually give you a return that is almost three times higher. This is what you call a “no-brainer” investment. CORRECTION The February 28 edition of the Post contained a letter to the editor titled “Voting for Ken Berrick for AC Transit Board. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department’s newest officer, Ashley Gallion, grew up in a tight-knit community where neighbors knew one another and kids played outdoors until nighttime. It was the kind of neighborhood that doesn’t exist in many places. When she first saw Piedmont, she knew she had found something special. “When I came for my first ride-along to see the department, I remember driving in and seeing the kids walking to school. Just seeing them feel safe enough to walk to school. It is exactly like what I had growing up in Morgan Hill, and it was what I always looked for once I left that community.” On January 12, the Piedmont Police Department (PPD) announced that Gallion completed her field training program, making her a fully sworn officer on the police force. She was born in 1996 in Gilroy, and grew up in Morgan Hill, where she lived, and San Jose, where she went to school. She graduated from Branham High School in 2014 and began attending San Jose State the same year, with a major in Psychology. However, she quickly learned that though she liked helping people, she didn’t necessarily like sitting behind a desk all day. She decided to go into law enforcement after a conversation with her grandmother about hostage negotiations. “My grandma had read something in a newspaper about hostage negotiating, and she brought it up to me. ‘You know, this is all the things you like intertwined into one. You get to use your psychology degree, but you get to help people, be outside, and really feel like you’re making a difference.” Photo by April Fitzgerald Officer Ashley completed her field training program on January 12 and is now a fully sworn officer with Piedmont Police Department. This was the turning point in her career. “It switched on something for me. That’s when I knew I wanted to go into law enforcement,” she said. In 2018, Gallion left SJSU to become a Community Service Officer with the San Jose Police Department. There she met Jessica Morey, now also a member of the PPD, and the two became close friends. Morey found her way to Piedmont through a mutual friend who put her in contact with Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. A ride-along was organized where Gallion and Morey could see the city, and she was impressed. “When Jessica and I left the city, we were both in such awe. We looked at each other and said this is where we belong.’” These days, Gallion doesn’t think about a job in hostage negotiation as much, but she still identifies with the sentiment of helping others in need. Overall, she hopes she can serve the Piedmont community well in her role. “I am here and ready whenever they need me, and I’m fortunate I have the opportunity to be a person they can count on,” she said.
articles.title: Officer Ashley Gallion joins police department

articles.text: Nicole Virgil, practitioner of Christian Science healing and public speaker, will present a talk, “Be set free,” on Sunday, March 24, at 2:00 p.m. at First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland, located at 1880 Mountain Blvd. in the Montclair district. The talk will focus on universal healing precepts found in the Holy Bible, especially in Christ Jesus’ life and teachings, showing how they are available for anyone to understand and experience through the lens of Christian Science. The talk is free, open to the community, and sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland. “Circumstances often present what appear to be significant obstacles to living freely, something that everyone wants to do,” Ms. Virgil says. “In this talk, we will examine liberty from a Biblical perspective; and see how real people today find their freedom from all kinds of physical, emotional and circumstantial restrictions that seem clearly beyond their control.” Sharing examples of healing from her own life and professional practice of Christian Science, Ms. Virgil will explain why Christian Science is both Christian and scientific, meaning that people can prove its effectiveness for themselves, as fully described in the book Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, written by the founder of the Christian Science movement, Mary Baker Eddy. Ms. Virgil will also touch on the life of Mary Baker Eddy, who came to understand, confirm, and teach what she felt was original Christian healing. Eddy herself said she was especially inspired by Jesus’ demand, “He that believes on me, the works that I do will he do also; and greater works than these will he do, because I go unto my Father” (found in the Gospel of John 14:12 in the Bible). For over 150 years, people around the world have worked to follow Christ Jesus in this practice of Christianity and continue to do so today, experiencing healings of physical ills and personal difficulties. Nicole Virgil has been a Christian Science practitioner for many years, helping people on a daily basis through this scientific approach to prayer. She travels from her home near Chicago to speak to audiences as a member of the Christian Science Board of Lectureship. articles.text: Lateefah Simon, a member of the BART board of directors, has emerged as the apparent frontrunner in the race for the 12th Congressional District, which has been held by Rep. Barbara Lee (D) since 1998. Lee is currently a candidate for the Senate seat of the late Dianne Feinstein. Simon, based in Emeryville, has raised more than $1.1 million according to the Federal Elections Commission and has received endorsements from Governor Gavin Newsom, Barbara Lee, and the California Democratic Party. In addition to her broad appeal, Simon has also shown interest in Piedmont in recent statements, including a willingness to taking over Lee’s speaking role at the annual Martin Luther King Jr. celebration in Piedmont if elected. “If I have the honor of being elected to Congress, I’ll be a voice for all residents of the 12th Congressional district, including Piedmont,” said Ms. Simon. “With my background as an Lateefah Simon organizer and community leader, I understand the importance of staying connected to the communities I serve. One of my top priorities will be to build a strong district office with accessible and responsive staff to provide constituent services.” Simon acknowledged that she would have big shoes to fill if elected to Lee’s seat in Congress. “It would be the honor of my life to continue the legacy of Congresswoman Barbara Lee by representing the East Bay in Washington. Congresswoman Lee has championed our East Bay values and stood up for peace and justice on the national stage [...] I plan on being a fighter for this community.” On January 31, Lee officially endorsed Simon. “After his 27 years of service, [Ron Dellums] passed the baton to me, and now I am excited and proud to endorse Lateefah Simon, my former student, to run this next lap of the race,” said Lee. When asked if she would take over Barbara Lee’s longtime speaker role at Piedmont’s annual MLK Jr. celebration if elected, Ms. Simon was enthusiastic. “Absolutely! I’d be honored to join the people of Piedmont in celebrating Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s legacy. Events like this are what keep the memory of the civil rights movement alive. Count me in.” The 12th Congressional District’s general election will be on November 5, 2024.
articles.title: Lateefah Simon emerges as frontrunner for Congress

articles.text: At the Special School Board meeting on Monday, March 4 cuts to next year’s classified school staff roster were approved. Unlike certified employees, the contract with classified staff does not require an advanced public hearing before announcing cuts. Together, with the planned cuts of 8.7 FTE to certified staff, the district aims to save $1.4 million next year. Also announced were reductions in hours for dozens of existing employees with the job titles: Special Ed Para I, Special Ed Para II, Assistive Technology Tech, and Library Media Tech. These reductions equate to 1.75 full time equivalent in salary. Nine employees with those titles at Piedmont High School are having their paid hours reduced from 33.35 hrs/wk to 31.25 hrs/week. The 2.1 hrs a week reduction for nine positions equates to a reduced payroll of 18.9 hr/wk. Two employees at Millennium High School will see the same reduction which equals 4.2 hrs/wk. Fourteen Piedmont Middle School employees are having their hours scaled back from 33.35 hrs/wk to 30 hrs/wk. The reduced hours at the three sites totals 1.75 full time equivalent in salary, when combined with the elimination of positions at 6.3 the total classified reduction looks more 8 full time jobs off the books for the district. The district equates the reduction in hours to more accurately reflect current working hours following a change in the bell schedules at the schools. APT President, Elise Marks, came to the defense of her colleagues, although they are in different unions. “Those people are still working full time jobs. They put in extra time all the time at brunch and lunch and after school and give all kinds of extra effort that they’re not actually paid for,” Marks told the Post. retirements,” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn said. “Remember this past year we could not find a chemistry teacher?” Looking side by side at the two versions of the cuts, the February 14 list was aimed at positions totaling 13.3 FTE and had the potential to save the district $2.4 million. The revised list of cuts, which was approved Monday, will save $1.4 million and affects 8.7 full time equivalent positions. These totals include cuts to certified, classified, and administrative positions. Measure H hopes to be able to bridge this gap. These “right-sizing” cuts, have been scaled back from 13.3 FTE to 8.7 FTE, made possible by entrusting residents of the city to help avert having to make another round of cuts following the 2024-2025 school year and a parcel tax.
articles.title: School Classified Staff also to be reduced

articles.text: As most people in Piedmont know, Piedmont’s School board is issuing major budget cuts to the art and dance departments, starting as early as March 15. I beg of our community to do all you can to reverse these harmful actions. Not only are teachers a vital part of the community and Piedmont’s culture, but art is key to teenagers’ development. As a current student I can state that art and dance are both activities that give me great joy and passion. For many, art and dance are escapes or creative outlets. In straining times for adolescents, they are key activities that help to release stress and improve mood. The thought of them possibly being cut from the school curriculum fills many with great sadness and frustration. Art has long been overlooked as nothing more than “pretty paintings” or modernistic statements few can understand. In reality, that is far from the truth. Art can take many forms and shapes, one of them being dance, also deemed unimportant by the school board and set for cuts. The school board has already faced major pushback from the community in response to their recent decision. I can vividly remember coming to school and having slips of paper on each desk, detailing the school board’s decision as well as instructions and a request to send an email to the board asking them to revoke the decision. But now I am begging our community to do the same. The reactions that have already been captured are truly valuable, showing the importance of these subjects to our students and staff. The subjects that the school board wishes to brush off like flies, leaves many in despair. Piedmont is a community-based city. Our combined resistance can and will spark change. –Daisy Seymour 8th grade, Piedmont Middle School
articles.title: Students need parents to help stop budget cuts

articles.text: As the world of standardized testing continues to evolve in a “post” pandemic era, many families wonder how AP exams, which take place each May, fit into their student’s college roadmap. We want to help sift through the enormity of information available on the internet and provide insight into some of the questions we are most frequently asked. • Do AP exams actually matter for college admissions? The short answer is yes. AP exams can be impactful for college admissions. Depending on exam scores, students may be eligible for specific merit scholarships or receive college credit. AP exams allow schools to evaluate a student’s readiness for the rigor of college courses. • My student signed up for an AP exam back in October; must she take the test? They do not have to take the test, but, unless there is an extenuating circumstance, most students should. If the test goes well, they have a great quantitative addition to their apps. • My student is doing well in the AP class. Will he do well on the AP exam? This is a tricky one. AP classes are not standardized like the exam; there is often great variety in rigor, grading, and expectations. The best way to know how a student will do on an AP exam is by taking a practice test. • If my student’s AP class isn’t doing much to prepare her for the exam, what can she do? All students who are enrolled in an AP course have access to “AP classroom”. This is a great resource for official practice problems and course content. If a student wants more individualized support, they can always talk to their teacher or engage a tutor. There are now a total of 39 AP courses (although few schools offer the full range of classes). APs are meant to be an opportunity for students to delve into topics of interest while also challenging themselves with college level coursework. While AP classes and exams can be an important factor in college admissions, their true intent is to help students gain important knowledge and skills that will help them succeed in college and beyond. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, March 6, 2024 SchOOLs School Classified Staff also to be reduced By Jay Russell At the Special School Board meeting on Monday, March 4 cuts to next year’s classified school staff roster were approved. Unlike certified employees, the contract with classified staff does not require an advanced public hearing before announcing cuts. Together, with the planned cuts of 8.7 FTE to certified staff, the district aims to save $1.4 million next year. Also announced were reductions in hours for dozens of existing employees with the job titles: Special Ed Para I, Special Ed Para II, Assistive Technology Tech, and Library Media Tech. These reductions equate to 1.75 full time equivalent in salary. Nine employees with those titles at Piedmont High School are having their paid hours reduced from 33.35 hrs/wk to 31.25 hrs/week. The 2.1 hrs a week reduction for nine positions equates to a reduced payroll of 18.9 hr/wk. Two employees at Millennium High School will see the same reduction which equals 4.2 hrs/wk. Fourteen Piedmont Middle School employees are having their hours scaled back from 33.35 hrs/wk to 30 hrs/wk. The reduced hours at the three sites totals 1.75 full time equivalent in salary, when combined with the elimination of positions at 6.3 the total classified reduction looks more 8 full time jobs off the books for the district. The district equates the reduction in hours to more accurately reflect current working hours following a change in the bell schedules at the schools. APT President, Elise Marks, came to the defense of her colleagues, although they are in different unions. “Those people are still working full time jobs. They put in extra time all the time at brunch and lunch and after school and give all kinds of extra effort that they’re not actually paid for,” Marks told the Post. Superintendent 1.0 Assistant to Superintendent 0.2 Total 6.3 FTE Students need parents to help stop budget cuts By Daisy R. Seymour As most people in Piedmont know, Piedmont’s School board is issuing major budget cuts to the art and dance departments, starting as early as March 15. I beg of our community to do all you can to reverse these harmful actions. Not only are teachers a vital part of the community and Piedmont’s culture, but art is key to teenagers’ development. As a current student I can state that art and dance are both activities that give me great joy and passion. For many, art and dance are escapes or creative outlets. In straining times for adolescents, they are key activities that help to release stress and improve mood. The thought of them possibly being cut from the school curriculum fills many with great sadness and frustration. Art has long been overlooked as nothing more than “pretty paintings” or modernistic statements few can understand. In reality, that is far from the truth. Art can take many forms and shapes, one of them being dance, also deemed unimportant by the school board and set for cuts. The school board has already faced major pushback from the community in response to their recent decision. I can vividly remember coming to school and having slips of paper on each desk, detailing the school board’s decision as well as instructions and a request to send an email to the board asking them to revoke the decision. But now I am begging our community to do the same. The reactions that have already been captured are truly valuable, showing the importance of these subjects to our students and staff. The subjects that the school board wishes to brush off like flies, leaves many in despair. Piedmont is a community-based city. Our combined resistance can and will spark change. –Daisy Seymour 8th grade, Piedmont Middle School School Cuts Continued from page 1 ruary 14. That meeting brought teachers, students, and parents to the defense of the programs they saw as important to a quality education. Technology teaching and technology coordinating services may now be the hardest hit, with a full time elementary position being eliminated, and two other part time positions being eliminated. An English class and a Spanish class are scheduled to be dropped at the high school along with one of the school’s two vice principal positions. The equivalent of one full time librarian job between PMS and PHS libraries is targeted to be eliminated. Current PHS librarian Kathryn Levenson is retiring at the end of the year. “We don’t know what that means yet. Will each library be open only half the time? Will we run the [PHS] Library with a media tech or close it!?” Levenson said. “These are not harmless cuts; we are going to really be struggling,” said Marks to the school board on Monday. Marks also mentioned that cutting a full-time nurse could be potentially dangerous for students. Science, computer classes and all STEM classes were conspicuously absent from the district’s trimming. “Subjects, such as science, are not listed [for cuts] because we are already down a teacher or we have already received some retirements,” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn said. “Remember this past year we could not find a chemistry teacher?” Looking side by side at the two versions of the cuts, the February 14 list was aimed at positions totaling 13.3 FTE and had the potential to save the district $2.4 million. The revised list of cuts, which was approved Monday, will save $1.4 million and affects 8.7 full time equivalent positions. These totals include cuts to certified, classified, and administrative positions. Measure H hopes to be able to bridge this gap. These “right-sizing” cuts, have been scaled back from 13.3 FTE to 8.7 FTE, made possible by entrusting residents of the city to help avert having to make another round of cuts following the 2024-2025 school year and a parcel tax. Thinking Outside the Classroom The school board held a special meeting in the drama classroom at the Alan Harvey Theater to approve budget cuts to staffing on Monday, March 4 READ IT IN THE POST The fast FAQs on AP exams By Ariel Rodriguez As the world of standardized testing continues to evolve in a “post” pandemic era, many families wonder how AP exams, which take place each May, fit into their student’s college roadmap. We want to help sift through the enormity of information available on the internet and provide insight into some of the questions we are most frequently asked. • Do AP exams actually matter for college admissions? The short answer is yes. AP exams can be impactful for college admissions. Depending on exam scores, students may be eligible for specific merit scholarships or receive college credit. AP exams allow schools to evaluate a student’s readiness for the rigor of college courses. • My student signed up for an AP exam back in October; must she take the test? They do not have to take the test, but, unless there is an extenuating circumstance, most students should. If the test goes well, they have a great quantitative addition to their apps. • My student is doing well in the AP class. Will he do well on the AP exam? This is a tricky one. AP classes are not standardized like the exam; there is often great variety in rigor, grading, and expectations. The best way to know how a student will do on an AP exam is by taking a practice test. • If my student’s AP class isn’t doing much to prepare her for the exam, what can she do? All students who are enrolled in an AP course have access to “AP classroom”. This is a great resource for official practice problems and course content. If a student wants more individualized support, they can always talk to their teacher or engage a tutor. There are now a total of 39 AP courses (although few schools offer the full range of classes). APs are meant to be an opportunity for students to delve into topics of interest while also challenging themselves with college level coursework. While AP classes and exams can be an important factor in college admissions, their true intent is to help students gain important knowledge and skills that will help them succeed in college and beyond. articles.text: The Readmont community discussion for this year’s selection, “Accountable” by Dashka Slater, will occur tonight, Wednesday, March 6, at 7:00 p.m. in the Piedmont High School library. articles.text: A couple of weeks ago two troops from the Piedmont Scout Council headed into the mountains for a weekend full of snow, fun, and fellowship. Though the two troops hadn’t planned on staying at the same place at the same time, it proved to be a fun coincidence. After braving traffic to get to the mountains on Friday evening, Scouts and leaders settled into their respective rooms at Clair Tappan Lodge, a legendary Sierra Club hostel in Norden near the Donner Pass. They took note of the chore lists on the walls and immediately signed up to help with setting tables, doing the dishes, and cleaning up. “I enjoyed skiing with my friends and playing ping pong at the lodge,” said Troop 1 Scout Ben Mittan. “It was a relaxing trip compared to the others we have done this year, and I loved all of it.” Saturday dawned bright and early with excellent food and time to make bag lunches for everyone. Some Scouts who skied rarely or never before headed to nearby Sugar Bowl for lessons in the morning. The rest of the Scouts hit the slopes before the rush of Bay Area skiers arrived. Scouts and adult volunteers from Piedmont Scout Troops 1 and 11 in front of Clair Tappan Lodge in Norden near Donner summit Anna Benson and Annabelle Malione of Troop 11 enjoy time in the snow. Scouts build snow forts in the fading light of the day in the mountains. Troop 1 Scout Susanna Cantrill and Ronan Price enjoy the snow. After practicing all day on the slopes, Scoutmaster Rob Kobal reviews the final requirements for a Snow Sports merit badge with Scouts at the lodge.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 6, 2024 9 Piedmont Scouts Continued from page 8 Scouts and adult volunteers play some board games at the lodge. “It was great!” said Mason Myers, a Troop 1 Scout “The snow was so white and fluffy and the lines were short, I thought I was in heaven. It was some of the best skiing of the year.” “It was fun to ski with my friends and also earn the Snow Sports merit badge. Back at the lodge we got to make snow forts, break giant icicles off the lodge and throw snowballs!” said Gabi Stein of Troop 1. After a full day on the slopes, the Scouts returned to the lodge and promptly headed for the hot chocolate. After that warm-up, they headed back to the snow for sledding and digging snow caves where some would spend the night. Dinner, board games, merit badge work, and other fellowship rounded out the evening’s activities. In Scouting, the snow sports merit badge is a fun offering, and Troop 11 Scoutmaster Rob Kobal made it available. It involves reviewing safety precautions, common first aid needed on the slopes, and basic skills to stay safe and have fun in the snow. “I’ve taught the snow sports merit badge using both snowshoeing and skiing,” said Kobal. “I enjoy seeing Scouts learn a skill and show off their prowess.” Scouts Isabelle Myers, Sean McKee, Theo Ferguson, and Drew Kobal enjoy a short rest between runs at Sugar Bowl. This is one of the adventures that Piedmont Scouts enjoy during the year, along with hiking, backpacking, camping, white water rafting, and summer camp. Scout troops serve youth 11-18 years old. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team season came to an end on Tuesday, February 27 in the first round of the Division 3 CIF State Tournament. Playing at No. 3 Valley Christian in San Jose, No. 14 Piedmont lost 72-43. PHS played a close first quarter and trailed 17-13. However, Valley Christian shut down PHS in the second quarter, limiting the Highlanders to just four points while scoring 15 to jump ahead 32-17 at halftime. Valley Christian continued to knock down all of its shots, including flurries of 3-pointers in the second half. It ends the Highlanders’ season with a 20-11 overall record Staff Photos Brit Burden departs with the Class of 2024. He’s among the new members of Piedmont’s 1,000 point club. Ravi Silverberg will be a returning senior to lead next year’s squad. Dillon Casey wraps up a productive sophomore campaign and will be among next year’s key players. and their first North Coast Section Finals appearance since winning the title in 2020. The Highlanders started the season shorthanded. Scott Cooley, a tall forward, was ruled ineligible due to transfer rules. The squad also lost senior Alex Anderson, also a forward, in the first game of the season due to a knee injury. “We rolled with the guys who got us here and we became a different team from the start of the season. I’m just proud of the effort everyone gave from start to finish,” coach Ben Spencer said. Anderson’s injury opened the door for sophomore Dillon Casey to enter the starting lineup. He became a mainstay and the team’s second-best scorer. “Dillon came in and made an impact instantly,” said senior Brit Burden, who finishes his high school career with over 1,000 points. The team loses several key players to graduation, including its leading scorer Burden. senior forward Declan Linnane, forward Thorin Holmes, guard Arjun Bornstein and forward Finn Burke. “I’m really proud of our seniors and what they gave over the last 20 games. I’m proud of our boys for the way they battled. We haven’t been to a Final or State in a while and now we’ve been to State two times in five years. There’s a culture we’ve developed and now its always about getting back to the finals and getting back to State,” said coach Spencer. In their wake, Piedmont will return a talented backcourt with Casey and Ravi Silverberg, P.J. Brayer also got valuable time as the season progressed, while Cash Panico and Lucas Malecki earned minutes as well. 72-43 loss to Valley Christian Piedmont trailed in striking distance down 17-13 by the end of the first quarter but were held to just four points in the second while allowing 15, down 32-17 at the half. Valley Christian stayed hot in the third quarter with 24 points with Piedmont adding 15, making it 56-32 entering the fourth. The Highlanders added 11 points in the fourth but conceded 16. Final stats: Burden led scoring with 19 points, Silverberg scored eight, Linnane had six, while Casey had four.
articles.title: Boys’ basketball season ends in State playoffs

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team got to the State Playoffs before losing on Tuesday, February 27 to Whitney in Rocklin in the first round of the Division 1 CIF State Tournament. Piedmont, the No. 9 seed, lost by 12 points 53-41, to the No. 8 ranked Wildcats. The Highlanders end their season with a 20-8 overall record and as co-champions of the Western Alameda County Conference. Although Piedmont held an early lead in the first quarter and battled to a 28-24 deficit in by halftime, they were held to three points in the third quarter. It was ultimately enough to set the two teams apart. Senior Natalia Martinez led the Highlanders with 16 points and concluded her high school career with 2,272 points. She will continue her basketball career at San Diego State later this year. “Nat’s one of the best players in Northern California, if not the best already, said coach Bryan Gardere. “She’s a really special player. She worked hard to put herself in position to go play Division 1 basketball on a great team. She always put in the extra minutes before school, before practice, at lunch or in free period.” Martinez was a four-year starter and started in every game since coming to the school in 2020. She’s the school’s record holder for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28. Martinez won back-to-back WACC Player of the Year awards and was the Post’s 2023 Athlete of the Year. She was also named 2022 Sophomore of the Year and 2021 Freshman of the Year. The team will lose Samantha Smith, Kat Melian, and Lindsey Wirgler to graduation. graduate. Smith was a role player in Piedmont’s D4 NCS Championship winning season in 2023. Sam Smith, who spent two years on varsity, is among the graduating players. Lindsey Wirgler, a senior, emerged as the team’s second leading scorer.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball season is off to a delayed start after having its opening games rained out on Thursday and Friday, February 29 and March 1. On Tuesday, March 5, the Highlanders season began in earnest, with a 12-2 thumping of Salesian at Humphries Diamond. It was a complete day, with eight hits and drawing eight walks to activate the 10-run rule to end the game after five innings. On the mound, senior John Olsen and George Bishop got the job done with a combined three hits allowed. Olsen got the win with four innings of work including two strikeouts and allowed no earned runs. “We have a lot of guys we’ll put on the mound and we trust them. John was great for us last year and he’ll throw a lot,” said coach Eric Olson, Senior Peter Krumins showed off his power hitting by going a perfect 3-for-3 with a pair of doubles that broke the game open. He finished with four RBIs and three runs scored. Catcher Will Parker, who hits in the three spot, also had a big afternoon, going 3-for-4 with a double and three RBIs. 12-2 over Salesian After a 1-2-3 top of the first by Olsen, PHS got the show started with a single by Markos Lagios, a walk by Krumins, and a single to bring in Lagios. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos then brought in Krumins in a fielder’s choice. Although Salesian scored twice in the top of the third to tie it at 2-2, it was the last time they got on the scoreboard. PHS scored three runs in the bottom half when Krumins slugged a double to left field, followed by Parker hitting a single. After Papahadjopoulos drew a walk, Brandon Dicke brought in Krumins on a ground out. Diego Delventhal then hit a single to right field to score Parker and Papahadjopoulos for a 5-2 score. Olsen then forced another 1-2-3 inning in the top of the fourth, leading to another 3-run inning. It started with Jack Meyjes reaching on an error, then loading the bases with walks to Ellis Moss and Lagios. Krumins hit a two-run single to score Moss and Meyjes. With one out, Papahadjopoulos drew another walk followed by Dicke bringing in Lagios on a fielder’s choice for an 8-2 lead. In the bottom of the fifth, Jordan Vo and Meyjes got things started with a pair of walks, then Lagios drew a walk to load the bases with one out. That’s when Krumins drove a shot to the left field fence for another double, bringing in Vo and Mayjes to score. Parker then stepped to the plate. On the second pitch of his at bat, Parker smacked a double of his own to deep center field, resulting in Lagios and Krumins crossing home to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Krumins went 3-for-3 with two doubles, three runs scored, four RBIs, and a Staff Photos Pitcher John Olsen got the start for Piedmont, throwing six strikeouts and allowing no earned runs. walk. Lagios went 1-for-2 with three runs, two walks, and a stolen base. Parker was 3-for-4 with a double, three RBIs, and one run. Papahadjopoulos had an RBI, run scored, and two walks. Dicke had two RBIs. Delventhal was 1-for-2 with two RBIs. Meyjes scored two runs and drew a walk. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) travels to San Leandro tomorrow, March 7, for a 3:30 p.m. game with the Pirates. They will host Justin-Siena in a traditional home opener on Saturday, March 9 at 12:00 p.m. Peter Krumins went 3-for-3 with two doubles and four RBIs. Will Parker was 3-for-4 with a double and three RBIs.

articles.text: Staff Photos Returning starter Ruby Guzdar scored five goals against Dublin. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got its season started in a big way, winning its first two games in the past week, They defeated Dublin 12-5 on the road Wednesday, February 28, and won handily 14-2 over HeadRoyce for their home opener at Witter Field on Monday, March 4. “It was really good we played that Dublin game. They were a very physical team, and our defense wasn’t really set. The Dublin game was helpful in putting that together. We really came together against Head-Royce,” coach Carlton Chan said. The pair of games was good preparation for some difficult competition. Piedmont plays at Acalanes tonight, March 6. The Dons are currently 3-1 and compete in North Coast Section’s Division 2 alongside Piedmont. Piedmont’s attack featured six different goal scorers against Dublin and different goal scorers against Head-Royce. Hallie Burden made an impact in face-offs, winning seven draws against Head-Royce and three versus Dublin. Ruby Guzdar, a leading scorer from last year, scored five goals against Dublin, and Laurel Bentley had a hat trick in the win over Head-Royce. “I said early on that Hallie was going to be important on the draw and she showed it today. Our plays are starting to come together,” Chan said. 14-2 win vs. Head-Royce PHS led 6-0 by the end of the first quarter and the route was on. It ballooned to 11-0 by halftime. With a running clock for the entire second half, PHS extended the lead to 13-1 through the third quarter and added one more goal in the final going. Piedmont wasted no time. Friedie Schickedanz scored a goal on the first possession of the game. Burden then scored two minutes later after drawing a shooting space penalty. Chloe Graham assisted Luisa Cole for a goal, and Graham scored with 4:52 left in the first period. Peyton Watson launched one in after another two minutes, and Guzdar capped off the quarter for a 6-0 advantage. In the second quarter, Watson scored after 33 seconds, while Burden made it 8-0 with 8:37 left in the half—then she scored again after another 45 seconds. Olive Litwin scored to make it 10-0 and activate the running clock with 5:34 left in the second Hallie Burden is making an impact in the face-off circle. She scored four goals against Head-Royce and won seven draws. Laurel Bentley had three goals against Head-Royce and two in the win over Dublin.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 6, 2024 13 Baseball opens season with big win over Salesian By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s baseball season is off to a delayed start after having its opening games rained out on Thursday and Friday, February 29 and March 1. On Tuesday, March 5, the Highlanders season began in earnest, with a 12-2 thumping of Salesian at Humphries Diamond. It was a complete day, with eight hits and drawing eight walks to activate the 10-run rule to end the game after five innings. On the mound, senior John Olsen and George Bishop got the job done with a combined three hits allowed. Olsen got the win with four innings of work including two strikeouts and allowed no earned runs. “We have a lot of guys we’ll put on the mound and we trust them. John was great for us last year and he’ll throw a lot,” said coach Eric Olson, Senior Peter Krumins showed off his power hitting by going a perfect 3-for-3 with a pair of doubles that broke the game open. He finished with four RBIs and three runs scored. Catcher Will Parker, who hits in the three spot, also had a big afternoon, going 3-for-4 with a double and three RBIs. 12-2 over Salesian After a 1-2-3 top of the first by Olsen, PHS got the show started with a single by Markos Lagios, a walk by Krumins, and a single to bring in Lagios. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos then brought in Krumins in a fielder’s choice. Although Salesian scored twice in the top of the third to tie it at 2-2, it was the last time they got on the scoreboard. PHS scored three runs in the bottom half when Krumins slugged a double to left field, followed by Parker hitting a single. After Papahadjopoulos drew a walk, Brandon Dicke brought in Krumins on a ground out. Diego Delventhal then hit a single to right field to score Parker and Papahadjopoulos for a 5-2 score. Olsen then forced another 1-2-3 inning in the top of the fourth, leading to another 3-run inning. It started with Jack Meyjes reaching on an error, then loading the bases with walks to Ellis Moss and Lagios. Krumins hit a two-run single to score Moss and Meyjes. With one out, Papahadjopoulos drew another walk followed by Dicke bringing in Lagios on a fielder’s choice for an 8-2 lead. In the bottom of the fifth, Jordan Vo and Meyjes got things started with a pair of walks, then Lagios drew a walk to load the bases with one out. That’s when Krumins drove a shot to the left field fence for another double, bringing in Vo and Mayjes to score. Parker then stepped to the plate. On the second pitch of his at bat, Parker smacked a double of his own to deep center field, resulting in Lagios and Krumins crossing home to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Krumins went 3-for-3 with two doubles, three runs scored, four RBIs, and a Staff Photos Pitcher John Olsen got the start for Piedmont, throwing six strikeouts and allowing no earned runs. walk. Lagios went 1-for-2 with three runs, two walks, and a stolen base. Parker was 3-for-4 with a double, three RBIs, and one run. Papahadjopoulos had an RBI, run scored, and two walks. Dicke had two RBIs. Delventhal was 1-for-2 with two RBIs. Meyjes scored two runs and drew a walk. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) travels to San Leandro tomorrow, March 7, for a 3:30 p.m. game with the Pirates. They will host Justin-Siena in a traditional home opener on Saturday, March 9 at 12:00 p.m. Peter Krumins went 3-for-3 with two doubles and four RBIs. VB = Boys’ Volleyball Girls lacrosse team opens season with pair of wins Staff Photos Returning starter Ruby Guzdar scored five goals against Dublin. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got its season started in a big way, winning its first two games in the past week, They defeated Dublin 12-5 on the road Wednesday, February 28, and won handily 14-2 over HeadRoyce for their home opener at Witter Field on Monday, March 4. “It was really good we played that Dublin game. They were a very physical team, and our defense wasn’t really set. The Dublin game was helpful in putting that together. We really came together against Head-Royce,” coach Carlton Chan said. The pair of games was good preparation for some difficult competition. Piedmont plays at Acalanes tonight, March 6. The Dons are currently 3-1 and compete in North Coast Section’s Division 2 alongside Piedmont. Piedmont’s attack featured six different goal scorers against Dublin and different goal scorers against Head-Royce. Hallie Burden made an impact in face-offs, winning seven draws against Head-Royce and three versus Dublin. Ruby Guzdar, a leading scorer from last year, scored five goals against Dublin, and Laurel Bentley had a hat trick in the win over Head-Royce. “I said early on that Hallie was going to be important on the draw and she showed it today. Our plays are starting to come together,” Chan said. 14-2 win vs. Head-Royce PHS led 6-0 by the end of the first quarter and the route was on. It ballooned to 11-0 by halftime. With a running clock for the entire second half, PHS extended the lead to 13-1 through the third quarter and added one more goal in the final going. Piedmont wasted no time. Friedie Schickedanz scored a goal on the first possession of the game. Burden then scored two minutes later after drawing a shooting space penalty. Chloe Graham assisted Luisa Cole for a goal, and Graham scored with 4:52 left in the first period. Peyton Watson launched one in after another two minutes, and Guzdar capped off the quarter for a 6-0 advantage. In the second quarter, Watson scored after 33 seconds, while Burden made it 8-0 with 8:37 left in the half—then she scored again after another 45 seconds. Olive Litwin scored to make it 10-0 and activate the running clock with 5:34 left in the second See Girls’ Lacrosse on page 32 Hallie Burden is making an impact in the face-off circle. She scored four goals against Head-Royce and won seven draws. Laurel Bentley had three goals against Head-Royce and two in the win over Dublin.

articles.text: Staff Photos John Champion had 19 kills on San Lorenzo and 18 on Mt. Eden, and is closing in on a school record. The PHS boys’ volleyball team wrapped up a productive first week by winning two of its their first three with matches on three consecutive days. They opened the season with a 3-0 win over Mt. Eden on Tuesday, February 27 in Hayward, lost 3-1 to St. Joseph at in Alameda the following day, and bounced back, shutting out San Lorenzo 3-0 in a home opener at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, February 29. All three were non-league matches. Mt. Eden and San Lorenzo competed in the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division, and Piedmont plays in the more challenging Foothill Division. St. Joseph, unlike its basketball teams, competes es in the Bay Counties Athletic League with small enrollment schools. Piedmont’s victories were expected over Mt. Eden and San Lorenzo, although it was the first appearances of a squad with 13 new players. “We don’t have a lot of players with a lot of experience. Our main system of offense is John [Champion], we’re going to keep giving it to #7 until he can’t hit any more. We’re figuring out a good rotation,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Champion is the team’s primary outside hitter, with 19 kills against San Lorenzo, 14 vs. St. Joseph, and another 18 in the season-opener against Mt. Eden. “At this point, what we need most is reps. Even though we had back-to-back-to-back games this week, it works out well for us to get that game experience,” Champion said. Shunji Higashi and Champion are only returning starters from last year. “We just need to keep getting practice together,” said Higashi. “I was trying to set up everyone today, but in the end, I started going straight to John when things got too close.” It was a good start for a team that will require time to mold. Cardenas is hopeful the team can continue putting the pieces together and qualify for North Coast Section playoffs for the third consecutive year. “We’re going to need a lot of practice time where we need to focus. I would love to make NCS; we’ve done well the last two years, and want to get there again,” Cardenas said. Shunji Higashi sets up a spike. He’s the team’s primary setter. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont starts its season with two low-scoring defensive losses. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team showed good defense in its first pair of games of the spring season, but fell 7-3 to Serra in San Mateo on Thursday, February 28 and 6-4 to Casa Grande on Friday, March 1 at Witter Field. Offensively senior Rylan Nelson and freshman Connor Fredericks, the younger brothers of Class of 2023 graduates Jack Nelson and Nate Fredericks, were the sparkplugs. Nelson scored three of Piedmont’s goals, two against Serra. Fredericks also scored three total goals, including two against Casa Grande. On defense, goalie Gus Von Metszch made eight saves against Casa Grande and 15 against Serra. The results were seen as encouraging defensive performances against difficult opponents. Piedmont’s full starting lineup has had limited time practicing together. “There was a fair amount of season overlap, so we had mixed numbers through the first two weeks of practice. We finally had full numbers when the winter season wrapped up,” explained first-year coach Jeff Lamb. Piedmont’s season ramps up next week. It plays Washington in Fremont for the Western Alameda County Conference opener tomorrow, March 7, and will face Div. 1 NCS opponent California at home on Friday. It also will play Div. 2 powerhouse Novato at Witter Field on March 12. 6-4 loss to Casa Grande Piedmont trailed 2-1 by the end of the first quarter and 3-2 by halftime. Casa Grande scored three goals in the third quarter while the Highlanders added one to make it 6-3 entering the fourth. PHS didn’t allow another goal in the remaining minutes, but only got one more on the board. Fredericks scored once in the first quarter at the 9:25 mark, but Casa Grande responded two minutes later and took the lead with 4:47 left in the first. Casa Grande extended the lead with slightly less than 10 minutes left in the second quarter, but Oliver Shafroth won the faceoff and scored a goal on the very next possession, 3-2. Rylan Nelson scored three goals in two games. Gus Von Metszch had eight saves against Casa Grande and 15 against Serra.

articles.text: Swain, a freshman, continues to excel Sebastien Swain (#18) placed eighth of 249 runners in the 800 meters at the Dan Gabor Invitational. Members of Piedmont’s track team traveled to Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton last week to compete in the annual Dan Gabor Invitational along with athletes from 47 other schools and hundreds of athletes. The meet It marked another impressive run by freshman Sebastien Swain, who placed eighth in a massive field of 249 runners in the 800 meter run. He clocked a time of 2:01.69, a very fast time for a freshman. “If you watched Seb’s race Saturday, you’ll be surprised to know it was only his third 800 ever. He got out nicely, settled in, and he and the winner pulled away from the pack at the end. He’s again broken his own PHS freshman record and is already one of the top 800 runners across all 155 schools in the North Coast Section,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. Also in the 800, sophomore Noah Sohn placed 67th in 2:14.71, freshman Thomas Ero was 79th in 2:16.56, and junior Oliver Horsley clocked in at 2:19.12. Xander Schulte-Sasse showed his experience and skill in the 3200, placing 10th of 111 runners in 9:39.52. Schulte-Sasse also placed 15th of 407 milers in the 1600, the largest field of the event. He posted a time of 4:31.86. Julien Lee also ran in the 3200 and 1600. He finished 21st in the 3200 with a time of 10:06.52, while he was 82nd in the 1600 in 4:53.59. Freshman Alex Schleuning ran the 3200, placing 83rd in 12:07.99. Sophomore Marius Arno competed in multiple events. He was 18th in the 300 hurdles in 47.10, was 73rd of 321 sprinters in the 100 in 12.16, and was 11th of 18 in the pole vault with a height of 9 feet, 6 inches. articles.text: Museo Italo Americano presents “Riccardo Rossati: Villa Arconati & Imaginary Worlds” at Fort Mason Center For Arts and Culture in San Francisco now through March 31. Italian artist Rossati was born in Rome into a family of painters, and studied under celebrated painters in China, Singapore, Thailand and Paris. Rossati is influenced by the alchemy of pigments, and said at a very young age that he discovered the art of oil painting. He studied the masters of the Italian Renaissance and modern expressionism at the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome. This exhibition features the enchanting Villa Arconati, a grand Baroque style palace nestled near the city of Milan. Rossati’s paintings provide a mesmerizing glimpse into the artist’s distinctive perspective of the ItalRiccardo Rossati ian historical site. Hours of the exhibit are Tuesday through Saturday, 12:00 to 4:00 p.m. and Sunday, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The exhibit will be on view through Sunday, March 31. To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://fortmason. org/event/museo-riccardo-ross a t i -v i l l a - a r c o n a t i -i m a g i - nary-worlds/.
articles.title: Riccardo Rossati art exhibit at Fort Mason through March 31

articles.text: Tickets are now on sale for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Art Bash, the museum’s major annual fundraiser that helps fund the museum’s education, family programs and community engagement events, benefiting over 150,000 people every year. This year’s Art Bash begins at 5 p.m. on Wednesday, April 24 with a cocktail reception and immersive dinner experience designed by iconic filmmaker and installation artist Isaac Julien. Julien’s filmmaking career began with his celebrated 1989 drama-documentary Looking for Langston, an exploration of the poet Langston Hughes and the Harlem Renaissance. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2017 Birthday Honors for services to the arts. Art Bash 2024 will feature photography and large-scale images from the artist’s series Ten Thousand Waves. The dinner program will be followed by a lounge experience for dinner guests at 8 p.m., and will include Solo to Symphony, a multidisciplinary installation conceived by Bay Area–based artist Richard Misrach, an American photographer known for his portrayal of deserts of the American West. A late-night party begins at 10 p.m. and includes art, live music, museum exhibitions and complimentary food and drink with ticket purchases. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse presents Rent, directed by Kimberly Dooley, playing onstage now through March 31. Based loosely on Puccini’s La Boheme but set in the East Village of New York City, Rent is a story about love, finding your voice and living for today. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, Jonathan Larson’s 1996 Broadway musical quickly became a pop cultural phenomenon. It was adapted into a musical drama film directed by Chris Columbus in 2005 to widespread acclaim. Larson’s Rent follows a year in the life of a group of impoverished young artists and musicians struggling to survive and create in New York City during the HIV/ AIDS epidemic. The Berkeley Playhouse production is co-directed by Peet Cocke, with musical direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Mel Martinez. Cast includes Sleiman Alahmadieh as Roger, Kassandra Lopez as Mimi, Tommy Lassiter as Mark, Anthony Rollins as Collins, Alex Rodriguez as Angel, Andrea Rae as Maureen, Lucca Troutman as Joanne, and Marshall Forte as Benny, with more cast members rounding out the ensemble. Run time is two hours and thirty minutes, with a fifteen-minute intermission. To purchase tickets, visit https://tickets. berkeleyplayhouse.org. The cast of Berkeley Playhouse’s Rent Photo by Ben Krantz
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse presents Rent now through March 31

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate its brass musicians with an all-brass concert at Davies Symphony Hall this Sunday, March 10. Trumpet, French horn, trombone, and tuba players will be led by conductor Brad Hogarth to bring the instruments’ big, bold and distinctive sound front and center. Hogarth is the Associate Professor of Conducting at San Francisco State University, and was recently named Associate Conductor of the Monterey Symphony. He is the music director and conductor of the Art Haus Collective and is also an accomplished trumpeter who performs regularly with a number of orchestras, including the Indianapolis Symphony and Louisville Orchestra. As a guest conductor, he has appeared with the Diablo Symphony Orchestra, the ECHO Chamber Orchestra, the San Francisco Wind Ensemble and the Oakland Municipal Band. The evening’s program will highlight concert music for brass, percussion, and timpani. The program includes Presto Barbaro from Symphonic Suite Photo by Kristen-Loken San Francisco Symphony brass musicians from On the Waterfront by Leonard Bernstein, Ottoni by Magnus Lindberg, Quatre Motets sur des thèmes grégoriens by Maurice Duruflé, A Moorside Suite by Gustav Holst, Variations on a Theme by Paganini Witold Lutosławski, and Chicago Skyline by Shulamit Ran. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Ticket s /2023 -24/SF- SY M PHO - NY-BRASS.
articles.title: SF Symphony’s brass ensemble in concert this Sunday

articles.text: Play ends on March 10 American Conservatory Theater’s production of Big Data ends on Sunday, March 10. Tickets are still available for showtimes this week. Written by Kate Attwell and directed by ACT’s Artistic Director and Tony Award winner Pam Mackinnon, Big Data is a modern-day love story awash in techPhoto by Kevin Berne Gabriel Brown (left), Rosie Hallett, and Michael Phillis in Big Data, on stage at ACT in San Francisco until March 10 nology and the dizzying possibilities of artificial intelligence. The play follows four young people. Sam loves Timmy, and Lucy loves Max, but they all succumb to the addiction of technology and smart devices. When Sam and Lucy’s parents make a shocking announcement, the family is forced to confront the technology that has distracted them from each other and the legacy they’ll leave behind. MacKinnon and Attwell reunite to bring this revolutionary piece to audiences, inspired by Attwell’s experience touring search engine platform Mozilla’s “Glass Room” pop-up interactive exhibit in San Francisco. The cast includes Gabriel Brown, Rosie Hallett, Julia McNeal, Michael Phillis, Harold Surratt, Jomar Tagatac and BD Wong. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/2023-24-season/big-data/. Please join us for the 16th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the Tower Chapel Friday, March 22 – Sunday, March 24 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. Free Admission!
articles.title: Last Chance to see ACT’s Big Data

articles.text: Oakland Ballet’s Dancing Moons Festival takes place in Oakland and San Francisco this Spring. Oakland Ballet will present its third annual Dancing Moons Festival March 14 through April 6 at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland and ODC Theater in San Francisco. The program is choreographed by all-Asian American Pacific Islander talent and will include a preview of the dance company’s Angel Island Project with choreography by Natasha Adorlee and Feng Ye. The project took inspiration from poetry carved by detainees held at the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station held thousands of immigrants through 1910 and 1940, mainly from China, Japan, India and the Philippines. “With captured imaginations, we take on a flight of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved in the walls by detainees,” Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig said. “The Angel Island Project helps us to trace who we are today by remembering from where we came.” Several selections will also be presented at the festival as works in progress, including Layer Upon Layer by Caili Quan (2022), Ballet des Porcelaines or The Teapot Prince by Phil Chan (original 1739; reimagined 2021), and highlights of Exquisite Corpse by Elaine Kudo, Seyong Kim, and Phil Chan (2023). For the first time since the festival’s inception, an exhibition of visual artists will be displayed at the cultural center. Artists include Asian Americans Sanjay Vora, Mark Shigenga and JaYing Wang. March 14 through 16 performances will take place at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland, and April 5 and 6 performances take place at the ODC Theatre in San Francisco. Showtimes vary. To purchase tickets, visit https://oaklandballet.org/ dancing-moons-festival/.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet Dancing Moons Festival begins March 14

Long before director/writer John Maloof conceived of creating the documentary film Finding Vivian Maier, he went to a local auction where he bought a cache of negatives, hoping that he might find something of interest for a history of his neighborhood that he was writing. Once home he looked at a few samples and concluded there was nothing he could use for his book. He put the box on a shelf where it remained for some time. Only later when he took a closer look, Maloof realized that the photographs, taken by a street photographer he had never heard of, a Vivian Maier, were surprisingly good. Beyond good – extraordinary, he decided. Wondering who this woman was, and assuming her work had been shown in galleries, he began a process of inquiry that would surprise him in countless ways. After acquiring more of Maier’s work, Maloof had some 100,000 negatives in his possession. As he soon learned, Maier (1926-2009) had shot hundreds of rolls of film, some never developed; many simply kept in their containers and left in cardboard boxes. He found no actual photos until he began to develop samples from the stacks of negatives. What he saw, in black and white (rarely in color), were haunting, stark, street photos shot with a Rolleiflex twin-lens reflex camera. The subjects were rarely posed, many pictures of the urban dispossessed, hundreds were unforgiving photos of those who, like so much flotsam and jetsam, reside on the edges of society. Most simply stared into the camera as if startled or curious. Maier and her camera might have been intrusive after the fact, but not in the moment. The moment shows an existenStreet photographer Vivian Maier is the subject of John Maloof’s documentary film Finding Vivian Maier. tial truth that is compelling. Most of her pictures, no matter the setting or subject, have a sense of melancholy, while others possess a penetrating bleakness, often raw and unadorned, street portraits of inner-city denizens, often invisible, except to Vivian Maier. There are also photos of children, some with an element of unexpected warmth and playfulness. What Vivian Maier created was art and her work is suffused with humanity in all its permutations. But then Maloof and co-director Charlie Siskel make two decisions that push Finding Vivian Maier, with all its potential, toward the mundane. First they structure the film using a documentary format of offering up background information using standard full-face interviews with those who knew Maier. As it turns out, Maier was a nanny, working in some of the toniest parts of Chicago, taking care of the children of the affluent. Her childhood was spent in France with her French mother and Austrian father. Gradually, it becomes clear that Maier is a damaged human being, reclusive, obsessive, a hoarder, suspicious of men, never married and, of course, childless. Some of the adults who were once under her care as children insisted she had a dark side and could be cruel, even physically abusive. Clearly, the contrast between her as a person and her work, which demonstrates an overriding compassion, suggests an inherent dissonance. And that is the second question begged: while the filmmakers manage to create a mystery of sorts, how important is it to know the details of an artist’s life while judging his or her work? Is it necessary to know that Hemingway killed himself? The essence of Finding Vivian

articles.text: Nicole Kidman and Aaron Eckhart in Rabbit Hole There are some life experiences from which there is no recovery. No matter how often the word “closure” is offered as an outcome, in truth, there will never be closure when parents lose a child. The only imponderable question is how those who face such tragedy endure. For that is what they must do. How they endure is the essence of Rabbit Hole. The film begins with Howie (Aaron Eckhart) and Becca (Oscar-nominated Nicole Kidman) clinging to their routines while they cope with canyons of distance between them. The tension is palpable. Only gradually is it revealed that the source of their pain – the spare conversations, the brittle quality to their relationship – is the loss eight months prior of their 4-year-old son. He chased their dog into the street and was hit by a car. The performances of both Kidman and Eckhart are brilliantly crafted. Each copes with grief in completely different ways. The contrasts are both a strength and a weakness. How they navigate this tortured road,

Their Of all the “Star Trek” films made to date, perhaps the most accessible is “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home,” receiving four Oscar nominations. You don’t have to be a Trekkie to enjoy this movie. Though it follows “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock” and the first few minutes of “Voyage Home” make a loose connection to “III”, “IV” easily stands The premise is deceptively simple: It’s the late 23rd century and a space probe of unknown origins is approaching earth, sending out a signal that is at first indecipherable. The force field from the probe is shutting down all electrical grids on earth and is, in effect, destroying the planet. The crew of the Enterprise, their starship destroyed, and having hijacked a Klingon vessel in need of repairs, is stranded on the planet Vulcan. Their plan is to return to earth and stand trial for crimes against the Federation. They pick up transmissions not only from the probe, but distress calls from earth. Finally breaking the probe’s code, they determine that it is sending out a series of whale calls, or humpback whale songs. Because whales are extinct in the 23rd century, the crew decides that the only solution is to travel back in time, to the late 20th century, beam up two whales, and return them to their time. And so they travel back in time, to San Francisco, landing the cloaked Klingon ship in Golden Gate Park. The crew then ventures forth, walking the streets of San Francisco in search of two whales and a nuclear energy source to power the ship. Their time in San Francisco is inspired. The juxtaposition of the crew with the locals makes for some interesting moments. An embedded joke is that even though they are all dressed in Starfleet uniforms (with the exception of Spock, who is wearing a white terry cloth robe and an aerobic headband to hide his ears), no one pays them any attention. This is, after all, San Francisco, which is very hip and laid-back. The encounters of the crew with the locals are wonderful, often comedic, and just restrained enough to never slide into parody. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, March 6, 2024 MOVIE FOR KIDS Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home By Chris Honoré The year was 1966 and a Sci Fi series called “Star Trek” debuted on television, promising to “boldly go where no man has gone before.” Now, some 44 years later, improbably, “Star Trek” has morphed into a cultural phenomenon resulting in not only television syndication of the original show, but spin offs, books, comics, video games and, for a time, a themed attraction in Las Vegas that drew thousands of what came to be known as “Trekkies.” In other words, Star Trek evolved from those early days into a worldwide entertainment juggernaut, resonating with generations of fans, and possessing a cult following wherein hard-core Trekkies peruse endless layers of narrative minutiae, characterization and predictive technology. In 1979 the first feature length film was made – “Star Trek: The Motion Picture” – launching what would become a successful franchise, starring the original multiethnic cast from the television series. Names such as Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Captain Kirk (William Shatner), Lt. Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), and “Bones” McCoy (DeForest Kelley) are now part of our lexicon, as is the phrase, “beam me up.” In fact, NASA named its prototype space shuttle the Enterprise after the fictional starship. Since the first “Star Trek” was screened, 10 movies have followed – the most recent, “Star Trek,” a prequel — with the The cast of Star Trek reprise their role in the movie Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home. 12th in preproduction, due to be released in June of 2012. Their appeal is indisputable. Of all the “Star Trek” films made to date, perhaps the most accessible is “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home,” receiving four Oscar nominations. You don’t have to be a Trekkie to enjoy this movie. Though it follows “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock” and the first few minutes of “Voyage Home” make a loose connection to “III”, “IV” easily stands alone. The premise is deceptively simple: It’s the late 23rd century and a space probe of unknown origins is approaching earth, sending out a signal that is at first indecipherable. The force field from the probe is shutting down all electrical grids on earth and is, in effect, destroying the planet. The crew of the Enterprise, their starship destroyed, and having hijacked a Klingon vessel in need of repairs, is stranded on the planet Vulcan. Their plan is to return to earth and stand trial for crimes against the Federation. They pick up transmissions not only from the probe, but distress calls from earth. Finally breaking the probe’s code, they determine that it is sending out a series of whale calls, or humpback whale songs. Because whales are extinct in the 23rd century, the crew decides that the only solution is to travel back in time, to the late 20th century, beam up two whales, and return them to their time. And so they travel back in time, to San Francisco, landing the cloaked Klingon ship in Golden Gate Park. The crew then ventures forth, walking the streets of San Francisco in search of two whales and a nuclear energy source to power the ship. Their time in San Francisco is inspired. The juxtaposition of the crew with the locals makes for some interesting moments. An embedded joke is that even though they are all dressed in Starfleet uniforms (with the exception of Spock, who is wearing a white terry cloth robe and an aerobic headband to hide his ears), no one pays them any attention. This is, after all, San Francisco, which is very hip and laid-back. The encounters of the crew with the locals are wonderful, often comedic, and just restrained enough to never slide into parody. There’s also a mild romantic tension (atypical to be sure) between Kirk and a marine biologist, Dr. Gillian Taylor (Catherine Hicks). The conflict in the film stems from the urgency of the hunt. Earth in the future is in peril; time is of the essence. Unlike other “Trek” films, there are no villains in “Voyage Home” – well, perhaps there are, meaning the whalers who have hunted the humpbacks to extinction, a reality that Spock points out is “illogical.” There is, of course, the probe, needed only as a brief catalyst for sending the crew back in time. The co-author and producer of “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home,” Harve Bennett, will make a guest appearance at Saturday’s screening and take questions at the end of the film. Bennett was born in Chicago in 1930 and has spent most of his life, since graduating from UCLA’s film school, producing television shows for ABC and CBS, as well as feature length films. He co-authored, produced, and made cameo appearances in four of the “Star Trek” films – “The Wrath of Khan”; “The Search for Spock”; “The Voyage Home”; and “The Final Frontier.” Now living in Ashland, he considers himself “semi-retired.” Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home.
