articles.text: Toda,y I found a hang tag on my door from the Piedmont Police informing me that PPD was moving ahead with the next phase of ALPR (Automated License Plate Recognition). This is a very good step. Chief Bowers has said in the past that the ALPRs play an extremely important role in combatting crime in the city. It also reminded me that I had been meaning to address this issue in the Post for many months, but I had not achieved a great enough level of crabbiness to do so. And even though Wiley is feeling pretty mellow today, he’s going to write the article anyway. My shrewd power of observation has led me to deduce that there are a lot of cars in Piedmont without front license plates. In fact, every time I have conducted an informal visual survey at the corner of Oakland and Highland, I have found that about half of the cars that go by have no front plates. My power of analytical thinking has led me to deduce that if a car has both front and back plates, it is significantly more likely to be recognized by the ALPR. And being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Let me repeat that: Being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Who are these scofflaws (what a great word)? Most of them are otherwise law-abiding citizens of Piedmont, who generally stop at stop signs, support our great police department, and keep voting to tax themselves to keep the city solvent. Most of them drive expensive cars like Audis, BMWs, Land Rovers, Range Rovers, Porsches, and Teslas. (Please note that I did not include Mercedes Benz in the above list. You seldom see a Mercedes with only one plate. Mercedes owners are old money, and old money people wouldn’t think of ignoring the law. They probably even tell the truth on their taxes.) Why do these scofflaws continue to thumb their noses at California Vehicle Code 5200(a) which states that “When two license plates are issued by the department for use upon a vehicle, they shall be attached to the vehicle for which they were issued, one in the front and the other in the rear.”? As Wiley sees it, there are two reasons: practicality and visual appeal. In the past few years, grilles on cars have grown so large (and ugly, IMHO) that there really isn’t much space below for a plate. Try attaching a license plate to a car where the grille takes up 90% of the front and let me know what happens. As for visual appeal, even Wiley will agree that a cool BMW or Porsche, with its sleek, tailored front styling, looks better without a plate disturbing its design. Installing a front plate would be like telling Zendaya (or Jennifer Anniston, if you are of Wiley’s generation) that she needs to do a better job on her makeup. But it is time for this lawlessness to come to an end. From a completely practical standpoint, the law makes sense. It makes it easier for ALPRs and police to recognize when something is out of whack. If CVC 5200(a) were enforced, any car without a front plate would be subject to a legal vehicle stop. I’m not saying that this would happen – PPD has enough on its hands that it wouldn’t and couldn’t. But it would give PPD the opportunity to conduct a vehicle stop if something didn’t seem right without being accused of racial or ethnic profiling. Now, Wiley is not saying that PPD should start enforcing the code tomorrow. Clearly, communication is key. PPD should choose a date several months in the future, publicize it widely, and begin putting notes on the windshields of parked cars without front plates informing the owners that they need to comply with the law. In other words, use a velvet glove. Finally, how do we deal with the outrage from Mr. Upstanding Citizen who gets his first ticket? Well, the ticket will be the “fix it” variety. So, MUC puts on the license plate that has been gathering dust in the garage, drives down to PPD HQ, and gets an officer to sign off on it. He then sends it in to the court and pays an administrative fee, probably $25. He and the missus may have to go without lattes from Starbucks for a day or two, but it will be an inexpensive life lesson. These days, it’s difficult to have a conversation with a Piedmont citizen without the subject of public safety coming up. As citizens, we need to do our part. We cannot rely on PPD, with its limited resources, to do everything. So, let’s make it easier for them to do their job and to protect us by putting those d**n front license plates on our cars. Note: Wiley’s wife drives a Tesla, which Wiley hates, but at least it has front and back license plates. Wiley Hoag is a Piedmont resident and the Piedmont Post’s Consumer Affairs columnist.
articles.title: CONSUMER AFFAIRS Let’s be “Up Front” on license plates

pages.text: Wednesday, March 6, 2024 21 Features CONSUMER AFFAIRS Girl and her Dog Farm Michelle Docter and Rita show their harvest. Tucked behind a wooden fence in Albany lies a backyard you may not expect. Monarch butterflies and bees dance from sweet peas to broccoli. The classic Bay Area clay soil is worked with rich compost. Almost every inch of arable land holds an edible crop. This backyard isn’t just a backyard – it’s a farm and home to a small CSA program, Girl And Her Dog Farm, run by Michelle Docter and her dog Rita. This small Community Supported Agriculture feeds a handful of families every other week from spring to fall. Veggies, fruits, herbs, and fresh flower bouquets are all grown organically within the front and back yards and crafted into a produce box for delivery. Neighbors stop by while we refresh garden beds to admire the zinnias or ask how to stop the deer from devouring everything. Though small in size, the farm is creating community around homegrown food. Whether it’s a next door neighbor or a CSA member, they not only know who grows this food, but they’re learning about the variety of carrots planted. They get to see our growing practices that take a carrot from seed to soil and to their plate. While we’d love to curate produce boxes for all our neighbors, our Bay Area backyard just won’t cut it. The limited space in the backyard kindled our garden consulting service, teaching others how to grow food in their own space. After apprenticing at the UC Santa Cruz Farm, I want to share the skills and knowledge I learned on a big scale farm to a small-scale backyard. Growing just a small kitchen garden to snip herbs for a family meal or sowing enough lettuce for a weekly salad is what we hope to inspire and help create for all our neighbors. To spark that inspiration in our favorite way, my sweet dog and I jump in front of the camera, creating helpful videos on Youtube and Instagram. We share tips and tricks in the garden from starting a compost bin to planting a bed of tomatoes. There’s almost always something to make our audience smile. I’m delighted to also be writing a monthly column for the Piedmont Post where I can share more in depth gardening advice. With spring right around the corner, it’s the perfect time to start that garden you’ve always dreamed of. Now is actually a great time to add compost to your desired planting space and sow seeds, like: peas, lettuce, arugula, spinach, carrots, and beets. If starting on your own feels too daunting, please reach out. I’m excited to be able to help neighbors grow their own backyard farms. Girl And Her Dog Farm is run by backyard farmer Michelle Docter in Albany, CA. It offers nacluard CSA produce, homebaked breads, and kitchen garden designs. In fact, every time I have conducted an informal visual survey at the corner of Oakland and Highland, I have found that about half of the cars that go by have no front plates. My power of analytical thinking has led me to deduce that if a car has both front and back plates, it is significantly more likely to be recognized by the ALPR. And being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Let me repeat that: Being recognized by the ALPR system is a matter of public safety. Who are these scofflaws (what a great word)? Most of them are otherwise law-abiding citizens of Piedmont, who generally stop at stop signs, support our great police department, and keep voting to tax themselves to keep the city solvent. Most of them drive expensive cars like Audis, BMWs, Land Rovers, Range Rovers, Porsches, and Teslas. (Please note that I did not include Mercedes Benz in the above list. You seldom see a Mercedes with only one plate. Mercedes owners are old money, and old money people wouldn’t think of ignoring the law. They probably even tell the truth on their taxes.) Why do these scofflaws continue to thumb their noses at California Vehicle Code 5200(a) which states that “When two license plates are issued by the department for use upon a vehicle, they shall be attached to the vehicle for which they were issued, one in the front and the other in the rear.”? As Wiley sees it, there are two reasons: practicality and visual appeal. In the past few years, grilles on cars have grown so large (and ugly, IMHO) that there really isn’t much space below for a plate. Try Let’s be “Up Front” on license plates attaching a license plate to a car where the grille takes up 90% of the front and let me know what happens. As for visual appeal, even Wiley will agree that a cool BMW or Porsche, with its sleek, tailored front styling, looks better without a plate disturbing its design. Installing a front plate would be like telling Zendaya (or Jennifer Anniston, if you are of Wiley’s generation) that she needs to do a better job on her makeup. But it is time for this lawlessness to come to an end. From a completely practical standpoint, the law makes sense. It makes it easier for ALPRs and police to recognize when something is out of whack. If CVC 5200(a) were enforced, any car without a front plate would be subject to a legal vehicle stop. I’m not saying that this would happen – PPD has enough on its hands that it wouldn’t and couldn’t. But it would give PPD the opportunity to conduct a vehicle stop if something didn’t seem right without being accused of racial or ethnic profiling. Now, Wiley is not saying that PPD should start enforcing the code tomorrow. Clearly, communication is key. PPD should choose a date several months in the future, publicize it widely, and begin putting notes on the windshields of parked cars without front plates informing the owners that they need to comply with the law. In other words, use a velvet glove. Finally, how do we deal with the outrage from Mr. Upstanding Citizen who gets his first ticket? Well, the ticket will be the “fix it” variety. So, MUC puts on the license plate that has been gathering dust in the garage, drives down to PPD HQ, and gets an officer to sign off on it. He then sends it in to the court and pays an administrative fee, probably $25. He and the missus may have to go without lattes from Starbucks for a day or two, but it will be an inexpensive life lesson. These days, it’s difficult to have a conversation with a Piedmont citizen without the subject of public safety coming up. As citizens, we need to do our part. We cannot rely on PPD, with its limited resources, to do everything. So, let’s make it easier for them to do their job and to protect us by putting those d**n front license plates on our cars. Note: Wiley’s wife drives a Tesla, which Wiley hates, but at least it has front and back license plates. Wiley Hoag is a Piedmont resident and the Piedmont Post’s Consumer Affairs columnist. articles.text: After some earlier wet Wednesdays this year, February 21 was a good time for the Walking on Wednesdays group, and a solid turnout of 37 walkers and one K-9 best were on hand to enjoy it. Piedmont students were on February break (Ski Week), so it was a good time to visit empty schoolyards. At El Cerrito Avenue they had to cross the first of a number of streets where bulbouts were being added to intersections on Oakland Avenue. The group continued down Oakland and onto Greenbank Avenue. They noted a charming Victorian home built in 1896 with a white picket fence, chairs, and a children’s swing in the front yard. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and climbed up Greenbank to Lake Avenue then onto Nace and Howard Avenues before continuing on Lake to Beach School. This part of Piedmont goes back to the city’s early days. The homes on Nace, Howard, and Lake were built started in 1908. The oldest Nace house was built in 1910. Egbert Beach Elementary School can tie its history to the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. On that April 18th morning thousands of people fled the city to the East Bay. Many decided not to return to San Francisco, and Piedmont grew ten times over the next year. Piedmont was incorpoThe original Beach School, which opened in 1913, was the second elementary school built in Piedmont is as many years following the city’s rapid expansion in the early twentieth century. rated the following year in September 1907. City leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The first school was named “The Bonita Avenue School” and later renamed after the land donor, Frank C. Havens. It opened in 1911. The Bonita Avenue School quickly filled, and in 1913 the Lake Avenue School was built. It had four teachers and 100 students in six grades. In 1918 the school was renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in honor of the first Piedmont resident killed in World War I. The rapid growth of Piedmont from 1920 to 1930 created school housing needs that could not be met with available school funds. Beach students were taught in cramped, wooden portables that were called “shacks” by the locals. In 1933 the school buildings were condemned as firetraps and an earthquake menace. They were torn down in 1934 and replaced by two buildings as part of the federal government’s WPA projects. The main wing was built in 1936, and the auditorium/classroom wing was added in 1940, an entire new building of eight classrooms, kindergarten, administrative area, library, health room and auditorium. The group then continued to the Linda Beach courts next to the school. Quincy Dong explained that in an attempt to address neighbors’ noise issues, there is no pickleball on Wednesdays. articles.text: It’s time to save the date for the third annual Piedmont Food Fest. The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival is returning to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 20 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. This volunteer event was created post-pandemic, three years ago as a way to build community through diverse food, drink. and music. It has evolved into a broader showcase of the Bay’s most distinctive cuisines, cultural performances, and community groups. It has also attracted over 3000 attendees and generated over $100,000 for local businesses. Attendees have appreciated the chance to spend the day connecting with each other amid a medley of flavors, sounds, and cultures – all gathered in one place. “Piedmont Food Fest was an absolute treat for the whole family – a not-to-miss community event centered around connection and diversity,” said Havens parent Katie Castles Shaffer. “We love the Piedmont Food Fest, Being able to spend an afternoon with friends and community and have our kids entertained with the kids zone makes this an event we’ll look forward to every year. We especially appreciate the organizers’ dedication to having diverse representation of food, vendors and entertainment.” added Piedmont resident Amanda Feldman. Piedmont Food Fest 3 will feature over 19 food vendors including Crazy Empanadas, Robert Dorsey Catering, La Santa Torta, Momolicious, Arthur Mac’s, Lahor Di Khushboo, The Chairman, and Oakland Bloom as well as beer & wine tasting from local favorites including Federation Brewing, Two Broads Ciderworks, and Deer Hill Vineyards. Main stage performances will include Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, O Hina’aro Tahitian Dance & Music, Beloved Little Circus, and the Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator. Junior food festers can look forward to an enhanced KidZone with both carnival and multicultural craft stations. Please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org to sign up for event updates as well as checking out Early Bird specials available through March. This event is free to attend and all are encouraged to invite friends and family to come for a memorable day in Piedmont.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Quick soda bread with whole wheat and walnuts St. Patrick’s Day is just around the corner and the American tradition of corned beef and cabbage will be making an appearance on our table. I look forward to this time of year when I begin seeing corned beef appearing at our markets. I’ve previously shared my colcannon recipe, my family’s favorite dish of the meal, and now I’m sharing a quick soda bread I also prepare. You can toast the walnuts for additional flavor, as well as the wheat germ (if adding), but often I skip the toasting step and the bread is very tasty. This dough is pretty forgiving so you can take it to a sweet direction by adding a bit of dried fruit, or in a savory direction with some freshly snipped herbs and a bit of grated or tiny cubed cheese. Quick Soda Bread with Whole Wheat and Walnuts Adapted from America’s Test Kitchen, March 2013 Makes a one-pound loaf (approximate weight depending upon add-ins) INGREDIENTS • 1-1/4 cup all-purpose flour • 1/2 cup whole-wheat flour • 2 tablespoons wheat germ, toasted, optional • 1 tablespoon granulated sugar • 3/4 teaspoon sea salt • 3/4 teaspoon baking soda • 1/2 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 cup walnuts, coarsely chopped • 7 fl. ounces, 7/8 cup, buttermilk, chilled and preferably whole fat • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly; plus an additional 1 tablespoon melted to brush over the baked loaf INSTRUCTIONS Adjust an oven rack to the lower-middle position. Preheat the oven to 400° F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper and set aside. Whisk the flours, wheat germ (if using), sugar, salt, baking soda and powder together. Stir in the walnuts. Add the two tablespoons of melted butter into the chilled buttermilk. The butter will clump a bit when added to the cold buttermilk, which is what you want. Stir to break up any large lumps. These lumps of butter will translate into small, small, airy pockets in the finished loaf. Stir with a spatula until the dough just barely comes together. There will be some pockets of unincorporated flour and the dough will be shaggy, not at all cohesive. Turn onto a lightly floured surface then knead and turn a few times until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork the dough. It will be sticky but manageable. Shape into about a 4-1/2 to 5-inch round, about 2-inches tall. Place on the parchment lined baking sheet. Slice a large cross, or plus sign (+), about 1/4-inch deep and coming to about an inch from the edges with a sharp knife. The slicing is important to guide the bread’s expansion whilst it bakes. Bake about 45–50 minutes until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean, or about 195° F on an instant-read thermometer. Rotate the pan around midway through the baking. Remove the bread from the oven and brush on the remaining one tablespoon of melted butter. Transfer the loaf to a wire rack to cool for at least 30 minutes before slicing. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com

articles.text: Dear Jim: I have water in my basement, and I’m experiencing flooding for the first time ever. I work out of my basement, so I need a permanent solution. Even the crawlspace next to it is wet and mold is developing. What should I do? Why is this happening? Most older homes in our area have inadequate drainage systems, and many have no drainage at all. Clay piping systems which were used as foundation drains when the homes were built were laid in small sections and are all filled with dirt and no longer working. Most downspouts still drain onto the ground next to your home, causing settlement problems and allowing water A new French drain is below the adjacent basement elevation. Dual membranes at the foundation provide additional protection. Flooded basements and crawlspaces need drainage help. inside. Add in climate change and extreme water events and this is a recipe for disaster. Why is this so difficult to fix? Most drainage work is done by landscapers, handymen, laborers or General Contractors who don’t understand the complexity of proper drainage. They make fundamental errors in designing their drainage solutions which often make the problems worse. The number of actual experienced drainage contractors in our area can probably be counted on one hand. What is the solution? Proper drainage generally consists of French Drains to handle underground water and separate downspout and area drains to handle surface water, and these are used in combination along with membranes to protect your foundation. Water needs to end up in either a drain field on your property or at the street. Sump pumps are most often only an external solution tied into your drainage system to remove water when the new drains can’t slope downhill to their endpoint. The location and depth of these drains and attention to detail particularly with the membrane system are crucial to their success. The Top 3 Things to remember: 1. Interior sump pumps are not the answer. When placed in your basement or crawlspace they typically only remove water directly adjacent to them. 2. You may need to go deep. French drains must extend at least a foot below the area they are trying to protect. Drainage that is too shallow will often make your problem worse. 3. Don’t fall for interior drainage solutions for your basement. While they are cheaper, drains on the inside next to your basement walls can undermine your foundations and don’t protect them from deterioration. articles.text: Bob Wright, a pillar of Piedmont Community Church, died on January 20, 2024 of a heart attack while on vacation in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany. He was 80, and quite literally “died with his boots on”, while heading up the mountain for the last ski run of the day. He left this world as he lived in it, full of life and tackling adventures head on. Born Robert Bruce Wright on January 22, 1943, he was the son of William Bruce Wright and Thelma Brown Wright of Topeka, Kansas. Despite losing his father at a very young age, Bob grew up in a loving family and enjoyed a happy childhood. He was very active in the local Episcopal Church, serving as an altar boy for many years. He attended Topeka High School, where he was well liked and admired by his peers. After graduating from high school, Bob left Kansas for California, where he attended the University of the Pacific in Stockton. It was there he met the love of his life, his future wife Judith Meadows (later Wright). The two of them started out as “just good friends”, but eventually realized that there was a lot more than friendship there. The first year of their relationship was one of long distance, as Bob had been accepted to a year-long study abroad program in Denmark. Their commitment to each other remained steadfast, and excited to start their lives together as a married couple, they were married on August 28, 1965. Early in his marriage, Bob felt the call to serve his country, and joined the Marine Corps, serving a tour in Vietnam in 1967. After the birth of their first child, he chose to leave active duty military service in 1969, and continue his commitment to the Marines as an officer in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. He served for over 20 years and reached the rank of Colonel before retiring with full military honors in 1992. In addition to his military service, Bob had a distinguished career as a telecommunications Sales Executive with Pac Bell/AT&T, the culmination of which was an overseas assignment as Vice President of International Sales for Southeast Asia. Upon retirement from AT&T and his return to the U.S. in 1998, Bob continued his life of service. He was active in the community, most especially in the Piedmont Community Church. His love Bob Wright, a longtime member of Piedmont Community Church, died on January 20 while skiing in Germany on vacation. for and devotion to God and his church family were an ever-present part of his life. He served on multiple church boards, as well as headed multiple committees, projects, and small groups within the fellowship. His acts of charity, assistance, leadership and mentorship touched the lives of thousands. Everyone who knew Bob knew of his insatiable sense of wanderlust. Bob and Judy travelled extensively, managing to visit dozens of countries on all seven continents. He was an avid hiker, fisherman, and of course, skier. He threw himself with enthusiasm into high-adventure activities like ziplining well into his 70s. He was particularly a fan of cruising, and visited many exotic locations via Viking Ocean, River, and Expedition ships. He was never happier than when traveling with friends and family and sharing adventures with them. Bob is survived by his wife Judith Wright, and children Lisa Wright and Mitchell Wright. He is preceded in death by his parents, William and Thelma, stepfather Lenel Shuck, and sister Patricia. Bob will always be remembered for his charitable heart and love of life. We will miss him every day. The memory of him will live on in the hearts of all those who loved him. Bob will be remembered at a Celebration of Life service on Saturday, March 23, at 11:00 a.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Memorial donations in his name may be made to a charity of choice.
articles.title: Bob Wright dies on January 20 at age 80

After graduating from high school, Bob left Kansas for California, where he attended the University of the Pacific in Stockton. It was there he met the love of his life, his future wife Judith Meadows (later Wright). The two of them started out as “just good friends”, but eventually realized that there was a lot more than friendship there. The first year of their relationship was one of long distance, as Bob had been accepted to a year-long study abroad program in Denmark. Their commitment to each other remained steadfast, and excited to start their lives together as a married couple, they were married on August 28, 1965. Early in his marriage, Bob felt the call to serve his country, and joined the Marine Corps, serving a tour in Vietnam in 1967. After the birth of their first child, he chose to leave active duty military service in 1969, and continue his commitment to the Marines as an officer in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. He served for over 20 years and reached the rank of Colonel before retiring with full military honors in 1992. In addition to his military service, Bob had a distinguished career as a telecommunications Sales Executive with Pac Bell/AT&T, the culmination of which was an overseas assignment as Vice President of International Sales for Southeast Asia. Upon retirement from AT&T and his return to the U.S. in 1998, Bob continued his life of service. He was active in the community, most especially in the Piedmont Community Church. His love Bob Wright, a longtime member of Piedmont Community Church, died on January 20 while skiing in Germany on vacation. for and devotion to God and his church family were an ever-present part of his life. He served on multiple church boards, as well as headed multiple committees, projects, and small groups within the fellowship. His acts of charity, assistance, leadership and mentorship touched the lives of thousands. Everyone who knew Bob knew of his insatiable sense of wanderlust. Bob and Judy travelled extensively, managing to visit dozens of countries on all seven continents. He was an avid hiker, fisherman, and of course, skier. He threw himself with enthusiasm into high-adventure activities like ziplining well into his 70s. He was particularly a fan of cruising, and visited many exotic locations via Viking Ocean, River, and Expedition ships. He was never happier than when traveling with friends and family and sharing adventures with them. Bob is survived by his wife Judith Wright, and children Lisa Wright and Mitchell Wright. He is preceded in death by his parents, William and Thelma, stepfather Lenel Shuck, and sister Patricia. Bob will always be remembered for his charitable heart and love of life. We will miss him every day. The memory of him will live on in the hearts of all those who loved him. Bob will be remembered at a Celebration of Life service on Saturday, March 23, at 11:00 a.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Memorial donations in his name may be made to a charity of choice. Democracy is not a spectator sport! Students also attended a performance at the Kennedy Center, visited museums including the Museum of African American History and Culture and the Holocaust Memorial Museum, and ended the trip by exploring Georgetown. “There were tight schedules but there was a lot of free time to hang out with friends and meet with other workshops. It was more fun than I had imagined,” said junior Toby Fleischer. “It was really eye opening,” said junior Alma Ruberto, “I realized that people who have different opinions are just normal people with nice personalities, even if I don’t agree with them on everything.” Ruberto and other Piedmont students had the opportunity to discuss prominent issues in the U.S. – like sexism, LGBTQ rights, and abortion rights – with other Close Up students. “The debating was my favorite,” Ruberto said. “That’s one of the things I wanted to do – actually talk to people from [throughout] the country [while] being in our nation’s capital. It was a lot of fun.” “We went to a lot of places in a short amount of time but it oddly never felt rushed,” said junior Raiyaan Shah. Shah also gave a closing speech at the farewell banquet at the end of the week, representing his workshop after getting strong encouragement from new friends in Arizona. “I thought it would be a fun new way to end the trip,” Shah said, “The Arizonians, being the master persuaders they are, convinced me I would do fine, and I guess I did!” “I had these moments when we were in the National Mall and walking back from the Botanical Gardens and I [thought], ‘That’s the Capitol. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, March 6, 2024 Street Repairs Continued from page 1 Despite the need for better street surfaces, Public Works claims that its funding limits the department’s ability to do major street repairs. “We always wish we had more money to spend. We want to improve conditions as much as possible, but we know that our chosen funding level is pretty much only good enough to keep things as they are but not to move it forward the way we want to,” said Gonzales. In terms of priority, Gonzales added that the streets for each resurfacing project are chosen carefully, and not necessarily in order of need. Sometimes, the department prioritizes the maintenance of existing roads with the heaviest traffic over the resurfacing of the worse streets. “In general, it is cheaper to perform maintenance on roadways [than to fully resurface streets]. That’s by far the most cost-effective thing to do to keep the roadways in good condition.” This year’s resurfacing project is expected to cost over $1.5 million. articles.text: A report delivered to City Council last week detailed an unusually high amount of overtime in the Piedmont Fire Department. During the annual midyear financial report presented on Tuesday, February 20, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore and Finance Director Michael Szczech explained that because of understaffing problems, which have plagued the department for several years, firefighters have had to work more overtime than typical. As a result, City Council has authorized an additional $125,000 to cover overtime costs through the end of the fiscal year. Szczech said that the overtime costs are mostly offset by the lower number of employees. Though the problem has been resolved in recent months and the department is now fully staffed, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said the period of low staffing and long hours had contributed to low morale at the station. Szczech sounded cautiously optimistic in his assessment of the Fire Department’s financial future. “The department, which was down as many as seven employees at one point, is now fully staffed. However, three of the new employees are attending the fire academy. So, overtime will continue to be high, but to a lesser extent in the second half of the year,” he said. “All fire departments are short right now,” explained Brannigan. Since the pandemic, there have been nationwide shortages of firefighters across the country, including in Piedmont. “It was very difficult for our current employees from late spring of 2023 until right about New Year’s this year. People were working a lot of extra shifts, and it was really starting to impact morale in their families.” Matters seem to have improved though, said Brannigan, with the addition of seven new hires in recent months. “It’s been challenging for sure, but we got some relief in December, and it’s much more manageable now,” he said. To prevent personnel shortages in the future, the department has adopted a proactive hiring policy. “We are working on ongoing recruitment, which is not something we’ve had to do in the past. We have more outreach going on and more defined communication paths with potential candidates. That brought in a bigger pool of qualified applicants and we now have a current list to draw from if needed more quickly,” said Brannigan.
articles.title: Fire Dept. overtime a result of earlier understaffing

articles.text: Editor: The evidence lies all around us of what under-funded municipalities look like. As a lifelong resident of the East Bay, what I’m seeing in our surrounding communities is demoralizing. While especially noticeable in emergency services, the deterioration appears to have impacted all civil services. The root cause may be debatable, but the one common complaint is funding, and lack thereof. Piedmont is an exception. Our police and fire departments still “work.” Our parks are maintained, and our recreation department continues to meet our needs. I’m grateful. Measure F maintains and improves the City services that we depend upon. Without it cuts will be made. Make no mistake. It won’t just be in our public security; it will be in other less appreciated amenities like our library contract with Oakland. Now more than ever, we need to protect city services. I join our City Council and strongly encourage passage of Measure F. –Chris Hart
articles.title: In favor of Measure F

articles.text: By: Hari Titan, Ph.D. Student enrollment has been going down due to 1) a declining birth rate, 2) increased expense for families to move to Piedmont, 3) families who can afford private schools, and 4) empty-nesters who remain in Piedmont. PUSD presented a budget workshop on January 11 to discuss possible cuts that would achieve the cost-of-living-adjustment (COLA) the union was seeking. Out of fear of a strike, I decided to analyze past budgets (bit.ly/PUSDBudget) myself and found a number of interesting things which I presented to district leadership. PUSD enrollment declined 14.8% (2014-23) despite a total funding increase of 47% over the same time period. This student enrollment decline was roughly 8% above the state’s average decline rate of 6.7%. State income taxes (including capital gains tax) went up much higher over those years and a fixed percentage of that goes toward TK-12 education. Had that not occurred, revenue from the state could have been roughly 8% higher. That’s the revenue “loss” referred to by PUSD in recent documents. The schools don’t really need that extra money because there are fewer students to support. Logically, if enrollment goes down by 8%, staff should correspondingly go down by a similar percentage. Deciding which smaller classes to merge and which staff to reduce is not easy. The resulting savings would help cover the COLA. Property taxes and our parcel taxes act as a bit of a buffer on the rightsizing needed since those funding sources are locked in for 8 years, independent of enrollment changes. I urge the community to review the Budget Workshop presentation attached to the January 11th board meeting. The presentation had a slide that revealed the downward enrollment trend, grade by grade. 12th and 11th grades in 2023 are well above 200 students, middle school grades are below 190, elementary grades below 175, with 1st and 2nd grades below 160 and the Kindergarten class at 135 students. Lower enrollment isn’t temporary and requires addressing staffing levels, not papered over with higher parcel taxes.
articles.title: Rightsizing in school district is right thing to do

It was first approved by voters in 1981, again in 1984, and has been approved every subsequent four years. It was last approved by Piedmont voters in 2020 and is set to expire on June 30, 2025. The City Services Tax funds core city services, includ- ing police, fire and paramedic services, the maintenance of parks, green spaces, stormwater, infrastructure, streets and public facilities, in addition to planning, library, recreation and other community services. On October 16, 2023, the Piedmont Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee (BAFPC) recommended to the City Council that a renewal of the tax be placed before the voters. The BAFPC evaluated the City’s 10-year financial projections and maintenance needs, concluding that long-term stable funding is essential for city services. The City Council took action to place the renewal of the tax on the March 5, 2024, ballot. The ballot measure proposes a 20% increase and a 12-year term to preserve existing service levels citywide, augment staffing for the emergency 911 communication center, and leverage new and improved technology. Measure F amounts to an estimated increase of less than $15 per month for most property owners. Please join us in support of the city services we all rely upon and vote Yes on Measure F. –Mayor Jennifer Cavanaugh Vice Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen Councilmember Conna McCarthy Councilmember Jennifer Long Councilmember Tom Ramsey City lagging on street repairs Editor: This letter is from a Piedmont Citizen who has lived in this beautiful city for over 30 years and has paid taxes throughout those 30 years. articles.text: Public Works estimates work to be completed by April 5 Residents may not have to worry about construction on Oakland Avenue much longer. The Piedmont Public Works Department has confirmed that the installation of the project to install bulb-outs at three intersections is on-track to finish by April 5. Construction workers are currently installing bulb-outs at the corners of Jerome Avenue and Oakland Avenue, El Cerrito and Oakland Avenue, and Nova and Magnolia Avenue. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that two bulb-outs have already been poured at each of the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito. The third location is a Y-intersection at Nova and Magnolia Avenue, where a former cluster of bollards has been removed. The total construction cost for this project is $773,885. Project funding includes a $50,000 contribution from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and approximately $600,000 from the State Gas Tax. “The increased [crime] activity is part of the formula, but we have always been understaffed with primarily one dispatcher on at any time that works the window, answers non-emergency and 911, while talking with the Police Department, Fire Department, and any other sources needed to support them. That can be overloading when something significant happens,” said Captain Chris Monahan. The first dispatcher position was filled earlier this month by new hire Rachel Ponce, who is currently in training. Measure F would increase the existing Parcel Tax’s rate by 20% (an additional $11-$19 per month for most households) and would change its term of renewal from every four years to every 12 years. Citizens can vote on Measure F via the California Primary election ballot on Tuesday, March 5. For information on the location of polling stations, visit www.sos. ca.gov/elections/polling-place.
articles.title: Bulb-outs more than halfway done

articles.text: Editor: Like so many others, am writing to express my strong support for Measure F. I know that sometimes it can feel like we’re pouring our (often large) tax contributions down a drain, that we’re throwing money into an oncoming tide of problems that we have very little ability to fix. But one of the many benefits of living in Piedmont is we get to be the direct beneficiaries of our local taxes. Our already outstanding emergency services will be made better by Measure F, and we will be even safer. Our streets will be even more beautiful. There will be even more shared space in which to enjoy our friends, neighbors, and larger community. Our recreation options will be even better. I urge everyone to vote yes with me on Measure F. –Max Roman
articles.title: Voicing strong support for Measure F

articles.text: As Piedmont residents for 50 years, we fully support Ken Berrick for the AC Transit Board of Supervisors. We have known Ken for over 30 years and know his lifelong advocacy and work with children, mental health, education, social services, and housing. Ken was the founder and CEO of Seneca Center, providing these services throughout the County and State. He worked closely with Counties and their departments on all levels to develop innovative programs which maximized Federal dollars and ensured successful outcomes. This election is not just about one issue. We have multiple issues that require expertise to solve. It’s about holding the County and its staff accountable and maximizing resources to get the job done. It’s about outcomes and follow through. Ken Berrick has done this in his work and will do this as a Board of Supervisor. Having worked with Ken as a fellow service provider in multiple Counties throughout the State, I can personally attest to Ken’s forward thinking and follow-through as well as his expertise in County and State issues and effective solutions. We cannot be swayed by emotions. We need to think strategically about who can win and do the best job for us, our district and County. Ken Berrick is the more viable candidate throughout our district. A vote for Chris will result in neither Chris or Ken being elected and open the election for an unwanted candidate from Oakland being elected. Let’s not let what happened in the Oakland Mayor’s election happen with this Board of Supervisors election. Vote for Ken Berrick for AC Board of Supervisor. –Mary Jane & Benton Gross Piedmont Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver
articles.title: Voting for Ken Berrick for AC Transit Board

I know that sometimes it can feel like we’re pouring our (often large) tax contributions down a drain, that we’re throwing money into an oncoming tide of problems that we have very little ability to fix. But one of the many benefits of living in Piedmont is we get to be the direct beneficiaries of our local taxes. Our already outstanding emergency services will be made better by Measure F, and we will be even safer. Our streets will be even more beautiful. There will be even more shared space in which to enjoy our friends, neighbors, and larger community. Our recreation options will be even better. I urge everyone to vote yes with me on Measure F. –Max Roman ent perspective, but I am no less enthusiastic in my support. I view Measure F through the lens of “paying it forward.” Since 1981, the residents of Piedmont have chosen to invest in back into this community, and though my family just got here, we are so grateful for the investment that has been made over the past four decades – we benefit from it every day. Renewing the City Services Tax now gives us the opportunity to support Piedmont so that future generations will continue to enjoy all that the city has to offer. It is our responsibility to do so. –Billy Deitch In support of Measure F Editor: The City Services Tax, Measure F, deserves support. articles.text: Photo by April Fitzgerald Officer Jessica Morey next to a police patrol car Community members may have seen new police office Jessica Morey, a former teacher, as she patrols city streets and at Cop on the Block events. “I was a teacher in a classroom for preschool-aged students,” she said in an interview, explaining there were similar motivations between the two careers. “It really does come down to the fact that I like helping people,” she said. On January 8 the PPD announced that Officer Morey completed her field training program, making her a fully sworn officer on the force. It is an achievement she is proud of and welcomes the responsibility. “I just feel very, very welcomed here. I’m happy to be here and start my journey as a sworn officer,” she said. Morey grew up in San Mateo and attended Carlmont High School. She went on to study at San Jose State University, where she earned a B.S. in Child and Adolescent Development. While she was in college, she taught preschool students and supervised children in an afterschool care program but overall felt that something was missing. “In my last semester I took a criminal justice class, and that’s when I realized after a few years of teaching I really wanted to do police work her way instead.” Morey found Piedmont based upon the recommendation of a friend. She was working as a Community Service Officer in the San Jose Police Department when a colleague approached her and her best friend, Ashley Gallion, now also a Piedmont Police officer. “He knew we both wanted to go sworn, and he put us in contact with Capt. Chris Monahan,” she said. Officer Morey remembers that during her first ride-along in Piedmont, it was a culture shock compared to her time in San Jose. “I remember driving with Officer Petit and Officer Diaz thinking that the city was so cute, and then Officer Diaz started rolling down the window and waving to everybody. In San Jose, people don’t wave at you unless they’re trying to get your attention or have you stop for them.” Morey said the interaction left an impression on her. “That was huge. [Ashley and I] applied as soon as we could, and then luck worked out that we both got hired.” She said she appreciates the culture of community policing in Piedmont. “I’m not just a name or a badge number in this city. I’m a face with a name and people will want to get to know me.”

articles.text: The City of Piedmont invites community members to apply for vacancies on seven commissions and committees. These volunteer positions serve as a way to learn more about the inner workings of City government and to become involved in local government. These positions will regularly hear reports from City staff about current and proposed services, policies, and programs and will help shape the direction these bodies take by providing valuable insight and resident perspectives. All vacant offices serve threeyear terms subject to a limit of two consecutive terms. Residents may apply online at www.piedmont.ca.gov/commissioner. Vacancies on the following commissions and committees will be available: Park Commission – Advises City Council on issues related to public parks and street trees. The commission meets regularly on the first Wednesday of the month at 5:30 p.m. The Park Commission currently has two vacancies and two incumbents on the commission are currently eligible to reapply. Planning Commission – Advises City Council on issues related to planning and building and makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. This commission requires approximately four hours per month in addition to its scheduled meeting time. The commission meets regularly on the second Monday of the month at 5:30 p.m. The Planning Commission has one vacancy and no incumbents on the commission are currently eligible to reapply. Recreation Commission – Advises City Council on issues regarding recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space, and other related issues. The commission meets on the third Wednesday of the month at 7:30 p.m. The commission has two vacancies and one incumbent on the commission is currently eligible to reapply. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee – Provides recommendations on the City’s annual budget, long-term financial projections, mid-year budget adjustments, and the City’s municipal services tax rate and renewal. The committee meets as needed. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee currently has two vacancies and two incumbents on the committee are currently eligible to reapply. Public Safety Committee – Advises on efforts to increase public participation in crime reduction and disaster preparedness. The committee meets quarterly, has two vacancies and one incumbent on the committee is currently eligible to reapply. Police and Fire Pension Board – Oversees the investment of funds in the legacy pension plan for Police Officers and Firefighters. The board meets quarterly. The Police and Fire Pension Board has one vacancy and one incumbent on the commission is currently eligible to reapply. Civil Service Commission – Oversees personnel issues (including classification) and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. The commission meets as needed. The Civil Service Commission currently has two vacancies and two incumbents on the commission are currently eligible to reapply. Applications are due by 5 p.m. on Friday, March 15. The City Council will appoint a total of 12 seats. Applicants must attend an in-person interview at City offices in the evening of Monday, March 25, to be considered for appointment. Interviews will be conducted by the City Council and will last roughly five minutes each. The interview schedule will be provided to applicants on Friday, March 22. For more information, contact the City Clerk’s office at 420-3040 or e-mail at cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: During a Piedmont School Board meeting on February 14, the school district announced a limited time incentive for teachers for early retirement of resignation – a one-time $40,000 payment, for veteran teachers at the top of the pay scale. The school district placed a deadline of Monday, February 26 for a decision. A minimum of 10 staff positions would be required to complete the offer. As of February 27, the school district had not receive enough applicants and the program will not be in effect. The proposal was contingent upon receiving that number to make the saving meaningful for the district. As of February 14, the district had around 30 teachers with senior qualifications, either on the maximum step and column of their salary schedule, or having been with the district more than 20 years. “I don’t think the objective was to reduce our teaching ranks, because we would be refilling.” said Finance Director Ruth Alahydoian. Employees that may have submitted their intent may rescind their retirement/resignation since the incentive program did not fulfill its requirements. The program was projected to save the district $100,000 in future years, with the $40,000 payments guaranteed by Piedmont Education Foundation. The typical advance notice date for teachers to retire was February 15. During the school board meeting, board members applauded the program as creative and a win-win, although board member Cory Smegal worried the deadline was too soon given Ski Week ending one day prior. The now failed proposal was also offered as a tantalizing option to limit the number of March 15 salary reduction notices that would be sent to teachers. “This offer is possible this year due to unique circumstances and is not likely to be available in future years,” the board document read.

The typical advance notice date for teachers to retire was February 15. During the school board meeting, board members applauded the program as creative and a win-win, although board member Cory Smegal worried the deadline was too soon given Ski Week ending one day prior. The now failed proposal was also offered as a tantalizing option to limit the number of March 15 salary reduction notices that would be sent to teachers. “This offer is possible this year due to unique circumstances and is not likely to be available in future years,” the board document read. articles.text: Linda Beach Cooperative Preschool welcomes families from Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and surrounding areas to an Open House on Saturday, March 16 from 10 a.m.-12 p.m. Parents are welcome to tour the warm and welcoming classroom and have a chance to meet the teachers and other families. The preschool has been a Piedmont fixture for more than 80 years. The school emphasizes the development of each child through independent and group play-based activities. Classroom adults always include two teachers and two or three parent volunteers. This allows for a maximum 5:1 child to adult ratio. LBCP offers gymnastics classes that allow for children to grow better body awareness and strengthen their gross motor skills. The M/W/F (4 year old) program also provides Spanish classes where children are introduced to the Spanish language and culture by native Spanish-speaking adults. Families are encouraged to participate in field trips to Tilden’s Little Farm, the Piedmont Fire Station, and Roberts Park. The cooperative preschool not only provides families the opportunity to watch their child grow in the classroom, but it also allows families to build and further develop their parent network. Through the experience of classroom participation, approximately once a month, parents have the unique opportunity to see their child in the context of their peers and to receive feedback from teachers and other parents about their child. All LBCP teachers became involved with Linda Beach as parents. The much-loved director, Shelley Kelly, has been an integral part of the school for 32 years. She is also the lead teacher for the 3-year old program and assists the 4-year old classroom. To sign up, take a tour, or learn more about Linda Beach Cooperative Preschool, visit Lindabeach. org.

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation has announced that this year’s Spring Fling will be co-chaired by three elementary school dads, Marco Gonzalez-Navarro (Havens), Michael Gross (Beach), and Max Roman (Wildwood). “This is our chance to ensure that essential programs are not lost, whether donating an item for the auction, organizing a parent-sponsored party, or coming to the Spring Fling Gala to bid.” said Gross, who is the President of Beach School Dads Club. “Last year’s Spring Fling raised enough to fund expanded counseling and lunchtime library coverage,” said Roman. PEF and the co-chairs aim for an exciting event schedule. This year’s Gala is scheduled for Saturday, May 4, in Oakland’s Jack London Square with a theme of an evening in Venice. “We hope parents have a fantastic time with friends and neighbors while showing how much we all support and care for Piedmont schools,” said Gonzalez-Navaro. The weeks leading up to Spring Fling will be packed with fun events that contribute to elementary school fundraising. The Comings & Goings Photography Project features local photographers taking candid photos of kindergarteners (Comings) and 5th Graders (Goings) as a sweet keepsake of their elementary school journey. Parent Sponsorships are a popular way to support the elementary schools while getting some fabulous exclusive perks. Volunteers are putting together theme parties such as Aloha to 5th Grade, High Chai Tea, and Spin and Sip – all benefitting the elementary schools. In April, look for the Spring Fling Online Auction featuring an array of fun items from local shops, restaurants, and entertainment venues. Sponsorships, Comings & Goings pre-orders, and more are available at PiedmontSpringFling.org. Funds raised through Spring Fling sponsorships, auctions and events directly support Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools. PEF works with the tri-school principals and parents club presidents to determine where the area of greatest need intersects with parent priorities. A trifecta of Piedmont dads, Michael Gross (left), Marco Gonzalez-Navarro, and Max Roman, will co-chair Spring Fling this year.

articles.text: Camp Joyful Voices is a sleepaway experience for 7-10 year olds Registration is now open for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir summer music camp, where kids get to sing under the stars with their friends. Camp Joyful Voices, the choir’s popular camp program for singers ages 7-10, has added a second week by popular demand and spaces are filling quickly. Created with young singers in mind, this weeklong sleepaway camp is the perfect opportunity for children to build confidence, deepen musical skills, and make new friends. With a supportive staff and skilled counselors, singers are sure to make lifelong memories and friendships while nurturing their love for singing. Children are encouraged to sing on hikes, at Turtle Pond, and around the campfire at night. Singers share cabins, compete for prizes for creative outfits during Spirit Days, and spend time reading, napping, writing letters, playing games, and bonding with each other. They swim and kayak at Turtle Pond, go on hikes to explore nature, watch sunsets, do arts and crafts, and share camp recitals and evening programs. By the time the last day of camp rolls around, the joy and memories are mixed with not wanting to leave. Join us this summer; we can’t wait to sing with you. Camp Dates Session 1: July 22 - July 28 Session 2: July 28 - August 3 Location: Walker Creek Ranch in Marin County, a 1700- acre site that includes forests, chaparral, grassland, 20 miles of hiking trails, and a great 4-acre swimming hole. Cost: $1700/week Sibling discounts, payment plans, and financial assistance are available. Save your spot for Camp Joyful Voices and sign up now. To learn more about Camp Joyful Voices and our other camp programs, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/camp or contact Camp Director Tate Bissinger at tbissinger@piedmontchoirs.org. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team suffered a 66-40 loss to Acalanes for fifth place in the North Coast Section Open Division on Wednesday, February 21 in Lafayette. The Dons kept a frequent press, two defenders against Piedmont’s leading scorer, Natalia Martinez. “It’s interesting because when you play in the Open Division, it’s a sign of respect and that you had a good year to be one of the top-six teams in the entire North Coast Section. But it’s very challenging, because every team is so good,” coach Bryan Gardere. Turnovers have played a factor in Piedmont’s postseason thus far, with 16 on Wednesday and 31 in the previous game against Carondelet. “I think some of our weaknesses are just taking care of the ball, so we have to figure that out. It’s hard to win games when you’re giving up a lot of turnovers in a 30-minute game,” Gardere said. But their season continued. The Highlanders received an automatic berth in the CIF State Tournament and were given the No. 9 seed in the difficult Division 1 ladder. They faced No. 8 Whitney in Rocklin last night, February 27. Results were not complete by Post time. Natalia Martinez pulls up for a 3-pointer against Acalanes.

articles.text: Staff Photos Coach Ben Spencer’s boys’ basketball team fell to University in the Div. 3 NCS Finals but qualified for the State Tournament. Piedmont High’s championship dreams fell short on Friday, February 23, as the boys’ basketball team, the No. 3 seed, fell to No. 1 seed University 65-55 in the Division 3 North Coast Section Finals at the University of San Francisco. On the way to the finals they defeated No. 2 Archie Williams 64-61 in San Anselmo on Tuesday, February 20. It was a great response to Piedmont’s early-season 93-61 loss to University on December 12, and coach Ben Spencer considers this year’s team one of the most special he’ has coached. “[University’s] press was a challenge for us in the fourth quarter. I’m not sure which team I’m more proud of—this team or the NCS Championship team we had [in 2020]. It’s a tossup. This group lost to University by 32 points [ in December]. As coaches and players we challenged each other the rest of the way to play 100 percent every game. For the next 24 games, we did that. We were right there,” he said. But Piedmont’s season isn’t over. By reaching the North Coast Section finals, they automatically qualified for the CIF State Tournament. They were placed in Div. 3 as the No. 14 seed and on Tuesday night, February 27, they faced Valley Christian in San Jose. Results were not available at press time. The game was back and forth with Piedmont holding leads briefly in the third and fourth quarters, including a 42-41 lead after Ravi Silverberg knocked down a 3-pointer to open the fourth quarter. Silverberg led the scoring with 23 points and senior leader Brit Burden finished with 16. The Red Devils kept a heavy press on the Highlanders through all four quarters, which Piedmont dealt well with until fatigue started to show during the late part of the game. PHS committed six turnovers in the final quarter. “Once the game started, I knew I had to be aggressive and my shots started falling, so I just kept shooting,” said Silverberg. “They’d trap in the post and have a second guy in the post, so it was tough to get inside. They had a great game plan and they were really good on-ball defenders,” said Burden. Burden had one of the best NCS semifinals performances in the last 10 years with 28 points in the semifinal win over Archie Williams, rarely missing when attacking the rim for layups. The 64-61 semifinal score looks a lot closer than the game actually was. PHS held a 52-33 lead entering the fourth quarter. The Peregrine Falcons landed a flurry of three-point shots in the final few minutes. “Brit’s performance was up there; he was a force. He set the tone early by going to the basket and drawing fouls. We just played physical against Archie. it was an unbelievable performance and hopefully we still have more basketball left,” added Spencer. 65-55 to University After a defensive first quarter, Piedmont led 10-9. The offense was going strong in the second quarter when Silverberg hit a 3-pointer to take a 20-19 lead at the 3:07 mark. But University went on a 10-0 run to take a 29-20 lead at halftime. In the third quarter, the Highlanders rallied with a 16-5 run to move in front 35-34 with 2:25 left. But University quickly responded with a layup and free throw by Gus Fried to go back ahead 37-35. Burden put Piedmont in the lead at 39-38 on a layup with 1:20 to go, but University’s Gus Parsons hit a 3-pointer to make it 41-39 Red Devils. Piedmont came out firing in the fourth with Arjun Bornstein feeding Silverberg for a 3-pointer to give the Highlanders a 42-41 lead 10 seconds into the quarter. It was the last time they held the lead. The Red Devils quickly got back in front with a pair of free throws by Cole Boake for the start of a 13-2 run that put University up 54-44. Both teams traded baskets in the remaining time, including five free throws by Burden and Silverberg with a pair of three-pointers. Final stats: Silverberg had 23 points, Burden had 16 points, Thorin Holmes and Dillon Casey both had six, Declan Linnane scored four. 64-41 over Archie Williams Piedmont got out to a 16-11 lead and led 37-23 at halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 52-33 entering the fourth quarter, while the Peregrin Falcons scored 28 points in the final Ravi Silverberg led scoring in the finals with 23 points against University.

articles.text: Piedmont’s track & field team sent three athletes to the 18th annual Skyline Invitational in Oakland on Saturday, February 24: sophomore pole vaulter Marcos Arno, senior sprinter and long jumper Breah Bell, and junior Sam Shelby making his season debut. Much of the PHS team was out of town for Ski Week. Shelby started his season in a big way. He finished fourth in the 100 meters in a field of 144 athletes with a time of 11.34. He’s poised for a strong spring season after a breakout campaign on the football team last fall, He was named WACC Offensive Player of the Year and an All-Metro selection by the SF Chronicle. “Sam picked up right where he left off in the 100m, missing his end of season PR by less than a tenth of a second,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. “He has more power than ever, so now we just need to build up his endurance and we’ll be good.” Photo by Becky Swain Breah Bell competed in the 100 meters, long jump and triple jump at the Skyline Invitational. Sam Shelby made his season debut in the 100 and 200 meters and in the long jump. Sprinter and relay runner Sam Shelby (second from right). Shelby also ran the 200 meters, placing 14th of 142 sprinters with a time of 23.81 seconds. He also made his high school debut in the long jump, placing ninth of 59 jumpers with a distance of 19 feet, 6.5 inches, a mark that was eighth best over the last decade at Piedmont High. “We pushed Sam to consider a third individual event and long jump makes sense. He comes down the runway with tons of velocity and after maybe just three hours total of long jump practice, he’s already just a couple steps away being an elite jumper. Saturday was the first time he ever officially jumped,” Assadi said. Bell, now a senior, competed in three events. She placed 14th of 114 athletes in the 100 meter dash with a time of 13.34.“ Breah blasted out of the blocks with more power and better form than I’ve ever seen from her. Now we just have to work on endurance and we’ll be cooking,” Assadi said. She was also 12th of 24 in the long jump at 15 feet, one inch, and 11th of 17 in the triple jump in 29 feet, 1.75 inches. “Breah is still working on the mechanics of her jumps, but her confidence is there and we like the direction she’s headed,” Assadi said. Arno, a sophomore, was ninth of 13 in the pole vault with a height of eight feet, seven inches. NEXT UP Piedmont will compete in the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton on Saturday, March 2 at 8:30 a.m.
articles.title: Track & Field team sends 3 to Skyline Invitational

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team starts its season after reaching the North Coast Section finals last year. They lost 11-10 in double overtime to Tamalpais. The Highlanders compiled a 14-4 record last season and won their sixth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference championship. A big change is underway, however. This year’s team has a new head coach, Jeff Lamb. Coach Al Yu unexpectedly left the team a few months ago. Lamb competed at Georgetown University during his college career. He coached at Arlington after graduating in 2012. Ny day he is Vice President of Seven Post Investment. “I grew up on the East Coast and received a scholarship to play at Georgetown. I played two years as a midfielder but fractured my femur, which put a stop to my playing career. After I graduated, I was an assistant at Washington-Liberty High School in Arlington, Virginia,” Lamb said. “I moved to the Bay Area about 10 years ago and made the move to Alameda. After a series of introductions and relationships with some parents in Piedmont with children in high school, they found out I played lacrosse in college. They asked if I was interested. I’ve always loved coaching and love the sport, so I wanted to lend a hand,” he added. Boys’ lacrosse has become one of the school’s top performing teams over the last decade and Lamb acknowledged the pressure to be quickly successful at Piedmont High. “The expectation levels are high. The reality is there were quite a few seniors who graduated. One of the important things is getting the new players and mid-level experienced players as Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team returns to Witter Field after reaching last year’s North Coast Section finals. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team is back at the Witter Softball Field for the spring season. The team went 4-13-1 last year and will be competing in the Shoreline Division of the Western Alameda County Conference this year against Hayward, San Lorenzo, and Tennyson. It marks a rebuilding year for the Highlanders after losing key players like Leah Bell, Morgan Hunt, Ginger Gardner, Hailey Ronen, and Gretchen Gerhardy with the Class of 2023. The team returns other key athletes, Miya Fujimoto, Sa’Mara Levi, and Angelina Wu. Fujimoto was a first-team All-League selection last year and Levi earned an Honorable Mention. “We have them coming back. We’ll need people to step up for us in key positions,” said coach Gene Denard. An ongoing issue with Piedmont softball has been the lack of a starting pitcher since the graduation of Izzy Epstein in 2022. Fujimoto, the shortstop stepped in to help on the mound as a sophomore and will continue as Staff Photos Piedmont’s softball team gets back on the Witter Softball Diamond next week. a junior. Wu and Ronen will also get time pitching. Levi and Wu will also be the headliners of the group. Wu is a speedy runner on the base paths and is a dependable glove in the infield. Levi, meanwhile, provides a big bat with a lot of pop. “It’s going to be the same thing. Fujimoto, Angelina, and Samantha will hopefully push us through the season. Right now, Miya Fujimoto is a headline returner. She’s a former All-League recipient and was the Post’s 2022 Freshman of the Year. Sa’Mara Levi is a key player from last year’s team who earned AllLeague honors as a freshman. we’re looking for people to step up as leaders and find their voice to be vocal,” Denard said. Returning players include Mia Leggett, Samantha Ronen, and Caitlin Boothby. They are also expected to have key roles. “We have some girls coming back and they will be important to fill those key roles. Caitlin and Samantha are back. Mia is our only senior this year,” Denard said. Piedmont gets its season started on Monday, March 4 hosting a game with St. Helena at 3:30 p.m. at Witter Field.
articles.title: Softball team returns to Witter

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont boys’ volleyball and coach Mariah Cardenas are back for the spring season. Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team is back at Binks Rawlings Gym for the spring season, but with a distinctly different roster than last year’s squad which posted a 14-7 record. This year’s team has only two returning starters. “We lost a lot of our main people, so we’re really starting over and starting completely fresh,” explained coach Mariah Cardenas. “We have a couple of returning varsity players, called up some JV players, and have some new players. Our main focus this year is to compete and have fun.” Shunji Higashi is a four-year starter and is a defensive cornerstone as the team’s Libero. John Champion is a three-year starter as an outside hitter and was a leader on last year’s team. Both are seniors. “They’re doing well. It’s shellshock to lose those seniors from last year who they played alongside for so long,” Cardenas said. After losing much of last year’s team, 2024 will be a learning experience for many on the court, compounded by the school not fielding a JV team. Two freshmen who have made an impact are Lukas Kim and Justin Amen, both with experience at the club level. “We have two freshmen who are looking like starters. They are really familiar with volleyball and have played club volleyball for a long time,” Cardenas said. Senior Spencer Sorensen-Wald is a new addition. He competed on the track team last spring. “Spencer has been a surprise. He’s just athletic and naturally skilled,” Cardenas said. Piedmont gets its season started tonight, February 28, with a match at St. Joseph in Alameda at 5:00 p.m. They play the following day in the home opener at Binks Rawlings Gym hosting league opponent San Lorenzo at 4:30 p.m. Shunji Higashi (left) is one of just two returning varsity athletes. John Champion is an outside hitter and will lead the team.
articles.title: Boys’ volleyball team back with new roster

articles.text: Piedmont MTB is back after racing in the Fun at the Fort event at Fort Ord to open its season. Pictured are Schuyler Sawicki (left), Max Rivera, and Mark Hsia after their varsity race Piedmont’s Mountain Bike team made its season debut on a bright and sunny Saturday, February 24, at the Fun at the Fort event at Fort Ord in the National Interscholastic Cycling League’s NorCal East Bay/Central Region. They brought 10 athletes which was raced on a four-mile course. In the five-lap varsity event, Max Rivera led the way for Piedmont by finishing 24th of 41 with a time of 1:18:53.64. Behind him was Mark Hsia in 25th, clocking a 1:19:03.50. Schuyler Sawicki was 34th with a time of 1:20:17.62, while Scanu came in 1:30:13.17. During the race, Scanu took a hard fall on the second lap. Rivera, Hsia, and Sawicki rode in a close pack on their way to the finish. Piedmont had two athletes in the four-lap JV1 race. Jasper Schuetz finished 12th of 45 in 1:02:53.06 after being hampered by a cold. Schuetz notably won nearly every event of last year in the sophomore category. Cary Ward, meanwhile, was close behind in 14th in 1:03:50.84. In the JV2 race, sophomores Caleb Canada and Asher Villarreal competed. Canada was 29th of 50 in 57:12.74 while Villareal was 45th in 1:11:06.86. Olive Reining raced in the girls’ JV2 race, clocking a 1:25:09.27. Piedmont’s MTB Junior Development team middle school riders also competed at Fort Ord on a shorter course. 8th grade rider Josephine Schuetz was ninth of 12 in 44:28.12. Rose Reining finished in 47:13.24. Sixth grade riders making their debut included Carter Lew in 22nd of 58, and Quincy Aguilar, who was 43rd in 31:21.73. Racing is only one part of being a member of the teams, which welcome riders who prefer mountain biking as an adventure. To learn more, see www.piedmontmtb.com. Mark Hsia leads Matteo Scanu around the bend during their varsity race.
articles.title: Mountain bike team makes debut at Fort Ord

articles.text: more than a month left in the season. The winter season is officially coming to a close at Piedmont High. Both the boy s’ and girls’ soccer teams reached the North Coast Section postseason, and both basketball teams qualified for and will play in the State Tournament. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite five moments from the recent sports seasons. Natalia Martinez sets school record with 52 points This has been a historic scoring season for senior Natalia Martinez, now with 2,256 career points going into Tuesday’s Division 1 CIF State Tournament against Whitney. On December 28, Martinez scored an historic number 52 points in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch in the San Diego Holiday Classic Tournament, It’s a score that coach Bryan Gardere believes tops the school’s best-ever player, Courtney Paris, who had a 12-year professional career in the WNBA and abroad, “The last player to do anything close to this was Courtney Paris, but I’m pretty sure she never had a 50-point game. It’s incredible; we’re seeing history before our eyes. But I’m not surprised. Nar has put a lot into this,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Martinez had nine games with at least 40 points this season and topped 2,000 career points one month ago on January 24 with Boys Basketball reaches NCS Finals Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team is also continuing its season in the CIF State Tournament after reaching the Division 3 North Coast Section Finals against University, losing 65-55 recently last Friday. Coach Ben Spencer described after the game that he was unsure if he was more proud of this team or the last one to reach the State tournament in 2020 when winning the D4 NCS title. Piedmont arrival in the State tournament marked a moment of triumph for the basketball program, reaching the semifinals each year since winning the D4 section banner, including losses to Branson in 2022 and 2023. Brit Burden was instrumental in getting the Highlanders back to the championship game with 28 points in a 64-61 win over Archie Williams in the semifinals. Burden scored his 1,000th career point in Piedmont’s 67-43 win over Alhambra in the NCS Quarterfinals on February 16. Boys Soccer defeats Berkeley for first time Piedmont finished its season with a 12-3-3 (W-T-L) overall record and reached the North Coast Section quarterfinals, where their season came to a close in a 3-1 loss to Archie Williams. Staff Photos Natalia Martinez made history by scoring 52 points in a game against Scripps Ranch in December. Brit Burden surpassed 1,000 career points in basketball and led the team to the North Coast Section finals. Enzo Bernales scores the game-winner against Berkeley in soccer. Photo by Scott Stratman
