articles.text: San Francisco corps de ballet on opening night of Swan Lake. A wondrous night unfolded at the Opera House as the S.F. Ballet’s swans floated in gracefully and flew off to the cheers of a sold-out house. For many, “Swan Lake” is the pinnacle of all ballet love-drama fantasies, a fairy tale that grips the heart with great endearment. This time with a very promising ballerina out of Sweden, Nikisha Fogo. The fairy-tale plot: innocent maidens are scooped up by the evil winged sorcerer Von Rothbart, transformed magically into swans, and subservient into all eternity. Subplot is a fickle human swain of lesser IQ, Prince Siegfried, falling in love with her, and later falling for the bot, Rothbart’s seductive look-alike Black Swan, the super-athlete, which leads to the demise of one and all, and to wet hankies throughout the house. “Well, yeah,” said the wise one. “But actually I read it as allegory, Rothbart being the bully major power swallowing up the less powerful defenseless neighbor in a quick war, like a shark after minnows.” Hmmmm…. Fairy tale or Weltpolitik, even after a century and a half, the “Swan Lake” experience conquers hearts and souls around the world while offering the dream role for all aspiring ballerinas. The opening night’s wronged heroine, Odette/Odile, was Fogo. Initially a habile technician in that tremulous first meeting with the prince, Ms. Fogo became an ever more poetic presence with him in that nonpareil act two, all white with those swan feathers embracing her hair. The Black Swan role suited her even better, calling on her playing the deceitful one reverberantly, combined with the requisite endurance to make 32 whipping fouettée spins in her solo variation, one of the greatest physical challenges in all ballet. These she spun off brilliantly to the exuberant house Feb. 23, without the creeping toward the footlights that fatigue often imposes. Photos by Lindsay Thomas If Fogo is not yet the ultimate swan queen, she is well en route, beloved by the admiring throng. Her Prince was Aaron Robison, a powerful partner with soaring jetée leaps and the knack for throwing her effortlessly toward the skies. Heightening the drama are her two prescribed backward falls, each time caught adroitly by the prince. In his best role ever, corps member Nathaniel Remez flew about the stage like a black crow from first to last, nearly earning audience boos for his malevolent Rothbart role. Not to be forgotten was the parade of snow-white enchanted swans in perfect alignment, sometimes 16, sometimes up to 30, that enkindled the audience all night long. And of course the quartet of fast-stepping cygnets in their rapid-fire show-stopper – deft contrasting segment by composer Tchaikovsky. Apart from the brass section, Martin West’s orchestra was unassailable. Please join us for our upcoming in-person seminar.
articles.title: Could Swan Lake be an allegorical tale?

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company is showing the West Coast premiere of Bees & Honey by Guadalís Del Carmen now through March 10. The two-person play follows Manuel and Johaira, a Dominican couple in New York City, as they navigate an unforeseen tragedy that upends their relationship and their lives. Johaira (Maribel Martinez) and Manuel (Xavier Pacheco) are an unlikely couple. The beautiful Johaira is an accomplished attorney and Manuel is a brutish auto mechanic, but sparks fly between them when they first meet at a club in New York City’s Washington Heights neighborhood. That meeting sets the scene for Bees & Honey, and their relationship through turmoil and tragedy. The play is inspired by the Juan Luis Guerra song “Como Abeja Al Panal,” and is fresh from its world premiere at New York’s Off-Broadway Manhattan Class Company Theater. Visit https://www.marintheatre.org/subscriptions-23-24/23- 24-shows to learn more and to purchase tickets. Photo by Julieta Cervantes Maribel Martinez and Xavier Pacheco in Marin Theatre’s production of Bees & Honey
articles.title: Bees & Honey at Marin Theatre Co. ends March 10

articles.text: Famed saxophonist to appear at SF Jazz Feb. 29 to March 3 Saxophonist Branford Marsalis at SF Jazz this week Branford Marsalis returns to San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz tomorrow, February 29, and will perform a series of concerts through March 3. Marsalis is a highly regarded composer and jazz tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughn Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras, and has performed with the New York Philharmonic, Chicago Symphony, Detroit Symphony, Dusseldorf Symphony, and North Carolina Symphony, Marsalis will be joined at Miner Auditorium by Joey Calderazzo on piano, Eric Revis on bass and Justin Faulkner on drums. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/23-24/branford-marsalis/ or call the box office at 415-788-7353. Performance times vary.
articles.title: Branford Marsalis to perform 4 shows at SF Jazz

articles.text: Show now open online until February 29 We all miss the days of the live San Francisco Tribal Shows at Fort Mason, the last exhibit was with a bang just before COVID lockdown in February 2020. In the three years that have followed, the show went virtual to keep us in touch with old friends. This year the beloved show was merged with the Whitehawk and the Objects of Art shows out of Santa Fe, with insufficient reference to the live show we have done in San Francisco for more than 30 years, What we remember as the SF show, with some of the classic SF participants, is now called the Virtual Whitehawk show. We are listing the link now so you won’t miss what 2024 has to offer. Dave and Nancy DeRoche have taken three ‘booths’ in this online virtual show, making splashes in our traditional areas of the arts of Africa, Oceania, Tribal Asia, and The Americas, including Pre-Columbian Art. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s exhibit, Por el Pueblo: The Legacy and Influence of Malaquías Montoya, celebrates Chicano identity with political imagery. The exhibition is on view in the museum’s Great Hall through June 30. Montoyo, now 85, is originally from Albuquerque, New Mexico. articles.text: Virginia Hong is a successful entrepreneur, an accomplished software developer, and, at her core, a genuine artist. Her journey unfolds as a passionate photographer who finds solace and inspiration in the quiet moments of life. Unlike conventional photographers, she captures moments not for the world, but for her own pleasure and meditation. She seeks out subjects and scenes that resonate with serenity, stillness, and tranquility similar to what she finds when she programs. Her large immersive prints are windows into a sanctuary of peace and quiet, inviting viewers to pause, breathe, and indulge themselves in a moment of quietude, allowing for an escape from their hectic lives. Her solo exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, amid the height of the COVID pandemic in August 2021, garnered significant attendance. Throughout 2024 the Piedmont Post will publish Hong’s photos monthly based upon her 2024 photography calendar, beginning with Emerald Bay in her series of photos of Lake Tahoe. The photo shown was taken just a short distance beyond Emerald Bay on Emerald Bay Drive. Following my sunrise session at Emerald Bay, I stumbled upon this captivating sight: a flawless reflection on the still lake, creating a fascinating texture reminiscent of arrows pointing towards the right on the horizon. Subtle light graced a handful of trees, adding highlights and a little bit of color to the composition. Emerald Bay, Lake Tahoe Photo by Virginia Hong Dreaming up the ideal retirement is your job. Those who are in the Classic instrument business have “proved” that classic instruments are better than any other instruments. Contemporary makers, on the other hand, have also conducted “impartial” tests. Their results prove that modern instruments are better than the old instruments. So, where do things stand? Is there actually an advantage to using a Strad? Of course there is. When you play on one of these instruments, you just know you sound better. Psychological advantages certainly help. articles.text: The past week was rather uneventful. The only thing to disturb the placidity was a dust- up which questioned a famous musical figure’s importance in posterity. The famous entertainer, Bing Crosby described it perfectly when he said: “difference of opinion is what makes horse racing.” Closer to home, the name Stradivarius can stir up considerable controversy. When famous people play the violin, they usually choose a Stradivarius violin. Queen Victoria always played on Stradivarius, and so did the last czar of Russia. Auto manufacturer Henry Ford had two Stradivarius violins in his collection. This reminds me of a story. One of the great child prodigy fiddlers of the 20th century was Grisha Goluboff. A German nobleman gave Grisha a priceless violin to use in his concerts. On his first day in office, Adolf Hitler demanded that Grisha return the violin immediately. The violin was duly returned. articles.text: Hollywood learned long ago that formula films work. Find a template and use it until it’s frayed and even then return, promising something familiar but with a twist. Take the road trip recipe. It can be a wonderful if sometimes predictable vehicle involving multiple characters, settings and encounters. As a genre, it’s as comfortable as an old sneaker, and easily slipped on. Everybody’s Fine is such a sneaker. In the setup, Frank (Robert DeNiro), a recently widowed and Society of the Snow is based on the crash of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 541 on October 13, 1972 Society of the Snow, submitted by Spain for the 2024 Oscar category of Best International Feature Film, is considered a dark-horse contender for an award. The film is based on the 2009 non-fiction book by Pablo Vierci which describes the crash of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 541. The plane had been chartered to fly a young Uruguayan rugby team to Santiago, Chile, for a much-anticipated match. For reasons never detailed in the film, the twin-engine prop plane lost power and went down high in the snow-covered Andes Mountains. As depicted in the movie, it was a violent crash that killed or injured many of the players as well as staff and pilots. The film is, in essence, a story of survival; however, it is about much more. Huddled together (16 of the 45 survived) in the mostly intact fuselage, and those not injured gradually ventured forth into the harsh sunlight only to find that they were on a glacier surrounded by impossibly high snow-covered mountains. It is a daunting moment as they grasp their total isolation. Convinced initially that they would be rescued, they waited, opening suitcases, searching for more clothing and anything that could be used to sustain them. But as days passed, their hope began to fade. Hunger and desperation began to overwhelm them. Their choices were stark and all but impossible to contemplate. They would either die from starvation or be forced to consider another alternative. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, February 28, 2024 MOVIE FOR ADULTS Society of the Snow a must-see Oscar nominated film from Spain Everybody’s Fine – light on story but with a fine cast By Chris Honoré Hollywood learned long ago that formula films work. Find a template and use it until it’s frayed and even then return, promising something familiar but with a twist. Take the road trip recipe. It can be a wonderful if sometimes predictable vehicle involving multiple characters, settings and encounters. As a genre, it’s as comfortable as an old sneaker, and easily slipped on. Everybody’s Fine is such a sneaker. In the setup, Frank (Robert DeNiro), a recently widowed and retired factory worker is shown readying the house and backyard for a visit from his four children who live in various parts of the country. He shops and vacuums and waters the plants and then sadly gets four phone calls conveying four excuses as to why they can’t come. Soon, they each promise. Soon they’ll visit. Frank is not content with soon, and against his doctor’s advice (he has health issues), he decides to visit them instead. He wants it to be a surprise. So, with suitcase in hand, his medication in his pocket, he hits the road: first, New York City to See Everybody’s Fine on page 29 Society of the Snow is based on the crash of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 541 on October 13, 1972 By Chris Honoré Society of the Snow, submitted by Spain for the 2024 Oscar category of Best International Feature Film, is considered a dark-horse contender for an award. The film is based on the 2009 non-fiction book by Pablo Vierci which describes the crash of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 541. The plane had been chartered to fly a young Uruguayan rugby team to Santiago, Chile, for a much-anticipated match. For reasons never detailed in the film, the twin-engine prop plane lost power and went down high in the snow-covered Andes Mountains. As depicted in the movie, it was a violent crash that killed or injured many of the players as well as staff and pilots. The film is, in essence, a story of survival; however, it is about much more. Huddled together (16 of the 45 survived) in the mostly intact fuselage, and those not injured gradually ventured forth into the harsh sunlight only to find that they were on a glacier surrounded by impossibly high snow-covered mountains. It is a daunting moment as they grasp their total isolation. Convinced initially that they would be rescued, they waited, opening suitcases, searching for more clothing and anything that could be used to sustain them. But as days passed, their hope began to fade. Hunger and desperation began to overwhelm them. Their choices were stark and all but impossible to contemplate. They would either die from starvation or be forced to consider another alternative. And therein resides the wrenching moral See Society of the Snow on page 29 Kate Beckinsale and Robert De Niro in Everybody’s Fine A d v a n c e o r $ 3 0 ( D O O R S t i c k e t s $ 2 4 a t c a s h / c h e c k o n l y a t t h e d o o r ! articles.text: In the Heart of the Sea is an epic seafaring tale, adapted from the 2000 best-selling non-fiction book by Nathaniel Philbrick. Set in 1819 during a period when the whaling industry was robust and sperm whale oil kept the lights burning and the wheels of the still nascent industrial revolution turning. Initially set in Nantucket, the film tells the story of the Essex, captained by the inexperienced George Pollard (Benjamin Walker), who was reluctant to turn to his first lieutenant, Owen Chase (Chris Hemsworth), fearful that he would seem weak. It was estimated that the journey of the Essex would last up to three years, depending on how long it took to fill its holds with 2,000 barrels of oil. After a year at sea and little oil to show for it, Chase and Pollard are told of an area off the southern coast of South America said to be superb hunting. The information comes with a grim caveat: there is a massive whale out there that without hesitation will ram a ship and breach its hull. Discounting the story, the Essex sets sail south by southwest, headed for the hunting grounds. The film opens with a writer, Herman Melville, hoping to convince one of the survivors, Tom Nickerson (Brendan Gleeson), to tell him the story of the great whale and the sinking of the ship. At first reluctant to reveal any details to Melville, Nickerson finally relents. In a series of long flashbacks, he shares the story while Melville painstakingly takes notes. The essence of the tale is not just about the whale – 100 feet long, barnacle-encrusted, battered and covered with white spots – but of the men’s survival in their lifeboats for 90 days. articles.text: From camping and hiking to water-based adventures to snow sports and service projects, these outings provide opportunities for personal growth, skill development, and meaningful connections with nature and community. ties, scouts not only acquire practical outdoor skills but also cultivate values of leadership, service, and environmental stewardship that will serve them well throughout their lives. That is why Troop 4 will continue to expand as new members join, and we will see you in the near future for more trips and outings. Join us at the Troop 4 Open House on Monday, March 4 from 7:30-8:30 p.m. at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School. Come discover the excitement of scouting and the countless opportunities for personal growth and outdoor exploration. Whether you’re interested in hiking, camping, or learning essential life skills, Troop 4 offers a supportive environment where boys and girls can develop leadership abilities and forge lifelong friendships. Come meet our dedicated leaders and scouts, explore our meeting place, and learn about upcoming activities. Don’t miss this chance to embark on a journey of discovery and fun with Scout Troop 4. Leadership Development Troop 4’s activities are not just about adventure and exploration; they also serve as a platform for leadership development. Through designated leadership roles within their patrols or crews, scouts have the opportunity to practice decision-making, communication, and problem-solving skills in real-world scenarios. Scout Leaders will often be the ones to take responsibility for the group; to lead their scouts to complete tasks. Guided by adult leaders and mentors, scouts learn to lead by example, inspire their peers, and navigate challenges with resilience and integrity. Water-Based activities For scouts who are drawn to aquatic adventures, activities such as canoeing, kayaking, and rafting provide exciting opportunities for skill development and exploration. Whether paddling down a peaceful river or navigating challenging whitewater rapids, scouts learn valuable lessons in teamwork, safety, and water conservation. These experiences not only build confidence in the water but also teaches scouts how to survive and use the water as an advantage in everyday life. Camping Camping lies at the heart of the Scout experience. Whether it’s a weekend getaway at a local campground or an extended expedition into the wilderness, camping trips offer scouts the chance to disconnect from technology and immerse themselves in the beauty of nature. In previous years, we camped through a lot of places such as rain and harsh weather at Sugarloaf Regional Park, American Whitewater River Rafting, and camping at the Ferguson Observatory. Moreover, camping builds teamwork and relationships between scouts as they work together to tackle challenges and share memorable experiences under the stars. You will make great memories, singing around the fire and making stories to lighten up the night sky. Snow sports From skiing to snowboarding to snowshoeing, our troop offers exciting opportunities for scouts to hone their skills on the slopes while building camaraderie and resilience. Whether carving through fresh powder or mastering the art of snowshoeing, our experienced leaders provide expert guidance to ensure safe and memorable experiences. With winter landscapes as our playground, scouts learn valuable lessons in teamwork, perseverance, and outdoor survival. Service Projects In addition to recreational activities, Scout trips often incorporate service projects that allow scouts to give back to their communities and the environment. Whether it’s participating in trail maintenance, beach cleanups, or conservation efforts, scouts learn the importance of environmental stewardship and civic responsibility. As of today, we have gone to a number of service projects, such as the Scouting for Food and the Tree Lot. Scouts not only use these service projects as a way to obtain merit badges and rank requirements, but also do them just to help the community. These service projects instill a sense of pride and purpose, empowering scouts to make a positive impact on the world around them while reinforcing the values of service and leadership. articles.text: An 8-month-old female tiger cub is now being rehabilitated at Oakland Zoo. As agents for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Oakland Zoo assisted with the rescue of an eight-month-old tiger cub illegally owned in the western U.S. Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff performed a thorough physical exam, CT scan, and bloodwork which found the female cub to have at least 10 ten improperly healed fractures. The fractures were determined to be the result of decalcification of her bones, a result of inadequate amounts of calcium and phosphorus in her diet. It resulted in the weakening of the bones and subsequent fracturing during normal young tiger activities. “I’ve treated over 100 cases of rescued big cats, and unfortunately, these injuries can lead to lifelong medical issues,” said Dr. Ryan Sadler, Senior Veterinarian at Oakland Zoo. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital team is working to build her calcium intake and develop a physical therapy plan to rehabilitate the atrophied muscles. Oakland Zoo is cautiously optimistic though the healing and restoration to full health will take some time. “Seeing this young tiger enduring such obvious suffering is extremely difficult. No animal should experience life in this way. We are grateful to serve in a role that gives her hope for brighter days ahead,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. Currently the tiger’s medical issues prevent her from performing natural behaviors like running and climbing. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital is working steadily to strengthen her through specialized enrichment. When she fully heals and is cleared medically, she will move to her new home in a large animal sanctuary. Oakland Zoo supported the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act (BCPSA), legislature approved in December 2022 that bans private ownership and public contact with big cats and imposes new restrictions on their commerce, breeding, possession, and use. BCPSA helps put an end to businesses that practice ‘cub petting’ for profit, as exemplified on the popular show “Tiger King.” Oakland Zoo underwent a thorough review by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) to obtain accreditation and has been in the forefront since 1988. Oakland Zoo is taking action to promote responsible pet ownership and to rescue and provide or find new homes for improperly owned animals. To support Oakland Zoo’s efforts to rescue and rehabilitate animals in need, please donate at oaklandzoo.org/ supportanimals. Dr. Alex Herman examines a rescued female tiger at the Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital.
articles.title: Illegally-owned tiger cub confiscated, brought to Oakland Zoo

pages.text: Wednesday, February 28, 2024 27 Features your Garden column by Josh Harkinson I have made some mistakes as a gardener. The biggest was planting a vegetable garden next to a 30-foot-tall oak tree. My wife insisted on it, but in all fairness, I’m the one who ran an irrigation line next to the trunk and didn’t notice for months that it was leaking. The oak was already weak. Though we’d cut down the invasive acacia trees that had blocked its sun, the irrigation caused it to develop root rot disease, an arborist later confirmed. (You should never water oaks in the summer). The leaves began dropping. I had to blow off the driveway almost daily. I held out hope for a turnaround—until a winter storm knocked it onto the roof of my neighbor’s Volkswagen Jetta. Not watering oak trees is easier said than done, especially if you have eight of them like I do. Almost anything I plant will be next to one. Eventually I found a solution: California natives. I’ve come to love my native plants. They’re usually low maintenance, easy on my water bill, and attract birds and bees. Early spring is a great time to plant them. In the sunny parts of my yard I grow ceonothus, the California lilac. There are some 50 species of this hardy shrub, ranging from the low-growing Ceonothus thyrsiflorus (creeping blue blossom) to the tree-like Ceonothus dark star, which in my yard grew more than 7 feet tall. All of them produce dense, brilliantly blue flowers in the spring, creating a bonanza for pollinators. Their only downside is that they don’t live very long – 10 years supposedly, but in my experience closer to five. Be sure to plant them in well-drained soil. For showy blooms later in the summer, try the freakishly gigantic matilija poppy. Also known as the California tree poppy, it grows an astounding 6 to 8 feet tall and wide. You won’t need to water it after it’s established, but you will need to keep its rhizomes from invading other parts of your garden and cut the whole plant down to the ground in the winter to promote spring flowering. I know that’s a lot of work, but the prolific yellow and white flowers are worth it. Four to 9 inches in diameter, they resemble sunny-side-up eggs. No wonder it was once in the running to be the state flower. For shadier areas under oak trees, I love ribes sanguinium, or the red-flowering currant. This deciduous shrub grows six feet tall (sometimes more) and in the spring produces delightful pink flowers on dangling racemes. In the summer the flowers turn into currants that are too bitter for humans but a hit with birds. The western redbud also puts on a nice show this time of year. For a low-growing, shade-tolerant plant, I’ve found success with the evergreen ribes viburnifolium, or Catalina currant, which quickly extends branches along the ground horizontally. Also worth mentioning for dry shade: the thimbleberry, with its big attractive leaves and red fruit – like a drier version of a raspberry – that were once a staple for Native Americans. Many California natives can eventually take on an unkempt, scraggly look if you don’t prune them. Personally, I like a bit of the wild feel, especially when it comes with foraging squirrels and blue jays, fluttering butterflies, and nesting Cooper’s hawks. Still, I feel no need to apologize to those squirrels for killing that oak tree given all the tomatoes, strawberries, and sunflowers they’ve stolen from our vegetable garden since then. I think we can call it even. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. articles.text: Nicholas “Nick” Baz, artist, father of six, died at his home in Eugene, Oregon on February 8, 2024. He was 78. Originally from Los Gatos, and a long time resident of Eugene, Oregon and Piedmont, California, Nick specialized in painting and printmaking, and had a unique, often intense symbolic expressionistic style. Many of his works are rife with deep spiritual themes, documenting his journey through life with religious imagery. Those who knew him may recall the bright, psychedelic colors of his paintings or the distinctive smell of his turpentine-based oil medium, which perfumed his studio. Born in Toledo, Ohio on October 6, 1945, he was the son of Toufic and Virginia Baz (née Little). Toufic immigrated from Lebanon after Nick’s grandfather died in the 1918 flu pandemic. Nick was the middle of three children, with an older brother, Chris, and a younger sister, Shawn. When he was young, he moved to California. Nick attended Los Gatos High School, where he met Sara Stanley, though the two did not form a relationship until after he graduated in 1964. They married in Santa Barbara in 1968, and their first child of six children was born the next year, Charis, Bronwyn, Rose, Alyssa, Zachary, and Naomi. In 1973, the couple moved to Eugene, Oregon and four years later Nick began what would become a 30-year career in broadcasting, working as a control room engineer for KEZI. During this time, Nick pursued further education for his lifelong artistic pursuits, graduating from the University of Oregon in 1992 with a baccalaureate degree in fine art. For most of his time in Eugene, Nick painted and lived in the Friendly St. neighborhood and attended Saint Mary’s Episcopal Church. After 40 years of marriage, Nick and Sara divorced in 2009, and he never remarried. The two maintained a friendly relationship and close ties to the family they built together. In 2008, Nick moved to the Bay Area, where he worked and lived on the premises of Piedmont Community Church as its Doorkeeper. He became an active member of the Men’s Bible Study which met every Saturday morning to discuss the inspiring Biblical writings of the Old and New Testament. During these group discussions, whenever Nick spoke, you could hear a pin drop because everyone appreciated the sincere and profound faith of this beloved member of their community. When word arrived of Nick’s death, Piedmont Community Church’s Associate Pastor, Don Ashburn, wrote, “Nick was one of the most deeply spiritual people I’ve ever known. I mean that both in the sense of his devotion to God as well as his concern for the spirits and wellbeing of other people.” The members of the Men’s Bible Study shared Pastor Ashburn’s feelings. After Nick was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2020, he began a courageous battle against it. When his doctors recommended regular walks following chemotherapy, Nick asked the members of the Men’s Bible Study if any of them wanted to walk with him and many eagerly accepted that invitation. Among the seventeen e-mail comments the church received about Nick’s passing, many mentioned the importance of Nick’s insights during these walks. Some examples were, “I cherished those days Nick Baz, the doorkeeper at Piedmont Community Church starting in 2008, died on February 8 in Eugene, Oregon. we took our walks (as healing for me as him)”, and “Nick has been so open and honest and generous with all of us it feels we are the ones who benefited while giving him support.” He made many friends in Piedmont, and towards the end of his residency there, Nick held an art show where he sold some of his paintings before moving back to Eugene in 2021. In 2022, he took a trip to France, where he painted plein air watercolor landscapes. When he returned to the U.S., those paintings spearheaded a sold-out art show in Oakland. After an unusually long battle with cancer, Nick died in his home on the morning of February 8, 2024, surrounded by people he loved. Nick Baz is survived by all six children along with 12 grandchildren. Nick’s art may be viewed on his website: nicholasbazart.com. A Celebration of Nick’s Life will be held on Saturday, March 16, 2024 from 2:00 to 4:00 pm in the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church doorkeeper Nick Baz dies on Feb. 8

articles.text: March 8 is International Women’s Day, a day for celebrating all the accomplishments of women around the globe. But many women still need to make up ground in one key area: retirement security. Women’s challenges in achieving a secure retirement are due to several factors, including these: • Pay gap – It’s smaller than it once was, but a wage gap still exists between men and women. In fact, women earn, on average, about 82 cents for every dollar that men earn, according to the Census Bureau. And even though this gap narrows considerably at higher educational levels, it’s still a source of concern. Women who earn less than men will likely contribute less to 401(k) plans and will ultimately see smaller Social Security checks. • Longer lives – At age 65, women live, on average, about 20 more years, compared to almost 17 for men, according to the Social Security Administration. Those extra years mean extra expenses. • Caregiving responsibilities – Traditionally, women have done much of the caregiving for young children and older parents. And while this caregiving is done with love, it also comes with financial sacrifice. Consider this: The average employment-related costs for mothers providing unpaid care is nearly $300,000 over a lifetime, according to the U.S. Department of Labor — which translates to a reduction of 15% of lifetime earnings. Furthermore, time away from the workforce results in fewer contributions to 401(k) and other employer-sponsored retirement plans. Ultimately, these issues can leave women with a retirement security deficit. Here are some moves that can help close this gap: • Contribute as much as possible to retirement plans. Try to contribute as much as you can afford to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan. Your earnings can grow tax deferred and your contributions can lower your taxable income. (With a Roth 401(k), contributions aren’t deductible, but earnings and withdrawals are tax free, provided you meet certain conditions.) At a minimum, contribute enough to earn your employer’s matching contribution, if one is offered, and try to boost your contributions whenever your salary goes up. If you don’t have access to a 401(k), but you have earned income, you can contribute to an IRA. Even if you don’t have earned income, but you have a spouse who does, you might be eligible to contribute to a spousal IRA. • Maximize Social Security benefits. You can start taking Social Security at 62, but your monthly checks will be much bigger if you can afford to wait until your full retirement age, which will be around 66½. If you are married, you may want to coordinate your benefits with those of your spouse — in some cases, it makes sense for the spouse with the lower benefits to claim first, based on their earnings record, and apply for spousal benefits later, when the spouse with higher benefits begins to collect. • Build an emergency fund. Try to build an emergency fund containing up to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money kept in a liquid account. Having this fund available will help protect you from having to dip into your retirement accounts for large, unexpected costs, such as a major home or car repair. It’s unfortunate, but women still must travel a more difficult road than men to reach retirement security. But making the right moves can help ease the journey. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a financial advisor in the Piedmont office at 370 Highland Avenue in Piedmont Tel 547-4589.
articles.title: How can women bridge the retirement gap?

articles.text: Rosanne Shaffer, better known and loved by all as Randi, passed away peacefully at her Piedmont home on the evening of February 18. It was her 89th birthday. Born on February 18, 1935, she was the daughter of James M. Flaherty and Nell Curran and grew up in Tulsa, Oklahoma with her two sisters, Mary Ellen and Sheila. Humor was the currency of love in the Flaherty household, a trait Randi embraced wholeheartedly and shared generously throughout her life. After relocating to New York in 1946, Randi graduated from White Plains High School and received a business degree from Westbrook College in Portland, Maine. She then began a career with American Airlines as a flight attendant that spurred a lifelong love of travel and forged enduring friendships with her fellow Kiwis. In 1959, Randi met and married the love of her life, Ron Shaffer. For 49 years, until Ron’s passing in 2012, they made Piedmont their home. With the arrival of their three children, Curran, Brad and Grant, family formed the bedrock of their life together. The Shaffer house thrived on a vibrant blend of humor and heart. Between Ron’s dry wit and Randi’s clever quips, laughter and joy filled every Randi often mused about her own obituary, saying, “Make sure you say I was funny.” She was funny. And kind and generous and mischievous and sporty. And really funny. In the great cocktail party of the afterlife, Randi is undoubtedly making fast friends, armed with a warm smile, a snappy one-liner and a Scotch on the rocks. Randi is survived by her children Curran Burfeind (David Burfeind) of Falmouth, Maine, Brad Shaffer (Tiffanie Shaffer) of Tiburon and Grant Shaffer (Alan Cumming) of New York City, She is also survived by five grandchildren that she adored: Connor, Grant, Riley, Zackary and Naimah; along with a brother-in-law and many nieces and nephews. She will be missed dearly by her family and an incredible group of friends whose compassion and devotion meant the world to her. She leaves a void that will be filled with echoes of her laughter and a readiness to find humor and joy in every moment. At Randi’s request, no memorial is planned at this time. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to The Cancer League in Oakland, Sutter VNA & Hospice in Emeryville or the charity of your choice. Randi Shaffer, a resident of Piedmont for 49 years, died on February 18 at age 89. corner of the Shaffer house. And every laugh was underpinned by an unshakable family bond and unconditional love. Randi operated on a firstname basis with the world, and her sense of humor was a gift she shared freely. She was a cherished member of various community groups in Piedmont, from the Garden Club to Hollyhock to The Cancer League – always ready to lend a hand or a joke, often blurring the lines between the two. Randi’s faith was a constant source of strength, and the Corpus Christi Church community remained a mainstay in her life.
articles.title: Longtime Piedmonter Randi Shaffer dies at 89

When word arrived of Nick’s death, Piedmont Community Church’s Associate Pastor, Don Ashburn, wrote, “Nick was one of the most deeply spiritual people I’ve ever known. I mean that both in the sense of his devotion to God as well as his concern for the spirits and wellbeing of other people.” The members of the Men’s Bible Study shared Pastor Ashburn’s feelings. After Nick was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2020, he began a courageous battle against it. When his doctors recommended regular walks following chemotherapy, Nick asked the members of the Men’s Bible Study if any of them wanted to walk with him and many eagerly accepted that invitation. Among the seventeen e-mail comments the church received about Nick’s passing, many mentioned the importance of Nick’s insights during these walks. Some examples were, “I cherished those days Nick Baz, the doorkeeper at Piedmont Community Church starting in 2008, died on February 8 in Eugene, Oregon. we took our walks (as healing for me as him)”, and “Nick has been so open and honest and generous with all of us it feels we are the ones who benefited while giving him support.” He made many friends in Piedmont, and towards the end of his residency there, Nick held an art show where he sold some of his paintings before moving back to Eugene in 2021. In 2022, he took a trip to France, where he painted plein air watercolor landscapes. When he returned to the U.S., those paintings spearheaded a sold-out art show in Oakland. After an unusually long battle with cancer, Nick died in his home on the morning of February 8, 2024, surrounded by people he loved. Nick Baz is survived by all six children along with 12 grandchildren. Nick’s art may be viewed on his website: nicholasbazart.com. A Celebration of Nick’s Life will be held on Saturday, March 16, 2024 from 2:00 to 4:00 pm in the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. Longtime Piedmonter Randi Shaffer dies at 89 Rosanne Shaffer, better known and loved by all as Randi, passed away peacefully at her Piedmont home on the evening of February 18. It was her 89th birthday. Born on February 18, 1935, she was the daughter of James M. Flaherty and Nell Curran and grew up in Tulsa, Oklahoma with her two sisters, Mary Ellen and Sheila. Humor was the currency of love in the Flaherty household, a trait Randi embraced wholeheartedly and shared generously throughout her life. After relocating to New York in 1946, Randi graduated from White Plains High School and received a business degree from Westbrook College in Portland, Maine. She then began a career with American Airlines as a flight attendant that spurred a lifelong love of travel and forged enduring friendships with her fellow Kiwis. In 1959, Randi met and married the love of her life, Ron Shaffer. For 49 years, until Ron’s passing in 2012, they made Piedmont their home. With the arrival of their three children, Curran, Brad and Grant, family formed the bedrock of their life together. The Shaffer house thrived on a vibrant blend of humor and heart. Between Ron’s dry wit and Randi’s clever quips, laughter and joy filled every Randi often mused about her own obituary, saying, “Make sure you say I was funny.” She was funny. And kind and generous and mischievous and sporty. And really funny. In the great cocktail party of the afterlife, Randi is undoubtedly making fast friends, armed with a warm smile, a snappy one-liner and a Scotch on the rocks. Randi is survived by her children Curran Burfeind (David Burfeind) of Falmouth, Maine, Brad Shaffer (Tiffanie Shaffer) of Tiburon and Grant Shaffer (Alan Cumming) of New York City, She is also survived by five grandchildren that she adored: Connor, Grant, Riley, Zackary and Naimah; along with a brother-in-law and many nieces and nephews. She will be missed dearly by her family and an incredible group of friends whose compassion and devotion meant the world to her. She leaves a void that will be filled with echoes of her laughter and a readiness to find humor and joy in every moment. At Randi’s request, no memorial is planned at this time. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to The Cancer League in Oakland, Sutter VNA & Hospice in Emeryville or the charity of your choice. Randi’s faith was a constant source of strength, and the Corpus Christi Church community remained a mainstay in her life. How can women bridge the retirement gap? March 8 is International Women’s Day, a day for celebrating all the accomplishments of women around the globe. But many women still need to make up ground in one key area: retirement security. Women’s challenges in achieving a secure retirement are due to several factors, including these: • Pay gap – It’s smaller than it once was, but a wage gap still exists between men and women. In fact, women earn, on average, about 82 cents for every dollar that men earn, according to the Census Bureau. And even though this gap narrows considerably at higher educational levels, it’s still a source of concern. Women who earn less than men will likely contribute less to 401(k) plans and will ultimately see smaller Social Security checks. • Longer lives – At age 65, women live, on average, about 20 more years, compared to almost 17 for men, according to the Social Security Administration. Those extra years mean extra expenses. • Caregiving responsibilities – Traditionally, women have done much of the caregiving for young children and older parents. And while this caregiving is done with love, it also comes with financial sacrifice. Consider this: The average employment-related costs for mothers providing unpaid care is nearly $300,000 over a lifetime, according to the U.S. Department of Labor — which translates to a reduction of 15% of lifetime earnings. Furthermore, time away from the workforce results in fewer contributions to 401(k) and other employer-sponsored retirement plans. Ultimately, these issues can leave women with a retirement security deficit. Here are some moves that can help close this gap: • Contribute as much as possible to retirement plans. Try to contribute as much as you can afford to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan. Your earnings can grow tax deferred and your contributions can lower your taxable income. (With a Roth 401(k), contributions aren’t deductible, but earnings and withdrawals are tax free, provided you meet certain conditions.) At a minimum, contribute enough to earn your employer’s matching contribution, if one is offered, and try to boost your contributions whenever your salary goes up. If you don’t have access to a 401(k), but you have earned income, you can contribute to an IRA. Even if you don’t have earned income, but you have a spouse who does, you might be eligible to contribute to a spousal IRA. • Maximize Social Security benefits. You can start taking Social Security at 62, but your monthly checks will be much bigger if you can afford to wait until your full retirement age, which will be around 66½. If you are married, you may want to coordinate your benefits with those of your spouse — in some cases, it makes sense for the spouse with the lower benefits to claim first, based on their earnings record, and apply for spousal benefits later, when the spouse with higher benefits begins to collect. • Build an emergency fund. Try to build an emergency fund containing up to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money kept in a liquid account. Having this fund available will help protect you from having to dip into your retirement accounts for large, unexpected costs, such as a major home or car repair. It’s unfortunate, but women still must travel a more difficult road than men to reach retirement security. But making the right moves can help ease the journey. articles.text: It’s time to save the date for the third annual Piedmont Food Fest. The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival is returning to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 20 from 11 am to 4 pm. This volunteer event created post-pandemic three years ago as a way to build community through diverse food, drink, and music has evolved into a broader showcase of the Bay’s most distinctive cuisines, cultural performances, and community groups that has attracted over 3000 attendees and generated over $100,000 for local businesses. Attendees have appreciated the chance to spend the day connecting with each other amid a medley of flavors, sounds, and cultures – all gathered in one place. “Piedmont Food Fest was an absolute treat for the whole family! A not to miss community event centered around connection and diversity.” remarked Havens School parent Katie Castles Shaffer. “We love the Piedmont Food Fest! Being able to spend an afternoon with friends and community and have our kids entertained with the Kids Zone makes this an event we’ll look forward to every year. We especially appreciate the organizers’ dedication to having diverse representation across food, vendors and entertainment.” said Piedmont resident Amanda Feldman. Piedmont Food Fest 3 will feature over 17 food vendors including Crazy Empanadas, Robert Dorsey Catering, La Santa Torta, Momolicious, Arthur Mac’s, Lahor Di Khushboo, The Chairman, and Oakland Bloom as well as beer & wine tasting from local favorites including Federation Brewing, Two Broads Ciderworks, and Deer Hill Vineyards. Main stage performances will include Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, O Hina’aro Tahitian Dance & Music, Beloved Little Circus, and the Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator. Junior food festers can look forward to an enhanced KidZone with both carnival and multicultural craft stations. To sign up, visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org, Check out Early Bird specials available through March. This event is free to attend and all are encouraged to invite friends and family for this memorable day in Piedmont. Roger Tsai is the principal organizer of Piedmont Food Fest. BALLET NOTES — The four Odette/Odile dancers this week are Wona Park, Sasha de Sola, Frances Chung and Fogo, stemming from four different countries…In some productions, the double role is split between two dancers, as occurred with ballet great Natalia Makarova doing Odette only in the Soviet Kirov ballet tour here in the 1960s….In the USSR, the denouement of “Swan Lake” was revised to produce a happy ending. Forgotten in all the hoopla was that the SFB – then a minor opera-ballet company – had given the U.S. premiere of the spectacle in 1940, under Willem Christensen, 45 years after the Petipa-Ivanov world premiere in Russia. Until 1940 U.S. audiences got a taste of the banquet with the touring Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo doing Act Two only, paired with “Scheherazade,” in sleek one-nighters. Their legendary ballerina Tamara Karsavina demonstrated the salient steps to the Christensen brothers here while on the tour, and the rest was history. Any thought that olden ballerinas could not emote was dispelled by choreographer John Cranko, who told me emphatically about Karsavina’s acting: “Oh, could she ever!!” Her father Platon Karsavin had been a favorite ballet pupil of Marius Petipa himself. articles.text: St. James Drive got a little more excitement than expected last Friday, February 23, around 2:15 p.m. when a large Monterey cypress tree fell on the street, obstructing foot traffic on the sidewalk and slowing road traffic. The City of Piedmont’s Public Works Department suspects high winds combined with the tree’s already saturated ground on a steep hill were to blame for the fall. No property was damaged, and there were no injuries. Public Works rushed to the scene within minutes and with a four-man crew began removal, which took six hours. The tree was cut into sections, loaded onto trucks and brought to the Corporation Yard. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales was pleased with the skill and effectiveness displayed by his department. “Large trees that close roadways are never quite routine. They’re always a little bit different, but it is something that our department does fairly often. I’m sure that as soon as they got that call, they knew what to do, and they were able to do it fairly quickly and get the roadway back open,” he said. The impact on traffic was minimal. Piedmont Real Estate Update February 2024 Did You Know? Over the past year, our monthly newsletter has focused on data, statistics, and market trends relative to Piedmont real estate, designed to give homeowners and potential buyers a deeper look at the marketplace. This month, we thought it would be interesting to share high-level information regarding two topics that may affect you as a current or future Piedmont property owner. People may not know that the city has, among other things, information and guidelines around rental properties and requirements for running a business out of your home available on their website. If you have recently purchased a home in Piedmont, it would be helpful to connect with the city to learn more about how it runs and what you can do to make your time here more pleasurable. If you want to know more, the City Code is available at Piedmont.city.gov, and the City Clerk’s Office is a helpful resource. Short-Term Rental Requirements (such as VRBO or Airbnb): A short-term rental is defined as less than 30 consecutive days with at least two consecutive nights and not more than 60 days in a calendar year. Other factors to consider: The rented space must be a part of the primary residence and cannot be in an ADU (whether permitted or unintended). They also cannot be located in a multi-family property. The short-term rental may be hosted or unhosted. A permit is required. When applying for the permit, you’ll need owner consent, evidence of insurance, and proof that the short-term dwelling meets safety requirements (smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, etc.). To renew a permit, you must apply before the expiration of your current permit. Business tax is required on any income earned. *Source: City of Piedmont website and City Code Rentals and Investment Properties Whether you’re buying a property in Piedmont as an investment or considering a short-term rental for your own use, there are some important facts to consider. Long-Term Rental Requirements:* Long-term rentals (30 days or more) are often a good option for people looking to provide housing or live in Piedmont themselves for the community, services, or schools. Below are a few things to remember as you consider a rental property: If you’re looking to rent a property that you own, the city requires homeowners to file an Intent to Rent form and pay annual rental tax. An annual business license is required each year on property that is rented or leased. The city of Piedmont does not have a rent control ordinance. However, Piedmont is in Alameda County, which may have rent and eviction controls that housing providers should consider. As always, if you are considering renting a property, we suggest you research the local laws and speak with an attorney if needed. Did you know the Piedmont Unified School District and the City of Piedmont are separate entities? Before signing a lease, contact the school district to learn more about the enrollment process and get tips for a successful transition into the school system. Home-Based Businesses In Piedmont, home occupation means a business conducted at a residence (a definition that doesn’t include renting a property), and comes with some regulation. The goal of the regulation is to accommodate the liberty to conduct economic activity in a home while preserving the residential feel of the neighborhood. The requirements are listed below, but we highly recommend contacting the City Clerk’s office for more detailed information and guidelines. Application to the City Clerk together with a fee; Notify adjacent residents of the intention to conduct a home business. Review of the application. No more than one room in the residence may be used in connection with the home occupation. Issuance of a home occupation permit. Business license tax. articles.text: Utility sprayed industry-strength chemicals near Blair Ave. reservoir East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) has confirmed that on January 29, 2024 at about 8:30 a.m., the water district sprayed chemicals containing glyphosate to eliminate weed growth near Reservoir Number One, an out-of-commission reservoir on Blair Avenue in Piedmont. Glyphosate is the active chemical in weedkillers like Roundup, which has generated controversy in recent years over its links to cancer. The City of Piedmont Public Works Department has stated it was not notified in advance of EBMUD’s plans and that it is in talks with EBMUD to “modify that behavior” in the future. Interest in EBMUD’s use of glyphosate in Piedmont began after former City Parks Commissioner Jukka Valkonen noticed signs in his neighborhood detailing the spraying. articles.text: Editor: I was shocked and frankly ashamed to read Joseph Gold’s “Seiji Ozawa a.k.a. the picture of Dorian Gray.” Although one need not slavishly follow the Latin maxim, “Of the dead, nothing but good is to be said,” I found Gold’s misguided attempt at “inside baseball,” with his entire focus on certain reportedly negative aspects of Ozawa’s musical career, to be in bad taste and certainly at odds with many of my own experiences of Ozawa’s music-making (for example, a stunning performance of Bartok’s Concerto for Orchestra, and one of his master classes for young conductors). A quick perusal of a number of obituaries of Ozawa will show how one can appropriately write about a career that was filled with many firsts, many high points, and, yes, the inevitable blemishes that can, in such a context, be mentioned. Gold suggests that Ozawa impressed only the “unsophisticated in the audience,” to which I would reply, “Please count me as unsophisticated.” –Tom Reicher

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in response to Joseph Gold’s brutish opinion piece about the recently deceased conductor Seiji Ozawa. As a member of the San Francisco Symphony for 32 years, I’ve had the opportunity to work with Mr. Ozawa as both a student at Tanglewood and as a professional in a couple of memorable returns he made to conduct the SFS. I always found him to be inspiring, supportive, engaging and professional. In particular, I fondly recall him coming in for one afternoon rehearsal and an evening concert of Beethoven’s 8th Symphony and Berlioz’ Symphonie Fantastique. Ozawa was well prepared, kind to the orchestra and, with his photographic memory, showed us everything he wanted and needed for the music through his elegant gestures with nary a word said. The orchestra rarely sounded as good and many of the Boston Symphony’s recordings from the Ozawa years are still favorites of mine both in terms of interpretation and sound. Most importantly, for Ozawa, it was never about him and always about the music. In the current era of social media where narcissism seems to be the norm, I look back on my own experiences with Seiji Ozawa as refreshing and truly special. –Jonathan Ring Grand Avenue 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to provide more background regarding concerns about the recent use of the herbicide Ranger Pro, by the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) near the reservoir on Blair Avenue in upper Piedmont (see letter of January 31 and article of February 14). Ranger Pro contains glyphosate, the active ingredient in the herbicide Roundup. Glyphosate products such as Roundup are one of the most widely used weed killers in the world. About 200 million pounds of Roundup are sprayed on U.S. crops each year. It may persist in soil for an extended period with a typical half-life of about 7 weeks, but which can be up to 6 months depending on soil conditions. The CDC has reported that up to 80% of Americans have been exposed based on having traces of it in their urine. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency or Research on Cancer (IARC) identified glyphosate, the world’s most used herbicide, as a probable human carcinogen. In contrast, the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Scientific Advisory Panel (SAP) met in December 2016 to consider scientific evidence and concluded that it was not likely to be carcinogenic if used as recommended. There were significant methodological differences in the reports contributing to the different results. In February 2020, the EPA published an interim decision which stated that there were no risks of concern to human health when glyphosate was used according to the label instructions. This decision was challenged in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and was vacated by the Court in July 2022 meaning that Court concluded that there were insufficient data to support the position that glyphosate did not adversely affect human health. Whatever the EPA position on glyphosate, it is notable that nearly $11 billion was awarded in 2022 to settle approximately 100,000 cases against Monsanto, the original manufacturer of Roundup until it was sold to Bayer in 2018, and there have been subsequent significant financial settlements. The potential adverse health effects of glyphosate include cancer, most notably non-Hodgkins’s lymphoma (NHL). The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2024 there will be more than 80,000 new cases of NHL in the United States and that more than 20,000 people will die from this cancer. It is one of the more common cancers of children, teens, and young adults. Glyphosate is a toxin for the nervous system. Recent reports suggest that glyphosate exposure may be associated with a higher overall risk of death. Exposure to glycoside in early childhood was recently shown to be associated with the development metabolic syndrome in late teenage or early adult years. Metabolic syndrome is a complex of heart disease risk factors which accelerate the development of heart disease, the leading cause of death in the U.S. At the city level, Piedmont’s Integrated Pest Management Plan (IPM) prohibits the use of glyphosate products. Glyphosate products are legal in California and State law does not allow the City to ban the use of these products by other entities (private property owners, including EBMUD) within Piedmont’s jurisdictional boundaries. So, what should we do about glyphosate? First, Roundup and other glyphosate products should be viewed as serious health hazards and their use and exposure to them should be avoided as much as possible. Second, the City should be proactive in discouraging its use by EBMUD and other private property owners in Piedmont. The State of California maintains a helpful website on integrated pest management (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/GENERAL/pesticides.html), a set of practices which minimize the use of herbicides. Requests for a reference list can be sent to me at ssidney3203@ gmail.com. Dr, Stephen Sidney, MD, MPH, is a 40-year Piedmont resident and retired epidemiologist with Kaiser Permanente Northern California.

articles.text: Editor: The mayor has proposed that all 132 apartments allocated by the new Housing Element to the Moraga Canyon planning area be built in Blair Park. These would include 62 units for low, very low, and extremely low-income families. She proposes this despite the fact that Blair Park is a former un-engineered landfill enclosed on 3 sides by impassable terrain and on the 4th by a major arterial that an earlier, city-commissioned EIR found unavoidably dangerous to access or cross due to sight lines shorter than those considered safe by Caltrans. Given that EIR, the Mayor’s proposal violates existing city policy that all new construction provide safe sight lines. When reminded of this violation, city staff responds that the Council need not acknowledge the prior EIR because the project it described was not approved. This response misleads Piedmont residents and the Council. The prior EIR found not only that Piedmonters would be put at risk by short sight lines if the then proposed project were approved, but also that the alignment of Moraga Avenue allows no access to Blair Park that meets Caltrans safety standards. That alignment has not changed. The mayor does not acknowledge that her proposal violates city policy by putting Piedmonters in unavoidably unsafe circumstances. But I plead with the remainder of the Council, and with our professional staff, to acknowledge that housing 132 families in Blair Park will not only physically and socially segregate those families from the remainder of Piedmont, but also put all of us who use Moraga Avenue in circumstances that neither Caltrans nor city policy deem acceptable. –Ralph Catalano, Ph D

This is definitely the case with Piedmont’s Measure F intended to make a modest increase (less than $15 a month in my case) in our Municipal Services Tax. It believes renewal of the Municipal Service Special Tax (“City Service Tax”) is necessary to help maintain critical city services and provide additional funds for public safety. The City Service Tax provides local funds for current operating costs to provide the quality services our community expects. These services are more essential than ever to address the increasing crime in the Bay Area, and it is unrealistic to assume the City’s existing resources are adequate to meet these challenges. An inspection by the Public Works Department determined that large amounts of mud caused by on-site drilling were traveling into nearby storm drains in violation of the Municipal Regional Permit (MRP), which mandates stormwater pollution prevention activities. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that workers from his department were sent to “remediate the site to the proper level of care,” following an unsatisfactory cleanup by contractors, and that Public Works will be billing either Shell or their contractors directly for the department’s services. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will launch a new online crime map through its portal on the City of Piedmont website on March 1. The new public-facing database will allow citizens to view the latest crime data in their neighborhoods and will also support new features such as custom alerts and notifications. The police department hopes that the newer, easier-to-use crime map will increase citizens’ awareness and promote greater transparency between PPD and members of the public. “The public wants to know what’s going on in their community and we want them to know what’s going on,” said Lisa Douglas, Support Services Commander at PPD. “It’s important to have that information available in a consumable and user-friendly way so that it builds trust and engagement.” Until recently, the PPD hosted its crime map on City Protect, another dedicated crime map website. However, problems with the system prompted the department to look at alternative providers. “We received complaints from the public about both [City Protect] itself being unresponsive and stopping its email notifications,” said Douglas. She also alluded to problems the department had with the previous software provider, including unexpected loss of connection. “It just didn’t perform satisfactorily for us,” Douglas added. The Department has not updated its crime map on City Protect since October 17, 2023, due partially to difficulties the department had using it. PPD will host the new crime map via Citizen Connect, a map-centric portal developed by tech company Tyler Technologies that specializes in allowing public agencies to view and analyze development trends in their area. The new crime map will also boast new features like custom alerts and notifications which can be set by users, as well as refined data tools, like the ability to draw a polygon around a certain neighborhood and find out what kind of activity is happening in that area. Upon its launch the crime map will have three months of data available from the police department’s computer-aided dispatch (CAD) and records management systems (RMS). Tyler Technologies is also the vendor for the CAD and RMS at the police department, which the department has said will make integrating their information into the new crime map even easier. The police department does not have a URL available for its crime map yet, but it plans on releasing a link to it through the City’s communication channels by its launch date.
articles.title: Police Dept. to launch new online crime map

articles.text: A new ADA-compliant ramp currently being built at Dracena Park has made considerable progress in recent weeks despite delays caused by rain. Workers from the City of Piedmont’s Public Works Department have cleared dirt from the terrain and laid concrete in its stead, resulting in a stark visual change in the landscape of the park. The project is still on schedule and Public Works estimates the ramp will be finished by the end of this month. “I think it melds very well into the park itself,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “If you didn’t know it was new, you never would. We’re glad the ramp doesn’t stand out in a negative way.” The ADA ramp has been built in spite of winter rains. “You don’t get quite the level of production you want [when it is raining]. You move slower when Workers with Piedmont’s Public Works Department lay concrete for the new ramp between rainy days. The ramp will be finished by the end of the month. you’re wet, have less ability to grab tools, the soil becomes wetter and harder to move around in. In terms of walking around the site with heavy equipment, it can be a safety issue,” he said. Gonzales also cited the need to comply with stormwater laws. “The mantra is ‘only rain down the drain.’ And if you’re making a muddy mess, you have to make sure the mud isn’t getting offsite and into the creeks and surrounding areas,” he said. The new pathway cuts an ADA-accessible route from Upper Dracena to Lower Dracena.

articles.text: After it rains, sometimes we get the chance to see a rainbow in the sky. But what causes a rainbow to form? Rainbows are created when sunlight is refracted by water droplets in the sky, resulting in a colorful display for us to observe. Did you know that this phenomenon can also be seen at night? However, instead of a rainbow, it is known as a moonbow. What causes a Moonbow? A moonbow is produced by the same process that forms a rainbow, with the Moon acting as the light source instead of the Sun. Earlier this year, observers were able to witness a moonbow in Oakland. When the right conditions align, it is a stellar sight to witness. However, such sightings are rare. Why is a Moonbow rare? Moonlight is significantly fainter than sunlight, which is why the circumstances in which you can see a moonbow, especially one with color are so rare. For a moonbow to appear, specific conditions must be met: a full or nearly full Moon, light rain, or sufficient moisture in the atmosphere to refract light, and clear skies to allow the Moon’s light to shine through. What if the moon is not completely full? A moonbow may still appear, but instead of displaying the typical colors we are familiar with, the moonbow will appear white or grey. While rainbows color our daytime sky, moonbows bring magic to our nighttime sky. They show us that even simple things like sunlight, moonlight, and raindrops can create something truly spectacular! articles.text: The benches outfront of Wildwood Elementary and a new safer landscaping layout were dedicated to retired Principal Carol Cramer and Administrative Assistant Christine Petersen on Friday, February 16. A crowd of 40 people were on hand to honor the decades of service from Cramer and Petersen and to hear about the improved safety of the pick up area. First year Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond opened the ceremony with a heartfelt message about the special team Cramer and Petersen were and the robust role they played in shaping the culture and community at the school and throughout the district. Cramer and Petersen both, started at PUSD in 1988, and both spoke to the crowd before cutting the big purple ribbons over the benches. Cramer emphasized it’s the relationships that make a place and make a community. Wendi Sue was the designer on the safety project, which made landscaping changes focused on making it easier for parents and children to see and find one another at the Wildwood pick up zone. Overgrown manzanita bushes had obstructed visibility and made for more challenges during pick up. Children can now safely sit on the benches after school while waiting for their caretakers to pull upfront. The garden space is now planted with native drought tolerant plants that are filling in the space. The Wildwood Parents Club (WPC) collaborated with the Dad’s Club and had the support of a private donor to make this project possible. Cramer and Petersen both, started at PUSD in 1988, and both spoke to the crowd before cutting the big purple ribbons over the benches. Cramer emphasized it’s the relationships that make a place and make a community. Wendi Sue was the designer on the safety project, which made landscaping changes focused on making it easier for parents and children to see and find one another at the Wildwood pick up zone. Overgrown manzanita bushes had obstructed visibility and made for more challenges during pick up. Children can now safely sit on the benches after school while waiting for their caretakers to pull upfront. articles.text: On Friday, February 16, the preschoolers of Piedmont Play School, a cooperative preschool at Hampton Park, visited the Piedmont Fire Department. Firefighters Nadder Shehadeh, Kevin Sauder and Lucas Romero gave the children a presentation on fire safety and the life of a fire fighter. articles.text: Part 2 in new class at Adult School A new class at Piedmont Adult School will guide participants in setting goals in order to achieve the life they want. The second of a three-part series, Catalyst for Success: Goal Setting Workshop for Personal and Professional Growth, will be taught by Jen Cavenaugh, executive leadership coach. The final class in the series will be Habit Hack: A Workshop for Cultivating Lasting Change. She holds an MBA from the University of Chicago and leadership certification training from the Co-Active Training Institute. Her seminars are designed to help individuals clarify their values, set goals and create lasting habits for professional and personal growth. • Catalyst for Success: Goal Setting Workshop for Personal and Professional Growth Tuesday, Feb. 27, 6:30-8:30 pm, $45. Participants will celebrate their past successes, visualize their dreams and create an action plan to build the life they have always wanted. To register, visit piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655.
articles.title: Goal-setting workshop at Adult School

articles.text: Piedmont Language School held its annual Lunar New Year celebration on Thursday, February 8, at the Guild Hall in the Piedmont Community Church. A strong turnout of young Mandarin students helped usher in the Year of the Dragon. All Mandarin students and their families were invited to come eat, drink, sing, dance and watch the young language students perform in a show for their families. Singing and dancing routines helped demonstrate what they have been learning. Piedmont Language School offers Mandarin classes after school from 3:20-4:20 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays for kids from TK-7th grades. The classes are held at Piedmont Middle School. For more information visit Piedmontlanguageschool.com. Mandarin students had a great time popping bubble wrap. Students in the after school Mandarin program march through the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church disguised as a dragon. articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club hosted a crowd of more than 130 guests at their 37th annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 10, in the Veterans Hall. Guests at the adults-only event paid homage to the 100th anniversary of Wildwood Elementary School by dressing in the style of the roaring 1920s. Volunteer parents decked out the venue in twenties era gold and black decorations, with old Piedmont news clippings on the walls and tables. A champagne tower greeted guests upon entry to the hall. The evening menu included Dungeness crab, baked salmon, New Kent Ferguson (left), Brian Crandall and Deb Crandall at the Crab Feed Wildwood dads with Wildwood School principal Melissa Daymond in a crab suit A crew of volunteer Dads started cooking five hours in advance in the Veterans Hall kitchen. Orleans spicy spinach, Tunisian spiced corn, scalloped potatoes, macaroni and cheese, garlic bread, and a tossed salad. “The food was amazing, I went back for thirds it was so good,” said Carolyn Pan, co-President of the Wildwood Parents Club. Two student bands provided live music, the Freshmen Jazz Combo and Juvenoia. Wildwood dad and DJ Ben Anderson kept the party going until the 11 p.m. closing time. Everyone had a blast snapping pictures in the Photo Booth too. It took 20 volunteer dads, 10 sponsors and 250 pounds of crab to pull off this event. “The most important thing about this event is how it brings the community together. For me, it was a wonderful way to enjoy a delicious dinner out with my wife, surrounded by friends and fun,” said Jake Strzelecki With nearly everyone buying into the flapper or pageboy aesthetics, Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond outdid them all by donning the famed crab suit at the event. The clocks were turned back 100 years in Veterans Hall on Saturday, February 10. Three-piece suits, ball gowns and caps were standard attire at the annual Wildwood Dads Club Crab Feed.
articles.title: Crab Feed honors Wildwood School’s 100th anniversary

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.
