articles.text: Brit Burden surpasses 1,000 career points Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team, the No.3. seed, defeated Archie Williams 64-61 last night in San Anselmo and will advance to the North Coast Section finals. With the win, Piedmont also has qualified for the CIF State Tournament as a Section finalist. The Highlanders got through the first two rounds of the Division 3 North Coast Section postseason, defeating No. 14 Sonoma Valley 40-34 in the opening round on Tuesday, February 13 and won 67-43 over No. 6 Alhambra in the quarterfinals on Friday, February 16, both games were played at Binks Rawlings Gym. On Friday night, Piedmont’s big win over the Bulldogs reversed an early-season 45-40 loss to Alhambra back on November 28. The Highlanders limited turnovers and found passing outlets in the low post. “We came out, played hard, and took care of the basketball,” said coach Ben Spencer. “The first time we played Alhambra, we lost by five [points] and couldn’t break their press or zone. We had 19 turnovers that game and it was arguably our worst game of the year.” The Highlanders have reached the NCS semifinals for five consecutive years. “We’re just excited to get Brit Burden surpassed 1,000 career points with a 19-point performance against Alhambra. Staff Photos Piedmont, the No. 3 seed, defeated Archie Williams and will play in the finals of the Division 3 North Coast Section. another shot at the semis. We’re both scored eight, P.J. Brayer put just excited to play. I told the boys up five, while Arjun Bornstein my birthday is March 1 and we scored two. hope to be practicing on March 1,” said Spencer. It marked a big improvement over their narrow first-round win over Sonoma Valley, where the Highlanders struggled to convert on shooting opportunities. “We didn’t make a lot of shots and were playing a little tight. This time, I think we got the jitters out and guys started making their shots,” said Spencer. 67-43 over Alhambra Piedmont came out hot in the first quarter, leading 19-10 and continued piling on the points in the second quarter to create a 37-21 advantage at halftime. The Bulldogs trimmed the lead to 47-34 in the third quarter, but the Highlanders offense stayed hot in the fourth to outscore Alhambra 20-9 for the 67-43 victory. During the fourth quarter, senior Brit Burden officially surpassed scoring more than 1000 career points. Burden was instrumental in Friday’s game by attacking the hoop and drawing fouls in the low post. He converted 11 of 13 free throws in his 19-point performance. Burden joins the 1,000 point club alongside former Piedmont greats including A.J. Harris (2023), JoJo Murphy (2022), Luke Harris (2021), and Luke Barrett (2020). Final stats: Burden had 19 points, Dillon Casey scored 14, Declan Linnane had 11, Thorin Holmes and Ravi Silverberg 40-34 over Sonoma Valley Piedmont held a narrow 9-5 lead by the end of the first quarter and took a 22-18 lead into halftime. Sonoma Valley cut PHS’ lead to 33-31, but the Highlanders’ defense prevailed in the fourth quarter to only allow three points while its offense put in seven, winning 40-34. Things got uncomfortably close in the third quarter with Sonoma Valley taking a fivepoint 28-23 lead midway through the quarter. But the Highlanders responded, scoring eight unanswered points to take a 31-28 lead, thanks to six points from Casey to put PHS back to the lead. Burden closed the quarter with a layup to give his team a 33-31 lead going into the final going. In the fourth, Burden scored five of PHS’ seven points. Final stats: Casey led with 18 points, Burden scored 16 points, Holmes and Silverberg had three. articles.title: Piedmont heads to the NCS Finals

articles.text: PHS vs. Carondelet tonight for 5th place Staff Photos After losing to Carondelet in the first round of the NCS Open Division, Piedmont plays Acalanes tonight for 5th-place, and then will enter the State tournament. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team bowed out of the North Coast Section Open Division with a 83-53 loss to No. 3 Carondelet on Thursday, February 15 at Binks Rawlings Gym. The steam has one more Open Division game for fifth place at Acalanes in Lafayette tonight, Wednesday, February 21. PHS automatically qualified for the CIF State Tournament after being moved up to the NCS Open Division. Piedmont’s placement in the brackets will come out on Sunday, February 25 with most first-round games occurring the following Tuesday. “That’s the best part with the Open Division [automatically qualifying for State]. We’re excited about that, but we have to learn from these [kisses] and get better,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Carondelet entered Piedmont’s gym with ab impressive 25-4 record. With a roster of 14 players compared to Piedmont’s six, the Cougars were able to effectively rotate players out when they got into foul trouble in the later going. The Highlander offense struggled in the first half and committed 24 turnovers. They trailed 47-15 at halftime against a physical opponent. Carondelet often double-teamed Natalia Martinez and pounced on passes at midcourt. Piedmont came out more composed in the second half only committing seven turnovers and converting 18 of 22 free throws. “We knew it was going to be a tough game,” said Gardere,” but we didn’t come out ready to Natalia Martinez scored 38 points including making 14 of 15 free throws. Lindsey Wirgler fights through contact for a layup.

articles.text: The Highlanders soccer season came to an end on Friday, February 16 at Witter Field, falling 3-1 to No. 7 Archie Williams in the Division 3 North Coast Section. PHS, the No. 3 seed, allowed all three goals in the first 25 minutes and scored their lone goal minutes before halftime. PHS ends its season with a 12-3-3 overall record in its first season in Div. 3 after being promoted last year. The visiting Peregrine Falcons played a composed game defensively, celebrating every tackle and clearance for 80 minutes. Their energy and momentum was impressive. “The difference was the intensity of the teams,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. “They came out really hungry and were the better team. They worked harder from the opening whistle and were more organized. The early goals hurt and those were our mistakes. We had a mountain to climb at 0-3,” he added. “They are obviously an organized side. The coach has been there awhile and they have big, strong boys. They knew how to stay organized and close out a game,” said Sullivan. Piedmont has some key players graduate this year: goalie Axel Saldanha, defenders Ben Elmquist and Andrew McLaughlin, striker Oliver Shafroth, captain midfielder Riley Stratman, and captain and four-year starting striker Aiden Woolwine. However a wealth of talent returns next season: forwards Bosco Lorin and Gianluca Bini, midfielders Jake and Logan Faucher, and Harper Mand, fullback Niko Markopoulos, fullback/ winger Jacques Saldanha, and central attacker Enzo Bernales, who was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2023. 3-1 loss to Archie Williams Archie Williams struck first in the 5th minute on a botched linkup. A pass back was mishandled and rolled to the Falcons’ left winger, who slotted it in. Three minutes later, the visitors drew a free kick slightly past midfield, and disaster struck again for Piedmont. This time, a long ball into the box was allowed to fall near the right post, settling nicely for an Archie Williams forward to score easily. Jacques Saldanha had a chance for Piedmont in the ninth minute after locating a long ball over the top and taking a shot that went high. AWHS’ goal keeper came out of net to challenge Jacques’ shot, colliding with the PHS winger but there was no call. Bernales also had a shot on target from a free kick a few yards above the penalty area, but the Falcons’ keeper was there. That chance led to a counterattack from Archie Williams, leading to a penalty awarded to the visitors after a collision in the box. The Peregrine Falcons’ initial PK attempt was saved by Axel Saldanha, but the shot deflected back to the penalty-taker for a goal in the 25th. Score 3-0. Stratman had a shot hit the crossbar in the 37th, while Logan Faucher had a header go wide in the 38th. Piedmont scored from a corner in first-half stoppage time when a cross into a crowded area was pushed home by Mand. In the second half, Piedmont had chances from Logan Faucher Staff Photos Piedmont exited the North Coast Section playoffs after falling to Archie Williams, 3-1. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team, seeded No. 7, lost 2-0 loss to No. 2 Cardinal Newman on Friday, February 16 in Santa Rosa in the Division 3 North Coast Section Quarterfinals. The Highlanders’ opened the playoffs with a strong 6-0 win over No. 10 Albany on Tuesday, February 13 at Witter Field. They compiled a record of 12-4-2 (W-T-L) this year. “Cardinal Newman are very good. We’ve played them a couple of times in year’s past. We knew it was going to be tough, but played very, very well. We had them on the ropes at times,” said PHS coach Dan Chubbock. Piedmont had its chances to score, including a penalty kick that was stuffed with around 10 minutes left in the game. “We kept it tight and created a few chances. It was a very endto-end game. We had the better of the opportunities in the second half. We won a penalty for a handball in the box, but their keeper made a really athletic save and tipped it onto the crossbar. Had the penalty gone in, maybe Sophomore Miranda Liu scored twice in the first round of the NCS playoffs. Juliana Thornborrow (left) and Elsa Wallway converge on a Cardinal Newman player. it’s a different story, but I’m happy with the performance,” Chubbock said. Making a difference in Friday’s game was the absence of two critical starters out with injuries – forward Lola Beihn, and talented midfielder Juliana Thornborrow who left the game after 15 minutes. “We lost Juliana, who came off injured, and we were without Lola as well. The players who were out there did great. It could’ve gone either way. I was proud of their performance,” Chubbock said. 2-0 loss to Cardinal Newman Cardinal Newman struck in the 8th minute into the first half after connecting with a header goal on a cross into the box from a corner. Then around the 46th minute in the second half on a rare Olimpico, where the Cardinals’ corner-kick taker bent her cross into the net at the far post. Despite the 2-nil score line, Piedmont had some looks. Their penalty kick came in the _ minute after CNHS committed a handball in the box. Wallway stepped to the spot, but her shot to the right of the keeper was stopped by a dive—tipping her shot onto the crossbar. Wallway had a look in the second half, but Cardinal Newman’s keeper successfully came out of net to pounce on the ball. Marshburn also had a shot attempt in the later going. 6-0 over Albany PHS hosted No. 10 Albany on Tuesday, February 13 and dominated in a 6-nil shutout victory. Piedmont led 3-0 by halftime with a goal by Liu in the 25th on a breakaway opportunity. Wallway made it 2-0 in the 38th by way of a penalty kick, slotting her shot to the keeper’s left. Liu scored once more in the 41st with a left-footed shot from a couple yards outside the 18-yard box using her weaker foot. In the second half, Symkowick scored in the 55th after launching in a shot on her first touch. Elia Kwong made it 5-0 in the 80th after gathering a loose ball in the area, while Eliza Hammond put a bow on the match with a goal in second half stoppage time, lobbing a shot over the keeper.

articles.text: The Highlanders’ boys’ tennis team is back on the courts for the 2024 season, bringing plenty of experience from last year’s team that went 15-8 overall and placed second in the Western Alameda County Conference. Back at the Corey Reich Tennis Center include four-year starters Monte Imburg and Ben Breber, along with 2023 Freshman of the Year Lucas Smolko. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s baseball team returns to Humphries Diamond for the spring season. Piedmont’s baseball team is back for the spring season, starting with a game at St. Mary’s in Berkeley this Saturday, February 24. The Highlanders went 14-11 last year in their first season in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. It caught everyone’s attention in the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs, advancing to the semifinals as the No. 8 seed. They lost a 11-10 barnburner against No. 5 Justin-Siena after upsetting No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 the previous round. The team lost key players to graduation, notably Michael Aikawa and Ryan McConathy. But a strong cast of players should provide a potent batting lineup. Returning starters include outfielder Markos Lagios, shortstop/ pitcher Peter Krumins, catcher Will Parker, outfielder/pitcher John Olsen, former first-baseman Dimitri Papahadjopoulos, infielder Diego Delventhal, and versatile utility players Brandon Dicke, and Ellis Moss. “We have 23 kids on the roster, so we’re going to need everyone. Players will have to play multiple positions and try positions they aren’t comfortable in just yet,” explained coach Eric Olson. Lagios was the Post’s Honorable Mention for 2023 Sophomore of the Year after batting .303 with 23 hits, 11 doubles, three triples, and 18 RBIs, He led the team with two home runs and 27 runs scored. “Markos is going to play center field and will lead off for us,” Olson said. “Peter could hit second and Will Parker will hit third; he’s going to be a stud.” Krumins s committed to play baseball for Northern Kentucky next year, takes over at shortstop for Aikawa and will be a pitcher. “We lost our ace last year with Michael Aikawa. He wasn’t a pitcher but he did a great job when we asked him. Peter Krumins can certainly do it,” Olson said. Delventhal was another player who impressed in the second half of the season. He’ll be a fulltime starter at second base. He was named Honorable Mention for 2023 Freshman of the Year after appearing 14 times for nine hits, two RBIs and three runs scored. In the NCS play offs, he had two hits, a run scored and an RBI against Justin-Siena. Olson is doing some mixing and matching to create a threeman starting pitching rotation. Krumins will get time as the No. 1 option, along with John Olsen, Papahadjopoulos, Seve Sanchez, and Ellis Moss, all with experience from last season. “Peter will throw, John Olsen is going to help out there, Dimitri Papahadjopoulos, Ellis Moss and Seve Sanchez will all get time and are all seniors. We’re hoping those five kids can step up,” Olson said. Piedmont plays its first game at St. Mary’s this Saturday at 1:00 p.m. before their home opener at Humphries Diamond against Encinal on Thursday, February 29 at 3:30 p.m. Peter Krumins, a senior leader, will be playing shortstop and pitching. Markos Lagios, a junior, enters his third year as a starter.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team is back in action for another spring season. They competed in the Grizzly Invitational on Saturday, February 17 at San Lorenzo High School. Piedmont’s boys team finished first and the girls’ team was second. The Highlanders are the last team to be displaced by the prolonged renovations of Witter Field. Their last roster of 110 athletes has had to split time training at Laney College, Witter Field, and running the streets of Piedmont. They even had to use a small area in Piedmont Park. “We’re basically doing Monday’s as a full team at Witter, Tuesdays and Thursdays the majority of the team is at Laney, and Fridays the sprinters are at Laney. The distance crew is mixing and matching at Witter, Laney and the Piedmont neighborhood,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. The big change for the boys’ team will be the absence of Parker Long, who has graduated. Returning as a team leader is distance runner Xander Schulte-Sasse, a senior, whose cross country season was cut short due to an injury. He’ll largely compete in the 1600 and 3200 events. Schulte-Sasse won the Grizzly Invitational’s 3200 with a time of 9:54.96 in a field of six and was second of 20 in the 1600 in 4:39.07. “Our expectation of him is to go out and pace the 1600 and 3200. Within the WACC, he’s got some competition at O’Dowd and Berkeley,” coach Assadi said of the senior runner. It’s also a big season for sprinter Sam Shelby, who is looking to take his breakout football season onto the track. He will compete in the 100, 200, 400, 4x100, and 4x400 relay teams. Last spring, he was a key memFreshman Team after qualifying for the CIF Cross-Country State Championship. Last Saturday, Swain won the 800 in 2:03.29 in a field of 15 half milers and was third of 20 in the 1600 in 4:39.58. “The No. 1 up-and-comer is Sebastien Swain. He’s already setting freshman records; Seb is someone who is a unique athlete,” Assadi said. Girls’ team The PHS girls’ track team will field a young roster led by sophomore Skylar Best. As a freshman last year, she competed in the 800, 1600, 3200, 4x400, and 4x800. She helped the 4x400 team – with Ella Yasar, Jamie Schwarz, and Emily Fitzgerald – place second in the WACC Championship, and fourth at the NCS Bayshore. “Skylar is one of those ultradiverse runners like Parker Long was last year. The question for her is what is her preference and where she can make the most impact,” Assadi said. Schwarz, a four year starter, will be a captain for the girls. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team returns to Witter Field after finishing 8-8 last season. Coach Carlton Chan said he had the largest turnout of players during his time at the school. He will be assisted by a former player, Kate Abel (PHS Class of 2019), who will coach the junior varsity team. “We have a lot of new kids, it’s probably the largest team I’ve ever had. We have 18 on varsity and the rest on JV. We have Kate Abel, who was an assistant coach last year, is now head coach of the JV team. She’s a former Piedmont athlete, played at Chapman, and is now coming full-circle,” coach Carlton Chan said. Last year’s team lost several key players to graduation: attacker Molly Ashton, goalie Lindsay Kottle, and middie/ attacker Eleanor Lavin. Lavin earned honors by being selected for the U.S. Lacrosse’s NorCal Senior All Star Game. This year’s team will include Ruby Guzdar as the incumbent leading scorer, Hailey Marshburn, goalie Friedie Schickedanz, and Jane Hempeck, Peyton Watson, Chloe Graham, and Luisa Cole. Guzdar has been named a team captain, along with Hempeck. “We have a lot of returners and we’re happy about that. I think they’re going to make a big impact. Jane will make a big impact on the defensive side and we’ll also get Hailey Marshburn back from soccer. She has a strong voice and is very good,” Chan said. Schickedanz played goalie last season, but will see more action in the field this year. “Now that Molly [Ashton] has graduated, Friedie is going to anchor that position. We’ve been trying to groom her to take that spot and she’s gotten pretty good,” Chan said. Watson is another young player who got time as a freshman and has been making her mark in training. “Peyton Watson is someone we’re excited about, she’s just gotten better and better. As a freshman, we saw glimmers of her ability and now she understands she’s faster, bigger, and stronger. In practice, she’s showing she can really take it to the hole. She’ll move around,” Chan said. Junior Annika Hattan-Kutter will debut as the starting goalRuby Guzdar is a captain and the leading returning scorer from last season. keeper. “Annika will get her first season as starting goalie. I told her, it’s the goal to be the starter and she needs to own it. She has a great attitude and is a good goalie. I think she can handle it,” Chan said. Chan is hopeful that this year’s team will emulate some similar aspects to Piedmont’s NCS Championship-winning team of 2020, which featured a lot of movement and cuts toward the net. “The good thing is, most of everyone are returners and understand the offense. We’re going to run a similar offense to where we’re cutting left and right. We’re going to bring back some offense from our NCS Championship days,” Chan said. Piedmont starts its season on Wednesday, February 28 at Dublin. Hailey Marshburn is a returner and a four-year starter.

articles.text: South African artist Zanele Muholi The first major exhibition of South African artist Zanele Muholi on the West Coast is now on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and will be available for viewing through August 11. The multimedia exhibition, entitled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, features over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present alongside paintings, sculpture and video. Eye Me celebrates the artist’s Black queer community in post-Apartheid South Africa and showcases issues of gender identity, representation and race. Muholi was born in Durban and currently lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. The museum has featured works by Muholi in the past, including Faces and Phases in the 2011 exhibition Face of Our Time. Their work was also featured in Public Intimacy: Art and Other Ordinary Acts in South Africa, co-organized by SFMOMA and the Yerba Buena Center for Arts in 2014. To learn more and to purchase passes to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/zanele-muholi-eye-me/.
articles.title: Zanele Muholi exhibition now on view at SF MOMA

articles.text: Theatre to host community night this Friday Photo by Kevin Berne Ixtlán and Oogie Push appear in Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Manhatta. Aurora Theatre Company’s current production of Manhatta is playing onstage now through March 10. The play by Mary Nagle follows two stories separated by centuries and focuses on the native Lenape people. The island of Manhattan in New York City was once known as Manahatta by the Lenape. The Dutch West India Company established a trade route with the native people in the 17th century but soon began to bargain for the island itself, effectively pushing out the Lenape tribes. Centuries later, a similar scenario plays out in the New York City housing market when inflated housing prices force out longtime city dwellers. Once again, greed causes many to lose their homes. Director Shannon Davis weaves the two narratives into a single story of avarice and loss through the eyes of a young Lenape woman, Jane Snake, who returns to her ancestral homeland. The cast includes Linda Amayo-Hassan as Bobbie, Livia Gomes Demarchi as Le-le-wa’ -you/Jane, Max Forman-Mullin as Jakob, Anthony Fusco as Peter Minuit, Ixtlán as Se-ket-tu-mayqua and Oogie Push as Toosh-kipa-kwis-i. A discussion of Manahatta will be hosted after the show on Friday, February 23, and Wednesday, February 28. An indigenous community night will also be held this Friday, February 23. featuring guest speaker and Ohlone healer Kathleen Grace. A pre-show reception will be held at 6 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024- season/Manahatta, or call the box office at 510-843-4822. The theater is located in downtown Berkeley at 2081 Addison Street.

articles.text: Visit the Conservatory of Flowers in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park this Saturday, February 24, for a guided tour of the Conservatory’s Magnolias. The Conservatory houses one of the most significant collections of Magnolias in the United States, with over 200 trees blooming from mid-January through March. The ancient flowering trees are endemic to Asia and the New World and do well in San Francisco’s mild climate. The conservatory cultivates species from across most of the world, from the Himalayas to Mesoamerica. A curated tour begins at 10 a.m. and will run for approximately an hour and a half. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, February 21, 2024 Arts & Entertainment Zanele Muholi exhibition now on view at SF MOMA Aurora Theatre presents Manhatta through March Theatre to host community night this Friday South African artist Zanele Muholi By Allyson Aleksey The first major exhibition of South African artist Zanele Muholi on the West Coast is now on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and will be available for viewing through August 11. The multimedia exhibition, entitled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, features over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present alongside paintings, sculpture and video. Eye Me celebrates the artist’s Black queer community in post-Apartheid South Africa and showcases issues of gender identity, representation and race. Muholi was born in Durban and currently lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. The museum has featured works by Muholi in the past, including Faces and Phases in the 2011 exhibition Face of Our Time. Their work was also featured in Public Intimacy: Art and Other Ordinary Acts in South Africa, co-organized by SFMOMA and the Yerba Buena Center for Arts in 2014. To learn more and to purchase passes to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/zanele-muholi-eye-me/. By Allyson Aleksey Aurora Theatre Company’s current production of Manhatta is playing onstage now through March 10. The play by Mary Nagle follows two stories separated by centuries and focuses on the native Lenape people. The island of Manhattan in New York City was once known as Manahatta by the Lenape. The Dutch West India Company established a trade route with the native people in the 17th century but soon began to bargain for the island itself, effectively pushing out the Lenape tribes. Centuries later, a similar scenario plays out in the New York City housing market when inflated housing prices force out longtime city dwellers. Once again, greed causes many to lose their homes. Director Shannon Davis weaves the two narratives into a single story of avarice and loss through the eyes of a young Lenape woman, Jane Snake, who returns to her ancestral homeland. The cast includes Linda Amayo-Hassan as Bobbie, Livia Gomes Demarchi as Le-le-wa’ -you/Jane, Max Forman-Mullin as Jakob, Anthony Fusco as Peter Minuit, Ixtlán as Se-ket-tu-mayqua and Oogie Push as Toosh-kipa-kwis-i. A discussion of Manahatta will be hosted after the show on Friday, February 23, and Wednesday, February 28. An indigenous community night will also be held this Friday, February 23. featuring guest speaker and Ohlone healer Kathleen Grace. A pre-show reception will be held at 6 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024- season/Manahatta, or call the box office at 510-843-4822. articles.text: B e r k e l e y S y m p h o n y announced on February 19 the appointment of veteran music and arts administrator Marion Atherton as its new Executive Director. Marion will join the organization immediately and will be working closely with Ming Luke, who has been serving as Interim Executive Director and Artistic Director, to ensure there is a smooth and seamless leadership transition. Marion Atherton brings over 25 years of arts management experience to the position. She most recently served as the Chief Operating Officer and Interim Head of School at the Crowden Music Center in Berkeley. Prior to that, she was the Executive Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Atherton’s experience includes successful fundraising and financial oversight, strategic planning, and community engagement. “We are thrilled to have someone with Marion’s experience and East Bay roots leading Berkeley Symphony as we begin the next 50 years of our history,” said Symphony Board President Rigel Marion Atherton has been appointed Executive Director of Berkeley Symphony. Robinson. “I am thrilled to lead Berkeley Symphony in its next chapter,” said Atherton. “As a longtime Berkeley resident, I have a personal investment in Berkeley Symphony's mission. I look forward to working with the Symphony's outstanding team of artists, staff, and Board members to continue its history of building community through world-class performances and educational programming.”
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony names Marion Atherton as new Executive Director

articles.text: and distinctive sound front and The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate its brass family with an all-brass concert at Davies Symphony Hall on Sunday, March 10. Trumpet, French horn, trombone, and tuba players will be led by conductor Brad Hogarth to bring the instruments’ big, bold center. Based in the San Francisco Bay Area, Hogarth is the Associate Professor of Conducting at San Francisco State University, and was recently named Associate Conductor of the Monterey Symphony. He is the music director and conductor of the Art Haus Collective. He is also an accomplished trumpeter and performs regularly with a number of orchestras, including the Indianapolis Symphony and Louisville Orchestra. As a guest conductor, he has appeared with the Diablo Symphony Orchestra, the ECHO Chamber Orchestra, and the San Francisco Wind Ensemble. The evening’s program will highlight with concert music for brass, percussion, and Timpani. The program includes Presto Barbaro from Symphonic Suite from On the Waterfront by Leonard Bernstein, Ottoni by Magnus Lindberg, Quatre Motets sur des thèmes grégoriens by Maurice Duruflé, A Moorside Suite by Gustav Holst, Variations on a Theme by Paganini Witold Lutosławski and Chicago Skyline by Shulamit Ran. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https://www. sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/ 2 0 2 3 -2 4 / S F- S Y M PH ON YBRASS. Brad Hogarth will lead a brass concert by members of San Francisco Symphony.
articles.title: SF Symphony presents all-brass concert on March 10

articles.text: San Francisco Opera continues its Schwabacher Recital Series with an evening performance on Wednesday, March 2. Tickets are available now. The recital series offers audiences an opportunity to hear upcoming gifted singers in an intimate setting. Since 1983, the series has featured renowned artists and has been instrumental in launching international careers. The evening’s performance features soprano Arianna Rodriguez, soprano Olivia Smith, mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz, bass-baritone Jongwon Han, and pianist Yang Lin. The artists will perform in a program curated by American tenor Nicholas Phan entitled The Secret Garden, composed of songs in English, German, Russian, Spanish, French and Korean. “Throughout the ages, poets and composers have been Mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz inspired by nature, finding meaning and metaphor for the human experience through our relationship with the flora and the fauna that surround us,” said Phan. “In this spirit, The Secret Garden is a bouquet of song, featuring songs by beloved composers such as Margaret Bonds, Lili Boulanger, Henry Thacker Burleigh, Ernest Chausson, Aaron Copland, Edvard Grieg, Franz Schubert, Richard Strauss and Ralph Vaughan Williams.” The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/schwabacher-recital-series/. Please join us for our upcoming in-person seminar.
articles.title: SF Opera’s Schwabacher Recital Series continues March 2

articles.text: Concert held at First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley Berkeley Symphony pays homage to the diversity of French music with a French Reverie concert held at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley this Sunday. The concert features French music from the Impressionist era to the present day, with a program that includes Debussy’s Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, Connesson’s A Kind of Trane honoring the legendary jazz icon John Coltrane, and Farrenc’s Symphony No. 3 in G minor. T he c onc e r t fe at u r e s acclaimed saxophonist Robert Young, the brother of Berkeley Symphony conductor Joseph Young. He has performed with numerous symphonies in the U.S., including the Wichita Symphony Orchestra, Charleston Symphony Orchestra and the University of Michigan Symphony Orchestra. He holds a teaching position at the University of North Carolina School of the Arts as Associate Professor of Saxophone. The concert begins at 4 p.m. A pre-concert chat will be held one hour before the performance, where guests will be invited to learn about the program’s cultural and historical context, along with guided listening. There will be live interviews with guest artists, composers, and orchestra musicians, and admission to the pre-show event is free to all ticket holders. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleysymphony. org/event/french-reverie/. Robert Young, brother of Berkeley Symphony conductor Joseph Young ®
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony presents ‘French Reverie’ concert this Sunday

articles.text: All art is introspective to some degree, but some pieces ask us to stop and reflect more than others. A woman sitting in a boat without oars contemplates her reflection. A red finch, frozen in an explosion of water from its’ bird bath. A wedding. A stormy night. A pair of hands reach toward heaven holding phones. This invitation to reflect is the goal of an exhibition titled “Moments that Give Pause,” now on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The show brings together the work of four Easy Bay artists, Carol Aust, Debra Collins, Leslie Vail Crisfield, and Gretchen McCondochie, all united by a theme of contemplating beauty. The artists worked in Artists Carol Aust (left), Debra Collins, Leslie Vail Crisfield, and Gretchen McCondochie a range of mediums and materials to bring the display to life, including traditional painting, Dawn by Debra Collins is an example of the artist’s work using cut paper. sewn fiber and cut paper. “I do figurative paintings of people traveling through emotional landscapes,” said Aust, an Oakland-based painter. Her paintings vary between depictions of intimate moments of beauty between family and lovers to lone figures in solitary situations. “I want all of my paintings to have a degree of mystery. I want the viewer to be able to look at it and have their own opinion of what each piece means,” she said. Leslie Vail Crisfield leans more heavily into her sense of solitude for her work. “I often travel and take myself on solo art retreats for my work. I’ve been to Joshua Tree by myself for a month, Sedona by myself. I just put myself in the car and go,” she said. This quality appears in her work through landscapes that use black and white to evoke a sense of seclusion and natural beauty. “I usually wind up with these stark light and dark things,” she said. Moments that Give Pause will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays, February 17 through March 3 from noon to 3 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonita Avenue. In Carol Aust’s Reflection, a woman sits calmly in a boat without oars, contemplating her image in the water. Gretchen McCondochie’s “Embroidered Bird” Splash 1 (left) and Splash 2 by Leslie Vail Crisfield depict an explosion of water in a birdbath.
articles.title: “Moments That Give Pause” art show at Center for the Arts

articles.text: Ongoing through March 3 Carol Aust & Friends Art Exhibit Four East Bay artists will have an exhibition titled Moments that Give Pause on Saturdays and Sundays, February 24 to March 3, from noon to 3 pm, with a closing reception on March 3 from 12–3 p.m. The artists use divergent materials – painting, fiber, and cut paper — but share a common theme of celebration in the moment. Saturday, March 2, 7 p.m. Dente Duo Guitar and Percussion Returning from France for a repeat engagement, classical guitarist Arthur Dente will perform a collection of his own compositions, accompanied by Steve Robertson on assorted percussion instruments. The works of J.S. Bach (Chaconne fr. Partita #2), Hector Villa-Lobos (Prelude #1), Isaac Albeniz (Asturias), and Francisco Tarrega (Recuerdos de la Alhambra) will be performed. Advance tickets are $24 at https://bpt.me/6124713, or $30 cash or check at the door. Sunday, March 3, 4:30 p.m. Duo SaBu Songs with the Piano Duo SaBu pianist Heidi Saario and tenor Erich Buchholz will perform an afternoon of romantic songs from England, Norway and Finland., to include the music of Vaughan Williams, Grieg, Sibelius, and Madetoja. Complete texts and translations will be provided. For lovers of piano, opera and song, this will be a fulfilling hour of music. Tickets are $25/$10 available in advance at http://www.eventbrite. com/e/804151788647, or at the door. Saturday, March 9, 6 p.m. Michael Stehr illustrated Art Lecture Artist and art historian Michael Stehr will take the audience on a two-block stroll in Rome in an illustrated lectured titled Two Blocks in Rome: Bernini, Borromini, e la Via del Quirinale. His talk will explore the work and influence of two 17th-century Italian artists: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was arguably the greatest sculptor of the 17th century, and is also known for outstanding architectural works, such as the colonnade enclosing the piazza before St. Peter’s. Francesco Borromini was a leading figure in the emergence of Roman Baroque architecture. Doors open at 5:30 for the 6 p.m. lecture. Admission is $20 at the door, cash only. Sunday, March 10, 3 p.m. Melissa Lam Solo Cello Recital Cellist Melissa Lam, 15, returns to PCA for her second solo cello recital on March 10. She performs with the California Chamber Orchestra and has played at major venues including Davies Symphony Hall. She was invited as the guest soloist to perform Elgar’s Cello Concerto at the prestigious Town and Gown Club’s annual luncheon in Berkeley last year. She has won several U,S, and international competition first prizes. The recital is free, with a suggested donation at the door. Sunday, March 17, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio Come to the PCA Classic Jazz Club for some late afternoon relaxation and the music of Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Anthony Pegram as they celebrate St. Patrick’s Day. This event is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing its magnificent Steinway grand piano. Relax in the intimate club-like environment with snacks and complimentary wine, enjoying familiar music and some of its history. Tickets are $25 in advance at https://bpt. me/6214927, or $30 at the door, cash or check only. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up-to-date vaccinations. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.

articles.text: Two Blocks in Rome: Bernini, Borromini, and Via del Quirinale Local artist and art historian Michael Stehr returns to Piedmont Center for the Arts on March 9 for another spirited foray into the world of art history. For this next adventure, Stehr takes the audience to his beloved Rome to consider one of his favorite walks: a two-block stretch along the Via del Quirinale. The highlight of this stroll is the unique ability to compare, practically side by side, major architectural achievements by two founders of the Italian Baroque style: Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Francesco Borromini. While both are regarded as founders of the same artistic movement, the two could not be more different as individuals. These personal differences are clearly manifested in their drastically contrasting aesthetics. Bernini’s more theatrical style is demonstrated at the first stop on the journey, at the small church of Sant’Andrea al Quirinale. After traveling a mere 100 yards, one stands at the door of Borromini’s San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, regarded by some art historians as the greatest building in all of Western art. Here, Borromini’s use of complex geometry is in full force, resulting in an exhilarating architectural encounter. This short walk through history has one more stop, at Santa Maria della Vittoria, before backtracking to the Palazzo Barberini, where Interior details of Borromini’s San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane in Rome both artists were working side by side, simultaneously, as they faced the same design challenge. Stehr’s 50-minute illustrated lecture on Saturday, March 9 will begin at 6 p.m.. Doors open at 5:30. $20 per person at the door. Cash only please.
articles.title: Michael Stehr art lecture on March 9

pages.text: Wednesday, February 21, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet Fast food…then and now By Joseph Gold We are going out to eat. We have to hurry because all the restaurants will be closed in Pompeii after August 24, 79AD. When we go out to a ball game or a show someplace, there are food vendors everywhere. Think of all of the food trucks and fastfood chains that we all know and love. Perhaps you already have in mind some of your favorite foods, like hotdogs and hamburgers, potato chips, and French fries, popcorn, and chocolate. Don’t forget the ketchup and the salt. But we are now finding out that the ancient Romans enjoyed the good life also. When Mt. Vesuvius erupted, it essentially froze the civilization in Pompeii and neighboring cities in place. We are The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet lucky that archaeologists are discovering new things all the time. It turns out that fast food joints are nothing new. Pompeii had at least 90 of these fast-food places. Let’s take a look back in time and get the picture as it was. Considering that Pompeii had about 90 fast food places, that’s practically one at every intersection. In many ways, these fast food restaurants were kind of like the restaurant buffets we have today. They were usually L-shaped or square with the food on display and somebody behind the counter to manage the restaurant and serve the food. The menu was proudly displayed on the wall in the form of a fresco. They had cash registers of sorts, looking more like a bowl filled with coins. And just like today, there was crime. The tough guys ate at the fast-food joints. The wealthy folks, known as patricians, dined at home. There was no ketchup, but the Romans smacked their lips with a stinky fermented fish sauce. Vinegar was used frequently, and so was honey and local herbs. There was no sugar and very little salt. These things were just too expensive. For main courses they had pork, goat, lots of grain and legumes, and they even had ice cream. Some of the popular delicacies will sound very strange to us. For instance, they loved honey roasted rodents, and flamingo tongues. For drinks, they had many forms of wine, and if the wine soured, they could refresh it with water and spices. “Hey waiter… Hurry up. I’ve got to get to the show. My favorite gladiator team is fighting for the world championship.” They sure knew how to enjoy their lives. They had to. Back then you were lucky if you lived to be 33 years old. articles.text: The Holdovers, put simply, is an extraordinary film, nominated by the Academy for a 2024 Oscar for Best Picture. From the first frame, it reminds audiences that movies are a remarkable medium for telling stories that convey an almost magical depth and breath when examining the human condition. It also possesses a deep bench of gifted actors, led by the genius of Paul Giamatti, nominated for Best Actor in a Leading Role. He inhabits the character Paul Hunham, a classics teacher at a New England boarding school. The year is 1970. He is considered by students and faculty to be a dedicated curmudgeon who long ago abandoned his conviction that he could make a difference in the lives of his students, whom he calls “troglodytes” and “smarmy Visigoths.” There is a sadness to the delight he seems to take in dropping graded blue book exams on their desks, most with large Fs and Ds. The narrative begins in earnest when Paul is called to the office of the headmaster and told that the Christmas holiday is approaching and during this two-week hiatus four students – who for various reasons – must remain at the school. They’re referred to as the “Holdovers.” Having no family, Paul is asked to watch over them, much to his consternation. As the school empties and parents arrive to pick up their sons, Dominic Sessa, Paul Giamatti, and Da’Vine Joy Randolph in The Holdovers Paul gathers his four charges in the library, and takes some pleasure in notifying them that they will use the two weeks for studying, meaning preparing for the next semester. While he is ignoring their groans and protests, a fifth student, senior Angus Tully, wonderfully portrayed by Dominic Sessa, walks in with his suitcase, clearly angrier than his usual mien. He has just received a phone call from his mother informing him that he will remain at school while she goes to St. Kits with her new husband. And so begins what becomes a road trip to Boston, one that includes the school’s food manager/cook, Mary, played by D’Vine Joy Randolph, who has been nominated for Best Actress in a Supporting Role. Also included is sharp-tongued student Angus, feeling abandoned, and of course Paul, driving his worn, nondescript sedan. The other four holdover students have been liberated, unexpectedly, by a wealthy parent of one of the boys, who arrives in a helicopter. The journey is nuanced, comical, and revelatory, focused almost completely on the bad-tempered, sullen then gradually transformative relationship between Angus and Paul. The Holdovers is beautifully written, superbly acted, and now streaming. The Holdovers. Directed by Alexander Payne. Starring Paul Giamatti, D’Vine Joy Randolph, Dominic Sessa. 2 hrs., 13 min. articles.text: Unknown is a roller coaster ride. It moves slowly at first, up a long incline and then gravity kicks in and it takes off. Of course, the film is full of holes. It’s improbable, defies all logic, but then what are action thrillers for but to seriously get the attention of the audience, ratchet up the intensity, and reveal answers to a puzzle ever so slowly. Botany professor Dr. Martin Harris (Liam Neeson) is visiting Berlin with his wife of five years, Elizabeth (January Jones). He’s slated to speak at an international conference. Harris and Liz arrive at their hotel when Martin discovers he is missing his briefcase containing all of his papers and his passport. Leaving Liz to check them in, he races back to the airport. On his way, he is involved in a car crash that sends his taxi into the river. He sustains a concussion that puts him into a four-day coma. When he wakes, his memory is sketchy – he can recall his name, his wife’s name, but little else. He has no papers and no identification. And so the mystery begins – and what a yarn it is. Martin drops down the rabbit hole with a nod to The Bourne Identity, to include some spectacularly wicked car chase scenes on the icy streets of Berlin (it’s a bitingly cold winter, adding to the ominous mood). It’s been a remarkable run wherein narratives were lifted from the pages of comic books that possessed a superhero. These are characters possessed of superhuman powers who use their abilities to triumph over evil in the form of some equally classic antagonists. Kids and many adults love this stuff. And now arrives on the big screen a lush, beautifully costumed big screen movie of sweeping vistas and stunning scenes, the Black Panther/T’Challa (Chadwick Boseman), a superhero who appeared for the first time in the 2016 Captain America: Civil War. In this incarnation, he has A scene from From Up on Poppy Hill From Up on Poppy Hill was written by Hayao Miyazaki, the father of director Goro Miyazaki, and is based on the manga story by Tetsuro Sayama. Absent the fantastical, devoid of that floating sense of the surreal so often embedded in Studio Ghibli’s animated features, Poppy Hill is a touching, straight-forward, unsentimental coming-of-age story about a strong-willed 16-year-old girl named Umi (Sarah Bolger) who meets and becomes much enamored with Shun (Anton Melchin), a member of a geeky group of boys who inhabit an aging wreck of a building out of which they run a newspaper. He is the editor. The story is set in Yokohama, overlooking a sweeping bay. The year is 1963, and Japan is only just beginning to fully emerge from the devastation of World War II. Umi, whose father was lost at sea, and whose mother is presently studying in America, helps her grandmother (Jamie Lee Curtis) run a boarding house. She is responsible for much of the cleaning and shopping while attending a nearby high school and struggling to keep up with her schoolwork. In the opening scenes, we see Umi raising a flag in homage to her greatly missed father. She is spotted by Shun who is working on his father’s tugboat. Umi soon meets Shun and learns about his and his friends’ resistance to the razing of an old building they occupy as part of urban renewal. The struggle is between reverence for the past and the urge by officials to move toward a new, more modern Japan. The Olympic Games are slated to arrive in Japan in 1964. Umi joins Shun and friends in a campaign protesting the removal of the building and the more time she and Shun spend together the deeper their connection grows. articles.text: Some years ago, I stumbled onto a bottle of wine with the unusual name of Alicante Bouchet on it. I had never heard of it so my expectations were very low. I was astounded with the quality of the wine. It was inky purple even at 15 years of age and had a luscious, perfumed nose of blueberries and roses. It was huge and intense on the palate with layers of complexity and a big mouthfeel. There were still tannins on the finish, but they were not harsh or unwelcome. That experience taught me to keep my eyes open for the varietal and try a bottle wherever I could find it. I noticed that some of the greatest Zinfandels produced by Ridge, my favorite producer, often had a hefty dollop of Alicante Bouchet added. On a recent wine trip to the Alentejo region of Portugal I discovered that Alicante Bouchet is the major grape produced in the area and that it is revered. In fact, the best Portuguese wine I had on the trip, Mouchao, was made from 100% Alicante. The grape was first cultivated in France in 1866 by Henri Bouchet as a cross of Petit Bouchet and Grenache. The result was to produce a grape with deep color and high quality. Alicante is a teinturier, a grape with red flesh, and is one of the few teinturier grapes in the world. Its deep color makes it useful for blending with light red wine. It was planted heavily during prohibition in California for export to the east coast. Its thick skin made it resistant to rot during the transportation process. Last month my friend Kent Rasmussen, also an Alicante fan, organized a tasting at his house of very old Alicante bottles he had in his collection. They came from Angelo Papagni, Ramsay and Kent Rasmussen labels and dated from 1972 to the late 90’s. We were astounded that the wines from the 70’s. At almost 50 years of age, they were still vibrant and alive and delicious. They were almost all drinking beautifully. That experience set me off on a hunt to find current Alicante Bouchet wines in production in California and arrange a tasting 2018 Carol Shelton Alicante Bouchet Blue Tooth
articles.title: Alicante Bouchet – California’s overlooked gem

On a recent wine trip to the Alentejo region of Portugal I discovered that Alicante Bouchet is the major grape produced in the area and that it is revered. In fact, the best Portuguese wine I had on the trip, Mouchao, was made from 100% Alicante. The grape was first cultivated in France in 1866 by Henri Bouchet as a cross of Petit Bouchet and Grenache. The result was to produce a grape with deep color and high quality. Alicante is a teinturier, a grape with red flesh, and is one of the few teinturier grapes in the world. Its deep color makes it useful for blending with light red wine. It was planted heavily during prohibition in California for export to the east coast. Its thick skin made it resistant to rot during the transportation process. Last month my friend Kent Rasmussen, also an Alicante fan, organized a tasting at his house of very old Alicante bottles he had in his collection. They came from Angelo Papagni, Ramsay and Kent Rasmussen labels and dated from 1972 to the late 90’s. We were astounded that the wines from the 70’s. At almost 50 years of age, they were still vibrant and alive and delicious. They were almost all drinking beautifully. That experience set me off on a hunt to find current Alicante Bouchet wines in production in California and arrange a tasting The Alicantes – ready to taste to see the current state of the wine. The following wines were presented to our tasting panel and passed with flying colors. • 2018 Carol Shelton Alicante Bouchet “Blue Tooth” This beautifully crafted wine comes from the Bastoni Vneyard in the Fountaingrove District of Sonoma County. Blackberry and vanilla oak aromas burst out of the glass followed by a big mouthful of blueberry pie and plum fruit. It has good acid without being astringent and finishes long and savory. 2018 Carol Shelton Alicante Bouchet Blue Tooth • 2020 Jessie’s Grove Alicante Bouchet This wine from Lodi was a bit shy on the nose with mild cherry aromas. It is soft and round in the mouth with medium bodied red fruit flavors. The finish is smooth and tannin free. • 2021 Carlisle Alicante Bouchet Pagani Ranch The 100-year-old Alicante vines from the Pagani Ranch in Sonoma Valley are probably the most famous in California. The wine shows a delightfully ripe and juicy nose with aromas of beef, black peppercorn, blackberries tobacco and baking spice. Full-bodied, the palate is focused and refined with black olive and plum flavors. It is reminiscent of a fine wine from Hermitage or Cornas with a spicy mid-palate and dusty tannins. Will last and improve for decades in the cellar. Excellent effort. • 2019 Cavaletti Alicante Bouchet Swayze Vineyard This wine comes from a 3000-foot elevation vineyard in the high desert of Los Angeles County. It is aged in French oak and has a bit of Cabernet Sauvignon and Tempranillo blended in. Scents of licorice, blueberry and a hint of coffee appear on the nose, while the medium to full-bodied palate is framed by silky tannins, leaving it easy to drink and enjoy. • 2018 Hatcher Alicante Bouchet Hatcher Winery is in the Sierra Foothills with a tasting 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday 11am-5:30pm Sunday 1pm-5pm for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org Ordaz Family Wines • 2022 Ordaz Family Alicante Bouchet This is a new winery to me and I was blown away by the quality of their Alicante offering. This tiny production wine (85 cases) offers an impressive nose of pepper, spices, dark wild berries and earth, followed by a medium-bodied juicy palate, it has a fresh core of fruit and concludes with a smoky and peppery finish. • 2020 Spangler Alicante Bouchet (TOP OF THE CLASS) Made in Roseburg, Oregon from grapes grown in Amador County this wine was the unanimous top choice of the tasting panel. It shows a beautifully complex nose of blackberries, currants, and leather, it is hugely mouth filling on the palate but not ponderous or over the top. Layered, complex and balanced it has structure to last for decades in the cellar. Beautiful job. Oregon-based Spangler was the top wine. room in Murphys and a winery in Vallecito. It has alluring scents of blackcurrants, violets and black pepper. The medium bodied palate has a “cool-climate” feel with loads of fresh acidity enlivening a core of dark fruit, pleasantly chewy tannins and a long, savory finish. It will pair widely at the table. • 2020 Dutchman Vineyard Alicante Bouchet This wine hails from San Joaquin County. It is detailed and pure, although it takes plenty of air to really open. Blackcurrant, plum and expresso are underpinned by smoked meats and earth. The full-bodied palate is powerful yet elegant, its concentrated mineral-driven fruit is framed by powdery tannins and focused acidity. It has a long finish and will develop complexity in the bottle for many years. • 2022 Scar of the Sea Alicante Bouchet Galleano Ranch Haili ng f rom a v i ne - yard planted in the 1920’s in Cucamonga Valley east of Los Angeles, these vines are dry farmed. It has dense aromas of blueberry jam, aniseed, honeysuckle, and grilled meats. The full-bodied palate has a concentrated core of nuanced fruit approachable tannins bright acidity and a long, spicy finish. Perfect with grilled ribs or burgers. • 2022 St. Amant Alicante Bouchet Lodi-based St. Amant has produced an attractive wine with aromas of cassis, violets and blueberries. The full-bodied palate has bold ripe fragrant fruit framed by rounded tannins and bright acidity, and a long, layered finish. It will benefit from 2 to 3 years in the bottle. • 2018 Harmony Wynelands Estate Alicante Bouchet The Harmony Alicante is bursting with scents of blueberry, raspberry, chocolate and bacon. The full-bodied palate has a concentrated core of savory fruit. Its gently chewy tannins and fresh acidity complement its depth of flavors and it has a smooth satisfying finish.

articles.text: Last Wednesday morning, the Walking on Wednesdays group was treated to finally having architect and urban planner Will Adams give them a tour of Mediterranean style architecture in Piedmont. Delayed for two weeks due to rain, it drew a large turnout of 56 walkers and two K-9 best friends. Will Adams is an architect, planner, urban designer, and a resident of 30 years. He writes the Piedmont Post’s Walking Piedmont column, and is a Wednesday walker too. A recent article was on Mediterranean style architecture. The Spaniards brought their style of constructing buildings with them when they colonized California which has similar geography and weather to Spain. Basic Spanish architecture from which the Mediterranean style is derived has been influenced by Moroccan, Italian, Portuguese, and French designs. One important overriding characteristic of this architecture is its asymmetry and informality. Generally, a more symmetrical design is more formal. Mission Revival, Spanish Colonial, Spanish Colonial Revival are some of the names given to sub-categories of this Mediterranean style. Will first led the group up Highland Avenue to the main entrance of Havens School and its adjoining Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. He asked the walkers to observe the main Mediterranean style characteristics with arches, courtyards, low slope terracotta roofs, high ceilings, exposed rough-hewn beams, off white stucco exteriors, thick walls, bell towers, and ironwork. In California Spanish Colonial times, the materials builders used were what was available locally. Will took the walkers to Oakland Avenue and to the corner with Bonita Avenue, Will paid compliments to designer Mark Becker’s 2010 school redesign. There is a richness in its detail and even in the sign in front of the playfield. The group continued on to the middle of Bonita. The steps in front of the west entrance provided a suitable location for a group photo. Meghan Bennett shared another group photo taken on almost the same spot and printed in an old newspaper showing all the students in front of the school, which was built in 1910. It was originally the Bonita Avenue School, and later renamed Frank C. Havens Elementary School after its land donor. The school cost $32,000 to build, was on two acres with cypress trees, and had 260 students and 12 teachers. Piedmont’s population in 1910 was 2,375. be considered a Mediterranean design due to the red tile roof and faux trellises in front. Will stressed how asymmetry can create visual interest. Walking to Guilford Avenue, they admired a home with an ornate Mediterranean style exterior. Will explained that traditional overhangs help prevent water leaks in exterior windows. There was enough time to finish the upper Wildwood Gardens loop and return to their starting point. The group expressed its thanks to Will Adams and looks forward to another tour of a different architectural style in Piedmont. She underwent an extensive and thorough exam under anesthesia to test for diseases like TB, SIV (non-human primate version of HIV), and rabies, along with blood work and a CT scan. During the exam, evidence of a pre-existing fracture in her left radius and ulna was discovered, likely due to trauma experienced during her private ownership. “In all likelihood, this injury is from the animal being housed inappropriately. The bones had healed but were malaligned, which can impact her movement. She appears to be compensating well, but we continue to watch her mobility closely,” said Dr. Ryan Sadler, Senior Veterinarian at Oakland Zoo. Estrela will remain in the care of the Oakland Zoo and housed in their Veterinary Hospital until she has completed her quarantine period. She will then move to a permanent home at the Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation Center in Texas. Animal care involves many factors beyond healthcare. Veterinary Hospital workers are keeping Estrela occupied with new enrichment items like puzzle feeders and foraging toys and providing her with audio-visual stimulation through music and videos. Estrela is building trust with her keepers and enjoys ‘grooming time’ with them through a barrier. Oakland Zoo has a history of rescuing animals from the illegal wildlife trade. Most of its residents are rescues, many of which were victims of a multi-billion-dollar industry. For years, animals confiscated by officials at San Francisco airport and ay the Port of Oakland have been brought to Oakland Zoo for treatment, care, and permanent sanctuary. “The best intentions of private owners, while understandable, in no way compensate for the innate needs of the individual animals housed as pets, many of which suffer the effects of chronic stress, malnutrition, and other maladies,” said Darren Minier, Director of Animal Welfare and Research at Oakland Zoo. Primates are social creatures, and only their fellow primates can meet their social needs. Estrela was kept alone in a parrot cage, an inappropriate housing for a complex species, and posed several health risks for her and the humans around her. Oakland Zoo continues to evaluate her for emerging signs of possible behavioral effects of long-term chronic stress. The popularity of e-commerce and social media has led to a rise in illegal exotic pet ownership. These platforms make it easy to advertise and showcase live animals, putting animal and human health at risk by spreading zoonotic diseases. Illegal wildlife trade is a significant threat to global wildlife, with thousands of species at risk of being traded unlawfully. It is considered the fourth most lucrative transnational crime, after drugs, human trafficking, and arms trafficking. To learn more about the Zoo’s efforts in Taking Action Against the Illegal Wildlife Pet Trade, visit Oaklandzoo.org/endthetrade. On January 20, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) and the Wildlife Confiscation Network (WCN) placed the monkey in Oakland after the owner was arrested on unrelated charges. Oakland Zoo was contacted after San Diego Zoo and Los Angeles Zoo could not take in the marmoset due to capacity and concerns related to other recent WCN rescues. The marmoset was kept in a large birdcage by her owners, which is not suitable housing for monkeys and their movements or behavior. The female marmoset has been affectionately named Estrela, Estrela the marmoset is under the care of the Oakland Zoo. Marmosets are native to South America. articles.text: On a recent Sunday with howling winds and an impending level 4 storm, 18 intrepid members of the Piedmont Seniors ventured to see Hello, Gorgeous!, a live tribute to Barbra Streisand at the Lesher Theatre in Walnut Creek. Though it was a very stormy day, the group felt fortunate that the power remained on throughout the performance. Hello, Gorgeous! is a sentimental journey starring Rebecca Clark, who portrays the vocalist-actress Barbra Streisand. She did an excellent impersonation of Streisand, belting out such favorite tunes from Funny Girl, A Star Is Born, and Yentl, as well as many of Streisand’s greatest hits such as Evergreen, The Way We Were, Second Hand Rose, You Don’t Bring Me Flowers, Memories, and many others. When Clark spoke to the audience, she even offered the same mannerisms and speech patterns as Streisand. Clark is no newcomer to show business. Like Streisand, she is also a native New Yorker, and has performed at The Aladdin and The Bellagio in Las Vegas, the Cannes Music Festival in France, and has toured with Bob Hope USO shows throughout Europe. Prior to the performance, the Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a delicious Italian lunch at Tomatina’s in downtown Walnut Creek. If you are interested in participating in either excursions or meetings of the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein the Coordinator at jepstein@ piedmont.ca.gov. The Piedmont Seniors meet monthly at 10 a.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall on the fourth Wednesday of each month. This is in addition to optional monthly excursions to museums and varied points of interest throughout the Bay Area. You do not need to be a Piedmont resident to join.

articles.text: While some people express a desire to be “treated with dignity”, and others plead to have dignity “maintained,” it’s not always clear what this means in practical terms. There are six definitions for dignity in the dictionary, and the word can start to sound a bit posh. Perhaps this one seems to be the most relevant: “bearing, conduct, or speech indicative of self-respect or appreciation of the formality or gravity of any occasion or situation.” Another way of putting it would be that one person’s actions show they care about another. “To me, dignity means a recognition of the person: as valued, and as an equal in any interactions, regardless of any infirmity or disability,” says Dr. G. Allen Power, M.D., a geriatrician, dementia expert and author of “Dementia Beyond Drugs: Changing the Culture of Care.” “It means recognizing that all people have certain basic rights. In the case of health care, these include the right to be informed of one’s medical diagnoses, the right to make choices regarding not only treatment decisions, but also all aspects of daily living,” he says. Treating people with dignity extends to those who no longer seem able to self-advocate. “Dignity also means recognizing older people and those living with dementia as adults; not infantilizing, talking down to, or seeing them as childlike,” Dr. Power says. “We support our parents and assist them to be as capable as possible, but we do not “parent” them.” Easier said than done Treating people with kindness and caring seems obvious and simple, but one man’s dignity is another man’s insult. Pride and dignity, while distinctly different feelings, can be in conflict when a person has to rely on another in some capacity. “There are many societal stigmas around both aging and dementia,” Dr. Power explains. “Society tends to value older people less than those who are younger and who are gainfully employed. We also attach a great deal of worth to our cognitive abilities, and those who are less able are devalued and marginalized.” Within society is a complex healthcare system that, according to Dr. Power, does not always set up people for dignified moments. “Our care systems that are more focused on tasks than people and are often very rigid,” he says. “As a result, the desires and needs of the individual are often lost in an inflexible care system, and many of the practices that result also rob people of their dignity. A perfect example is rotating care staff at our convenience, which subjects people to receiving showers and other personal care from a parade of strangers.” Dementia can add another layer of challenges for all parties when striving for dignity. “There are many myths and stigmas around dementia that fuel people’s fears, and lead them to believe that the person is “fading away,” is incapable of being engaged meaningfully, or having input and choice in daily living. These beliefs set up a series of self-fulfilling prophecies, where we expect less of people and therefore do not provide an environment in which they can be more, and then their inability to do more reinforces our view that they are incapable,” he says. Give It a Try If you have a loved one who needs care and are concerned about respecting their dignity, try Dr. Power’s suggestions for how to consciously treat them with the decency that they want: • Learn and use optimal communication techniques so that people are well understood and can understand you. Also, learn how they prefer to be addressed. • • • • • • • • • • Never enter a person’s room or apartment without identifying yourself and securing permission to enter and engage with them. Engage the person as an equal: at eye level, spoken to as an adult, with appropriate pacing and enunciation for them to hear you; and with body language and attention that shows your openness and sincerity. Always connect with the person before launching into any task. Solicit frequent input and have the person direct all care as far as she is able. Check in frequently. I teach the acronym “SEE”: Slow down, Engage, Empower. Do tasks with people, not to them or for them. “No” means “no.” Never force care on a person who is declining. Do not argue with or deny what people are feeling or expressing. Seek to understand their perspective. Engage the person during any tasks; do not treat them like an object. Always describe the person with words that you would want used to describe you. Do not use pejorative labels or terms that objectify or blame people. Be open to learning from the person. I have heard it said that in any interaction, we should always assume that the other person is smarter than we are! articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Chris Moore for the position of Supervisor of District 5 on the Alameda County Board of Supervisors. pages.text: Wednesday, February 21, 2024 29 Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I am trying to get my estate in order so I can update my trust. One of my friends recommended I keep myself organized on my computer. I have no idea how to even get started. My attorney wants my updated beneficiary list and changes. How do I begin? -Lissa R., Oakland Dear Lissa: When you realize how valuable a tool a computer can be to get yourself organized for things like managing your beneficiary list for your trust and will, managing your medical expenses, etc., it helps with the stress of getting ready for the inevitable. Since I am assuming you don’t plan to try to create your will and trust by yourself without an attorney, here are some ways to get organized. 1. Create a folder for all of the documents you need and create You might label it Trust and Will 2024. In this folder, you can keep scanned documents to help you get organized, bank account, account, numbers, and any documents that you create. 2. Get your documents in order It’s very likely that your financial planner or stockbroker has a guide how to organize your documents to make it easier for your executor or family members to proceed in the event of your death. You should organize things like investment accounts, bank, accounts, and assets. If you are making a trust for the first time, you should know the limits of what you can have before things go to probate. If you have a lot of money in your checking account, for example, you should make sure it doesn’t exceed the limit to necessitate probate. Assets are subject to probate if they are not in trust, jointly held, or if a beneficiary designation is not in place. As a reference, decedent estates had to be probated when assets subject to probate exceeded $184,500 for persons who passed away in 2023. And assets aggregate maximum value threshold for 2023 was $25,000. Each item’s value cannot exceed $5000. So if you have artwork worth more than $5000 apiece, you want make sure that is put in the trust. Again, it’s important to talk to your financial advisor about the state of your accounts. You can keep copies of investment statements, bank statements, etc. in your organizational folder. 3. Create a spreadsheet Your Mac comes with spreadsheet, word processor, and presentation software. The spreadsheet software is called Numbers. Of course, many of us have Microsoft products, and that case you can use Excel if you have that on your computer. Then you can make headings for the types of beneficiaries that you may have. The headings can be family, friends, and nonprofits and charities. For the nonprofits and charities, you will need their addresses, their EIN numbers phone numbers and or email. If you’re not even sure which charities to choose, you can use a well-known site like charitynavigator.org. This very useful site gives you ratings for the charities, as well as all of their contact and Tax ID information. There are also some nonprofit groups on this site. For personal beneficiaries, it’s a good idea to have addresses, phone numbers, and current email addresses. A spreadsheet is also incredibly useful to list your investment and bank account, their numbers, who the beneficiaries are, and contact info for customer support whether it be your financial advisor or bank representative. 4. Talk to your family members This sounds easy, but it’s often very difficult to talk to your children or relatives who will be handling your estate upon your death. But it’s a necessary conversation. Who will be the executor? It’s not an easy job and it takes somebody that can persevere in dealing with beneficiary, payouts, sale of property of necessary, etc. You also want to make sure that you have medical and durable power of attorney in place. You also must make sure that your family members that will be handling your estate have access to your passwords, bank account, and can actually get into your computer. You can create what’s known as a legacy contact on your iCloud account, this would allow these contacts, usually relatives, to have access to all of your Apple iCloud data after your death. You can also share your folder with family members through Google Drive or Dropbox 5. Fill out a Healthcare Directive and Memorial Plan This is an important aspect of trust and will planning. In a healthcare directive, you are determining how you would like to be treated if your condition becomes terminal. It’s important that your children or relatives have a copy of this, and they understand your wishes. A memorial plan indicates how you would like your remains to be handled whether for example burial with a service, cremation, or donation to science. These documented wishes should also be kept in your trust and will folder. Planning for our inevitable demise is uncomfortable, but the more that you do now, the less your beneficiaries will have to deal with after your death. If you find it difficult to talk with your family members alone, you can do that with your financial advisor and family all together. articles.text: In a letter to City Council, the Piedmont League of Women Voters has raised concerns about Measure F, the City’s proposal to extend the renewal of Parcel Tax (also called the City Services Tax) from every four years to every twelve. Although the League appears resolute in presenting its concerns, its position has put it at odds with the opinions of city leadership, present and past. Until last week, Measure F enjoyed near-universal support in Piedmont ahead of the upcoming March election day. In total, the ballot item suggests raising the Parcel Tax by a modest amount (an estimated $12-21 per month for most residents) and extending the renewal of the tax from every 4 years to every 12. No one could begrudge it was going to a good cause either – the Parcel Tax accounts for 7% of the City’s general fund. However, the League of Women Voters is urging voters to slow down and consider just what they are getting with Measure F. Their letter to the City Council on January 30, raised concerns that Measure F’s twelve-year term removes an important tool for voters – the ability of voters to hold their politicians accountable by their purse strings. “Measure F’s twelve-year term removes an important means of accountability for voters: the need to seek approval of a special tax on a regular basis,” the letter reads. The League also suggested that the City’s “lack of comprehensive long-range planning” may mean more special taxes and bond measures may follow after Measure F “as soon as November 2024.” Not everyone shares their concerns, however. “The Voters and residents have other ways of holding City Council responsible for their financial managements and a lot of that is just through elections and who they vote into office,” said Bob McBain, former mayor and current member of the Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee for the City of Piedmont. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s Public Works Department has confirmed that workers from East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) used glyphosate chemical sprays to eliminate weed growth near Reservoir Number One, an out of commission reservoir on Blair Avenue in Piedmont. Glyphosate is the active chemical in weedkillers like Roundup and has generated controversy in recent years over its links to cancer. In March 2015, the World Health Organization classified glyphosate as “probably carcinogenic to humans.” “My head came off today when I saw this sign at the reservoir on Blair Ave.,” said Jukka Valkonen, former Park Commissioner for the City of Piedmont, and a resident living near the reservoir. In a letter to the community printed January 31 in the Piedmont Post, Valkonen described seeing a sign posted at the reservoir detailing the use of these chemicals. “So how long have they been poisoning us, our pets, wildlife, and the environment?” The sign was taken down shortly after the spraying finished. “I think residents’ astonishment and anger is not unwarranted,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “It was essentially a heavy-duty version of Roundup.” Gonzales clarified that it was not the city’s decision to use glyphosate chemicals for weed control. “EBMUD has their own integrated pest management plan, and that plan does allow for the use of pesticides if you use the ‘least invasive methods’ for removal, and those methods fail for whatever reason. In this case, EBMUD decided that those earlier methods were ineffective,” he said. articles.text: Editor: We’ve lived in town for over 20 years and like many of our neighbors, we chose Piedmont over other East Bay cities for its strong public schools. Resources no doubt account for a good part of PUSD’s success. Voter-backed local school taxes and a generously endowed foundation supplement state funding, helping maintain facilities, student-support services, and extracurricular activities. Without its dedicated and talented teachers, though, Piedmont – despite its wealth and widely shared commitment to education – might have attractive campuses, but it wouldn’t have the schools that drew folks to town in the first place. The Association of Piedmont Teachers has been working fairly and openly to secure a decent contract for its members, even as the district pleads poverty and pushes teachers toward direct action. Piedmonters eager to protect what truly makes the town rich, and who want security for all the major players in their kids’ everyday lives, would do well to support APT’s campaign. Piedmont teachers make PUSD a regional standout. Fair compensation, including wages and benefits commensurate with the tremendous value our teachers bring to town, is the least we owe them. –Matthew M. Goldstein, Ph.D. Laura E. Ruberto, Ph.D. Grand Avenue Editor:
