articles.text: Don Dare makes an excellent point in his opinion piece about the Shell recharge station. Without knowing what the demand will be, the Piedmont Planning Commission should authorize no more than a 6AM to 10 PM charging time. This would be consistent with prior CUP approvals and would indicate whether Piedmont needs or wants an overnight charging station. Currently, virtually all EV owners charge their cars from their homes. Piedmont should assess the demand for a charging hub before providing an invasive all-hours supply. –Neil Joeck Nova Drive 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS

articles.text: To be a Super Bowl quarterback is to be famous. The average American may not be able to name the United States Secretary of State, yet it is more than likely that they can tell you that Brock Purdy is the quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers and that Patrick Mahomes is the quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs, the two teams that played in tomorrow’s Super Bowl. An average citizen may also be able to tell you that both Purdy and Mahomes can be accurately described as young, poised and as having “good field vision.” These famous athletes see what their opponents are trying to do and, in the moment, respond accordingly. They make accurate, almost instantaneous, decisions based on the rapidly changing picture before them. This week’s gospel story, the Transfiguration of Jesus, gives three of his disciples, Peter, James and John, an opportunity, like Super Bowl quarterbacks, to develop and demonstrate good field vision; the occasion to see the big picture and to respond accordingly. On a mountain top away from the crowds, the three are given a vision of the eternal identity of their friend and teacher. Before their eyes his clothes become dazzling white, he engages in conversation with the quintessential law-giver Moses and the quintessential prophet Elijah. A cloud overshadows them and from the cloud a voice proclaims, “This is my Son, whom I dearly love. Listen to him.” Good field vision on their part was to recognize Jesus’ divine identity, and that he is the teacher of teachers, the prophet of prophets, that he is truly God in our midst. On that mountain top they are given the opportunity to see that Jesus does not stand apart from the tradition of the law and the prophets but is a living expression of that tradition. The average American may not be able to name the United States Secretary of State, yet it is more than likely that they can tell you that Brock Purdy is the quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers and that Patrick Mahomes is the quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs, the two teams that played in tomorrow’s Super Bowl. An average citizen may also be able to tell you that both Purdy and Mahomes can be accurately described as young, poised and as having “good field vision.” These famous athletes see what their opponents are trying to do and, in the moment, respond accordingly. They make accurate, almost instantaneous, decisions based on the rapidly changing picture before them. This week’s gospel story, the Transfiguration of Jesus, gives three of his disciples, Peter, James and John, an opportunity, like Super Bowl quarterbacks, to develop and demonstrate good field vision; the occasion to see the big picture and to respond accordingly. On a mountain top away from the crowds, the three are given a vision of the eternal identity of their friend and teacher. Before their eyes his clothes become dazzling white, he engages in conversation with the quintessential law-giver Moses and the quintessential prophet Elijah. A cloud overshadows them and from the cloud a voice proclaims, “This is my Son, whom I dearly love. Listen to him.” Good field vision on their part was to recognize Jesus’ divine identity, and that he is the teacher of teachers, the prophet of prophets, that he is truly God in our midst. On that mountain top they are given the opportunity to see that Jesus does not stand apart from the tradition of the law and the prophets but is a living expression of that tradition. Piedmonters know the value that their city government provides and have been willing to fund needed services for over 40 years through the Special Municipal Services Tax, commonly known as the Parcel Tax. Over time, the necessary services provided by our city government have expanded. In 1981, who would have imagined many of the programs that the city currently provides and expenses it now incurs. Over the years, our City Council has proven itself to be a wise financial steward of the taxpayer dollar. The Council scrutinizes, amends, and approves a budget annually. This budget process is conducted entirely in public and members of the Piedmont community actively participate by sharing their opinions and priorities with the Council and staff. Measure F on the March 2024 ballot asks Piedmonters to be willing to continue to fund needed services, allow city government to be able to adapt to the changing needs of the Piedmont community, and to be able to continue the bedrock mission of providing the high level of service we demand from our city government. As a fellow Piedmont resident, I urge you to vote yes on Measure F. –John O. Tulloch Former City Clerk tion in 1981. We have lived in Piedmont since 2003. When we first arrived, we had only lived in large cities and were baffled by the constant parcel tax discussions in Piedmont. We couldn’t understand why our property taxes weren’t enough to fully fund Piedmont’s wonderful schools and city services. Fast forward to the present. If you jump in and get involved in Piedmont, you cannot help but learn that it’s an extraordinarily well-run city blessed with forward-thinking, sensible, responsible volunteers who take their stewardship extremely seriously. Measure F is an excellent example. By project i ng modest increases (the largest parcels in Piedmont would see their parcel tax increase by less than the price of one latte a week!) and forecasting the budget twelve years into the future, the city will be able to undertake long-range planning and avoid the cost and effort of multiple renewal campaigns. These are the kinds of winwin solutions we all desperately ache for our civic leaders at the state and national level to come up with. We are grateful for the extraordinary services paid for by Measure F – police, paramedic services, parks, public facilities, fire response, streets & sidewalks, recreation, stormwater infrastructure. articles.text: State program provides up to $3,000 to eligible households The City of Piedmont is encouraging residents with eligible homes to apply for the Earthquake Brace+Bolt program. From now through February 21, Piedmont homeowners may apply for the state retrofit grant and receive up to $3,000 to make their homes more resilient to earthquakes. Registration is only open for 30 days once per year. The Earthquake Brace + Bolt program is a state program that offers eligible homeowners grants of up to $3,000 to help offset the cost of seismic retrofits that would brace the walls of older homes and bolt houses to their foundations. These steps reduce the potential for damage or collapse in the event of an earthquake. Homes that qualify for the program are typically built before 1980 (but are more prevalent before 1940), have a raised continuous perimeter concrete foundation, may sit on level ground or a low slope, and may have woodframed walls (often called “cripple walls”) in the crawl space under the first floor. To apply for a retrofit grant, residents may visit www. earthquakebracebolt.com and complete the online registration form by February 21. The program website also hosts a helpful list of qualifications for homeowners unsure if their property is eligible. Once registration closes, grant recipients will be selected through a random drawing. Residents will be notified via email if they have been selected or placed on the waitlist. If selected, residents will still need a City of Piedmont building permit to complete the retrofit. Households with an annual income of less than $87,000 may be eligible for greater funding opportunities of up to $7000 in addition to the initial $3000 amount. For more information about the Brace+Bolt program, visit www.earthquakebracebolt.com. For questions about seismic retrofits, contact the City’s building department at 420-3050 or buildingpermits@piedmont. ca.gov. against or in support of Measure F. articles.text: The magical experience of talking with grown-ups No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling mind blown when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world - from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share in, but that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. We remember, often very clearly, how people made us feel when we were children. • An uncle who looked at your drawings and scribbles with an artist’s perspective, recognizing your use of shape, line and color • A neighbor who gave you the time to fully explain your thoughts and feelings, asking follow-up questions that showed you were really being heard • A teacher who pulled you aside to share that the assignment you turned in was more than good - it left them awed and they want to know how you felt while working on it These adults made us feel like we were more than ‘just a kid’. Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. So how do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising coming from a camp director, but I recommend sending them to camp. Photo by Sebastián León Prado The relationship between a grown-up and child is very important. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. Wonderful, magical, kind, kidsat-heart counselors and staff who we hired for their innate ability to see children for the wonders they are. Not perfect angels or naive brats, but smallish humans who have their own unique interests, attributes and lenses through which they see the world. keeping our ratios tight (camper to staff 1:2 overall and 1:5 in cabins), we create opportunities every day for a camper to experience the magic of being seen. I am proud to report that we see those special moments all the time: an adult turning on their listening ears, seeing not ‘just a kid’, but a person they are happy to give their full heartfelt attention to. Affirmed. Interesting. Valuable. Creative. Loved. Special. Whatever wonderful feeling was felt, it was felt because someone took the time to help them feel the goodness that was already in themself. At Camp Augusta, we believe there is something awesome in every child, we need only to take the time to notice. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. has been Camp Augusta’s director for more than 20 years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and program philosophies can be found at www. campaugusta.org. This article originally appeared in the Post on February. 1, 2023. Tours for 5th and 8th grade families at PMS and PHS have also been successful. Thomasson attended a high school tour in November which had around 35 participants. Additional campus tour dates at PHS and PMS will take place on Tuesdays on March 19, April 16, and May 21. Sign up at: Piedmont.k12.ca.us/details/~board/ district-news/post/school-tours. Tours at elementary schools have already ended for the year. “We moved up our open enrollment date in order to encourage resident families to enroll earlier in order to capture as many resident families as possible. We will continue to refine our information processes and hope to see increased enrollment in our schools,” said Hawn. Nearly all Bay Area schools have seen drops in enrollment since 2018. Piedmont School District is targeting students who are residents, encouraging them to stay in Piedmont instead of going to private schools.

Amy Moorhead directed the show and was choreographer and producer. Sandra Peter served as Vocal Director and Trevor Meseroll conducted the orchestra. The performances were based on a play by John Van Druten and stories by Christopher Isherwood as well as the book by Joe Masteroff. The play takes place in Berlin in 1929-1930 in pre-Nazi Germany and brings to life the Sophomore Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles in Piedmont High School’s production of the musical Cabaret. Sophomore Amelia Addington played a leading role as Sally Bowles, sophomore Theo Fergason was the male lead, Clifford Bradshaw, and junior Caitlin Boothby was the emcee at the Kit Kat Club. articles.text: On Friday, February 9, members of Girl Scout Troop 33943 met with Piedmont High School seniors Lola Biehn and Izzy Grimmer to help boost the message about their Period Product Drive. Izzy and Lola have worked to enforce the installment of menstrual product dispensers installed in Piedmont schools. The Flow Club was created to address the concerns the Girl Scouts had. Zayda Weber explained, “We started this drive to help people in need of access to period products. Once we started hanging posters, we saw some kids react with a negative take and make fun of it. Witnessing this, we see how important it is to work to end period stigma. Periods shouldn’t be seen as something weird or gross, but as something healthy and normal.” Please help Troop 33943 by donating new, unopened packages of menstrual products. All products will be donated to Alameda County Food Bank and Oakland Elizabeth House Shelter for Women with Children. The collection goes until March 10. The following items are being sought: New, unopened packages of tampons, menstrual pads, period underwear, and menstrual cups. Collection bins are located at: • Donation stand at the corner of Oakland and Grand Ave. • Beach Elementary • Havens Elementary • Millennium High School • Piedmont High School • Mulberry’s Market Collection Bin at the corner of Oakland and Grand Avenue. Izzy Grimmer, Zayda Weber, Emma Syhabout, Sicheng Wu, Elizabeth Ackerman, Sai Ahuja, Olivia Chan and Lola Biehn are helping with the donation drive.
articles.title: 7th Grade Girl Scouts partner with PHS Flow Club

articles.text: Piedmont School District has announced the nominations for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The previous winners are: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000) Lisa Lomenzo (2001) jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002) jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003) Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004) Cynthia Gorman (2005) Grier Graff (2006) Julia Burke (2007) Maude Pervere (2008) jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009) Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010) Andrea Swenson (2011) June Monach (2012) Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013) Ray Perman (2014) Jennifer Fox (2015) Katie Korotzer (2016) Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018) Cathy Glazier (2019) Sue Smegal (2020) Ken Li (2021) Eileen Ruby (2022) David Ragones in 2023 Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and at Oakland’s McClymonds High School. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was an early supporter of Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by School Board member Dewey Watson in Hecht’s memory. The deadline for nominations is March 15. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 8, Board of Education meeting. Nomination forms are available in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue, or online at https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J92iTb6870oZbIRotoHW8rM3MUmCS8bORuf- 7c1hcCmY/edit?pli=1.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 14, 2024 9 Piedmont Play Schoolers host Lunar New Year parade By Oriana Syed Piedmont Play School, a cooperative preschool located at Hampton Park, held its Annual Lunar New Year Parade on Friday, February 9. Dressed in red, the children walked hand in hand with their teachers and caregivers around the field. Leading the parade was teacher Raven Ritchie in a dragon costume that the kids Kids made their own cut-out dragon masks for the parade. Preschoolers made a dragon costume for teacher Raven Ritchie to wear. Preschool teacher Raven Ritchie leads the parade dressed as a dragon. made for her earlier in the week. The parade was the culmination of a week of exploring how Lunar New Year is celebrated around the world. “At Piedmont Play School we value teaching children about various cultures and traditions. It is important for us to recognize not only our classroom community but the greater community around us,” said Ritchie. While much of the focus this past week was on Chinese New Year, the preschoolers also learned about Lunar New Year celebrations in other countries. Ritchie talked about the differences in celebratory garments for the new year and noted how celebrations can be similar but unique. “We try our best to share about different cultures respectfully through the use of examples through books, videos and crafts,” she explained. The children decorated personal masks for the parade and collaborated on making the lead dragon head constructed from boxes, paper, and embellishments. One child, who herself celebrates Lunar New Year at home, shared with Ritchie how happy she was to be celebrating this most special day at school. “Making the dragon head together as a class was a fun and engaging way to show our appreciation for the beautiful holiday that is Lunar New Year,” said Ritchie. Photos by Oriana Syed Piedmont Play School preschoolers march around Hampton Field during their Annual Lunar New Year parade. Adults help usher kids through the parade celebrating Lunar New Year. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Staff Photos Senior Brit Burden scored 19 points in a close win over Castro Valley, including three clutch free throws in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team finished its regular season last week with two more wins, defeating San Leandro 57-38 on the road on Wednesday, February 7 while beating Castro Valley 44-37 at Binks Rawlings Gym two days later. The Highlanders end ed their regular season with a 17-9 overall record and third place in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. “We wanted to wrap up our season going 4-0 in league. We didn’t win league this year, so our next goal is to win North Coast Section,” said coach Ben Spencer. “We’re the No.3 seed and Archie Williams is #2. I just want us to go out there, defend, and rebound. That’s what we were looking for over these last couple of games.” The Highlanders honored their seven seniors on Senior Night against Castro Valley: Arjun Bornstein, Alex Anderson, Thorin Holmes, Brit Burden, Finn Burke, Scott Cooley, and Declan Linnane. Piedmont earned the No. 3 seed in the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs and hosted No. 14 Sonoma Valley on Tuesday, winning 40-34. 44-37 win over Castro Valley Piedmont trailed through the first quarter 11-7. With both teams playing tough defense in the second quarter, PHS cut the Trojans lead to 16-14 going into halftime. Both teams traded points in the third quarter to make it 30-28, but Piedmont dominated the final quarter, taking the lead early with 16 points for the 44-37 victory. Burden continued his impressive work attacking the basket, scoring five of his 19 points in the fourth quarter in addition to 3 of 4 free throws. Holmes, another senior, also knocked down 3 of 4 free throws in the fourth quarter. Final stats: Burden had 19 points, Ravi Silverberg had eight, Holmes had seven, Linnane had five, Dillon Casey scored four, Bornstein had one. 57-38 win vs. San Leandro PHS went up 17-8 in the first quarter and carried a 26-18 lead into halftime. The Highlanders came out firing in the third quarter with 17 points while allowing 12, making it a comfortable 43-30 Thorin Holmes converted 3 free throws in the win over Castro Valley. lead into the fourth. They scored 14 more in the fourth, conceding eight toward the victory. Final stats were not provided. articles.text: Highlanders receive No. 6 seed; moved up to NCS Open Division Staff Photos Piedmont’s basketball team honored its six seniors on Senior Night: Sam Smith (left), Natalia Martinez, Erinn Gardere, Lindsey Wirgler, Arshiya Ranjitkar, and Kat Melian. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team claimed both of its final games of the season to share the league championship with Bishop O’Dowd with a 7-1 league record. The Highlanders bowled over San Leandro 74-24 on Wednesday, February 7 at Binks Rawlings Gym for Senior Night, and dominated Castro Valley 62-34 two days later at the Trojans’ gym. As a result, Piedmont was moved up to the Open Division of the North Coast Section playoffs and given a No. 6 seed. PHS will host No. 3 Carondelet on Thursday, February 15 at Binks Rawlings Gym and gain an automatic bid to the CIF State Tournament. The Highlanders were awarded a home-bid by the draw from a hat by the league’s athletic directors. The Highlanders celebrated its six seniors at the start of Wednesday’s game: Natalia Martinez, Lindsey Wirgler, Sam Smith, Kat Melian, Erinn Gardere, and Arshiya Ranjitkar. Martinez put on a dazzling show with 40 points against San Leandro and Castro Valley, including a perfect 10 for 10 three-pointers against the Pirates, a Piedmont school record. “The rim was on fire. I knew I wasn’t going to miss and if I was going to miss, it’d be a contested shot. I just thought, ‘I’m gonna keep shooting.’ From the beginning of the game, I knew I was on fire. I thought, ‘Just keep shooting like Stephen Curry.’,” said Martinez. Martinez goes down as one of Piedmont’s leading scorers in the company of Courtney Paris, Ashley Paris, Casey Morris, and Trinity Zamora. “I remember my freshman year with Kai [Johnson] being the only senior. I remember beating O’Dowd. Having Kai step up as the only senior made me want to do that when it was my time as a senior. All the players who were here before me really paved the way,” said Martinez. Wirgler joined the team as a junior but had to sit out last season due to transfer rules. She entered the starting lineup this year to become the team’s second leading scorer. “It’s been an up-and-down journey, but I’m glad to be here with this crew. Most importantly, we just have to finish this year out, we’ve been working way too hard to celebrate now. For me, my journey here has been different and I’ve been able to grow throughout every year of high school. Being a senior, I’m grateful to just be at the point where I can reflect back on how I’ve gotten here,” said Wirgler. “It’s a culmination as a long but fast four years. It’s great to look back at all that’s happened and be able to celebrate. Joining last year with such a strong team, I didn’t get a lot of playing time, but I learned a lot from that experience and put in work over the summer. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team claimed both of its final games of the season to share the league championship with Bishop O’Dowd with a 7-1 league record. The Highlanders bowled over San Leandro 74-24 on Wednesday, February 7 at Binks Rawlings Gym for Senior Night, and dominated Castro Valley 62-34 two days later at the Trojans’ gym. As a result, Piedmont was moved up to the Open Division of the North Coast Section playoffs and given a No. 6 seed. PHS will host No. 3 Carondelet on Thursday, February 15 at Binks Rawlings Gym and gain an automatic bid to the CIF State Tournament. The Highlanders were awarded a home-bid by the draw from a hat by the league’s athletic directors. The Highlanders celebrated its six seniors at the start of Wednesday’s game: Natalia Martinez, Lindsey Wirgler, Sam Smith, Kat Melian, Erinn Gardere, and Arshiya Ranjitkar. Martinez put on a dazzling show with 40 points against San Leandro and Castro Valley, including a perfect 10 for 10 three-pointers against the Pirates, a Piedmont school record. “The rim was on fire. I knew I wasn’t going to miss and if I was going to miss, it’d be a contested shot. I just thought, ‘I’m gonna keep shooting.’ From the beginning of the game, I knew I was on fire. I thought, ‘Just keep shooting like Stephen Curry.’,” said Martinez. Martinez goes down as one of Piedmont’s leading scorers in the company of Courtney Paris, Ashley Paris, Casey Morris, and Trinity Zamora. “I remember my freshman year with Kai [Johnson] being the only senior. She entered the starting lineup this year to become the team’s second leading scorer. “It’s been an up-and-down journey, but I’m glad to be here with this crew. The Highlanders end ed their regular season with a 17-9 overall record and third place in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. “We wanted to wrap up our season going 4-0 in league. articles.text: Highlanders in NCS playoffs on Friday Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s soccer team honored its nine seniors on Senior Night: (front) Charlotte Davies (left), Hailey Marshburn, Lily Caldwell, Malea Hartford, Elle Ruegg; (back) Sara Broach, Amy Derr, Lola Biehn, and Clio Salzer. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team capped its highly successful season with an exciting 2-1 win over rival Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 6 at the recently reopened Witter Field. They held Berkeley to a scoreless draw on Friday, February 9, bringing their record to 11-2-3 (W-T-L) overall and 5-2-3 in league, second place behind Castro Valley. Entering the post-season North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 7 seed, Piedmont walloped No. 10 Albany 5-0 last night, February 13, in the first round. The Highlanders celebrated their nine seniors on the roster before the O’Dowd game: Charlotte Davies, Amy Derr, Hailey Marshburn, Lily Caldwell, Sara Broach, Lola Biehn, Malea Hartford, Elle Ruegg, and Clio Salzer. 1-0 draw with Berkeley In a back-and-forth match, Berkeley kept a defensive look causing Piedmont to have trouble finding rhythm on the attack. The Yellowjackets assigned its top defender, Camila Vasquez, on Piedmont’s Elsa Wallway, resulting in limited looks at goal from the aggressive freshman forward. The result meant Castro Valley captured the WACC’s Foothill Division title and Piedmont tied with Berkeley for second place in the league. 2-1 over Bishop O’Dowd Coach Dan Chubbock started the game with all of the seniors, subbing in lead attackers Miranda Liu and Wallway after 10 minutes. Quickly after Liu and Wallway entered the pitch, Piedmont drew its first chance when Juliana Thornborrow weaved through the defense to send a pass out wide to Elle Ruegg. The right back sent in a low cross to Liu charging toward net, but the Dragons’ defender got a foot on the ball before colliding with Liu. Liu had another look later in the first half on some great interplay. Louisa Symokowick sent a laser pass to Thornborrow, who flicked a pass on a first touch to Liu running in behind. Liu’s shot was stopped on a foot save by BOD’s keeper, and the score remained 0-0 at halftime. At the 50th minute, Piedmont broke the deadlock after Wallway drew a penalty kick. It come moments after she beat multiple defenders to draw a free kick on the left side of the penalty area. Wallway took the initial free kick, sending a cross that was returned to her via a defensive header. Retrieving the ball, Wallway patiently waited for two defenders to come her way, darting to the right, before intricately moving into the box and drawing contact on her back by the over pursuing defender. Wallway calmly buried the PK at the right post. With 10 minutes left in the game, Bishop O’Dowd tied the game. Players celebrate on the field in the final moments of their 2-1 win over Bishop O’Dowd. It was their first game at Witter Field this season.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team tied rival Bishop O’Dowd 2-2 on Tuesday, February 6 at the Dragons’ field in Oakland, but suffered a narrow 1-0 loss to its other rival, Berkeley, two days later on Senior Night. At the end of it regular season it was able to play its first home game on its own field. PHS finished with an 11-3-2 (W-T-L) overall record. It celebrated its six seniors prior to Thursday’s game: Axel Saldanha, Ben Elmquist, Oliver Shafroth, Andrew McLaughlin, Aiden Woolwine, and Riley Stratman. Piedmont’s loss to Berkeley came on a late goal in the 73rd minute. Against O’Dowd, Piedmont trailed 0-2 before rallying to score twice in the second half, both on penalty kicks, “Beating Berkeley earlier in Photo by Scott Stratman Goalkeeper Axel Saldanha stops a penalty kick in the final moments against Bishop O’Dowd. the season meant this would be a tough game, they were really motivated. We fought until the end and it was unfortunate to concede with less than 10 minutes to go,” said coach Todd Sullivan following the loss to Berkeley. Thursday’s game was a milestone for Sullivan, who has coached the Highlanders in 150 games since being named head coach. Based on the success of the team, they were promoted from the Shoreline Division to the more competitive Foothill Division during his time at the school. “Even Berkeley’s coach at the end praised us for coming back from 2-nil down to O’Dowd. This program is now well established and the top schools are looking over their shoulder. It’s probably my strongest season as a Piedmont coach to have 11 wins in a schedule as tough as ours,” said Sullivan. PHS enters the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 2 seed. They hosted No. 15 Novato on Tuesday, February 13 for the first round. Game details will appear in next week’s Post.

He was fifth at the NCS Bayshore at 41 feet, 10.75 inches. at the WACC Championship in 51.57. Bell also competed in the triple jump, and was 10th of 26 in 14 feet, 2.5 inches at the NCS Bayshore meet. Finn Burke was a three-year varsity athlete in water polo and competes on the basketball team this winter. Breah Bell was a pass rusher and running back on the flag football team, and is a sprinter on the track team. FINN BURKE Water Polo & Basketball Staff Photos Miguel Long was an All-League defensive back on the football team last fall and competes in jumping events on the track and field team. BREAH BELL Flag Football & Track and Field MIGUEL LONG Football & Track and Field Miguel Long, a senior, is a two-sport athlete with football in the fall and track and field in the spring. Long is a two-year starter on the football team and earned second-team All-League honors as a defensive back. He was key to Piedmont’s 29-26 win over Newark Memorial and win the team’s Shoreline Division title, He had two interceptions during both of Newark’s final two offensive drives. Breah Bell, another senior, competed on the flag football team in its inaugural season in the fall as a pass rusher. She is a sprinter and jumper on the track team in the spring. She helped the flag football team go 4-6 and finish fourth in the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament. She contributed as a pass rusher and running back. On the track team, Bell reached NCS Bayshore meet as a member of the 4x100 sprint relay team alongside Miranda Liu, Ella Yasar, and Darcy McKee. They finished second of eight Finn Burke, a senior, was a key starter on the water polo team last fall. He is a member of the current basketball team as a forward. He earned second-team All-League honors on the NCS Championship-winning water polo team last fall. In water polo, Burke often lined up in the Hole set as a versatile scorer, passer, and defender. He scored in Piedmont’s 13-9 NCS Semifinals win over Marin Academy, and had three goals in a 15-8 win over Castro Valley to take third place in the WACC Tournament. This winter, the basketball team finished its regular season with a 17-9 overall record and enters the Division 3 NCS playoffs as the No. 3 seed—placing him on two NCS contending teams this school year.

articles.text: Seeing my brother at the starting line shaking, I wonder what it’s like. The shot goes off. He’s gone. The speed he pedals at is something foreign to me; the fighting spirit that he possesses is unknown to me. After tens of minutes he comes around the final stretch. I see him finish – dead last. The months of training all for nothing. Day after day, week after week, he didn’t seem himself. “Is this normal?” I asked myself. “Is he ok?” This concept of mental pain felt very distant to me. I had never gone through it. Once I joined crew, I learned that competing in sports isn’t just a physical battle, it’s a mental one, too. Mental struggles of professional athletes In 1989, Clint Malarchuk, an NHL goalie had his jugular vein cut by a skate during a game. He survived this injury and was somehow able to come back a few weeks later. While this side of the story has a happy ending, Malarchuk was mentally destroyed. It was a trauma undiagnosed. In the years to come, he started drinking and taking painkillers regularly. Back then, mental health struggles were often viewed as a sign of weakness than an illness and where seeking help wasn’t an option. You fight through the pain silently. In 2008 when Malarchuk attempted suicide, it wasn’t taken lightly. That was the turning point where coaches and fans realized the pain athletes were going through. Acknowledgement of this topic began to reduce the number of struggling athletes, but a significant percent of them still suffer from burnout, depression, or anxiety. One of the big reasons is the competitive environment and social stigmas. The feeling of having to do the same thing day after day or even loss after loss takes so much mental fortitude. Having to adjust your lifestyle to be aligned with your team can be a daunting task. While professionals are on a completely different spectrum of athletic ability, there are obvious connections regarding mental health when compared to an everyday athlete. As a high school rower, I’ve seen how these struggles relate to my experiences. I often find myself thinking about not doing as much as I should have. However, to counteract this, Luca Vieira, now a college athlete, advised me: “Convince yourself you’re the best.” An athlete’s take on the topic Luca is a rowing coxswain at UC Berkeley. He and his team have secured multiple titles including at Henley Royal Regatta, one of the largest and most popular races in the world. Regattas are the pinnacle in rowing, as each crew prepares tirelessly for months on end to compete for a mere six minutes. The best way to keep going in races is in his words, “Convince yourself that you’re the best”. Having self confidence is the mindset that is key to winning. Luca’s ‘open book’ relationship with his coach has been one of the most valuable to him, and the key to that is to not be afraid of asking questions. His most important priority is keeping focused on his boat and not the other boats. When you are not ‘In the zone’ the boat feels much more out of sync and affects your overall speed. Emotional maturity is extremely important because the inability to hold back whatever comes to mind can create rifts in the team, leading to a loss of focus. Making a Difference As a young athlete, I’m passionate about spreading awareness about mental health challenges. I want to use my voice to help people care about this issue. We each have the power to make a real impact and it starts with us, the young athletes. Evrim Duransoy is a Sophomore at PHS and is a rower on the Oakland Strokes varsity team.
articles.title: The mental stress in sports

The shot goes off. He’s gone. The speed he pedals at is something foreign to me; the fighting spirit that he possesses is unknown to me. After tens of minutes he comes around the final stretch. I see him finish – dead last. The months of training all for nothing. Day after day, week after week, he didn’t seem himself. “Is this normal?” I asked myself. “Is he ok?” This concept of mental pain felt very distant to me. I had never gone through it. Once I joined crew, I learned that competing in sports isn’t just a physical battle, it’s a mental one, too. Mental struggles of professional athletes In 1989, Clint Malarchuk, an NHL goalie had his jugular vein cut by a skate during a game. He survived this injury and was somehow able to come back a few weeks later. While this side of the story has a happy ending, Malarchuk was mentally destroyed. It was a trauma undiagnosed. In the years to come, he started drinking and taking painkillers regularly. Back then, mental health struggles were often viewed as a sign of weakness than an illness and where seeking help wasn’t an option. You fight through the pain silently. In 2008 when Malarchuk attempted suicide, it wasn’t taken lightly. That was the turning point where coaches and fans realized the pain athletes were going through. Acknowledgement of this topic began to reduce the number of struggling athletes, but a significant percent of them still suffer from burnout, depression, or anxiety. One of the big reasons is the competitive environment and social stigmas. The feeling of having to do the same thing day after day or even loss after loss takes so much mental fortitude. Having to adjust your lifestyle to be aligned with your team can be a daunting task. While professionals are on a completely different spectrum of athletic ability, there are obvious connections regarding mental health when compared to an everyday athlete. As a high school rower, I’ve seen how these struggles relate to my experiences. I often find myself thinking about not doing as much as I should have. However, to counteract this, Luca Vieira, now a college athlete, advised me: “Convince yourself you’re the best.” An athlete’s take on the topic Luca is a rowing coxswain at UC Berkeley. He and his team have secured multiple titles including at Henley Royal Regatta, one of the largest and most popular races in the world. Regattas are the pinnacle in rowing, as each crew prepares tirelessly for months on end to compete for a mere six minutes. The best way to keep going in races is in his words, “Convince yourself that you’re the best”. Having self confidence is the mindset that is key to winning. Luca’s ‘open book’ relationship with his coach has been one of the most valuable to him, and the key to that is to not be afraid of asking questions. His most important priority is keeping focused on his boat and not the other boats. When you are not ‘In the zone’ the boat feels much more out of sync and affects your overall speed. Emotional maturity is extremely important because the inability to hold back whatever comes to mind can create rifts in the team, leading to a loss of focus. Making a Difference As a young athlete, I’m passionate about spreading awareness about mental health challenges. I want to use my voice to help people care about this issue. We each have the power to make a real impact and it starts with us, the young athletes. Evrim Duransoy is a Sophomore at PHS and is a rower on the Oakland Strokes varsity team. pages.text: Wednesday, February 14, 2024 15 HIKING WITH JON By Jonathan Comeaux [Reprinted from February 2023] There is no better time for viewing reservoirs and lakes than following the rains. Just nine miles from Piedmont is a trail that will make you forget that you’re in the hustle and bustle of Hiking the Kings Canyon Loop by San Leandro Reservoir the Bay Area with the Kings Canyon Loop off of Canyon Road on the way to Moraga. Parking at East Bay MUD’s Valle Vista Staging Area, the Kings Canyon Loop is a moderately challenging trail that walks alongside the Upper San Leandro Reservoir. Hiking the loop requires 6.4 miles of walking and around 950 feet in elevation gain. The reservoir is the highest it’s been in years, providing fantastic views for the majority of your hike. Walking along the northern portion of the reservoir, there’s a continuous great view of the rolling East Bay hills as you walk along the winding trail. It’s a great location for birding A close view of the San Leandro Reservoir from the Kings Canyon Loop Trail Staff Photos The San Leandro Reservoir is the highest it’s been in years thanks to recent rains. The final portion of the Kings Canyon Loop Trail with the San Leandro reservoir to the left California newts can be spotted walking along the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Electricity towers are overhead on the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Watch out for several muddy and slick areas on the trail. The Kings Canyon Loop trail brings hikers underneath groves of Oak trees. or catching sight of little critters. On multiple occasions, California newts were spotted passing by on the trail. As for the difficulty of the trail, about 75 percent of the trail was manageably flat, but once you hit the 4.5 mile mark, the trail noticeably ramps up in elevation gain—providing 460 feet in ascent in just half a mile – so roughly half of the day’s elevation gain is in one portion of the trail. It’s worth mentioning that about 10 sections of the trail were oversaturated and muddy, making it difficult to walk through without slipping. Be advised to use caution and patience when passing over slippery surfaces. After walking alongside the reservoir for those 4.5 miles, the trail takes into the hills and narrows down from over 10 feet wide to just a few feet in some sections. It traverses underneath groves of Oak trees and eventually provides an overhead view of the reservoir. At the 6-mile mark, you come to an intersection to continue on the Kings County Loop Trail to your left or to an added trail, Rimer Creek Trail to the right. The Posts’ suggestion is to take the trail on the left which leads back to the reservoir. The trail on the right adds a mile to your afternoon of hiking, but featured some of the most saturated portions of mud throughout the day. Despite being a magnificent trail, it is severely underrated. In 7.5 miles of hiking around noon on a Saturday, The Post passed just 21 other hikers.

articles.text: On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. United States, 1984) — a contemporary envisioning of a Chinese mother goddess, rendered in a dangling complex of ceramic forms — mingle interrogations of utopian ideals, the experience of migration, and what it means to be a woman protagonist. Fresh approaches to well-established genres also boldly defy expectations. What appears to be a traditional Chinese landscape painting by Wu Chi-Tsung (b. Taiwan, 1981) is in fact formed from sculptural layers of crumpled photosensitive paper, while an experimental film by TT Takemoto (b. United States, 1967) peers beneath the surface of documentary footage of Japanese American women factory workers to reveal an intimate social atmosphere. “At a moment of heightened turmoil domestically and around the globe, Into View feels so needed right now, entwining concepts like mythology, cosmology, political uprisings, social intimacy and ecology as viable alternatives to our current systems and empowering audiences to rethink possibilities in their own lives,” said Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art & Programs Naz Cuguoglu. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org. articles.text: Oakland Museum will have lion dancers this Saturday for Lunar New Year. The Oakland Museum of California will host its 23rd Annual Lunar New Year celebration this Saturday, February 17, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Family-friendly activities celebrate the Year of the Dragon, including storytime in the lecture hall, interactive lion dances, and a variety of food offerings from Bay Area-based Asian and Pacific Islander chefs. Guests are invited to create paper dragon puppets and paper dragon danglers and learn about and sample a variety of tea with local tea company Far Leaves Tea founder Donna Lo. The event will take place rain or shine. Festival tickets are $10 and include access to all Lunar New Year performances and activities, as well as entry to all galleries. To purchase tickets, visit https://museumca. org/event/23nd-annual-lunarnew-year-at-omca-year-of-thedragon/.
articles.title: Oakland Museum to celebrates Lunar New Year on Saturday

articles.text: A new exhibition at the Legion of Honor showcases the history of San Francisco through fashion. Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style features iconic collections of 20th and 21st-century women’s fashion in the United States and the Bay Area. The exhibition includes over 100 pieces, some loaned by local collectors of haute couture. It is the first major presentation of the museum’s own costume collection. A wide range of fashion is represented, from French dressmakers to Japanese avant-garde designers. Designs by Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, Christopher John Rogers, Comme des Garçons, Rei Kawakubo, Kei Ninomiya, Junya Watanabe, Yohji Yamamoto and Rodarte are on display. “These garments echo the evolving urban landscape of San Francisco, a city populated by structures that push the confines of modern architecture, likewise made by advanced engineering and with state-of-the-art industrial materials,” said Laura Camerlengo, curator of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Fashioning San Francisco is on display through August. Visit https://www.famsf.org/exhibitions/fashioning-san-francisco to learn more. Fashioning San Francisco features over 100 clothing items from famous designers.
articles.title: Fashioning San Francisco exhibit now on view at Legion of Honor

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater premieres Big Data onstage at the Toni Rembe Theater tomorrow, February 15. Written by Kate Attwell and directed by ACT’s Artistic Director and Tony Award winner Pam Mackinnon, Big Data is a modern-day love story awash in technology and the dizzying possibilities of artificial intelligence. The play follows four young people. Sam loves Timmy, and Lucy loves Max, but they all succumb to the addiction of technology and smart devices. When Sam and Lucy’s parents make Michael Phillis stars in Big Data. a shocking announcement, the family is forced to confront the technology that has distracted them from each other and the legacy they’ll leave behind. MacKinnon and Attwell reunite to bring this revolutionary piece to audiences, inspired by Attwell’s experience touring search engine platform Mozilla’s “Glass Room” pop-up interactive exhibit in San Francisco. The cast includes Gabriel Brown, Rosie Hallett, Julia McNeal, Michael Phillis, Harold Surratt, Jomar Tagatac and BD Wong. The play will be performed through March 10. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/2023-24-season/big-data/. Kronos Quartet will perform at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on March 2.
articles.title: Big Data premieres on stage at ACT tomorrow

articles.text: Jazz vocalist Dianne Reeves will perform four concerts at SF Jazz Thursday through Sunday, February 22 - 25. A Grammy Award winner, Reeves is noted for her scores of R&B, gospel, Pop, Latin and Blues tracks and is considered one of the most proficient jazz vocalists today. She draws inspiration from Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday. Reeves has released numerous albums since 1987. Her most recent recorded album was Beautiful Life in 2014. Two years later she was recognized by the National Endowment for the Arts as the 2018 Jazz Master, the nation’s highest honor in the genre. Reeves continues to tour, most recently with the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra and Samara Joy, performing American jazz standard and holiday classics. All performances begin at 7 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/23-24/dianne-reeves/. Jazz vocalist Dianne Reeves to perform at SF Jazz for four evenings February 22-25.
articles.title: SF Jazz presents Dianne Reeves at Miner Auditorium Feb 22-25

articles.text: Renown quartet celebrating 50th year on March 2 The internationally acclaimed Kronos Quartet celebrates its 50th anniversary with a performance on Sunday, March 2, at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley. Entitled Five Decades, the program features the world premiere of Segara Gunung (Ocean-Mountain), a Cal Performances co-commissioned work by composer Peni Candra Rini, as well as excerpts from Michael Gordon’s gfedcba, a new work written for the group. Other music includes Severiano Briseño’s El Sinaloense (The Man from Sinaloa) arranged by Osvaldo Golijov, Sofia Gubaidulina’s Quartet No. 4, Steve Reich’s Triple Quartet, and Nicole Lizée’s ZonelyHearts, a multimedia work. An introductory eight-minute film by Sam Green, titled Kronos at Fifty will be shown. Founded in Seattle in 1973, Kronos Quartet has received more than 40 awards, including three Grammy Awards and the Polar Music, Avery Fisher, and Edison Klassiek Oeuvre Prizes. More than 1000 works have been written for the group, which has been praised for the inclusiveness of its repertoire. Kronos Quartet is the most well-known and nationally recognized string quartet that hails from San Francisco. Quartet members are David Harrington and John Sherba (violin), Hank Dutt (viola), and Paul Wiancko (cello). To purchase tickets, visit https://calperformances.org.
articles.title: Kronos Quartet returns to Zellerbach Hall

articles.text: Oakland Ballet will present its third annual Dancing Moons Festival March 14 through April 6 at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland and ODC Theater in San Francisco. The program is choreographed by all-Asian American Pacific Islander talent and will include a preview of the dance company’s Angel Island Project with choreography by Natasha Adorlee and Feng Ye. The project took inspiration from poetry carved by detainees held at the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station held thousands of immigrants through 1910 and 1940, mainly from China, Japan, India and the Philippines. “With captured imaginations, we take on a flight of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved in the walls by detainees,” Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig said. “The Angel Island Project helps us to trace who we are today by remembering from where we came.” Several selections will also be presented at the festival as works in progress, including Layer Upon Layer by Caili Quan (2022), Ballet des Porcelaines or The Teapot Prince by Phil Chan (original 1739; reimagined 2021), and highlights of Exquisite Corpse by Elaine Kudo, Seyong Kim, and Phil Chan (2023). For the first time since the festival’s inception, an exhibition of visual artists will be displayed at the cultural center. Artists include Asian Americans Sanjay Vora, Mark Shigenga and JaYing Wang. Performances on March 14-16 will take place at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland. The performances on April 5-6 will take place at the ODC Theatre in San Francisco. To purchase tickets, https://oaklandballet.org/dancing-moons-festival/. Oakland Ballet’s Dancing Moons Festival takes place in Oakland and San Francisco this Spring.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet Dancing Moons Festival begins March 14

articles.text: This column usually sings the praises of musicians and concerts. Not this time. Seiji Ozawa died the other day. He was a flamboyant conductor, to be sure. In fact, he was one of the most prominent conductors in the world of music. I, however, was not a fan of his. This is a column that could have been written in 1970. I attended one of Seiji Ozawa’s concerts with the San Francisco symphony in the Opera House. The Orchestra was on stage, ready to begin the concert. Ozawa ran onto stage as if he had been poked in the backside. He leapt to the podium and without acknowledging the applause or his musicians, he began to conduct. He gesticulated like a man insane. I thought he was imitating a rabbit suffering convulsions. The musicians of his orchestra looked bewildered. Perhaps he impressed some of the unsophisticated in the audience. Ozawa’s career continued to the stratosphere. His salient features as a conductor were precision of attack. He was concerned entirely with attack and little else, it seemed. Every orchestra he ever conducted produced an impoverished tonal quality. When he left San Francisco to conduct the Boston Symphony, the results were the same. The Boston Symphony’s former warm and rich tone became thin and scrappy. It is also interesting to note that controversies followed him. His relationships and interpersonal contacts with his musicians left much to be desired. What follows is an example: When I came to San Francisco, Philip Karp was the first chair contrabass player in the SF Symphony. He was a very respected musician among his colleagues. Sometime later I noticed that Karp was sitting last chair in the bass section. I found out what happened from some reliable sources. Ozawa summoned Karp and told him that he was disenchanted with a lack of discipline
articles.title: Seiji Ozawa a.k.a. the picture of Dorian Gray

articles.text: The Rite of Spring will feature 30 dancers from 14 African countries and assembled through a collaboration between Germany’s Pina Bausch Foundation, Senegal’s École des Sables, and the UK’s Sadler’s Wells. Cal Performances at UC Berkeley will present a special double-billed program of The Rite of Spring by choreographer Pina Bausch and a new companion piece, common ground[s] by Germaine Acogny and Malou Airaudo. The production will premiere on Friday, February 16, at 8 p.m., with performances on Saturday and Sunday, February 17-18. This will be the first-ever performance of Bausch’s Rite of Spring choreography in the Bay Area, a piece widely regarded as one of the most influential dance works of the 20th century. “This is the first time that [The Rite of Spring] is done not with an existing company, but with dancers who came together specifically for this piece,” explained Salomon Bausch, Pina Bausch’s son and the Executive Director of the Pina Bausch Foundation. The Rite of Spring will feature 30 dancers from 14 African countries, all assembled through a collaboration between Germany’s Pina Bausch Foundation, Senegal’s École des Sables, and the UK’s Sadler’s Wells Ballet Company. “I’m very excited to see the impact of their personalities and their diverse dance backgrounds on the piece but also vice versa; how the piece influences the dancers, both as artists and as human beings,” said Bausch. “I’ve always felt that this was an African dance,” said dancer Germaine Acogny, “The rituals are the same. And that music has an extraordinary pagan, terrestrial power. I even wonder whether Stravinsky was possessed when he composed it.” The Rite of Spring first premiered in 1913 in Paris, performed by the acclaimed Ballet Russes. In a controversial decision, a relatively-unknown Igor Stravinsky decided to base the composition and ballet on traditional Russian pagan rituals and folk dances, causing a near-riot on opening night. A moderated post-performance discussion will take place on Friday, February 16, and post-performance community conversations will be held on Saturday and Sunday, February 17 and 18. Tickets are $38–$86. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances.org, by phone at 642-9988, and in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m.

articles.text: Frank Langella as David Frost and Michael Sheen as Richard Nixon in Frost/Nixon Richard M. Nixon, the only U.S. president ever to resign from office, sat down with David Frost for a series of interviews several years after Nixon had resigned from office. Frost, whose career had taken a downward turn, needed a sensational moment that would bring him back into the spotlight. Nixon, living in exile in San Clemente, California, was eager to have the opportunity to find himself once again stage center in hopes of having the opportunity of if not at redemption, then certainly at putting his own spin on what had come to be known as Watergate – a harrowing and breathtaking scandal which had eventually brought down his administration. Who would have thought that this protracted interrogation would make not only good theater (the Broadway play was written by Peter Morgan), but also good filmmaking. In essence, Frost/Nixon is a prolonged conversation in which the two men face off in the living room of a suburban Los Angeles home. Where’s the drama in that? And yet, there is a palatable tension as the Nixon-Frost camps negotiate first the payment ($600,000) for the interviews with Nixon’s agent, Swifty Lazar (Toby Jones), and then the interviews themselves. Nixon, like a veteran prizefighter, bobs and weaves, selling his legacy like a hustler on a used car lot, while Frost tries to lay a glove on him without much luck. At least not initially. What makes the film remarkable is Frank Langella’s performance as Nixon. It’s a stunning piece of acting. Langella does not so much impersonate Nixon, he interprets the man’s mannerisms: his hunched, forward leaning walk; his deep, resonant voice; the jowly, perspiring visage, eyes shifting, assessing. Langella completely inhabits the character and creates a Nixonesque persona that is both powerful, believable and tragic. From almost the first frame, it is Nixon on the screen and Langella has vanished completely. Michael Sheen accomplishes the same thing, though his interpretation of Frost is less a physical presence and more the personification of Frost: carefully coiffed television personality, toothy smile, affable, made famous by his compelling interviews with famous people. Does Frost ultimately get the “get” he so desperately needed, one that would in effect be the trial that Nixon escaped due to Gerald Ford’s blanket pardon? Or does Nixon manage to turn the interviews into his bid for national absolution while making his case that he was a statesman of considerable accomplishments both domestically and internationally (Nixon did open the door to China). Therein is the tension in the film, two men using the reductive power of television as they joust, mano a mano. No matter the outcome, it is evident that Nixon was a brilliant politician who was fatally flawed. His life is reminiscent of a Greek tragedy, the pain of the years etched in his face, and that of his wife, Pat Nixon, who appears in one strained scene. Though he reached the pinnacle of power, Nixon was never able to free himself from the pathologies that framed his entire life, from those tenacious feelings of inferiority that loomed whenever he encountered the Brahmins of politics, perhaps best represented by John Kennedy. As Henry Kissinger was reported to have said of Nixon, “Imagine what he might have become had someone loved him.” Frost/Nixon. Directed by Ron Howard. Starring Frank Langella, Michael Sheen, Toby Jones and Rebecca Hall. Docudrama. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated R. Released in 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/ prime/apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIE FOR ADULTS Brilliant acting on view in Frost/Nixon

articles.text: Perhaps it’s time to banish that all too familiar line, “This is a chick flick;” no matter that the genre is still alive and well in Hollywood. Yet there are also films about women who live very different lives and have very different definitions of what completes them. Case in point would be It’s Complicated. This is a woman’s movie to be sure; however, the target demographic is women 40 and older. Nancy Meyer (Baby Boom, Something’s Gotta Give, The Holiday) has been writing and directing romantic comedies about mature women for the better part of two decades. Her protagonists have had enough life experience to make insightful comparisons (that was then, this is now), bridling when things begin to feel hauntingly familiar. It’s Complicated has at its center the incomparable Meryl Streep, portraying Jane Adler, divorced for over a decade from Jake, played by Alec Baldwin. As a middle-aged woman, Jane has it all – a gorgeous, semi-rural home in Santa Barbara; a prosperous, up-scale bakery and café; three grown children; and is an accomplished chef. But still no man in her life. And therein is the rub. At her son’s NYU graduation (the whole family gathers in Manhattan), she unexpectedly has drinks and dinner with Jake with much dancing before and after. Jake is attending the ceremony without his younger wife, Agness (Lake Bell) – buff and demanding and the mother of 5-year-old Pedro. Drunk, swept away by familiar emotions and alcohol, they fall into bed and into an affair resurrecting all kinds of issues that long ago had resolved, or at least buried. Jane is suddenly the other woman and completely unhinged by events. Jake is energized, captivated and even jealous of Jane’s casual flirtations with her architect, Adam (Steve Martin). The situation makes for engaging comedy. What Meyers does, and does well, is focus on a certain type of woman – mature, professional, once wounded, affluent and feeling she has been sleeping alone for far too long. Jane’s circle of friends, all contemporaries, equally attractive, are at first shocked when told about Jake; yet they remain supportive. Meyer is adept at creating a world that is more fantasy than reality, possessing a bright patina, a bit Disneyesque, lacking any semblance of grit and inspired, it seems, by Crate and Barrel, Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin in It’s Complicated
articles.title: Meryl Streep, Alec Baldwin star in It’s Complicated

And yet, there is a palatable tension as the Nixon-Frost camps negotiate first the payment ($600,000) for the interviews with Nixon’s agent, Swifty Lazar (Toby Jones), and then the interviews themselves. Nixon, like a veteran prizefighter, bobs and weaves, selling his legacy like a hustler on a used car lot, while Frost tries to lay a glove on him without much luck. At least not initially. What makes the film remarkable is Frank Langella’s performance as Nixon. It’s a stunning piece of acting. Langella does not so much impersonate Nixon, he interprets the man’s mannerisms: his hunched, forward leaning walk; his deep, resonant voice; the jowly, perspiring visage, eyes shifting, assessing. Langella completely inhabits the character and creates a Nixonesque persona that is both powerful, believable and tragic. From almost the first frame, it is Nixon on the screen and Langella has vanished completely. Michael Sheen accomplishes the same thing, though his interpretation of Frost is less a physical presence and more the personification of Frost: carefully coiffed television personality, toothy smile, affable, made famous by his compelling interviews with famous people. Does Frost ultimately get the “get” he so desperately needed, one that would in effect be the trial that Nixon escaped due to Gerald Ford’s blanket pardon? Or does Nixon manage to turn the interviews into his bid for national absolution while making his case that he was a statesman of considerable accomplishments both domestically and internationally (Nixon did open the door to China). Therein is the tension in the film, two men using the reductive power of television as they joust, mano a mano. No matter the outcome, it is evident that Nixon was a brilliant politician who was fatally flawed. His life is reminiscent of a Greek tragedy, the pain of the years etched in his face, and that of his wife, Pat Nixon, who appears in one strained scene. Though he reached the pinnacle of power, Nixon was never able to free himself from the pathologies that framed his entire life, from those tenacious feelings of inferiority that loomed whenever he encountered the Brahmins of politics, perhaps best represented by John Kennedy. As Henry Kissinger was reported to have said of Nixon, “Imagine what he might have become had someone loved him.” Frost/Nixon. Directed by Ron Howard. Starring Frank Langella, Michael Sheen, Toby Jones and Rebecca Hall. Docudrama. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated R. Released in 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/ prime/apple tv. Meryl Streep, Alec Baldwin star in It’s Complicated By Chris Honoré Perhaps it’s time to banish that all too familiar line, “This is a chick flick;” no matter that the genre is still alive and well in Hollywood. Yet there are also films about women who live very different lives and have very different definitions of what completes them. Case in point would be It’s Complicated. This is a woman’s movie to be sure; however, the target demographic is women 40 and older. Nancy Meyer (Baby Boom, Something’s Gotta Give, The Holiday) has been writing and directing romantic comedies about mature women for the better part of two decades. Her protagonists have had enough life experience to make insightful comparisons (that was then, this is now), bridling when things begin to feel hauntingly familiar. It’s Complicated has at its center the incomparable Meryl Streep, portraying Jane Adler, divorced for over a decade from Jake, played by Alec Baldwin. As a middle-aged woman, Jane has it all – a gorgeous, semi-rural home in Santa Barbara; a prosperous, up-scale bakery and café; three grown children; and is an accomplished chef. But still no man in her life. And therein is the rub. At her son’s NYU graduation (the whole family gathers in Manhattan), she unexpectedly has drinks and dinner with Jake with much dancing before and after. Jake is attending the ceremony without his younger wife, Agness (Lake Bell) – buff and demanding and the mother of 5-year-old Pedro. Drunk, swept away by familiar emotions and alcohol, they fall into bed and into an affair resurrecting all kinds of issues that long ago had resolved, or at least buried. Jane is suddenly the other woman and completely unhinged by events. Jake is energized, captivated and even jealous of Jane’s casual flirtations with her architect, Adam (Steve Martin). The situation makes for engaging comedy. What Meyers does, and does well, is focus on a certain type of woman – mature, professional, once wounded, affluent and feeling she has been sleeping alone for far too long. Jane’s circle of friends, all contemporaries, equally attractive, are at first shocked when told about Jake; yet they remain supportive. Meyer is adept at creating a world that is more fantasy than reality, possessing a bright patina, a bit Disneyesque, lacking any semblance of grit and inspired, it seems, by Crate and Barrel, See It’s Complicated on page 27 Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin in It’s Complicated

articles.text: What can be enriching, even surprising, is to watch a foreign film and be immediately struck by the profound differences that exist between cultures – some deeply subtle, others far more blatant, evident in interactions, mannerisms, the scaffolding of life itself, all so unique and so compelling. Departures offers the audience such an opportunity for it constructs a tender and at times unsettling bridge between the living and the dead. Briefly, the film tells the story of Daigo (Mashiro Motoki), a young cellist and member of the Tokyo Symphony Orchestra. He is married to Mika (Ryoko Hirosue). Unexpectedly, the orchestra is disbanded and Daigo and Mika return to the prefecture of Yamagata and to his old family home, which he inherited when his mother passed away. He must find work and opportunities for cellists are rare. He answers an ad in a newspaper for a “departures” assistant. Thinking it’s a travel agency, Daigo goes to the office to apply. What he discovers is that the job is for a “departed” assistant, and the position entails “encoffination” of the deceased, an elaborate ritual of washing and dressing a loved one and then slowly placing the body into a coffin as the grieving family and friends look on. Daigo is at first repelled by the work, so much so that he Mashiro Motoki in a scene from Departures can’t share with Mika what the job involves. But he is also touched by the profound tenderness that his mentor, Mr. Sasaki (Tsutomu Yamazaki), exhibits as each step is slowly carried out. He is also struck by the impact this ceremony has on the family – the ritual is a gift, a farewell, a closure. American critics have faulted Japanese films for being overly sentimental, and Departures has its moments. But it is also beautifully acted and courageous in its intent. When it won an Oscar for Best Foreign Film, there was an audible gasp from those who believed it was not the best of a strong field; the voting Academy, however, disagreed. If a film has the power to touch the audience, to elicit an emotive response, then it has achieved far more than most films. And the willingness of director Yojiro Takita to explore this subject intimately, while telling the story of how two young people come to terms with Daigo’s work is compelling from the first frame. Departures explores a facet of the human condition from which we almost reflexively turn, away and it does so with insight and subtlety. Departures. Directed by Yojiro Takita. Starring Masahiro Motoki, Tsutomu Yamazaki, Ryoko Hirosue, Kazako Yoshiyuki. In Japanese with English subtitles. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on VUDU. articles.text: Kids loved the video scoundrel Ralph (John C. Reilly), the origin star of Wreck-it-Ralph. And though a sequel was planned, it took more than a few years to finally create and release Ralph Breaks the Internet. It was worth the wait. Six years have passed spent in the Litwak Arcade, home to BFF Vallelope Von Schweetz (Sara Silverman) and Ralph. Needing a special part for her Sugar Rush game, Vallelope finds a path, through a router, into the World Wide Web with Ralph close behind. Already kids are wondering if Ralph will break something — and then what? What the pair discover is that they are totally unprepared for this amazing place, and in order to complete their search they will need the support of the internet locals – called the netizens – to assist them in navigating what proves to be very unfamiliar electronic territory. The interior of the internet looks like a mall-sized unexpected world where they meet puzzling and interesting inhabitants such as an entrepreneur named Yesss (Taraji Henson) who is the head algorithm, so to speak, and the soul of a place named Buzztube. There are even pop-ups which appear in strangely sweet shapes (Beyoncé as a corn chip?), and lots of workers running Social Media. In this wildly colorful mix is embedded a nice message that stresses that not everyone has to like the same thing or do the same stuff. But then the internet Ralph returns in the sequel Ralph Breaks the Internet

articles.text: The sun was shining as I drove across the Bay Bridge and the shimmering bay was filled with sailboats competing in a regatta. I was headed to one of my favorite wine tastings of the year - the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting in San Francisco held this year at One Market on the Embarcadero on January 27. Zinfandel is not really native to California – most ampelographers from UC Davis now believe it came to California from Croatia in the 1800s, but it’s certainly the trademark grape of the state; there was even a bill before the state legislature to declare it the official state wine (the Cabernet and Pinot producers protested). Ninety nine percent of the world’s Zinfandel is grown in California and because there is no French equivalent it is the closest thing we have to a native son. World class Zinfandels are still much less expensive than world class California Cabernets but unfortunately the price is edging upward. Most of the wines listed below retail for between 25 and 50 dollars. These wines can often be found at lower prices at places like the Wine Club in SF or on Wine.com. The wonderful thing about Zinfandel is how versatile it is in pairing with food. It goes great with salmon, steak, burgers, pasta or pizza to say nothing of enjoying a glass all on its own. The size of the tasting at One Market was bigger this year and it appears that ZAP has returned to its pre-Covid participation levels. There were so many old standby producers as well as some new kids on the block that I was excited to meet. The overall quality was extremely high. making my job of discerning the best wines very tough. At the end of the day, the following wines were the ones that stood out. They are the cream of the crop. • 2021 Hartford Family Zinfandel Dina’s Vineyard Dina’s Vineyard is a 10-acre plot planted over 100 years ago by Italian immigrants in the Russian River Valley. The wine offers up notes of cinnamon, anise, black tea, and forest floor over a core of blackberries, cassis, and blueberry jam. Medium to full-bodied, it packs in the earthy layers on the palate with a chewy texture and a long savory finish. • 2021 Perlegos Zinfandel Stampede Vineyard, $32 Hailing from the Lodi area, the 2021 Perlegos conjures notions of plums, raspberries and fruitcake with touches of dusty soil and sandalwood. Full-bodied, richly fruited and wonderfully layered, it has a solid frame of tannins and bright acidity finishing with a lively lift. • 2021 Corkwood Cellars Zinfandel Steele Vineyard This was a new producer to me, and it appears they are up to good things. The wine from a 100-year-old vineyard in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada reveals a medium to deep garnet color and a nose of blackberries and blueberries with hints of baking spice, garrigue and tilled earth. The full-bodied palate delivers a lot of fruit, supported by firm, chewy tannins and just enough acid, finishing with great length and balance. • 2018 Stef Zinfandel - Sensational This wine is aged three years in neutral barrels and is made from Dry Creek Valley grapes. It exhibits a sensational nose of black raspberry and berry fruit, a supple, full-bodied, expansive, savory mouthfeel, wonderful purity, heady glycerin and has a long, satisfying finish. This sensuous Zinfandel can be drunk over the next 5 years. • 2019 Lava Cap Old Vine Zinfandel The Lava Cap winery in the El Dorado AVA in the Sierra foothills is a perennial favorite. It is graced with expressive dark red fruit, flowers, mint, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries round out the finish. • 2021 Limerick Lane Zinfandel Estate Cuvee, $85 This Russian River Zin is augmented with a good portion of Syrah, Mourvedre and Petite Sirah. The Estate Zin is a beautiful effort, giving off a tight but promising nose of raspberry and briery fruit intermingled with notions of oak, pepper and leather. The wine from a 100-year-old vineyard in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada reveals a medium to deep garnet color and a nose of blackberries and blueberries with hints of baking spice, garrigue and tilled earth. The full-bodied palate delivers a lot of fruit, supported by firm, chewy tannins and just enough acid, finishing with great length and balance. • 2018 Stef Zinfandel - Sensational This wine is aged three years in neutral barrels and is made from Dry Creek Valley grapes. It exhibits a sensational nose of black raspberry and berry fruit, a supple, full-bodied, expansive, savory mouthfeel, wonderful purity, heady glycerin and has a long, satisfying finish. This sensuous Zinfandel can be drunk over the next 5 years. • 2019 Lava Cap Old Vine Zinfandel The Lava Cap winery in the El Dorado AVA in the Sierra foothills is a perennial favorite. It is graced with expressive dark red fruit, flowers, mint, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries round out the finish. • 2021 Limerick Lane Zinfandel Estate Cuvee, $85 This Russian River Zin is augmented with a good portion of Syrah, Mourvedre and Petite Sirah.
