It will drink well for 6 to 7 years. • 2021 Miro Zinfandel Bastoni Vineyard, $32 This is Miro’s 20th anniversary vintage, and this bottling shows they are improving with age. It displays a deep garnet-purple color and delivers pronounced blueberries, and plum preserves notes with hints of baking spices, dried herbs, and potpourri. Very big, full-bodied, rich, and seductive in the mouth, it packs in the spice and berry preserves, finishing with incredible length. This wine cries out for some BBQ ribs. • 2019 Alexander Valley Vineyards Sin Zin, $24 (BEST VALUE) This ripe and shall we say hedonistic wine displays a deep garnet-purple color and delivers pronounced blueberries, and plum preserves notes with hints of baking spices, dried herbs, and potpourri. Very big, full-bodied, rich, and seductive in the mouth, it packs in the spice and berry preserves, finishing with incredible length. This wine would partner great with grilled burgers. • 2021 Macchia Prestigious Zinfandel, $40 Macchia does not make wines for the timid or faint of heart. This fruit comes from the famous Grandpere Vineyard one of the oldest in California. A sweet vanilla oak nose cascades out of the glass followed by opulent rich berry fruit on the palate and a long full finish. This wine should be drunk over the next 5 years. • 2021 Once and Future Zinfandel Old Hill Vineyard, $55 It was great to see Joel Peterson at the tasting. As founder of Ravenswood Winery, he is truly one of the giants in the world of Zinfandel. In this new project he is using grapes from the famous Old Hill Vineyard, a mixed field blend of over 40 different varieties. It’s an amazing place that he has been working with since the 80’s. It shows blueberry and vanilla notes intermixed with cherries and black currant fruit. It is a well-made, seriously endowed, full-bodied, spicy Zin that should last decades in the cellar. • 2019 Three Old Vine Zinfandel, $30 This wine comes from some ancient sandy vineyards in Contra Costa County. An excellent deep ruby/plum colored Zinfandel with sweet, briary, black cherry and currant fruit. Medium-bodied texture and a plush mid-palate. The alcohol tips over 15% but is nicely hidden by the lush fruit. • 2020 Quivira Black Boar Zinfandel, $55 Deep purple in color, the wine exhibits some wood notes but that component is well-balanced by the fleshy concentrated black berry and plum flavors. Notions of earth and tar also make an appearance in this full-bodied, ripe Zinfandel. • 2021 Biale Zinfandel Stagecoach Vineyard, $55 Biale has long been one of my favorite Zin producers, but this is first time I have written about their Stagecoach bottling. The wine reveals aromas of ripe blueberry and cherry fruit with hints of spice and earth on the palate. Medium-bodied, with nicely integrated wood and no hard edges. Great with pizza or pasta. • 2020 Dry Creek Zinfandel Wallace Ranch, $46 Dry Creek is one of the pioneering wineries in Sonoma County. This Zin is fortified with a splash of Alicante Bouchet – always a good thing. The wine reveals aromas of ripe raspberry and cherry fruit with hints of exotic spices and earth on the palate. Medium bodied with nicely integrated tannins with no hard edges. • 2021 Bricoleur Zinfandel Rockpile Vineyard, $65 The high elevation Rockpile Vineyard is known for making some of California’s most concentrated and powerful zinfandels. The wine exhibits excellent ripeness along with abundant briary fruit, a hint of pepper and a long, heady finish. • 2019 David Clinton Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard, $35 This is a fine expression of Sonoma’s Dry Creek Valley Zinfandels. The area produces perfectly balanced wines that are not ponderous or over the top and tend to smell more of cherries and blackberries than raisins or prunes. Good acid and a refreshing finish. • 2020 Epoch Zinfandel Paderewski Vineyard This “big boy” Zin (15.5%) from Paso Robles is packed with unctuous flavors of plums, blueberry jam and cherry pie. The big, round, luscious, finish goes on forever. It cries out for a big rack of BBQ ribs. • 2019 Storrs Rusty Ridge Zinfandel In the wine world Santa Clara County sometimes gets overlooked, but this high-quality Zin shows what the region can do. It has deep purple color, black and red fruit f lavors, medium body lots of glycerin and a dense but balanced palate. Very well made. • 2022 Christopher Cellars Zinfandel Cherryhouse Vineyard T h i s w i ne f r om t he Mokelumne River AVA was new to me. It was aged in 40% new French oak which gives a sweet richness to the nose. It is a lush wine with lots of cassis, blackberry and plum fruit. There are notes of leather and earth and good structure on the long finish. • 2021 Van Ruiten Family Old Vine Zinfandel, $25 This intense spicy wine has jammy aromas of black cherries and plums, followed by medium-bodied, fleshy flavors with loads of glycerin and an opulent mouthfeel. Should last for 6 to 7 years in the cellar but is plenty delicious now. • 2021 Hendry Zinfandel Blocks 7 & 22, $42 Napa Valley has budded over most of its Zinfandel grapes to the more lucrative, Cabernet Sauvignon so I am always glad to see Hendry hanging in there with its wonderful Napa Zin. This has a deep ruby/purple color as well as a profound core of cherry, currant and raspberry fruit loads of spice box and pepper, authoritative flavors and a super long finish. • 2020 Dashe Zinfandel Todd Brothers Ranch $44 East Bay’s own Dashe Cellars (Alameda) has long been a producer of opulent crowd-pleasing wines. It has a complex nose of figs, smoked meats, sweet cherries, currants and earth. Medium bodied with good acidity, it is elegant, well-delineated and vibrant with a satisfyingly savory finish. • 2021 We Know Jack Zinfandel Rockpile, $78 This was a new label to me from the wonderful Rockpile AVA. Big, tangy, sweet aromas of black raspberries, cherries and spice box are followed by a fleshy, full-bodied offering with gorgeous purity, a lovely texture and enough acidity to provide vibrancy and uplift. This opulent wine is delicious now and should last for nearly a decade in the cellar. • 2021 Tres Sabores Por Que No?, $38 This is a blend of Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot. It offers a deep, saturated ruby/purple color as well as a big, sweet bouquet of blackberries, cherry liqueur, licorice, wood and dried herbs. Powerfully built, with a layered, opulent texture, and good purity this is a mouth-filling delicious blend to drink over the next 4 to 5 years. • 2020 J. Dusi Paper Street Zinfandel, $68 A big Paso Robles Zin, the Paper Street charges out of the gate with plums, cherries and raspberry pie with a touch of herbs and baking spices. The full-bodied palate is laden with red and black berry layers, supported by chewy tannins and invigorating freshness, finishing long and peppery. • 2017 Cast Late Harvest Zinfandel Late Harvest zinfandel used to much more popular than they are today and I miss them. I think this was the only one at the tasting. This “mini-port” without the fortification is rich and luscious with tons of sweep plum and prune flavors and ethereal perfumy nose. It has plenty of acid to avoid being cloying or tiring on the palate. This beautiful wine would be an elegant way to end a meal or just sipped alone by the fireside.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 14, 2024 23 Garden column by Josh Harkinson While at Tahoe on Friday, my kids and I rode a ski lift to the top of Palisades’ Siberia Ridge and encountered a white-out. Back at home this Monday morning, I’m looking out the window at my currants and camelias in full bloom with a weather forecast of highs close to 60. I never cease to be amazed by our microclimates. Spring starts early in our part of the East Bay – and so do serious gardeners. The best-long term defense against weeds is a thick layer of mulch. This month’s heavy rains have turbocharged the weeds. Crabgrass, clover, Algerian ivy, Scotch broom are all on a rampage. Get them out before they go to seed, or you’ll regret it. Though plucking weeds can be meditative, now might be a good time to get smarter about controlling them. I know people who swear by what I call synthetic methods of weed control. If you use anti-weed fabric, make sure it’s staked down or else racoons will pull it up to look for worms underneath. Personally, I don’t like the idea of covering my yard in polyester or using ecologically damaging weed killer, though I’ll admit to sometimes spraying it on cracks in my driveway after the rains have stopped and there’s less chance of it seeping into the Bay. The best-long term defense against weeds is a thick layer of mulch. I’ve discussed using leaves from your own trees, but if that’s not enough then try the attractive redwood chip bark mulch from American Soil and Stone in Richmond. You can pick it up by the bag, or for the most cost-effective option, order it by the truckload and have it dumped in a pile on your driveway. Not every weed is your enemy. The plants range from one to four feet in height. They produce attractive fall colors before dropping their leaves in the winter, though, owing to our mild climate, some keep their foliage year-round. There’s only one catch to planting blueberries: you must first add peat moss to the soil to make it more acidic. articles.text: Ken Li & Valerie Ng will celebrate 40 years of marriage on February 29. Piedmonters Ken Li and Valerie Ng have been married for nearly 40 years but will only be celebrating their 10th anniversary at the end of this month. They were married on Leap Year’s Day in Texas in 1984. Li, a prominent figure in town with decades of experience piloting the Piedmont Scouting Venture Scout program and Ng, a medical doctor, don’t usually make a fuss of celebrations or Valentine’s Day. However, with their once-in-every-four-year anniversary on the rise, they decided to reminisce their tale of courtship to the Post. They met in Dallas in the spring of 1982 after being set up for a blind date by a friend on Ken’s soccer team, and a classmate of Valerie. Their first date was anything but common. Valerie was in the middle of finals week for medical school and was letting off some steam with a pack of 10 classmates. Ken was invited to join, to see a matinee of Conan the Barbarian. “My group is pretty rowdy. It’s a Rocky Horror Picture Show with every movie. So we went to see Conan, and we were yelling and screaming,” recalled Valerie. “She shows up and I’m expecting to just meet her, but she shows up with like nine guys and her,” said Ken. “Then we go up to the theater to the front row and they have to sit all in a row in the front row. They start heckling at the movie while we’re watching.” Valerie remembered the day well, laughing about mocking Arnold Schwarzenegger’s deaf display of acting. “My thought was, if he could tolerate me and my friends, he had potential,” Valerie said with a smile. Ken survived the trial. They had a real date after that. A year and a half later, they were living together and an idea came to Ken. “It was February 28th and it was a leap year. And so I said, ‘Hey, wouldn’t it be cool to get married on a Leap Day?’” Ken recalled. T hey b ot h l i ke d t he impromptu idea. “So I go to work and I tell the secretary, ‘I’m taking the afternoon off to get married,’” said Ken. Ken, who grew up outside of Boston, and Valerie, who grew up in Oakland, were married in Texas on the spur of the moment. The couple relocated back from Texas to the West Coast for Valerie’s medical residency. They found a place in Piedmont, and started a family, and the rest is history. Ever since, Valerie has tirelessly worked, building an impressive medical career as a pathologist. Ken, similarly, shows high devotion to the Piedmont Scouting program and Piedmont Community Service Crew. For their 40th anniversary the couple will celebrate by Valerie taking a one-week vacation. Whether they refer to it as their 40th or 10th anniversary, their longevity is admirable. What is their secret? “I would just say we are not demanding of each other,” said Valerie. “I think that’s right, we do things together, but we can entertain ourselves so, there’s not a lot of pressure,” said Ken with a smile.
articles.title: Ken Li & Valerie Ng – a Leap Year’s Day marriage

articles.text: Neil and Beverly Rothenberg have been married for nearly 48 years. Beverly Rothenberg will never forget the time her husband, Neil, took off running down the street in Berkeley on one of their first dates. “We were out one night and there was this woman who was walking nearby who had her bag stolen,” she said. “Neil goes tearing after the guy without even batting an eyelash.” The thief eventually ducked out of sight, but the memory stayed with Beverly. “His quick action, I thought, was something really admirable.” Neil and Beverly met at UC Berkeley in 1972. The two had seen each other around the tennis courts before. “I was on the team at Cal and Beverly played recreationally,” said Neil. “I think the first time, it was Beverly who asked me out.” “He said no,” laughed Beverly, so I invited him over for dessert.” “It was the second time,” he jumped in. “She invited me over for dessert when I accepted. I remember exactly what it was— apple strudel.” And so began Neil’s love of Beverly’s cooking. One of the first things he would come to love about her. The couple dated for three years before they were engaged. “And this time, it was definitely me asking her,” Neil confirmed. He proposed to Beverly in the kitchen of their Berkeley apartment while she was cooking dinner. Beverly agreed enthusiastically. “There was a lot of jumping up and down.” They were married in Southern California, at Neil’s parents’ house in Tarzana. A second reception was held in Oakland, so they could include as many of their friends and family members as possible. “We didn’t have very much money, so we did everything on the inexpensive side,” said Neil. “In fact, we had a judge come to the house to marry us. I remember my dad slipping him 50 bucks afterwards for performing the ceremony!” After 48 years of marriage, Neil and Beverly still admire much about each other. “I think my favorite thing is that she has always looked out for me. That no matter what, she’s always loved me,” said Neil. “And it’s good to have Beverly to talk to before I do anything rash,” admitted a man sometimes known for quick thinking and quick action. “Neil is really good with our kids,” said Beverly. “He was the dad who did all of the coaching and the dad everybody knew at school. I admire that it was always important to him.” When asked if they had any Valentine’s Day plans, Neil and Beverly said they didn’t give the holiday too much thought these days. “There are so many more important things than just showing up one day a year,” said Beverly. “It’s the everyday things that you have to do. That’s way more important to me than flowers on a day.” Neil agreed wholeheartedly.
articles.title: A couple who found love on the tennis court

articles.text: Debbie Dare and Joe Gold celebrating their anniversary at Italian Colors. No couple is perfect, some say, but Piedmont’s Joseph Gold and wife Debbie Dare exist in defiance of that sentiment. Joe and Debbie were married in 1990, and have laughed, dined and performed their way to happiness, one day at a time, year after year, ever since. Joe and Debbie, both musicians, met in Berkeley at Ifshin Violins, where Debbie now works. They decided to cook a meal together. Neither music nor culinary pursuits can be said to be their matchmaker however, because that title belongs to Joe’s son, Raphael, also a professional musician. At the age of four, he acted as a real-life Cupid uniting the two. Debbie recalls Joe’s son saying to Debbie: “I have a special name for you. I’m going to call you Mom.” She told Raphael at the time that she thought Mom was a wonderful name, but they should ask his dad if that was going to be okay. “Raphael was sitting in his highchair at the time, and he just took his fist and pounded the table,” Debbie said with a grin. He said, ‘that doesn’t have anything to do with him. That’s between you and me.’” – Joseph Gold Joe corroborated the story, “My first wife died and my son, four years old, he was thinking it would be nice to have a mother. Debbie was his choice. He told her it was his decision and that my opinion didn’t count,” said Gold. Joe and Debbie share passions beyond music – for things within life that can only be matched by the love they reciprocate for one another. Joe’s column in the Post, The Musical Gourmet, frequently combines philosophy with culinary and musical insights. Joe’s parents taught him to cook and Debbie’s dad was an excellent chef. “We dine, it’s very important. My recipes are easy to do, easy to assemble, they don’t take long and they look good,” said Gold. Food unites them as much as music as the pair travels the world teaching and performing violin and viola. They have performed in Romania, Germany, and Spain, including at the Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna. The globetrotting couple fortuitously concluded an extended stay in Spain at the end of February 2020. They spent a romantic 2020 Valentine’s Day taking a cooking class in Barcelona on the art of making paella. Joe Gold and Debbie Dare will be celebrating their 34th year of marriage this year. Please join us for our upcoming in-person seminar.
articles.title: Joe Gold and Debbie Dare a true match by Cupid

articles.text: When Chad Olcott started dating Laura Pochop, the first thing he noticed was her mind. “If anyone knows my wife, she is the smartest person in the room wherever she goes,” he said. At the same time, Laura was falling in love with Chad’s voice. “The first things I realized I liked were his funny little accents and impressions,” she said. They had laughter, chemistry, and attraction. The stage was set for romance, with only one problem. They couldn’t tell anyone that they were dating. “It was a secret office romance,” laughed Olcott. “So, we had to be discreet.” Chad and Laura met at the non-profit organization City Year in 1993. He was Executive Director and she was Development Director. “It was this place that takes young people and puts them into full-time community service, kind of like an urban Peace Corps,” he explained. It was “a young, upstart company and a young office, filled with bad copiers and broken coffee machines,” he recalled, but also an office with the woman of his dreams in it. Together, they were asked to set up a branch of the company in Providence, RI, where they worked. Although they were in very different parts of the company – Laura’s work was administrative and Chad did mostly field work – the two eventually started spending time together after hours. As time went on, they developed a mutual respect and admiration for one another that blossomed into a relationship. On their first Valentine’s Day, the couple didn’t want to run into any trouble with their HR department, but Chad wanted Laura to know he was thinking of her. “So, I brought her favorite Dunkin’ Donuts iced coffee to her desk with three scoops of sugar,” he recalled. The only person who knew they were dating was their coworker and friend Lauren Dutton, now a Piedmont resident herself. After celebrating a milestone at work, Dutton pulled the two aside and asked them pointblank: “Is there something going on between you two?” The couple admitted gleefully. “And that’s how Lauren Dutton was there the first night we actually kissed,” recalls Chad. Chad and Laura moved into a small home in Providence in 1994. The stars aligned in 1995, and when Laura was accepted into the Stanford Graduate School of Business, a position opened up for Chad at City Year’s headquarters in San Jose. The two were West Coast-bound. In 1996, Chad and Laura were married at Hammersmith Farm in Newport, RI, a venue famous for being the location where John F. Kennedy and Jackie held their wedding reception. But Hurricane Fran made an appearance, and the event became windy and wet, but memorable. “It was the summer of Alanis Morrisette’s song “Ironic,” so everyone there was singing: ‘It’s like rain on your wedding day!’” These days, Chad and Laura usually opt for a more low-key Valentine’s Day celebration with a few friends over for a Valentine’s Day potluck this year. But that doesn’t mean the two are any less smitten with one another. “I love her smile and her dance moves,” said Chad. “And she’s an amazing cook.” “Nobody makes me laugh the way he does,” said Laura. “And he is a phenomenal father.” Photo by Chad Olcott Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop have been together for over thirty years. ®
articles.title: A secret office romance turns into a 26-year marriage

articles.text: If you’re a business owner, you always have a lot to do and a lot to think about. But have you put much thought into how you’ll eventually leave it all behind? Even if you’re a few years away from that day, it’s a good idea to create an exit strategy. If you’re like most other owners, most of your net worth may well be tied up in your business – so how you exit that business can have a big impact on your finances and your retirement. As you begin the exit strategy process, you’ll need to examine some basic questions, such as how much you want for your business and how much it’s worth. But you’ll especially need to plan for the mechanics of your exit — that is, just how you’re going to sell or transfer ownership of it. Essentially, you have three main options: • Internal sale or transfer – You could sell or transfer your business to someone affiliated with the company, such as a family member, business partner or even a group of employees. The advantages of this method are that you’ll have greater control over the timing of your exit, and you’ll be able to provide greater continuity for your employees, clients and suppliers. One potential disadvantage is that your net sales proceeds may be less than what you’d get from selling the business to an unrelated third party. • External sale or transfer – The biggest benefit of selling or transferring your business to an unrelated third party is that you can potentially maximize your net sales proceeds. But you’ll need to consider some tradeoffs, too. For one thing, a sale to an outside person or business usually requires a long and possibly expensive due diligence process. Also, you’ll have less control over the timing of your exit than you would if you sold the business to an internal source. • Liquidation – If you liquidated your business by selling all your assets and shutting down operations, you could end up with far fewer net proceeds than if you sold the business to an internal or external source. However, you could raise cash pretty quickly. But if you chose to liquidate or dissolve your business, it could potentially be disruptive for your employees, clients and suppliers. Because everyone’s situation is different, there’s no clearcut formula for deciding which of these exit options is right for you. And it isn’t simply a matter of numbers, either, because you’ll need to consider some intangible factors, too. How will your family be affected by your choice? How would you feel if your business was in someone else’s hands, or no longer existed? You’ll need to work out these issues, along with the financial ones, before you decide on your business exit strategy. Fortunately, you don’t have to go it alone. You may want to consult your financial, legal and tax advisors, and possibly work with a commercial banker and a business evaluation expert. By drawing on several sources of expertise, you can feel more confident that you’ll make a decision that’s appropriate for your needs. One final suggestion: Don’t wait too long before you begin putting together your exit strategy. Time goes fast, and when the time comes for you to say goodbye to your business, you’ll want to be prepared. articles.text: There was a turnout of 16 readers of the First Mondays Reading Group met on February 5 at the Community Hall to discuss the 2021 non-fiction The Code Breaker written by American historian and journalist Walter Isaacson. It is a biography of Jennifer Doudna, the winner of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her work on the CRISPR system of gene editing. The book debuted at number one on The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list. When Doudna was in sixth grade, her father gave her a paperback titled The Double Helix. After she read it, Doudna became fascinated by science and was driven to understand how nature works. Later she became interested in the competition to discover the genetic code of life and to turn discoveries into inventions. From her passion, she would help make one of the most important biological advances since the discovery of the structure of DNA. With collaborators she created an easy-to-use tool that can edit DNA. It can transform the human race and is known as CRISPR. It has opened a new world of medical advances, but also raises moral questions that Isaacson presents in the book. After helping to discover CRISPR, Doudna became a leader in addressing these moral issues and, with her collaborator Emmanuelle Charpentier, won the Nobel Prize in 2020. The Code Breaker was another good read for the group because some loved it, while for others there were varying degrees of “not so much.” It really was varying degrees because the book’s subject matter, and especially the ethical questions it raises were important to the group. For those. Who loved it, the book covered a lot of ground well. The science Isaacson described is cutting edge and relevant to our current and future lives. Additionally, Isaacson provides this information in a way that the general, non-science-oriented person can understand, something that was appreciated by the group. The book gave the readers views of the cooperation, but also the competition within the field of scientific research as well as the related business opportunities. The Code Breaker also provides women, like Doudna, the recognition they deserve. However, The Code Breaker’s length was a negative for some readers, long and tedious, Parts of the book were interesting, but others weren’t. A shorter, more concise young adult version would have been preferred by some, and in fact was enjoyed by one reader when that was the only edition of the book available at the library. Isaacson’s “scatter shot approach” in presenting his material may have been intended to keep the reader’s interest but was not orderly for some. The presentation of the ethical issues and questions related to CRISPR were particularly engaging and thought provoking for the group. Should we use our new evolution-hacking powers to make us less susceptible to viruses? What about preventing depression? Should we allow parents, if they can afford it, to enhance the height, strength, or intelligence of their children? These are hard questions. CRISPR has huge potential benefits, but also significant dangers that society must understand, the book explains. With the discussion complete, future books were considered. The group had previously selected Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis for March and I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou for April. Lois Price presented three new candidates for May and Perestroika in Paris by Jane Smiley was selected. The next discussion will be on March 4 at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee. Registration is required at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. On hand for the monthly Monday reading group were: Rich Seigel, Bob Hall, Rob Smith, Laura Goldman, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Melba Yee, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Martin Levy, Sarah Johnson, Ken Young, Hilary Honore, Lois Price, Phil Witte, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus.

articles.text: Last week’s Wednesday Walkers included Mark Davis, Lois Price, Rick Eigenbrode, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Karen Sullivan with K-9 best friend Cooper, Will Adams, Bob Wong, rob Smith, Jim Kuo, Quincy Dong, Charlene Louie, Claudia Bach, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Karen Sullivan brought her husband, Tom Sullivan, to walk with them. Last week 16 hardy members of the Walking on Wednesdays group (and one K-9 best friend) showed up with raincoats and umbrellas. The group decided on a walk closer to the Exedra in case the rain got worse. They headed to the Hazel Lane loop and surrounding streets. The walkers went down Highland Avenue to its corner with Requa Road where they stopped for some history of the area. At the start of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have good educations, so she got Isaac Requa to build a one-room schoolhouse on his property at what is now the end of the Requa Place cul-de-sac. She hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children. This was the very first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Long leased the house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane. She also hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and California families, and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913. Soon after more classrooms and a gymnasium were added. The school had dormitory rooms for up to 70 students from first grade through high school. In 1924 there were 186 students, and in 1928 there were 21 teachers and 42 graduating seniors. However, the Stock Market crashed in 1929 and the following Depression created financial difficulties for many of the school’s parents. Piedmont High was less expensive and Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and the school closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The walkers passed the tall redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane, site of the entrance to the original Ransom Bridges School, The school itself was at what is now 141 Hazel Lane. They admired the Albert Farr craftsman design of the home and took a group photo in front of it. The walkers also noted the neighborhood’s first house at 152 Hazel Lane, and completed the rest of loop, which took them back to Requa Road. The group retraced their steps and decided that despite the rain they weren’t finished for the morning. They crossed Highland and went on Caperton Avenue to Mountain Avenue. The walkers sloshed down to Craig Avenue where they noted a beautiful Italian Victorian, built in 1883 and originally owned by Hugh Craig, Piedmont’s first mayor. Originally on Highland Avenue (then Vernal), the house was put on log rollers and pulled by horses to its current location, 55 Craig Avenue. The walkers went up Craig and found the somewhat secret back driveway to the Community Church. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. pages.text: Wednesday, February 14, 2024 29 Walking on Wednesday Water resistant walkers show up for Wednesday Walk Last week’s Wednesday Walkers included Mark Davis, Lois Price, Rick Eigenbrode, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Karen Sullivan with K-9 best friend Cooper, Will Adams, Bob Wong, rob Smith, Jim Kuo, Quincy Dong, Charlene Louie, Claudia Bach, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Karen Sullivan brought her husband, Tom Sullivan, to walk with them. By Dick Carter Last week 16 hardy members of the Walking on Wednesdays group (and one K-9 best friend) showed up with raincoats and umbrellas. The group decided on a walk closer to the Exedra in case the rain got worse. They headed to the Hazel Lane loop and surrounding streets. The walkers went down Highland Avenue to its corner with Requa Road where they stopped for some history of the area. At the start of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have good educations, so she got Isaac Requa to build a one-room schoolhouse on his property at what is now the end of the Requa Place cul-de-sac. She hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children. This was the very first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Long leased the house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane. She also hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and California families, and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913. Soon after more classrooms and a gymnasium were added. The school had dormitory rooms for up to 70 students from first grade through high school. In 1924 there were 186 students, and in 1928 there were 21 teachers and 42 graduating seniors. However, the Stock Market crashed in 1929 and the following Depression created financial difficulties for many of the school’s parents. Piedmont High was less expensive and Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and the school closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The walkers passed the tall redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane, site of the entrance to the original Ransom Bridges School, The school itself was at what is now 141 Hazel Lane. They admired the Albert Farr craftsman design of the home and took a group photo in front of it. The walkers also noted the neighborhood’s first house at 152 Hazel Lane, and completed the rest of loop, which took them back to Requa Road. The group retraced their steps and decided that despite the rain they weren’t finished for the morning. They crossed Highland and went on Caperton Avenue to Mountain Avenue. The walkers sloshed down to Craig Avenue where they noted a beautiful Italian Victorian, built in 1883 and originally owned by Hugh Craig, Piedmont’s first mayor. Originally on Highland Avenue (then Vernal), the house was put on log rollers and pulled by horses to its current location, 55 Craig Avenue. The walkers went up Craig and found the somewhat secret back driveway to the Community Church. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: At its most recent meeting, Piedmont City Council heard from Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun about the City’s plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont. Recently hired to the role, Deniz Ergun has been tasked with helping the City meet ambitious climate goals. During their July 17, 2023 meeting, the City Council approved amendments to their Climate Action Plan 2.0, vowing to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 50% by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality no later than 2045. During her presentation on Monday, February 5, Ergun identified three main items she recommended the City prioritize in 2024 and early 2025 to help meet this goal –developing a building electrification strategy, promoting the adoption of electric vehicles (EV), and increasing community engagement. On developing a building electrification strategy, Ergun suggested a task force to “establish a pathway for the equitable transition of Piedmont’s existing homes and businesses to carbon net zero emissions.” She also explained the importance of this component, as residential buildings accounted for almost half of the greenhouse gas emissions in the City. “The other half are from transportation,” she continued. articles.text: The Beach school community took full advantage of a break in the rain on Saturday, February 3, to celebrate the Year of the Dragon. Over 120 people attended the Lunar New Year event organized by the Beach Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging committee at Beach School. Guests feasted on traditional new year dishes, including long noodles, japchae, turnip cake, and sticky buns. Beach parent Janet Cheng showed kids how to make norigae, a decorative Korean pendant hung from a hanbok, and Susan Chenshu led kids in a Chinese paper cutting activity. Betty Rojas also used play-doh to teach kids how to make mooncakes. articles.text: Editor: The common Piedmont refrain is that people come for the schools but stay for the city. For more than 15 years as a Piedmont volunteer, as a commissioner, city council member and as mayor, scores of folks shared with me their impressions of living here: the well maintained parks, the safe and well-lighted sidewalks, and the immediate police and fire response time. Through the years I always enjoyed hearing Piedmonters’ praise for city services. But it was all hearsay until my 87-year old father fell and I couldn’t get him up. Before I hung up the phone with the 911 dispatcher, I could hear the fire department sirens coming down Oakland Avenue. For my elderly father, Piedmont’s response time was critical. The rapid response time is almost unheard of in any other city in Alameda County.. How is our response time excellent while neighboring jurisdictions struggle? articles.text: Editor: As long-time residents of Piedmont we support Measure F. For forty plus years we, the citizens, have supported the parcel tax as a way of providing enhanced city service for police, fire, recreation and public works. Although we all can complain about something, Piedmont’s services are better than any of the surrounding communities largely because we tax ourselves for good city services. Measure F is a continuation of the city services parcel tax that keeps our community safe, our parks usable and recreation programs serving all ages. –Linnea Graff and former school board member Grier Graff REVIEWERS

articles.text: Measure F and the Overall Tax Burden in Piedmont The following letter was sent on January 30 to Piedmont City Council. Editor: The Piedmont league of Women Voters is writing to express concern about Measure F specifically, and more broadly about the piecemeal process for asking Piedmont voters to approve bond measures and special taxes. Our concerns are two-fold. First, while we understand that the City seeks predictable revenue, Measure F’s twelve-year term removes an important means of accountability to voters: the need to seek approval of a special tax on a regular basis. Second, we fear that due to the lack of truly comprehensive long-range planning by the City, Measure F will not be the end of additional special taxes or bond measures through 2037. mont’s taxpayers are currently subject to a sewer tax, a school bond and taxes, a parcel tax, a pool bond, and – in some areas – a utilities undergrounding bond. When the Council approved Measure F for the March 2024 ballot, the Council commented that the $245,000 per year equipment budget in Measure F would not cover all costs for improved City services. The Council even suggested that it might return to voters as soon as November 2024 to request an additional increase in the parcel tax. For many years, it has been known that costly seismic retrofitting is needed for Piedmont’s public safety buildings. The Council has recently contemplated, as part of the housing element, options that could include making improvements to the corporation yard, relocating a sports field, and offering City-funded incentives to developers. These possibilities were not included in the City’s 10-year General Fund financial projections on which the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee based its Measure F recommendation. The league believes that all of the growing needs for City services must be considered as a part of the City’s long-range planning.

articles.text: Editor: Up for discussion at next week’s Planning Commission meeting is the Conditional Use Permit application by Shell Recharge to demolish the old Shell station at 29 Wildwood Avenue and replace it with an Electric Vehicle charging hub. I support the city’s stated goals and commitment regarding EVs and EV infrastructure, and would like to welcome Shell to the neighborhood. However, I firmly oppose their application to establish an unprecedented 24/7 operation at this location. Since the implementation of the CUP process in Piedmont in 1990, no CUP applicant doing business along the Grand Avenue corridor has ever applied for permission to operate before 6 am or after 10 pm. I would venture to say that in the 100 plus years of Piedmont’s incorporation, no business located along this corridor has ever legally done so. The Piedmont Design and Review Guidelines describe the Grand Avenue Commercial District as “fundamentally defined by the surrounding residential buildings and the residential form of Piedmont itself.” The proposed site shares a property line with two private residences. There are four more residences across the street on Wildwood. Many more homes on Wildwood, Fairview, Grand and Olive are within eyesight and/or earshot of the property. These residents are entitled to enjoy the same peace and quiet in the overnight hours that every other Piedmont resident appreciates. To suggest otherwise insults one’s intelligence. In previous Piedmont Post articles announcing the planned charging hub, Jeremy Randolph, Shell Recharge Program Manager, has stated both Shell’s commitment to being a good neighbor and their intention to operate 24/7. These goals are incompatible. A visit to the area in the overnight hours will make it clear to anyone what an unwelcome intrusion 24/7 would be. Hopefully, the Planning Commission and Shell Recharge will make the smart choice and create a win/ win/win situation, compatible with both the city’s and Shell’s goals and with the “residential form of Piedmont itself.” –Don Dare Wildwood Avemue HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY
articles.title: Shell Recharge 24/7

articles.text: Editor: I am reaching out to convey my concerns regarding the potential consequences of a teachers’ strike, which may inadvertently hinder their pursuit of higher pay rather than support it. While I empathize with teachers advocating for fair compensation, it is crucial to examine the wider repercussions a strike could have on parental support, enrollment, and the overall financial health of our schools. Various factors have been identified as contributors to the current financial challenges our schools are grappling with, such as state funding, community contributions, and enrollment levels. Regrettably, a strike would not tackle the problem of insufficient state funding and could potentially worsen the situation by reducing revenue from both enrollment and community support. The increasing shift of parents moving their children to private schools in our community is evident. It’s also noteworthy that a significant number of parents have openly expressed their consideration of making this transition. I’m concerned a strike could push more parents in that direction, which would lead to significant consequences for vital funding. This would impact enrollment, and we must acknowledge that, whether we prefer it or not, the most substantial donations to our schools often come from individuals who can afford private education. In conclusion, all stakeholders must engage in open dialogue to find alternative solutions that prioritize fair compensation for teachers while also ensuring the financial stability of our schools. A collaborative approach will better serve the interests of our educators, and, most importantly, our students. – Concerned Elementary and Middle School Parent from left to right.
articles.title: Consequences of a teachers’ strike

pages.text: Wednesday, February 7, 2024 3 Clarifying teachers’ union position on impasse By Dr. Elise Marks Editor: I wanted to respond to last week’s letter to the editor that stated that “It appears APT has no interest in negotiating, and perhaps at the direction of CTA is marching towards a strike arm-in-arm with other Coalition members, regardless of any offer from PUSD.” I think it’s important that the public understand the actual nature and function of the East Bay Coalition. The letter said that joining the Coalition means Piedmont educators are “[l]etting outsiders drive APT’s agenda.” In fact, the Coalition arose organically from many years of conversations among East Bay educators, including Piedmont teachers, about the difficulty of surviving here on a typical teacher’s salary, and about how the current teacher shortage is driving schools to a crisis point. All local schools are struggling to attract good teachers as the current generation of veterans retires in increasingly large numbers, while the teacher credentialing programs that should be training a new generation have distressingly (but understandably) low enrollments. Low teacher pay is a systemic problem, and the East Bay Coalition rose out of the desire for a systemic solution. Everyone in the coalition is an actual working educator in the East Bay. Each union that joined the coalition did so freely, in the hope that standing together we’d have a better chance of making positive change. Piedmont educators voted overwhelmingly to join the coalition each year. Common bargaining standards each year were built by group consensus. We recognize meeting the standards is harder for some districts since funding structures differ. But we’ve also watched Piedmont slip lower in comparison to other local districts in compensation over the past few years. Last year’s 7.5% increase was among the lowest in the Coalition, and unlike several other local districts, we received no increase in district contributions to health care premiums. For this year, given inflation and a dramatic spike in Kaiser costs, an 8.22% salary increase is actually the minimum needed to avoid an effective compensation cut. That’s why we stood firm by the Coalition bargaining standards to the point of going to impasse. And we’ve watched as many surrounding districts have indeed settled their contracts at or above the 8.22% COLA. Others have gone to impasse with offers much higher than PUSD’s current offer. Now that we’re in mediation, we’re no longer obligated to hold to the Coalition standards, much as we believe they are good ones. We are absolutely–and always have been–bargaining in good faith to reach a fair and reasonable agreement that allows Piedmont educators to afford to stay here and ensure our students get the superb educations they deserve. –Elise Marks is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers Consequences of a teachers’ strike Editor: I am reaching out to convey my concerns regarding the potential consequences of a teachers’ strike, which may inadvertently hinder their pursuit of higher pay rather than support it. There are four more residences across the street on Wildwood. Many more homes on Wildwood, Fairview, Grand and Olive are within eyesight and/or earshot of the property. These residents are entitled to enjoy the same peace and quiet in the overnight hours that every other Piedmont resident appreciates. To suggest otherwise insults one’s intelligence. In previous Piedmont Post articles announcing the planned charging hub, Jeremy Randolph, Shell Recharge Program Manager, has stated both Shell’s commitment to being a good neighbor and their intention to operate 24/7. These goals are incompatible. A visit to the area in the overnight hours will make it clear to anyone what an unwelcome intrusion 24/7 would be. Hopefully, the Planning Commission and Shell Recharge will make the smart choice and create a win/ win/win situation, compatible with both the city’s and Shell’s goals and with the “residential form of Piedmont itself.” –Don Dare Wildwood Avemue ATLAS HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY Old Fashioned Service and High-Quality Installations www.AtlasHeating.com 510-629-6021

articles.text: Barbara Lee (D), U.S. Representative for California’s 12th Congressional District (which encompasses Piedmont, Oakland, and most of Northern Alameda County) is running for the U.S. Senate seat formerly occupied by the late Senator Diane Feinstein. As a leading candidate, along with Adam Schiff (D), Katie Porter (D), and Steve Garvey (R), Lee’s run for senate has added fire to the already exciting race since she announced her candidacy in February 2023. Her candidacy has also raised questions about who will take Lee’s her long-held seat in the House of Representatives. “Senator Feinstein was a friend, a mentor, and a role model who, from being the first woman elected as mayor of San Francisco to being the first woman to represent California in the U.S. Senate, broke many glass ceilings for others behind her,” said Lee. “It’s time to keep breaking glass ceilings. I’m running to be California’s Senator, and only the fourth Black woman ever to serve in the Senate, because I am a consistent progressive who has never backed down to fight for working people – whether it’s affordable, accessible health care, climate justice or an economy that works for everyone.” Lee also called on the residents of Piedmont to go to the polls on election day. “I am committed to the unfinished work of advancing equality for all and would be honored to have the people of Piedmont’s support to be their representative U.S. Senate candidate Barbara Lee in the U.S. Senate,” said Lee. Lee was elected to Congress in 1998. Her bid for a seat in the Senate has raised questions of who her successor in the House of Representatives will be. Of nine candidates currently running in the primary election the frontrunner appears to be Lateefah Simon, a BART board of directors member, whose campaign donations measure more than seven times that of the next highest-fundraising candidate. The California Primary election will be on March 5, 2024. The last day to register for the primary election will be on February 20, 2024. The 12th congressional district’s general election will be on November 5, 2024. For more information on your local poll station, visit the California Secretary of State’s website at www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ polling-place. articles.text: The arrival of the Year of the Dragon will be celebrated by the Piedmont Asian American Club at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School this Friday, February 9 from 5:30-7:30 p.m. Around 80 student and adult volunteers from PAAC will host the Lunar New Year event highlighted by performances, crafts, a lion dance and dim sum. With the exception of calligraphy, all the craft and game tables will be new this year. Attendees will delight in making a dragon puppet, a lucky mandarin, paper fan and a spin drum. “Growing up in Asia, Lunar New Year is a festive and important holiday. It’s Thanksgiving and Christmas combined into one where everyone travels near and far to spend time with friends and family,” explained PAAC board member Della Chow, “I’m so grateful that we can bring a piece of this tradition to Piedmont.” Last year during the first year of the event, a capacity crowd of over 350 people enjoyed the hands on activities, food options and student performances. “The students’ performance will not only brings Lunar New Year’s joy and celebration to the community but also showcases their learning and understanding of Chinese culture and arts,” said PHS and PMS Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia. “Some have been studying for decades, while others are just getting started, but we dedicated one to two months of preparation for this performance.” The playhouse will be flooded with arts and crafts tables for active participation. This year, gourmet desserts, boba drinks and panang curry from local Piedmont businesses, including BakeSum, Tea on Piedmont and Salisa Skinner, will be available for purchase. This event is sold out, and at capacity. Unfortunately, walk-ups will not be admitted. Last year’s PAAC Lunar New Year celebration featured lion dancers at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse.
articles.title: PAAC Lunar New Year Celebration at Driscoll Playhouse on Friday

articles.text: As part of this year’s International Holocaust Remembrance Day on January 27, approximately 200 San Francisco East Bay Jewish community members came together to honor and remember victims of the Shoah and spread the urgent message: “Never Again Is Now”, linking the responsibility to never forget with the urgent need to remain vigilant against the current rising tide of antisemitism. With a generous sponsorship from Eileen Ruby, president of the Jewish Community Federation of the Bay Area, organizers from the Jewish Community of Piedmont, including Donna Friedman Meir, Nicki Gilbert, Sari Kaplan, Melanie Marcus, Lili Naveh, and Sharon Sagiv, developed a moving program with local Jewish community leaders, bringing a focus on Holocaust survivors, the atrocities of October 7 in Israel, and recent local antisemitic attacks. The event began at the gates of the Home of Eternity Jewish Cemetery in Oakland, where many survivors are laid to rest. Aliza Grayevsky Somekh, the visionary behind this event and owner of Israeli-owned catering company Bishulum San Francisco, opened the ceremony and Rabbi Mark Bloom of Temple Beth Abraham led the attendees in prayers. “International Holocaust Remembrance Day is our day not only to remember, it is our day to remind the whole world how fast things can go tragically wrong. It is time to act and bring our community together,” said Grayevsky Somekh. Participants shared stories with each other as they walked in a candlelight vigil along Piedmont Avenue to Pomella, an Israeli-owned and operated restaurant. “It is our privilege to provide respite and comfort to our community,” said Mica Talmor, chef and owner of Pomella, which has become an impromptu meeting place for Jewish community members since October 7, and has also endured antisemitic attacks and a loss of business. Rabbi Bloom, NCSY Youth Director Tani Polansky, and Beth Jacob Congregation Rabbi Gershon Albert of Oakland led a musical havdalah service, after which Holocaust survivors, Sanne DeWitt, 89, and Magda Silberman, 95, shared their experiences as young people during the Holocaust. At the age of four, Ms. DeWitt was smuggled from Germany to Holland, and then traveled by ferry to England, eventually ending up in the south of Wales. “Courage is in the DNA of the Jewish people,” she said. “Just as we rose after the Holocaust, we will rise again.” Ms. Silberman survived the Auschwitz and Ravensbrook concentration camps, work camps and munition factories in Germany. As a young and able person, she was forced to sort through the belongings of murdered Jews, and had access to shoes, clothes and food, which kept her alive through death marches, starvation and horrendous conditions. Ms. Silberman reminded attendees to “never give up hope, value family and good friends, and keep the story of the survivors alive. The second and third generation must continue the work of telling the stories of survivors.” Additional speakers included Yoav Harlev, the organizer of the group of volunteers who stand in daily vigil on the Highway 24 overpass in Lafayette with posters demanding the release of the hostages, and Dorit Dorenz, a victim of a recent antisemitic attack in nearby El Cerrito. “In unity there is strength,” said Dorenz as she courageously encouraged the crowd to work together to stand up against antisemitism. Harlev, who grew up on Kibbutz Kissufim along the border with Gaza and Israel, is connected to at least 105 of 136 hostages still in captivity. “I’m shattered and hurting inside. It is my calling to make sure that we don’t lose sight of these innocent hostages that are there, suffering every day,” he said. Event organizer Donna Friedman Meir reminded all those present that, “Never Again is Now. It means that in this moment we must stand together, we must show up for each other in whatever ways we can: support local Jewish and Israeli businesses, show up when advocacy is needed, be good neighbors, check in with one another, and educate the next generation.” The event ended on a note of hope with a heartfelt rendition of “One Day” by Matisyahu, and Israel’s national anthem, “Hatikvah” – literally “The Hope.”
articles.title: Piedmont Jewish families honor International Holocaust Remembrance Day

articles.text: Beer snobs rejoice; the craft-brewing event of the year is about to begin. SF Beer Week will kick off this weekend with its annual Opening Gala on Pier 35, Saturday, February 9 from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. Organizers expect more than 100 craft breweries, including local favorites like Russian River Brewing Co., to be on site. A ticket for $95 gives beer lovers access to unlimited tastings as well as exclusive and pre-release access to hundreds of new and special releases from indie craft brewers across the Bay. This will be the first year that the Opening Gala has made a return since COVID. SF Beer Week is a celebration of the Bay Area’s vibrant craft beer culture since 2009, Other Beer Week events will take place in the East Bay at Hop Grenade, Trumer, Cellarmaker, and Beer Baron. For a full list of events, visit sfbeerweek.org/activities. Tickets are available online at sfbeerweek.org. Tickets will not be sold at the door. SF Beer Week was founded in 2009 and now involves more than 100 independent breweries across the Bay Area.
articles.title: SF Beer Week Returns to SF and East Bay

articles.text: Girl Scouts in Troop 33943: Sai Ahuja, Elizabeth Ackerman, Zayda Weber, Emma Syhabout, Imogen Weber, Shaan Ahuja, Josie & Georgie. Not pictured: Sicheng Wu and Olivia Chan. On Saturday, January 27, Piedmont Middle School 7th grade Girl Scouts in Troop 33943 gathered to work on posters, donation bins and paint a donation stand for their 2024 Service Project, a Period Product Drive. “We are doing the drive to help people who have periods to have better access to period products for their physical and mental health. We are doing this drive to help eliminate period poverty,” explained Zayda Weber. Troop 33943 also partnered with Lola Biehn, president of the Flow Club at Piedmont High School, who also works to improve community access to sustainable period products. From February 1 to March 10 Girls Scouts in Troop 33943 will be collecting new, unopened packages of tampons. menstrual pads, period underwear, and menstrual cups. Please donate new, unopened period products into collection bins located at: • Mulberry’s Market • Donation Stand at the corner of Oakland and Grand Ave • Beach Elementary • Havens Elementary • Piedmont Middle School • Millennium High School • Piedmont High School Troop 33943 has partnered with Oakland Elizabeth House, a residence for women with children, and Alameda County Food Bank to distribute the donated products to the community. Dr. Amy Vallerie, a Troop Leader and the Regional Lead for Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology at Kaser Oakland noted, “Periods are the number one loss of productivity for school and work for women of a reproductive age. And adding stigma, embarrassment and inability to access appropriate menstrual products, in addition to pain, heavy menstrual cycles, sometimes period related migraines - Is just adding more and more barriers towards young women achieving their full potential.” “We do this drive because many people cannot afford period products,” explained Sicheng Wu. “This drive helps these people get their needs met, which improves their health. I’m proud to be part of it.”
articles.title: Girl Scouts launch donation drive for period products

articles.text: Piedmont School District has announced the nominations for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The previous winners are: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000) Lisa Lomenzo (2001) jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002) jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003) Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004) Cynthia Gorman (2005) Grier Graff (2006) Julia Burke (2007) Maude Pervere (2008) jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009) Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010) Andrea Swenson (2011) June Monach (2012) Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013) Ray Perman (2014) Jennifer Fox (2015) Katie Korotzer (2016) Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018) Cathy Glazier (2019) Sue Smegal (2020) Ken Li (2021) Eileen Ruby (2022) David Ragones in 2023 Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and at Oakland’s McClymonds High School. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was an early supporter of Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by School Board member Dewey Watson in Hecht’s memory. The deadline for nominations is March 15. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 8, Board of Education meeting. Nomination forms are available in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue, or online at https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J92iTb6870oZbIRotoHW8rM3MUmCS8bORuf- 7c1hcCmY/edit?pli=1.
articles.title: Nomination period open for annual Art Hecht Award

articles.text: Love is in the air – it’s February. It’s easy to think that the opportunity for creativity around Valentine’s Day is in crafting cards, making homemade Valentines cookies or planning the ultimate date night. But, what if the actual act of creativity for Valentine’s Day is the process of creating relationships themselves? Building a relationship of any kind–marriage, significant other, friendship, parent/child–is a creative process because it requires constant growth, curiosity and openness to possibility to continuously nourish and deepen the connection between people. When you meet someone new, you have to be open to getting to know them, you have to take a risk to put yourself out there to possibly be rejected and you have to get deeply curious about the other person. Openness, risk-taking and curiosity are three core traits of creativity. Fun fact: A recent study from Northwestern University found that people who have a creative mindset find their life partners more desirable and attractive longer than those who do not regularly practice creativity. Huh? How does creativity connect to finding your hubby or wife attractive? Well, creative people are willing to play with each other, try new things and reinvent to keep things new and fresh. And let’s face it, if you are in a marriage and you have children, it is easy to get stuck in a romantic rut. So a willingness to get creative helps avoid just being in the same routine day in and day out. We don’t often give ourselves credit for the creativity it requires to get to know a new person and then to maintain intimacy through a whole series of different types of challenges. Even in friendships we are in constant problem-solving mode, which is a form of creativity. We have busy lives and we need to figure out how to find time to hang out or we might not have the same hobbies or interests and have to find common ground. For this Valentine’s Day, take a moment to notice how you have brought creativity to the relationships that means the most to you: • Have you expressed appreciation in a fun or novel way? • Have you created intimacy through vulnerability and revealing your emotions? • Have you found opportunities for play and laughter? • Have you made plans that bring people together to form meaningful connections? • Have you overcome obstacles and deepened bonds? Why not celebrate love and creativity all at once pm February 14 and long after? Nina Meehan speaks and coaching on creativity, communication and connection. https:// gocreate.zone/
articles.title: Love is the ultimate creative act

On Saturday, January 27, Piedmont Middle School 7th grade Girl Scouts in Troop 33943 gathered to work on posters, donation bins and paint a donation stand for their 2024 Service Project, a Period Product Drive. “We are doing the drive to help people who have periods to have better access to period products for their physical and mental health. We are doing this drive to help eliminate period poverty,” explained Zayda Weber. Troop 33943 also partnered with Lola Biehn, president of the Flow Club at Piedmont High School, who also works to improve community access to sustainable period products. And adding stigma, embarrassment and inability to access appropriate menstrual products, in addition to pain, heavy menstrual cycles, sometimes period related migraines - Is just adding more and more barriers towards young women achieving their full potential.” “We do this drive because many people cannot afford period products,” explained Sicheng Wu. “This drive helps these people get their needs met, which improves their health. I’m proud to be part of it.” Thinking Outside the Classroom Love is the ultimate creative act By Nina Meehan Love is in the air – it’s February. It’s easy to think that the opportunity for creativity around Valentine’s Day is in crafting cards, making homemade Valentines cookies or planning the ultimate date night. But, what if the actual act of creativity for Valentine’s Day is the process of creating relationships themselves? Building a relationship of any kind–marriage, significant other, friendship, parent/child–is a creative process because it requires constant growth, curiosity and openness to possibility to continuously nourish and deepen the connection between people. When you meet someone new, you have to be open to getting to know them, you have to take a risk to put yourself out there to possibly be rejected and you have to get deeply curious about the other person. Openness, risk-taking and curiosity are three core traits of creativity. Fun fact: A recent study from Northwestern University found that people who have a creative mindset find their life partners more desirable and attractive longer than those who do not regularly practice creativity. Huh? How does creativity connect to finding your hubby or wife attractive? Well, creative people are willing to play with each other, try new things and reinvent to keep things new and fresh. And let’s face it, if you are in a marriage and you have children, it is easy to get stuck in a romantic rut. So a willingness to get creative helps avoid just being in the same routine day in and day out. We don’t often give ourselves credit for the creativity it requires to get to know a new person and then to maintain intimacy through a whole series of different types of challenges. Even in friendships we are in constant problem-solving mode, which is a form of creativity. We have busy lives and we need to figure out how to find time to hang out or we might not have the same hobbies or interests and have to find common ground. For this Valentine’s Day, take a moment to notice how you have brought creativity to the relationships that means the most to you: • Have you expressed appreciation in a fun or novel way? • Have you created intimacy through vulnerability and revealing your emotions? • Have you found opportunities for play and laughter? • Have you made plans that bring people together to form meaningful connections? • Have you overcome obstacles and deepened bonds? Why not celebrate love and creativity all at once pm February 14 and long after? articles.text: Last autumn, I traveled to Maui with my family. It was my first time in Hawaii, and I was more than excited to experience the beauty of the island. I had one goal in mind: to enjoy their traditional shaved ice. Due to the fires, we stayed on the South side of the island. However, on October 8th, the West side was ‘reopened’. Eager to see the other side of the island we climbed into our rental car and We were struck with horror when we saw the ruins. Blackened trees dotted the parched landscape, and buildings stood half supported. Destruction was everywhere, whispered in the air, through the time that seemed to stand still, in the sickening feeling of sadness that touched all of us. Disheartened, we headed back to our condo. As we traveled through the mountains, we spotted a shaved ice sign, and, with the motivation of treating ourselves to the iconic Hawaiian dessert, we pulled into Lorraine Shaved ice, where we were greeted by a kind and welcoming couple. Like many small, owner-run businesses on Maui, Lorraine Shave Ice in Kahakuloa has suffered due to the lack of tourists who avoided visiting the island as an effect of the deadly fires. Also like many small, owner-run businesses on Maui they all care deeply about the island and the people who come to experience the beauty. To see the destruction and negative impact on these humble businesses is truly heart wrenching. There has been a lot of controversy surrounding the reopening, with people arguing that the island needs time to heal, others claiming that tourism could be beneficial to the island as one of its main revenue streams. I’m not going to say if one party is wrong, but I will say what needs to be said: Maui needs to heal. While one side argues that Maui needs the isolation to repair and rejuvenate, the other believes that tourism will aid them, especially in the economical sense. However, the strain that the fire has pushed upon the island and its inhabitants is a pain no one person can imagine. So much rich history and culture, destroyed. As the new year dawns on us, we focus on healing and improving ourselves for the coming year. With the giving spirit and hope for renewal, the new year is that perfect time to help this beautiful island to revive itself. Daisy Seymour is an eighth grader at Piedmont Middle School. Lorraine Shaved Ice, a family-owned business in the mountains of Hawaii was heavily impacted by the loss of tourists after the devastating fires on Maui in August 2023.
articles.title: The Healing of West Maui

articles.text: The 55th Annual Leonard Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will officially use the artwork of PHS senior Kira Pan as the poster for the event. The famed competition, founded by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, will use the theme “A Rose By Any Other Name Would Sound As Sweet,” which coordinates with the artwork. Pan’s poster will be used in all publicity for the event including the cover for the program. For her effort, Pan will receive a large framed copy of the poster, two tickets to the show and a $200 prize. “I’ve always loved the annual Bird Calling Contest at Piedmont and am excited to contribute to the tradition,” said Pan. PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson will serve as Chair of the Bird Calling Contest Committee, her final year at the school. “In the early days of the Bird Calling Contest, our posters were commissioned from professional artists. In more modern times, we have turned to the amazing talent of our Piedmont High School artists,” stated Levenson. Pan served as the graphics editor of The Piedmont Highlander (TPH) last year, where she honed skills as a digital artist. She is currently the co-editor-in-chief of TPH and continues to contribute art for the school publication. “My inspiration for the piece was the bluebird because I love their bright colors and how they’re believed to symbolize good luck. Working in TPH has taught me how to integrate design elements cohesively, so I decided to incorporate the rose theme into the microphone drawing and have the bluebirds hold up the banner,” explained Pan. The theme “A Rose By Any Other Name Would Sound As Sweet” is taken from William Shakespeare’s play Romeo and Juliet. The bird calling acts are composed of groups of students performing for local celebrity judges. Acts are scored on authenticity of call, information about the bird provided by the students, poise of delivery, creativity and artistry. For decades, the winning Piedmont bird callers would appear and perform on the Johnny Carson Show and later on the David Letterman Show. The Bird Calling Contest will take place on Friday, March 29, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School. Tickets, which go on sale on March 1, are $25 for general admission and $15 for students. PHS senior Kira Pan’s winning poster design. ®

articles.text: Seven fifth graders – Nicholas Phung Theodore Gottscalk, Nicholas Phung, Maxwell Howng, Brendan Edesses, Andrew Lee, Madison Kao, and Julian Huang – made a presentation about the Lunar New Year at Wildwood Elementary School. Theodore and his mom, Stefanie Wong, have been doing this presentation since he was in kindergarten. This year, he switched it up and invited his friends to present with him. He does this presentation every year to spread awareness and acceptance of the Chinese culture. Stefanie started presenting when Theo was six. This was because she experienced racism when she moved to a new school in Canada where she and her sister were the only Asian kids in the school. As a result, Stefanie wanted to teach children about her culture and ethnicity. She does this Theo Gottschalk teaches his classmates how to say “Happy New Year” in Chinese. Photos by Carolyn Pan Madison Fishman has a question for her classmate Maxwell Howng as Nikias Moulatsios, Ms. Tang, Max Centeno, and James Wilson look on. at Lunar New Year and Mid Autumn Festival presentations at Wildwood. In Nicholas’s part of the presentation, he talked about why the first day of the Lunar New Year moves around in the Chinese calendar. Then Maxwell informed the crowd about some traditions for Lunar New Year. After that, Brendan told the class how certain foods can have different meanings. Finally, Madison described some taboos that are important during the Lunar New Year. Following that Theo taught his peers some things to say in Mandarin like “ni hao”. And finally they ended the presentation with Julian naming what animals in the coming years will be. Now in their last year at Wildwood School, they hope that another family or group will continue this tradition every year in the coming years. In this game, participants try to guess which object will appear on the dice. In Vietnamese culture, kids are taught to be generous if they win and gracious if they lose, as well as to give to others during Tết what they hope to receive in the new year. This year’s celebration also brought a wishing tree and raffle. Participants wrote down their wishes for the new year and hung them on the Wishing Tree, which is a traditional part of many Lunar New Year celebrations. Raffle winners Dalia Doebelin, Roland Lee, James Chew, and Kian got to take home large lucky red envelopes filled with surprises from Taiwan, dragon stuffies, and balloons. Siblings Tina and Dominic Campanile’s names were also each drawn, which bodes well for a lucky new year ahead! articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s entire sixth grade braved the rain on Monday, January 22, to go on a field trip to the Academy of Sciences in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. The trip was a joint effort between the Core teachers and the Science teachers, which aimed to provide an experiential aspect to concepts learned in both Social Studies and Science this school year. The group of approximately 180 students, 50 parent volunteers, and seven teachers visited seven “stations” with various learning goals. The African Hall’s special exhibit, the Human Odyssey, took students through the evolution of early humans, reinforcing the very first unit of study from their social studies class last August. Students noted the special structures of cnidarians such as jellyfish and anemones in the aquarium. Echinoderms such as sea cucumbers and urchins, Mollusks such as scallops and octopus, and Arthropods such as crab and shrimp as well as all of these animals’ interactions with one another in their environment. In a reptile hunt that took students all over the museum from the aquarium to the swamp to the rainforest, the focus was on the various adaptations the reptiles have to live in a variety of environments. There were two special exhibits on display, Hidden Wonders and Color of Life. In Hidden Wonders, there were collections of various animals, plants and fossils from around the world. Students investigate the content of an aquarium during the “Marine Invertebrate Seek and Find.” Andrew Meyer, Holden Fasteau, Kenji Holt, and Jane Saunders explore the interactive map that shows early human migration patterns and their connection with climate change. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, February 7, 2024 Piedmont 6th graders explore Academy of Sciences By Anjuna Lohnes Piedmont Middle School’s entire sixth grade braved the rain on Monday, January 22, to go on a field trip to the Academy of Sciences in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. The trip was a joint effort between the Core teachers and the Science teachers, which aimed to provide an experiential aspect to concepts learned in both Social Studies and Science this school year. The group of approximately 180 students, 50 parent volunteers, and seven teachers visited seven “stations” with various learning goals. The African Hall’s special exhibit, the Human Odyssey, took students through the evolution of early humans, reinforcing the very first unit of study from their social studies class last August. Students noted the special structures of cnidarians such as jellyfish and anemones in the aquarium. Echinoderms such as sea cucumbers and urchins, Mollusks such as scallops and octopus, and Arthropods such as crab and shrimp as well as all of these animals’ interactions with one another in their environment. In a reptile hunt that took students all over the museum from the aquarium to the swamp to the rainforest, the focus was on the various adaptations the reptiles have to live in a variety of environments. There were two special exhibits on display, Hidden Wonders and Color of Life. In Hidden Wonders, there were collections of various animals, plants and fossils from around the world.
