articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team is rolling as its regular season nears its end. They defeated Alameda 4-0 on Tuesday, January 30 at Chabot College, and shut out Encinal 4-0 two days later at Estuary Park in Alameda. The results extended the Highlanders’ winning streak to four matches, all by shutout victories with 12 goals during the current stretch. It keeps them in contention for the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill division title. Piedmont carries a 10-1-3 overall record (W-T-L) and has 13 points toward the Foothill Division standings with a 4-1-3 league record. With two matches left in the regular season, the Foothill Division is only separated by a couple of points with Castro Valley in first with 15 points, and Piedmont in a 30way tied for second place with Berkeley and Bishop O’Dowd with 13 points. PHS and O’Dowd played a critical match on Tuesday, February 6, but results were not complete by Post time. The Highlanders finish its season at Berkeley on Friday, February 9. 4-0 over Encinal Piedmont’s win over Encinal avenged a 2-1 loss to the Jets on January 16. The Highlanders laid on the pressure in Thursday’s meeting with several early shots. Miranda Liu broke through on a left-footed shot in the first half on an assist by Elsa Wallway. In the buildup, Juliana Thornborrow dribbled through the attacking third until sending a pass to Wallway, who flicked on a pass through the back line on her first touch to Liu. The second goal was scored by Thornborrow, who took a few touches into the box before unloading a right-footed shot to the top-right bin—making it 2-0 going into halftime. Wallway scored in the early minutes of the second half after receiving a pass from Lola Beihn. She unloaded a shot from the left side through the area, sending a Photos by Todd Marshburn Elsa Wallway scored twice against Alameda and had a goal and assist versus Encinal. Miranda Liu had two goals against Encinal and scored once against Alameda. Juliana Thornborrow had a goal and assist against Alameda and another assist in the win vs. Encinal. deflection off an Encinal defender into net. Piedmont’s last goal was scored by Beihn in the late minutes, when she launched a shot from nearly 30 yards past the keeper who was far off her line. 4-0 over Alameda Piedmont came out hot with a goal in the first 10 minutes when Thornborrow played a long through pass to Liu charging through the defense. In a 1-on-1 situation, Liu scored on a rightfooted shot past the keeper. Wallway scored next on a free kick from the far left side about 10 yards outside the area, lobbing a shot to the far post over the keeper and into net. Wallway made it 3-nil in the second half, this time from a shot around the top-right of the penalty box, bending a shot to the far post. Liu scored the fourth on a longshot seven yards above the penalty area, curling a rightfooted shot perfectly placed above the keeper. Tuesday vs. Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont hosted Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 6. See next week’s Post for match details. articles.title: Piedmont on 4-game winning streak after pair of 4-0 wins

articles.text: The Highlanders wrapped up a productive week with two wins to create a three-game winning streak. They defeated St. Joseph in Alameda 67-55 on Monday, February 5 and dominated Alameda 58-39 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Wednesday, January 31. PHS now holds a 15-9 record going into its final two games of the season. “We try to go one game at a time, but I knew St. Joe would be one of our toughest games. It was our third game against them and when you play anyone that many times, it’s going to be tough,” said coach Ben Spencer. “They were playing for their playoff lives.” Piedmont will travel to San Leandro tonight, February 7, and host Castro Valley two days later, when the team will honor its six seniors on the roster: Brit Burden, Arjun Bornstein, Finn Burke, Thorin Holmes, Declan Linnane, and transfer student Scott Cooley. With two wins, PHS could set itself up nicely for a high seeding in the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs. “Right now, we can more consistent with our energy levels on the defensive end. We just need to lock in defensively, trusting each other, and play for each other,” said Burden. “We have to get ready for NCS, and these games are preparing us for that. It’s good to get some wins and get on a roll going into NCS,” said junior guard Ravi Silverberg. Burden had a strong 23-point performance in Monday’s win over St. Joseph, building stronger into the second half as he adjusted against the Pilots’ tall forward Gabriel Enyinwa. “Gabe’s a great player. I’ve been matching up against him since freshman year and it’s always fun to go against him. Those type of players just push me and make me better,” said Burden. Against the Hornets, everything was falling into place for Silverberg, who led scoring with 18 points. “The drive was there the whole game, so I just kept attacking. I didn’t feel like anyone could guard me, so I just kept attacking. I got to the rim a lot and the points added up,” said Silverberg. 67-55 over St. Joseph Piedmont led 14-13 by the end of the first quarter and 27-25 at halftime. With a big 22-point third quarter, Piedmont created some breathing room at 49-37, and added 18 more points in the final going. There were four lead changes in the third quarter until Dillon Casey put PHS up 33-31 after drawing a foul on a layup. It was the start of an 11-0 scoring run to put the Highlanders ahead 41-31. The Pilots battled in the fourth to narrow the deficit to one possession at 53-51, but from there Piedmont scored 12 unanswered points to jump ahead 65-51 in the late minutes. Final stats: Burden had 23 points, Linnane had 13 points, Casey scored 11, Silverberg had 10, Bornstein scored six, while PJ Brayer and Thorin Holmes has two. Staff Photos Brit Burden carved up St. Joseph with 23 points, and also had 14 against Alameda. Declan Linnane (33) knocks down a 3-pointer against St. Joseph.

articles.text: When mentioning the athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can be easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers in college. In this week’s issue, we take a look at Ana Romanczuk of track and field, Kai Johnson of basketball, and Gavin Horne of track and field. Photo courtesy of Chapman Athletics Ana Romanczuk, PHS Class of 2022, is a sophomore on Chapman University’s track and field team. Photo courtesy of Morgan State Athletics Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, is a junior on Morgan State’s basketball team. In 2022-23, Johnson appeared in 29 games at Weber State and totaled 18 rebounds, seven assists, seven steals, and two blocked shots. As a freshman, she played in 26 games and had 19 points, 14 steals, 16 rebounds, three assists, and one block. For Piedmont, she was a team captain her final two years. She was a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball team, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2018, 20-11 in 2019, 21-7 in 2020, and 15-3 in 2021’s shortened pandemic season. Chapman, Track Ana Romanczuk, PHS Class of 2022, is a sophomore on Chapman University’s track and field team and getting ready for the start of her season. At Chapman, Romanczuk competes in the shot put, discus throw, and hammer toss. Last year, she competed in all three events at the 2023 SCIAC Track and Field Championship in April. At the championship meet, Romanczuk was 14th of 21 in the hammer toss with a distance of 31.67 meters, was 21st of 27 in the discus with a distance of 26.40 meters, and was 32nd in the shot put with 6.32 meters. Romancuzk primarily competed in shot, discus, and pole vault in high school. She reached the NCS Bayshore Championship in the discus, where she was 19th with a distance of 66 feet, 3 inches. Photo courtesy of Pitzer Athletics Gavin Horne, PHS Class of 2021, is entering his junior season on PomonaPitzer’s track and field team. Morgan State. Basketball Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, was a four-year starter at Piedmont High and was named our Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a senior. She’s currently a junior at Morgan State after transferring from Weber State following her sophomore year. So far this season, Johnson has appeared in 18 games and started once, playing in 80 minutes for 13 total points, six rebounds, and two steals. The Bears are currently 7-15. Pomona-Pitzer, Track Gavin Horne, PHS Class of 2021, is a junior on Pomona’s track and field team, competing primarily in their jumping events. He’s getting ready for the start of their spring season. He reached the SCIAC Track and Field Championships on April 29-30, where he competed in the long jump and triple jump. In the long jump, Horne was 15th of 24 with a height of 5.78 meters. As for the triple jump, Gavin finished 14th of 17 with a distance of 11.34 meters. His long jump at the SCIAC Championship marked a personal record for him, while he also reached a distance of 11.42 meters in the triple jump at the PLNU Invitational on March 25.

articles.text: Piedmont Fencing Team is halfway through its season and quickly approaching the prestigious Junior Olympics in Charlotte, North Carolina on February 16-19. Piedmont High juniors Teresa McKay and Oliver Greenebaum have already qualified for the tournament, and former Piedmont resident Sophie Choi is also hitting high levels for the club which trains at the community church. “Teresa, Oliver and Sophie all qualified for Junior Olympics and also qualified for Nationals in the summer. We’re about mid-way through our schedule and we’re doing really well,” said veteran coach David Sinkkonen. Since the Post covered the Piedmont Fencing Team in July last year following the National Championship in Phoenix, several of the club’s top fencers have progressed tremendously. McKay has earned two Bronze medals for third place finishes thus far, improving her win ratio in overall matches from 19 percent last year to 42 percent currently. “Teresa has been putting up great numbers. In fencing, you lose more than you win. It’s kind of like the baseball batting average, so for her to have that high of a percentage says a lot. She’s awesome,” said Sinkkonen. McKay has 34 wins so far this season. She finished third at the Air Force ROC in Colorado Springs on October 1 in the Division 2 women’s foil ladder and was third of 11 at the Wasatch Fencing RYC/ RJCC on September 23 in Utah in the junior women’s ladder. She recently competed in the women’s Division 1-A at the Battle of the Bay in San Jose. She will compete in the junior and cadet women’s categories at the Junior Olympics. Sophie Kim (left) and Teresa McKay will be representing Piedmont Fencing Team at the Junior Olympics. Oliver Greenebaum (left), a junior at Piedmont High School, has qualified for the Junior Olympics. “Teresa has had an excellent season and has increased her rating to E and D all in one weekend [at the Air Force ROC]. She was able to qualify for Junior Olympics, which is awesome. There are college recruiters looking at her,” said Sinkkonen on Teresa’s development. Greenebaum has also earned two Bronze medals in 2023/2024, putting together a win ratio of 36.3 percent with 41 wins. His ratio has improved by seven percent over the last year. On January 1, he competed in the Hangover Open in Denver, where he increased his rating. “He’s doing pretty darn well. He had a tournament in Denver and earned his D rating and also qualified for Junior Olympics,” said Sinkkonen.
articles.title: Piedmont Fencing Team approaching Junior Olympics

articles.text: Yosemite National Park’s annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls is starting this week and stretching through the end of the month. The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracting light shining off of Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 through the end of the month, requiring clear skies around sunset and assuming sufficient water is flowing from Horsetail Falls. In order to manage the popularity of the Firefall, Yosemite National Park is enforcing reservations to enter February at www.Recreation.gov. A current weather forecast shows a clear week of mostly sunny skies coming within the next week from February 10 through February 18. February 20-22 has some forecasted snow in the area, while the following week from February 23-29 is forecasted for mostly cloudy skies. articles.text: On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. United States, 1984) — a contemporary envisioning of a Chinese mother goddess, rendered in a dangling complex of ceramic forms — mingle interrogations of utopian ideals, the experience of migration, and what it means to be a woman protagonist. Fresh approaches to well-established genres also boldly defy expectations. What appears to be a traditional Chinese landscape painting by Wu Chi-Tsung (b. Taiwan, 1981) is in fact formed from sculptural layers of crumpled photosensitive paper, while an experimental film by TT Takemoto (b. United States, 1967) peers beneath the surface of documentary footage of Japanese American women factory workers to reveal an intimate social atmosphere. “At a moment of heightened turmoil domestically and around the globe, Into View feels so needed right now, entwining concepts like mythology, cosmology, political uprisings, social intimacy and ecology as viable alternatives to our current systems and empowering audiences to rethink possibilities in their own lives,” said Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art & Programs Naz Cuguoglu. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org. articles.text: Lee Mingwei: Rituals of Care, the Taiwanese American artist’s first survey exhibition in the U.S., will open at the de Young Museum in San Francisco on Saturday, February 17, to run through July 7. The show features seven projects made between 1995 and 2024 that place visitors at the center of interactive acts of generosity and care, asking how art can be a conduit for social connection and healing. Mingwei spent his formative years in San Francisco. Inspired by personal experiences of loss and resilience and major world events such as 9/11, the Iraq War and the COVID-19 pandemic, Mingwei (b. 1964) has, over the course of his career, created participatory mixed-media installations and performances that transform ordinary gestures like writing, sweeping, mending, or breathing into rituals of engagement and solace. The Letter Writing Project (1998–present) draws from the human need to communicate thoughts and feelings left unsaid, keenly felt by the artist after the death of his maternal grandmother. Consisting of three writing booths and an accessible writing station, the latter project invites visitors to write the letter they have always meant to send but never have, and to decide whether to address their letters and have the museum post them, or leave the letters unsealed for others to read. In The Mending Project (2009–present), Lee Mingwei transforms the simple act of sewing into an opportunity to connect. Visitors are invited to bring items of clothing that need mending to the installation, which consists of a table, two chairs, and a wall of colorful, cone-shaped spools of thread. Unlike a traditional tailor, who would try to hide repairs, Lee Mingwei’s mending and that of the volunteers activating the installation is done with the idea of celebrating the act. Hauntingly current in the context of world events, Guernica in Sand (2006–present) comments on the cyclical nature of creation and destruction. Created at the height of the Iraq War, Guernica in Sand draws on the Tibetan Buddhist mandala tradition to remake and unmake Pablo Picasso’s famous painting Guernica (1937). Halfway through the exhibition, the work is both completed and erased, simultaneously. From noon to sunset, Lee Mingwei invites audience members to enter the piece and walk across the sand as he works to finish the image. The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park) is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 seniors, $11 students, youth free) are available at famsf.org or at 888-901-6645.

articles.text: The 56th California International Antiquarian Book Fair is returning to San Francisco from Friday to Sunday, February 9 to 11, at Pier 27. The fair, held by the Antiquarian Booksellers’ Association of America, is widely recognized as one of the world’s largest exhibitions of antiquarian books for sale. More than 100 exhibitors from around the world will present rare books, maps, illustrations, historical documents and ephemera on a vast array of subjects. The fair encompass art, science, medicine, literature, history, gastronomy, fashion, first editions, Americana, philosophy, and children’s books. This year, the fair welcomes international exhibitors from the UK, Argentina, Australia, Austria, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany and The Netherlands. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, February 7, 2024 Arts & Entertainment Lee Mingwei’s “Guernica in Sand” (2006-present) will be one of the interactive installations on view at the artist’s first U.S. survey exhibition, running at the de Young from Saturday, February 17 through July 7. Lee Mingwei exhibit opens at de Young Feb. 17 By Selen Ozturk Lee Mingwei: Rituals of Care, the Taiwanese American artist’s first survey exhibition in the U.S., will open at the de Young Museum in San Francisco on Saturday, February 17, to run through July 7. The show features seven projects made between 1995 and 2024 that place visitors at the center of interactive acts of generosity and care, asking how art can be a conduit for social connection and healing. Mingwei spent his formative years in San Francisco. Inspired by personal experiences of loss and resilience and major world events such as 9/11, the Iraq War and the COVID-19 pandemic, Mingwei (b. 1964) has, over the course of his career, created participatory mixed-media installations and performances that transform ordinary gestures like writing, sweeping, mending, or breathing into rituals of engagement and solace. The Letter Writing Project (1998–present) draws from the human need to communicate thoughts and feelings left unsaid, keenly felt by the artist after the death of his maternal grandmother. Consisting of three writing booths and an accessible writing station, the latter project invites visitors to write the letter they have always meant to send but never have, and to decide whether to address their letters and have the museum post them, or leave the letters unsealed for others to read. In The Mending Project (2009–present), Lee Mingwei transforms the simple act of sewing into an opportunity to connect. Visitors are invited to bring items of clothing that need mending to the installation, which consists of a table, two chairs, and a wall of colorful, cone-shaped spools of thread. Unlike a traditional tailor, who would try to hide repairs, Lee Mingwei’s mending and that of the volunteers activating the installation is done with the idea of celebrating the act. Hauntingly current in the context of world events, Guernica in Sand (2006–present) comments on the cyclical nature of creation and destruction. Created at the height of the Iraq War, Guernica in Sand draws on the Tibetan Buddhist mandala tradition to remake and unmake Pablo Picasso’s famous painting Guernica (1937). Halfway through the exhibition, the work is both completed and erased, simultaneously. From noon to sunset, Lee Mingwei invites audience members to enter the piece and walk across the sand as he works to finish the image. The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park) is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 seniors, $11 students, youth free) are available at famsf.org or at 888-901-6645. Into View at Asian Art Museum By Selen Ozturk On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. United States, 1984) — a contemporary envisioning of a Chinese mother goddess, rendered in a dangling complex of ceramic forms — mingle interrogations of utopian ideals, the experience of migration, and what it means to be a woman protagonist. Fresh approaches to well-established genres also boldly defy expectations. What appears to be a traditional Chinese landscape painting by Wu Chi-Tsung (b. Taiwan, 1981) is in fact formed from sculptural layers of crumpled photosensitive paper, while an experimental film by TT Takemoto (b. United States, 1967) peers beneath the surface of documentary footage of Japanese American women factory workers to reveal an intimate social atmosphere. “At a moment of heightened turmoil domestically and around the globe, Into View feels so needed right now, entwining concepts like mythology, cosmology, political uprisings, social intimacy and ecology as viable alternatives to our current systems and empowering audiences to rethink possibilities in their own lives,” said Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art & Programs Naz Cuguoglu. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org. articles.text: Nora: A Doll’s House, Scottish playwright Stef Smith’s innovative take on Henrik Ibsen’s classic play, is being performed at City Lights Theatre in San Jose through Sunday, February 18. It’s 1918. And 1968. And 2018. Nora: A Doll’s House, Scottish playwright Stef Smith’s innovative take on the Ibsen classic, sets the action in three decades in a show being performed at City Lights Theatre in San Jose through Sunday, February 18. Nora plays the part in the play of the flawless wife and mother. But she has a secret that threatens to upend her seemingly perfect existence. Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen challenged social norms and outraged audiences when his work A Doll’s House debuted on-stage in 1879. Smith’s new iteration of the play looks back at the roles that women have played during the fight for female suffrage, the swinging sixties, and the modern day, and wonders how far we’ve really come. In an interview with The Standard (U.K.), Smith said she chose the years 1918, 1968 and 2018 because they represent important chapters in women’s history: the first time women were allowed to vote in Britain, legal acknowledgement of reproductive rights in Britain and the aftermath of the #MeToo movement. Three actresses alternate playing Nora and her closest friend, Christine, but Nora’s husband Thomas is always portrayed by the same man. “It’s like the men are in stasis, they find themselves trapped in time, whereas the women have to be more malleable and change with the times,” Smith said. Nora: A Doll’s House premiered in 2019 at Citizens Theatre in Glasgow, followed by an acclaimed production at the Young Vic Theatre in London. Raves have included “beautiful and explosively significant” (The Scotsman), “an explosive couple of hours” (The Herald) and “a radical, stunning reworking of the play” (British Theatre). Smith calls her work “predominantly political, seeking to unearth unheard stories.” Her other plays include Girl in the Machine, Enough, and Human Animals. Smith also writes for the screen, with credits including the BBC Scotland coming-of-age drama Float. Director Angie Higgins is making her City Lights directing debut but is a career veteran, having helmed shows at Limelight Theater, Utopia Theatre Project, Broadway West, Northside Theatre Company, Santa Clara Players and Silicon Valley Shakespeare, where she has been Artistic Director for the past 10 seasons. Tickets ($28-$67) for the play at City Lights Theater (529 S. Second St.) are available at cltc. org, or through the box office at 408-295-4200.
articles.title: A Doll’s House at City Lights Theatre through Feb. 18

articles.text: Cal Performances at UC Berkeley will present a special double-billed program of The Rite of Spring by choreographer Pina Bausch and a new companion piece, common ground[s] by Germaine Acogny and Malou Airaudo. The production will premiere on Friday, February 16 at 8 p.m., with performances on Saturday and Sunday, February 17-18. This will be the first-ever performance of Bausch’s Rite of Spring choreography in the Bay Area, a piece widely regarded as one of the most influential dance works of the 20th century. “This is the first time that [The Rite of Spring] is done not with an existing company, but with dancers who came together specifically for this piece,” explained Salomon Bausch, Pina Bausch’s son and the Executive Director of the Pina Bausch Foundation. The Rite of Spring will feature 30 dancers from 14 African countries, all assembled through a collaboration between Germany’s Pina Bausch Foundation, Senegal’s École des Sables, and the UK’s Sadler’s Wells Ballet Company. “I’m very excited to see the impact of their personalities and their diverse dance backgrounds on the piece but also vice versa; how the piece influences the dancers, both as artists and as human beings,” said Bausch. “I’ve always felt that this was an African dance,” said dancer Germaine Acogny, “The rituals are the same. And that music has an extraordinary pagan, terrestrial power. I even wonder whether Stravinsky was possessed when he composed it.” The Rite of Spring first premiered in 1913 in Paris, performed by the acclaimed Ballet Russes. In a controversial decision, a relatively-unknown Igor Stravinsky decided to base the composition and ballet on traditional Russian pagan rituals and folk dances, causing a near-riot on opening night. A moderated post-performance discussion will take place on Friday, February 16, and post-performance community conversations will be held on Saturday and Sunday, February 17 and 18. Tickets are $38–$86. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances.org, by phone at 642-9988, and in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m. Germaine Acogny (back) and Malou Airaudo pose for a promotional photo for their new companion piece, common ground[s].
articles.title: Pina Bausch’s The Rite of Spring comes to Zellerbach Hall

articles.text: For more than two decades, Kitka Women’s Vocal Ensemble’s annual Wintersongs concerts have explored songs from across Eastern Europe that summon the return of light and hope in times of difficulty and darkness. On Friday, February 9 and Saturday, February 10 at 8 p.m. the ensemble will perform Wintersongs in Candlelight at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. Featuring seasonal songs from Balkan, Baltic, Caucasian, Mediterranean, and Slavic lands, Wintersongs highlights include music expressing gratitude and wonder for the miracle of creation; folk carols that bestow blessings upon family and friends gathered around hearth fires and feast tables; hymns of faith and devotion to divine beings; humorous songs that heal with laughter; songs that summon hope for rebirth and renewal; and choral callings for peace on Earth. Kitka is an American women’s vocal arts ensemble inspired by traditional songs and vocal techniques from Eastern Europe and Eurasia. Founded in 1979 as an offshoot of the Westwind International Folk Ensemble, Kitka began as a grassroots group of amateur singers from diverse ethnic and musical backgrounds who shared a passion for the stunning dissonances, asymmetric rhythms, intricate ornamentation, and resonant strength of traditional Eastern European women’s vocal music. For four decades, the ninewoman Oakland ensemble has developed a vast, breathtaking repertoire of traditional songs from the Balkans, Caucasus and Slavic lands, as well as new material composed for the group drawing on those traditional vocal practices. Traveling to rural communities in Armenia and Bulgaria, Ukraine and Georgia, Serbia and Turkey, they’ve gathered songs and communed with elders who are often the last links to centuries-old traditions. A frequently occurring symbolic word in Balkan folk songs, “Kitka” means bouquet in Bulgarian and Macedonian. Tickets are $25-$50 at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, 114 Montecito Avenue (near Lake Merritt) are available at stpaulsoakland.org/concerts. The Kitka Women’s Vocal Ensemble will perform at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland on Friday and Saturday, February 9-10.
articles.title: Kitka vocal ensemble comes at St. Paul’s Episcopal on Feb. 9-10

articles.text: Four East Bay artists will showcase their work at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont. The exhibition, titled Moments that Give Pause, will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays, February 17 to March 3, from noon to 3 pm, with an opening reception on February 17 from 6 pm to 9 pm. These artists use divergent materials – painting, fiber, and cut paper – but share a common theme of celebration in the moment. Their exhibition is an invitation to pause from the intensity of life and to contemplate beauty. Featured Artists Carol Aust is a figurative painter based in Oakland. Her acrylic paintings depict people on journeys through emotional landscapes. Her work can be viewed at www.carolaust.com. Debra Collins creates delicate and intricate hand cut paper works of “internal meanderings.” Her work can be viewed at www. debraacollins.com. Carol Aust, “Mother and Child #49,” acrylics on panel, 16”x20” Gretchen McCondochie, “Embroidered Bird,” embroidery thread, 3”x3” Leslie Crisfield explores the contrast of light and dark and “wow moments” that stop her in her tracks. Her acrylic paintings can be viewed at www.lesliecrisfield.artcall.org. Gretchen McCondochie creates mixed media pieces, textiles, drawings and paintings that reflect her need for nature and stillness. Her work can be viewed at www.instagram.com/gretchendailydrawing. At the opening reception, live music of jazz standards will be provided by the Backyard Trio, with Chris Cooper on guitar, Jessie Ortiz on piano, and Baird Wheatley on saxophone. For more information, contact Carol Aust at carol.aust.art@ gmail.com .
articles.title: Exhibit at PCA features four East Bay artists

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate the Lunar New Year with their Year of the Dragon concert and banquet with 4 p.m. pre-concert festivities, a 5 p.m. performance and a 6:30 p.m. post-concert feast on Saturday, February 17 at Davies Symphony Hall. Lunar New Year is the most important holiday for many cultures in East, South and Southeast Asia, and is celebrated by people of Asian descent worldwide. This year’s celebration marks the 24th anniversary of the SF Symphony’s signature event, an elegant celebration of the Lunar New Year drawing upon vibrant Asian traditions past and present. The celebration begins at 4 p.m. with pre-concert lobby festivities open to all ticket holders, featuring an array of entertainment and activities including dragon dancers, fortune readers, calligraphy artists, and cultural performances. Conductor Mei-Ann Chen and the orchestra will then open the concert with Li Huan-Zhi’s energetic Spring Festival Overture and Phoon Yew Tien’s joyful New Year Greetings. The orchestra will then perform Jasmine Flower, a folk song from China’s Jiangsu province, which was arranged for orchestra by Li Wenping in 1999. The program continues with Flower Drum Song from Feng Yang and Girl from Da Ban City from Huang Ruo’s Folk Songs for Orchestra, originally commissioned and performed by the San Francisco Symphony at their 2012 Chinese New Year concert. Also on the program is Vivian Fung’s Pizzicato, which features sounds inspired by two Chinese instruments — the pipa and qin — as well as Indonesian gamelan music. Violinist Paul Huang will join the Symphony to play music from Tan Dun’s violin concerto, Fire Ritual, originally written for and premiered by violinist Eldbjørg Hemsing. Concluding the program are Che Chang’s Ali Mountain Evergreen, a piece that evokes the staggering scale of Ali Mountain in Taiwan, and Chen Ge Xin’s Gong Xi Gong Xi, a popular Chinese Lunar New Year song that translates to “Congratulations” or “Wishing You Happiness and Prosperity.” The post-concert Lunar New Year Banquet begins at 6:30 p.m. in Zellerbach Rehearsal Hall, located at 300 Franklin Street at the rear of Davies Symphony Hall. This event will feature a lucky draw and live music. The banquet will be catered by McCalls Catering & Events, with lighting design by Got Light. The décor for the event will feature hanging screens that highlight the many ways that Lunar New Year is celebrated across different cultures. Proceeds from the event support the Symphony’s artistic, education, and community programs. Tickets for the concert ($39- $109) and information about individual and full banquet table reservations can be found for purchase at sfsymphony.org, or through the box office at 415-864-6000. San Francisco Symphony’s Lunar New Year concert returns on Saturday, February 17.
articles.title: SF Symphony celebrates Lunar New Year with Feb. 17 concert

Friday, February 9, 7 p.m Diluvian String Quartet Chamber Concert For their fifth appearance in Piedmont, the Diluvian String Quartet’s winter recital will be another fun and diverse musical journey. On the program includes Mozart’s Adagio and Fugue in C minor, a short, profound score that he adapted from an earlier work for two pianos; a fresh, humorous quartet from 1919 by Germaine Tailleferre, the only female of the group Les 6; Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, written in 1905; and Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous. articles.text: Certain topics used to be off-limits. Many of us learned to avoid controversial topics such as politics and religion. That was a very good policy. Let’s open the discussion with a very famous phrase which was uttered by one of the most controversial politicians ever. The phrase “Share the wealth” was used by Louisiana Governor Huey Long. Controversial he certainly was. The accusation of “demagogue” fits him very well. Now that I have your attention, let’s analyze how “share the wealth“ is a very good policy in the world of arts. Concert touring has changed greatly over the years. Not so many years ago, concert artists traveled from city to city by train. Let’s use this as a jumping off point and take it from there. A concert tour of the West Coast might start in Seattle, then continue to Portland. Next they would come to the Bay Area and play three concerts, one in San Francisco, another concert in Oakland, and a final concert in San Francisco. Then they’d play in San Jose, take the train to Santa Barbara, Los Angeles and finish in San Diego. Intercontinental plane travel put an end to this type of concert tour. We sometimes read of sister cities. Piedmont has a sister city, Cuneo, Italy, thanks for the efforts of Loretta Breuning and City Council member Jeff Wieler. I’ll bet only a few remember this connection. The last time I heard about Cuneo was when I was there in 2002 playing a concert. The mayor of Cuneo gave me a medal. The big-time concert artists have their own concert circuit. The others have to struggle for an existence. Perhaps, if we would work together, eve r yone cou ld benef it. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is our city’s gem. Quite obviously many of our citizens agree. The advice to share the wealth remains valuable, especially if you avoid the politics. Piedmont Center for the Arts
articles.title: Sharing the wealth

articles.text: This weekend, February 9 through 11 four-time Grammy Award-winning bass virtuoso Stanley Clarke will perform with his band at Yoshi’s in Oakland. Born in Philadelphia, Clarke has been a constant force in American music since the early 1970s with the success of the jazz-fusion group Return To Forever, founded with Chick Corea and Lenny White. Along the way, he has collaborated with Quincy Jones, Stan Getz, Art Blakey, Paul McCartney, Jeff Beck, Keith Richards, Aretha Franklin, Stevie Wonder, Chaka Khan, The Police and Herbie Hancock, and has shared the stage with Bob Marley and Miles Davis. Clarke’s creativity has been rewarded with gold and platinum records, Grammy Awards, and Emmy nominations. In 2022 he was selected by the National Endowment for the Arts as one of its four new Jazz Master honorees. He also was Rolling Stones’ first Jazzman of the Year. articles.text: The singer and composer Danielle Wertz will be performing music from her newest album, Other Side, for two 7 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. shows on Friday, February 16 at SFJAZZ. “A masterful ballad interpreter” (NYC Jazz Record), the New York City-based vocalist and 2015 Thelonious Monk competition finalist weaves together elements of jazz, folk and her own voice used as an instrumental texture, to create an intimate musical world. A finalist in both the Ella Fitzgerald Jazz Vocal Competition and the Mid-Atlantic Jazz Vocal Competition, Wertz released her 2017 debut album Intertwined in collaboration with Israeli pianist Tal Cohen — a sparkling collection of standards and newer compositions which was ranked #4 on Capital Bop’s list of “Best DC Jazz Albums of 2017.” In addition to her solo career, Wertz is an avid collaborator, featured on recording projects alongside musicians Elena Pinderhughes, Braxton Cook, Justin Rock and Ambrose Akinmusire, among others. With Other Side, Wertz braves essential questions of the human experience with nuanced expression and deep feeling. Born of the introspection and examination that the pandemic forced upon us all, the album pairs her own lyrical compositions based in personal stories with carefully chosen covers like the Rogers and Hart classic “Spring is Here,” imbued with the longing and anger created by a world in lockdown. Tickets ($25) for the shows at SFJAZZ (201 Franklin St.) are available at sfjazz.org, or through the box office at 415-788-7353. The singer and composer Danielle Wertz will be performing music from her newest album, Other Side, for two evening shows on Friday, February 16 at SFJAZZ.
articles.title: Danielle Wertz plays SFJAZZ Feb. 16

articles.text: Viggo Mortensen and Kodi Smit-McPhee in The Road No doubt the world of Cormac McCarthy, author of the novel The Road, is bleak and austere. Recall his dark and nihilistic book, No Country for Old Men, also adapted to the screen by the Coen brothers. It won four Academy Awards, one for best picture. The Road is perhaps the most severe of all of McCarthy’s stories and director John Hillcoat follows the novel closely. The film is set during a post-apocalyptic period, one that has caused an ecological disaster, not unlike a nuclear winter. What happened is never made clear. The skies are leaden, a perpetual mist falls, all is grim and gray. A father (Viggo Mortensen) and his son (Kodi Smit-McPhee), ten years after the catalytic event, are on a road headed to the Pacific Ocean. Few people have survived the long torturous decade. Most have starved, been killed or committed suicide. The father and son are faced with overwhelming odds; they are desperate for food and constantly fearful of those they might meet along the way. The fragile patina of civilization has been scraped away, revealing the most sinister aspects of the human condition. They hide constantly from predators who will resort to anything to stay alive. Anything. All taboos have been broken. The intersection, between order and chaos, between laws and anarchy, intrigue McCarthy, and it’s an intersection that is explored in withering detail in The Road. The post-apocalyptic setting of this film is unrelentingly stark, with only a glimmer of hope embedded in this harsh, dystopian tale. The performances of Viggo Mortensen and Kodi SmitMcPhee are impressive. And with the exception of brief backstory, focusing on the mother (Charlize Theron), it is the father and son who make the journey, and it is their bond of love, their will to survive against all odds, that make for a compelling tale. Some might feel that The Road is too forbidding to be enjoyed. Yes, it is desolate; however, it is also far from the spectacle of most contemporary, apocalyptic blockbusters that assume that to hold filmgoers’ attention they must be overwhelmed by high volume drama, dazzled by seamless CGI, and taken for a harrowing ride. The Road is the antidote to such an assumption. The Road. Directed by John Hillcoat. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Charlize Theron and Robert DuVall. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R. Released 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIE FOR ADULTS The Road – a post apocalyptic story of survival

articles.text: Max has all the right stuff to make it a winning movie for kids, say 10-years-old and up. It’s got a young teen boy, Justin (Josh Wiggins), feeling angry and rebellious, alienated from his strict ex-marine dad (Thomas Haden Church) and his kind mom (Lauren Graham). His brother, Kyle (Robbie Amell), is in Afghanistan where he and his squad are constantly on patrol for the bad guys. Along with Kyle goes Max, a trained military dog, wearing his own flak jacket, always scouting ahead, on the lookout for danger. Kyle is killed while on patrol and Max is sent back to the states to a small town in Texas. The dog (a Belgian Malinois) suffers from post-traumatic-stress as a result of the loss of Kyle and the ambush. As a result, his career over. Max is about to be put down. Justin and his mom and dad rescue Max, feeling he represents a tangible connection to their lost son, Kyle. Max, until he meets Justin, is, angry, snarling and lost. Eventually, they win each other over and team up. With the help of Justin’s friends, Chuy (Dejon La Quake) and Carmen (Mia Xitlai), a sweet love interest for Justin, they solve a Hardy Boys-type mystery involving some gangster types dealing in stolen guns and involving brother Kyle’s ex-marine buddy Tyler (Luke Kleintank), a stealthy villain. The last act has some intense action scenes where Justin and Max are both in harm’s way. As is Justin’s dad. The movie is sentimental and unabashedly schmaltzy. Indeed. In other words, it’s perfect summer fare for kids. Better than some the of big tent blockbusters. This is a straightforward boy and his dog movie, right out of the ‘50s. And it’s a perfect 4th of July movie (there is even a parade in act two). It also bears witness to the courage exemplified by what we refer to as “war dogs,” those canines that have a long and distinguished history, dating back to WWI. Be sure and stay for the credits. Max. Directed by Boaz Yakin. Starring Josh Wiggins, Thomas Haden Church and Lauren Graham. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated PG. Released 2015. Streaming on VUDU/prime/max/apple tv.
articles.title: Max – all about a dog in wartime

Everything is icky, they want to go home, and dig in their snobbish custom made heels, refusing to help out. Things are dire. Isabel’s brothSee Nanny McPhee on page 32 Max – all about a dog in wartime By Chris Honoré Max has all the right stuff to make it a winning movie for kids, say 10-years-old and up. It’s got a young teen boy, Justin (Josh Wiggins), feeling angry and rebellious, alienated from his strict ex-marine dad (Thomas Haden Church) and his kind mom (Lauren Graham). His brother, Kyle (Robbie Amell), is in Afghanistan where he and his squad are constantly on patrol for the bad guys. Along with Kyle goes Max, a trained military dog, wearing his own flak jacket, always scouting ahead, on the lookout for danger. Kyle is killed while on patrol and Max is sent back to the states to a small town in Texas. The dog (a Belgian Malinois) suffers from post-traumatic-stress as a result of the loss of Kyle and the ambush. As a result, his career over. Max is about to be put down. Justin and his mom and dad rescue Max, feeling he represents a tangible connection to their lost son, Kyle. Max, until he meets Justin, is, angry, snarling and lost. Eventually, they win each other over and team up. With the help of Justin’s friends, Chuy (Dejon La Quake) and Carmen (Mia Xitlai), a sweet love interest for Justin, they solve a Hardy Boys-type mystery involving some gangster types dealing in stolen guns and involving brother Kyle’s ex-marine buddy Tyler (Luke Kleintank), a stealthy villain. The last act has some intense action scenes where Justin and Max are both in harm’s way. As is Justin’s dad. The movie is sentimental and unabashedly schmaltzy. Indeed. In other words, it’s perfect summer fare for kids. Better than some the of big tent blockbusters. This is a straightforward boy and his dog movie, right out of the ‘50s. And it’s a perfect 4th of July movie (there is even a parade in act two). It also bears witness to the courage exemplified by what we refer to as “war dogs,” those canines that have a long and distinguished history, dating back to WWI. Be sure and stay for the credits. Max. Directed by Boaz Yakin. Starring Josh Wiggins, Thomas Haden Church and Lauren Graham. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated PG. Released 2015. Streaming on VUDU/prime/max/apple tv.

articles.text: The spirit of friendly competition, creativity and community engagement came alive last weekend at the 19th Annual Girl Scout Pinewood Derby. On the afternoon of Saturday, February 3, Girl Scouts from Piedmont, Oakland and Emeryville met at the gymnasium of Piedmont Community Church (PCC) to race their handcrafted cars against one another. Since last year, Piedmont Middle School’s 7th grade Girl Scout Troop 33587 has taken over as host of the derby from Troop 31765. Several of Troop 33587’s girl scouts participated in the derby when they were Daisy Scouts, but this year they had a chance to give back to the derby racing community by running the event. Brownie Girl Scouts, excited, nervous and energetic, lined the hallway waiting for their cars to be weighed in at the registration table. The racers could make last-minute additions of weight or repairs at the workbench in the gymnasium before they handed their cars over to this year’s car manager, Girl Scout Charlotte Phung from Troop 33587. Soon, it was time for the competition to start. Parent Rob Edesses began the festivities with a brief introduction to the competition’s rules, then passed the mike to the two announcers, Girl Scouts Devon Porter and Junie Waters Worthen. With their energetic and outgoing commentary, the duo raised the energy of the audience before the competition had even begun. “Three, Two, One, Go!” called A full house was in the gym for the Brownie race. In the aftermath, girls congratulated the creators of the winning cars and consoled those whose cars had lost. As the evening closed on the event’s final race, the feeling of the crowd changed. The room fell more silent before each race’s end as people held their breaths in anticipation of the winner. After the Girl Scout’s finish line judge, Victoria Mbise, picked up the winning car, more screams rang out. articles.text: At Chinese New Yar celebrations people wear red clothes, decorate with poems on red paper, and give children and single people “crisp lucky money” in red enveloples or “hong bao.” Gung Hay Fat Choy - May you be Happy & Prosperous. Lunar New Year is the longest and most important celebration in Asia, celebrated by millions of people in China, Vietnam, Korea, and Singapore for two weeks. The Chinese year 4722, Year of the Dragon, began on Feb. 10, 2024. The Chinese use the lunar calendar, which has 13 months which explains why Lunar New Year changes every year. Breathing Fire into the New Year Legend has it that in ancient times, Buddha asked all the animals to meet him on Chinese New Year. But only twelve animals came. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The strong, hardworking Ox was in the lead. Suddenly, the clever Rat, jumped on the Ox’s back, he did not even feel the little thing getting a free ride. At the last second before reaching shore, the Rat jumped on land, winning the race! The Ox came in second, the Tiger third, and so it went... the happy-go-lucky Pig took his time and came in last... and the Chinese Zodiac and its twelve signs were born. Being a sacred animal in Chinese culture and mythology, everyone’s bet was on the Dragon to take home the top prize. But along the way, the Dragon stumbled upon a village suffering from drought. He took pity on them and used his powers to send them rain before finishing the race. He finished in fifth place behind the Rat, Ox, Tiger and Rabbit. Buddha named a year after each animal and the cycle would repeat every 12 years. He announced that the people born in each animal’s year would have some of that animal’s personality. Because of their status as a favorite animal, Dragons are seen as confident, idealistic and ambitious. Dragon years are considered the most auspicious years of any in the Chinese Zodiac. All the zodiac animals are real-life, non-mythical animals except the dragon. The dragon is considered the most powerful of all the zodiac signs. As the only fictional creature among the 12 zodiac animals, the Dragon occupies a lofty status in Chinese culture, representing success and imperial power, as well as authority, dignity, honor, success and luck. Chinese people regard themselves as descendants of the Chinese dragon, with emperors exclusively entitled ‘The Dragon’. People born in the Year of the Dragon are believed to be ambitious, energetic, and charismatic, often inspiring others with their passion and enthusiasm. They are considered to be natural leaders, confident and unafraid to take risks, making them magnetic personalities in social and professional circles. These traits together make someone a powerful, strong authority figure. Accordingly, people born in the year of the dragon are thought to make integrity-bound politicians, natural entrepreneurs, and leaders of our communities, revolutionary idealists, and forward-thinking visionaries who connect with the people around them. traditional dessert during Lunar New Year is a sweet fried crescent dumpling made with sugar, shredded coconuts, roasted peanuts and sesame seeds. This article was taken from a welcoming speech by Mary Geong, Oakland Rotary Club’s past president, at a Lunar New Year banquet in Oakland. What does Lunar New Year signify? Similar to the Western New Year, Lunar New Year symbolizes letting go of the past and ringing in the present. Celebrations are focused on removing the bad and the old and welcoming the new and the good. The Lunar New Year also is an important time for spending time with family to show one’s love and gratitude. People will pay their respects to their ancestors and older family members. Its significance is similar to Thanksgiving or Christmas among Western cultures. “ At Chinese New Year celebrations people wear red clothes, decorate with poems on red paper, and give children and single people “lucky money” in red envelopes. Red symbolizes fire and good luck, which according to legend can drive away bad luck. The fireworks that shower the festivities also drive away evil spirits. I see many of you are wearing red tonight. Tangerine/orange represents prosperity because the color resembles the color of gold coins. articles.text: You could see them coming from every direction, dozens of kids from K-5th grade and their families descending upon the Piedmont Community Church Gymnasium for the Annual Pinewood Derby. Races were held by age group every hour throughout the day. Piedmont BSA Cub Scouts held their competition in the morning, while the Girl Scouts of Northern California, Oakland Service Unit, held theirs in the afternoon. The Pinewood Derby is a Scouting tradition dating back to the 1950s. These days, the annual event is held by most packs around the country and works in the same way, regardless of location: Scouts race small, driverless wooden cars down a sloped track. The cars are powered only by gravity. With an adult’s help, each Pinewood Derby car is built by the child using a standard kit that includes a wooden block, plastic wheels, and metal axles. Prizes are awarded based on speed, design, and construction. Races started soon after check-in was complete. The competition was a double-elimination bracket, so each car raced twice to determine the event’s ultimate winners. Individual races typically lasted less than four seconds while the day’s especially fast cars usually clocked in at just over three. Winners in each category were provided with a certificate detailing their name and category. The Piedmont Council BSA serves youth in kindergarten through age 21 with programs designed to build character, fitness, citizenship and leadership. From building a pinewood derby car at home to completing a 70-mile hike in New Mexico, Piedmont Council BSA helps youth and their families form lasting memories and build valuable skills. For more info visit www.piedmontbsa.org or email contact@piedmontbsa.org. Photo by Atlantis Langowski A division of cars sits on a table after check-in, ready for their races.

articles.text: Piedmont dads and Scouting parents David Cole and Greg Wolff, who have helped organize the annual Pinewood Derby for last four years, have completed their final lap and are now headed to the pit. The two each have boys who have now aged out of the program and decided that this year was time to take their leave. Both Cole and Wolff helped behind the scenes. Both are involved with Piedmont Makers and have opened their workshops to groups of derby racers in the past. Asked why they were involved with the Pinewood Derby for so many years, Wolff said that he did it for the kids. “The kids will come to us with a perfectly visualized derby car in their mind, so helping them realize that dream has been such a kick,” said Wolff. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, February 7, 2024 Pinewood Derby a showcase for creativity By Atlantis Langowski You could see them coming from every direction, dozens of kids from K-5th grade and their families descending upon the Piedmont Community Church Gymnasium for the Annual Pinewood Derby. Races were held by age group every hour throughout the day. Piedmont BSA Cub Scouts held their competition in the morning, while the Girl Scouts of Northern California, Oakland Service Unit, held theirs in the afternoon. The Pinewood Derby is a Scouting tradition dating back to the 1950s. These days, the annual event is held by most packs around the country and works in the same way, regardless of location: Scouts race small, driverless wooden cars down a sloped track. The cars are powered only by gravity. With an adult’s help, each Pinewood Derby car is built by the child using a standard kit that includes a wooden block, plastic wheels, and metal axles. Prizes are awarded based on speed, design, and construction. Races started soon after check-in was complete. The competition was a double-elimination bracket, so each car raced twice to determine the event’s ultimate winners. Individual races typically lasted less than four seconds while the day’s especially fast cars usually clocked in at just over three. Winners in each category were provided with a certificate detailing their name and category. The Piedmont Council BSA serves youth in kindergarten through age 21 with programs designed to build character, fitness, citizenship and leadership. From building a pinewood derby car at home to completing a 70-mile hike in New Mexico, Piedmont Council BSA helps youth and their families form lasting memories and build valuable skills. For more info visit www.piedmontbsa.org or email contact@piedmontbsa.org. Photo by Atlantis Langowski A division of cars sits on a table after check-in, ready for their races. Pinewood Derby volunteers retire from roles By Atlantis Langowski Piedmont dads and Scouting parents David Cole and Greg Wolff, who have helped organize the annual Pinewood Derby for last four years, have completed their final lap and are now headed to the pit. The two each have boys who have now aged out of the program and decided that this year was time to take their leave. Both Cole and Wolff helped behind the scenes. Both are involved with Piedmont Makers and have opened their workshops to groups of derby racers in the past. Asked why they were involved with the Pinewood Derby for so many years, Wolff said that he did it for the kids. “The kids will come to us with a perfectly visualized derby car in their mind, so helping them realize that dream has been such a kick,” said Wolff. Cole concurred. “There is nothing as pure as the excitement of those kids and it is a real honor to offer something that they will remember for a long time,” he said. Lunar New Year is the longest and most important celebration in Asia, celebrated by millions of people in China, Vietnam, Korea, and Singapore for two weeks. The Chinese year 4722, Year of the Dragon, began on Feb. 10, 2024. The Chinese use the lunar calendar, which has 13 months which explains why Lunar New Year changes every year. Breathing Fire into the New Year Legend has it that in ancient times, Buddha asked all the animals to meet him on Chinese New Year. But only twelve animals came. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The strong, hardworking Ox was in the lead. Suddenly, the clever Rat, jumped on the Ox’s back, he did not even feel the little thing getting a free ride. At the last second before reaching shore, the Rat jumped on land, winning the race! The Ox came in second, the Tiger third, and so it went... the happy-go-lucky Pig took his time and came in last... and the Chinese Zodiac and its twelve signs were born. Being a sacred animal in Chinese culture and mythology, everyone’s bet was on the Dragon to take home the top prize. But along the way, the Dragon stumbled upon a village suffering from drought. He took pity on them and used his powers to send them rain before finishing the race. He finished in fifth place behind the Rat, Ox, Tiger and Rabbit. Buddha named a year after each animal and the cycle would repeat every 12 years. He announced that the people born in each animal’s year would have some of that animal’s personality. Because of their status as a favorite animal, Dragons are seen as confident, idealistic and ambitious. Dragon years are considered the most auspicious years of any in the Chinese Zodiac. All the zodiac animals are real-life, non-mythical animals except the dragon. The dragon is considered the most powerful of all the zodiac signs. As the only fictional creature among the 12 zodiac animals, the Dragon occupies a lofty status in Chinese culture, representing success and imperial power, as well as authority, dignity, honor, success and luck. Chinese people regard themselves as descendants of the Chinese dragon, with emperors exclusively entitled ‘The Dragon’. People born in the Year of the Dragon are believed to be ambitious, energetic, and charismatic, often inspiring others with their passion and enthusiasm. They are considered to be natural leaders, confident and unafraid to take risks, making them magnetic personalities in social and professional circles. These traits together make someone a powerful, strong authority figure. Accordingly, people born in the year of the dragon are thought to make integrity-bound politicians, natural entrepreneurs, and leaders of our communities, revolutionary idealists, and forward-thinking visionaries who connect with the people around them. traditional dessert during Lunar New Year is a sweet fried crescent dumpling made with sugar, shredded coconuts, roasted peanuts and sesame seeds. Similar to the Western New Year, Lunar New Year symbolizes letting go of the past and ringing in the present. Celebrations are focused on removing the bad and the old and welcoming the new and the good. The Lunar New Year also is an important time for spending time with family to show one’s love and gratitude. People will pay their respects to their ancestors and older family members. articles.text: Local with Lisa: SWEAT Many people are setting ambitious fitness goals as the new year rolls in. If you’re one of them, look no further than SWEAT, a fitness studio on College Avenue in Oakland’s Rockridge neighborhood. I had the pleasure of sitting down with Cassie Hecker, the owner of SWEAT and a Wildwood mom, to learn more about her innovative approach and what inspired her to open this boutique studio. The SWEAT Experience SWEAT offers a distinctive workout that combines high-intensity lifting with a focus on dumbbells, kettlebells, and body weight exercises. “We’re all about building up the big muscles while keeping the intensity up, so you’re also getting a good cardio workout,” she explained. The beauty of SWEAT’s approach is its versatility; it caters to a wide range of fitness levels and is ideal for busy individuals, including parents and tech professionals who may have limited time for exercise. Elaborating on its inclusivity, she said, “It’s for anyone. Honestly, it’s tailored towards super busy parents or tech people who don’t have much time. They’ll get a couple of workouts in a week, and they get their cardio and strength training. They get their mobility work in those few precious hours they have to themselves,” she said. The journey and Inspiration With two SWEAT locations, one on College Ave. and another on San Pablo Ave., Cassie’s journey in the fitness industry is rooted in her passion for health and wellness. “I’ve been in fitness for 20 years. I started doing this when I was in college. We moved to San Francisco from Ohio with the intention of opening a gym. I took what I thought was the most effective for busy working parents,” Cassie shared. Post-Pandemic Recovery Both SWEAT locations offer the same exceptional workout in SWEAT is located at 5410 College Avenue. two different settings. While the original College Avenue location is inside, the newer San Pablo location is outside. It was how the gym dealt with the challenges brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic. Setting, achieving fitness goals With the new year, many people set fitness goals, but Cassie advises positive reinforcement. “I think it’s best if you set a very specific goal and you set up a system to reward yourself. Maybe that goal is to eat five servings of vegetables every day, and on the days that you do, you give yourself some sort of reward. It could be buying new workout clothes, and then the days that you don’t, you just ignore them versus punishing yourself. You need to give yourself wins.” The SWEAT Recovery Room One of the unique services SWEAT offers is its Recovery Room at each location. Each location will have one private room that you can rent for 30 minutes that will have an infrared sauna and a cold plunge. The infrared sauna offers various health benefits, including increased metabolism, improved immune system function, and muscle recovery. Following the sauna, clients can take a plunge into cold water, which reduces inflammation and energizes the body. Why a cold water plunge? A cold-water plunge produces a rush of endorphins and adrenaline. “The endorphins you feel after you’re out of there, but also the recovery. That shock to your system, that cold, reduces all the inflammation I just put in your body when you lift. It will all be gone when you get out of that tub and you’ll be ready to hit that next workout. But also, you want to do it earlier in the day because of the amount of endorphins and adrenaline that you have is just like having three cups of coffee,” she said. Cassie Hecker’s passion for fitness and her innovative approach at SWEAT make it a compelling choice for anyone looking to achieve their fitness goals this year. Whether you’re a busy parent or seeking an efficient and effective workout routine, SWEAT offers a comprehensive fitness solution that may be just what you need to make 2024 your healthiest year yet. SWEAT is located at 5410 College Avenue. Tel. (510) 697- 2899. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Coconut Mochi Cake is a traditional treat during Lunar New Year. February 10th marks the Lunar New Year of the Dragon. It is said that the lunar year harnesses the powers of its zodiac animal, so we are in for a favorable year as dragons symbolize strength and good fortune. A tradition in most Chinese families at Lunar New Year is nian gao (translation “Year Cake”), a steamed cake made of sweet rice flour and minimally processed cane sugar. We decorate it with sesame seeds and dried Chinese dates (jujubes) and steam it in a bed of bamboo leaves. This recipe is a twist, using coconut milk, granulated sugar, and baking the cake in a standard, 350°F oven. It’s an easier approach, especially if you do not regularly steam foods with a large steaming set-up. “Mochi cakes” have become very mainstream these days, with mochi as the sweet rice flour base in place of wheat flour. The cakes are adored for their soft and bouncy texture and are gluten-free. Coconut Mochi Cake – aka Chinese Nian Gao for Lunar New Year Adapted from What to Cook Today Makes one 8-inch round cake INGREDIENTS • 1/4 cup flaked coconut, unsweetened • 1-1/4 cup glutinous, sweet rice flour • 1 cup granulated sugar • 1/ 8 teaspoon salt • 2 extra-large eggs • 1-1/2 cups whole-fat coconut milk • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted then cooled slightly; plus additional butter for the pan • 1/2 teaspoons coconut extract INSTRUCTIONS Toast the coconut flakes in a small, shallow pan over medium heat, stirring frequently, about five minutes until the edges of the flakes just begin to turn golden. Remove from the heat, transferring to a dish if needed to stop the browning. Set aside. Generously butter the sides of the cake pan and line the bottom with parchment paper. Position an oven rack one-third from the bottom of the oven. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Melt the 2 tablespoons of butter then transfer to a medium bowl. Add the 2 eggs and coconut extract then mix until combined. Add the coconut milk and mix again until well combined. (If the coconut milk as separated, warm it in a small saucepan over very low heat to re-emulsify. The coconut fat will melt at about 75°F – 80°F.) Mix the sweet rice flour, sugar, and salt together in a large bowl. Make a well in the center of the dry ingredients and add the liquid ingredients, stirring with a whisk to achieve a smooth, thin batter. Try to remove any lumps, straining if needed before pouring into the prepared pan. Bake for 30 minutes then remove from the oven and sprinkle on the reserved toasted coconut atop. Return to bake an additional 20 – 25 minutes until the cake is golden brown and the center is just barely set. A toothpick inserted into the center of the cake should come out with a few sticky bits, but not wet. Total baking time is about 50 – 55 minutes. Remove the cake from the oven and let cool for several hours before attempting to remove from the pan and cut. The cake is very soft and needs time to cool and set. Overnight in the refrigerator is also fine. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok at: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers last week included Matt Gerhardt, Rick Eigenbrode, Mike Henn, Dottie Hutch, Christina Miller, Ken Hubbert, Maricela Negron, Mark Davis, Peggy Shultz, Will Adams, Marianne Jakus, Jim Kuo, Helen Dong, Lois Price, Rob Smith, Lori Austin, Martin Levy, Pat Keller, Elizabeth Richter, Sharona Fischrup, and Dick Carter. In 2023, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group lived a charmed weather life. It never rained on Wednesday mornings. However in January, the threat of rain had to be part of their plans for weekly walks. Last Wednesda, rain was forecast for later in the day, so it was an opportunity for the group to live up to their “we walk rain or shine” mantra. Twenty-one walkers with umbrellas were at the Exedra Wednesday morning. A planned walking tour by architect Will Adams was postponed a week for better weather. The group went up Highland Avenue, turned up Oakland Avenue, and stopped in front of a house on the corner. This area was a bit of a Bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters like Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. However, before them Frank C. Havens and his nephew, George Sterling, were residents in the area. His house was built in 1898 and might have been an early office for Havens, who was a local real estate developer in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries. He partnered with Francis “Borax” Smith, a businessman who made his fortune in borax mining, to create the Realty Syndicate in 1895, and they developed many of Oakland and Piedmont’s neighborhoods. Interestingly, both Havens and Sterling married their secretaries, and Sterling and his wife lived two houses up from this corner. The house at Highland and Oakland has a wonderful late 19th/early 20th Century look, with gables of different sizes and a witch cap roof in the front. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake. After Piedmont became a city in 1907, home construction boomed. These streets were part of Wickham Havens’ (Frank’s son) Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development. The walkers wondered if Havens’ “Alta Piedmont” resulted in the later references to “Baja Piedmont” for the streets below Highland. The group made a left turn on the one-block Hardwick Avenue and went up the Langdon Court cul-de-sac to enjoy their first cloudy view of San Francisco. The walkers returned to Hardwick, then on Blair and back to Highland to start the climb up Pala. They went on Mesa, enjoying more great homes built between 1906 to 1960, then it was up Pala to the Scenic-Pala steps where they climbed the 161-foot set of stairs. At the top, they went up Scenic for expansive views of the Bay and Mountain View Cemetery. An about-face took the walkers back down Scenic to more wonderful, cloudy San Francisco views and Blair Avenue. Going down Blair, the group quickly came to the house in which Jack London wrote his classic novel Call of the Wild. A closer look at the house found a fun, small street sign on a side gate that reads, “City of London Museum.” At this point, the walkers made their way directly down Blair to Highland and the Exedra before the sprinkles turned into the forecasted shower. It had been a fun, two-mile walk with wonderful homes, history, views, and friends on an only little-wet Wednesday morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

They went on Mesa, enjoying more great homes built between 1906 to 1960, then it was up Pala to the Scenic-Pala steps where they climbed the 161-foot set of stairs. At the top, they went up Scenic for expansive views of the Bay and Mountain View Cemetery. An about-face took the walkers back down Scenic to more wonderful, cloudy San Francisco views and Blair Avenue. Going down Blair, the group quickly came to the house in which Jack London wrote his classic novel Call of the Wild. A closer look at the house found a fun, small street sign on a side gate that reads, “City of London Museum.” At this point, the walkers made their way directly down Blair to Highland and the Exedra before the sprinkles turned into the forecasted shower. It had been a fun, two-mile walk with wonderful homes, history, views, and friends on an only little-wet Wednesday morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Girl Scout Pinewood Derby will be held this Saturday, February 3, in the Piedmont Community Church Gymnasium. Beginning at 3:00 p.m., local Girl Scouts will cheer, shout, and send their creations down the track as they compete to see who has the fastest car in town. Prior to this weekend’s race, the Girl Scouts held a practice run for the Pinewood Derby on January 27, providing an opportunity to test their handmade cars on the same race track that will be used for the real competition. “It was super busy – a steady stream of kids coming from the Scouts BSA, the Girl Scouts, and their parents,” said Carolyn Pan, a Girl Scout Leader for Troop 33587 and organizer for this year’s Girl Scout Pinewood Derby. “The kids had so much fun. All they wanted to do was run the cars down the track. In fact, it might have been more fun than the actual race,” joked Pan. The Girl Scout practice run allowed them to iron out any problems with their cars before race day, letting them fine-tune their vehicles for maximum speed. articles.text: In a move toward accessibility, the City of Piedmont’s Public Works Department has begun work on the construction of an ADA-compliant access ramp in Dracena Park, The project will cost $89,649 and will connect the areas of Lower Dracena and Upper Dracena with a low-incline pathway. Director of Public Works Daniel Gonzales stressed the importance of the ramp installation. “There’s no accessible pathway that leads there right now. This would be the only ADA-compliant access point we’d have in Dracena Park,” he said. Public rights-of-way and facilities are required to be accessible to persons with disabilities under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990. These statutes prohibit public agencies from discriminating against persons with disabilities by excluding them from services, programs, or activities. The city first received a request for ADA access to an off-leash dog park in mid-2023. articles.text: Editor: With a heavy heart I express my deep concern about the threat of a teachers’ strike in Piedmont. I genuinely appreciate the dedication of our teachers, most of whom approach their roles with passion and dedication, and I recognize the validity of their requests for increased compensation. However, I am extremely uneasy about the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) aligning with a regional coalition of unions led by the California Teachers Association (CTA). This coalition, seemingly formed just to coordinate labor action, introduces a divisive “us vs. them” mentality that betrays APT’s stated commitment to negotiate in good faith. It’s becoming increasingly clear that the list of demands that members of the Coalition have presented to their employers does not account for the unique differences of each district, budget, enrollment, or demographics. Letting outsiders drive APTs agenda is damaging to the sense of community, collaboration, and trust that makes PUSD the special district many of us moved here for. Why else would APT essentially declare in “impasse” back in August before negotiations even began? Why else would they pre-emptively authorize strike action before mediation is complete?
