articles.text: And we certainly don’t want to see cuts beyond what’s being proposed, but what are we supposed to do? We’re told, don’t you understand? The district just doesn’t have enough money to help teachers with this. Well, we do understand. We see the budget numbers, and believe me, we understand the nature of the problem all too well. All of us here are intimately familiar with what it’s like not to have enough money to cover expenses. We live it every single month of our personal lives. This budget shortfall is real, but it cannot keep falling on educators’ shoulders. Many times in the past, we’ve agreed to make sacrifices to keep the district solvent. We gave up full health insurance coverage in 2011. We agreed to four straight years of furlough days after the last financial crisis. We’ve signed contract after contract below COLA [Cost of Living Adjustment] and below CPI [Consumer Price Index]. Perhaps that’s led to a tacit assumption that teachers will always somehow figure it out. Teachers are known for being able to do that. [There is] an assumption that teachers can take the hit, teachers can absorb the damage. Teachers are used to sacrificing their own well-being again and again and again. But we’ve hit a hard limit at long last. And that brings me to the announcement I have to make tonight. As many in the community are already aware, Piedmont’s educators have taken the almost unprecedented step of holding a strike authorization vote. Before I formally announce the outcome of the vote, I want to clarify what a strike authorization vote means. It is not a vote to immediately strike. Here’s the language: APT members were asked to vote yes or no on. ‘I authorize the APT Executive Board to call for a legal strike at the appropriate time if no agreement is reached once the contract bargaining process has been exhausted.’ Okay, in other words, a majority yes vote means we are still committed, as we have been, to going through the mediation process, and if necessary, the fact-finding process, with full good faith in pursuit of a fair contract resolution. However, should that process fail, a majority yes vote empowers APT leadership to call a strike at any point up until we sign a new contract. It does not have to be immediate. Again, a majority vote would be sufficient for authorization. We asked for authorization from every member of APT, and the result was overwhelming. Nearly 96% yes votes for authorization. That is an extraordinary number for Piedmont teachers. I’ve been here for 24 years. This is not a striking district, not a striking group of people, so the fact that we got 96% yes votes really tells you how desperate people are. Let me be very clear to you and to the whole community. APT’s goal will always be to avoid a strike. We want to be in the schools and classrooms teaching and supporting our students. We fully understand how disruptive a strike would be to our students. Lord knows we don’t want to lose a single minute of precious instructional time, and we don’t want our students to be stuck at home, right? We’ve all been through that, and we don’t want it again. We are deeply aware about how disruptive a strike would be to families and working parents, but we cannot sign a contract that amounts to a literal ongoing pay cut for Piedmont’s educators.”

articles.text: The Year of the Dragon will be celebrated in Piedmont’s Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens Elementary School on Friday, February 9, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) will host the annual Lunar New Year event highlighted by performances, crafts, a lion dance and dim sum. “It’s the Year of the Dragon, a year of energy and excitement. Let’s celebrate it together,” said PAAC Co-President Cassindy Chao. Last year a capacity crowd of more than 350 people enjoyed hands-on activities and instrumental and vocal performances by the Honors Mandarin class. “We welcome our community. We’re doing this for our children for their futures as citizens in a diverse community that welcomes them,” said Chao. The event will include arts and crafts tables for kids, and gourmet desserts, boba drinks and panang curry available for purchase by local Piedmont businesses, including BakeSum, Tea on Piedmont and Salisa Skinner. Last year’s event attracted many local Piedmont leaders and reached maximum enrollment prior to doors opening. Tickets are suggested to be reserved in advance by February 4 by emailing piedmontpaac@gmail.com or using the QR code. articles.text: Photo by Echa Schneider Carl Schmits, Managing Director of Equipment Standards for USA Pickleball, shows a new noise-reduced paddle. The City of Piedmont held a public demonstration of new sports equipment last week designed to reduce the sound of pickleball play. On Wednesday, January 24, at Linda Beach Courts, the city displayed newly developed sound absorption panels for noise-dampening, sound monitoring tools, and new pickleball paddles that “have been tested to reduce noise by more than 50%” according to the city. Approximately 15 people, including City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, were present at the demonstration on Wednesday, January 24. Among the more interesting equipment shown off was a remote sound monitoring service by the company SLN/CR (pronounced “silencer”). At the event, USA Pickleball representative Carl Schmits teased a SLN/ CR device that would provide real-time noise updates on local pickleball courts and, if a pre-set noise threshold was exceeded, alert city officials, club directors, and even local police departments. The device would be “plug and play,” and require very little in terms of installation or upkeep. “We’re excited to partner with USA Pickleball to showcase emerging technology and equipment at Linda Beach Courts,” said Bayon Moore. “We are a community of learners and this demonstration will accelerate our education as we continue to explore creative ways to support Piedmont’s active, engaged pickleball community while also being good neighbors.” Bayon Moore’s comment about being “good neighbors,” as well as the location of the demonstration, is likely a reference to the noise complaints of neighbors near the Linda Beach Courts. Since October 2023, the City of Piedmont has been involved with a lawsuit from a group of private citizens who claim that the City violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) by dedicating the courts without properly reviewing the noise effects it would have on the local community. Richard Drury, an attorney for the group of private citizens, said that the demonstration was a positive development for the neighborhood, but would not affect their lawsuit. “If anything, it proves that our lawsuit is meritorious,” said Drury. “We are arguing that the city should have done CEQA review to analyze feasible mitigation measures. Now the city has basically proven that we are right and there are feasible ways to reduce noise. [...] The city’s actions actually prove that they skirted the law.” As a matter of policy, the City of Piedmont does not comment on pending litigation.
articles.title: Noise-reducing pickleball equipment shown to city

Since October 2023, the City of Piedmont has been involved with a lawsuit from a group of private citizens who claim that the City violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) by dedicating the courts without properly reviewing the noise effects it would have on the local community. Richard Drury, an attorney for the group of private citizens, said that the demonstration was a positive development for the neighborhood, but would not affect their lawsuit. “If anything, it proves that our lawsuit is meritorious,” said Drury. “We are arguing that the city should have done CEQA review to analyze feasible mitigation measures. Now the city has basically proven that we are right and there are feasible ways to reduce noise. [...] The city’s actions actually prove that they skirted the law.” As a matter of policy, the City of Piedmont does not comment on pending litigation.

articles.text: Piedmont School District has announced that they are now accepting nominations for the annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The previous winners are: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000) Lisa Lomenzo (2001) jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002) jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003) Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004) Cynthia Gorman (2005) Grier Graff (2006) Julia Burke (2007) Maude Pervere (2008) jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009) Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010) Andrea Swenson (2011) June Monach (2012) Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013) Ray Perman (2014) Jennifer Fox (2015) Katie Korotzer (2016) Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018) Cathy Glazier (2019) Sue Smegal (2020) Ken Li (2021) Eileen Ruby (2022) David Ragones in 2023 Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and at Oakland’s McClymonds High School. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982 and was an early supporter of Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by School Board member Dewey Watson in Hecht’s memory. The deadline for nominations is March 15. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 8 Board of Education meeting. articles.text: Ten Piedmont Middle School baseball players and their families will be traveling to Cuba during Spring Break, April 5-11, for a cultural exchange to see and experience the country through a love of baseball. The Piedmont team will be playing games against some of Cuba’s finest young players and will receive baseball training from experienced Cuban coaches. This trip is designed to be a once-in-a-lifetime experience for the students who will have the opportunity to play competitive baseball on Havana’s storied fields, meet and interact with Cuban youth, and develop memorable relationships. They will not only visit this beautiful island and learn about its history as they practice their Spanish speaking skills, but more importantly they will gain a valuable perspective about one of the world’s most unique countries. This exchange program is coordinated by Baseball Beyond Borders, a non-profit founded by former professional Cuban baseball player Michel Rodriguez, owner of 365 Baseball and Softball Academy. Michel started this organization to support the Cuban people and offer American kids the unique opportunity to connect with Cuban youth through a shared passion for baseball. The group is fundraising to support financial needs of players making the trip, uniforms, balls and the cost of a professional coach. Players will also be collecting baseball gear to donate to the Cuban youth baseball community. To help send the Piedmont team to Cuba and for more information, contact Mike Gray at mjgray@gmail.com. Piedmont Middle School students who will travel to Cuba during Spring Break include: Ryan McMurtry (left), Aidan Stewart, Mason Gray, Dylan Toyama, Jack Dahling, Ben McMurtry, Orion Sachs, Jonah ChaFoster, and Zachary Cha-Foster. Not pictured: Clemens Conrad.
articles.title: 10 middle school students going to Cuba

articles.text: If you’re in a relationship, here is your reminder that Valentine’s Day is coming up. If you happen to be single, hopefully you can get yourself some nice flowers and/or buy some of the chocolate on sale the day after Valentine’s Day. Since it’s the month of the most romantic holiday, I thought I would share some tips from Positive Psychology about love and relationships. I am a Positive Psychology and Relationship coach for neurodivergent people and anyone else who needs some help improving their lives. For those that aren’t familiar, positive psychology is a concentration within the greater field of psychology that looks at the science behind wellness and improving people’s lives. Relationships are fundamental for overall well being so much so that the World Health Organization has actually declared that loneliness is actually worse for your health than smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Since relationships are so fundamental to overall well being, I typically work on improving the relationships in my client’s lives and helping them to build new connections as well. For clients already in romantic relationships, one of the things that I work on is practicing expressing gratitude to your partner. For clients that are single and hoping to date, one of the solutions I offer is developing an understanding of one’s personal strengths throughout the dating process. Whether or not you’re in a romantic relationship, expressing gratitude to the people in your life is important. When you’ve been in a relationship for a long time, it’s easy to slip into a pattern where you’re not giving your full attention and appreciation to your partner often enough. Expressing gratitude is pretty much as simple as it sounds but remembering to do it can be more difficult. If you want to try this out, make a pact to say thank you to your partner once every day for something they’ve done or something you like about them. For clients who are single, one of the solutions I offer is being aware and having an understanding of their personal strengths throughout the dating process. Strength Spotting is the practice of noticing what you are good at and then relying on that strength during difficult moments and dating is full of difficult moments. For example, if one of your strengths is humor, then finding a way to laugh about a date that doesn’t exactly go as planned is a great way to utilize that strength. No matter your relationship status, Valentine’s Day is a great time to reflect on both romantic and platonic connections in your life. I feel so grateful to be able to work with people on building and improving their relationships with others and I appreciate you taking the time to learn a little bit more about positive psychology. Please don’t hesitate to reach out to me if you want to explore anything discussed in this article or want help improving the relationships in your life. Erica Monical is a Positive Psychology and Relationship Coach. You can contact her at mindsglowing@gmail.com or 415-689-8812.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post visited Beth Black’s freshman period 2 English class on Friday, January 26, to witness 9th graders pitch their topics of research which they will work on for the next nine weeks. Students in Black’s class – and all freshman students – have embarked upon the annual “I-Search” projects in which they will write four detailed essays, after some deep examination which includes an in-person interview. Seated in a circle, akin to a roundtable, Black instructed her students on “Topic Day” to state their choice of topic, three main questions they have, one fact and who they plan to interview. Selected topics showed a wide landscape of interests for students. The variety exemplified the strength of the project, which is to motivate students by allowing them to pick any topic. Some of the topics of research selected by students included “Dreams- Why they happen” by Gianluca Richmond, “The Dark side of K-Pop” by Ava Saephan, and “Pushing kids into sports too early” by Thomas Ero. In Black’s class students provided “audience support,” by giving suggested readings, videos and aspects to consider. For example, Claire Aubrecht plans to interview a plastic surgeon for her article exploring Beauty Standards. Brynne Jones added Piedmont High School English teacher Beth Black implores her students to dive deep into their topics. to the discussion to mention the 1800s practice of women cutting back their hairlines to achieve the aesthetic of the time, which was to have a large forehead. Black encouraged her students, to reach out to anyone, even famous or important people, to let go of reservations about the importance of their inquiry. Black mentioned a student last year who, through a lawyer, was able to correspond with a death-row inmate. “It’s not hard to reach out,” she said to her class, “it’s not difficult to try. It’s just an email or a phone call.” The freshman will learn valuable research skills such as writing a proposal and making a distinction between sources of information. The main essay will be four to six pages with at least five relevant sources. Black’s students took the task seriously, showing some care and forethought. Zoe Synder plans to look at the ethics of space exploration, while Yiyou Fang will conduct a study about “Free will.” The annual I-Search project has a free choice assignment aspect that allows students to show their skills in a medium of their choice. Seven options for students include: reviewing a nonfiction film, creating a visual aid, or observing a relevant site or activity. For the next nine weeks all PHS freshman English students will be completing their I-Search assignments, and learning crucial techniques to conduct and independently motivated inquiry. Freshman English class in Room 32 at PHS

articles.text: Amelia Addington plays the role of Sally Bowles. Piedmont High School presents the musical Cabaret the weekend of February 1-4 at the Alan Harvey Theater. Directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead. This Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draws to a close, explores the exhilarating life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. The use of swastikas and military uniforms have been omitted. Memorable songs from Cabaret include “Willkommen,” “Perfectly Marvelous,” “Money,” “Maybe This Time,” and the title song, “Cabaret”. More than 70 Piedmont and Millennium High School students are involved in this PG-13 version of the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal Direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to impact its audience and performers. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Schultz,” said sophomore Ben Wakefield. “The Israel-Hamas War, which unfolded during our rehearsal period, did impact my feelings about performing in Cabaret. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical. Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present.” Senior Ellie Broscow, who plays the role of Fräulein Schneider, added, “Cabaret is an incredibly important musical to me and has been for quite some time. My love for the show has definitely grown throughout the rehearsal process as I’ve realized just how relevant the themes still are, 58 years since its premiere on Broadway in 1996. The themes of anti-Semitism especially resonate with me after the events of October 7th. I have seen how the world has turned against the Jewish people throughout history, and Cabaret addresses a particularly intense period, 1929, or the rise of Hitler. The vivid anti-Semitism that existed then has continued to increase, especially right now, and we simply cannot turn a blind eye to it any longer. I hope that Cabaret will continue to be performed for years to come.” The show opens Thursday, February 1, with performances Friday through Sunday, February 2-4, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Ave., Piedmont. Tickets may be purchased online at https://www. showtix4u.com/event-details/ PHSCabaret or at the door for an additional $2.00 per ticket. Performances will be held at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts, 1428 Alice Street, Oakland, on February 9-11 and 16-18. A shot at college, internet fame, and attention from the one they like – the stakes are high at Plain Springs High’s first ever Dance-a-thon. As the demonic DJ transports them to dance crazes throughout history, each contestant must face their deepest desires and greatest weaknesses. Only one couple will walk out with “The Prize” and the rest won’t make it out alive. Commissioned by YMTC in 2014, Don’t Stop Me is a musical dance-a-thon to the death from Tony Award-nominated composer/lyricist Dave Malloy and award-winning playwright and former Julliard School fellow Krista Knight. The show features 21 student actors and five creative apprentices from cities throughout the Bay Area. One adult professional Charlotte Ragones Dahlia Saffouri actor, local favorite Kevin Singer, plays the role of the disc jockey. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, including Director Jennifer Boesing, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Janet Collard. The show includes a 7-piece pop/techno band playing Dave Malloy’s orchestrations. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $17–$38, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. YMTC offers one “pay what you will” performance on Friday, February 16, to provide affordable musical theater to all in the community. ABOUT YMTC YMTC is the Bay Area’s premiere pre-professional musical theater training organization. It brings together the Bay Area’s most talented and dedicated young performers – as well as students of technical theater and student musicians – with professional directors, designers, choreographers and musicians.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: First-ever league win over Berkeley Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team is surging at the right time. As its season winds down, the Highlanders put themselves in position to compete for the Western Alameda County Conference title after defeating Berkeley 1-0 on Tuesday, January 23 on the road, and against Castro Valley 1-0 two days later at Chabot College in Hayward. The victory over Berkeley marks the school’s first-ever win against the Yellowjackets since joining the Western Alameda County Conference in 2012. Berkeley routinely competes for the WACC Foothill Division crown and the top division of North Coast Section. PHS, meanwhile, was recently promoted to Div. 3 in the NCS. The team’s success is a reflection of the program’s growth under eight-year head coach Todd Sullivan. “It’s a very good week,” he said. “Our win over Berkeley was the first time we’ve ever done it as a varsity program in my years. It was a huge, huge defensive effort against Berkeley and we deserved the result. We improved in the second half but just didn’t have a lot of quality. But a win is a win,” he added. Piedmont’s game-winner against Berkeley came early from Enzo Bernales in the 24th minute when cleaning up a loose ball in the box. Against Castro Valley, Aidan Woolwine scored in the first minute of second-half stoppage time at 81’. It was a miracle-goal, where Woolwine sent a cross from the right wing to the far post, the ball bounced off the turf and was mishandled by CV’s keeper who landed on the ball and punched it into net for an own goal. “It was a cross. I was looking for either Bosco [Lorin] or Enzo in the back, and I guess I hit it weird and it had some spin to it. The goalie didn’t really know what to do with it, but a goal’s a goal. We count those around here,” said Woolwine with a laugh. The Highlanders now look ahead to the final four-games of its regular season schedule and have a chance to wrap up its Staff Photo Aidan Woolwine looks up in disbelief after scoring the game-winner in the 81st minute against Castro Valley. Photos by Scott Stratman Enzo Bernales (left) sends a right-foot volley for the game-winning goal against Berkeley. season on an inspirational note. With the possibility of Witter Field finally being available for games after a seven-month delay, Piedmont should be able to host Berkeley for a season-finale at Witter on February 8. I’ve wanted to play there from the jump. We wanted to get our season rolling because I know these guys are going to be pumped playing at Witter. It means everything to me. I am ready to get our NCS Championship run on,” said Woolwine “Berkeley is going to be looking for revenge and we learned about Bishop O’Dowd. The boys are massively motivated, not just to for a high ranking in Division 3 (NCS playoffs), but to get back to Witter. Some of these boys are really chomping at the bit to get a Witter appearance before they graduate,” said Sullivan. 1-0 shutout of Castro Valley Against Castro Valley, the Trojans controlled much of the early action with a chance that was saved by Axel Saldanha. Bernales had a shot blocked in the 23rd, while striker Oliver Shafroth had a shot blocked in the 36th. Harper Mand had a header from a corner go wide in the 37th. In the second half, Bosco Lorin had a looping header bounce off of the crossbar in the 51st minute. Woolwine had a good opportunity in the 63rd after receiving a long-ball from Bernales, but his shot sailed. After shot attempts by Andrew McLaughlin and Bernales couldn’t find home, the match went into stoppage time still tied at 0-0. That’s when Woolwine sent a long cross targeting the far post in the 81st minute. Castro Valley’s keeper mistakenly fell on Woolwine’s pass and pushed it into the net for an own goal. 1-0 win vs. Berkeley Sullivan converted his usual 4-3-3 formation to a 4-4-2 diamond to compress the midfield. articles.text: PHS romps: 55-20 over San Leandro, 64-47 over Castro Valley Staff Photos Natalia Martinez scored her 2,000th career point at Piedmont High School with a left-handed layup against San Leandro. Piedmont senior Natalia Martinez, a four-year starter on the basketball team, continued to etch herself into Piedmont High history. Finishing with 24 points in a 55-20 win at San Leandro on Wednesday, January 24, and officially scored her 2,000th career point for the Highlanders. She added 31 more points in a 64-47 win over Castro Valley two days later at Binks Rawlings Gym. Her record-setting 2,000th point came with 6:15 left in the fourth quarter against San Leandro after forcing a steal at midcourt, then racing to the hoop for a left-handed layup finish. “It’s going to take me a few days to process it all,” she said. “Honestly, I was going up with my left hand and I was thinking, ‘Don’t miss this.’ If this was how I’m going to do it, I thought a lefthand layup was the perfect way to get it,” she said. Martinez came to Piedmont by way of Millennium High as a freshman in 2020 and scored the historic number in her hometown of San Leandro. “It’s a reflection of how much work she’s put in and a testament to the time she’s put in,” said a proud coach, Bryan Gardere. “It’s always fun to watch players reach these different milestones and being able to celebrate it with her family and her team. It’s been a long journey. She started during COVID and had a shortened season, so she lost 10-15 games. “It’s going to be exciting to watch what she does with her career, and I’m excited for her,” Gardere added. Martinez is the second player in as many years to reach the figure after Trinity Zamora finished her career with over 2,000 points and 1,400 rebounds in 2023. Zamora is now at San Diego State, where Martinez will be playing next season. With five games left in the regular season, Piedmont holds a 15-4 overall record and is 4-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents. The team is on track for its second consecutive WACC title and a high seeding in the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs. Next week will be an important time to recapture the league crown. Piedmont faces Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland today, January 31, and face Alameda on Friday, February 2. 55-20 win over San Leandro Piedmont led 17-5 by the end of the first quarter and 28-8 by halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 45-13 in the third quarter, adding 10 more in the fourth while allowing seven for the 55-20 final. Martinez started the second half with eight points, but found her rhythm in the third quarter. Starting with converting three free throws, Natalia hit a 3-pointer after grabbing a rebound and turning up court, followed by Shakila Zuberi grabNatalia Martinez celebrates with her teammates as she comes off the court.

articles.text: PHS girls post 2-0 wins over Berkeley, Castro Valley Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored both goals in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Berkeley. In a highly successful week for the Piedmont High girls’ soccer team, the Highlanders defeated Berkeley 2-0 on Tuesday, January 24 and Castro Valley 2-0 two days later. Both matches were at Chabot College in Hayward. The pair of wins brings Piedmont’s record to 8-1-3 (W-T-L) overall and 2-1-3 against league competition. Castro Valley is currently in first-place of the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division at 4-1-1, and perennial contender Berkeley is 3-0-3. PHS has three matches left in its regular season. “We’re hitting form at the right time. It’s coming together nicely,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “Our second-half against Berkeley was some of the best football I have seen us play, including from previous seasons.” Piedmont is marching towards the end of its regular season with the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs on the horizon. An added motivation will be being able to play on Witter Field after playing the full season without a home field. PHS will host its first home game at Witter on Tuesday, February 6 against Bishop O’Dowd and will honor its eight seniors on the roster. “We’ll be having our first real home game at Witter on February 6 against O’Dowd for our Senior Night. The girls are really excited to get back to Witter, we really want to get a crowd,” said Chubbock. Liu leads PHS to 2-0 over Berkeley Berkeley controlled much of the first 20 minutes, but Piedmont stabilized and began to find rhythm towards the latter portion of the first half. Piedmont came out firing in the second half and got on the board In the 50th minute when Miranda Liu scored after receiving a pass from Elsa Wallway through the back line. Liu got around Berkeley’s center back for a first-touch shot that clanged off of the left post and into net. Liu struck again in the 61st minute, this time when outside back Elle Ruegg sent a long ball from the right side over the defense. Using her speed, Liu sprinted past the defense to create a one-on-one with the goalie. She took a touch around the keeper at the top of the penalty area for an easy tap in. 2-0 over Castro Valley Both teams traded possession for the entirety of the game, and the outcome looked like it would end in a 0-0 deadlock. But with four minutes left. coach Chubbock rotated Wallway from her forward role and into Hailey Marshburn’s usual central midfield spot. Moments later, Wallway wove her way into space around the top of the penalty area, rifling a shot from distance. It forced a diving save by CV’s keeper, but the ball rebounded back it into play. Marshburn instinctively pounced on the loose ball in front of the net, slotting it into net from close range. In the final minute, Castro Valley had a last gasp at goal on Lola Beihn launched in a goal from 45 yards out against Castro Valley to give PHS a 2-0 lead. Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont will play its first game at Witter Field on Tuesday, February 6, when it will host Senior Night. articles.text: Staff Photos Dillon Casey led scoring with 18 points against Bishop O’Dowd and Berkeley. He also scored 10 on El Cerrito. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team ran into some tough competition last week, losing to Bishop O’Dowd by five points at home 51-46 on Thursday, January 25, and lost to Berkeley 63-47 on the road on Saturday, January 27. The Highlanders got back on track with a dominant 62-15 win over El Cerrito at Binks Rawlings Gym on Monday, January 29. “We had two really tough games last week,” said coach Ben Spencer. “We had Bishop O’Dowd on the ropes and were up 46-41 with two minutes to go. They closed the game on a 10-0 run. We played good basketball, but missed a couple of open shots and they made them.” “Against Berkeley, we played them tough but didn’t shoot the ball well. The energy was there and the enthusiasm was there. We had a two-possession game late in the game, but didn’t make that big shot when we needed,” Spencer said. Piedmont now goes into a critical portion of the regular season with four games to play. They’ll host Alameda tonight, January 31, before traveling to St. Joseph in Alameda on Monday, February 5 and at San Leandro two days later. PHS closes its regular season against Castro Valley at Binks Rawlings Gym on February 9. “We have a big one against Alameda, and St. Joe is 4-4 against league teams as well. We’d love to finish the league on a strong note. Our last four games are league games, and going 4-0 against them would help push us to NCS,” said Spencer. 51-46 to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont had a strong first quarter to lead 13-7, but Bishop O’Dowd came back to tie 21-21 at the half and the two teams battled in the third quarter with 16 points apiece. However, the Dragons outscored Piedmont 14-9 in the fourth quarter to win, 51-46. BOD effectively shut down Piedmont’s leading scorer, Brit Burden, who was held to five points in the game. Sophomore Dillon Casey rose to the occasion and scored 18 points to lead the team. Final stats: Casey finished with 18 points, Declan Linnane Brit Burden scored 16 on Berkeley and 14 against El Cerrito, but was limited to five points against Bishop O’Dowd. P.J. Brayer drives in against El Cerrito.

articles.text: While mentioning the current athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can be easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers after moving on to college. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on February 2021. Morgan Hill is the site of a 1,147 acre park known for its waterfalls. On the eastern side of the Santa Cruz Mountains is Uvas Canyon County Park which you can reach at the end of the private Sveadal community on Croy Road. Hikers will be greeted to the sound of babbling brooks immediately when entering the park on the Waterfall Loop trail along Swanson Creek. The first and smallest cascade, Granuja Falls, provides a fitting welcome to visitors after the first bridge. After another half mile, hikers will find the base of the Black Rock Falls on the right. Follow the water up the narrow path to find the roughly 20-foot tall waterfall that passes over a black rock face barring its name. Returning back to the Waterfall Loop Trail for just 0.2 of a mile brings walkers to an intersection with the base of Upper Falls on the left, and a walkway to Basin Falls –which seemed to be the most thriving of the park after the rain. Basin Falls is about 15 feet, flowing down stones as it feeds into Swanson Creek. A fallen tree sits in its center to provide a clear perspective of its size. Returning to the Waterfall loop reunites you with Upper Falls, a two tiered cascade that is also around 15 feet. Passing the Black Rock Falls is around 20 feet and feeds into Swanson Creek. Upper Falls is about 15 feet and is situated near Basin Falls. articles.text: SF Ballet’s principal dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance in Marguerite and Armand on Wednesday, February 14. San Francisco Ballet Principal Dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance on Wednesday, February 14 at 7:30 p.m. dancing the role of Marguerite in Sir Frederick Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco from February 9 to 14. Born in Shanghai, Tan joined SF Ballet as a soloist in 1995 and was promoted to principal dancer two years later, making her the youngest and first Chinese principal dancer in the company’s history. Her unprecedented 29-year career at SF Ballet exemplified her devotion to dance and a passion to create art that is as elegant as it is human. Her repertoire has encompassed nearly 100 classical, neoclassical, and contemporary ballets choreographed by George Balanchine, Sir Kenneth MacMillan, John Neumeier, Christopher Wheeldon, Helgi Tomasson, Yuri Possokhov, Edwaard Liang, and Wayne McGregor, among others. Most notably, she has memorably interpreted classical characters such as Giselle, Aurora and Odette/Odile, as well as contemporary characters such as the Little Mermaid. As an international ambassador of ballet, she has been a symbol of ballet across the world. Since 2002, she has served as the artistic director and co-choreographer for the Tan Yuan Yuan and Her Friends production in China. In 2016, she established the Tan Yuan Yuan International Ballet Art Studio in partnership with the Shanghai Theater Academy. This community of patrons promoted ballet as a popular art form in China, enhanced cultural exchange between the U.S. and China, and gave rise to SF Ballet’s first two China tours in 2009 and 2015. Tan has been awarded the Mayor of San Francisco Art Award in 2018 and in 2022. She also received SF Ballet’s inaugural Silver Artists Society award in 2022, recognizing her 27th anniversary with the Company and longstanding contributions to SF Ballet. “Her grace, skill, versatility, and strength have helped her become the first Chinese prima ballerina in the United States and one of the greatest Chinese ballerinas of all time. She has gracefully served as a cultural ambassador for San Francisco and the U.S., said Mark Farrell, former San Francisco mayor. “I am indebted to my mentors and teachers, whose wisdom, encouragement, and belief in my potential have been instrumental in my success,” said Tan. “To my dancer colleagues, thank you for the shared moments of triumph. Through collective dedication and hard work, we have created a legacy that goes beyond individual accomplishments.” Tickets ($29-$465) to Yuan Yuan Tan’s farewell performance on February 14, or to prior performances of Marguerite and Armand February 9 to 14, may be purchased online at sfballet.org or by calling 415-865-2000.
articles.title: Yuan Yuan Tan final performance at SF Ballet on Feb. 14

articles.text: Opera San José’s 40th anniversary season continues with a thrilling production of Giuseppi Verdi’s Rigoletto, from February 17 through March 3. With some of the most memorable opera music of all time, including the signature aria “La donna è mobile,” this gripping work tells the tale of the jester Rigoletto, his innocent daughter Gilda, and the corrupt Duke of Mantua, whose callous treatment of women launches a storm of vengeance, murder and tragic self-sacrifice. The production is led by visionary director Dan Wallace Miller, acclaimed for his work with Seattle Opera and other national companies, with guest conductor Jorge Parodi making his OSJ debut. Rigoletto, Verdi’s 16th opera, is widely considered the first of the composer’s middle career masterpieces. The three-act opera made its world premiere at Teatro La Fenice in Venice, Italy on March 11, 1851, and was based on Victor Hugo’s controversial 1832 play Le Roi s’amuse (The King Amuses Himself). Set in 16th century Mantua, Italy, the opera follows a jester who struggles to balance the conflicting nature of beauty and evil in his life. “Rigoletto is one of opera’s timeless tragedies and Verdi’s most popular works as it embraces the many emotions we have as humans from cruel mockery and white-hot rage to heart-melting despair and undeniable love for family. This beloved opera is an indestructible, eternal testament to the sacrifices we make for our job, our loved ones and our honor,” said Opera San José General Director Shawna Lucey. The OSJ production features an exciting roster of talented singers, including baritone Eugene Brancoveanu in the title role of Rigoletto. Soprano Melissa Sondhi, Opera San José’s Wadhwani Artist-in-Residence who starred earlier this season as Juliet in Romeo and Juliet, returns in the role of Gilda, and tenor Edward Graves, recently seen as Gastone in San Francisco Opera’s La traviata, makes his Opera San Jose debut as the Duke of Mantua. “Classically Curious” night for Rigoletto will be held Friday, February 23, bringing together people ages 21 to 40 who are interested in deepening their involvement with opera. This program was created to introduce new audiences to opera, offering discounted tickets, behind-thescenes opportunities and social events that will connect young adult opera lovers. More information can be found at go.operasj.org/ClassicallyCurious. Tickets ($55–$195) for the performance at California Theatre (345 South 1st St., San Jose), are available at operasj.org, or by calling the box office at 408-437- 4450.
articles.title: Rigoletto opens at Opera San José Feb. 17

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes back Grammy-winning jazz pianist and composer Brad Mehldau to Zellerbach Hall this season for a concert on Sunday, February 10 at 8 p.m. He will perform the Bay Area premiere of his solo piano composition, 14 Reveries, along with selections from his Suite April 2020. Mehldau explores the terrain between improvisation and composition and influenced by French Impressionism. In his second performance of the 2023–24 season, he offers a recital of the work that reflects both jazz and classical influences, melding the two with pop sensibilities. “14 Reveries reflects on the interior experience we create from our own consciousness, independently of those around us... a meditation on the space a composer leaves between specific directions in the score that lets the beauty of the music reveal itself as it allows for new discovery,” he said. In a review of Mehldau’s world premiere performance of 14 Reveries in September 2023, the London Jazz News described it as “a new work which is neither straightforward nor simple, but is manifestly a very personal and special statement from one of the great musicians of our time.” As a pianist, Mehldau is widely praised for lyricism balanced with heady abstraction and innovation rooted in tradition. His influences and prolific recorded output have ventured into rock, pop, electronic music, bebop, blues and spiritual music. To date, he has released 12 trio recordings of original compositions and new arrangements of jazz standards and pop songs. He first performed at Cal Performances in 2006with the Brad Mehldau Trio with Larry Grenadier and Jeff Ballard. The group is now regarded among the great piano trios of jazz history. Tickets ($42-$98) for the show at Zellerbach Hall are available at calperformances.org, by phone at 642-9988 or in person at the ticket office Tuesday through Friday 12 to 5:30 p.m., and Saturday through Sunday 1 to 5 p.m. Cal Performances will present jazz pianist Brad Mehldau at Zellerbach Hall on Sunday, February 10.
articles.title: Brad Mehldau at Zellerbach Hall Feb. 10

articles.text: At any major U.S. museum exhibition, it is generally considered “poor form” to jump onstage, pull historic and priceless fashion pieces from their mannequins, and then try them on in a nearby mirror—usually to the horror of any nearby museum docents. Luckily, the de Young Museum has the next best thing. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style is the newest major exhibition to launch at the de Young Museum and the first ever to let audiences “try on” its dresses by using augmented reality mirrors provided on-site. The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (FAMSF) has partnered with Snap Inc., the parent company of the popular social media app Snapchat, to provide an experience they say will “bridge the gap between the digital and the physical” according to a press release. “This project showcases how Snapchat can support the arts by using augmented reality in innovative, impactful, and stylish ways,” said Rajni Jacques, Global Head of Fashion & Beauty at Snap Inc. “Our partnership with the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco is a testament to how augmented reality can infiltrate culture, encourage creativity and self-expression, and bring historic couture to life like never before.” The museum said that Fashioning San Francisco will examine the role of style as a marker of social identity. The exhibition draws mainly from the significant costume collections of the FAMSF, including a rich selection of high fashion and haute couture ensembles generously donated by Bay Area women philanthropists. The outfits featured include a 1955 “Soirée de Paris” dress by Yves Saint Laurent, a 1985 lamé outfit by San Francisco designer Kaisik Wong, and a 1987 velvet gown by Valentino. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style will be on view at the de Young Museum through August 11, 2024. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park. Tickets may be purchased online at www.famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Tickets may also be purchased in person at the admissions desk on a first-come, first-serve basis. The outfits featured in Fashioning San Francisco showcase the city’s history through its variety of trends over the years. One museum-goer “tries on” one of the dresses featured in the exhibition by using the museum’s augmented reality mirrors. ®
articles.title: Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style debuts at de Young Museum

articles.text: The first major survey exhibition of Native Indian artist Duane Linklater is on view at Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) through February 25. Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) will present the first major survey exhibition of Canadian Duane Linklater, the celebrated Omaskêko Ininiwak artist whose work explores the contradictions of contemporary Native Indian life. The exhibit Duane Linklater: mymothersside features more than 30 works by this artist, who has over the past decade become a leading voice in the contemporary art world, with important contributions to the 2022 Whitney Biennial and the 2023 Bienal de Saõ Paulo, in Brazil. The exhibition will survey the wide scope of Linklater’s practice, which encompasses painting, sculpture, video and performance. Based in North Bay, Ontario, Linklater has been celebrated for a conceptual and material practice that interrogates what he calls “the physical and theoretical structures of the museum” in relation to the exclusion of indigenous cultures past and present. His work references ancestral traditions from Moose Cree First Nation – from hunting to fur trading to berry gathering – alongside popular bands and films of his youth, including the English rock band The Cure and the American blues musician Taj Mahal. The exhibit includes structures made with teepee poles, highlighting the artist’s interest in reassembling one of the most ubiquitous symbols of Indigeneity. The large-scale architectural installations will be displayed alongside Linklater’s draped and folded teepee cover paintings, shaped canvases the artist uses a combination of digital printing and natural dyeing techniques. “We’re thrilled to partner with Duane Linklater on bringing his first survey museum exhibition to Berkeley, which will give our audiences the opportunity to discover one of today’s most vital and engaging artists,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director Julie Widholm. “Duane’s interest in reimagining the role of Indigenous art in traditional museum spaces engages the critical questions we want to explore at BAMPFA.” Berkeley Art Museum is located at 2155 Center Street on the UC Berkely campus. Hours of operation are 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($14 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa.org, or in-person at the museum desk.
articles.title: Duane Linklater show at Berkeley Art Museum through Feb. 25

articles.text: The 56th California International Antiquarian Book Fair is returning to San Francisco from Friday to Sunday, February 9 to 11, at Pier 27. The fair, held by the Antiquarian Booksellers’ Association of America, is widely recognized as one of the world’s largest exhibitions of antiquarian books for sale. More than 100 exhibitors from around the world will present rare books, maps, illustrations, historical documents and ephemera on a vast array of subjects. The fair encompasses art, science, medicine, literature, history, gastronomy, fashion, first editions, Americana, philosophy, and children’s books. This year, the fair welcomes international exhibitors from the UK, Argentina, Australia, Austria, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany and The Netherlands. An impressive number of U.S. exhibitors also highlight the This extremely rare first edition 1832 print will be on view at the California International Antiquarian Book Fair from February 9 to 11. It depicts what is believed to be one of the first machine-learning devices in history. wealth of material available stateside. One of the rare maps exhibited will be Augustus Chevalier’s stunning large-scale 1911 map of San Francisco, the premier map of the city following the San Francisco Earthquake and one of the most impressive and beautiful urban plans in the history of American mapmaking. The fair also boasts offerings in every conceivable genre including the first-ever catalog on the history of artificial intelligence from Novato book dealer Jeremy Norman. pages.text: Wednesday, January 31, 2024 17 Duane Linklater show at Berkeley Art Museum through Feb. 25 The first major survey exhibition of Native Indian artist Duane Linklater is on view at Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) through February 25. Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) will present the first major survey exhibition of Canadian Duane Linklater, the celebrated Omaskêko Ininiwak artist whose work explores the contradictions of contemporary Native Indian life. The exhibit Duane Linklater: mymothersside features more than 30 works by this artist, who has over the past decade become a leading voice in the contemporary art world, with important contributions to the 2022 Whitney Biennial and the 2023 Bienal de Saõ Paulo, in Brazil. The exhibition will survey the wide scope of Linklater’s practice, which encompasses painting, sculpture, video and performance. Based in North Bay, Ontario, Linklater has been celebrated for a conceptual and material practice that interrogates what he calls “the physical and theoretical structures of the museum” in relation to the exclusion of indigenous cultures past and present. His work references ancestral traditions from Moose Cree First Nation – from hunting to fur trading to berry gathering – alongside popular bands and films of his youth, including the English rock band The Cure and the American blues musician Taj Mahal. The exhibit includes structures made with teepee poles, highlighting the artist’s interest in reassembling one of the most ubiquitous symbols of Indigeneity. The large-scale architectural installations will be displayed alongside Linklater’s draped and folded teepee cover paintings, shaped canvases the artist uses a combination of digital printing and natural dyeing techniques. “We’re thrilled to partner with Duane Linklater on bringing his first survey museum exhibition to Berkeley, which will give our audiences the opportunity to discover one of today’s most vital and engaging artists,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director Julie Widholm. “Duane’s interest in reimagining the role of Indigenous art in traditional museum spaces engages the critical questions we want to explore at BAMPFA.” Berkeley Art Museum is located at 2155 Center Street on the UC Berkely campus. Hours of operation are 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($14 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa.org, or in-person at the museum desk. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style debuts at de Young Museum By Matt Simons At any major U.S. museum exhibition, it is generally considered “poor form” to jump onstage, pull historic and priceless fashion pieces from their mannequins, and then try them on in a nearby mirror—usually to the horror of any nearby museum docents. Luckily, the de Young Museum has the next best thing. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style is the newest major exhibition to launch at the de Young Museum and the first ever to let audiences “try on” its dresses by using augmented reality mirrors provided on-site. The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (FAMSF) has partnered with Snap Inc., the parent company of the popular social media app Snapchat, to provide an experience they say will “bridge the gap between the digital and the physical” according to a press release. “This project showcases how Snapchat can support the arts by using augmented reality in innovative, impactful, and stylish ways,” said Rajni Jacques, Global Head of Fashion & Beauty at Snap Inc. “Our partnership with the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco is a testament to how augmented reality can infiltrate culture, encourage creativity and self-expression, and bring historic couture to life like never before.” The museum said that Fashioning San Francisco will examine the role of style as a marker of social identity. The exhibition draws mainly from the significant costume collections of the FAMSF, including a rich selection of high fashion and haute couture ensembles generously donated by Bay Area women philanthropists. The outfits featured include a 1955 “Soirée de Paris” dress by Yves Saint Laurent, a 1985 lamé outfit by San Francisco designer Kaisik Wong, and a 1987 velvet gown by Valentino. Fashioning San Francisco: a Century of Style will be on view at the de Young Museum through August 11, 2024. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park. Tickets may be purchased online at www.famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Tickets may also be purchased in person at the admissions desk on a first-come, first-serve basis. The outfits featured in Fashioning San Francisco showcase the city’s history through its variety of trends over the years. One museum-goer “tries on” one of the dresses featured in the exhibition by using the museum’s augmented reality mirrors. ® R&S OVERHEAD R&S OVERHEAD GARAGE DOOR, INC. GARAGE DOOR, INC. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony & Friends continues its Chamber Series with Spirited Impressions on Sunday, February 4 at 4 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts. This vibrant and romantic concert will feature piano trios exploring a wide range of French music, including Gabriel Fauré’s Piano Trio No. 1 in D Minor; Arthur Honegger’s Sonatine for Violin and Cello; Bay Area composer Jean Ahn’s A Flashback of Ravel; and Claude Debussy’s Piano Trio in G Major. Musicians Alison Lee, piano; Sarah Elert, violin; and Douglas Machiz, cello, will present Faurè’s marvel of color, energy, and contrast in his Piano Trio, followed by the vivacity of Honegger’s Sonatine. Audiences will find themselves immersed in a Parisian landscape, with the striking melodies of Jean Ahn’s homage to Ravel’s Impressionist works, with a contemporary twist. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will celebrate the Lunar New Year with their Year of the Dragon concert and banquet with 4 p.m. pre-concert festivities, a 5 p.m. performance and a 6:30 p.m. post-concert feast on Saturday, February 17 at Davies Symphony Hall. Lunar New Year is the most important holiday for many cultures in East, South and Southeast Asia, and is celebrated by people of Asian descent worldwide. This year’s celebration marks the 24th anniversary of the SF Symphony’s signature event, an elegant celebration of the Lunar New Year drawing upon vibrant Asian traditions past and present. The celebration begins at 4 p.m. with pre-concert lobby festivities open to all ticket holders, featuring an array of entertainment and activities including dragon dancers, fortune readers, calligraphy artists, and cultural performances. Conductor Mei-Ann Chen and the orchestra will then open the concert with Li Huan-Zhi’s energetic Spring Festival Overture and Phoon Yew Tien’s joyful New Year Greetings. The orchestra will then perform Jasmine Flower, a folk song from China’s Jiangsu province, which was arranged for orchestra by Li Wenping in 1999. The program continues with Flower Drum Song from Feng Yang and Girl from Da Ban City from Huang Ruo’s Folk Songs for Orchestra, originally commissioned and performed by the San Francisco Symphony at their 2012 Chinese New Year concert. Also on the program is Vivian Fung’s Pizzicato, which features sounds inspired by two Chinese instruments — the pipa and qin — as well as Indonesian gamelan music. Violinist Paul Huang will join the Symphony to play music from Tan Dun’s violin concerto, Fire Ritual, originally written for and premiered by violinist Eldbjørg Hemsing. Concluding the program are Che Chang’s Ali Mountain Evergreen, a piece that evokes the staggering scale of Ali Mountain in Taiwan, and Chen Ge Xin’s Gong Xi Gong Xi, a popular Chinese Lunar New Year song that translates to “Congratulations” or “Wishing You Happiness and Prosperity.” The post-concert Lunar New Year Banquet begins at 6:30 p.m. in Zellerbach Rehearsal Hall, located at 300 Franklin Street at the rear of Davies Symphony Hall. This event will feature a lucky draw and live music. The banquet will be catered by McCalls Catering & Events, with lighting design by Got Light. The décor for the event will feature hanging screens that highlight the many ways that Lunar New Year is celebrated across different cultures. Proceeds from the event support the Symphony’s artistic, education, and community programs. Tickets for the concert ($39- $109) and information about individual and full banquet table reservations can be found for purchase at sfsymphony.org, or through the box office at 415- 864-6000. San Francisco Symphony’s Lunar New Year concert returns on Saturday, February 17.

articles.text: Part 1 If the film industry is a barometer, it seems we have turned a corner and found a semblance of long-awaited normalcy with this year’s announcement by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences of its list of movies released in 2023 to be honored. This 96th Academy Awards ceremony, with all its incandescent glitter and haute couture, will take place at the Dolby Theater in Hollywood on March 10, 2024. It will be televised live on ABC beginning at 4:00 p.m., with late night host Jimmy Kimmel as host. Of course, the question begged is does the return to normalcy mean that the filmmaking industry has found its pre-pandemic audience? Will millions again tune in to the awards ceremony having seen some, if not most, of the movies nominated? We’ll see. Find below those categories that seem to garner moviegoers’ attention. Look for Part 2 in next week’s paper.

Germaine Tailleferre was the only female member of the group of “les 6”, a group of French composers forging a new voice in the early 20th century. In this quartet, we can hear her fresh, humorous voice, written over the course of 2 years and published in 1919 at the end of the Great War. A superb talent, her music is sadly not heard often enough. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. Intended to be part of a full length string quartet, this piece is no doubt a short musical journey through the joys and fears of young love. Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous, begins with two notes and is said to be a musical way of saying his wife’s name, Clara. Always lyrical, tonally lush, and beautiful, it is a work not to be missed.

I raised my hand and asked: “what about PDQ Bach?” You see, I wanted to show my erudition. Michael Tilson Thomas was seated on my right. He looked at me and said: “Haven’t you heard of Peter Schikele?” I realized that I had made a grievous historical error. I tried to save face and pretended that I knew who he was talking about. In reality, I had absolutely no idea. And in that way Professor Peter Schickele got the last laugh. That’s the way comedy works. A superb talent, her music is sadly not heard often enough. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. Intended to be part of a full length string quartet, this piece is no doubt a short musical journey through the joys and fears of young love. Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous, begins with two notes and is said to be a musical way of saying his wife’s name, Clara. Always lyrical, tonally lush, and beautiful, it is a work not to be missed. articles.text: And it is in this sweet spot that Stephen King resides, coming at it from a myriad of angles with a prolific talent that seems without end. What King understands, and this is his genius, is that it is part of human nature to carry a nugget of unresolved uneasiness, of a willingness to suspend one’s disbelief, and enter into that dark geography that haunted us as kids. It’s why standing on the top step of a dark basement, the ominous smells wafting up, then turning on the light switch and finding that the lights aren’t working so resonates. And therein is the power and effectiveness of the film It. Using the image of the benign and joyful clown, King takes the expected and transforms it into the most frightful. Part of the brilliance of this film, set in the small town of Derry, Maine in 1989, is that it opens with seven middle-schoolers, all just released from school with the summer stretching before them. At the outset they are not a crew, though each resides on that outcast edge of the school experience. A scene from It They slowly come together and tentatively share their individual encounters with a shape-shifting clown called Pennywise (Bill Scarsgard). In fact, the initial set up of the movie begins with Bill Denbrough (Jaeden Lieberher) constructing a small boat made out of heavy paper for his younger brother, Georgie (Jackson Robert Scott), who wants to go outside and play in the rain and float the boat in the water-filled gutters while he chases behind. That is until the boat disappears into a storm drain. Of course Georgie kneels down and looks into the opening and there, holding the boat, is Pennywise. What is also immensely important is that Pennywise begins to represent those moments of disbelief and then terror, eliciting from the kids their personal anxieties and apprehensions and unresolved fears that will remain with them for a lifetime. Realize that you are not watching a horror film per se. Though King is thought of as a master of the genre, it’s a shallow definition. Know that it is not Pennywise who is at the center of the story; rather, it is the kids, as a group and as individuals, that give this film its essence and texture. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 31, 2024 MOVIE FOR ADULTS By Chris Honoré When I was 11 years old, my dad took me to see a sci-fi film titled The Thing. I was simultaneously riveted and terrified. There was one scene in which the Thing, an enormous, manlike creature from another world. stood on one side of a door and two scientists stood on the other side, debating about turning the knob. It’s a familiar trope, but for me as a kid whose imagination could slip into overdrive at even the prospect of walking down the stairs into a dark, dank basement, that moment to this day remains unforgettable. I think of it as the metacreepy, hair-raising sweet spot. Put another way, it’s that place where our labyrinth of fears reside, fears that can define part of our childhood. Kids are not as insulated from the terrifying as are adults who are more jaded by their life experiences. Using the image of the benign and joyful clown, King takes the expected and transforms it into the most frightful. Part of the brilliance of this film, set in the small town of Derry, Maine in 1989, is that it opens with seven middle-schoolers, all just released from school with the summer stretching before them. At the outset they are not a crew, though each resides on that outcast edge of the school experience. A scene from It They slowly come together and tentatively share their individual encounters with a shape-shifting clown called Pennywise (Bill Scarsgard). In fact, the initial set up of the movie begins with Bill Denbrough (Jaeden Lieberher) constructing a small boat made out of heavy paper for his younger brother, Georgie (Jackson Robert Scott), who wants to go outside and play in the rain and float the boat in the water-filled gutters while he chases behind. That is until the boat disappears into a storm drain. Of course Georgie kneels down and looks into the opening and there, holding the boat, is Pennywise. What is also immensely important is that Pennywise begins to represent those moments of disbelief and then terror, eliciting from the kids their personal anxieties and apprehensions and unresolved fears that will remain with them for a lifetime. Realize that you are not watching a horror film per se. Though King is thought of as a master of the genre, it’s a shallow definition. Know that it is not Pennywise who is at the center of the story; rather, it is the kids, as a group and as individuals, that give this film its essence and texture. Each is dealing with standing at the top of the basement stairs and finding that the light switch is broken and with massive amounts of will each takes one step then a second into that space defined by their own imaginations. The novel It is over 1,000 pages long and is divided into two parts. This film adaption focuses just on the kids; it’s also subtitled, while the end credits roll, as Chapter One. In the denouement of Chapter One, the seven kids stand in a circle and take an oath, swearing to return to Derry if ever need be. And so they do in chapter two. articles.text: Thomasin McKenzie and Ben Foster in Leave No Trace Leave No Trace opens with a father, Will (Ben Foster), and his teenage daughter, Tom (Thomasin McKenzie), preparing chopped kindling for a fire. Slowly the camera pulls back and it gradually becomes obvious that where they are staying is not a temporary shelter, erected for one night before moving on. There is a permanence to what is revealed: a tent, a canopy of tarps, one to trap rainwater, a small butane cook stove; this is home. The place is Forest Park, a 5,000-acre wilderness just outside Portland, Ore., and Will and Tom are, in effect living off the grid. It’s an interesting distinction, the term “living off the grid,” and being homeless, living on the urban streets of a city like Portland. For Will and Tom, it’s a purposeful choice to live in a place apart and for them being “off the grid” is a term of art, a philosophy, a value judgment as well as a kind of lifestyle shorthand. And so, stripped of all extraneous societal distractions, Leave No Trace has at its center the tender and subtle relationship between father and daughter as they go about their self-sufficient days, gathering mushrooms, greens, preparing meals, rehearsing what they must do if discovered by “them.” On occasion, they walk into town to buy necessary supplies using money Will receives from selling his veteran PTSD meds to homeless vets. As for backstory, the cause of Will’s intentional retreat, with Tom, into the woods, is only hinted at. There is a moment, in the dead of night, when he wakes to the sound of a helicopter overhead that only he can hear. Hyperventilating, he struggles to find firm ground. It is Will who has constructed their lives as they are, to leave as soft a trace as possible. And Tom mirrors his gentle spirit, something that is reflected in their spare conversation and silent interaction all of which convey the depth and strength of their bond as well as their fundamental kindness. And it is that bond that frames this remarkable and moving film, an allegory, a poem, really, so beautifully made, so intimately told, so universal, an exemplum of how life can ever so unexpectedly shift the prism through which we observe its elusive meaning. Tension is introduced when the “the grid” intrudes into Tom and Will’s delicately eco-balanced lives. It is painful to watch as Tom opens up to other aspects of life and to community while Will’s reflexive reaction is to retreat. Leave No Trace is directed by Debra Granik whose breakout film was Winter’s Bone. She is a gifted filmmaker who can capture in image and interaction the muted vagaries of the human condition, most especially that period in a young person’s life often referred to as the rite of passage. The performances offered by Ben Foster, one of the best actors working today, and Thomasin McKenzie, a Kiwi who is new to Hollywood, are simply exceptional. Each is able to capture with a subdued expression, a discerning glance, emotions that require no exposition. Even for Will it is impossible to go through life in the presence of others and leave no trace. This is a truth that bears down on him; however, at great personal cost, he still must try. Leave No Trace. Directed by Debra Granik, Starring Ben Foster, Thomasin McKenzie, Jeff Kober. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/apple tv.

articles.text: Let’s say you’re about 12 or 13 and looking to spend a couple of hours being severely entertained, wanting the world outside to drop away, the demands of peers and school to vanish. What better way to escape than to scrunch down on the sofa and watch Race to Witch Mountain starring Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock. Witch Mountain is a smorgasbord of stuff that kids enjoy: two teenage ETs, Sara (AnnaSophia Robb) and Seth (Alexander Ludwig), whose space craft crashes on earth, and are desperate to return home. Government agents, led by Burke (Cirian Hinds), having recovered their ship and are in the hunt to find the aliens so they can study them in a federal facility. Plus there’s an alien ironclad terminator sent to kill them; a super-sized father figure in the form of Jack Bruno (Johnson) who has taken them under his muscular wing. There are lots of edgy chase scenes and close calls; an ET/SF Las Vegas convention with tons of Trekies and Star War geeks; and loads of piled-on special effects. Just perfect. Of course, kids will watch Race to Witch Mountain uncritically, ignoring the lame plot and dialogue. Nor will said filmgoers point out to their peers that Seth and Sara, who have a truckload of ET powers, don’t always use their powers, even when in a really, really tight spot. Case in point would be Sara, who can shoot energy bolts using the tip of her finger and holds off, even with the Feds closing in. Wouldn’t you use the standby energy bolt? But no matter, this is a spiffy movie that will keep young moviegoers pretty much riveted. Race to Witch Mountain. Directed by Andy Fickman. Starring Dwayne Johnson, AnnaSophia Robb, Alexander Ludwig, Carla Gugino and Cirian Hinds. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/ prime/Disney+/apple tv. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Spanish-style Red Lentil Soup is a classic warm meal on a cold winter night. This is the time of year when we look to lighten up our meals and lighten up cooking duties after months of large holiday meals. This soup checks the boxes for both and can be made from a well-stocked Piedmont pantry. Bonus: it scales up nicely to feed a crowd! The list of ingredients looks long, but many of the items are “staples” in many kitchens. The spices and even vegetables can be changed up to suit your taste. I’m not a fan of cooked carrots; I think they can take the dish in a too-sweet direction. But if that’s what you love about carrots, then you know what to do… Note: Soaking the saffron in liquid (wine or water) in preparation for cooking is called “blooming”, which draws the most flavor out of the most expensive spice (by weight) in the world. Spanish-Style Red Lentil Soup Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil • 1 medium onion, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1 cup • 2 stalks celery, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1 cup • 1 red pepper, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1 cup • 2 small carrots, diced in 1/4-inch bits, about 1/ 2 cup • 3 – 4 cloves garlic, minced, about 1 tablespoon • 1 bay leaf • 2 teaspoons Mediterranean oregano, dried • 1 tablespoon sweet paprika • 1 teaspoon smoked paprika • 1/2 teaspoon piment d’esplette, or to taste (substitute cayenne pepper) • 1/8 teaspoon saffron threads, crumbled and “bloomed” in 2 tablespoons of dry white wine or water • 1 can diced tomatoes, 14.5 ounces (Use fire-roasted for extra flavor, but regular are fine.) • • • • • • 1-1/2 cups dried red lentils 1 quart low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth 2 cups of water, or as needed to obtain desired consistency Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste Fresh lemon wedges and additional extra-virgin olive oil to drizzle at serving Parsley for garnish INSTRUCTIONS Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a 4-quart saucepan over medium-high heat until it just begins to shimmer. Add the onion and celery, stir together and sauté until softened – about 3 minutes. Add the red pepper, carrots, and garlic and continue cooking until the all are softened and aromatic – another 3–4 minutes. Add the bay leaf, oregano, both paprikas, and piment d’esplette, then stir well to combine. Add in the saffron and the blooming liquid, and canned diced tomatoes. Finally add the 1-quart of stock and 2 cups of water. Stir all to combine well. Cover and bring to a slow boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer until the lentils are tender, about 20-30 minutes. With an immersion blender, use short bursts to coarsely puree the soup. Alternatively, remove about half of the soup to a food processor or regular blender and pulse a few times to achieve a coarse texture. Add the pureed portion back to the pot. The soup should be a bit chunky. Taste and adjust seasonings to suit. Ladle the soup into bowls, then drizzle with olive oil and a spritz of fresh lemon juice. Garnish with flat-leaf parsley and serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 8, 2020.
articles.title: Spanish-Style Red Lentil Soup

Finally add the 1-quart of stock and 2 cups of water. Stir all to combine well. Cover and bring to a slow boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer until the lentils are tender, about 20-30 minutes. With an immersion blender, use short bursts to coarsely puree the soup. Alternatively, remove about half of the soup to a food processor or regular blender and pulse a few times to achieve a coarse texture. Add the pureed portion back to the pot. The soup should be a bit chunky. Taste and adjust seasonings to suit. Ladle the soup into bowls, then drizzle with olive oil and a spritz of fresh lemon juice. Garnish with flat-leaf parsley and serve.
