articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson We all know that winter isn’t peak fruit season. Yes, this time of year brings plenty of citrus, and one can certainly harvest what the French call les fruits de mer, including delightful Dungeness crab. But don’t be fooled by the paucity of locally grown fruit at the grocery store. Now is the perfect time to start planting and pruning fruit trees in your garden. A few winters ago, I ordered bare-root fruit trees through the mail. I was nervous. It seemed counterintuitive that one could ship saplings halfway across the country without soil. It took me a week to get around to planting them, and then I had to wait two months to see what would happen. I was pleasantly surprised – they all leafed out beautifully. Bare-root fruit trees usually cost less than the ones in pots and are almost as easy to plant. The hole you dig should be twice as wide as the spread of the tree’s roots but not too deep. To keep the bare roots from compacting, ask a friend to hold the tree in place while you fill in the soil. Make a mound with a donut around it to catch irrigation water. Ideally, the trunk will be one to two inches above ground level once you fill in the soil. I’ve been particularly happy with my bare-root apple trees. The variety known as Arkansas Black, as the name suggests, has a deep purple skin that is nearly black at maturity. In keeping with the French / espalier theme, Diane Louvel, a French friend visiting from New York, stands next to a cherry tree. Josh Harkinson stands next to an apple tree with espalier. The Pink Pearl, a yellow apple with strikingly pink flesh, was developed in 1944 by Northern California breeder Albert Etter by crossing a conventional apple with red-fleshed Russian crab apple. Both varieties grew quickly, fruited profusely in the second year, and taste great. Fruit trees don’t necessarily require a lot of space. During the Middle Ages, Europeans wanted to plant them inside castle courtyards. The technique they developed, now known as espalier, is a French word deriving from the Italian spalliera, meaning “something to rest the shoulder (spalla) against.” It refers to the trellises that train the branches of fruit trees to grow horizontally, but there are also espalier techniques that require little in the way of infrastructure. Espalier works best with apples and pears. I planted my apple trees next to a waist-high picket fence and allowed them to shoot straight up. After they’d shed their leaves for the winter, I bent the branches sideways until they were parallel with the fence and secured them with twine. The following winter, I pruned to maintain the two-dimensional shape. I cut off most of the twigs but retained some of the tallest new shoots – two- or three-feettall growths from the original espaliered branches – and bent them back the other direction, securing them with twine. After a couple of years, I had a living fence that was more than six feet tall. For other types of fruit, you can often find dwarf varieties adapted to our climate. It’s a bit too cold in this part of the East Bay for sweet cherries, but I have a dwarf sour cherry tree that produces bucketloads of fruit every year and makes fantastic pies. And while pomegranates also prefer more heat than we get, I planted a pomegranate hedge on the south-facing edge of my driveway, which acts like a heat island. After about five years it has started to yield some great fruit. The only problem comes in late fall when I must choose between scratching my car or lopping off some nice pomegranates before they’ve ripened. As the French and Americans would say, c’est la vie. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening.

articles.text: A few longtime members of the Piedmont Seniors celebrate the holiday season at the Claremont Country Club. On December 14, a total of 50 Piedmont Seniors and guests had a special holiday luncheon at Claremont Country Club. The Garden Room was festively decorated with strands of garlands attached to the ceiling as well as a colorful Christmas tree by the fireplace. The occasion was augmented by a pianist who played both holiday and other well-known tunes. Adding to the festivities, there was an optional gift exchange where the group selected wrapped packages with others who brought gifts to swap. The luncheon consisted of butternut squash soup, cordon blue chicken breast, spinach and mushroom crepes, and ice cream dosed with chocolate sauce. To make this get-together even sweeter there were assorted holiday candies at each place setting. This luncheon has become an annual tradition, as the Piedmont Seniors look forward to marking the holiday season each year. The Seniors have been going to the Claremont County Club during the holidays for approximately 20 years. The Claremont Country Club was established in 1897 and has become a favorite spot as it is conveniently located near Piedmont and upper Rockridge areas. The Claremont’s Tudor style clubhouse has become a sanctuary for those seeking a respite from the “hustle and bustle” of everyday life. If you are interested in learning more about the Piedmont Seniors, including meetings and excursions, contact Janet Epstein, Coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.us. The Seniors are a very welcoming group and are always looking to meet new members. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to participate in the activities. Pictured are Jim Ayotte (left), Gregory Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Mona Jamieson, and Fred Pemberton. Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 3820 Broadway, Oakland

Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Article reprinted from Piedmont Post on January 18, 2023. Dear MacMama: I just brought home a new MacBook Air, and the salesperson at the Apple store told me I can use iCloud to sync my items from my older computer to my new one. How does that work exactly? I don’t actually understand how iCloud works. –Oliver D., Piedmont Dear Oliver: Simply said, Apple’s iCloud is a storage service that can both store your files and sync them across all your devices. But there is much more to iCloud. We use it to sync contacts, reminders, calendars, and photos. We use it to store documents, folders, and passwords. If your computer has OS Catalina or later, when you turn on location services, you can use it to find misplaced iPhones, air pods, and Apple watches. If we use Air Tags, we can keep track of almost any item like wallets, keys, and anything to which we can attach an Air Tag. If your older Mac had OSX Yosemite or later, you can turn on iCloud Drive, enable “Desktop and Documents” and then all items on your desktop and in your “documents” folder will be stored in iCloud. They will still exist on your computer, and any other device in which you were signed in with the same Apple ID and have enabled iCloud Drive. This is great for people who have more than one device and need to keep their files in sync. So, for example, since I have iCloud enabled, if I work on a file in one computer, as soon as my other computer connects to the Internet, that file will be updated. And all my files are on both machines. If the operating system on your old computer is current enough and iCloud is enabled, you can set up the new computer, sign into iCloud, and these files will be downloaded onto your new computer. The same goes for photos, contacts and calendars. But this is not a complete solution for moving all your data over. For example, if you purchased Microsoft applications, Adobe applications, any non-Apple applications that don’t come on your machine from the factory, these will not transfer over with iCloud. And if you organize your mail into local folders, meaning the folders that exist in Apple Mail under the heading “On My Mac”, these will also not transfer over. So, in some cases, using Time Machine (assuming you have been backing up your old machine with Time Machine to an external drive) is a better way to transfer your data from an old machine to a new one. There are so many features in iCloud that it would take much more than this column to explain them all. Even if you use Time Machine on an external drive from your previous computer, in many cases, it is still prudent to enable iCloud to store and sync your desktop and documents. This acts as a cloud back up and makes these files accessible on your iPhone and iPad on the “Files” app, assuming the operating system on your device is current enough. There have been so many times that I have been without my computer, and somebody needs a file very quickly, and I have been able to email it by accessing my computer files right from my iPhone. Of course, keeping all our personal data, as well as sensitive data in a cloud storage system has its risks. Although Apple takes privacy seriously and protects your information by encrypting it when it’s in transit and storing it in an encrypted format, there are always security risks. It’s really important to use a secure password for your Apple/iCloud ID. It’s not just Apple that has security risks. Dropbox, Google Drive, any cloud storage is vulnerable to security breaches. But used wisely, with a good secure password, iCloud can be a real timesaver.. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: The start of the New Year gives us a good reason to start anew. It’s time to take another look at the level of care we provide. If we can improve one area to make our caregiving lives a little easier, life will be better for us and our loved ones. Why not build on the momentum of others setting and working toward their New Year’s resolutions? While some focus on the typical goals to lose weight, eat right and stop smoking, how about setting a goal to find a healthy balance between self-care and care for a loved one? Easier read than done, right? Yet, you can avoid the potential for caregiving burnout when you use the right tools. Three Tips for Caregivers There are a number of tools to help caregivers better manage and even lighten the load. We’ll begin with three important ones. 1 Learn as much as you can to know what to expect. Most of us have wondered, how hard can it be to provide care for someone? Let’s just say, there’s more to it than meets the eye. Avert the sinking feeling knowing that what you see is just the tip of the iceberg. The massive responsibility you’ll undertake is hidden and you’ll have to dive deeper to learn about what you should expect. Let’s say you’re caring for a person with dementia, learn what kind of dementia; it could be Alzheimer’s, Lewy body, vascular, Parkinson’s, or rarer forms such as frontotemporal. It is important to also learn what stage of the disease a person is. In the early stages of dementia, a person is fairly independent with minimal care needs. Later on, cognitive impairing diseases like Alzheimer’s, require continual reminders and then assistance with the activities of daily living such as eating, toileting, bathing and dressing. 2 Find others like you in a support group. Caregiving can be an isolating experience. There are thousands of caregiver support groups that meet in-person and online around the world. Ideally, find and attend a few focused on people caring for the same disease or illness. Participate in a few until you find one you feel comfortable attending that meets your needs. Depending on where you live, you could attend one in person while receiving respite care for your loved one. Get help in locating appropriate support groups by contacting organizations’ hotlines. You could also attend online and, for a change of pace, attend one in another area or country; although, it will be harder to learn about local resources. We all need someone who speaks the same language, understands and laughs at the same jokes. We need someone who has our back when we feel uncertain and weakened by the weight of our responsibilities. Find the right support group and you’ll find these and more. 3 Get Help: You Can’t Do It Alone. No (wo)man is an island. We’re all interconnected and need one another if we’re to survive and thrive. Fortunately, there are resources to help caregivers for the long run. You’ve undoubtedly heard, caregiving is not a sprint, it’s a marathon. In any long distance race the key to crossing the finish line is to pace yourself. For us slower runners, it includes taking water, bathroom and snack breaks thanks to the volunteers at various points along the route. Similarly, there are many resources along the caregiver’s journey. It makes sense to pace yourself while taking regular respites to regain enough balance and energy to finish this caregiving marathon. Start the New Year right and use these three tools to lighten your caregiving load as you balance self-care with care for your loved one. Learn as much as you can about your care recipient’s disease or illness, attend a support group in person or online, and use your community’s resources such as in-home and adult day care in order to cross the finish line of caregiving. articles.text: It had rained earlier in the morning and it looked like there could be some more last Wednesday, however, the uncertain weather didn’t stop 24 walkers and one K-9 best friend from a stroll in central Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesday group decided to revisit the history of Walter Blair, the first European settler on the area, and go the site of his original Blair’s Park on what is now the north side of Moraga Avenue. This park was an attraction Blair created to get people to come to his Piedmont Springs Hotel that he built in 1872, and where the Exedra is today. Blair came to California from Vermont during the gold rush in 1852 at the age of 22 with $100. In 1852 he purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. His land was most of the area between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia and Grand Avenues. Blair’s original home was where 111 Highland Avenue is today with its back on today’s Waldo Avenue. He started as a dairy farmer and established Blair’s Dairy at the corner of today’s Blair and El Cerrito Avenues. His cattle grazed in pastures that ran to Grand Avenue. He also developed a quarry where Dracena Park is today. The walkers went down Highland Avenue and found the site of Blair’s home. When they got to the end of the street more of Blair’s history was shared. He was an entrepreneur and partnered with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to Piedmont Avenue. In 1878 he decided to build his own line from where the Piedmont Avenue line ended at the gates of the Mountain View Cemetery to the Piedmont Springs Hotel. To increase ridership in 1884 Blair developed 40 acres of the land between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park, which he named “Blair’s Park.” It had an entrance arch at what is now the corner of Highland and Moraga Avenues and offered many ascensions. Many of these picnickers and hotel guests purchased land and became Piedmont’s early residents. Blair died in 1888 and was only 57 years old. Blair Avenue in Piedmont is named for him. After his death Blair Park was purchased in 1890 by a company that operated a cable car up Oakland Avenue. However, the company went into receivership in 1893. Blair’s heirs owned the park land, but in 1897 all of Blair’s remaining 235 acers, including Blair’s Park, were for sale. In 1901 the park was abandoned, and in 1902 Frank C. Havens’ land development syndicate owned the park land. By 1913 the land was vacant, but in 1917 builder Guy Turner built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue and at least six more in 1922. The walkers looked across Moraga Avenue where the original entrance to Blair Park was located and took a group photo. They made their way down Moraga passing Turner’s homes and came to the gate entrance of a nine-unit apartment building that was built in 1914. Two gardeners were working in the yard, and the group asked if they could come in. Permission was granted and the group enjoyed Walter Blair the beautiful garden and view of San Francisco. The group continued down Moraga to the Oakland/Piedmont city line at Pleasant Valley Avenue, and went on Ronada Avenue, to Parkside Drive cul-de-sac, and then up to Ronada, Ramona, and Estrella Avenues. A right on Bonita Avenue and a left on Park Way brought got the walkers to Waldo and Blair Avenues, and a chance to once again remember Walter Blair. They arrived back at the Exedra just as the moisture could no longer to be called mist. The group had escaped the rain and enjoyed a fun three-mile walk and an almost entirely dry morning together. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. On hand for last week’s Wednesday Walk were: Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Judith Lee, Charlene Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Land, Lisa Euphrat, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Peggy Shultz, Gloria DaSilva, Rick Eigenbrode, Lori Austin, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Maricela Negron, Dottie Hutch, Dave DeRoche, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Christiana Miller, Elizabeth Richter, Claudine Bach, and Dick Carter. 12-MONTHS FINANCING 0% INTEREST WE PAY TAX SALE* *on all installed jobs CL#788850

pages.text: Wednesday, January 31, 2024 25 Starting the New Year right: 3 tips for caregivers By Benjamin Bloom The start of the New Year gives us a good reason to start anew. It’s time to take another look at the level of care we provide. If we can improve one area to make our caregiving lives a little easier, life will be better for us and our loved ones. Why not build on the momentum of others setting and working toward their New Year’s resolutions? While some focus on the typical goals to lose weight, eat right and stop smoking, how about setting a goal to find a healthy balance between self-care and care for a loved one? Easier read than done, right? Yet, you can avoid the potential for caregiving burnout when you use the right tools. Three Tips for Caregivers There are a number of tools to help caregivers better manage and even lighten the load. We’ll begin with three important ones. 1 Learn as much as you can to know what to expect. Most of us have wondered, how hard can it be to provide care for someone? Let’s just say, there’s more to it than meets the eye. Avert the sinking feeling knowing that what you see is just the tip of the iceberg. The massive responsibility you’ll undertake is hidden and you’ll have to dive deeper to learn about what you should expect. Let’s say you’re caring for a person with dementia, learn what kind of dementia; it could be Alzheimer’s, Lewy body, vascular, Parkinson’s, or rarer forms such as frontotemporal. It is important to also learn what stage of the disease a person is. In the early stages of dementia, a person is fairly independent with minimal care needs. Later on, cognitive impairing diseases like Alzheimer’s, require continual reminders and then assistance with the activities of daily living such as eating, toileting, bathing and dressing. 2 Find others like you in a support group. Caregiving can be an isolating experience. There are thousands of caregiver support groups that meet in-person and online around the world. Ideally, find and attend a few focused on people caring for the same disease or illness. Participate in a few until you find one you feel comfortable attending that meets your needs. Depending on where you live, you could attend one in person while receiving respite care for your loved one. Get help in locating appropriate support groups by contacting organizations’ hotlines. You could also attend online and, for a change of pace, attend one in another area or country; although, it will be harder to learn about local resources. We all need someone who speaks the same language, understands and laughs at the same jokes. We need someone who has our back when we feel uncertain and weakened by the weight of our responsibilities. Find the right support group and you’ll find these and more. 3 Get Help: You Can’t Do It Alone. No (wo)man is an island. We’re all interconnected and need one another if we’re to survive and thrive. Fortunately, there are resources to help caregivers for the long run. You’ve undoubtedly heard, caregiving is not a sprint, it’s a marathon. In any long distance race the key to crossing the finish line is to pace yourself. For us slower runners, it includes taking water, bathroom and snack breaks thanks to the volunteers at various points along the route. Similarly, there are many resources along the caregiver’s journey. It makes sense to pace yourself while taking regular respites to regain enough balance and energy to finish this caregiving marathon. Start the New Year right and use these three tools to lighten your caregiving load as you balance self-care with care for your loved one. Learn as much as you can about your care recipient’s disease or illness, attend a support group in person or online, and use your community’s resources such as in-home and adult day care in order to cross the finish line of caregiving. Walkers visit Walter Blair’s original property By Dick Carter It had rained earlier in the morning and it looked like there could be some more last Wednesday, however, the uncertain weather didn’t stop 24 walkers and one K-9 best friend from a stroll in central Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesday group decided to revisit the history of Walter Blair, the first European settler on the area, and go the site of his original Blair’s Park on what is now the north side of Moraga Avenue. This park was an attraction Blair created to get people to come to his Piedmont Springs Hotel that he built in 1872, and where the Exedra is today. Blair came to California from Vermont during the gold rush in 1852 at the age of 22 with $100. In 1852 he purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. His land was most of the area between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia and Grand Avenues. Blair’s original home was where 111 Highland Avenue is today with its back on today’s Waldo Avenue. He started as a dairy farmer and established Blair’s Dairy at the corner of today’s Blair and El Cerrito Avenues. His cattle grazed in pastures that ran to Grand Avenue. He also developed a quarry where Dracena Park is today. The walkers went down Highland Avenue and found the site of Blair’s home. When they got to the end of the street more of Blair’s history was shared. He was an entrepreneur and partnered with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to Piedmont Avenue. In 1878 he decided to build his own line from where the Piedmont Avenue line ended at the gates of the Mountain View Cemetery to the Piedmont Springs Hotel. To increase ridership in 1884 Blair developed 40 acres of the land between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park, which he named “Blair’s Park.” It had an entrance arch at what is now the corner of Highland and Moraga Avenues and offered many ascensions. Many of these picnickers and hotel guests purchased land and became Piedmont’s early residents. Blair died in 1888 and was only 57 years old. Blair Avenue in Piedmont is named for him. After his death Blair Park was purchased in 1890 by a company that operated a cable car up Oakland Avenue. However, the company went into receivership in 1893. Blair’s heirs owned the park land, but in 1897 all of Blair’s remaining 235 acers, including Blair’s Park, were for sale. In 1901 the park was abandoned, and in 1902 Frank C. Havens’ land development syndicate owned the park land. By 1913 the land was vacant, but in 1917 builder Guy Turner built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue and at least six more in 1922. The walkers looked across Moraga Avenue where the original entrance to Blair Park was located and took a group photo. They made their way down Moraga passing Turner’s homes and came to the gate entrance of a nine-unit apartment building that was built in 1914. Two gardeners were working in the yard, and the group asked if they could come in. Permission was granted and the group enjoyed Walter Blair the beautiful garden and view of San Francisco. The group continued down Moraga to the Oakland/Piedmont city line at Pleasant Valley Avenue, and went on Ronada Avenue, to Parkside Drive cul-de-sac, and then up to Ronada, Ramona, and Estrella Avenues. A right on Bonita Avenue and a left on Park Way brought got the walkers to Waldo and Blair Avenues, and a chance to once again remember Walter Blair. They arrived back at the Exedra just as the moisture could no longer to be called mist. The group had escaped the rain and enjoyed a fun three-mile walk and an almost entirely dry morning together. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. On hand for last week’s Wednesday Walk were: Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Judith Lee, Charlene Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Land, Lisa Euphrat, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Peggy Shultz, Gloria DaSilva, Rick Eigenbrode, Lori Austin, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Maricela Negron, Dottie Hutch, Dave DeRoche, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Christiana Miller, Elizabeth Richter, Claudine Bach, and Dick Carter. articles.text: The Number 11 streetcar on the right-of-way between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues in 1948. was what then was the newly built Transbay Terminal in San Francisco. Cars travelled east and west on the top level of the bridge. Electric trains served other parts of the East Bay. The A Train covered downtown Oakland, and the B Train travelled through the Lakeshore and Trestle Glen neighborhoods. The E Train went to Berkeley to the Claremont Hotel. In Berkeley, the F Train travelled on Shattuck to Solano, the G Train served Westbrae, the H Train travelled on Monterey Avenue, and the K Train ran on College Avenue. Today, some AC Transit buses use the same letters to identify their routes. End of the Line The last Piedmont streetcar operated until 1948. With the proliferation of automobiles after World War II, electric streetcars were no longer considered efficient. Buses, later run by AC Transit District, took over the streetcar routes. The C Train continued to run to San Francisco until 1958 when streetcars on the Bay Bridge were discontinued. The Oakland Tribune described this poignant time as “sad, exuberant, quiet, noisy, confused and orderly.” That last ride was standing room only. Homeowners along the train’s route came out to wave goodbye, as the motorman saluted back. The C Train at the small Oakland Avenue station at Latham that provided shelter to waiting passengers in 1940. Legacy The Number 11 and 12 streetcar lines and the C Train also left a legacy of vacant right-ofway land. The right-of-way for the Number 11 between Sunnyside and Linda became the beautifully landscaped Linda Park and the energetic Linda Avenue Dog Park across from Beach School. The Number 12 streetcar on Fairview Avenue had no dedicated right-of-way. When the C Train stopped running, its right-of-ways were filled with houses. Today, three narrow houses occupy the right-of-way along Latham. The land between Ricardo and York became more back yard space for adjacent houses. New houses were built on York near Arroyo. The C Train also shared the right-of-way on Arroyo with the Number 10 streetcar before it As the C Train curves to the right toward its route to Latham and Oakland, the Number 10 streetcar descends Arroyo toward Piedmont Avenue.

It was the longest Key Route line in Piedmont and ran from Piedmont Avenue and 41st to Crocker Park. There were two other streetcar lines and an electric train in Piedmont that provided convenient, reliable and inexpensive transportation to other neighborhood cities, downtown Oakland and San Francisco. The Number 11 streetcar ran from 7th and Broadway in Oakland up Oakland Avenue into Piedmont. At the Oakland Avenue Bridge it turned left and continued onto the rightof-way that ran between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues. At Lake Avenue, the streetcar ran on Linda Avenue to Piedmont Avenue and to the end of its line at the Piedmont Avenue Station. (The route up Oakland Avenue from Grand Ave. was too steep for electric streetcars.) The Number 12 streetcar also traveled from downtown Oakland, but it served another part of Piedmont. It ran up Grand Avenue and up Fairview Avenue beside the strip park. It ended at Oakland and Jerome Avenues. From there, passengers could cross Oakland Avenue to board the C Train to San Francisco. Taking the C Train to San Francisco When the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, the Key System added electric train service to San Francisco. (The Key Route had became the Key System in 1923.) The electric C Train began service to Piedmont in 1939 and offered direct transportation from Piedmont to San Francisco every 20 minutes. Each train had a smoking section and “card tables were provided for commuters used to such diversions when they rode the ferries.” Many Piedmont commuters caught the C Train from the small Spanish-style waiting station at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street. From there the train travelled along Latham, then between the houses on Ricardo and York. Two stops allowed more passengers to board before the train left Piedmont for the station at 41st Street and Piedmont Ave. and on to the Bay Bridge. The lower level of the new Bay Bridge was reserved for trucks and trains. The electric trains ran on parallel tracks on the south side of the bridge, and trucks used the north side. The Contour Trail goes for about 1.1 miles and provides some uphill climb to your day, meaning it’s not just a scenic nature hike, but a fitting lower body workout. The trail also surrounds you with the aroma of California Bays, the sprawling red bark of Manzanita, and A view of Swanson Creek. You’ll walk over the creek to continue on the Contour Trail. Triple Falls is our final of five thriving waterfalls in the park. It’s the tallest at around 50 feet. a towering second-growth redwood here and there. Intersecting with the Alec Canyon Trail, turn right to head just slightly less than a mile to Triple Falls, the final landmark of the day and the tallest of the waterfalls at around 50 feet, a small trickle compared to the other four. Our Uvas Canyon loop to hit every waterfall is approximately 5.2 miles and topped out at 1,273 feet in elevation gain. The Post passed 44 hikers on the day, but over 36 of which came on the initial walk on the Waterfall Loop given its popularity. It is also one of the few dog friendly parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains, so it is safe to bring your pooch without fear of repercussion. It’s also worth mentioning that 24 hour advance reservation for parking, otherwise you’ll be parking on the road leading in. For parking information, visit https://parks.sccgov.org/santaclara-county-parks/uvas-canyon-county-park or search “Uvas Canyon County Park” in your device—it will be the first option in search engines. articles.text: Ballot item would renew City Parcel Tax for 12 years Piedmont City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore will provide an informational report on Measure F, a renewal of the Municipal Services Parcel Tax (City Services Tax) during a series of presentations at multiple city commission and committee meetings this month. Measure F, which will be on the March 5, 2024 ballot, would renew the City Services Tax for 12 years instead of the usual four and increase its tax rate by 20%- -an increase of between $12 and $21/month for most households. The City Council placed this renewal on the ballot at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. “The presentations before our citizen-led bodies will provide reliable and factual information on Measure F,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. “The City encourages everyone to participate in expressing what is important to them on Election Day. On March 5th, voters will be defining service level expectations for Piedmont.” The city’s decision to extend the term of the tax to 12 years is an attempt to increase the city’s ability for long-term planning. “This tax accounts for about 8 to 10% of general fund revenues,” said Echa Schneider, Communications Manager for the city. “Without knowing that money is going to be there, it makes it hard for the city to plan long term.” Schneider also added that the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committees have been encouraging the city to make this change for the past 15 years. The city briefly considered extending the term of the tax in 2019 but decided against it after the upheaval caused by the COVID-19 epidemic. The next presentation on Measure F will be on Thursday, January 25, at 5:30 p.m., at the Public Safety Committee meeting. All meetings will be held in City Council Chambers at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. The Planning Commission meeting can also be viewed online or on KCOM-TV (Comcast Channel 27 or AT&T U-verse Channel 99). Measure F Presentation Schedule • Public Safety Committee: Thursday, January 25, 5:30 p.m. • Planning Commission: Monday, January 29, 5:30 p.m.
articles.title: City to host presentations about Measure F

articles.text: Negotiations between Piedmont Unified School District and the Piedmont teachers union, the Association of Piedmont Teachers, will resume with the state-appointed mediator on Friday. Piedmont teachers will be busy advocating for themselves prior to that, by reducing their workloads for two days, picketing in Piedmont Park on Tuesday, and announcing the result of their Strike Authorization vote during tonight’s school board meeting. Discussions have yet to bear a formal resolution since Ken Glenn was announced as a state-appointed mediator on December 14. “We are at a point where I think the community needs to understand that either we are going to not have enough teachers willing to work in Piedmont, or have to face very, very, deep cuts in order to raise compensation,” said Dr. Elise Marks, president of APT. Teachers enacted a two day “work to rule” action beginning yesterday, Tuesday, January 23, in which teachers have coordinated to only do work that they have direct contractual obligations to do. This equates to an elimination of anything extra teachers commonly do including: class prep time, staying after school, and opening classrooms to students or clubs at lunch. articles.text: Havens dad Jeff Hoffman won the 16th annual Havens Dads Club Poker Night tournament, on Friday, January 19, in the Veterans Hall with two pairs, queens over twos, to defeat Melissa Clark. During the four and half hour Texas-Hold-Em tournament, 148 other poker players were eliminated in a benefit that raised $52,000 for Havens Elementary School. Hosted by Dads Club President Roger Tsai, the event would not have been possible without 18 volunteers and many sponsors. Measure F, which will be on the March 5, 2024 ballot, would renew the City Services Tax for 12 years instead of the usual four and increase its tax rate by 20%- -an increase of between $12 and $21/month for most households. The City Council placed this renewal on the ballot at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. “The presentations before our citizen-led bodies will provide reliable and factual information on Measure F,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. “The City encourages everyone to participate in expressing what is important to them on Election Day. On March 5th, voters will be defining service level expectations for Piedmont.” The city’s decision to extend the term of the tax to 12 years is an attempt to increase the city’s ability for long-term planning. “This tax accounts for about 8 to 10% of general fund revenues,” said Echa Schneider, Communications Manager for the city. “Without knowing that money is going to be there, it makes it hard for the city to plan long term.” Schneider also added that the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committees have been encouraging the city to make this change for the past 15 years. The city briefly considered extending the term of the tax in 2019 but decided against it after the upheaval caused by the COVID-19 epidemic. The next presentation on Measure F will be on Thursday, January 25, at 5:30 p.m., at the Public Safety Committee meeting. All meetings will be held in City Council Chambers at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. The Planning Commission meeting can also be viewed online or on KCOM-TV (Comcast Channel 27 or AT&T U-verse Channel 99). articles.text: Editor: I am a 40+ year resident of Piedmont. Because of Piedmont’s location relative to larger urban areas, there is increasing evidence of a need for enhanced city services, particularly for public safety. And of course, there is also the ongoing need to maintain and improve city property and utilities like parks, streets and storm drains. Quality city services like those we enjoy need to be paid for, and continuing this tax which we’ve regularly renewed for decades is how we need to pay for those services. For those reasons, I hope Piedmont’ Measure F succeeds in obtaining the necessary two-thirds vote for passage. –Michael Henn

articles.text: Editor: The City of Piedmont’s Parcel Tax was first implemented more than 40 years ago when its then leaders found the cap that Proposition 13 placed on property tax revenues left them unable to fund the basic services Piedmonters expected. Since that time, the cap on property taxes has remained. The cost of basic services, however, has increased. Moreover, events in the world around us, including most especially in Oakland, cause us to demand increased services for Piedmont. We are fortunate to have financially savvy citizens to analyze what level of taxation is necessary to meet the need. Voters must do their part and vote YES ON MEASURE F. articles.text: City of Piedmont ranks highest in county for clarity The nine Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the March 5, 2024 election, were evaluated in December 2023 and January 2024 by the Alameda County Chapter of the California Civil Grand Jury Association, (ACCGJA). The measures were evaluated for accuracy and fairness pursuant to the criteria established by the association for each type of ballot measure, e.g. Bond Measure, Tax Measure and The collective scores represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who are Civil Grand Jury Association members (up to 15 allowed). The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should be included in each type ACCGJA is not evaluating the merits of the measures. We are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the 75-word ballot question put to the voters. State law requires ballot labels to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure, and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure”. Unfortunately, many jurisdictions violate the law by exaggerating the benefits and glossing over the costs, as well as adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. No one other than the agency promoting the measure is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this, there is a need for active and consistent monitoring and evaluation of local government’s ballot language. This current ACCGJA effort implements the findings of 2021 Alameda County Civil Grand Jury report, “The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of BalCity of Piedmont, Measure F To increase funding for essential police, fire, and paramedic services, maintain parks, greenspaces, and public areas, and preserve recreation, public parks, recreation and public works, and community services, shall Ordinance 771 N.S. be adopted to renew the City of Piedmont’s expiring four-year parcel tax with a twelve-year parcel tax with annual rates between $743 and $1,254 per single family residential parcel, $1,254 or $1,882 per commercial parcel, or $515 per multi-family dwelling unit, subject to CPI adjustment, raising approximately $3,272,000 annually? Type: Parcel Tax, Vote required: 2/3 SCORE: 4.2 Comments: This measure was only minimally scored down from the maximum of five for failing to explain the amount of the increase in taxes relative to the existing similar tax that was being renewed. articles.text: The Year of the Dragon will be celebrated in Piedmont’s Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens Elementary School on Friday, February 9 from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) will host the annual Lunar New Year event highlighted by performances, crafts, a lion dance and dim sum. “It’s the Year of the Dragon, a year of energy and excitement. Let’s celebrate it together,” said PAAC Co-President Cassindy Chao. Last year a capacity crowd of more than 350 people enjoyed hands-on activities and instrumental and vocal performances by the Honors Mandarin class. “We welcome our community. We’re doing this for our children for their futures as citizens in a diverse community that welcomes them,” said Chao. The event will include arts and crafts tables for kids, and gourmet desserts, boba drinks and panang curry available for purchase by local Piedmont businesses, including BakeSum, Tea on Piedmont and Salisa Skinner. Last year’s event attracted many local Piedmont leaders and reached maximum enrollment prior to doors opening. Tickets are suggested to be reserved in advance by February 4 by emailing piedmontpaac@gmail.com or using the QR code. Last year’s Lunar New Year celebration organized by the Piedmont Asian American Club included colorful lion dancers.
articles.title: PAAC Lunar New Year event at Havens on Feb. 9

articles.text: State program to provide up to $3,000 for eligible households The City of Piedmont is encouraging residents to apply for the Earthquake Brace + Bolt retrofit program. Now through February 21, Piedmont homeowners may apply for a state retrofit grant and receive up to $3,000 to make their homes more resilient to earthquakes. Registration is only open for 30 days once per year. The Earthquake Brace + Bolt program is a state program that offers eligible homeowners grants of up to $3,000 to help offset the cost of seismic retrofits that would brace the walls of older homes and bolt houses to their foundations. These steps reduce the potential for damage or collapse in the event of an earthquake. Homes that qualify for the program are typically built before 1980 (but are more prevalent before 1940), have a raised continuous perimeter concrete foundation, may sit on level ground or a low slope, and may have woodframed walls (often called “cripple walls”) in the crawl space under the first floor. To apply for a retrofit grant, residents may visit www.earthquakebracebolt.com and complete the online registration form by February 21. The program

articles.text: The Troubadours will be busy in February as they celebrate Valentine’s Day on February 14 with Heart-O-Grams in collaboration with ASB. On Valentine’s Day, members of the Troubadours will accompany students from ASB as they go from classroom to classroom delivering paper telegrams and spreading holiday cheer with their harmonious voices. The Troubadours are a wellknown, completely student-run a capella group that’s been serenading Piedmont since 1968. Between their infectious energy and melodic voices, the Troubadours have a long-standing reputation at the high school for being creative, performance-oriented, and fun. “It’s just kids who are passionate about music and have a common goal of learning music together and spreading joy and performing for others as well,” said senior Cat Pasion. There are three directors, two program directors, and a musical director, all of whom are seniors elected by other members. The directors run rehearsals, schedule gigs, organize bonding events and retreats, teach, arrange and select music, and hold auditions. “I had never been in a fully student-run organization but I think it really teaches our leaders how to become responsible and be able to learn the skills we need for future jobs,” said junior Lauren Brenner. Brenner has been a part of the Troubadours since her freshman year. The Troubadours just finished a busy winter season, as many organizations look for holiday carolers for events. The Troubs perform routinely during December at Scott’s Restaurant in Jack London Square, at private gatherings, and at local events, including the annual Piedmont Tree Lighting ceremony. Last month, the group made their annual delivery of Holiday-O-Grams amidst the stressful weeks of preparations for final exams. The Holiday-O-Grams are a short break during class that helps put everyone in the holiday spirit. The week prior to deliveries, students can buy small notes for friends that members of ASB deliver to each classroom as the Troubs, in their festive costumes, sing to their peers. “It was so much fun. I just loved dressing up and bombarding all the classrooms with songs,” said freshman Ben Ramakrishnan. “It’s the highlight of my day,” said junior Kaeli Yeung. “It brightens up the school atmosphere, “ said junior Teresa McKay. Holiday-O-Grams were not only a highlight for students, but for teachers as well. “I can’t stop smiling every time they walk into the room because it’s just so joyful,” said History teacher and Yearbook Adviser Melanie McCauley. “I love that the Troubs are so comfortable coming in and singing in front of everyone. I love it when I see students, ones I had no idea could sing, all of a sudden come in and start belting out songs. I hope it never goes away.” The Troubadours will also hold a Spring Concert in May. The Troubadours are available for hire for private events. For more information, contact program directors Axel Saldanha or Melina Markowitz at thepiedmonttroubadours@gmail.com The Troubadours, Piedmont High School’s a cappella vocal ensemble, shown during their busy holiday season in December.
articles.title: Troubadours prepare for Heart-O-Gram Valentine deliveries

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation’s (PEF) Giving Campaign resulted in donations of $3.4 million from 1,160 households in support of Piedmont schools. The number of donors, and the total amount donated, increased from last year. According to PEF Board Chair Tonya Antonucci, “This increase is a tremendous accomplishment. PUSD enrollment has declined, but we’re seeing both a higher rate of community participation and an increase in the dollar amounts donated.” Antonucci credits the leadership of Co-Chairs Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn for the campaign’s success. The PEF board and Giving Campaign committee, the PUSD School Board, and the boards of Havens and PMS parents clubs all achieved 100% parent participation in the campaign. Overall 66% of PUSD parents made a contribution this year compared with 62% last year. Winning the class level competition was transitional kindergarten (TK) with 83% parent participation. Of the six schools, Havens came out ahead with 82% participation with Havens’ Kindergarten parents leading at 92% participation. A party to celebrate TK families is being planned for early spring. Co-Chair Kim Hunter said, “We thank everyone who contributed. This has been a lot of work and a lot of fun, and seeing the community come together for something this important is so rewarding.” Catie Osborn added, “It has made me realize how important each individual is when making sure our schools succeed. And how much more we have to do. There’s a lot of work still to be done at the national, state and local levels.” “That’s why we’re both stepping up again to chair next year’s Giving Campaign,” said Hunter. “We know we can count on everyone to help us out again.” Funds raised through the Giving Campaign will be granted to PUSD for use during the 2024- 25 school year. For more information on the grant process and this year’s grant distribution, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/ Our-Impact.
articles.title: Giving Campaign raises $3.4 Million

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting tonight Wednesday, January 24 at 7:00 p.m. at City Hall. The meeting is shaping up for high drama as the teachers union has ramped up its visibility in town with picketing, and two days of coordinated “work to rule” action. The teachers union will reveal the results of their Strike Authorization Vote at tonight’s board meeting. The five school board members, led by President Veronica Anderson Thigpen will be joined by Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Teachers Union President Elise Marks will give the result of the Strike Authorization Vote to the board and the community during the Board President’s announcement. Outside of the ongoing impasse over teacher salary negotiations, the meeting will have several topics of wide interest. An announcement will be made that the application period for the annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award has opened, and that the school district will recognize February as Black History Month. A summary of the Governor’s Proposed State Budget for 2024-25 and its potential impact on Piedmont School District will be provided by Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The update is coming on the heels of the January 10 release of Governor Gavin Newsom’s Proposed State budget. The results of a financial audit of the district will also be presented as a review and action item. The agenda for the board meeting can be found at Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/SB_Meetings/ViewMeeting.aspx- ?S=36030373&MID=27600 The board meeting can be attended in person at City Hall, or participated in remotely via Zoom.us/j/82270330787

The final class period at Piedmont High on Tuesday let out at 3:25, and by 3:30 p.m. a critical mass of teachers were joined by supporting parents, community members and students. Marks explained the two days of action are a common form of protest used by unions as they build towards striking. It is a tactic of engagement for teachers as a reminder to administrators and the public of the extra work teachers perform but is often taken for granted. Tonight, Wednesday, January 24, towards the start of the 7:00 p.m. school board meeting at city hall, union leadership will announce the results of a strike authorization vote recently conducted by the teachers union. If members of the union voted in favor, the union leadership would have the power to declare a strike. A strike is not on the horizon anytime soon, and it could only be executed if the current mediated negotiations stall, and then after a subsequent three-person fact finding panel makes an effort at remediation. “It would not be a fast process. We absolutely would not blindside the community. If it comes to a strike, it will be a while from now,” said Marks. “We don’t want to have to do that,” Marks said of a strike, “But we’ve been waving the red flag and screaming and yelling and saying we’re in a terrible situation financially. From the rides to the petting zoo and Alice in Wonderland maze, a day of fun is a few blocks away from Piedmont. All shows on the stage of Fairyland’s Storybook Puppet Theater are original productions, featuring scripts, costumes, music, and sets designed by their talented puppeteers. Check their website prior to your visit to make sure they are open in the event of rain. Oakland Zoo Oaklandzoo.org 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 Guests can see the amazing animals during the day and stay for an illuminated lantern landscape at night. Glowfari, the zoo’s glowing lantern festival, will continue through January 28. The zoo has new mountain lion cubs and a new baby giraffe. Check in advance for tickets to tour the vet hospital on select days. Chabot Space & Science Center Chabotspace.org 10000 Skyline Blvd., Oakland 336-7300 Chabot is open Wednesday-Sunday. Enjoy the out of this world exhibits and the shows in the planetarium and megadome to experience space and science on the biggest of big screens. Every Friday and Saturday night the Chabot Observatory Deck has a free telescope viewing from 7:30- 10:30 p.m. weather permitting. Check out Chabot’s night time Solstice event Dec. 21 and Chabot’s New Years (afternoon) balloon drop. Calif. Academy of Sciences Calacademy.org Golden Gate Park, 55 Music Concourse Dr., S.F. (415) 379-8000 California Academy’s four-story rainforest has everything from butterflies to the bioluminescent depths of the “twilight zone.” Kids will enjoy vicariously joining the colony of endangered African penguins, and their imaginations will take off while visiting the Steinhart Aquarium. Glimpse the rich ecosystems of the California Coast, the Philippine Coral Reef and the swamp as well. The Academy is open everyday 9:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m. and with late opening of 11:00 on Sundays. Look into a membership for early morning admission. Want to do something special for Valentine’s Day? Order your custom Chocolate-Dipped Strawberries Premium strawberries courtesy of Village Market Proceeds will help PCSC Crew members repair homes in Oakland, cook meals for the homeless, and the many projects they undertake during the year. Piedmont Community Service Crew is a coed teenage Venturing unit with the Piedmont Scout Council. Place your order online at http://tinyurl.com/pcscvalentines2024 Piedmont Teachers Continued from page 1 ing papers or emailing parents. As school let out on Tuesday at the six school sites, teachers locked their classrooms and headed for Piedmont Park to picket. The final class period at Piedmont High on Tuesday let out at 3:25, and by 3:30 p.m. a critical mass of teachers were joined by supporting parents, community members and students. Marks explained the two days of action are a common form of protest used by unions as they build towards striking. It is a tactic of engagement for teachers as a reminder to administrators and the public of the extra work teachers perform but is often taken for granted. Tonight, Wednesday, January 24, towards the start of the 7:00 p.m. school board meeting at city hall, union leadership will announce the results of a strike authorization vote recently conducted by the teachers union. If members of the union voted in favor, the union leadership would have the power to declare a strike. A strike is not on the horizon anytime soon, and it could only be executed if the current mediated negotiations stall, and then after a subsequent three-person fact finding panel makes an effort at remediation. “It would not be a fast process. We absolutely would not blindside the community. If it comes to a strike, it will be a while from now,” said Marks. “We don’t want to have to do that,” Marks said of a strike, “But we’ve been waving the red flag and screaming and yelling and saying we’re in a terrible situation financially. The district is really going to be struggling to get and retain teachers. And we’re kind of being met with silence,” she added. APT members with healthcare through the school district were hit with larger new increases to their premiums in December, costs which are at the forefront of why they are asking for 8.22% raises. With further planned increases to Kaiser medical insurance approaching and the district not planning to take on those costs, Marks says some teachers are looking at changing school districts right now, during this school year. “There are other districts, literally, where I could earn $70,000 more a year for doing the same job,” confirmed Marks. Tonight’s school board meeting can be watched and participated in through public comment via Zoom.us/j/82270330787 Approximately 100 teachers rallied at the Exedra with picket signs at 3:30 p.m. on Tuesday, January 23, to create public visibility for their stalemate with Piedmont School District. articles.text: Piedmont High School presents the musical Cabaret the weekend of February 1-4 at the Alan Harvey Theater. Directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead, this Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close, explores the exhilarating life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. The use of swastikas and military uniforms have been omitted. Memorable songs from Cabaret include “Willkommen,” “Perfectly Marvelous”, “Money”, “Maybe This Time”, and the title song , “Cabaret”. More than 70 Piedmont and Millennium High School students are involved in this PG-13 version of the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal Direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to impact its audience and performers. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Schultz,” said sophTheo Ferguson (left) (Cliff Bradshaw), Amelia Addington (Sally Bowles), Caitlin Boothby (Emcee), Ellie Broscow (Fräulein Schneider), and Ben Wakefield (Herr Schultz) omore Ben Wakefield. “The Israel-Hamas War, which unfolded during our rehearsal period, did impact my feelings about performing in Cabaret. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical. Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present.” Senior Ellie Broscow, who plays the role of Fräulein Schneider, added, “Cabaret is an incredibly important musical to me and has been for quite some time. My love for the show has definitely grown throughout the rehearsal process as I’ve realized just how relevant the themes still are, 58 years since its premiere on Broadway in 1996. The themes of anti-Semitism especially resonate with me after the events of October 7th. I have seen how the world has turned against the Jewish people throughout history, and Cabaret addresses a particularly intense period, 1929, or the rise of Hitler. The vivid anti-Semitism that existed then has continued to increase, especially right now, and we simply cannot turn a blind eye to it any longer. I hope that Cabaret will continue to be performed for years to come.” Performances are February 1, 2, 3, and 4 at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Ave., Piedmont. Tickets may be purchased online at https://www. showtix4u.com/event-details/ PHSCabaret or at the door for an additional $2.00 per ticket. articles.text: Highlander Robotics Team 8033’s SPARK fundraiser will be held on Friday, January 26 at 7 p.m. at a lovely central Piedmont home. Enjoy a talk by a local tech luminary that is sure to spark conversation while you enjoy delicious wine and food. This event directly supports Piedmont’s Highlander Robotics Team 8033, a program designed to empower youths to be leaders in STEM. Tickets are now on sale through our website www. frc8033.com The event features Bryan Cantrill’s talk Intelligence Is Not Enough about AI and ethics, a timely topic for parents of kids interested in STEM. Cantrill is a software engineer who has spent over a quarter of a century at the hardware/software interface. He is the co-founder and CTO of Oxide Computer Company, the creator of the world’s first commercial cloud computer. Formerly CTO of Joyent and Distinguished Engineer of Sun Microsystems, Cantrill is a sought-after speaker in the tech industry for his ability to colorfully connect strong values to current best practices. As the Scoutmaster of Piedmont’s Troop 1, he is also committed to leadership formation of our youth. History of team Highlander Robotics Team 8033 was founded in 2019 to provide access to engineering through competitive robotics for high school students of Piedmont and nearby Bay Area communities. Our student-led approach is designed to empower our youth to become leaders in the growth of STEM education while advocating for gender parity in tech. We are role models in our community by embracing a culture of excellence and innovation in a fun and collaborative environment. Team 8033 is the capstone robotics program for the largest community-based FIRST league in the country, organized by Piedmont Makers. We partner with Piedmont School DisBryan Cantrill is the featured speaker at a fundraiser on January 26 for Highlander Robotics. trict to have our homebase in the Mary G. Ross engineering lab at Piedmont High School. We are the only competitive community-based FRC team in a 25-mile radius and now have team members from 15 high schools who otherwise would not be able to participate in FRC. Beyond access to the robust network of Bay Area FIRST FRC teams, we provide hands-on experience with our lab equipment and technology; engagement with expert mentors and speakers from STEM companies; and opportunities for field trips to top companies. Because it is a community-based team, it does not receive funding from schools. The team’s goal is to cover half of its $80,000 annual budget from contributions from the community and from corporate donations. Please join us for SPARK and help this valuable program thrive for current and future young people interested in STEM. Tickets for the fundraiser are limited and can be purchased through the website www. frc8033.com or at Eventbrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ spark-an-8033-fundraiser-tickets-792852612507?aff=oddtdtcreator). Wines have been graciously donated by Wente wines. For questions. contact Larraine at lms@larraineseiden.com or Natalia at natferretti@gmail. com

articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council’s annual Pinewood Derby will take place on Saturday, February 3, at the Piedmont Community Church Gymnasium. Watch as local Cub Scouts race fast, colorful, and creative cars of their own creation against their peers. Check-in for the race begins at 8:30 a.m. The first race will begin at 9:00 a.m. An open practice will be held in the church gym one week before the race on Saturday, January 27, from 10 a.m. to 12 noon. Cubs can test their cars on the official tournament track and make adjustments prior to race day. Parents may register their Scouts online at www.piedmontbsa.org. Registration is $5 per Cub Scout. Registration closes at the end of the day on Thursday, February 1. For more information about the Pinewood Derby contact Eris Turner at the Scout office at eturner@piedmontbsa.org, or call 547-4493.
articles.title: Pinewood Derby returns on February 3

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School woodshop was filled with a steady flow of racers during the Girl Scouts’ annual Pinewood Derby workshop last Saturday, January 20. Girl Scouts and their parents banded together to create their cars from start to finish while volunteers stood by to help Scouts throughout the process, including designing their cars, cutting them from blocks of wood, and decorating them afterward. “We have Scouts from about a dozen troops signed up so far from the Oakland-Piedmont-Emeryville Service Unit area,” said Carolyn Pan. “It’s a fun way for girls to gather, build, and compete. The girls have fun with their cars [...] and at the races, you’ll hear all the Girl Scouts cheering for each other and their friends and family.” Overall, Pan said she was as excited for the upcoming Pinewood Derby as the adults helping their kids build cars at the workshop. This will be the first year that her troop is in charge of organizing the event. “We are still learning the Mother Tory Roman and daughter Beazy show the painting process during the Pinewood Derby workshop. The Girl Scout Pinewood Derby will be held in the Education Building at Piedmont Community Church, 10 Highland Way, on Saturday, February 3, from 3:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. Contact Carolyn Pan via email at carolynpan@yahoo.com to register and to arrange a car kit pickup. Registration is $20 and includes a car kit, trial run at Piedmont Community Church, race registration, certificate award, and patch.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Staff photo – Pouyan Assadi Head track & field coach, Piedmont High School Witter Field is expected to open on February 5, two months later than expected. The track will be out of service until later this summer, effectively displacing the track and field team with 104 athletes. Construction on the renovation of Witter Field hasn’t gone as planned in the slightest. After having an initial target date of November 2023, the field’s completion has been pushed back continuously, leaving fall and winter sports teams forced out of town for home games. According to Piedmont High athletic director Bradley Smet, some sports can return to Witter Field starting February 5, but with strings attached. One bright note is Smet’s assurance that the girls’ and boys’ lacrosse teams will have a full spring season at Witter Field. “Right now, we have work that’s happening on February 1. They are re-laying asphalt that needed work after a section of the field degraded that they did not anticipate. That led to additional work. As long as weather cooperates, we’ll be able to get back on the field by February 5,” Smet said. But Smet explained that repairs to the track won’t start until June and won’t be completed for one month. It means that the track and field team of 10 athletes will not have a training or competition site for its upcoming season. “They are doing the work on the track over summer. My understanding is that Witter Field would be shut down, once again, in June in order to lay the track surface,” said Smet. “As long as there are no more delays, we’re looking at opening things back up again in July,” Smet said. The track and field team has been forced to find a training site off campus with completion of the track not expected until late summer. They’ll be splitting time at Laney College and Witter Field’s turf field going forward. “We’re going to use a combination of Witter Field and Laney, which will be the home-base. We’re going to try and mix in Witter,” said head track and field coach Pouyan Assadi. “We’re envisioning that we’ll have the field available for short sprint workouts. Soccer and lacrosse will be prioritized, but we’ve talked to those coaches and they are very understanding of the situation. We’re all working through this together.” “The asphalt-track will be available, but I envision us doing short sprint workouts on Witter Field itself. We’ll use Laney for hurdles, jumps and pole vaults, and we’ll use the Witter weight room and the hills in the neighborhood as well,” Complications at Witter Field have strongly impacted the school’s running programs going back to the fall. Without a track to train on, Assadi has been forced to host practices at local parks. He stressed the importance of how an adequate running surface plays a factor in student-athletes’ health and well-being, in addition. tain Xander Schulte-Sasse’s season was cut short last fall. He’s eying a return to distance events in track this spring bit without a home field track. Longtime resident and distance running coach Steve Zirkelbach said, “It’s been hard on the kids. We’re doing the best we can with the hand we have been dealt. As a coach of young runners, one of my biggest concerns has been the increased risk of injuries from exclusively running on hard surfaces. Not having the track’s softer running surface significantly increases risk of injury. I believe some of the injuries we sustained last fall may have been avoided if we trained on a more forgiving surface. It’s a bummer that hundreds of Piedmont kids have been displaced.” “There seems to be something unpredictable every four weeks. We get the disappointing news along with the rest of the public. I’m a coach, I’m also a dad, and I pay taxes in town. Not just in property tax, but the extra money I spent to have a house here is because of the great public schools which presumably has excellent decision-makers. “It sure would be nice to know some details; my intention is to be here 20-plus years,” Assadi said. A November completion would’ve allowed the football team to finish its season on a home field. The squad won the 2023 WACC Shoreline Title and a berth in the post-season North Coast Section playoffs all while training on a portion of the outfield of the baseball field. Both soccer teams are coming off 2023 NCS title-winning seasons, but they have been forced split their home games at Chabot College in Hayward and Estuary Park in Alameda. Both teams hosted practices at Laney College this season. A February 5 start date would allow Piedmont’s boys’ and girls soccer teams to play their first home games at Witter Field in 62 days – since the season started two months ago on December 5. The girls’ soccer team’s critical home match with rival Bishop O’Dowd on February 6 is its next to last game of the regular season. “Coaches have been asked to be very creative. The problem is with the rain coming down, all the plyometric and sprint workouts we want to do on softer surfaces to protect the kids’ knees, ankles, feet and joints are being done in Piedmont Park, which isn’t flat anywhere. “Also, the Rec. Department has asked us to use a smaller space so we don’t take up too much space for the regular patrons. We found another patch of grass, but its muddy and the kids are going home dirty. We’re probably able to do 25-40 percent of what we’d normally do. “The coaches have been creative. We’ll still be able to accomplish quite a bit this season,” Assadi said. articles.text: Staff Photos Brit Burden led the way with 21 points against Marin Catholic and 25 points against San Leandro. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team reeled in three more wins last week to extend its winning streak to five games. They defeated San Leandro 61-50 at home on Wednesday, January 17, beat Castro Valley 56-42 on Friday, January 19 at the Trojans’ home court, and traveled to Kentfield the following day for a 56-44 victory over Marin Catholic. (Final stats against Castro Valley were not provided.) The five-game winning streak has coincided with the return of senior forward Declan Linnane. The two-sport (also water polo) provides stability in the low post, defense, and is a player who can knock down a 3-pointer in the corner in critical moments. “It’s great to have Declan back. He’s like a shutdown cornerback on the left side. This 3-2 zone that we have has given a bit of an identity defensively. With his water polo background, he deflects four or five passes a game because he’s so long,” said coach Ben Spencer of the senior. “I’m just happy to be back,” said Linnane. “It was tough sitting out and watching the team battle, but other guys got a lot of minutes and that was good for them.”. A big part of this year’s team is sophomore guard Dillon Casey, emerging as a starter following senior forward Alex Anderson’s injury in the first game of the season. “I’m definitely learning from the upperclassmen and taking in all I can from them. It’s been an easy transition; my teammates have made it really easy. As a point guard, protecting the ball is one of the most important parts of the game, so that’s something I’m working on,” said Casey The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 12-7 overall and 4-2 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents. They enter another critical week with rematches against Bishop O’Dowd tomorrow, Thursday, and with Berkeley on Saturday. Declan Linnane has been a big part of Piedmont’s five-game winning streak. Thorin Holmes makes a layup against San Leandro.

articles.text: Photos by Eric Taylor Sam Smith knocked down a team-leading 16 points Gym the following day. The wins bring the team record to 13-3 overall and 2-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division teams. Alameda is having a surging year with an 13-4 record, and Lincoln of Stockton carries a 16-5 record. The Hornets used a strategy of double-teaming Piedmont senior guard Natalia Martinez, the team’s top scorer. But coach Bryan Gardere found a way to guide his team to victory. Piedmont looks ahead to a pair of league games this week, raveling to San Leandro for a game tonight, January 24, and a game with Castro Valley ton Friday. 53-50 victory over Alameda Piedmont trailed 10-9 after the first quarter, but went ahead 26-23 by halftime. Alameda stormed ahead in the third quarter to lead 41-37, only to see the Highlander offense come alive with 16 points in the final quarter and holding their opponents to nine points. Martinez, who has had multiple 40-point games this season and one for 52 points, was shut out in the first quarter for the first time all season, leading to a pair of 3-pointers by Sam Smith and one by Lindsey Wirgler. In Piedmont’s 17-point second quarter, Smith was key with two more 3-pointers, while Shakila Zuberi had one of her own. Martinez put up four points, including a pair of free throws. Piedmont scored 11 points in the third period with 3-pointers by Zuberi and Wirgler, while Martinez had three points via an and-one layup. In the fourth, Zuberi converted one more 3-pointer and a pair of free throws, while Wirgler also knocked one down. Despite the score line, Piedmont dominated possession in the second half with O’Dowd. “[There was] a little bit of nervous energy around the start of the game [against O’Dowd] and I think it carried through in the start of the first half. But we kept going and the last 10 minutes was outstanding, I felt we deserved a second goal. I’m proud of how they dug in and kept going,” said coach Todd Sullivan. 3-1 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Bishop O’Dowd scored both of its goals within one minute in the first half.
