articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team suffered two narrow losses to Western Alameda County Conference opponents last week, falling 1-0 to rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, January 18, and taking a 2-1 loss to Encinal on Tuesday, January 16. The pair of losses extends the Highlanders’ winless run to four matches and still seeking their first league victory. PHS dominated possession against Encinal but couldn’t find the finishing touch. The Highlanders came close to scoring on multiple occasions against O’Dowd as well, but the Dragons were able to sit defensively after taking a 1-0 lead in the ninth minute. “I felt we’re playing well; we just need to figure out how to solve the problems to break down the other teams. We couldn’t do it against Encinal and couldn’t do it tonight [against O’Dowd]. But you hear the girls. They are happy and enjoying it; they know they are putting forward a good team effort. We’ll keep plugging away,” said coach Dan Chubbock Staff Photos Freshman Elsa Wallway was shoved down in the box against Bishop O’Dowd, but there was no penalty call. Amy Derr sends in a long ball in the final moments against O’Dowd. Piedmont looks to regroup after a pair of narrow league losses. following the result to O’Dowd. 1-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont nearly struck first in the fourth minute of the game when Miranda Liu tracked a long pass into the penalty area. But the Dragons’ keeper came far out of net to get a hand on Liu’s shot. The ball skipped back towards the net but a BOD defender raced back to clear it off the line. Three minutes later O’Dowd struck after playing a long ball into space to their speedy striker, who caught Piedmont’s defense in a vulnerable spot and slotted in her shot in a one-on-one situation. From there, the Dragons sat deeper, having their keeper far up the penalty box waiting to pounce on forward passes to Liu. After a couple of shot attempts, Wallway was involved in a controversial no-call in the 35th minute. She dribbled into the box with two defenders chasing her and fell to the ground after taking a shove in the back. The referee waived his arms to signal no foul. In the second half, Wallway had a shot through traffic in the 55th minute, and PHS drew corner kicks in the 66th and 75th. A ball was played short to Wallway and tried to bend in a shot from the top of the box, but it went narrowly wide of the far post. Piedmont had one final free kick in second half stoppage time, when Amy Derr sent in a long ball from midfield. The pass fell into a dangerous area, but the Highlanders didn’t put contact on the ball and the Dragons’ keeper made the claim. 2-1 loss to Encinal On a cold and stormy night at Chabot College in Hayward, Piedmont couldn’t find the finishing touch past Encinal’s keeper. Lola Beihn had a shot on target in the early going, but the Jets’ GK was in good position. Encinal scored in the first half after a ball trickled around without clearance, it fortunately fell to an attack to send in a low shot for the score. As the rain continued, massive puddles on the field began slowing down every pass, leading to difficulties in Piedmont’s quick-moving and fluid style. Liu had a near chance midway through the first after beating two defenders to put herself one-onone with the goalie, but her leftfooted shot clanged off the crossbar. Liu had another shot hit off the crossbar minutes later. Wallway tied the match in the second half, using her speed to pounce on a loose ball around midfield and wheel her way into a one-on-one situation. She took a touch as the Encinal keeper rushed out, sending in a shot to the empty net. Wallway had another shot on target moments later. PHS continued pressing forward for a goal with multiple shots being saved or going narrowly wide. But disaster struck in last minute of the game when Encinal had one of its only attacks in the second half, where their forward sent in a beautiful arcing shot from the top of the box.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of St. Mary’s Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020 and a redshirt junior at St. Mary’s College, was named West Coast Conferences Player of the Week on January 2. Two of Piedmont High School’s former basketball stars are having impressive collegiate seasons. Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020 and now a redshirt junior at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, is in the midst of a career year. He was recently named West Coast Conference Player of the Week after leading his team to a 66-46 win over Kent State on December 29. During the game, he scored a career-high of 19 points, converting seven of nine shots from the field, including two 3-pointers. He also grabbed six rebounds including three offensive boards, to go along with one blocked shot. Since then, Barrett scored 14 points and had seven rebounds in an 81-70 win over UC San Diego, and he scored 17 points and had six rebounds in a 74-49 win over Santa Clara. The Gaels are now 13-6 and 4-0 in conference play, in first place in the WACC. Barrett has appeared in all 19 games thus far, averaging 16.1 minutes per game, totaling 94 points with 33 field goals and 10 three-pointers, to go along with 10 assists and 10 steals. He’s been active on the boards with 64 rebounds, including 34 offensive grabs. St. Mary’s finished last season ranked No. 22 in the country after going 27-8. They received the No. 5 seed in the NCAA Tournament, defeating No. 12 VCU 63-51 in the first round before losing 70-55 to UConn. As a sophomore, Barrett made an appearance in the Gaels’ 82- 53 win over Indiana in the first round of the NCAA Tournament. While at Piedmont High he helped lead the school to the North Coast Section Div. 4 championship. He was named Athlete of the Year by the Post in his senior year. As a sophomore, Harris helped lift Carleton College to the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference championship with an 86-76 win over St. Johns on February 26, where the guard scored 19 points. Harris was second on the team in scoring with 16.4 points per game achieved double-digit points in 20 of 24 games last season, including eight games with at least 20 points. He led Carleton with 92 assists, was second on the team in field goals with 159 made, and was third in rebounds with 132. Carleton finished last year with a 24-4 overall record before losing 81-77 to St. Norbert in the first round of the Division 3 NCAA tournament. He graduated from Piedmont High as another all-time great, finishing with over 1,200 career points as a three-year starter in three highly successful years: 21-11 in his sophomore year, winner of the North Coast Section championship in 2020 with a 24-6 record, and 11-5 in the pandemic shortened 2021 season. Harris was named Athlete of the Year by the Post in 2021. LUKE HARRIS Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, is a junior at Carleton College in Northfield, Minnesota and recently surpassed 1,000 collegiate points after scoring 23 against Macalester on January 10. The Knights are currently 9-6. Harris has appeared in all 15 games and is averaging 31.9 minutes per game. He’s recorded 324 points with 103 field goals and 13 three-pointers, converting 44.6 percent of his field goals to go along with 51 assists and 31 steals. Luke Harris, Class of 2021, recently surpassed 1,000 collegiate points with Carleton College. He was Piedmont Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2021.

articles.text: Tucked away in Leona Heights Park in the Oakland Hills is a towering seasonal waterfall of over 100 feet that comes alive following a consistent rain. A gushing waterfall and creek would be enough to send droves of hikers to Mt. Tamalpais and Marin County at a moment’s notice, but hidden in your own backyard is an equally mystifying experience and far fewer hikers on the trail. Leona Heights is an Oakland gem where you can find groves of redwood and oak trees, flowers in bloom, a running creek, and the foundation of a building that has since been covered in artwork and graffiti. The park itself only has two access points. The base of the park can be reached from Mountain Boulevard, where the York Trail runs alongside Horseshoe Creek through second-growth redwood trees. It intersects with the McDonell trail, which takes you to the top of the park across from Merritt College and sweeping views of the Bay Area. Beginning at the York Trail the waterfall is just less than a half mile from the trailhead. Hiking up to the former Merritt College lot is a bit over 1.5 miles uphill, making it around a 3-mile trip back to your car on Mountain Boulevard. In addition to being Oakland’s only natural waterfall, Leona Heights is also home to Oakland’s only Old Growth redwood tree, named Old Survivor. Towering Another view of the waterfall as Horseshoe Creek runs alongside. Horseshoe Creek flows through Leona Heights Park. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: All-male comic drag ballet company to perform on Jan, 27 & 28 Les Ballet Trockadero de Monte Carlo, the world’s foremost all-male comic drag ballet company, will perform a pair of back-to-back shows on Saturday, January 27 and Sunday, January 28 at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall in celebration of their landmark 50th anniversary season. Les Ballet Trockadero de Monte Carlo, or the Trocks as they are affectionately called, are a wildcard ballet company comprised of highly skilled ballet performers in drag. Over five decades of performance, the Trocks have developed a performance that combines superb ballet technique with expert slapstick and comic timing that manages to pay homage to ballet history even as it relishes mocking the genre’s conventions. The 16 male members of the company dance delicate, traditionally female roles en pointe, taking on outrageous faux-Russian stage names and fabricated backstories to match. “You have to know an awful lot about something in order to make fun of it successfully,” said Robert Carter, the senior memTrocks members Olga Supphozova (Robert Carter) (left), Lariska Dumbchenko (Raffaele Morra), Ida Nevasayneva (Paul Ghiselin), and Sveltlana Lofatkina (Fernando Medina Gallego) ber of the troupe. “Over the time that I’ve been with the company, we’ve become respected and included in the top list of companies in a lot of cases sometimes. We tour extensively and I’ve never knocked the company’s ‘charm’ because it has kept me gainfully employed all these many years,” he joked. Besides their world-class technique, part of the Trocks’ appeal includes their over-the-top showmanship. Ballerinas take the stage with tongue-in-cheek names like “Varvara Laptopova” and “Nadia Doumiafeyva.” “We’re trying to emulate the grand personalities of these characters from a long time ago, like from the Ballet Russes and people were Russian-izing their names to be taken seriously,” explained
articles.title: Les Ballet Trockadero de Monte Carlo Celebrates 50th anniversary at UC Berkeley

articles.text: Principal ballerina leaves an unprecedented and high-profile role in the world of dance San Francisco Ballet Principal Dancer Yuan Yuan Tan will give her final performance with San Francisco Ballet on Wednesday, February 14, at 7:30 p.m., dancing the role of Marguerite in Sir Frederick Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand at the War Memorial Opera House. Tan will also dance with former SF Ballet Principal Dancer Tiit Helimets in a selection from Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight at the company’s 2024 Opening Night Gala on Wednesday, January 24, 2024. The veteran dancer made headlines earlier this month when she announced her departure from the company after a record-breaking 29 seasons. Tan joined SF Ballet in 1995 as a soloist. In a meteoric rise through the ranks, she advanced to the coveted role of Principal Dancer within two years, making her the youngest principal dancer in the company’s history at age 20. Now 47, she is the longest-dancing principal with SF Ballet to date. Over her long and memorable career, Tan has danced in nearly 100 classical, neoclassical, and contemporary ballets choreographed by the likes of George Balanchine, Sir Kenneth MacMillan, John Neumeier, Christopher Wheeldon, Helgi Tomasson, Yuri Possokhov, Edwaard Liang, and Wayne McGregor, among others. In a recent statement, Tan took a moment to thank her fans for their support over the years. “Finally, to the San Francisco audiences over the last three decades, I express my sincere thanks. Bausch’s seminal and towering The Rite of Spring (1975) — staged in the Bay Area for the first time ever — is performed by an ensemble of over 30 dancers from 14 African countries, assembled through a collaboration between Germany’s Pina Bausch Foundation, Senegal’s École des Sables, and the UK’s Sadler’s Wells theater. The work’s companion piece, common ground[s], is a new duet co-created and danced by septuagenarians Germaine Acogny, known as the “mother of African contemporary dance,” and Malou Airaudo, a longtime collaborator with Bausch. The duet contemplates the performers’ lived experiences, their relationship to dance across generations, and their identities as mothers, daughters, grandmothers and granddaughters. “This is the first time that The Rite of Spring is done not with an existing company, but with dancers who came together specifically for this piece,” said Salomon Bausch, Pina Bausch’s son and Executive Director of the Pina Bausch Foundation. “I’m very excited to see the impact of their personalities and their diverse dance backgrounds on the piece but also vice versa — how the piece influences the dancers, both as artists and as human beings.” Tickets ($33-$96) for the show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@ calperformances.org or by phone at 642-9988. Les Ballet Trockadero de Monte Carlo, or the Trocks as they are affectionately called, are a wildcard ballet company comprised of highly skilled ballet performers in drag. Over five decades of performance, the Trocks have developed a performance that combines superb ballet technique with expert slapstick and comic timing that manages to pay homage to ballet history even as it relishes mocking the genre’s conventions. The 16 male members of the company dance delicate, traditionally female roles en pointe, taking on outrageous faux-Russian stage names and fabricated backstories to match. “You have to know an awful lot about something in order to make fun of it successfully,” said Robert Carter, the senior memTrocks members Olga Supphozova (Robert Carter) (left), Lariska Dumbchenko (Raffaele Morra), Ida Nevasayneva (Paul Ghiselin), and Sveltlana Lofatkina (Fernando Medina Gallego) ber of the troupe. “Over the time that I’ve been with the company, we’ve become respected and included in the top list of companies in a lot of cases sometimes. We tour extensively and I’ve never knocked the company’s ‘charm’ because it has kept me gainfully employed all these many years,” he joked. In honor of one of the most significant and popular American composers of all time, famed jazz pianist Marcus Roberts, National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master drummer Jason Marsalis and bassist Marty Jaffe bring a modern interpretation to George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue, which celebrates its 100th birthday in 2024 and is regarded as one of the most important American musical works of the 20th century. To commemorate this milestone, Roberts gives the piece a fresh, new twist with his version of Rhapsody in Blue, which was first performed with his trio and the Grant Park Symphony Orchestra in Chicago in 1995. “Roberts radically reconceived the piano part, using Gershwin’s basic melodic material to create new themes, unexpected harmonies and bracing, utterly modern dissonances,” said the Chicago Tribune. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) celebrates its 87th season with the 2024 Winter Concert this Saturday, January 27 at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church, 7:30 p.m. This year marks Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 34th season as YPSO’s Music Director and Conductor and features an inaugural collaboration with a longstanding Bay Area institution, the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO). The two groups will feature BCCO classical soprano singer Vuyiswa Sigadi and solo violinist Henry Stroud, the YPSO concertmaster. A sophomore at Berkeley High School, he is the winner of this season’s YPSO concerto competition. The concert opens with American composer Kenji Bunch’s Supermaximum, a contemporary composition that explores themes of resilience and determination. YPSO will then perform the first movement of Camille SaintSaëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 in B Minor, Op. 61. According to the program notes of Orrin Howard, the violin concerto’s “first movement revolves around a bold, dramatic first theme, a songful contrasting theme, and fistsful of rapid scales, arpeggios, and double stops.” Closing the program is Francis Poulenc’s Gloria, a choral and orchestral masterpiece that reflects the composer’s unique blend of sacred and secular influences. Poulenc’s Gloria is a joyous and vibrant work, featuring lush harmonies and intricate textures which will be led by BCCO Music Director Ming Luke, Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. YPSO’s mission is to “encourage young people to become exemplary musicians and young musicians to become exemplary people”. The organization performs four regular concerts per season. In addition, they reach out through programs such as Bread and Roses and the Bay Area Music Project to bring music into the lives of the surrounding community and encourage the civic development of its students. Tickets ($20-$30) for the event at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church (1801 Lacassie Avenue) are available online at ypsomusic. org/tickets.
articles.title: YPSO Winter Concert this Saturday

articles.text: The first retrospective of artist Pacita Abad, on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, will have its last day this Sunday, January 28. Featuring over 40 major works, including many rarely seen by the public, this exhibition is the most significant U.S. presentation of the artist’s multifaceted and mesmerizing art practice. Throughout her 32-year career from the 1970s to the early 2000s, If My Friends Could See Me Now (1991), one of the many trapunto paintings by the artist Pacita Abad at SFMOMA. The exhibit closes this Sunday, January 28. Abad centered the triumphs and adversities of people on the periphery of power, as seen in her Social Realist, Immigrant Experience and Masks and Spirits series. This exhibition celebrates an artist whose vibrant and inventive practice generated thousands of daring artworks—from intricately constructed underwater scenes to abstract compositions—and whose themes are as urgent today as they were two decades ago. Abad was born on 1946 in Basco, Philippines; and died 2004 in Singapore. She traveled and lived in over 60 countries in her lifetime including Bangladesh, Papua New Guinea, the Dominican Republic, Kenya, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Sudan and Yemen. San Francisco in particular was a place of creativity for Abad, as the city inspired her artistic career in the early 1970s. Abad interacted with myriad communities through her travels, incorporating a diversity of artistic traditions and techniques – from Korean ink brush painting to Indonesian batik and Nigerian tie-dye – into her expansive practice. These lessons found their greatest expression in her trapunto paintings: canvases that she painted, stuffed and embellished with buttons, cowrie shells, beads and mirrors. She created hundreds of these magnificently textured works, occasionally enlisting the help of family members and friends, thereby evoking the communal cultures that inspired her. “When curator Nancy Lim and I learned that this exhibition was being planned, we knew that it had to come to San Francisco, the city that inspired Pacita Abad to commit her life to artistic expression,” said Eungie Joo, curator and head of contemporary art at SFMOMA. “While some of the works gathered here were shown locally during Abad’s lifetime, this is the first exhibition to reveal the profundity of her prolific practice.” SFMOMA is open from 10 a.m. through 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday (closed Wednesday), and 1 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 for adults, $25 ages 65+, $23 ages 19-24, free 18 and younger, free for members) are available online at sfmoma.org, or in-person at the museum counter.
articles.title: Pacita Abad art exhibit closes this Sunday at SFMOMA

articles.text: Sound Sculpture by MASARY Studios, featured at Glow: Discover the art of light, on view at the SF Exploratorium through this Sunday, Jan. 28. The San Francisco Exploratorium’s annual celebration of luminous artworks, Glow: Discover the art of light, will run through this Sunday, January 28. Visitors can compose music with light, play LED-lit dungeon crawl games, and see themselves in mechanical mirrors through the work of seven artists. Among the large-scale light and sound installations are Sound Sculpture by MASARY Studios and Flux by Collectif Scale. Build dynamic musical compositions by moving Sound Sculpture’s portable location-aware cubes around, changing the rhythm and pitch as the cubes shift. Meanwhile, the Exploratorium presents the U.S. premiere of Flux, which showcases 48 twirling rods of white light that appear to twist and coil – put on a headset to immerse yourself in synchronized compositions by Grégory Sémah. Experience interactive artworks by Robin Baumgartner, including Quantum Jungle, a mathematically accurate model of a quantum object, and Line Wobbler, a challenging LED dungeon crawl game where hand-eye coordination is key. Crystal Paintings by Maria Constanza Ferreira reveals the hidden, brilliant patterns found in crystals, and you can also view a selection of Ferreira’s short films in the Osher Gallery 1 Microcinema. Chaco Kato’s Color Study makes its U.S. premiere at the show, featuring constantly changing colors and geometric patterns projected onto a solid but seemingly weightless artwork made of thousands of pieces of string. Also featured is a returning Glow favorite: Luke Jerram’s Museum of the Moon, which shows every cliff and crater of the moon at an approximate scale of 1:700,000. The Exploratorium, located at Pier 15, is open from 12 noon to 5 p.m. on Sunday, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Tickets are $39.95 for adults and $29.95 for youth 4-17 and seniors 65+), and are available online at exploratorium.edu, or by phone at 415-528-4444.
articles.title: Glow exhibit at Exploratorium through January 28

articles.text: Botticelli Drawings, a major exhibition drawing together the complete graphic output of one of the world’s most famous artists for the first time, is on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco through Sunday, February 11. A quintessential artist of the Italian Renaissance, Alessandro di Mariano di Vanni Filipepi — better known as Sandro Botticelli — is known for some of the world’s greatest paintings, from La Primavera (1477–1482) to the Birth of Venus (1485–1486). Among the first artists to make drawing central to his design practice, Botticelli developed a new visual style for the era, elevating the line as the primary force behind his figures and their movement. A prolific portraitist, he made a practice of drawing from life, one that would become an artistic standard in Renaissance Florence and beyond. Yet despite the centrality of drawing to Botticelli’s work, less than three dozen confirmed drawings by the artist survive today. Although these drawings are key to the masterworks driving his continued popularity, Sandro Botticelli, Study of the head of a woman in profile (“La Bella Simonetta”), 1848, is part of the exhibition Botticelli Drawings on view at the Legion of Honor through February 11. there has been no major exhibition dedicated to Botticelli’s art of drawing — until now. articles.title: Groundbreaking exhibition of Botticelli Drawings at Legion of Honor through Feb. 11

articles.text: Emerald Bay, Lake Tahoe Virginia Hong is a successful entrepreneur, an accomplished software developer, and, at her core, a genuine artist. Her journey unfolds as a passionate photographer who finds solace and inspiration in the quiet moments of life. Unlike conventional photographers, she captures moments not for the world, but for her own pleasure and meditation. She seeks out subjects and scenes that resonate with serenity, stillness, and tranquility similar to what she finds when she programs. Her large immersive prints are windows into a sanctuary of peace and quiet, inviting viewers to pause, breathe, and indulge themselves in a moment of quietude, allowing for an escape from their hectic lives. Her solo exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, amid the height of the COVID pandemic in August 2021, garnered significant attendance. Throughout 2024 the Piedmont Photo by Virginia Hong Post will publish Hong’s photos monthly based upon her 2024 photography calendar, beginning with Emerald Bay in her series of photos of Lake Tahoe. The photo shown was taken last April early in the morning about an hour after sunrise. The silence was deafening. There was no sign of any living thing around me. That, plus the stillness of the water, and the quality of the morning light, had all the ingredients begging to be recorded.
articles.title: The art of Virginia Hong, photographer

Meanwhile, the Exploratorium presents the U.S. premiere of Flux, which showcases 48 twirling rods of white light that appear to twist and coil – put on a headset to immerse yourself in synchronized compositions by Grégory Sémah. Experience interactive artworks by Robin Baumgartner, including Quantum Jungle, a mathematically accurate model of a quantum object, and Line Wobbler, a challenging LED dungeon crawl game where hand-eye coordination is key. Crystal Paintings by Maria Constanza Ferreira reveals the hidden, brilliant patterns found in crystals, and you can also view a selection of Ferreira’s short films in the Osher Gallery 1 Microcinema. Chaco Kato’s Color Study makes its U.S. premiere at the show, featuring constantly changing colors and geometric patterns projected onto a solid but seemingly weightless artwork made of thousands of pieces of string. Groundbreaking exhibition of Botticelli Drawings at Legion of Honor through Feb. 11 By Selen Ozturk Botticelli Drawings, a major exhibition drawing together the complete graphic output of one of the world’s most famous artists for the first time, is on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco through Sunday, February 11. A quintessential artist of the Italian Renaissance, Alessandro di Mariano di Vanni Filipepi — better known as Sandro Botticelli — is known for some of the world’s greatest paintings, from La Primavera (1477–1482) to the Birth of Venus (1485–1486). Among the first artists to make drawing central to his design practice, Botticelli developed a new visual style for the era, elevating the line as the primary force behind his figures and their movement. A prolific portraitist, he made a practice of drawing from life, one that would become an artistic standard in Renaissance Florence and beyond. Yet despite the centrality of drawing to Botticelli’s work, less than three dozen confirmed drawings by the artist survive today. Although these drawings are key to the masterworks driving his continued popularity, Sandro Botticelli, Study of the head of a woman in profile (“La Bella Simonetta”), 1848, is part of the exhibition Botticelli Drawings on view at the Legion of Honor through February 11. there has been no major exhibition dedicated to Botticelli’s art of drawing — until now. Germaine Tailleferre was the only female member of the group of “les 6”, a group of French composers forging a new voice in the early 20th century. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. pages.text: Wednesday, January 24, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet Sigmund Freud as music critic By Joseph Gold This article was inspired by a conversation I had with the nephew of Sigmund Freud many years ago. While some of it is fanciful, much is based on the information I got from N. Freud. Hey, Sigmund! You missed your calling. You should have been a music critic. I’d like to know your opinions on some of the immortal musicians of the past. “Johann Sebastian Bach was a giant in many ways. First, he stood about six feet four and was solid in every respect. Once he made up his mind to do something, you better get out of the way. You can hear these things in his music. Everything was always in perfect proportion, and his music dances all the way. I know that some people criticized him for being a conservative, but his harmonic vocabulary was so advanced that he always sounded modern. Mozart and Beethoven should be considered together. Beethoven was a great admirer of Mozart. That should be proof enough. As everyone probably knows, both Mozart and BeethoThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet ven suffered from a variety of psychological illnesses. Mozart was one of the first people who was noted to have Tourette’s syndrome. He would frequently blurt out scatological comments. This mercurial personality is readily observed in his music. He’ll state an idea and then do about face. Everything is always kept in perfect symmetry, however. Beethoven did similar things because his excitable personality was extreme to the point of irascibility. He was noted to have had a very bawdy sense of humor. That brings us to Paganini… the greatest virtuoso of all time. He considered Beethoven to be the greatest genius in the history of music. All I can say about him at this time is that his multifold talents caused all of music to be thrust into outer space. Franz Liszt never made any recordings but we have a good idea how he actually sounded. Almost all contemporary reports assure us that Emil von Sauer performed in a very similar manner to his master, Franz Liszt. Sauer always took his time and had a soft, velvety touch at the keyboard. Oh, how I wish that modern pianists would take note of this fact. But they all seem to be in a hurry to play faster and louder, as if it’s a competition. I’d like to mention the French composer-pianist St-Saens at this time. We are fortunate that he made a number of recordings and a silent film. His recordings prove that he played his music exactly as written. He would object strenuously if someone didn’t observe what he wanted.” Perhaps we should keep some of these things in mind when we attend concerts. I kind of wonder if every performance deserves a standing ovation. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony & Friends continues its Chamber Series with Spirited Impressions on Sunday, February 4 at 4 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts. This vibrant and romantic concert will feature piano trios exploring a wide range of French music, including Gabriel Fauré’s Piano Trio No. 1 in D Minor; Arthur Honegger’s Sonatine for Violin and Cello; Bay Area composer Jean Ahn’s A Flashback of Ravel; and Claude Debussy’s Piano Trio in G Major. Musicians Alison Lee, piano; Sarah Elert, violin; and Douglas Machiz, cello, will present Faurè’s marvel of color, energy, and contrast in his Piano Trio, followed by the vivacity of Honegger’s Sonatine. Audiences will find themselves immersed in a Parisian landscape, with the striking melodies of Jean Ahn’s homage to Ravel’s Impressionist works, with a contemporary twist. The musical “Tour de France” will be complete with one of Debussy’s earliest works, the sweet and sentimental Piano Trio. about experiencing lush and immersive music when musicians are playing so close that audiences can hear every nuance and breath, and feel every vibration and phrase,” said Ming Luke, Interim Executive Director of Berkeley Symphony. “Berkeley Symphony’s chamber concert Spirited Impressions brings us to France, perfect for a romantic February, with piano trios of Debussy, Fauré, Honegger, and Berkeley composer Jean Ahn.” Spirited Impressions provides a perfect pairing with Berkeley Symphony’s next Symphonic Series concert, French Reverie, on Sunday, February 25 at 4 p.m. at First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. The later symphonic concert will feature Dr. Robert Young, brother of Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young in A Kind of Trane, a riveting saxophone concerto by Guillaume Connesson, as well as one of the most famous impressionist works, Claude Debussy’s Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. articles.text: A scene from The Boys in the Boat To opine that the recently released The Boys in the Boat is old-fashioned filmmaking should not be regarded as criticism, but rather as high praise. It is an extraordinary and moving true story, based on the 2013 bestselling historical work by Daniel James Brown. The film opens in 1935, during the height of the Great Depression with scenes of a shantytown, also known as a Hooverville, its frayed inhabitants destitute and desperate. The camera reveals a young man, Joe Stanz (Callum Turner), living alone in the back of an abandoned wreck of a car. We soon learn that he is enrolled at the University of Washington, and while standing before the school registrar is told that he is behind in his tuition payments and is given a grace period of two weeks to pay or “find other educational arrangements.” Jobs are scarce, unemployment stalks the nation, and Joe, who is studying engineering, is urgently looking for work without success. From a classmate he learns that if he can qualify for the Washington junior varsity rowing team, that spot will include room, board, and help with tuition, plus parttime work. His problem is that he has never rowed before, and the opening slots are severely limited, amounting to only eight places plus a coxswain. On the first day of the tryouts, a crowd of young men show up. Standing before them is head rowing coach, Al Ulbrickson (Joel Edgerton), who tells them, in the starkest terms, that what they are about to embark on is “the most difficult team sport in the world.” The physical demands on the body and the mind are punishing, the skill sets necessary involve a concentrated synchronization that is like no other sport. And the eight-man shell is not comprised of eight individuals but represents a singular, harmonious effort. When the names of those selected for the JV team are announced, Joe is one of them. And so the world of rowing, unrelenting in its demands, is revealed through an intense montage of training, exercises, conditioning and endless rowing. The field of play is a wide ribbon of water near the university where the athletes endlessly practice in single sculls and in eight-man shells with their coxswains seated in the stern. One such is Bobby Moch (Luke Slatterly), setting the rhythm and number of strokes. To the surprise of Ulbrickson, the JV boat proves unexpectedly fast, proving to be stronger and faster than the varsity boat. This fact leads to a number of difficult decisions for the coaching staff, which ultimately leads to the JV boat being selected to represent Michael Paul Stehr Founder and Principal Artist Head of a Woman in Near Profile Looking down to the Left 1468–1470 The Virgin and Child…

articles.text: There was a time when on Saturday afternoons I sat in the balcony of the Laurel Theater in Oakland and watched what were then state-of-the-art adventure movies. They were intense. Riveting. And filled with one grand chase scene after the next. Often they were serials that defined the word cliffhanger. Just as the car of Don Winslow of the Navy was being chased by nefarious villains wearing fez hats and thick mustaches, it slams through the guard rail on a blind curve and soars out into space, jagged rocks waiting below. The scene would cut to the words, “To Be Continued Next Week.” These films embraced the minimalist tradition of screenwriting. Lots of action, harrowing moments in which our hero Don barely escapes, an abundance of fight scenes, and easily identifiable villains. There was little dialogue, character development or backstory. This wasn’t about Don’s conversations other than yelling to a gorgeous, helpless, terrified blonde, “Take the wheel!” on a careening speedboat while Don crawls to the stern to fight off the bad guys who’ve jumped on board. Adventure movies then, as now, were loud, exaggerated, fists landing on jaws, guns drawn and fired wildly. The film cuts were as staccato-like as anything produced today; the filmmakers knew our attention spans were short. Lots of action, harrowing moments in which our hero Don barely escapes, an abundance of fight scenes, and easily identifiable villains. There was little dialogue, character development or backstory. This wasn’t about Don’s conversations other than yelling to a gorgeous, helpless, terrified blonde, “Take the wheel!” on a careening speedboat while Don crawls to the stern to fight off the bad guys who’ve jumped on board. Adventure movies then, as now, were loud, exaggerated, fists landing on jaws, guns drawn and fired wildly. The film cuts were as staccato-like as anything produced today; the filmmakers knew our attention spans were short. In fact, if Don began talking too much to his sidekick or his marginal love interest, you See Night at the Museum on page 31 A scene from The Boys in the Boat By Chris Honoré To opine that the recently released The Boys in the Boat is old-fashioned filmmaking should not be regarded as criticism, but rather as high praise. It is an extraordinary and moving true story, based on the 2013 bestselling historical work by Daniel James Brown. The film opens in 1935, during the height of the Great Depression with scenes of a shantytown, also known as a Hooverville, its frayed inhabitants destitute and desperate. The camera reveals a young man, Joe Stanz (Callum Turner), living alone in the back of an abandoned wreck of a car. We soon learn that he is enrolled at the University of Washington, and while standing before the school registrar is told that he is behind in his tuition payments and is given a grace period of two weeks to pay or “find other educational arrangements.” Jobs are scarce, unemployment stalks the nation, and Joe, who is studying engineering, is urgently looking for work without success. From a classmate he learns that if he can qualify for the Washington junior varsity rowing team, that spot will include room, board, and help with tuition, plus parttime work. His problem is that he has never rowed before, and the opening slots are severely limited, amounting to only eight places plus a coxswain. On the first day of the tryouts, a crowd of young men show up. Standing before them is head rowing coach, Al Ulbrickson (Joel Edgerton), who tells them, in the starkest terms, that what they are about to embark on is “the most difficult team sport in the world.” The physical demands on the body and the mind are punishing, the skill sets necessary involve a concentrated synchronization that is like no other sport. And the eight-man shell is not comprised of eight individuals but represents a singular, harmonious effort. When the names of those selected for the JV team are announced, Joe is one of them. And so the world of rowing, unrelenting in its demands, is revealed through an intense montage of training, exercises, conditioning and endless rowing. The field of play is a wide ribbon of water near the university where the athletes endlessly practice in single sculls and in eight-man shells with their coxswains seated in the stern. One such is Bobby Moch (Luke Slatterly), setting the rhythm and number of strokes. To the surprise of Ulbrickson, the JV boat proves unexpectedly fast, proving to be stronger and faster than the varsity boat. articles.text: Lat week’s Walking on Wednesday group included Bill Ahern, Irene Thompson, Quincy and Helen Dong, Joanne Larson, Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kellogg, Sherry Jacobs, Melba Yee, Swee Ling Chen, Kat Lang, Helene Farber, Chuck Oraftik, Lori Austin, Nancy Henn, Tina Shum, Rick Eigenbrode, Stella Houston, Sharona Fischrup, Martin Levy, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Mike Henn, Peggy Shultz, Maricela Negron, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Matt Gerhardt, Nancy and Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Elizabeth Richter, Phil Witte, Ken Hubbert, Pat Keller, Adrienne Hamlin, Edith Lee, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Joyce Ahern, Claudine Bach, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kuo, Noemi Alvarado and Mark Davis, and Dick Carter. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 47 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday, January 17. There is some impressive Piedmont City and School District construction going on around town. Two new “bulb-outs,” also called “curb extensions,” are being built at the intersections of Oakland and El Cerrito Avenues and Oakland and Jerome Avenues. At Nova and Magnolia Avenues, a new traffic island is in the works, too. Steel beams have been erected for the new building at the Piedmont Community Pool site. Additionally, Witter Field and its track are getting new surfaces. The walkers thought it would be interesting to check out all of them, so a loop to all five was selected as the morning’s route. The group went down Magnolia Avenue to look at the progress on the pool. They were able to see a lot more than on past visits. The construction fence that surrounds the project had been pulled back in places. The shape of the facility with its building and two pools could be better envisioned now that the steel beams are up, and at the back is a massive, new, concrete retaining wall. The project was approved by voters in November 2020, and $19.5 million worth of bonds were authorized at that time when interest rates were low. The new facility replaces the original mid- 20th Century Piedmont Pool that was leaking water each day and no longer met the community’s needs. Designs for the new aquatics center were developed with extensive community input. However, the building’s size had to be reduced and other modifications made in May 2022 when construction bids came in higher than expected. Incremental funding was obtained to make the facility a unique all-electric design. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation led fundraising for landscaping. Construction started on January 27, 2023 with expectations that pool should open later this year. The group then went down Magnolia to the foot of El Cerrito Avenue to see the Witter resurfacing project. The new artificial turf looked good, but it appeared work needed to be done on the track. It was reported that cracks in large portions of the track’s surface had been discovered. Additional work and $155,500 more from Piedmont School District are needed to complete this approximately $4.9 million project to be funded by a State facilities grant. It was started in June 2023, but the expected February completion day is in question now. After Witter Field, they headed to Magnolia to Nova to see the first of the City’s street projects, a new traffic island. The site’s old bollards will be removed and curbing work has started. Then, it was up Nova to Jerome and Oakland Avenue to see the first of the bulb-outs. City Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said these curb extensions will make the areas safer by increasing pedestrian visibility, shortening road-crossing distances, and reducing vehicle speeds by narrowing the streets. Construction began on January 8 and is expected to be completed in three to four months. Traffic control by a construction flagman was helpful in getting the parade-like column of walkers across Oakland Avenue. Next it was up Oakland to see the bulb-out at El Cerrito Avenue. There was a significant carve out of the sidewalk, but no work was being done on it at the time. The total construction cost for the three locations is $773,885. Funding comes from a $50,000 Piedmont Beautification Foundation contribution and approximately $600,000 from the State Gas Tax. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: • Plunder Road (U.S., 1957), 7:30 p.m. From its thrilling opening, in which a crew of hooded robbers steal gold bullion from a train during a driving rainstorm, director Hubert Cornfield’s third feature film never stops moving. Gang leader Gene Raymond and his truck-driving cohorts (including Elisha Cook Jr.) desperately try to abscond with the score of a lifetime. • Hardly a Criminal / Apenas un Delincuente (Argentina, 1949), 9 p.m. The best Argentine noir of the 1940s tells the tale of a clever banking clerk who embezzles money from his employer and tries to get caught, since a loophole in the Argentine justice system will free him after six years behind bars — when he intends to reclaim the hidden loot. Part caper, part prison picture, this acclaimed drama earned Argentine director Hugo Fregonese a career in Hollywood.

articles.text: • Across the Bridge (U.S., 1957) 1:30 p.m. In this adaptation of a Graham Greene tale, Rod Steiger gives a compelling performance as an arrogant industry captain caught embezzling. Fleeing to Mexico, he impulsively switches identities with another rider and throws the body off the train. Unfortunately, his choice of victim lands him in a worse predicament. The film won rave reviews and great box-office receipts in England but remains virtually unknown in the U.S. • Zero Focus / Zero no Shōten (Japan, 1961), 3:30 p.m. In this many-layered crime mystery, newlywed bride Teiko Uhara sees her husband Kenichi off on one last business trip to his old office, and eagerly anticipates his return so they can start their new life. But Kenichi mysteriously vanishes and when the police move too slowly, tenacious Teiko begins her own investigation. This cross between slow-burning character study and thriller is tense and spellbinding. articles.text: Nestled in the heart of France, the Rhone Valley is a historic wine region extending from Lyon in the north to the Camargue area near the Mediterranean Sea in the south. Enriched by the Rhone River, which originates in the Swiss Alps and meanders through its valleys, the Rhone region has over 2,000 years of viticulture history dating back to the ancient Greeks. This picturesque landscape not only holds a profound historical and cultural significance but also serves as the nurturing ground for a diverse range of grape varieties, giving birth to some of the world’s most esteemed wines. The first cultivated vines in the Rhône valley were possibly planted around 600 BC. Syrah and Viognier are speculated to be the two most prominent grape varieties in the Northern Rhône. Some believe that Greeks brought Syrah grapes from the Persian city of Shiraz. Others say that the grape came from the Sicilian city of Syracuse, from whence the Romans sailed up the Rhône valley with Syrah and Viognier grapes. After the collapse of the Roman Empire, Popes gave fresh impetus to a flourishing wine trade in the region. In 1737, the King announced that all casks for resale should have the brand name C.D.R. (Côtes du Rhône). Just over 100 years later, wines from other parts of the region were added to the C.D.R. definition. Usually, Rhône reds are produced with Syrah and Grenache. Other red Rhône varietals are Mourvedre, Counoise, and Cinsault. Expect a fruity flavor and aroma that you’ll never forget. Indeed, Rhône whites feature a variety of flavors according to the dominant grape. The most common white Rhône varietals are Roussanne, Marsanne, Grenache Blanc, Viognier, and Clairette Blanche. The northern region of Rhône has a cooler climate because of the mistral wind that blows through the area. This region accounts for a very small percentage of total Rhône wine production. However, the Northern Rhône produces the most exclusive wines. Syrah is the only allowed grape variety here, but most of the AOCs allow a small amount of Marsanne or Roussanne in the blend. Cornas AOC is the exception, where any red wine must be 100% Syrah. The Southern Rhône wine region benefits from a modern Mediterranean climate. It has warmer summers and milder winters. The south region boasts an amazing variety of grapes. Two categories of wine are ‘Left’ and ‘Right’, which actually refer to the banks of the Rhône River. The left category features bigger wines with fuller and fruitier flavors. The Southern boasts a wealth of appellations that stretch from either side of the river into the mountains and valleys. The following wines represent some of the wonderful Rhone wines that are available on the market today. The Rhone wines also provide a good bargain. With the prices of Bordeaux and Burgundy wine skyrocketing, it is nice to find that all the wines reviewed here are less than $30.

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, January 24, 2024 Tudor Style Architecture By Will Adams Because England had such a strong cultural influence on early America, it was inevitable that we would inherit various architectural styles as well. While walking through Piedmont it is easy to come across the prominent Tudor style and its variants, maybe one of the most lasting of our British legacy. The Tudor we see in Piedmont today is really Tudor Revival, which was an early 1900’s reinvention of the medieval prototypes from the English Tudor dynasty of the 16th century. The Tudor style is characterized by steeply pitched, front facing gable roofs. There are, however, frequent variations and exceptions in this “playful” style of architecture with hipped roofs sometimes used in conjunction with the gables. What we end up with is a stately looking architecture that is also picturesque – the feeling of a country estate, which seems to be aesthetically suited for the large single family lots we have here. The popularity of this style in the early 1900’s was to a large degree an alternative to the modernism that was being developed in Europe with machined components and lack of ornamentation. People wanted a more handcrafted feeling that ended up being expressed in Tudor homes. As a matter of fact, the Tudor style was closely associated with the Arts and Crafts movement which was being developed at the same time for many of the same reasons. I often wonder why a certain architectural style becomes popular and then remains so for so many years. I think that certainly one reason is because these styles were well developed over a long period of time. Proportions, material selections, and detailing conventions were worked out over the years on different buildings until they became….fine architecture! Certainly. this was the case on the cathedrals that took hundreds of years to build. After building a part of it, seeing it for a few years or even decades, the sponsors and architects were able to re-design and correct functional and aesthetic components, sometimes even changing the architectural style completely. In any case, the Tudor style developed into an appealing and See Walking Piedmont on page 32 The “half-timbered” facade along with the steeply pitched gable roofs on typically two-and three-story buildings make the Tudor style easy to recognize. Intricate lower-level brick or stonework is also a common component as seen in these fine Piedmont homes. Not all Tudor homes are large manors. Tudor cottages with many of the signature hallmarks are also built. As discussed previously, this variation in building scale adds immensely to the vibrant texture and aesthetic vitality of the city of Piedmont. Artful, informal, even whimsical detailing is often found in the Tudor style. Chimneys and beautifully proportioned dormers both play a big part in the picturesque results.

After a half of a mile, the foundation of a factory building is covered with artwork from muralists in the area. It’s an area that provides this writer’s favorite lesser-known view of the Oakland hills, where you have an intimate sight of the Mormon Temple overlooking Oakland, Emeryville, and San Francisco. articles.text: desirable architecture all over this country. The visual giveaway of course is the half-timbered walls, consisting of a squared heavy timber frame structural system originally infilled with masonry or a stucco like mixture know as wattle between the timbers. The timber frame became unnecessary a long time ago, but the look was so favored and enduring that it continues to be imitated as a decorative motif instead of a structural necessity. Another attractive characteristic of the Tudor is the sophisticated window compositions, often very vertical and large, but made up of small divided lites (panes) which were all that were available until the early 20th century. The intricate detail and sense of scale resulted in an attractive character that is popular still today, as anyone who has glanced at a Marvin or Pella window catalogue can attest. Piedmont Real Estate Update January 2024 Happy New Year! As we welcome 2024, we hope everyone enjoyed the holidays and found time to relax with family and friends. Our newsletter series began one year ago, and we greatly appreciate the positive feedback we’ve received. Each month, we aim to discuss a topic that’s timely and relevant to our readers. Research and analysis are at the core of our business; we firmly believe leveraging data creates value for our clients as they navigate the dynamic Bay Area real estate market. If there is ever something you’d like to know more about, we’d love to hear from you! It may be information that other readers would find helpful and warrant a deeper look. As we close the books on 2023, we thought it would be worthwhile to look back at median prices over the last three years in Piedmont, Berkeley, and Oakland. An unprecedented rise in interest rates began in March 2022 and had notable repercussions on the local housing market. Both the number of home sales and the median prices of homes sold were impacted. Rates are expected to come down in 2024 if inflation continues to lower and hits the Fed’s 2% target. If we don’t see an improvement in inflation, or if it rises again, we may see more rate hikes. We’ll keep a close eye on the market and always welcome a discussion about buying or selling strategies. In Piedmont, the number of home sales in 2023 was down 32% from 2021. However, the median home price was only down 5% during that same period. This speaks to the low level of available inventory but also points to the value Piedmont holds even during a slow market. articles.text: As 2023 closed out and 2024 waited to take stage center, I found myself thinking about time. It’s abstract, invisible. And yet, ultimately, it’s all we have. The infinite is the finite and therefore, gradually, even painfully, we come to understand that time is of the essence. We acknowledge its presence in our lives by marking its passage, making the intangible tangible: birthdays, anniversaries, holidays. We glance at clocks, wear time on our wrists, check our cell phones, keep calendars, name the months that become years. All of the above brings me to that global celebration of a year ending and another beginning, often prompting, for many of us, a silent or shared New Year’s Resolution, one predicated on a promise. Indeed, resolution, resolve, resolute are all strong words that convey intent. But I would suggest that a NYR not be too weighted or require a monastic, disciplined effort. Best to gently frame it for the long haul. Neither guilt nor nudging disappointment should be the outcome. When I considered a resolution for 2024 the words “Be Kind” came to mind. Embedded in this resolution is the belief that kindness is underrated, especially in this moment of national acrimony, made manifest in the tone of our national discourse and sense of discontent. Place that discontent in the context of politics and it’s a dark, divisive, worrying tableau. The antidote to this national mood is to be kind at every opportunity, and be mindful that every interaction, however brief or transactional, can be defined or reframed by kindness. Once again, time is, indeed, of the essence. Best wishes for 2024. These dreaded days typically come when a politically expedient choice conflicts with the interests of the community at large. I suspect that state housing laws have ruined more than a few days for members of the Piedmont City Council. Another such day will likely dawn on January 22 when the Council chooses a preferred option among four alternative plans for housing 60 low-income families in Moraga Canyon. 50 years of research, as well as simple decency, urges that the low-income units be integrated into the remainder of the new Moraga Canyon neighborhood which will also include 72 market-rate units. For these reasons, as well as others having to do with land use and infrastructure constraints, consultants to the city have proposed that all four options keep the 132 units together rather than separated by major thoroughfares or difficult to traverse terrain. Three of the options would place the 132 units on the cemetery side of Moraga Avenue while a fourth would put all the units in Blair Park. Unfortunately, a politically expedient “hybrid” option could emerge with market-rate housing on the cemetery side of Moraga and low-income families segregated into Blair Park. Why would this hybrid be politically expedient? Because, first, it would please the powerful land-development lobby. articles.text: Deniz Ergun hired to help city meet climate goals In late November 2023, the City of Piedmont hired Deniz Ergun as its new sustainability program manager. Ergun will be responsible for implementing the city’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 and ensuring the city’s compliance with state and federal regulations, among other tasks. Ergun is originally from Oakville, a suburb in Toronto, Canada. Her family emigrated from Turkey a few years before she was born, and she grew up in a Turkish household. She attended Iroquois Ridge High School where a school trip to Costa Rica sparked her love of nature. “That specific trip really just sparked my love of nature. We were in the rainforest the whole time, and I just couldn’t believe how alive everything was. That completely changed the direction of the careers I was looking at,” she said. While pursuing her undergraduate degree at Guelph University, where she majored in wildlife biology, Ergun noticed a pattern developing in her studies. No matter the biome, the greatest threat to wildlife always seemed to be the climate crisis. “I came out of that four-year program deciding I want to focus moving forward on solutions.” She went on to earn a master’s degree in Building Sciences at Toronto Metropolitan University, where her research on reclaiming construction resources from demolished buildings won awards from the university’s Department Staff photo Deniz Ergun, the new sustainability program manager for the City of Piedmont. of Architectural Sciences. “Even in a very technical field, I was still very much drawn to an environmental emphasis in my work,” she said. After working with start-ups and local governments, she and her husband moved to California in 2022. “I knew that I wanted to continue doing work in for municipality and in government. So, when this opportunity popped up in Piedmont I started to look into the sustainability efforts that the city had been making it looked like a good fit for me.” Her first impressions of Piedmont were quite warm. “The first thing I noticed when I started at City Hall was that it was a really welcoming environment. I’m used to working in a jurisdiction that’s a lot bigger, and I felt like everyone made an effort to say hello. I got to do a tour and essentially meet most of the people I work with, which isn’t always the case. These guys really cared about who I was as an individual,” she said. Ergun is married to her husband, Brent Dienst, and together they have a two-year-old child. Ergun said she is hopeful for the future of the city’s climate goals. “This city has already done a lot, and now we’re trying to achieve some really ambitious greenhouse gas emission reduction goals. Now, it’s, ‘How are we going to build on the work that’s already been done?’ I’m hoping to do that in a way that brings the community into the plan because it’s not something that the city can do alone.”
articles.title: City welcomes new sustainability program manager

articles.text: Construction begins at intersection of Nova & Magnolia Ave. The traffic island at the intersection of Nova Ave. & Magnolia Ave., dubbed “Bollard Island” by community members, may not have its signature nickname for much longer. The Public Works Department recently began a construction project that will replace Bollard Island with a raised concrete-curbed median traffic island, thus eliminating the need for its plastic bollards. Additionally, a single bulb-out will be added at the corner of the island closest to 101 Magnolia Ave as part of a “traffic calming” measure. “The goal of the bulb out is to narrow roadways,” explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We’re trying to give pedestrians less distance to cross and give vehicles a lesser area to navigate. When vehicles are given more space, the faster they’re able to go.” Gonzales said that the new island, when finished, will be a greater safety aid to the community than the use of bollards. “The original bollards were not placed in a way that made them an effective traffic calming measure. This project is meant to rectify that.” For more information on construction projects in your area, please contact the Public Works Department at 420-3050 or email Director Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov. Staff photo Soon, Bollard Island will lose its signature plastic bollards in favor of a raised, concrete-curbed meridian.
articles.title: “Bollard Island” to lose its bollards

articles.text: Piedmont resident Chris Moore to run on a platform of public safety Piedmont resident and local activist Chris Moore has decided to run for 5th District County Supervisor on a platform that highlights public safety as his campaign’s number one concern. Following the unexpected retirement of longtime Supervisor Keith Carson, Moore is one of nine candidates running for the 5th District seat, which includes Albany, Piedmont, Emeryville, Berkeley, and sections of north and west Oakland. Moore has been a resident of Piedmont for 22 years and is a former member of the City of Piedmont’s budget committee. Readers may also recognize Moore from his activities with Piedmont Neighbors Together, a local activist group that promotes public safety reform and crime prevention. The group gained the attention of the community in September 2023 during a surprise demonstration outside Piedmont City Hall ahead of Police Chief Jeremy Bowers’ quarterly crime report. The group advocated for change in Piedmont’s crime prevention strategies, emphasizing a need for greater police deterrence. Since then, Moore has continued to be active in local politics. Moore kicked off his campaign at a launch party on Saturday, January 13, at Le Cheval in Oakland. The location is no doubt symbolic, as Le Cheval was one of several businesses in Oakland that closed in 2023 citing rising crime. “Over 6,000 businesses chose not to renew their business licenses in Oakland last year, and that is because of the crime problem. So, yes, I want to support public safety and stop this excessive and violent crime aimed at our local businesses,” said Moore. If elected, Moore said he will use his position as County Supervisor to further public safety in the 5th District by allocating funding away from organizations without “actionable results” on public safety and placing them with organizations that have more of an effect on preventing crime. “I’m not doing this for the politics. I’m doing this for the people of Alameda County. I truly am,” he said. Moore is one of two Piedmont residents running for this position. Lorrel Plimier, president of the Piedmont League of Women Voters, is also running for a seat on the County Board of Supervisors. For more information on Chris Moore’s campaign, voters can visit www.chrismooreforsupervisor.com. Election Day will be on March 5, 2024. For more information on your local poll station, visit the California Secretary of State’s website at www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place. Photo by Thomas Hawk Chris Moore talks with a supporter on Saturday, January 13, at the launch of his campaign as a candidate for a seat on the Alameda County Board of Supervisors.
articles.title: Local activist runs for county supervisor

articles.text: At its meeting on Wednesday, January 10, Piedmont School Board members were advised by middle school, high school and Millennium HS counselors on what kind of counseling most helps their students. Prefacing the counselors’ presentation, PHS English teacher and Association of Piedmont Teachers union president Dr. Elise Marks said, “We all know that our students are extremely high achieving, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t also high-needs. Our kids push themselves hard and need support.” Compared to nearby districts like Oakland and Berkeley, which “may have only one counselor for every 300 or 400 students,” PHS is at about the maximum ratio recommended by the American School Counseling Association of one counselor for 250 students. “Because we lost a PMS counselor at the start of this year, their caseload is now [1 per 415 students].” This caseload entails “organized chaos,” said Piedmont Middle School counselor Amy Sharp. “It’s a juggling act to make a daily plan prioritizing middle school students’ needs with everyone’s schedules,” she said. Collaboration has been a key to direct student support, she added. Large groups are especially helpful for academic counseling like grade-level skills, attendance and orientations, while common student needs like tech use and [its mental health effects] often involve large meetings with parents, administration and the wellness center. At the high school level, mental health support is more deeply intertwined with other areas of counseling like academic management, personal lives and future plans, said PHS counselor Amanda Carlson. PHS counselors collaborate frequently with the College and Career Center, and much one-on-one talk involves juggling graduation requirements with personal time management and lifestyle health, while also encouraging interests that students may not know they could pursue as careers. articles.text: Though Piedmont students and parents are already halfway through the school year, a new calendar year brings with it new state laws. Here are some of the most important measures passed by the California legislature taking effect in January 2024. Media literacy in every grade Per AB 873, California’s K-12 public school students will be required to learn from media literacy instruction which will help them identify fake news posted online while also being able to tell the difference between legitimate news articles and paid advertising. Critical engagement with online media content will be incorporated into the four core curricula of English language arts, mathematics, science and history / social science. Prohibited suspension for willful defiance SB 274 extends an existing prohibition against suspending students for willful defiance in grades 6 through 12, effective through July 1, 2029. “Willful defiance” includes students disrupting school activities or defying the authority of a teacher or administrator. Licensed school nurses AB 1722 allows school districts to hire licensed vocational nurses to be supervised by a credentialed school nurse if a credentialed nurse is not available to fill the licensed nurse’s job. Excused religious and personal absences Under existing law, students cannot be excused from school for more than four hours per semester to attend a religious retreat. AB 1503 expands this provision, allowing students to be excused for a full day. Although religious retreats are the only “justifiable personal reason” specified in the digest of this bill, others include “an appearance in court,” “attendance at a funeral service” and “attendance at an employment conference.” Expanded punishment for hate crimes AB 2282 increases the consequences for anyone who “places or displays hate symbols on private and nonprivate property, with the intent to terrorize another.” These symbols include Nazi swastikas, nooses, and desecrated crosses or other religious symbols. Although the increased prison sentence and maximum fines apply to hate crimes in general, the bill also expands the places where hate symbols are banned, to include K-12 schools, colleges, universities and public spaces. Involuntary leave salary AB 472 requires a classified school district or community college employee “placed on an involuntary leave of absence while the employee has criminal charges, a criminal investigation, or an administrative matter pending,” to be fully compensated for the leave period if the investigation concludes in the employee’s favor. Opioid overdose prevention SB 10 requires any school serving grades 7 through 12 to establish safety plans including protocols for responding to an opioid overdose. The bill encourages “county offices of education to establish a County Working Group on Fentanyl Education in Schools, as provided, for the purposes of outreach, building awareness, and collaborating with local health agencies regarding fentanyl overdoses.” Adequate school meals SB 348 requires “each school district, county superintendent of schools, and charter school to make available a nutritionally adequate breakfast and … lunch, free of charge during each school day, to any pupil who requests a meal, without consideration of the pupil’s eligibility for a federally funded free or reduced-price meal.” It also requires schools to “provide pupils with adequate time to eat, as determined by that school district, county superintendent of schools, or charter school.” Firing a superintendent or assistant superintendent Per SB 494, school districts can’t fire a superintendent or assistant superintendent at a special or emergency school board meeting, or within 30 days after the board’s first meeting after an election. To fire without cause, the board would have to hold a regular public meeting with a 72-hour notice.
articles.title: New school laws to take effect this month

articles.text: Piedmont Play School welcomes all interested families to its open house this Saturday, January 20, from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. at 401 Hampton Road, Piedmont. Meet the teachers, hear from current parents, and learn about this play-based cooperative preschool for children ages 3-5 years The Open House is for parents only. Those interested may RSVP to orianasyed@piedmontplayschool.org. If you’re new to the area, Piedmont Play School is located at Hampton Field in the most picturesque park setting. If you aren’t new to Piedmont, you might know that Piedmont Play School was established in 1958 by a small group of parents wanting to start a parent cooperative school. Piedmont Play School was first located at the Piedmont Community Church then moved adjacent to Wildwood Elementary, for three years below Community Hall, and currently is at the cozy cottage building at Hampton Field. It has 18 students ages 3 to 5, three teachers and one volunteer parent each day. Classes are in session from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Monday to Friday. Its calendar year is similar to Piedmont School District. As a cooperative, every parent takes on a job to help class run smoothly. Michelle Ritchie started teaching at the school in 2013 and became its Director three years later. She knows she has big shoes to fill after hearing about the legendary, dedicated teachers that came before her. Ritchie’s staff works every day to keep the school’s legacy thriving and to give the students a wonderful preschool experience based on their needs and interests. “I am a huge advocate of learning through play and I feel honored and privileged to serve our local community,” Ritchie said. “My co-teachers and I strive to provide a safe and nurturing environment where children can feel comfortable to express themselves and make lifelong companions.” Rewards of the co-op model are abundant – the opportunity to have more insight into your child’s day, have a tight-knit community that strives to organize extracurricular family activities and friendships that can last a lifetime. If you are interested in more information, plan on attending the Annual Open House on Saturday, January 20 from 10 am-12pm. For more information, e-mail orianasyed@piedmontplayschool.org. Director and head teacher Michelle Ritchie enjoys playing with the children at Piedmont Play School.
articles.title: Piedmont Play School open house on January 20

New school laws to take effect this month By Selen Ozturk Though Piedmont students and parents are already halfway through the school year, a new calendar year brings with it new state laws. Here are some of the most important measures passed by the California legislature taking effect in January 2024. Media literacy in every grade Per AB 873, California’s K-12 public school students will be required to learn from media literacy instruction which will help them identify fake news posted online while also being able to tell the difference between legitimate news articles and paid advertising. Critical engagement with online media content will be incorporated into the four core curricula of English language arts, mathematics, science and history / social science. Prohibited suspension for willful defiance SB 274 extends an existing prohibition against suspending students for willful defiance in grades 6 through 12, effective through July 1, 2029. “Willful defiance” includes students disrupting school activities or defying the authority of a teacher or administrator. Licensed school nurses AB 1722 allows school districts to hire licensed vocational nurses to be supervised by a credentialed school nurse if a credentialed nurse is not available to fill the licensed nurse’s job. Excused religious and personal absences Under existing law, students cannot be excused from school for more than four hours per semester to attend a religious retreat. AB 1503 expands this provision, allowing students to be excused for a full day. Although religious retreats are the only “justifiable personal reason” specified in the digest of this bill, others include “an appearance in court,” “attendance at a funeral service” and “attendance at an employment conference.” Expanded punishment for hate crimes AB 2282 increases the consequences for anyone who “places or displays hate symbols on private and nonprivate property, with the intent to terrorize another.” These symbols include Nazi swastikas, nooses, and desecrated crosses or other religious symbols. Although the increased prison sentence and maximum fines apply to hate crimes in general, the bill also expands the places where hate symbols are banned, to include K-12 schools, colleges, universities and public spaces. Involuntary leave salary AB 472 requires a classified school district or community college employee “placed on an involuntary leave of absence while the employee has criminal charges, a criminal investigation, or an administrative matter pending,” to be fully compensated for the leave period if the investigation concludes in the employee’s favor. Opioid overdose prevention SB 10 requires any school serving grades 7 through 12 to establish safety plans including protocols for responding to an opioid overdose. The bill encourages “county offices of education to establish a County Working Group on Fentanyl Education in Schools, as provided, for the purposes of outreach, building awareness, and collaborating with local health agencies regarding fentanyl overdoses.” Adequate school meals SB 348 requires “each school district, county superintendent of schools, and charter school to make available a nutritionally adequate breakfast and … lunch, free of charge during each school day, to any pupil who requests a meal, without consideration of the pupil’s eligibility for a federally funded free or reduced-price meal.” It also requires schools to “provide pupils with adequate time to eat, as determined by that school district, county superintendent of schools, or charter school.” Firing a superintendent or assistant superintendent Per SB 494, school districts can’t fire a superintendent or assistant superintendent at a special or emergency school board meeting, or within 30 days after the board’s first meeting after an election. To fire without cause, the board would have to hold a regular public meeting with a 72-hour notice.

articles.text: Piedmont High School actors will perform the dark musical Cabaret, directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead, Thursday through Sunday, February 1 to February 4 at the Alan Harvey Theater on the school campus. Written by John Kander and Fred Ebb, the story is set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close. It explores the exhilarating and tumultuous life in Berlin as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. (The director has chosen to eliminate the use of swastikas and military uniforms in this production.) Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to have an impact its audience and performers. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Shultz,” explained PHS sophomore Ben Wakefield. “The Israel-Hamas War, which The Tony Award-winning musical Cabaret premieres at Piedmont High School on Thursday, February 1, and runs through February 4. unfolded during our rehearsals, did impact my feelings about performing in the show. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical.” “Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present,” Wakefield added.” More than 60 high school students are involved in the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal Direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Performances are at 7 p.m. Tickets are $30 reserved, $25 adult general admission, $24 65+, $16 youth) and are available online at showtix4u.com/ event-details/80097 and at the box office. For more information, contact PHS theater director and choreographer Amy Moorehead at amoorhead@piedmont.k12.ca.us.
