articles.text: 2024 is here, and this year we’ll have the opportunity to witness a spectacular sight – a total solar eclipse. A total solar eclipse occurs when the moon travels between the Sun and Earth, fully blocking the face of the Sun. When the moon reaches this point where it fully blocks the Sun, it has reached totality. During this period of totality, the skies will darken, and the outermost portion of the Sun will become visible. This is known as the Sun’s corona, and it is usually concealed by the brightness of the Sun. Eclipses allow us to witness the Sun in a truly unique way and this year we will be having the chance to witness the last total solar eclipse visible from the contiguous United States until 2044. The Path of Totality The eclipse will take place on April 8, 2024, and its path of totality will extend through parts of Mexico, the United States, and Canada. To witness the total solar eclipse, observers will need to be within the path of totality. This year’s total solar eclipse is projected to last slightly over four minutes and the closer to the center of the path, the longer the period of totality will last. If you are viewing from outside the path of totality you may still have the chance to experiA solar eclipse will take place on April 8, 2024. ence a partial solar eclipse. A partial solar eclipse happens when the moon travels between the Sun and Earth, partially blocking the surface of the Sun. Observe Safely It is never safe to observe the sun without using proper specialized eye protection. Always remember to use special solar glasses, also known as eclipse glasses. When purchasing eclipse glasses ensure they meet international standards for filters used to view the Sun. It is also never safe to observe through unfiltered camera lenses, binoculars, or telescopes. Separate professional solar filters must always be used. Eclipses are an incredible sight to see but remember safety comes first. The Countdown Begins As we begin counting down the days, we invite you to join us at Chabot Space & Science Center where we’ll have the chance to experience this celestial event from Chabot’s Observation Deck. In Oakland, we will be in 34% totality, meaning 66% of the Sun’s face will be covered by the Moon. To learn more visit chabotspace.org. Isabel Lopez Ramirez is with Chabot Space and Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in the Oakland hills.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Celestial Event of the Year: A Total Solar Eclipse

articles.text: The Havens Dads Club will host its 16th Annual Havens Poker Night this Friday, January 20 at the Veterans Hall. A beginner tutorial starts at 6:00 p.m., the first cards will be dealt at 6:30 p.m. and the night will continue until the sold-out field of competing bluffers and betters are whittled down to one champion. All proceeds from the event will support Havens Elementary School projects. Previous projects included partial funding for the Becker Field replacement, the Ellen Driscoll mural, lunch tables and awnings on campus, and playground blocks. The tournament, themed “All in the for Kids,” will feature professional card dealers and poker tables, with an unlimited re-buy-in format to allow for players on full-tilt to utilize their gambling skills. Adult beverages for sale will include cocktails, beer, and wine with Havens Dad mixologist Peter Day in charge. articles.text: My name is Kane Crawford-Jakubiak, and I am a Life Scout in Piedmont Troop 11. I am working on my Eagle Scout Project with the Piedmont Historical Society. My project will help the Piedmont Historical Society by video recording interviews of former Piedmont Scouts and scouters from the 1930’s-1990’s who are willing to share their stories of what it was like to be a Scout or scouter in Piedmont back then. The goal of the project is to help the Piedmont Historical Society document and preserve this unique aspect of Piedmont’s history. I will be working with current Piedmont Scouts to video record the interviews. Piedmont is one of the oldest Scouting Councils in the country and Scouting has always been an important part of our community. I hope my project will be able to preserve these stories for future generations. If you are interested in telling your Scouting story, please contact me to set up a time for an interview. I can be reached at piedmontscoutinghistory@gmail.com.
articles.title: Calling all former Piedmont Scouts and Scouters

articles.text: “Roaring Twenties” theme on Feb. 10 celebrates Wildwood Elementary’s 100th anniversary The Wildwood Dads Club will host its annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 10 in the Veterans Hall from 6 to 11 p.m., with dinner starting at 7:00 p.m. The event will celebrate the 100th anniversary of Wildwood Elementary School. Tickets for this year’s event, themed “The Roaring Twenties,” are now on sale – and going fast, said Scott Zengel, President of the Wildwood Dads Club. With the addition of drinks and dancing, the club expects over the capacity of 150 Crab Feed attendees at this year’s event, which will include fresh Dungeness crab, oven-roasted salmon, New Orleans-style spicy spinach, baked macaroni and cheese, scalloped potatoes, coffee and— back by popular demand— tuxedo chocolate mousse cake for dessert. “Given that we’re taking a page out of the history books, the whole event will be focused on the period when Wildwood Elementary was founded, and we’ve been working with the Piedmont Historical Society to put together a presentation on the history of the school to share at the feed,” Zengel said. “The Crab Feed is our biggest event of the year, and we sell out every year, so we’re excited to bring the community together to eat delicious crab, dance and give back to Piedmont.” All proceeds will benefit the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s Sustainable Landscaping Project for the Piedmont Community Pool, Zengel added The crab feed is an adults-only event which includes bottomless beer and wine and dancing after dinner from 8:30 to 11 p.m. Specialty cocktails are available for purchase as well. Per the theme, this year’s dress code is Roaring Twenties-themed. Entertainment will be provided by DJ Ben Anderson, a Wildwood dad. For tickets ($75-$125), see wildwooddadsclub.org/crab-feed.
articles.title: Wildwood Crab Feed tickets selling fast

articles.text: Renee Taharka, 3rd grade Let us stand up Let us push through the barriers that hold us back To let go of the prejudice and stereotypes that float around us Let us be the ones that open our eyes to the people Let us be a concerned generation The ones who see the problems And the solutions Let’s be the ones who solve the wrongs that we all commit To help heal the wounds that no one will ever admit Let us remain awake through a great revolution Let us open our eyes to find a solution To see the world as other people see it Maybe then we can find resolution Let us be the ones who fix these mistakes Let us be the ones who stop the flames Let us be the generation who remains awake this feeling every day. Some people never feel this. Some people cause this. by bullying. Or by cyberbullying. But no matter what or who it is, this shouldn’t be an everyday feeling. Over the past couple years, it feels as if bullying, racism and sexism have just faded away. People are only thinking about the current violence, and wars. People have started to think, “if it’s not me then why would I care?” But when people just give up and stop helping, then think of how much worse it’s getting for people experiencing this. I do see that violence is a major issue. Many people are being robbed, and having their belongings stolen. But some people just let other issues go. For example, when a family sits down at a dinner table, no one says, “racism is a major issue, and it needs to stop.” Instead, everyone goes straight to the violence, and how annoying it is that their car window was broken last night. When people influence other people, it spreads. For example, when a parent, or trusted adult tells a young child about racism and bullying, they can learn to prevent bullying and stand up for others being bullied. If a child doesn’t learn about this, they may not recognize the fact that they are being bullied. For example, a young child goes to school. Let’s say they’re in preschool. They get bullied, or an older kid says a racist comment to them. They are unaffected and continue with their day. This is because their parents have yet to tell them what racism is and how bad it is. Now that’s just horrible. Someone saying a racist comment to an innocent child who is unaware. Another big issue is cyberbullying. Unlike bullying, you can’t really prevent cyberbullying without reporting it which takes a while. Cyberbullying can be done in different ways. One may hack or steal passcodes, while another may bully in a text, or in a game chat. You may think this is not a big deal, but when you think about it, you know that it is. One reason is because it may hurt even more when someone says a racist or rude comment online than in person. This may be because you don’t necessarily know who the person is, or because you can’t fully understand people in a text or chat. This may be a problem because when you are talking to someone in person you can understand their tone and see their facial expressions, but when you are online you don’t really know how the person is feeling. All of these issues relate, because racism is a form of bullying, and bullying can happen online (cyberbullying). All of these issues must come to a stop. pages.text: Wednesday, January 17, 2024 9 Art & Essay winners from 3rd annual MLK Jr. Showcase Piedmont’s 27th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 15, concluded with the display of Piedmont student artwork and literature in the Alan Harvey Theater. This was the third year Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) has hosted the student showcase, with 40 submissions from K-12 students. Recordings of student voices read aloud some of the poems projected onto the stage. But no matter what or who it is, this shouldn’t be an everyday feeling. Over the past couple years, it feels as if bullying, racism and sexism have just faded away. People are only thinking about the current violence, and wars. People have started to think, “if it’s not me then why would I care?” But when people just give up and stop helping, then think of how much worse it’s getting for people experiencing this. I do see that violence is a major issue. Many people are being robbed, and having their belongings stolen. But some people just let other issues go. For example, when a family sits down at a dinner table, no one says, “racism is a major issue, and it needs to stop.” Instead, everyone goes straight to the violence, and how annoying it is that their car window was broken last night. When people influence other people, it spreads. If a child doesn’t learn about this, they may not recognize the fact that they are being bullied. For example, a young child goes to school. Let’s say they’re in preschool. They get bullied, or an older kid says a racist comment to them. They are unaffected and continue with their day. This is because their parents have yet to tell them what racism is and how bad it is. Now that’s just horrible. Someone saying a racist comment to an innocent child who is unaware. Another big issue is cyberbullying. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Natalia Martinez dazzles with 41 points Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team appears to still be the class of the Western Alameda County Conference after defeating Bishop O’Dowd 59-50 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Wednesday, January 10. They also walloped league foe St. Joseph 72-33 on Friday, January 12 before losing a non-league game to Rancho Christian, 55-45, at an MLK Showcase at St. Mary’s of Stockton on Saturday, January 13. The victory over O’Dowd puts Piedmont on-track for its second-consecutive WACC title. “We haven’t played since December 30 and we knew it wouldn’t be the cleanest game. We knew O’Dowd would get back into the game. We got off to a good start, which was great to see after falling behind in some games before the break,” said coach Bryan Gardere. It was another phenomenal game for senior guard Natalia Martinez who finished with 41 points. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up a solid week with two wins and a loss in their last three games. After losing by 20 points to Western Alameda County Conference foe Alameda, 58-38, on Wednesday, January 10 at home, they followed up with a 58-47 league win over St. Joseph on the road and pulled out a 2-point victory over former state champion Fremont of Oakland, 48-46, in the MLK Showcase at Merritt College on Monday, January 15. Piedmont twice held double-digit leads against Fremont before the Tigers went on scoring runs in the third and fourth quarters. Piedmont had to overcome 25 turnovers to achieve its victory. “Fremont is a really long and athletic team. Doing film-study, we knew they had players who could score with the best of them. I think we did a good job shutting down their best player” said coach Ben Spencer. “It’s hard to win games [like that], but we never gave up the lead.” Senior forward Brit Burden led with 26 points against Fremont and had a big week with 16 points against Alameda and 24 against St. Joseph. Burden has shown improvement in each appearance with his ability to finish at the rim and draw fouls. “I’ve been working on my preparation before games and that’s translating. You just have to control getting to the hoop and finishing,” said Burden. Spencer is seeing how Burden can take control of games. He had a huge block to end the game. “He’s figured out after the Novato game that he’s going to be the best player on the floor offensively and defensively. He made a huge block, His length is tremendous and now over the last five games, he’s drawn a lot of fouls” said Spencer. The Highlanders now look ahead to another big week of games, playing league rival San Leandro today, January 17, and Castro Valley on Friday, January 19 before traveling to Marin Catholic in Kentfield on Saturday. 48-46 win over Fremont Piedmont held Fremont to just four points in the first quarter, 10-4, and led 25-17 at halftime. The Highlanders took a seven-point 41-34 lead into the fourth quarter and closed out with just seven points in the final going, but good enough to win 48-46. In the third, PHS built a comfortable 12-point lead at 36-24, but the Tigers went on a 10-0 scoring run to make it a two-point game, 36-34. The Highlanders had a 7-0 scoring run at the end of the third to start of the fourth period up 43-34. Fremont scored eight straight points off of turnovers to put itself one-point behind at 45-44. With one minute left, Burden dished off a pass to Dillon Casey who knocked down a 3-pointer, 48-44. After a basket by Fremont, 48-46, they had a chance to hit a game-winning 3-pointer with 20 seconds left, but Burden was there to block the shot. Piedmont retained possession and successfully killed the clock. Final stats: Burden finished with 26 points, eight rebounds, three assists, three steals, and one block. Casey had 10 points, Ravi Silverberg had eight, while Thorin Holmes and P.J. Brayer had two. 58-47 victory over St. Joseph Piedmont led 17-14 in the first quarter and 27-24 by halftime. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team remained undefeated season with 3-0 wins over Mt. Eden on Friday, January 12, and San Lorenzo two days earlier. Both matches were played at Chabot College in Hayward. The pair of games brings the Highlanders’ record to 6-1-0 overall (W-T-L) and 1-1-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents after tying 2-2 with Castro Valley the previous week. “We threw it away against Castro Valley after being up 2-0 with 10 minutes to go. But I like our response since then, I think our intensity is great and we’re working really hard on the defensive end,” said coach Todd Sullivan. “We have a solid group of 11 and know our set-team now. It’s a case of the players getting more comfortable with each other and understanding each other’s game,” The Highlanders scored all three goals against Mt. Eden in the first half, and piled on two second-half goals against the Grizzlies of San Lorenzo. “I think we’re getting stronger. In the early portion of the schedule, we were struggling to finish. In the first half [against Mt. Eden], we were doing a great job at finishing and connecting passes. The game got chippy in the second half, but we managed to keep the clean sheet, so shoutout to our defenders,” said Bosco Lorin, who scored two goals and an assist against Mt. Eden. Piedmont looks ahead to a critical week of league matches on the road. They face San Leandro tonight, January 17, play at Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, and face Berkeley on Tuesday, January 23. The Dragons are currently 8-1-1 and the Yellowjackets are 11-0-1. “One of our strengths has been playing together and I think that’s how we’ve pulled a lot of our results. That’s going to be important as we transition into the latter part of the season,” said captain Riley Stratman. “We just need to keep practicing, stay sharp, and stay healthy. We need to treat these upcoming games like we’ve treated the rest of these teams. They are tough teams, but we’re a strong team, too. If we stay confident, we can beat anyone,” added Lorin. 3-0 over Mt. Eden After having a few shot attempts wither go wide or blocked by Mt. Eden, Piedmont broke through in the 14th minute when Lorin sent a pass from the left wing to Jacques Saldanha, who lobbed a ball over the Monarchs’ goal keeper on his first touch in the 14th minute. Eden. Jacob Faucher scored on a free kick against San Lorenzo. Enzo Bernales has two assists against Mt. Eden and a goal against San Lorenzo.

articles.text: Staff Photos Miranda Liu (left) and Elsa Wallway celebrate Wallway’s first goal against Alameda. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team posted a 2-2 draw with Alameda on the road on Thursday, January 11, but lost 3-0 to Castro Valley at Chabot College two days earlier. The results bring its record to 6-1-1 (0-1-1 in league). Returning from Winter Break means the Highlanders are getting several players back from their club schedule, including sophomore striker Miranda Liu, the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2023. “I think we were good enough to win [against Alameda], I though they did well. It’s always tough to come to Thompson Field (slick and bumpy), and we dealt with it fairly well. It’s obviously great to bring back strong players from their club teams. I thought we had a good second-half against Castro Valley,” said coach Dan Chubbock. The Highlanders initially led 1-0 over Alameda before allowing a goal prior to halftime and another in the 52nd minute. But Piedmont tied the match in the 70th minute but couldn’t find the back of the net for a game-winner. “Coming into the season is always a big shock because we all are coming from our club teams and we have to gel in just a week or two. The early portion of the schedule is always tough, so now it’s just trying to mesh and became as cohesive as we can,” said senior Lola Beihn. Both Piedmont goals were scored by freshman Elsa Wallway in an impressive varsity debut. She played the club season with the De Anza Force. “Miranda had a great assist on the first goal and I was just able to slip it behind their defense into the net. The second half goal was a great press out of the back. It honestly feels great and I feel super fortunate to play with these girls and this team,” said Wallway. 2-2 draw with Alameda Piedmont had a couple of shots on target in the first half prior to the first goal with Julianna Miranda Liu with a chip shot goal attempt against Alameda.

articles.text: Editor: On the week of January 15-22, Piedmont Key Club will be running a soccer equipment drive at Piedmont High and Piedmont Middle School, and Havens Elementary. This drive is for any type of soccer equipment, from balls to cleats, shin guards, and even athletic clothing. Donations will go to the charity, Soccer Without Borders, an organization that reaches out to students and kids in the community through soccer. They focus especially on making a space for newcomer youth (refugees and immigrants) to connect with their peers and community by providing resources and training for soccer teams. together and help children develop social and developmental skills through the sport of soccer. Look for the donation bins and posters throughout the PHS, PMS, and Havens campuses. –Sabrina Olliphant PHS Key Club president

articles.text: With an enrollment size typically around 900 students, you will often see recurring faces at Witter Field, Binks Rawlings Gym, Humphries Diamond, and Witter Softball Field. Here is a feature-piece on three influential athletes at the school who are competing in multiple sports. OLIVER SHAFROTH Soccer & Lacrosse MARKOS LAGIOS Football & Baseball Junior Markos Lagios is the football team’s starting quarterback and will be entering his third year as a starter on the baseball team this spring. He recently was named as a second-team AllMetro selection by the San Francisco Chronicle. Last fall, Lagios led the Highlanders to a 7-4 record and a berth in the North Coast Section playoffs. It was the school’s first league title since 2015. In 2023, Lagios completed 62 percent of his passes in 2023 for 1,941 passing yards, 22 touchdowns and just three interceptions. Lagios also ran for 788 rushing yards, averaging over five yards per carry, and added 13 more touchdowns to his tally, giving him 35 total scores. In baseball Lagios plays both centerfield and third base, Last year he hit for a .303 average with 23 hits, 11 doubles, three triples, 18 RBIs and led the team with two home runs and 27 runs scored. The Highlanders went 14-11 last spring after being bumped up to the WACC’s Foothill Division. They reached the NCS Semifinals as the No. 8 seed and upset No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 in the quarterfinals and beating No. 9 Branson 4-3 in a 12-inning opening round win. Photo by Todd Marshburn Hailey Marshburn is a four-year starter on both the soccer and lacrosse varsity teams. Oliver Shafroth, a senior utility player on the soccer team is also a former first-team AllLeague recipient on the lacrosse team. He has appeared as a midfielder and a defender in coach Todd Sullivan’s soccer lineup, making a difference with his strength, comparable to former player Jack Nelson. Shafroth will be entering his third year on the varsity lacrosse team. He led the team last season as their primary faceoff specialist, and helped lead them to their sixth consecutive league championship in 2023. He recorded one assist and dominated the faceoff circle in Piedmont’s 14-6 win over Bishop O’Dowd in the title game by claiming 12 face-offs. Piedmont finished last year with a 14-4 record and reached HAILEY MARSHBURN Soccer & Lacrosse Hailey Marshburn wears the captain’s armband for the girls’ soccer team this winter. She plays midfield and also has the speed to move out wide as a fullback. Marshburn has scored once so far this season, Last year, she scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s sudden-death 2-1 win over No. 1 seed University to claim the North Coast Section title. Marshburn is a four-year starter on the lacrosse team and was often tasked to move the ball upfield with her speed and elusiveness. She was among Piedmont’s leaders in ground ball recoveries. Staff Photos Markos Lagios finished the football season and looks ahead to baseball in the spring.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Sailing Club is getting ready for its season starting February 3, with an introductory clinic the week before, on Sunday, January 28. As part of the Encinal Yacht Club High School Sailing Program, participants attend regular practices at the yacht club in Alameda and will be in several weekend regattas in the Bay Area and Southern California. The regattas are organized by the Pacific Coast Interscholastic Sailing Association (PCISA). Sophie Hess, a Piedmont High junior, joined the team in the fall. “I have loved being on the sailing team because it’s a great way to take advantage of the opportunity to actually sail pretty close to home. It is amazing to go to school then drive to Alameda, rig a boat and enjoy a gorgeous sunset from the water. It is an amazing experience. As a beginner to sailing, I felt a bit intimidated; but everyone has been so welcoming and friendly.” PHS senior Peter Stokes joined the team as a sophomore. “Small boat sailing is the most involved and fun type of sailing, it can be as competitive as you want it to be and offers a great way to meet people from other schools in the Bay,” he said. Team captain Mica Jorcino, a senior, joined the EYC high school sailing program as an 8th grader and is currently hoping to continue sailing in college. “I’ve been able to learn so many new skills and have gained so much knowledge as I get out of my comfort zone. It’s a super welcoming environment and I have loved seeing our team grow with so many people and incredible coaches these past five years,” she said. For more information reach out to Mica Jorcino at 24micaelajo@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or visit tinyurl.com/PHSsailing. Photos by Sophie Hess Mica Jorcino and Peter Stokes, PHS Seniors, at the NorCal regatta in the San Francisco Bay off of Richmond. The Encinal Yacht Club Jr. Sailing Program works in partnership with a number of East Bay high schools who have teams or clubs that participate in the Interscholastic Sailing Association.
articles.title: PHS Sailing Club gears up for spring season

HAILEY MARSHBURN Soccer & Lacrosse Hailey Marshburn wears the captain’s armband for the girls’ soccer team this winter. She plays midfield and also has the speed to move out wide as a fullback. Marshburn has scored once so far this season, Last year, she scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s sudden-death 2-1 win over No. 1 seed University to claim the North Coast Section title. Marshburn is a four-year starter on the lacrosse team and was often tasked to move the ball upfield with her speed and elusiveness. She was among Piedmont’s leaders in ground ball recoveries. PHS Sailing Club gears up for spring season Piedmont High School’s Sailing Club is getting ready for its season starting February 3, with an introductory clinic the week before, on Sunday, January 28. As part of the Encinal Yacht Club High School Sailing Program, participants attend regular practices at the yacht club in Alameda and will be in several weekend regattas in the Bay Area and Southern California. The regattas are organized by the Pacific Coast Interscholastic Sailing Association (PCISA). Sophie Hess, a Piedmont High junior, joined the team in the fall. “I have loved being on the sailing team because it’s a great way to take advantage of the opportunity to actually sail pretty close to home. Team captain Mica Jorcino, a senior, joined the EYC high school sailing program as an 8th grader and is currently hoping to continue sailing in college. “I’ve been able to learn so many new skills and have gained so much knowledge as I get out of my comfort zone. It’s a super welcoming environment and I have loved seeing our team grow with so many people and incredible coaches these past five years,” she said. pages.text: Wednesday, January 17, 2024 15 HIKING WITH JON By Jonathan Comeaux The rains from earlier this month have tapered off, but the impact can be seen in flowing streams and creeks. Winter hiking is the best time to visit the local waterfalls, and the Post has ventured to several in the Bay Area. Here’s a collection of local waterfalls to see: Uvas Canyon’s Waterfalls Loop Trail, Morgan Hill In Morgan Hill’s Uvas Canyon County Park are a collection of five accessible waterfalls in 5.2 miles of total hiking. Waterfall hikes to consider You’ll still require 1,273 feet in elevation gain to see all five in the entire loop—but four of those waterfalls within the first 1.6 miles—making the last long trip to Triple Falls, and optional excursion if you’re worried about tired legs. Cataract Creek, Mt. Tamalpais Watershed The Cataract Falls Trail in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed is a 4.8 out-and-back with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. There are two trailheads, parking on Bolinas Fairfax Road will provide just a 0.5 walk to the first waterfall and another 0.2 to its most famous Helen Markt Falls. Should you walk the entire Cataract Falls Trail, you will encounter cascades along cataract creek. Murietta Falls, Del Valle Regional Wilderness Murietta Falls in Livermore’s Del Valle Regional Park is considered the highest waterfall in the entire Bay Area at an elevation of near 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness, where a small stream cascades over 100 foot cliff-face – meaning this location should only be taken by experienced hikers looking for a challenge. Staff Photo You can see Helen Markt Falls in 0.7 miles of hiking in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed along Cataract Creek. Alamere Falls is thriving and currently is its most active in several years. Photo courtesy of AllTrails SPRING SEASON 2024 JAN 22ND-MAY 10TH SKYLINE LACROSSE Join the Journey to Greatness REGISTER www.skylinelacrosse.com GIRLS AGES 7-14 Staff Photo Uvas Canyon County Park has five waterfalls to enjoy, including four in the first 1.5 miles. Photo courtesy of AllTrails The waterfall at Murietta Falls in the Dal Valle Regional Wilderness is thriving after snow touched down in the area in late December. Photos courtesy of AllTrails Dawn Falls in Mt. Tamalpais can be seen in just 1.5 miles of hiking. The entire day required 12.1 miles of hiking and near 5,000 feet in elevation gain; it is considered a good training spot for those interested in Half Dome. Alamere Falls, Point Reyes National Seashore The trek to Alamere Falls is a total of 13.6 miles and an elevation gain of 1,811 feet taking the Coastal Trail to the Wildcat Campground. There is a shortcut at 4.5 miles, but it requires scrambling down a steep ravine to the beach and should only be done by experienced hikers who are comfortable with scrambling. Proper footwear is needed. Dawn Falls, Mt. Tamalpais We visited Dawn Falls in November, and it was a trickle off a large cliff-face. But fellow hikers online describe that its intensity picked up after the rain in the winter months. The walk to the location takes just 1.4 miles at around 500 feet in elevation gain through lush redwoods. The walk is popular and we passed 49 people in the trek to Dawn Falls.

articles.text: Sin Wai Kin and Gabriel Chaile exhibits on view As part of MATRIX, an exhibition series that provides artists with an experimental platform to make and show new work, the internationally recognized visual artists Sin Wai Kin and Gabriel Chaile have opened their first U.S. solo exhibitions at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA). Best known for category-defying performances and moving image works, Sin will present new work in MATRIX 284 / Sin Wai Kin: The Story Changing. In addition to a recent video work, Dreaming the End (2023), Sin’s six-channel video work The Breaking Story (2022) will spill out from the galleries and into the museum’s public space. The Toronto-born artist draws on references ranging from Cantonese and Peking opera to early performances in London’s experimental drag scene, in which their popular onstage persona pastiched an idealized version of Western femininity. Since then, the artist’s view has grown to encompass an expanding universe of characters who explore how social narratives are understood and transformed. Sin’s MATRIX exhibition will remain on view at BAMPFA through March 10, 2024. MATRIX 283 / Gabriel Chaile: No hay nada que destruya el corazón como la pobreza centers upon Chaile’s large-scale sculptural commission, which he completed onsite in collaboration with the UC Berkeley Art Practice department during a residency preceding the exhibition. Born in San Miguel de Tucumán, the Lisbon-based artist Gabriel Chaile, Rosario Liendro, 2022. In the artists’ first U.S. solo exhibitions, the works of Chaile and Sin Wai Kin are on view at Berkeley art Museum. has been celebrated worldwide — including at the 59th Venice Biennale last year — for his soaring, anthropomorphic clay sculptures that expand on the forms, rituals and traditions of pre-colonial cultures in his native Argentina. Chaile’s practice intertwines indigenous mythology and contemporary social and political references, including Tucumán Arde (Tucumán is Burning), a series of “happenings” by the artist that expose the region’s widespread poverty from the 1960s onward, following the federal government’s closure of key sugar mills. Chaile’s MATRIX exhibition, the title of which translates to “Nothing destroys the heart like poverty,” will remain on view at BAMPFA through April 14, 2024. The museum is located at 2155 Center Street and is open from 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($14 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa. org, or walk-up at the museum desk.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will celebrate its 87th season with its Winter Concert on Saturday, January 27 at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church at 7:30 p.m. This year’s event marks Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 34th season as Music Director/Conductor, and features an inaugural collaboration with a longstanding Bay Area institution, the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO). The two groups will feature BCCO classical soprano singer Vuyiswa Sigadi and solo violinist Henry Stroud, the YPSO concertmaster, a sophomore at Berkeley High School and the winner of this season’s YPSO concerto competition. The concert opens with American composer Kenji Bunch’s Supermaximum — a contemporary composition that explores themes of resilience and determination. According to Bunch, “this body of work serves as a singular example of a group of oppressed people resorting to, of all things, art for spiritual and, at times, physical survival under the most needlessly cruel of circumstances.” Following this, YPSO will perform the first movement of Camille Saint-Saëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 in B Minor, Op. 61. According to program notes writer Orrin Howard, the violin concerto’s “first movement revolves around a bold, dramatic first theme, a songful contrasting theme, and fistsful of rapid scales, arpeggios, and double stops.” Closing the program is Poulenc’s Gloria, a choral and orchestral masterpiece that reflects the composer’s unique blend of sacred and secular influences. Poulenc’s Gloria is a joyous and vibrant work, featuring lush harmonies and intricate textures. The orchestra and chorus will be led by Ming Luke, BCCO Music Director. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. YPSO’s mission is to “encourage young people to become exemplary musicians and young musicians to become exemplary people”. The organization presents four regular concerts per season. In addition, they reach out through programs such as Bread and Roses and the Bay Area Music Project to bring music into the lives of the surrounding community and encourage the civic development of its students. Tickets ($20-$30) for the event at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church (1801 Lacassie Avenue) are available online at ypsomusic. org/tickets. Young People’s Symphony Orchestra will celebrate its Winter Concert on Saturday, January 27, marking its 87th season and inaugural collaboration with the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra. articles.text: Lineup includes stand-up comics, actors, improv troupes SF Sketchfest begins tomorrow, marking the return of the Bay Area’s largest annual comedy festival. From January 18 through February 4, audiences can watch prominent stand-up comedians Maria Bamford, Marc Maron, Joel Kim, Matt Braunger and others perform alongside local comedians and celebrity guests like Bob Odenkirk, Weird Al Yankovic, and Eric Idle of Monty Python’s Flying Circus in a variety of stand-up shows, live podcasts, variety shows, and musical performances. This year’s festival boasts more than 175 comedy shows across 17 different venues in the city. A full lineup is available online at www.sfsketchfest.com. SF Sketchfest was founded in 2001 by Bay Area comics David Owen, Cole Stratton, and Janet Varney as a way to showcase the talents of Bay Area sketch comedy groups. Since its inception, the event has grown rapidly into a nationally recognized comedy festival that mixes national headliners, local favorites, and the best up-and-coming groups from throughout North America for nearly a month of sketch, improv, stand-up, and alternative comedy. Tickets are available online at www.sfsketchfest.com. Sold-out shows may still have a limited number of tickets available at the venue’s box office the night of the show. A line begins approximately 60-90 minutes before showtime, and any available seats will be sold on a first-come, firstserved basis. Photo by SF Sketchfest This year’s festival boasts more than 175 comedy shows across 17 different venues around the city.
articles.title: SF Sketchfest kicks off tomorrow

articles.text: Multiple Grammy nominee R&B singer-songwriter Terry Steele performs a concert this Sunday, January 21 at 7 p.m. at Yoshi’s in Oakland. The music reflects the legacy of singer-songwriting Luther Vandross, alongside special tributes to Whitney Houston and Aretha Franklin. Steele, a two-time American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishing (ASCAP) Award Winning Songwriter, has toured internationally for decades as a professional recording artist, with concert performances in Russia, Japan, China, Germany, Brazil, Jamaica, Israel, England and all throughout the U.S. As a songwriter, Steele has written for or collaborated with artists as Whitney Houston, Dionne Warwick, Starship, Hiroshima, Patti Labelle, Stevie Wonder, Diana Ross, The Spinners, Barry White, The Pointer Sisters, Arif Mardin, Natalie Cole, George Duke and saxophonist Richard Elliott. As the principal writer of the blockbuster hit, Here And Now, (recorded by the late Vandross), Steele won a Grammy nomination for “Best Rhythm and Blues Song” in 1990. Separate concert on January 23 Two days later, on Tuesday, January 23 at 8 p.m., multiple Grammy nominee, Guggenheim Fellow and MacArthur Fellow Terry Steele will perform at Yoshi’s this Sunday, January 21, and the Miguel Zenón Quartet, pictured, will take the stage on Tuesday, January 23. Miguel Zenón performs with his jazz quartet as one of the most groundbreaking and influential saxophonists and composers of his generation. Born and raised in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Zenón has released fifteen recordings as a jazz leader, including the Grammy nominated El Arte Del Bolero (2021). As a composer he has been commissioned by SFJAZZ, NYO Jazz, The New York State Council for the Arts, Chamber Music America, Logan Center for The Arts, The Hyde Park Jazz Festival, The John Simon Guggenheim Foundation, MIT, Spektral Quartet, The Hewlett Foundation, Peak Performances, PRISM Quartet and many of his peers. In addition, Zenón topped both the Jazz Artist of the Year and Alto Saxophonist categories on the 2014 Jazz Times Critics Poll and was selected as the Alto Saxophonist of the Year by the Jazz Journalist Association in 2015, 2018, 2019 and 2020 (when he was also recognized as Arranger of the Year). Doors for each show at Yoshi’s (510 Embarcadero West) open half an hour in advance. Tickets ($35-$69 for Terry Steele, $29- $69 for Miguel Zenón Quartet) and more details are available at yoshis.com.
articles.title: Terry Steele, Miguel Zenón Quartet coming to Yoshi’s

articles.text: The Diluvian String Quartet will perform their winter recital, Love Notes. at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, February 9 at 7 p.m. The public is invited to come and enjoy a romantic Valentine’s recital. Oozing with passion (and cheese), the program will include Germaine Tailleferre’s debut String Quartet, Robert Schumann’s most famous 3rd String Quartet, and other works by Mozart and Webern. Doors Open at 6:45 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at Eventbrite or at the door. A dessert reception and drinks will follow the concert. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. This will be their fifth appearance in Piedmont and will be another fun and diverse musical journey. On the program is Mozart’s Adagio and Fugue in C minor, a short, profound score that Mozart adapted from an earlier work for 2 pianos. This piece, written toward the end of Mozart’s life, was a tribute to the baroque era, and has entertained audiences since the late 18th century. Germaine Tailleferre was the only female member of the group of “les 6”, a group of French composers forging a new voice in the early 20th century. In this quartet, we can hear her fresh, humorous voice, written over the course of 2 years and published in 1919 at the end of the Great War. A superb talent, her music is sadly not heard often enough. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. Intended to be part of a full length string quartet, this piece is no doubt a short musical journey through the joys and fears of young love. Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous, begins with two notes and is said to be a musical way of saying his wife’s name, Clara. Always lyrical, tonally lush, and beautiful, it is a work not to be missed. The Diluvian String Quartet – Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello – will perform a Valentine concert in Piedmont on Saturday evening, February 9.
articles.title: Love Notes Diluvian Quartet concert at PCA on Feb. 9

articles.text: The chamber quartet Ives Collective comes to Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco for a hybrid, in-person, and livestreamed concert on Sunday, January 28 at 4 p.m. The quartet – comprised of violinist Kay Stern, violinist and violist Susan Freier, cellist Stephen Harrison and pianist Elizabeth Schumann – will play Mélanie Bonis’ Soir et Matin for Piano Trio, Op. 76; Dame Ethyl Smyth’s String Trio in D Major, Op. 6; and Bonis’ Piano Quartet No. 1 in B-flat major, Op. 69. Presenting powerful live music through fresh and informed interpretations of established masterworks and under-appreciated gems, the quartet continues its commitment to presenting lesser heard works by women composers. Program notes The composer Bonis just missed studying at the Paris Conservatoire under Fauré. Like many talented women of her time, her parents discouraged her studies, forcing her to drop out as soon as she became engaged. It wasn’t until 1891 that she was recognized through a musical competition, one that she entered The chamber quartet Ives Collective comes to Old First Presbyterian Church for a hybrid concert on January 28. under the name M. Bonis. The jury awarded her first prize, initially mistaking her for a man. Piano Quartet in B-flat major, Op. 69 is a wonderful example of Bonis’ feel for melody and atmosphere. Dame Ethel Smyth, born in 1858 like Bonis, nevertheless led a very different life from her French contemporary. She was an avid member of the women’s suffrage movement. Despite suffering the same bigotry toward her work that plagued other female composers – her father was very much opposed to her work – she became the first female composer to be granted a damehood. Her ambitious String Trio, like so much of her chamber music, has only recently been resurrected. The Ives Collective was formed in 2015 by Co-Artistic Directors Susan Freier and Stephen Harrison following the disbanding of their group under the name Ives Quartet. The music background of the musicians includes San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, the Metropolitan Opera, Opera Parallèle and many university faculties and festivals. Tickets ($25 in-person general admission; $20 suggested donation for online live-stream) for the concert at Old First Presbyterian Church (1751 Sacramento St.) are available at oldfirstconcerts.org, or by phone at 415-474-1608.
articles.title: Ives Collective at Old First Presbyterian on Jan. 28

articles.text: World Harmony Chorus will present a free vocal concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Tuesday January 30 at 7:30 p.m. Audience members will enjoy hearing songs from Brazil, Ukraine, Galicia, Kenya, Korea, and Iceland. Hear stunning a cappella arrangements of traditional songs that feature unique musical traditions, unfamiliar languages and polyrhythms. Bring friends who like to sing and stay for refreshments. World Harmony Chorus is a community chorus that welcomes participants of all ages and ability levels. At our Friends & Family Concerts, we perform our current repertoire and then invite the entire audience to join us in learning and singing a couple of new songs. No singing experience is required. Tryouts on February 13 Try a free choral tryout on February 13 at 7:00 p.m. then join weekly rehearsals on Tuesday evenings. No auditions are needed; just show up at the first rehearsal at Berkeley Shambhala Center, 2288 Fulton Street, #203, in Berkeley. Singers at all levels are welcome! Director Betsy Blakeslee has directed choruses in multiple countries. Arranger Daniel Steinberg is one of the foremost a cappella world music arrangers. ®
articles.title: World Harmony Choral concert at Center for the Arts

Ives Collective at Old First Presbyterian on Jan. 28 By Selen Ozturk The chamber quartet Ives Collective comes to Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco for a hybrid, in-person, and livestreamed concert on Sunday, January 28 at 4 p.m. The quartet – comprised of violinist Kay Stern, violinist and violist Susan Freier, cellist Stephen Harrison and pianist Elizabeth Schumann – will play Mélanie Bonis’ Soir et Matin for Piano Trio, Op. 76; Dame Ethyl Smyth’s String Trio in D Major, Op. 6; and Bonis’ Piano Quartet No. 1 in B-flat major, Op. 69. Presenting powerful live music through fresh and informed interpretations of established masterworks and under-appreciated gems, the quartet continues its commitment to presenting lesser heard works by women composers. Program notes The composer Bonis just missed studying at the Paris Conservatoire under Fauré. Like many talented women of her time, her parents discouraged her studies, forcing her to drop out as soon as she became engaged. It wasn’t until 1891 that she was recognized through a musical competition, one that she entered The chamber quartet Ives Collective comes to Old First Presbyterian Church for a hybrid concert on January 28. under the name M. Bonis. The jury awarded her first prize, initially mistaking her for a man. Piano Quartet in B-flat major, Op. 69 is a wonderful example of Bonis’ feel for melody and atmosphere. Dame Ethel Smyth, born in 1858 like Bonis, nevertheless led a very different life from her French contemporary. She was an avid member of the women’s suffrage movement. Despite suffering the same bigotry toward her work that plagued other female composers – her father was very much opposed to her work – she became the first female composer to be granted a damehood. Her ambitious String Trio, like so much of her chamber music, has only recently been resurrected. The Ives Collective was formed in 2015 by Co-Artistic Directors Susan Freier and Stephen Harrison following the disbanding of their group under the name Ives Quartet. The music background of the musicians includes San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, the Metropolitan Opera, Opera Parallèle and many university faculties and festivals. Tickets ($25 in-person general admission; $20 suggested donation for online live-stream) for the concert at Old First Presbyterian Church (1751 Sacramento St.) are available at oldfirstconcerts.org, or by phone at 415-474-1608. READ IT IN THE POST Love Notes Diluvian Quartet concert at PCA on Feb. 9 The Diluvian String Quartet will perform their winter recital, Love Notes. at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, February 9 at 7 p.m. The public is invited to come and enjoy a romantic Valentine’s recital. Oozing with passion (and cheese), the program will include Germaine Tailleferre’s debut String Quartet, Robert Schumann’s most famous 3rd String Quartet, and other works by Mozart and Webern. Doors Open at 6:45 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at Eventbrite or at the door. A dessert reception and drinks will follow the concert. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. This will be their fifth appearance in Piedmont and will be another fun and diverse musical journey. On the program is Mozart’s Adagio and Fugue in C minor, a short, profound score that Mozart adapted from an earlier work for 2 pianos. This piece, written toward the end of Mozart’s life, was a tribute to the baroque era, and has entertained audiences since the late 18th century. Germaine Tailleferre was the only female member of the group of “les 6”, a group of French composers forging a new voice in the early 20th century. In this quartet, we can hear her fresh, humorous voice, written over the course of 2 years and published in 1919 at the end of the Great War. A superb talent, her music is sadly not heard often enough. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. Intended to be part of a full length string quartet, this piece is no doubt a short musical journey through the joys and fears of young love. Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous, begins with two notes and is said to be a musical way of saying his wife’s name, Clara. Always lyrical, tonally lush, and beautiful, it is a work not to be missed. The Diluvian String Quartet – Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello – will perform a Valentine concert in Piedmont on Saturday evening, February 9. articles.text: Sick children doing daily battle with debilitating and potentially lethal diseases turns the word entertainment on its head. And yet it is a theme that’s familiar in Hollywood. Extraordinary Measures is about a rare affliction known as Pompe’s Disease, a form of muscular dystrophy that strikes children at an early age, all too often truncating their young lives; most don’t live to be older than eight or nine years. The symptoms are enlarged organs and muscles that atrophy to the point where they can’t lift an arm to throw a small ball. It has to do with a missing enzyme that converts sugar in their muscles. Imagine the agony of those parents who watch their children slowly say goodbye, growing weaker and less resilient as months and then years pass and time grows ever shorter and symptoms become increasingly life threatening. The film Extraordinary Measures is based on the true story of a father and mother, John and Aileen Crowley (Brendan Fraser and Keri Russell), who refuse to quietly say goodbye to their son and daughter who are both afflicted with Pompe’s Disease. John, after reading all the literature, desperate for any possible breakthrough, sets out in search of a research scientist, Doctor Robert Stonehill (Harrison Ford), who is doing groundbreaking work regarding enzymes. He is also perpetually cranky and under-funded. As Crowley, a Harvard MBA, finds high finance money, Stonehill concentrates on the cure. The game clock, sadly, is ticking for the Crowley children who are both in crisis. Time is of the essence. Surprisingly, the weakest part of Extraordinary Measures is the portrayal of Stonehill by Ford. Scientists, of course, can be eccentric and reclusive; however, if they’re likable and seem to have a good heart, well, that is redemptive. But if they’re self-absorbed, selfish and uncaring, then they’re decidedly unattractive. Sadly and surprisingly, Stonehill is the latter. Ford’s performance reminds viewers that he often plays someone who is short-tempered, out of sorts and verging on anger (all without a sense of humor, a quality that often saves Bruce Willis as he plays Bruce Willis over and over again). Ford is a huge movie star and someone who audiences clearly enjoy spending time with. In this film, however, he is miscast. The partnership between the parents and Stonehill is never satisfactory. Instead Stonehill finds the parents and his fellow scientists intrusive and a distraction and too often becomes petulant – not endearing qualities. They detract from the film consistently, until the end of act three when Stonehill softens, but by then it’s too late. Extraordinary Measures. Directed by Tom Vaughn. Starring Harrison Ford, Brendan Fraser and Keri Russell. 1 jr., 46 min. Rated PG. Released 2010, Now streaming on VUDU/prime/ apple tv. articles.text: Saoirse Ronan stas in The Lovely Bones The film The Lovely Bones, based on Alice Sebold’s bestselling book, immediately lets the audience know two things: Susie Salmon (Saoirse Ronan), a 14-year-old, is murdered, and the man who lures her into an underground room where he rapes and kills her is a seemingly a benign neighbor, George Harvey played by Stanley Tucci. The question that Susie asks after this horrific event in a haunting voiceover, is, “Will there be justice? Will Harvey, a serial predator, be found out?” Sebold uses a familiar narrative device: Susie, a lovely, quintessential teen, now dead, is trapped in an incandescent purgatory, a morphing place called “the in-between.” And it’s from that vantage point she watches her parents cope with the loss of their beloved daughter. Both are devastated, mired in a wrenching grief, and relentlessly pushing the case detective who has no leads or suspects. The film is predicated on a reality that no parent ever wants to encounter, which is that beneath the patina of societal civility resides an unadorned evil and a pathology that is incomprehensible. Predators are ever with us. And our children, hobbled by their inherent innocence, cannot be completely protected. Had director Peter Jackson explored that truth without dressing the film up with an over-thetop psychedelic view of “the in-between,” The Lovely Bones would have been a far edgier and engaging film. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Saban’s Power Rangers is an unabashed movie for older kids and teens with lots of CGI action and other wild, over-the-top stuff that kids will really like. Personally, I’m a sucker for origin films and the first act (plus part of act two) is a good one. You have five kids who all look like they are on the Student Council, but somehow end up in detention (think the Breakfast Club). Each one feels powerless and definitely misunderstood until they aren’t, which doesn’t happen until well into act three. But therein is the real story of The Power Rangers and all other comic book movies that take wimpy kids and give them super powers. What adolescent doesn’t wish he or she had some serious mojo? You can start with Spiderman and go through the deep Marvel and DC Comics bench and it’s all about power and how it’s used. Kids love this idea. It’s brilliant. In Power Rangers, you have five young people who are given the gift (just the way that Harry Potter was) and now it’s up to them to make use of it. Of course, act two and three of this nostalgic reboot, based on a 1993 TV series, get nuts with Naomi Watts showing up as ultracampy Rita Repulsa, who is evil incarnate and wants to lay waste to all, including the bucolic town’s Krispy Kreme donut shop. Really. But here’s the deal: Rangers is all about friendship, bonding, and finally morphing. It’s also got a quirky robot named Alpha 5, portrayed by Bill Hader, as well as a very cool space ship buried deep in a quarry. The kids could have gone back to school and hassled some bullies (one does get his mild comeuppance), but they have bigger things to do. Like save their families and their town. This is a popcorn movie. But a good one for kids and even their parents. Saban’s Power Rangers. Directed by Dean Iaraelite. Starring Dacre Montgomery, Naomi Scott and RJ Cryer. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Saban’s Power Rangers trilogy. M I C H A E L

articles.text: Survey of Retro and Mid-Century Jewelry by Sacha Grippando Sacha Grippando will present a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on February 1 at 6 p.m. featuring the jewelry collection of American actress Elizabeth Taylor. Jewelry from the 1930s–1960s is bold, colorful and extravagant. Elizabeth Taylor and the Duchess of Windsor amassed what are considered today to be the best collections of jewelry from the 20th century. They both had amazing taste and a passion for important gemstones and innovative and avant-garde design. As the majority of their collections were acquired as gifts from their husbands, these collections are truly legacies of love. Both women led extraordinary lives that were very public. They were often vilified, criticized and at certain points in their lives portrayed as “the most hated women in the world” by the press. This pair of lectures will focus on jewelry from these two collections from the 1930s to the 1960s, as both feature the best of the best from this time period, and will include gorgeous photos and discussions on some of their most important pieces of jewelry from the ‘30s to the ‘60s, along with fascinating stories about these women and their controversial lives. The February 1 lecture explores the collection of Elizabeth Taylor, who shared the Duchess’ love of jewelry and also has some of the best examples from the 1950s-60s. Her collection was also the result of gifts from her husbands, predominantly from Mike Todd and Richard Burton. It was not until later in her life that she purchased pieces on her own, her first being the Prince of Wales brooch that had belonged to the Duchess of Windsor. She purchased it from the Duke and Duchess of Windsor sale at Sotheby’s in 1987. Taylor’s collection was considered the best collection of important gemstones and jewelry in the world. She was an ardent admirer and collector of pieces from Bulgari, the Italian jewelry firm that came to the forefront during this period, helped greatly by her purchases and her very public wearing of their finest pieces. She was also a collector of famous gemstones like the 33.19 ct. Krupp diamond, the 68 ct. Taylor-Burton diamond and the 16th-century pear- shaped pearl, famously known as La Peregrina, that was once owned by King Philip II of Spain (1527-1598). Continuing her illustrated Lecture Series exploring the Jewelry Arts: Sacha Grippando Gemologist

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is ringing in 2024 with the world premiere of playwright Minna Lee’s My Home on the Moon from January 25 through February 24. In this epic sci-fi journey into the metaverse, business is booming for a formerly failing Vietnamese pho restaurant in the middle of a gentrified neighborhood after it receives help from a mysterious marketing consultant. Things are not all they seem as the restaurant’s waiter, Mai, discovers that artificial intelligence-powered simulations may be taking over reality. With the help of her friends and family, and armed with delicious pho, Mai must learn to reckon the perfection of artificial life with the welcome imperfection of reality. A finalist in the 2024 Bay Area Playwrights Festival and semi-finalist at Ashland New Plays Festival, My Home on the Moon received developmental readings at UC Santa Cruz’s Rainbow Theater Festival and Denver, Colorado-based arts collective Bucharest Inside the Beltway. For tickets ($15-$100) and more information about the performance at SF Playhouse (450 Post Street), visit sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677-9596 Marketing consultant Vera (Rinabeth Apostol) learns the art of cooking pho from Mai (Jenny Nguyen Nelson) in the world premiere of My Home on the Moon at San Francisco Playhouse January 25 through February 24.

articles.text: The Lesher Center for the Arts Repertory Company opens its 2024 season with the remarkable hit solo show, Every Brilliant Thing, on view through January 28. Making a list of things that make life worth living would get different responses from different people, and what would be at the top? Family? Ice cream? The even-numbered Star Trek films? For the lead character in this uplifting play, it’s his mother. This surprising and immersive theatrical experience by Duncan Macmillan and Jonny Donahoe delves into the human experience with playfulness and love. With poignant humor and joy, Every Brilliant Thing takes audiences on a journey through favorite moments such as falling in love, as well as grief, healing, and discovering and rediscovering all that life has to give. Directed by celebrated Bay Area fixture Jeffrey Lo and starring Oakland Theater Project Co-Artistic Director William Thomas Hodgson, the story is filled with opportunities for warm, fun audience participation. The show premiered at the Ludlow Fringe Festival, then it was performed off Broadway at Barrow Street Theatre where it was filmed for HBO. It was deemed a “heart-wrenching, hilarious play” by The Guardian; The New York Times called it “captivating.” Time Out London lauded the work as “gloriously funny and exceptionally warm,” while The Independent said it “finds a perfect balance between conveying the struggles of life, and celebrating all that is sweet in it.” For tickets ($35-$40) visit LesherArtsCenter.org or call the box office at (925) 943-7469. Lesher Center for the Arts is located at 1601 Civic Drive in Walnut Creek. William Thomas Hodgson stars in Every Brilliant Thing at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek through January 28.
articles.title: See Every Brilliant Thing at Lesher Center through Jan. 28

articles.text: Cult of Love will be performed by Berkeley Repertory Theatre from January 26 through March 3. Cult of Love, written by Leslye Headland and directed by Trip Cullman, will open at Berkeley Repertory Theatre on Friday, January 26, for a five-week run. Cult of Love is a ruthless comedy about a deeply Christian family, the Dahls, devoted to their belief that all one needs is love. The four Dahl siblings were brought up with a devotion to Jesus and each other. Now adults with their own distinct beliefs and years of emotional wariness, they gather once again for the holidays at their childhood home, singing joyous carols and recreate family traditions. However, repressed feelings and conflicts about the siblings’ upbringing shatter the family’s façade of forced cheer, and all hell soon breaks loose. Bold and provocative, Cult of Love dares to challenge our perceptions of family to examine what’s truly needed for deep faith and love to persist. “All families are inherently complicated, but in Leslye Headland and Trip Cullman’s hands, they are also dynamic, dramatic, and wildly entertaining,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “I’m delighted to welcome this incredibly gifted cast and creative team to Berkeley Rep.” Tickets ($22.50–$134) may be purchased at the box office or online at berkeleyrep.org/shows/ cult-of-love, or by phone at 647- 2949. Berkeley Rep’s Roda Theater is located at 2015 Addison Street.
articles.title: Cult of Love opens at Berkeley Rep Jan. 26

articles.text: La Coulée Verte and Bois de Vincennes Previsouly printed in the Piedmont Post on February 24, 2021. The winter months are dwindling, but Paris restaurants, cafés, museums, theatres, department stores, and every imaginable entertainment remains closed. Worse, Paris may be experiencing a third wave of Covid-19 with the spreading United Kingdom mutant dubbed the UK-variant. France continues to enforce curfews and ban international travel with no end in sight, though England is predicting some normalcy by mid-May. For now, Paris parks are open, and as the days gently warm, there are greenbelt options to get some fresh air while practicing social distancing. Paris, though not ranked in the world as a green city, has more than 400 parks. Many agree the most admired are Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden at the Louvre, and Bois de Boulogne in the 16th arrondissement. Buttes-Chaumont at Belleville in the 19th district is an enchanting city park in the Luxembourg style but with a more intimate aura as a country place. Plus, it’s generally not as crowded with tourists. Jardin des Serres d’Auteil is a secret garden of greenhouse exotics at the southern tip of Bois de Boulogne. The Jardin des Plantes, the city’s vast botanical garden whose roots took hold for apothecary herbs to treat the Renaissance royals, is a top choice. On its grounds are the National Natural History Museum and academies for botany, mineralogy, and geology, while the gardens and natural history museum are a magnet for energetic children on school tours. La Coulée Verte, from the Bastille to Bois de Vincennes A high line park was built atop an obsolete railway spur from the Place de la Bastille to Bois de Path along Coulée Verte where an obsolete train track used to be. Aligre market between Bastille and Nation plazas is a good place to pick up fresh produce, meat, fish, deli, and charcuterie before trail walking or afterwards to carry home for dinner. Vincennes, and since its opening in 1993 is a popular greenway. If the idea of converting an elevated train line into a parkway seems familiar, the New York City High Line was inspired by the Paris trail and opened in 2007, running from the meatpacking district to 34th Street. The stairway entrance to this Paris elevated parkway is at the back of the Opéra Bastille along Rue de Lyon. The park, called the “green river”, is not an exact translation of La Coulée Verte. And earlier moniker was Promenade Plantée (the planted promenade). The walkway is a mile and a half of easy strolling through an assorted green trail of paths laden with roses, plantings, and flower gardens, wild greenery, a short canal. At varying locations, it branches into wider spaces with bench seating. Further along, the pathway narrows over the Jardin de Reuilly and snakes downhill to street level for bicyclists and walkers who will arrive at the entry to Bois de Vincennes in another mile and a half. Trail walkers may wish to bring food and drinks on sunny days and choose a scenic spot to picnic at Reuilly park. A favorite Bastille location, Marché d’Aligre with open stalls and covered counters stacked with produce and fresh foods, is open six days a week. A lot of the trail fun is the sheer elevation – walking on a raised platform places you eye to eye with the third or fourth level of buildings. One is peering over the railings at street intersections and gazing at apartments with The Opéra Bastille that opened to grand fanfare in 1989 was built on the spot that Gare de la Bastille occupied from 1859 to 1969. This second opera house designed for the Paris general populace is immense in size, holding: 2,745 seats; a 500-seat amphitheatre; a 230-seat studio theatre; set and costumes workshops; rehearsal rooms; and offices. Controversy has dogged the project including criticism about “disappointing” acoustics. glimpses of balconies and people walking below: it’s an urban adventure. Once you reach Reuilly, it’s decision-time with a half dozen options. From here you can take the stairs to street level to the Viaduc des Artes and stroll by workshops, cottage businesses, cafés, and retailers along Avenue Daumesnil, where the walk returns strollers to the Bastille. More options open when you decide to walk the entire Coulée Verte and reach the Bois de Vincennes. One may alternately catch the 46 bus on Avenue Daumesnil headed south and ride the mile and a half to the park. Vincennes is the largest park in Paris with crisscrossing foot trails clocking some 50 miles in length. Bicycle trails are also abundant. At the entry to Vincennes, Palais-Porte Dorée is an intriguing museum full of curiosities from the time of the French Colonial Exhibition in 1931, and a glorious example of the Art Deco age. Inside the park is a zoo that children love. Lac Daumesnil along Avenue Daumesnil is the park’s largest lake and entertains patrons with rentals of rowboats, bicycles, and pony rides around the lake for kids. Parc Floral is the site for international flower shows and filled with beauty when the tulips and daffodils are in bloom. From Parc Floral and across Lac des Minimes is a tropical plant garden. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, January 17, 2024 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Previsouly printed in the Piedmont Post on February 24, 2021. The winter months are dwindling, but Paris restaurants, cafés, museums, theatres, department stores, and every imaginable entertainment remains closed. Worse, Paris may be experiencing a third wave of Covid-19 with the spreading United Kingdom mutant dubbed the UK-variant. France continues to enforce curfews and ban international travel with no end in sight, though England is predicting some normalcy by mid-May. For now, Paris parks are open, and as the days gently warm, there are greenbelt options to get some fresh air while practicing social distancing. Paris, though not ranked in the world as a green city, has more than 400 parks. Many agree the most admired are Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden at the Louvre, and A visit to Paris High Line and Vincennes Woods La Coulée Verte and Bois de Vincennes Bois de Boulogne in the 16th arrondissement. Buttes-Chaumont at Belleville in the 19th district is an enchanting city park in the Luxembourg style but with a more intimate aura as a country place. Plus, it’s generally not as crowded with tourists. Jardin des Serres d’Auteil is a secret garden of greenhouse exotics at the southern tip of Bois de Boulogne. The Jardin des Plantes, the city’s vast botanical garden whose roots took hold for apothecary herbs to treat the Renaissance royals, is a top choice. On its grounds are the National Natural History Museum and academies for botany, mineralogy, and geology, while the gardens and natural history museum are a magnet for energetic children on school tours. La Coulée Verte, from the Bastille to Bois de Vincennes A high line park was built atop an obsolete railway spur from the Place de la Bastille to Bois de Path along Coulée Verte where an obsolete train track used to be. Aligre market between Bastille and Nation plazas is a good place to pick up fresh produce, meat, fish, deli, and charcuterie before trail walking or afterwards to carry home for dinner. Vincennes, and since its opening in 1993 is a popular greenway. If the idea of converting an elevated train line into a parkway seems familiar, the New York City High Line was inspired by the Paris trail and opened in 2007, running from the meatpacking district to 34th Street. The stairway entrance to this Paris elevated parkway is at the back of the Opéra Bastille along Rue de Lyon. The park, called the “green river”, is not an exact translation of La Coulée Verte. And earlier moniker was Promenade Plantée (the planted promenade). The walkway is a mile and a half of easy strolling through an assorted green trail of paths laden with roses, plantings, and flower gardens, wild greenery, a short canal. At varying locations, it branches into wider spaces with bench seating. Further along, the pathway narrows over the Jardin de Reuilly and snakes downhill to street level for bicyclists and walkers who will arrive at the entry to Bois de Vincennes in another mile and a half. Trail walkers may wish to bring food and drinks on sunny days and choose a scenic spot to picnic at Reuilly park. A favorite Bastille location, Marché d’Aligre with open stalls and covered counters stacked with produce and fresh foods, is open six days a week. A lot of the trail fun is the sheer elevation – walking on a raised platform places you eye to eye with the third or fourth level of buildings. One is peering over the railings at street intersections and gazing at apartments with The Opéra Bastille that opened to grand fanfare in 1989 was built on the spot that Gare de la Bastille occupied from 1859 to 1969. This second opera house designed for the Paris general populace is immense in size, holding: 2,745 seats; a 500-seat amphitheatre; a 230-seat studio theatre; set and costumes workshops; rehearsal rooms; and offices. Controversy has dogged the project including criticism about “disappointing” acoustics. glimpses of balconies and people walking below: it’s an urban adventure. Once you reach Reuilly, it’s decision-time with a half dozen options. From here you can take the stairs to street level to the Viaduc des Artes and stroll by workshops, cottage businesses, cafés, and retailers along Avenue Daumesnil, where the walk returns strollers to the Bastille. More options open when you decide to walk the entire Coulée Verte and reach the Bois de Vincennes. One may alternately catch the 46 bus on Avenue Daumesnil headed south and ride the mile and a half to the park. Vincennes is the largest park in Paris with crisscrossing foot trails clocking some 50 miles in length. Bicycle trails are also abundant. At the entry to Vincennes, Palais-Porte Dorée is an intriguing museum full of curiosities from the time of the French Colonial Exhibition in 1931, and a glorious example of the Art Deco age. Inside the park is a zoo that children love. Lac Daumesnil along Avenue Daumesnil is the park’s largest lake and entertains patrons with rentals of rowboats, bicycles, and pony rides around the lake for kids. Parc Floral is the site for international flower shows and filled with beauty when the tulips and daffodils are in bloom. From Parc Floral and across Lac des Minimes is a tropical plant garden. articles.text: Anybody ever had a crush on a movie star? I have. Ingrid Bergman in Casablanca. Diane Keaton in Annie Hall. Jessica Lange in Tootsie. And then there’s Shirley MacLaine in The Apartment. I fell for her when the movie came out in 1960, and Piedmont movie fans got to revisit her charming, pixie performance at last week’s meeting of the Second Thursday Flix Fest in the Center for the Arts. Helmed by Billy Wilder, famed director of Double Indemnity, Sunset Boulevard and Some Like It Hot, The Apartment was a big hit in its day, winning several awards for its actors and creators and a Best Director Academy Award for Wilder. Young and at his sly, engaging best, Jack Lemon plays insurance worker C.C. Baxter, who lends his Upper West Side apartment to company bosses for offthe-books affairs with female employees. When his manager, the coolly self-serving Mr. Sheldrake (Fred MacMurray), begins using Baxter’s pad in exchange for promoting him, Baxter’s heart sinks when he discovers that Sheldrake’s mistress is Fran Kubelik (Shirley MacLaine), the elevator girl at work whom Baxter is crazy about. Tension, and comedy with real consequences, arises as our hero has to decide between the girl he loves and punching up his career. The Piedmont audience generally liked the movie, noting how society has changed from the era of the film, with its blatant sexism and racism (one attendee said it was Billy Wilder’s dark satire of the period), compared to our more enlightened time. We still have a long way to go regarding gender and racial equity in the workplace, people noted. They liked the handsome black and white photography and especially enjoyed Jack Lemon’s performance. The next Flix Fest showing is the 1995 Italian classic, Il Postino, on February 8th. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the Film Fest takes place in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Those attending are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223
