articles.text: Like many of you, I have a lot of demands on my time: Earning a living, raising two kids, staying fit, keeping in touch with friends, reading the news…. the list goes on. So while feeling a bit overwhelmed and indecisive this morning, I did what I always do in such moments – I spent a solid two hours gardening. I trimmed the lawn, weeded crab grass from around my perennials and native grasses, and raked up four wheelbarrows of oak leaves. I dumped the leaves on my front flower bed, around the perennials I’d just liberated. I almost never throw oak leaves away. They make great mulch, and their presence compliments the natural feel of my oak woodlands habitat. – Marcus Tullius Cicero I felt great about triumphing over those winter weeds before they got unruly. And just as important, being out in the sun and getting the blood flowing lifted my mood and cleared my mind. Not a second too soon, either, as I come to today’s news: I am pleased to introduce myself as the new gardening columnist for the Piedmont Post. I know what you’re thinking. If you’re a gardener, like me, then you’ve already read my bio and you’re wondering in the crotchety manner of gardeners: “What makes this guy qualified?” And if you’re not a gardener, then you’re trying to figure out how I could possibly entertain you every week. Let me just say that I have unlimited stories about gardening. Let’s start with this one. When I was in middle school in the early 1990s, my friend Eric Fowler and I founded our own lawn care business. We were 14 and could not legally drive, but that wasn’t a problem: We had go-karts. Eric is the one who figured out how to make it work. He went to Sears and bought a small trailer of the sort meant to be towed by a riding lawnmower. He put his Honda push mower in Meet Josh Harkinson, the Piedmont Post’s new garden columnist. the trailer and attached it to his go-kart. And that’s how we got around town. We called our company Precision Lawn Care. Our precision did not extend to the legalities. Go-karts are not street legal, so we spent a lot of time worrying about the police. Whenever we saw a squad car, we’d pull into a driveway to make it look like we were at someone’s house. Eventually the police chased us down. An officer got out, told us he’d seen what we were doing and thought it was very enterprising. He had been thinking about it, and wouldn’t arrest us – as long as we kept the trailers attached to the go-karts to make ourselves more visible to drivers. I have learned a lot over the past dozen years about gardening natives and edibles on a property of 10,000 square feet of hilly oak forest, riparian creekfront, and sunny meadow. One of the two side-side houses was built as the personal residence of the early 20th-Century architect Frederick Reimers, whose father, Johannes Reimers, was a noted landscape architect. I’ve tried to keep his spirit alive. I’m looking forward to sharing more gardening stories. Before any more of January slips away, I want to remind you to fertilize your citrus trees. I like to use E.B. Stone Organics Citrus & Fruit Tree Food sold at Ace Garden Center in Piedmont. They say the best time is during the rainy season after the fruit has set. Your oranges and lemons might be looking almost ready to eat by now, but as I told my tree-climbing daughter today, don’t pick them early, or all at once. They will taste sweeter and last longer if you keep them on the branch until the moment you eat them. Josh Harkinson spent 12 years as a staff writer for Mother Jones Magazine in San Francisco. He graduated from Duke University in 1999 with a degree in Environmental Science and Policy, and from the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism in 2002. He lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. 12-MONTHS FINANCING 0% INTEREST WE PAY TAX SALE* *on all installed jobs CL#788850

articles.text: There was a good turnout of 19 readers showed up to discuss Station Eleven at a gathering of the First Mondays Reading Group on January 8 in the Community Hall. The book is a novel by Canadian writer Emily St. John Mandel published in 2014. It appeared on best-of-year lists and has sold over 1.5 million copies. Additionally, a ten-part version of it premiered on HBO Max in December 2021. The novel takes place before and after a fictional flu pandemic, the “Georgia Flu,” has devastated the world, killing almost everyone. The story starts during a King Lear performance in Toronto when an aspiring paramedic, Jeevan Chaudhary, watches as the famous actor playing Lear, Arthur Leander, has a heart attack. Jeevan tries unsuccessful to resuscitate him, and he then comforts one of the child actors, eight-year-old Kirsten Raymonde. Jeevan leaves the theater and receives a call from a doctor friend. He warns Jeevan to get out of the city, as a deadly flu is spreading rapidly and will soon become a full-blown pandemic. Many people who gather The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson will be the February book up for discussion to mourn Arthur die within three weeks. After fruitlessly waiting for weeks in an apartment for something positive to happen, Jeevan starts a wandering journey to find a new life. Twenty years later, Kirsten is part of a nomadic group of actors and musicians known as The Travelling Symphony. They perform Shakespeare plays and classical music throughout the region. Kirsten can remember little of her life before “Year Zero,” but she clings to a set of graphic novels given to her by Arthur before his death. They are titled Station Eleven. Mandel’s story follows the different characters as they try to survive in this post-apocalyptic world with past and present lives intertwined. Some of them make it, others don’t, but Mandel leaves her readers with hope that civilization is emerging again. The readers started their discussion answering a basic question: did you like Station Eleven or not? All but four said they did. The negative respondents made their case first, saying they weren’t interested in the genre. The plot didn’t interest them and character development was lacking. The post-apocalyptic world was depressing. Some found the first part of the book intriguing, but lost interest in the characters’ ongoing attempts to survive in this harsh world, and not always successfully. The story was obviously the basis for a TV series, which it was. The novel was not a page turner for them, but rather work to get through. However, most readers enjoyed the book. They enjoyed Mandel’s writing style and found her messages relevant and important. The motto “survival is not enough” from the Star Trek movie, is repeated in the story. The readers agreed with the importance of the arts, culture, community, and family for a meaningful life that Mandel suggests. It was also agreed that the book’s impact was greater for the readers today than it would have been in 2014 when it was writStation Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel ten. The group could more easily envision a post-apocalyptic world in our current Covid times. The vision of hope at the story’s end was also appreciated. Some readers thought resourceful survivors, and especially young people, would find ways to continue on. What was probably most appreciated about Station Eleven was how thought-provoking the book is, and the questions it poses. What is really important and needed in our lives? How would we react in survival situations? What types of relationships do we and society need? It was also said that the discussion provided a deeper understanding of the book and these issues. For all, it was a worthwhile conversation and reinforced the value of the First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson for February and Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis for March. Darby Gragg presented three new candidates for a book selection and I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou was picked for April. The next discussion will be on February 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate. Registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4.

Some of them make it, others don’t, but Mandel leaves her readers with hope that civilization is emerging again. The readers started their discussion answering a basic question: did you like Station Eleven or not? All but four said they did. The negative respondents made their case first, saying they weren’t interested in the genre. The plot didn’t interest them and character development was lacking. The post-apocalyptic world was depressing. Some found the first part of the book intriguing, but lost interest in the characters’ ongoing attempts to survive in this harsh world, and not always successfully. The story was obviously the basis for a TV series, which it was. The novel was not a page turner for them, but rather work to get through. However, most readers enjoyed the book. They enjoyed Mandel’s writing style and found her messages relevant and important. The motto “survival is not enough” from the Star Trek movie, is repeated in the story. The readers agreed with the importance of the arts, culture, community, and family for a meaningful life that Mandel suggests. It was also agreed that the book’s impact was greater for the readers today than it would have been in 2014 when it was writStation Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel ten. The group could more easily envision a post-apocalyptic world in our current Covid times. The vision of hope at the story’s end was also appreciated. Some readers thought resourceful survivors, and especially young people, would find ways to continue on. What was probably most appreciated about Station Eleven was how thought-provoking the book is, and the questions it poses. What is really important and needed in our lives? How would we react in survival situations? What types of relationships do we and society need? It was also said that the discussion provided a deeper understanding of the book and these issues. For all, it was a worthwhile conversation and reinforced the value of the First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson for February and Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis for March. Darby Gragg presented three new candidates for a book selection and I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou was picked for April. The next discussion will be on February 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate. Registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. articles.text: The forecast of rain showers didn’t scare off 21 intrepid members of the Walking on Wednesday group from showing up at the Exedra last Wednesday. Umbrellas were deployed and the shower quickly disappeared. On hand were: Denise Frankoff with her K-9 best friend Chester, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sherry Jacobs, Noemi Alvarado, Ken Hubbert, Meghan Bennett, Jim Kuo, Pat Keller, Sharona Fischrup, Mark Davis, Albert Chen, Mike Henn, Rick Eigenbrode, Bill Ahern, and Dick Carter. During their walk the week before the group had visited the Piedmont High campus and talk about the school’s past students. The group thought it would be fun to revisit Clint Eastwood, who had been mentioned as a PHS student. A past Piedmont Historical Society article by Gail Lombardi had identified a Hillside Avenue address as Clint’s childhood home, and the group thought it would also be fun to make it an initial destination. The walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue and up Bonita Avenue and past the former home of Clint’s father, Clinton Eastwood, Sr. He was a PHS grad and later a business executive. The group went down Park Way to Hillside and stopped in front of the Eastwoods’ home. Clinton Eastwood Jr. was born in 1930 and is now 93 years old. Eastwood was nicknamed “Samson” by hospital nurses because he weighed 11 pounds 6 ounces at birth. He attended Piedmont Middle School, and from January 1945 to 1946 he attended Piedmont High School. He transferred to Oakland Tech and graduated in 1949. The Eastwood biography presents the story of a teenager from a middle class family who had a circle of good friends but felt alienated from the wealthy and homogeneous Piedmont culture of the time. He rebelled against it and the people associated with it. After high school, Eastwood did different jobs, served in the army, and got started in acting. After many unsuccessful auditions, he was given a minor role in Revenge of the Creature in 1955, which was a sequel to the Creature from the Black Lagoon, and the rest is more history. The group continued down Park Way to Dracena Park. They zig zagged through the park’s trails, going up the seldom-walked upper east trail. They walked through the redwoods along the main trial to the upper trial along Park Way. The walkers made their way Monticello to Lorita Avenue. In the front yard of a home at the corner they discovered two trees with unique, gnarly bark trunks. The cork oaks are a primary source of cork for wine bottles and cork flooring. The group made their way up to the top of this cul-de-sac and found a hidden, narrow path that returned them to Monticello. Across the street is Arroyo Avenue and down it the group went. Charlene Louie lives there and reminded them that the Key System 10 Line train ran down it during the first half of the 20th Century. The group went onto Lower Grand Avenue and went up Holly Place to York Avenue and another path that connects to Ricardo Avenue and the foot of Dracena Park. They returned to the Exedra by way of Blair Avenue and San Carlos Avenue to Magnolia. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group can there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Boothby family’s first foster dog was a seven-pound puppy that had been thrown over the Oakland Animal Services (OAS) fence where a bush broke his fall. “He had a rough start in life,” said Cindy Boothby, who began volunteering at Oakland Animal Services after hearing news reports of overcrowding there. “He was so comfortable at our house,” she said of her first foster, named Flan. “I realized he could get some training and love and how much better it was for him at our house than at the shelter.” The puppy was adopted within two weeks and the Boothby family has gone on to foster another five puppies, each adopted within a month. “We foster one, take a break, and then when we are ready we foster another. It’s been incredibly rewarding,” she said. With the post-Covid return to in-person work, rising inflation, and Oakland’s affordable housing crisis, an increasing number of animals are being surrendered to OAS. The shelter is over-capacity with intake of medium and large-size dogs outpacing adoptions and a continuing influx of puppies. As an open admission shelter, OAS must accept all dogs, whether or not it has open kennel space. As a result there is a deadline by which they must be adopted, rescued, or fostered. “The changes we have made in the last three years, as well as the tremendous community support that we have received, has made it possible to maintain a historically low euthanasia rate for dogs, but our work is growing harder. We need the help of this community to make sure every one of these great dogs finds a new family,” said Ann Dunn, Director of Oakland Animal Services. Dunn is asking the public to save the life of animals by adopting a dog. Those who want to help but cannot adopt are encouraged to foster through a program funded by Friends of Oakland Animal Services. Piedmonter Jessica McDevitt fostered a senior dog when she learned he otherwise would have to be euthanized the next day for lack of space. “Looking at his sweet photos and video on the OAS website, I couldn’t stand the thought of him being put down,” said McDevitt. After being fostered by McDevitt for three weeks, he was adopted by a couple looking for a senior dog. “He’s leading the ideal life now,” said McDevitt. “He went camping the first night he was adopted and plays with his adopters’ other two dogs.” According to Dunn, fostering saves animals’ lives, alleviates shelter overcrowding and stress, and provides a chance for dogs to become reaccustomed to a home environment, increasing their chances of adoption. OAS provides fosters with initial supplies, ongoing medical services, and support. Dunn says those interested in learning more about fostering or ready to pick up a foster puppy or dog matched to the needs of their household can drop by the shelter on Thursdays from 12-7 p.m. to speak with a foster coordinator or select a foster puppy or dog. Puppies can be fostered individually or in pairs. For more information, e-mail: dogfostering@oaklandsanimals. org. Oakland Animal Services Dog Foster Coordinator Vivian Chu (left) with Caitlin, Cindy, and Andrea Boothby and foster puppies of Piedmont.

It is also in act one that we bear witness to the abiding grief of her parents and sister and brother, while George Harvey struggles with his demons a mere 50 yards away. Will he kill again? And will his next victim be Susie’s sister? But as the tension builds, the narrative breaks and Susie is running through undulating, surreal fields or along golden beaches. It’s a bit jarring. That isn’t to say that had her point of view been used sparingly that it couldn’t have been effective. There were moments when it was essential to the plot. But the key word is “sparingly.” There are many fine performances in this film beginning with Saoirse Ronan who captures in a hundred different ways the intense, vulnerable, innocent teen-tween girl. Mark Wahlberg and Rachel Weisz, as Susie’s father and mother, are both excellent. As is Susan Sarandon in a cameo role as the boozy, far from domestic grandmother who arrives wanting to help. And then there’s Stanley Tucci who delivers a quiet, nuanced portrayal as the malevolent and disturbing neighbor. Tucci is such a fine actor that to watch him work is reason enough to see The Lovely Bones. He defines character actor. Always in the background, always extraordinary, a chameleon in his ability to change his appearance, his mannerisms, down to his walk and gestures. He is never the leading man, but always astonishingly good in supporting roles. His career stretches back to 1985, and it’s not hyperbole to say that he has done it all, receiving countless nominations for his fine performances to include winning two Golden Globes. Recently, he played Meryl Streep’s husband in Julie and Julia, and was memorable in The Devil Wore Prada as Streep’s assistant. He is so good, so accomplished in his roles that he makes his craft seem effortless, and it is not uncommon to wonder if he was there at all. But of course he was, essential to every frame of The Lovely Bones. So many of Hollywood’s headline performers are famous for playing themselves, over and over. Audiences enjoy watching them fill the screen, their familiarity comfortable and predictable. They define the term movie star. But Tucci defines the term “actor,” for he can disappear into a role so completely that his character is remembered, not Tucci. The Lovely Bones. Directed by Peter Jackson. Starring Saoirse Ronan, Rachel Weisz, Stanley Tucci and Mark Wahlberg. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/MAX/ apple tv. articles.text: Each year as the lighting of Piedmont’s Holiday Tree approaches, Piedmont residents are invited to greet their Piedmont friends by way of donations to PBF’s Holiday Greeting Fund. This year, in addition to PBF’s regular Funds, donors were provided the opportunity to support the upcoming reforestation of Dracena Park. PBF is pleased to report that a large group of Piedmont families a extended holiday greeting to their Piedmont friends while responding generously to the funding opportunities offered by PBF. Almost $30,000 was contributed to PBF, including $8,300 for the Dracena Park project and $11,000 for its General Fund and $8,000 donated to the Sports Facilities Endowment. This is PBF’s newest permanent fund and is expected ultimately to become a vital source of money to properly maintain Piedmont’s many sports facilities. Coupled with other gifts, most notably the $250,000 for landscaping at the Piedmont pool, 2023 is PBF’s most successful year ever. PBF thanks all who donated and is pleased to provide the names of the donors to the Holiday Greeting Fund. Special thanks are extended to the underwriters who financed the city-wide mailing inviting everyone to Piedmont Lights Up, as the greatly expanded evening is now known. articles.text: and is open as an attraction to tour the chapel commissioned by Saint Louis in the 13th C. and the donjon completed in 1380. This donjon is a heavily fortified tower standing 170 feet tall and built within the medieval fortress. The tower’s walls are six-feet thick; surrounded by a moat, along with gunports, impenetrable wooden doors, and iron-bar latches. The donjon was where the Royals took refuge once the castle walls were breached by the enemy as a last chance to survive. The Vincennes military training field was decommissioned shortly after Lucky for the future, when Louis-Napoléon III granted the forests of Boulogne and Vincennes in 1855, the sites were professionally designed in the early Victorian style, a romantic vision that still works for today’s visitors. The two parks are legendary, conceived with artistry The latest 19th C. scientific methods were applied to construct lakes and drainage systems; roads and foot trails; and install flora and tree plantings of species numbering in the thousands. Each park has a hippodrome for horse racing, and VinThe Vincennes woods date Lac Daumesnil, the largest of four lakes at Vincennes, offers rowboat rentals, bike rentals, and pony rides for the kids around the lake. back to Gallo-Roman times when Paris was called Lutetia, and Romans referred to the forest as Vilcena. Of the two parks, Bois de Boulogne is stately and more prestigious: its boundary conjoins the 16th district’s west side, a locale with vast wealth, truly astounding mansions, private academies, and well-located foreign embassies. articles.text: Ken Betts Suds Machine on Piedmont Avenue recently closed temporarily and will re-open in March, according to owner Carla Betts. The popular car wash, which includes a gas station, closed due to construction required by the state concerning gas station fuel storage. Betts is using the time to install new car wash equipment and ensure an even better experience for customers after renovations. California now mandates that single-walled storage tanks that store gasoline must be replaced with double-walled ones by the end of 2024. Betts says she chose to perform their renovations now rather than later because it resulted in the “least loss of sales,” compared to the rest of their year. Other gas stations owned by Betts did not require construction because they already had double-walled storage tanks. However, Betts admitted that factors outside her control may delay the re-opening of the car wash past March. The biggest obstacle to re-opening remains the lengthy regulatory processes required of the gas station site. “Some of the dirt at the site is contaminated as a result of the single-walled tanks. So, there have been lots of regulatory officials coming to check the dirt,” she added. Overall, Betts looks forward to re-opening as soon as possible. “We want the people of Piedmont and Oakland to come back when we reopen. We want the car wash to be the best it can be when that happens. When it reopens, it’s going to be a brand-spanking new type of car wash,” she said. Staff Photo Ken Betts Suds Machine closed temporarily to upgrade its gas tanks and car washing equipment.

If you would like to read it for yourself you can find it on page 162 of Parting the Waters: America In The King Years 1954-63, by Taylor Branch. It was January 1956 and the Montgomery Bus Boycott was in its second month. The tensions and demands Dr. King faced were immense. Because he was regularly receiving threatening phone calls, some his friends armed themselves and began to drive him everywhere he needed to go. There was also pressure from the boycott participants and community supporters. How long would the boycott continue? How much longer would their lives be disrupted? Was any progress being made? Were King and the boycott leaders up to the task or were they in over their heads? As historian Branch records the story: After another long day King buried his face in his hands at the kitchen table. He admitted to himself that he was afraid, that he had nothing left, that the people would falter if they looked to him for strength. Then he said as much out loud. He spoke the name of no deity, but his doubts spilled out as a prayer, ending, “I’ve come to the point where I can’t face it alone.” As he spoke these words, the fears suddenly began to melt away. He became intensely aware of an “inner voice” telling him to do what he thought was right. Such simplicity worked miracles, bring a shudder of relief and the courage to face anything. It was the first transcendent religious experience of his life…It confirmed for him his belief that the essence of religion was not a grand metaphysical idea but something personal, grounded in experience – something that opened up mysteriously beyond the predicaments of human beings in their frailest and noblest moments. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee invite the public to the 27th annual Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 15 from 11 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. at Piedmont High School’s Alan Harvey Theatre, 800 Magnolia Avenue. With a theme of Remain Awake, the event will feature keynote speaker Dr. Amber Johnson, Assistant Vice Chancellor and Chief of Staff in the Division for Equity & Inclusion at UC Berkeley. Also speaking are Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, and Piedmont Mayor Jen Cavenaugh. The celebration event will feature the Oakland Interfaith Youth Choir and winners of the Art & Essay Showcase. Four days before he was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee on April 4, 1968, Dr. King delivered a sermon at the National Cathedral in Washington, D.C. Speaking about what he viewed as the evils of racism, poverty and militarism, Dr. King commented that “one of the great liabilities of life is that all too many people find themselves living amid a great period of social change and yet they fail to develop the new attitudes, the new mental responses that the new situation demands.” Dr. King noted that as citizens of one world, we are inextricably connected: “We are tied together in the single garment of destiny, caught in an inescapable network of mutuality. Whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly.” He issued the following challenge: “Let us stand up. Let us be a concerned generation. Let us remain awake through a great revolution.” Register to attend the event at: tinyurl.com/PADCMLK. The public is invited to Piedmont’s 27th annual MLK Day celebration on Monday, January 15 at the Alan Harvey Theater from 11 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The magical experience of talking to grown-ups No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling mind blown when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world - from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up, the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share in. But that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. We remember, often very clearly, how people made us feel when we were children. • An uncle who looked at your drawings and scribbles with an artist’s perspective, recognizing your use of shape, line and color • A neighbor who gave you the time to fully explain your thoughts and feelings, asking follow-up questions that showed you were really being heard • A teacher who pulled you aside to share that the assignment you turned in was more than good - it left them awed and they want to know how you felt while working on it Photo by Sebastián León Prado The relationship between a grown-up and child is very important. These adults made us feel like we were more than “just a kid.” Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. So how do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising coming from a camp director, but I recommend sending them to camp. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. Wonderful, magical, kind, kid-at-heart counselors and staff who we hired for their innate ability to see children for the wonders they are. Not perfect angels or naive brats, but smallish humans who have their own unique interests, attributes and lenses through which they see the world. and keeping our ratios tight (camper to staff 1:2 overall and 1:5 in cabins), we create opportunities every day for a camper to experience the magic of being seen. I am proud to report that we see those special moments all the time: an adult turning on their listening ears, seeing not ‘just a kid’, but a person they are happy to give their full heartfelt attention to. Thinking Outside the Classroom How sweet it is to be seen by you The magical experience of talking to grown-ups By Randall Grayson No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling mind blown when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world - from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up, the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share in. But that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. Photo by Sebastián León Prado The relationship between a grown-up and child is very important. These adults made us feel like we were more than “just a kid.” Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. So how do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising coming from a camp director, but I recommend sending them to camp. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. articles.text: Piedmont High School presents the musical Cabaret, directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead. The Kander and Ebb musical, set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close, explores the dark, exhilarating, and tumultuous life of Berlin’s natives and expatriates as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. The use of swastikas and military uniforms will not be in this production. More than 60 Piedmont High and Millennium High School students are involved in this PG-13 version of the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Winning a Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to impact its audience and performers. Sophomore Ben Wakefield expresses it well. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Shultz,” he said. “The Israel-Hamas War, which unfolded during our rehearsal period, did impact my feelings about performing in Cabaret. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical. Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present.” Performances are February 1, 2, 3, and 4 at 7:00 pm in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Ave., Piedmont. Tickets may be purchased online at https://www. showtix4u.com/event-details/ PHSCabaret or at the door for an additional $2.00 per ticket.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Victory over Berkeley, narrow loss to O’Dowd Staff Photos Brit Burden scored 29 points against Berkeley and 12 in a game with Bishop O’Dowd. Piedmont’s boys basketball team returned from Winter Break by splitting its opening two Western Alameda County Conference games. The Highlanders lost by five points, narrowly 57-52, to Bishop O’Dowd at the Dragons’ home gym on Thursday, January 4. Two days later Piedmont defeated Berkeley, last year’s league champions, 66-55 at home in Binks Rawlings Gym. “Our game plan was great and our boys executed really well,” said coach Ben Spencer. “Our guys battled and rebounded really well. We played tough in the second half of both games.” The 11-point win over the Yellowjackets and former PHS coach Mike Hudson was a huge response to the loss at O’Dowd. The Highlanders have been doing it shorthanded without starting forward Declan Linnane in both games, and senior forward Alex Anderson suffering a season-ending injury in the first game of the season. “We’re down two starters and Dillon [Casey] was even dealing with the flu during the week. Our players battled and that’s all you want as a coach – to come out and compete,” said Spencer. “It was a tough loss to O’Dowd, it feels like we’re always so close to beating them. But it got us in the right mindset for Saturday’s game. We put up a fight and got good looks. It’s the next-man-up mentality; we have depth and everyone stepped up big,” said senior leader Brit Burden. Piedmont played tough defensive games against both O’Dowd and Berkeley, turning up the intensity after falling behind in the first quarter of both games. PHS trailed 14-13 in the early going against the Dragons, while they were behind 15-10 at the end of the first quarter against Berkeley. “We started playing with more energy. When we’re communicating on the floor, we play more as a group. We switched to a zone against Bishop O’Dowd, and we know when we’re in a zone that we’re all in it together. When one person is lagging it messes up the entire zone,” added Burden. 66-55 win over Berkeley Piedmont trailed 15-10 to end the first quarter but gained a 30-28 lead at halftime. The Highlanders then stormed ahead 49-38 in the third quarter, while both teams closed out with 17 points in the final going for the 66-55 victory. In Piedmont’s 20-point second quarter, sophomore Dillon Casey and Burden scored eight and seven points respectively, and guard Ravi Silverberg put up five. In the third, Burden dominated Berkeley on the floor with 12 points, driving into the paint for layups and field-goal attempts. Silverberg, meanwhile, had four points from the line. Burden continued to show his versatility with seven points including one 3-pointer in the fourth. Final stats: Burden scored 29 points, Casey had 22, Silverberg had nine, while Thorin Holmes and Lucas Malecki had three points. 57-52 to Bishop O’Dowd The two sides traded points in the first quarter with the Dragons leading 14-13 after a 3-pointer. But PHS took the lead at 18-17 going into the second. O’Dowd regained the lead at 34-32 at halftime, only to see PHS jump back in the lead at 42-40 going into the fourth quarter. In the fourth quarter, O’Dowd hit a pair of 3-pointers to lead Dillon Casey had 22 points in Piedmont’s win against Berkeley and led the scoring with 19 points against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Markos Lagios elected to All-Metro Team by Chronicle Piedmont High’s return to playing football came with success, going 7-4 overall towards the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline title and a berth in the first round of the D5 North Coast Section playoffs. Making his mark as a receiver, return specialist, and defensive back was junior Sam Shelby, who was recently named the San Francisco Chronicle’s Player of the Year for the East Bay region. “He’s a hidden gem. He has a huge upside and really blossomed as our season unfolded,” said PHS offensive coordinator and veteran coach Paul Perenon. Shelby was also named to the Chronicle’s All-Metro first-team and The Mercury News’ All-Bay Area News Group second-team. Quarterback Markos Lagios was named to the Chronicle’s AllMetro second-team. “Markos is a special player. I don’t know how he wasn’t named to the Bay Area News Group Team; someone had to throw Sam the ball. We are so proud of both of them,” said Perenon. Piedmont’s 29-26 win over Newark Memorial on November 3 marked the first time PHS has won a league banner since 2015, also the last time they won the Shoreline Division. The winning touchdown came on an 80-yard pass from Lagios to Shelby with 5:27 left. Lagios suffered a knee injury Staff Photos Sam Shelby was named the Chronicle’s regional Player of the Year and first-team All-Metro, and also was named by Bay Area News Group to the second team. Sam Shelby was named the WACC Shoreline Division’s Offensive Player of the Year. Quarterback Markos Lagios earned second-team All-Metro honors by the Chronicle.

articles.text: Piedmont‘s girls’ soccer team walked out of 2023 on a high note, obliterating the Arroyo the Arroyo Dons 9-0 at Estuary Park in Alameda on Friday, December 22. The win continued the Highlanders’ undefeated record at 6-0-0 to start the New Year. Piedmont led 5-0 through the first half and added four more goals in the second. Malea Hartford, who was a two-sport athlete with flag football, bagged a firsthalf hat trick and added one more goal in the second half. It didn’t take long for Piedmont to get on the board, with fullback Elle Ruegg uncorking a perfect pass through the defense to Malea Hartford charging through the back line—sending a shot skipping past the keeper. The Highlanders then showcased great interplay on its second goal, where Ryo Woltag sent a pass to Hartford, who flicked a pass back to Juliana Thornborrow on her first touch. Thornborrow then sent a ball through the defense to Woltag in the box, who slotted home a hard right-footed shot. On the third goal, it started with Hailey Marshburn sending a hard shot towards above the keepers head. The Arroyo GK initially made the save, but bobbled the ball to the ground. There to poach the loose ball was Hartford, adding her second goal. Ruegg then put in Piedmont’s fourth goal of the first half. This time it came on Piedmont fluidly moving the ball downfield with incisive passes. This time, Lola Biehn found Ruegg charging down the right wing, leading to the fullback sending a rightfooted shot over the keeper’s head to the far post. For the fifth, Hartford found her hat trick after Biehn made good work of her defenders. In the build up, Biehn weaved her way around a pair of Dons’ center backs before letting the ball roll onto Hartford, who rocketed in a right-footed shot on her first touch for the goal. In the second half, Thornborrow scored Piedmont’s next goal quickly after the break when Photos by Todd Marshburn Malea Hartford had four goals in Piedmont’s 9-0 win over Arroyo. Darcy McKee scored had two goals against the Dons.

articles.text: Freshman Sebastien Swain was a breakout star on Piedmont High’s cross country team last fall, becoming the only runner at the school to qualify for the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park on Saturday, November 25. In doing so, he was selected for the All-State Freshman Team for Division 4 runners by Prep CalTrack on December 24. He was 67th of 201 runners at the state meet with a time of 16:41.3. His appearance at the State means Piedmont has sent at least one runner to the CIF Cross-Country Championship for 35 consecutive years. It’s something Swain didn’t entirely see coming once he first suited up in Purple and White. “It means a lot to me [to qualify for State]. I’m still really excited that I was just able to get there; it’s not something a lot of people get to do. It’s something I thought wasn’t even on the table before NCS when I qualified,” said Swain. From the first practice of the season, it was apparent Swain would be a standout runner in his debut year. “Sebastien showed up to our time trial before the season started and clocked the third-fastest time,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “Sebastien has an impressive amount of poise and concentration when he is racing. We see it in practice and have observed this focus throughout the season.” According to Zirkelbach, Swain achieved a freshmen record for Piedmont High at Woodward Park, eclipsing Mark Ceraldi’s time of 16:59 set in 2003. “Seb’s performance was the 3rd fastest freshman runner in his race. He set the PHS Freshman record for the course, one that goes back 20 years to Mark Ceraldi in 2003,” said Zirkelbach. Distance runner Sebastien Swain was named to the AllState Freshman Team by Prep CalTrack. He finished 67th of 201 runners at the State Championship with a time of 16:41.3. Swain punched his ticket to State by finishing 13th of 140 runners with a time of 16:29.5 at the NCS Championship on November 18 at Hayward High amidst stormy conditions. articles.text: Staff Photos Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills is considered an “ecological gem” because of its year-round display of blossoming plants. It has an ideal canopy for rain cover. With some rain in the forecast over the next week, looking out the window could be daunting for some hikers feeling those gray and gloomy vibes. But luckily for us in the Bay Area, there is a wealth of parks to choose from where hikers can avoid the wet weather with help of vast tree coverage. So grab your rain gear, hiking boots, and consider this group of five areas where you can enjoy some hiking even when it’s raining. Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve is a small treasure in the Oakland Hills. East Bay Regional Parks District (EBRPD) calls Huckleberry an “ecological gem” because of its year-round display of blossoming plants. The canopy of California Bays, Redwood trees, and Manzanita make it an ideal and small 3.4 mile loop. Manzanita trees, with their vibrant red burl, are currently in bloom. EBRPD has a list of plants currently blooming at the park. Redwood Regional A local favorite, Redwood Regional Park, is a default location for residents in the Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont hills. Several trails provide extensive tree coverage. Consider the French Trail, Chown Trail, Madrone Trail, Fern Trail, and Redwood Peak Trail as hikes that will put you beneath the canopy of trees. The West Ridge Trail provides an avenue where you can find each of the trailheads, parking at the Redwood Bowl Staging Area. Another connecting trail, which is well covered, is the Stream Trail, with parking at Canyon Meadow Staging Area. Joaquin Miller Adjacent to Redwood Regional Park on Skyline Boulevard, you’ll find trails with more foot traffic compared to the former, but equal amount of tree coverage along the Big Trees Trail, Sequoia Bayview Trail, Palos Colorados Trail, and the Sunset Trail. San Mateo: Purisima Creek Redwoods Traveling to San Mateo County; Purisima Creek’s Harkins Ridge provides a beautiful but rigorous journey through the hills surrounding San Mateo. Its trails beneath tree canopy are ideal for the rain. Consider the Purisima Creek Trail, which will go by the active Purisima Creek, where you can walk by large stumps of old growth trees with some second-growth trees scattered throughout the area. Marin: Cataract Falls Moving north to Marin County, the north end of Mt. Tamalpais has one of its most popular trails, the Cataract Falls Trail, where you’ll see a display of redwood trees towering over you. The rain will further enable the cascade of waterfalls along Cataract Creek, which will line your entire walk. Although less than four-miles, you’ll gain over 1,000 feet in elevation over steep steps and tree roots. It’s a perfect time to find mushroom while hiking on trails. Redwood Regional’s sprawling redwoods provide great cover from the rain.

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, January 10, 2024 Sebastien Swain named to All-State Freshman Team By Jonathan Comeaux Freshman Sebastien Swain was a breakout star on Piedmont High’s cross country team last fall, becoming the only runner at the school to qualify for the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park on Saturday, November 25. In doing so, he was selected for the All-State Freshman Team for Division 4 runners by Prep CalTrack on December 24. He was 67th of 201 runners at the state meet with a time of 16:41.3. His appearance at the State means Piedmont has sent at least one runner to the CIF Cross-Country Championship for 35 consecutive years. It’s something Swain didn’t entirely see coming once he first suited up in Purple and White. “It means a lot to me [to qualify for State]. I’m still really excited that I was just able to get there; it’s not something a lot of people get to do. It’s something I thought wasn’t even on the table before NCS when I qualified,” said Swain. From the first practice of the season, it was apparent Swain would be a standout runner in his debut year. “Sebastien showed up to our time trial before the season started and clocked the third-fastest time,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “Sebastien has an impressive amount of poise and concentration when he is racing. We see it in practice and have observed this focus throughout the season.” According to Zirkelbach, Swain achieved a freshmen record for Piedmont High at Woodward Park, eclipsing Mark Ceraldi’s time of 16:59 set in 2003. “Seb’s performance was the 3rd fastest freshman runner in his race. He set the PHS Freshman record for the course, one that goes back 20 years to Mark Ceraldi in 2003,” said Zirkelbach. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is ringing in 2024 with the world premiere of playwright Minna Lee’s My Home on the Moon from January 25 through February 24. In this epic sci-fi journey into the metaverse, business is booming for a formerly failing Vietnamese pho restaurant in the middle of a gentrified neighborhood after it receives help from a mysterious marketing consultant. Things are not all they seem as the restaurant’s waiter, Mai, discovers that artificial intelligence-powered simulations may be taking over reality. With the help of her friends and family, and armed with delicious pho, Mai must learn to reckon the perfection of artificial life with the welcome imperfection of reality. A finalist in the 2024 Bay Area Playwrights Festival and semi-finalist at Ashland New Plays Festival, My Home on the Moon received developmental readings at UC Santa Cruz’s Rainbow Theater Festival and Denver, Colorado-based arts collective Bucharest Inside the Beltway. For tickets ($15-$100) and more information about the performance at SF Playhouse (450 Post Street), visit sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677-9596 Marketing consultant Vera (Rinabeth Apostol) learns the art of cooking pho from Mai (Jenny Nguyen Nelson) in the world premiere of My Home on the Moon at San Francisco Playhouse January 25 through February 24.
articles.title: World premiere of My Home on the Moon at SF Playhouse Jan. 25

articles.text: The Lesher Center for the Arts Repertory Company opens its 2024 season with the remarkable hit solo show, Every Brilliant Thing, on view through January 28. Making a list of things that make life worth living would get different responses from different people, and what would be at the top? Family? Ice cream? The even-numbered Star Trek films? For the lead character in this uplifting play, it’s his mother. This surprising and immersive theatrical experience by Duncan Macmillan and Jonny Donahoe delves into the human experience with playfulness and love. With poignant humor and joy, Every Brilliant Thing takes audiences on a journey through favorite moments such as falling in love, as well as grief, healing, and discovering and rediscovering all that life has to give. Directed by celebrated Bay Area fixture Jeffrey Lo and starring Oakland Theater Project Co-Artistic Director William William Thomas Hodgson stars in Every Brilliant Thing at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek through January 28. Thomas Hodgson, the story is filled with opportunities for warm, fun audience participation. The show premiered at the Ludlow Fringe Festival then was performed off Broadway at Barrow Street Theatre where it was filmed for HBO, It was deemed a “heart-wrenching, hilarious play” by The Guardian; The New York Times called it “captivating.” Time Out London lauded the work as “gloriously funny and exceptionally warm,” while The Independent said it “finds a perfect balance between conveying the struggles of life, and celebrating all that is sweet in it.” For tickets ($35-$40) visit LesherArtsCenter.org or call the box office at (925) 943-7469. Lesher Center for the Arts is located at 1601 Civic Drive in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: See Every Brilliant Thing at Lesher Center through Jan. 28

articles.text: Due to popular demand, award-winning actor and playwright Dan Hoyle’s critically acclaimed one-man show Border People has been extended at The Marsh San Francisco with performances through Saturday, January 13, this weekend. Based on Hoyle’s conversations and interviews from South Bronx housing project courtyards, refugee safe houses on the Northern Border with Canada, and travels along the Southwestern U.S. border and into Mexico, Border People offers an intimate, poignant and funny look at the borders that many people negotiate in their everyday lives. Hoyle began work on the show after the presidential election of Donald Trump in November 2016, working with increased urgency to complete the play as the American immigration debate continued to grow more polarized and heated on both sides. This solo show has been greeted with widespreaed critical acclaim, earning the highest rating from the San Francisco Chronicle, which wrote “this is what it is to witness a master of his craft. Dan Hoyle is one of our theatrical gems,” and praised the production as “a testament to the core-to-nerve ending commitment and courage” of those living on borders of any kind. Theatermania wrote, “Border People is the most engaging evening I’ve spent in the theater in a long time. This is a show that anyone who considers themselves a well-informed citizen should see.” Border People, developed with and directed by Charlie Varon, will continue through January 13 at The Marsh, 1062 Valencia Street in San Francisco. For tickets ($25-$35 sliding scale, $50 and $100 reserved) and more information, see: themarsh.org. articles.text: Cult of Love will be performed by Berkeley Repertory Theatre from January 26 through March 3. Cult of Love, written by Leslye Headland and directed by Trip Cullman, will open at Berkeley Repertory Theatre on Friday, January 26, for a five-week run. Cult of Love is a ruthless comedy about a deeply Christian family, the Dahls, devoted to their belief that all one needs is love. The four Dahl siblings were brought up with a devotion to Jesus and each other. Now adults with their own distinct beliefs and years of emotional wariness, they gather once again for the holidays at their childhood home, singing joyous carols and recreate family traditions. However, repressed feelings and conflicts about the siblings’ upbringing shatter the family’s façade of forced cheer, and all hell soon breaks loose. Bold and provocative, Cult of Love dares to challenge our perceptions of family to examine what’s truly needed for deep faith and love to persist. “All families are inherently complicated, but in Leslye Headland and Trip Cullman’s hands, they are also dynamic, dramatic, and wildly entertaining,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “I’m delighted to welcome this incredibly gifted cast and creative team to Berkeley Rep.” Tickets ($22.50–$134) may be purchased at the box office or online at berkeleyrep.org/shows/ cult-of-love, or by phone at 647- 2949. Berkeley Rep’s Roda Theater is located at 2015 Addison Street.
articles.title: Cult of Love opens at Berkeley Rep Jan. 26

articles.text: Berkeley Community Chorus & Orchestra to collaborate In an inaugural moment for the local music scene, two of Berkeley’s long-standing musical institutions, the Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) and the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO), will join for a single performance, YPSO’s annual Winter Concert on January 27 at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church. YPSO proudly continues its 87th season, with Maestro David Ramadanoff celebrating an impressive 35 years as Music Director/Conductor. Leading a talented ensemble of 100 young musicians, ages 11 to 21 from cities spanning the Bay Area, from Napa to Pleasanton, Maestro Ramadanoff continues to inspire and guide the orchestra towards new heights. In a season brimming with activity, YPSO is performing the second of four subscription concerts, showcasing its talents at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, and embarking on a 9-day, 3-concert summer tour to Japan in June 2024. YPSO’s Winter Concert will feature works spanning three different centuries: Kenji Bunch’s Supermaximum, the first movement of Saint-Saëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 featuring soloist Henry Stroud (winner of this year’s YPSO concerto competition), and Poulenc’s Gloria in collaboration with the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO), featuring soprano soloist Vuyiswa Sigadi. Bunch’s Supermaximum is a contemporary composition that explores themes of resilience and determination, in which Bunch draws inspiration from the reallife experiences of individuals facing extraordinary challenges. He has created a musical narrative that speaks to the strength of the human spirit. Following this, YPSO will perform the first movement. In program notes, Orrin Howard has written of Saint-Saëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 in B Minor, Op. 61, “The first movement evolves around a bold, dramatic first theme, a songful contrasting theme, and fistsful of rapid scales, arpeggios, and double stops.” This piece will feature YPSO concertmaster Henry Stroud, a sophomore at Berkeley High, and winner of this season’s YPSO concerto competition. Closing the program is Poulenc’s Gloria, a choral and orchestral masterpiece that reflects the composer’s unique blend of sacred and secular influences. It is a joyous and vibrant work, featuring lush harmonies and intricate textures. YPSO is collaborating on this piece with Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra, a longstanding Berkeley music organization led by Ming Luke (https://bcco.org/ upcoming-collaborations/). History of YPSO Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The 2023-24 season is its 87th. YPSO’s mission is to “encourage young people to become exemplary musicians and young musicians to become exemplary people”. The organization puts on four regular concerts per season. In addition, they reach out through programs such as Bread and Roses and the Bay Area Music Project to bring music into the lives of the surrounding community and encourage the civic development of its students. YPSO will also host a free open dress rehearsal program on Friday Jan 26 at 6 p.m. for families with young children, elementary/ middle school classes accompanied by a teacher, and senior cit-
articles.title: YPSO Winter Concert to be performed Jan. 27

articles.text: Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival, an annual benefit concert by five principal youth orchestras, will take place at Davies Symphony Hall on Sunday afternoon, January 14, at 3 p.m. Hosted by San Francisco Symphony, the concert includes musicians from San Francisco Youth Orchestra, Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, California Youth Symphony, and Golden State Youth Orchestra. They will perform the music of Leonard Bernstein, Valerie Coleman, Manuel de Falla, Arturo Marquez, Piotr Tchaikovsky, and Ralph Vaughan Williams. Serving as MC will be former Piedmont resident and KPIX anchor Wendy Tokuda. Tickets are $25 General Admission, $70 reserved seating, and half price for age 7 and under. Online tickets are available at sfsymphony.org. Proceeds from the festival will benefit nonprofit organizations serving homeless and underserved youth in each orchestra’s local community. YPSO’s portion of the proceeds will benefit its community partner, the Bay Area Music Project (BAMP), a nonprofit, social change through music program that addresses social, emotional, cultural, and academic needs of children in grades K-12 in underserved communities in the immediate Bay Area. articles.text: ‘Seen’ by Laura Paladini to be the first ever curated exhibit at Alma Rise Alma Rise Gallery in Berkeley has announced its newest exhibition, “Seen,” will feature the work of Piedmont artist Laura Paladini. The exhibit, which contemplates the “enigma of invisibility” according to a press release, will open this Friday, January 12 during an opening reception from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m. at the gallery. Piedmonters may recognize Paladini from her previous involvement in the Piedmont Art Walk. She has worked with clients from her interior design firm in Piedmont for over 20 years. However in 2020, Paladini shifted her career focus to exploring the creative freedom of painting. Most of her work in recent years has been with oils on paper, wood panels, and canvas. “Laura was among the first artists I approached when we launched the gallery,” said Lupe Muller, the Executive Director at Alma Rise Gallery. Muller personally curated this show after being impressed by Paladini’s work. “I am personally really captivated by the authenticity embedded in her paintings and how she often shines a light on those we usually choose not to see.” “Seen” is an exploration of invisibility that examines societal norms, perceptions, and the ongoing struggle for recognition, something that resonates with Paladini personally. “I’m hoping that ‘Seen’ makes people examine the struggles other people are having, unseen, and that it presents them in a way that audiences can identify with,” said Paladini. Alma Rise Gallery is at 1600 Shattuck Ave, Suite 126 in Berkeley. “Seen,” will be on display from Friday, Jan 12 – Friday, Feb 9. Admission for this event will be free. No reservations are required for opening night. The show will be open every Saturday 1 p.m. – 4 p.m. or by appointment via email at info@almarisegallery.org. Artist Laura Paladini is shown next to a work titled His Domain, one of her most personal pieces featured in the new exhibition.
articles.title: Piedmont artist featured at Alma Rise Gallery

If they need some assistance, the homeroom teacher will be there to provide it. Every student should be required to take at least one music class during secondary school. For the students who do not play a musical instrument, music appreciation is ideal. School service should be another requirement. It can include chorus, instrumental music, and participation in a marching band. Foreign language should also be a requirement and should begin in elementary school and continue throughout secondary school. Other countries require this; why don’t we? We should also require at least one semester of school service, which could include community service. A number of subjects come to mind: kids can work on the school newspaper, help clean up the campus, assist the various athletic teams (including being a cheerleader), and work in the cafeteria or in the office. articles.text: Dan Flanagan and Trio Solano will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, January 13 at 7 p.m. The trio will performs string trios by Schubert, Sibelius and Beethoven, then will be joined by pianist Michael Seth Orland for Fauré’s epic Piano Quartet #1. Trio Solano consists of Dan Flanagan (violin), Paul Ehrlich (viola), and Vicky Ehrlich (cello). Each piece on the program will be accompanied by projections of period paintings, tying the concert in with Flanagan’s acclaimed international concert project, The Bow and the Brush, which comprises new works for violin composed by Flanagan and colleagues, each inspired by a fine art masterwork. The Bow and the Brush is expected to have its world premiere at Carnegie Hall later this Spring. The Ehrlichs (cello and viola) perform internationally and throughout North America, as well as locally with the San Francisco Symphony and Opera and Ballet Orchestras, along with several smaller groups all over the Bay Area. This concert at PCA is world-class music in Piedmont, with the added pleasure of fine art masterpieces of the period projected with each piece of music. Tickets ($25) are available at https://www.bpt.me/6201377 or $30 cash or check at the door.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The film Extremely Loud/ Incredibly Close opens with what has become an iconic image of 9/11: the falling man. We bear witness to an individual dropping some 125 stories through the air, escaping a consuming fire but unable to escape the final outcome. Another image captured in the film, one that will forever be with us, is the scene of a brick wall. It’s only been a few days since the Twin Towers collapsed. In the dark of night, the camera slowly moves from right to left, revealing countless photographs of the missing, along with messages, many a plea to call home. At the foot of the wall are lighted candles and bouquets of flowers. In essence, the wall is a heartbreaking memorial to those who will likely never return and are lost forever amid the rubble and steel that now lies where the towers once stood. But there is more to this haunting and extraordinary film one that tells the story of a nine-year-old boy, Oskar Schell (Thomas Horn), who lost his father on what he refers to as “the worst day.” School had let out early on Tuesday, September 11, for reasons that are initially unclear to Oskar. He arrives home, and as usual checks the family’s message machine. Unexpectedly, message one is his father’s voice (Tom Hanks), a call from the 125th floor of one of the towers where he has been attending a meeting. Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each building vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, instead observing the ceremony from a distance. A year passes and finally, reluctantly, Oskar enters his father’s den and begins to look through his things. And when he is taking down a box, he knocks a blue vase off the shelf, breaking it. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, Thomas Horn and Tom Hanks star in Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” Attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt. It was a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera to take their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud/ Intensely Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And, ultimately, why? Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close. Directed by Stephen Daldry. Starring Tom Hanks, Thomas Horn, Sandra Bullock, Max von Sydow. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13. Made in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime?Apple tv. Review by Chris Honoré Tully is many things: well acted, possessing a truly fine ensemble led by Charlize Theron, and a script, written by Diablo Cody (Juno), that is smartly brittle with a wide thread of authenticity. If this film can be characterized as a comedy (as it has been in the trailers), well, it’s a dark comedy. A close-to-the-bone depiction of parenting and motherhood that is raw and honest with not a hint of the Hollywood patina that so often disguises Charlize Theron, Asher Miles Fallica, and Lia Frankland in Tully and finds the house clean, Sarah eating her cereal, and a dozen cupcakes on the table. Tully is already gone. Marlo’s days become a slow-moving montage of Tully arriving each evening, sitting with the baby, explaining that she, Tully, is there not to just take care of Mia but to take care of Marlo. Gradually, Marlo is transformed, remembering once again how to breathe, and finding welcomed remnants of who she was… when? A decade ago? Her ennui lifts as Tully imparts not just encouragement but wisdom and insights that Marlo may have once known but has long ago forgotten. All of this leads to act three, which is completely unexpected and is, in its distinctive way, provocative and puzzling. It asks the audience to sort events out absent any exposition. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, January 10, 2024 MOVIE FOR ADULTS Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close a gripping film about 9/11 Review by Chris Honoré The film Extremely Loud/ Incredibly Close opens with what has become an iconic image of 9/11: the falling man. We bear witness to an individual dropping some 125 stories through the air, escaping a consuming fire but unable to escape the final outcome. Another image captured in the film, one that will forever be with us, is the scene of a brick wall. It’s only been a few days since the Twin Towers collapsed. In the dark of night, the camera slowly moves from right to left, revealing countless photographs of the missing, along with messages, many a plea to call home. At the foot of the wall are lighted candles and bouquets of flowers. In essence, the wall is a heartbreaking memorial to those who will likely never return and are lost forever amid the rubble and steel that now lies where the towers once stood. But there is more to this haunting and extraordinary film one that tells the story of a nine-year-old boy, Oskar Schell (Thomas Horn), who lost his father on what he refers to as “the worst day.” School had let out early on Tuesday, September 11, for reasons that are initially unclear to Oskar. He arrives home, and as usual checks the family’s message machine. Unexpectedly, message one is his father’s voice (Tom Hanks), a call from the 125th floor of one of the towers where he has been attending a meeting. Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each building vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, instead observing the ceremony from a distance. A year passes and finally, reluctantly, Oskar enters his father’s den and begins to look through his things. And when he is taking down a box, he knocks a blue vase off the shelf, breaking it. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, Thomas Horn and Tom Hanks star in Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” Attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt. It was a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera to take their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud/ Intensely Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And, ultimately, why? Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close. Directed by Stephen Daldry. Starring Tom Hanks, Thomas Horn, Sandra Bullock, Max von Sydow. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13. Made in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime?Apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Coraline The stop-motion, animated feature Coraline is a tour de force of imagination. Made in 2009 in this reviewer’s hometown, Ashland, Oregon, it is a dark fantasy horror film written and directed by Henry Selick, and based on Neil Gaiman’s novella of the same name. Though made to be shown in stereoscopic 3-D, even in 2-D it is vivid and rich with a panoply of colors and strange and interesting characters. But, for all of its technical wonder and labor-intensive filming – the characters are three-dimensional figures that are moved ever so slightly, a single frame at a time – it’s hard to enthusiastically recommend this film for children. It is a sinister narrative which takes a young girl’s fantasy and turns it into a gothic nightmare. All fairytales have a distinctly dark side to them. Dorothy follows the yellow brick road only to meet the Wicked Witch. Alice falls down the rabbit hole into a world that is not simply benign. And certainly Harry Potter, for all of his deft ability with magic, encounters evil that takes many forms and threatens his very existence. And so it is with Coraline who has recently moved from Michigan to Ashland, Oregon. She and her parents have moved into a Victorian rooming house called the Pink Palace (remember the one in San Francisco in the 1960’s? This one, however, is filled with eccentric boarders. Feeling lonely and bored, and finding her parents distracted and cranky as they work intensely on a gardening catalogue (her mother is especially curt and preoccupied), Caroline explores the house and soon discovers a hidden door in her room that opens into a narrow tunnel (a rabbit hole?) and a parallel world. In this mirror universe, however, her new parents are attentive to her every need, and her room wonderfully inviting. The only disconcerting aspect is that everyone she meets has buttons instead of eyes. It’s something she is willing to overlook. So seductive is this new world, where flowers bloom in the moonlight, where all is a kaleidoscope of colors, she begins to find it harder and harder to return to her real life and her real parents. And, of course, her new mother encourages her to remain forever. It all seems so perfect. But as a talking cat suggests, perhaps there is more to this parallel world than first meets the eye (or button). And perhaps all of this good will and attention is a bit suspicious. What child doesn’t fantasize about a world in which they are the center of attention, a world in which they feel powerful and have more than a modicum of control over their own lives. Or a world suddenly without parents who draw boundaries and make rules that seem so arbitrary. The culmination of this fantasy was captured perfectly in the film Home Alone, when Kevin wakes up in his house and discovers everyone is gone. He wished them gone, and suddenly his wish has come true. He quickly sets out to create a life in which he rules. It’s a rush until it isn’t. Like Kevin, Coraline is soon confronted with more than she can handle; what initially was exciting becomes deeply frightening. Will she be able to find her way back to her real world and once again be able to embrace her parents? Nothing is certain. What is surprising about Coraline is that none of the characters are particularly attractive. Even Coraline herself is feisty and a bit ill-tempered. That’s not to say that she should be Disneyesque or a Cinderella-type character, but there has to be an emotional bridge built between the young audience and Coraline. A young neighbor, Wybie, wants to befriend Coraline, but in return she accuses him of being a stalker. Parental warning Young children ever so easily blur the lines between what is real and what is fantasy and might find the last half of Coraline too intense, its foreshadowed sinister edge morphing into full-blown evil. The strength of this film is that it is so wonderfully imagined. Based on Neil Gaiman’s book which has sold over a million copies worldwide, there clearly is something about the story that resonates with kids. No doubt, all kids love to be scared, a little. Call it the jeepers creepers effect. On a larger-than-life screen, however, its impact may be more than some youngsters can handle. Coraline. Stop-motion animation. Directed by Henry Selick. Starring the voices of Dakota Fanning and Teri Hatcher. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG
