articles.text: If there is genius in the stories of Nicolas Sparks, it’s that he writes with a deft understanding of his audience. From The Notebook to Message in a Bottle to Nights in Rodanthe, Sparks delivers wildly popular melodramas that aim to give the heart of the reader an emotional tug. He has to date written 14 novels. In the hands of a good director and screenwriter, his books make for solid, if formulaic movies that never fail to entertain. Dear John is directed by the talented Swedish film director Lasse Hallstrom, the husband of equally famous actress Lena Olin. Sparks’ story aims at tween and teen girls, and he nails it. I saw the movie on a Friday afternoon, just after school had let out for the weekend, and the theater was filled with teenage girls, all tightly packed in the center of the theater. This shouldn’t have been a surprise for Dear John stars two movie Channing Tatum as John Tyree, home on leave from his tour of duty with the Army’s Special Forces, and Amanda Seyfried as Savannah Curtis, a lovely, coltish college student, spending her spring break on the coast of South Carolina, near Charleston, where John lives. The time is late spring; several months before 9/11. Okay, the film is a Hallmark card. But that’s not a criticism. Sparks is a master at creating relationships defined by intense bonding, followed by separation, heartache, obstacles to unrequited love, a heart-wrenching surprise or two, and a denouement that generally satisfies. Savannah and John have an intense, glowing, sun-kissed two weeks together as they play and talk and cavort like two young seals in the gentle Atlantic surf. He is polite and withdrawn while she, in contrast, is open and direct. Their mutual attraction, however, is palpable. And through the lens of Hallstrom’s camera, all is soft, burnished, wrapped in an appealing yellow glow. Even the few war scenes are seemingly benign. Of course given the title of the film, John and Savannah will face a time apart, their only connection countless letters as John is sent around the world on classified assignments with his Special Forces team. Savannah, waiting, longing, goes to class, walks the campus, and decides that she would like to devote her life to working with autistic children (there’s an aside where she wonders if John’s father, played by the incomparable Richard Jenkins, might be mildly autistic). Recall that this is a melodrama. There will be roadblocks to John and Savannah being reunited, beginning with the 9/11 terrorist attack in New York City, and its impact on John’s time in the service. Though Dear John heads toward its inexorable climax, Hallstrom/Sparks will not make it easy. At one especially emotional point in the film (and there are many), young teens in the theater could be heard sniffing and trying not to breathe. For good reason. This is a nifty teen melodrama and there’s no doubt that those girls, filled with romantic impulses, enamored with the idea of love and finding a John themselves, will be swept away by this movie. These are the same girls that kept James Cameron’s “Titanic” afloat, so to speak. And they may do the same for Dear John. Dear John. Directed by Lasse Hallstrom, Starring Channing Tatum, Amanda Seyfried, Richard Jenkins and Henry Thomas. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Streaming om VUDU/Netflix/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: For many families throughout the Bay, Lunar New Year – which this year is the Year of the Dragon – is one of the most anticipated times of the year. Though Lunar New Year officially starts February 10, Children’s Fairyland is beginning the fortune-filled celebration early, for three days from January 26 through January 28. On the lunar calendar the dragon symbolizes success, honor, luck, nobleness and power. It is a supernatural creature, supreme in its talent and excellence. Families can ring in the Year of the Dragon early with an explosive weekend of family fun at Children’s Fairyland in Oakland. articles.text: Dear Abby: We are looking for pugs and people to join us for a happy Pug Yoga session on Saturday, February 10th at 2 p.m. at the Sports Basement Community Room, 2727 Milvia Street, Berkeley, for a fun fundraiser for Pug Rescue NorCal. Bring your yoga mat and pug and watch the pugs as they show you how to do a beautiful downward dog better than any human. The donation is $32 per human and pugs are free. Tricks & licks to all, –Jen and Rex, the Pug who loves yoga Dear Jen & Rex: That sounds like lots of fun and a few sore muscles, but it looks like it’s a pugs only event, so I can’t join you. Still, I looked at the site and I can easily donate to your pug mission. Thanks for letting us know. I suspect a lot of our plucky Piedmont Pugs will show their pug love for their fellow pugs-in-rescue and have a good romp at this party. What a hoot. A big bow wow to all. –Abby Dear Abby: What are the healthiest dog breeds? My dear dog-friend Turk just passed and I would like to avoid that feeling for a while. He lived to be nine…63 in dog years. Far too short. –Silvia Dear Silvia: I’m so sorry to hear about Turk. Getting a new puppy (or a new older dog) is definitely worth thinking through the health concerns that affect certain breeds. While I’m not sure if you prefer big or small review, but here’s the top three to get you started. 1. Australian Cattle Dog. We see these occasionally around Piedmont. The Guinness Book of Records says the World’s Oldest Dog was an ACD named Bluey, that lived to the ripe age of 29 in human years, 203 in dog years. 2. Poodles tend to have long, healthy lifespans of up to 18 years, regardless of whether they are Standard, Miniature or Toy. Eye and joint issues tend to affect them in their older years. 3. Border Collies tend to be lovable and vigorous and healthy for most of their lives which can be 12-18 years. Deafness and epilepsy can affect them when they get long in the paw. Certain breeds like bulldogs are known to develop respiratory issues. Pugs can commonly suffer from eye infections. Frenchies, which became the top U.S. dog breed last year, can suffer from excessive itching and licking as well as respiratory issues. Talk with other Piedmonters who own these breeds and they’ll tell you the true tale. Mutts and crossbreeds are commonly thought to be healthier than some purebreds, but there’s no guarantee that the dog you pick won’t develop something which turns into a hefty vet bill. Lots for you to chew on. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.
articles.title: Selecting a new dog

While I’m not sure if you prefer big or small review, but here’s the top three to get you started. 1. Australian Cattle Dog. We see these occasionally around Piedmont. The Guinness Book of Records says the World’s Oldest Dog was an ACD named Bluey, that lived to the ripe age of 29 in human years, 203 in dog years. 2. Poodles tend to have long, healthy lifespans of up to 18 years, regardless of whether they are Standard, Miniature or Toy. Eye and joint issues tend to affect them in their older years. 3. articles.text: Most wine historians believe that the first place on earth to make wine was the modern country of Georgia. The roots of Georgian viticulture have been traced back by archeology to when people of the South Caucasus discovered that wild grape juice turned into wine when it was left buried through the winter in a shallow pit. This knowledge was nourished by experience, and from 6000 BC inhabitants of the current Georgia were cultivating grapes and burying clay vessels known as kvevris in which to store their wine ready for serving at ground temperature. When filled with the fermented juice of the harvest, the kvevris are topped with a wooden lid and then covered and sealed with earth. Some may remain entombed for up to 50 years. With a diverse and unique microclimate, there are about 500 grape varieties in modern Georgia. Wine vessels of every shape, size and design have been the crucial part of pottery in Georgia for millennia. Ancient artifacts attest to the high skill of local craftsmen. Among vessels, the most ubiquitous and unique to Georgian wine-making culture are probably the kvevris, very large earthenware vessels with an inside coat of beeswax. Georgia ranks second (in terms of volume) in grape production in the former Soviet Union behind Moldova. Its wines had a high reputation in the Soviet Union. Currently, the wine is produced by thousands of small farmers (using primarily traditional techniques of winemaking), as well as certain monasteries and modern wineries. According to the Minister of Agriculture of Georgia, wine production has increased from 13.8 million 750ml bottles in 2009 to 15.8 million bottles in 2010. In 2009, Georgia exported nearly 11 million bottles of wine to 45 countries. Noted British Wine writer Oz Clarke writes the following about the wines of Georgia. “Georgia has preserved and cherished a wine culture more closely linked to its past than any of the other countries. It certainly makes wines whose tastes are completely, utterly removed from the experience of any normal modern wine drinker. And it uses methods of winemaking that you couldn’t invent in a modern world; you could only inherit them through the mists of time, maybe as far back as human records go.” I recently had the opportunity to taste some Georgian wines and was pleasantly surprised by both the quality and the originality of tastes. If your wine drinking has gotten into a bit of a rut, trying these wines would be a great way to break out. 2019 Marnaveli Rkatsiteli This is a light, refreshing white wine made from the Rkatsiteli grape and grown in the Kakheti region of Georgia. It reminds me of a Sancerre or a really crisp Chenin Blanc with abundant floral and citrus notes. It finishes clean and sharp and A typical Georgian wine cellar with underground Kvevri jars.

Walkers explore high school and Witter Field By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group had a good turnout of 33 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra on January 3 for their first walk of 2024. Piedmont students weren’t due back to school until January 8, so the walkers had a chance to walk the Piedmont High campus and see the construction progress on Witter Field. Some PHS history was shared. In 1916, Piedmont land developer Frank C. Havens was in financial trouble. He wanted to sell the Piedmont Park to raise funds. The Piedmont School Board wanted to purchase 13 acres of the park for a new high school, but Havens wouldn’t sell less than its entire 27 acres. The City of Piedmont wanted to save the park from development, but did not have money to purchase the remaining parkland. In November 1916, Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to purchase the land. The land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase 14 acres of the park if the City would reimburse them. The School District could buy the 13 acres it wanted and the City could have its park. Alexander purchased the land in 1921. One year later voters passed a bond issue and the City reimbursed Alexander and his partners. Construction began immediately on the high school in 1921 and Piedmont Junior High School was added in 1924. The walkers headed off for the high school. They took a path behind the Exedra along the top of the park that led them to a back entrance to the school. They walked down a breezeway to an open area in front of the Student Center and the Library. More PHS history was shared there. In 1974, the original school building was declared unsafe under state earthquake laws and was demolished, albeit with some difficulty due to the strength of the concrete. By the mid-2010s, this construction was also deemed earthquake unsafe and these buildings had to be demolished too. The school was reconstructed following voters’ passage of a “H1 Measure.” A new STEAM building and a new theater were built and opened in the fall of 2021. The school’s most famous non-graduate attendee is probably Clint Eastwood. According to research from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi, Clint excelled in P.E., but received poor grades in other classes. Classmates said he was interested in girls and cars. Clint attended PHS until January 1946, but transferred to Oakland Tech and graduated in 1949. The walkers continued past Millennium High School. It was established in 2000 at the start of the new Millennium. The group then went past the Binks Rawlings Gymnasium, and walked down “PE Hill” to Witter Field and the field house with lockers and offices for coaches. Standing on the balcony overlooking the field they could see that the new turf was in place with “Piedmont” written on it. The athletic field was originally added to the school in 1924. Witter Field was reconstructed and rededicated as the Witter Sports Complex in 1998 with a new synthetic turf field that was replaced in 2007. By 2023 this turf was worn out too. The field’s drainage also didn’t work well and the field often flooded in heavy rains. The repair price tag was $4,156,933. Thankfully, State Modernization Funds were available to pay for the project. They were like matching funds for Piedmont’s Measure H1 Bond. The group went down the stairs and walked over for a look at the baseball field. They circled back and checked out the relatively new, little-known field on Bern Court below the middle school. Piedmont Soccer Club got permission a few years ago to create this turf field for their youth practices. The walkers continued on past the PHS softball field to the lower entrance to Piedmont Park for their return to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. On hand for last Wednesday’s walk were Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Charlene Louie, Tina Shum, Stella Houston, Mary Carter, Claudine Bach, Brenda Ferrero, Kat Lang, Jim Kuo, Phil Witte, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Alan Goldhammer, Mark Davis, Mike and Nancy Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Nadine Guffanti, Noemi Alvarado, Rick Eigenbrode, Albert Chen, Peggy Shultz, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Mike Hagerty, Sharona Fischrup, Martin Levy, Helen and Quincy Dong, Rob Smith, Bob Wong, Priscilla Wanerus, Jim Kellogg, Lori Austin, and Dick Carter. articles.text: When walking through Piedmont, it is interesting and fun to recognize, and try to name the various architectural styles employed in the homes and municipal buildings in town. As we have noted previously, this is in fact a big part of the aesthetic appeal of the place – the opposite of a large tract development all of the same architectural type. There are various reasons why certain styles were (and are) chosen for a building, including response to local climate, geography, material availability, as well as simply preference or architectural fashion. To begin with, because Piedmont lies on latitude 38, the same as the Mediterranean Sea, and because many early California settlers were from that area, it is only natural that the imported culture would include architectural inspiration from the surrounding countries, primarily Spain. Like a culture’s language and art, architecture is constantly evolving, constantly changing. It must, since “new” things like automobiles, appliances and superior construction materials and methods didn’t even exist when the styles we are still emulating first came into use. Although Mission Revival, Spanish Colonial, Spanish Colonial Revival are some of the names given to sub-categories of the Mediterranean Style family, it is well to remember that even the baseline style (“Spanish”) is only a snapshot of an architecture at one point in time, itself derived from previous iterations. Confusing? It can be. Architectural scholars can spot a certain type of detail on a building and know exactly how it fits into the historical timeline, but they often disagree on a number of things, including the various labels. But, back to the Mediterranean style. Although the variations share many recognizable characteristics (see photos), they all were, and continue to be, eclectic, meaning they are derived from a range of different sources. The basic Spanish architecture from which Mediterranean style is derived has itself been influenced by Moroccan, Italian, Portuguese, and French designs. One important overriding characteristic of this architecture is the informality. This is reflected in the relaxed asymmetry of the design, in both the plans and elevations (generally the more symmetry, the more formal the style). Another clue is the extensive use of inside/outside spaces. The “outdoor rooms” we discussed a few months ago are very comPhotos and Sketches by Will Adams The most common way to identify architectural styles is from the exterior. Any good work of architecture has a strong consistency between the exterior and interior design. In the Mediterranean styles, this is often reflected in high ceilings, exposed rough- hewn beams, textured plaster walls, and of course the continuation of the employment of arched openings. The floor plans are often L shaped, to form “enclosed” exterior courtyards, patios and terraces. This finely proportioned Piedmont home is less rustic still, with “cleaner” (more finished) lines, additional detailing and ornamentation (classically inspired). However, it retains all of the characteristics of the Mediterranean Style buildings. I would also call this Spanish Revival. It is a beautiful work of architecture.

The floor plans are often L shaped, to form “enclosed” exterior courtyards, patios and terraces. The Mission Revival style is characterized by arcades, arched openings, thick walls, low slope red barrel tile roofs and is generally white in color. It is the simplest, least adorned of the Mediterranean types certainly due to the remoteness (and lack of skilled labor) of the actual California missions from which it was derived. Somehow there is a grace and timeless beauty to these architectural forms that account for their popularity still, as seen in these fine examples in Piedmont. mon, formed by building walls and arcades, resulting in small patios, and/or large courtyards. These all have a strong connection via large doors with many lites (windows) to the interior rooms. Arched openings of windows, doors, and arcades are pervasive and normally in irregular compositions of various types and shapes, further contributing to the informality of the design. Regardless of the often subtle differences of the various subgroups, this style of architecture is generally a very casual one with warm character, well suited to the climate and attitudes of California and Piedmont. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on February 24, 2021. Bids will be publicly opened via an online Zoom meeting at 2:30 p.m. on February 8th, 2024. The Zoom meeting login information can be found in the bid documents. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1770 et seq. of the California Labor Code the Director of Industrial Relations for the State of California has ascertained the current general prevailing rate of wages for employer purposes, in Alameda County, State of California. Not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for work of a similar character in Alameda County and not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for holiday work fixed as provided in the California Labor Code shall be paid to all workers engaged in performing the project. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1771.1 of the California Labor Code, A contractor or subcontractor shall not be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal, subject to the requirements of Section 4104 of the Public Contract Code, or engage in the performance of any contract for public work, as defined in Chapter 1 of Part 7 of Division 2 of the California Labor Code, unless currently registered and qualified to perform public work pursuant to Civil Code Section 1725.5. Please note: It is not a violation of Section 1771.1 for an unregistered contractor to submit a bid that is authorized by Section 7029.1 of the Business and Professions Code or by Section 10164 or 20103.5 of the Public Contract Code, provided the contractor is registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5 at the time the contract is awarded. Any bids submitted without proof that Bidder and any listed subcontractor(s) are currently registered and qualified to perform public work, pursuant to Labor Code Section 1725.5, shall not be accepted by the City. In accordance with California Civil Code Section 1771.4, the project is subject to compliance monitoring and enforcement by the Department of Industrial Relations. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid class A California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price for the base bid without consideration of the bid price for any additive or deductive items. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. meda County, California. Shelby finished the year with 63 receptions, averaging an eye-popping 17.7 yards per catch for 1,117 yards and 14 touchdowns. He also put together 403 rushing yards on 33 attempts, averaging 12.2 yards per carry for eight more touchdowns. As the team’s kicker, he also converted 30 point after attempts. Lagios was just as effective, helping lead Piedmont to several victories. He completed 62 percent of his passes and had 1,941 passing yards and 22 touchdowns with only three interceptions. Lagios also ran for 788 yards, averaging over five yards per carry, and scoring 13 touchdowns for a total of 35 scores on the season. Shelby will be on the track team in the spring as sprinter, running the 100- and 200-meter dash and as a member of the 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams. articles.text: There is no other way to say it—2023 started off with a bang, literally. A lightning strike destroyed a redwood sequoia on Crocker Avenue on January 10 with a divine crack that sent debris in a 100-foot radius of the event and “sounded like a bomb,” according to Resident Fran Wolfe. The lightning strike came after two weeks of heavy storms, flooding, and mudslides in the city which caused multiple road closures and fallen power lines. However, as if to offset the sudden destruction in the city, omens of creation loomed on the horizon for Piedmont. On January 19, Wickman Development & Construction began construction on the new Community Pool, a $23.8 million construction project that promised to enrich the city and provide local swimmers a central hub for the aquatics community. The Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization raised the last funds required for the project, receiving donations from local organizations and individuals. The specter of increased crime also reared its ugly head in Piedmont this year, a trend that began in January and held true over the year. Staff photos On April 6, Rosanna Bayon Moore began her role as the new City Administrator, succeeding Sara Lillevand. In 2023, construction work on the community pool created a new retaining wall and concrete foundations for its buildings among other stark visual changes. Recreation Commission voted to proceed with a five-month trial period of exclusively pickleball play at the Linda Beach Tennis Courts, with polarizing response from the community. Supporters of the trial emphasized the importance of adding play spaces to decrease wait times. Opponents criticized the decision’s abrupt nature and the lack of discussions held with neighbors of the court. City Council confirmed the hiring of Rosanna Bayon Moore as the new City Administrator at a meeting on February 21. She was to take over after the retirement of Sara Lillevand in April. At the same meeting, City Council voted to create a Climate Task Force to implement plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030. A 30-year-old man was pistol-whipped and shot in the wrist on February 28, one of only two shootings in Piedmont in the last decade. The victim, who was not a Piedmont resident, was transported to Highland Hospital for non-life-threatening injuries. The school year starts in August and runs through May — quite an incongruous timeline compared to the calendar year; nevertheless, the last 12 months in Piedmont schools were actionpacked. articles.text: As the Post celebrates its 26th year of publication, a smile may come to the faces of our readers as they see a list of the top newspapers in the country. 1. The Wall Street Journal is read by the people who run the country. 2. The Washington Post is read by people who think they run the country. 3 The New York Times is read by people who think they should run the country and who are very good at crossword puzzles. 4. USA Today is read by people who think they ought to run the country, but don’t really understand The New York Times. They do, however, like their statistics shown in pie charts. 5. The Los Angeles Times is read by people who wouldn’t mind running the country if they could find the time, and if they didn’t have to leave Southern California to do it. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. The Boston Globe is read by people whose parents used to run the country and did a poor job of it, thank you very much. The New York Daily News is read by people who aren’t too sure who’s running the country and don’t really care as long as they can get a seat on the subway. The New York Post is read by people who don’t care who is running the country as long as they do something really scandalous, preferably while intoxicated. The Miami Herald is read by people who are running another country but need the baseball scores. The San Francisco Chronicle is read by people who aren’t sure if there is a country, or that anyone is running it; but If so, they oppose all that they stand for. There are occasional exceptions, such as if the leaders are handicapped minority feminist atheist dwarfs who also happen to be illegal aliens from any other country, or galaxy, provided, of course, that they are not Republicans. The National Enquirer is read by people trapped in line at the grocery store. The Piedmont Post is read by people who quietly run everything but the country, and who prefer a smaller newspaper for Where In the World Are We photo ops when they travel.

articles.text: Was 2003 our first full year when we felt as if the pandemic was truly behind us? Or for those of us who lived through it, will it always be a memory, however dim? On occasion, spanning some three years, I wrote occasional essays titled The Pandemic Diaries. Those vignettes attempted to capture, like a snapshot, what we endured. For us, who lived through those endless months, trailing into years, upon reflection they can still seem surreal. I realize now I was often searching for an analog – a fragile comparison. What follows below is but one example. For millennia artists – writers, painters, sculptors, photographers, and more recently filmmakers – have been driven to capture their meditations on periods of extreme dislocation, suffering and uncertainty. We carry with us those images of the pandemic, many memorialized, of eerily empty streets; of gowned and shielded health care workers, their exhaustion written in their vacant stares; the haunting whisper of ventilators connected to the desperately ill; stretching lines of cars waiting at food banks; school halls and classrooms eerily silent, waiting; stores, both large and small, shuttered; refrigerator trucks idling near hospitals, shrouded in a fearful finality. We lived in the all of it, the arc of history bending toward the unknown. I recall seeing a now famous photograph taken by Dorothea Lange in 1936 at the height of the Great Depression, a period in our history often used as an analog to profound social disconnection, sustained uncertainty, deep personal loss, and economic ruination experienced by so many during the pandemic. The stark image by Lange was of a migrant mother and her three

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee invite the public to attend the 27th annual Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 15, from 11 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. at the Alan Harvey Theatre on the high school campus, 800 Magnolia Avenue. The theme of this year’s free event is Remain Awake. Featured speakers include Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, Piedmont Mayor Jen Cavenaugh, and keynote speaker Dr. Amber Johnson, Assistant Vice Chancellor and Chief of Staff in the Division for Equity & Inclusion at UC Berkeley. The event will include the Oakland Interfaith Youth Choir and the annual Art & Essay Showcase. Just four days before he was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, Dr. King delivered a sermon at the National Cathedral in Washington, D.C. Speaking about what he viewed as the evils of racism – poverty and militarism – Dr. King commented that “one of the great liabilities of life is that all too many people find themselves living amid a great period of social change and yet they fail to develop the new attitudes, the new mental responses that the new situation demands.” Dr. King noted that citizens of one world are inextricably connected: “We are tied together in the single garment of destiny, caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, and whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly.” He issued this challenge: “Let us stand up. Let us be a concerned generation. Let us remain awake through a great revolution.” Register to attend the event at tinyurl.com/PADCMLK. The City of Piedmont will celebrate Martin Luther King, Jr. Day on January 15 at the Alan Harvey Theater at 11 a.m.
articles.title: “Remain Awake” MLK Day celebration on Jan. 15

Our EBSCO database alone is over $10,000 per year, equal to our entire reduced budget this year,” said Librarian Kathryn Levenson. “Last year we were excited to be able to subscribe to a digital edition of the New York Times for each student and staff member, costing $1,600. Our Social Sciences Department teachers rely on this resource for their students. “Each year we search for grants to make up the disparity between expenditures and budget. articles.text: It’s the New Year – time for the annual game known as “New Year’s Resolutions.” The game goes like this. On December 31st, you make all these promises to yourself and plans. And for the first few days of January, you are, in fact, resolute – purposeful, determined, and unwavering – in those plans and promises. But by January 10 or thereabouts, real life has started up again, and with it the twists and turns of the unexpected have arrived. Can your resolutions ride those waves? Can they sustain the inevitable surprises of day-to-day existence? For most of us, the answer is NO. Research suggests that only 9% of people actually keep their New Year’s Resolutions. Which explains why the gyms across the country are packed on January 3rd and empty by January 22nd. This year, why not commit to something that is sustainable? The Creative Path is a way of walking through the world, where we allow for the discovery to be part of the journey to the destination. When you begin a creative process, you have a general sense of the outcome that you want, but the nature of a creative endeavor is that you can’t know the exact end point. So, the creative path keeps you heading in approximately the right direction, but if the path zigs when you thought it would zag, you can accept that shift as part of the journey. What does this look like in real life? Let’s use the most typical new year’s resolution, losing weight. A resolution might look like this: “I will lose 20 pounds in 2024.” Statistically, you are not likely to actually make this goal. But the creative path looks more like this, “I am exploring getting my body healthier this year through daily physical exercise that is enjoyable and fueling myself with food that makes me feel good.” With this approach, there is a much higher chance that you will follow this plan because you know what your daily work is, and you know the outcome that you are aiming towards, but it also allows for the flexibility that will be needed for long term commitment. So, as you look at your resolutions this year, maybe let go of the resolute and invite in flexibility and openness. The creative path can lead to positive outcomes and allow for the bumpy times as well. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Coach specializing in Creativity. https://gocreate. zone/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Why be resolute when you can walk the Creative Path?

Book Drive underway for PHS Library The Piedmont High School Parent Club and PHS Book Advocacy Club hosted a successful Book Drive on November 22 and announced an ongoing fundraising and Book Drive for the Ambassador Christopher Stevens Memorial Library at PHS. “It takes about $18,000- $22,000 a year for our databases, book processing supplies and 100 or so new books for our student collection. Our EBSCO database alone is over $10,000 per year, equal to our entire reduced budget this year,” said Librarian Kathryn Levenson. “Last year we were excited to be able to subscribe to a digital edition of the New York Times for each student and staff member, costing $1,600. Unfortunately, we do not have the funds to pay for our subscription this year and are seeking donations. Our Social Sciences Department teachers rely on this resource for their students. “Each year we search for grants to make up the disparity between expenditures and budget. We had about $5,000 rolled over from last year’s grants to purchase new books.” How to help close the $7,000 gap 1. Ask your organization to make a grant to the library. 2. Donate with a check made payable to PUSD with a memo “For PHS/MHS Library Books” 3. Make a monetary donation at the School Store on Infinite Campus (https://piedmontca. infinitecampus.org/campus/ portal/piedmont.jsp). 4. Request a matching donation: Ask your employer to match your donation for your charitable contribution using PUSD tax ID# 94-2503182. 5. Purchase books from the Amazon Gift Registry (https:// www.amazon.com/registries/ gl /g uest-view/38P3Y DB- 7N5I7Q): Donate a new book to the library for your student’s birthday or graduation, and it will be acknowledged with a book plate. See over 200 book titles requested by teachers and students. Search gift registries for “PHS & MHS Library” and “Books We Would Like.” 6. Donate Books at the high school office: The library seeks gently used books appropriate to high schoolers that are no older than five years old from the publication date and have dust jackets for hardcovers. A special request is for a world atlas (the current atlas is 2004). For more information contact Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us. To reserve tickets ($75- $125), see wildwooddadsclub.org/ crab-feed. Thinking Outside the Classroom Why be resolute when you can walk the Creative Path? By Nina Meehan It’s the New Year – time for the annual game known as “New Year’s Resolutions.” The game goes like this. On December 31st, you make all these promises to yourself and plans. And for the first few days of January, you are, in fact, resolute – purposeful, determined, and unwavering – in those plans and promises. But by January 10 or thereabouts, real life has started up again, and with it the twists and turns of the unexpected have arrived. Can your resolutions ride those waves? Can they sustain the inevitable surprises of day-to-day existence? For most of us, the answer is NO. Research suggests that only 9% of people actually keep their New Year’s Resolutions. Which explains why the gyms across the country are packed on January 3rd and empty by January 22nd. This year, why not commit to something that is sustainable? The Creative Path is a way of walking through the world, where we allow for the discovery to be part of the journey to the destination. When you begin a creative process, you have a general sense of the outcome that you want, but the nature of a creative endeavor is that you can’t know the exact end point. So, the creative path keeps you heading in approximately the right direction, but if the path zigs when you thought it would zag, you can accept that shift as part of the journey. What does this look like in real life? Let’s use the most typical new year’s resolution, losing weight. A resolution might look like this: “I will lose 20 pounds in 2024.” Statistically, you are not likely to actually make this goal. But the creative path looks more like this, “I am exploring getting my body healthier this year through daily physical exercise that is enjoyable and fueling myself with food that makes me feel good.” With this approach, there is a much higher chance that you will follow this plan because you know what your daily work is, and you know the outcome that you are aiming towards, but it also allows for the flexibility that will be needed for long term commitment. So, as you look at your resolutions this year, maybe let go of the resolute and invite in flexibility and openness. The creative path can lead to positive outcomes and allow for the bumpy times as well. articles.text: On December 21, the last day before winter break, Coral Yeh, a Piedmont Girl Scout in Ambassador Troop 33426, held a bake sale and t-shirt sale in Piedmont Park to fundraise for Yeh’s Girl Scout Gold Award project. The Gold Award is the highest award for Girl Scouts in grades 9-12. It demonstrates extraordinary leadership in developing sustainable solutions to local, national, and global challenges that girls are personally passionate about. For her project, Yeh partnered with ocean conservation nonprofit Blue Endeavors to create a program that collects information related to ocean conditions at the Silver Bank marine area north of the Dominican Republic, a key breeding ground for humpback whales, a key species tied to the health of these ecosystems. Her program will place a buoy to collect environmental data that will be paired with whale surveying that connects ocean conditions to whale health parameters. The data from the buoy will be available on an open-source platform to be used by scientists, educators and politicians to make necessary changes for the health of the planet. This program will be available for future students to go on expeditions to collect this data and be made available through Blue Endeavors in their efforts to educate citizens of all ages on all ocean topics in the hopes of creating ocean advocates. Future students will maintain the buoy and sustain the program. Additionally, Yeh will be creating a curriculum component that will explain the biology, ecology, threats and current state of whales. The curriculum will explain how data collection works through buoys and teach audiences the important role of Humpback Whales in the overall balance of their ecosystem. This will be done using recorded discussions with experts that will be hosted on the Blue Endeavors website. The program will be accessible to scientists and politicians but also curated for educators of high school students and available to the general public. Yeh’s project needs $10,000 to purchase the Sofar data buoy that will be placed in Silver Bank Dominican Republic. The goal is to sell 333 t-shirts, available for $30 in navy or heather gray. If you would like to support the project and buy a shirt, they are $30. Those interested in helping the project may email Coral Yeh at yehcoral@gmail.com, and she will send a link to a Google form to order the shirts. Piedmont Girl Scouts Coral Yeh (right) and Sabrina Olliphant had a fundraiser in Piedmont Park on December 21 for Yeh’s Gold Award Scout project on oceanography and humpback whale health.

articles.text: Learn a new language or improve your existing skills with a French, Spanish and Italian language class at Piedmont Adult School starting in January. French levels 1A, 1B, 2 and 3 start the week of January 8. The in-person classes are taught by Jean Monnier, who has been teaching at the Adult School since 2007. Previously Monnier taught at UC Berkeley, Head Royce and Campolindo High Schools. In addition, he has written multiple papers and books on French involvement in the California Gold Rush and other topics. Spanish Intermediate 1, 2 and 3 classes also start in person the week of January 8. Instructor Afsaneh Olinga has been with the Adult School for nine years. Previously, she taught Spanish at all levels at Skyline High School for 19 years. She also taught at Oakland Adult and Career Education for four years. Spanish Beginning 1 and 2 classes will start the week of February 26 and will be taught by Helmi Waits. She has been teaching at the Adult School since 2012. Class schedules and rates are available at piedmontadultschool. org. Register for these and other classes at this website, or by calling 594-2655.

articles.text: Attention middle schoolers! The holidays will soon be over and you’re probably in debt for a couple presents. Your only choices are hoping your parents forgot about it or not earning an allowance any more. But wait! There is one more option - delivering the Piedmont Post. Delivering the Post is a great opportunity for you to do a few things, especially if you’re looking for a way to learn independence and reliability…and earn some money. I am a paper delivery girl and have to admit it’s not about wearing a newsboy style cap while triumphantly flinging papers that miraculously land on the middle of the door mat. Here is an easy-to-follow tip: For starters, never fling your papers, no matter how good your aim is. What will you gain? You will develop life skills and learn personal management with your earnings. I think the best part is talking to all the people you meet along the way. One interaction that sticks in my head happened when I was delivering papers to a house with a lot of steps. A man came up to me and said, “I know they are on vacation so let me take it for you.” He told me that when he was young he had a paper route. He then went on to describe how he did it. Apparently, he and a few friends used to stand on the back of a truck and tossed the papers to the houses. I told him that it sounded like fun. “Oh it was, especially the Sunday papers,” he replied. It’s connections like that that make me smile. Other things that make me smile are times like once when I was delivering a paper as soon as I turned around, the door opened and the owner said, “Thank you!” It’s the happiness of what they see in the paper and us - the people delivering them. That’s why we do it. To apply for a paper route, send an email with your name, grade in school, and your contact information to: news@piedmont-post.com.
articles.title: Calling all middle schoolers

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church dazzles community with frozen fun Photos by Michael Barber Rev. Scott Kail gives Evan Jahn a push on the tallest of two sledding hills fashioned from bales of hay and nearly 20 tons of snow. Madison Clopton enjoys a ride down the sledding hill. The usually dry parking lot of Piedmont Community Church was transformed on Friday afternoon, December 22 into a winter wonderland for the church’s firstever Snow Day. Using 20 tons of imported snow, the church created two sledding hills on the driveway from Craig Avenue to the back of the church and provided sleds for kids and adults. The free event was hosted by NextGen, PCC’s youth ministry. With an estimated 1,500 community members attending, it was an over-the-top success. “It wasn’t just kids playing,” said Kerry Persichitte, the church’s NextGen Director. “We had a lot of adults playing with their kids. We even saw Dottie Hutch, our liaison to our Senior community, going down the hill on a sled. And she’s 82!” “I think snow just really dives into our memories we may have as a child and creates this magical place where we can be a kid, no matter our age,” continued Persichitte. “We can put aside all of the other things in life and just have a little fun in nature.” Although the snow was the main attraction, two bounce houses were also on site, one gingerbread-themed and one snowman-themed. There was also free hot cocoa for children, a face painter, a balloon artist, opportunities to sing Christmas carols, a snow playground safe for toddlers for making snow angels, and building a snowman. , plus a Red Sauce Meatball food truck in the courtyard. Even Santa and his elves showed up to greet children and parents as they played in the snow. “I would say this is just the beginning,” said Persichitte. “Keep your eyes open for more similar events.” Children take advantage of the rare opportunity to make snowballs in Piedmont. Three-year-old Liam Li is thrilled by his time on the sledding hill. Two sledding hills were made in back of Piedmont Community Church Middle School students Lucy and Lauren double up on the snow tube. Santa paid a visit to the Snow Day event. The church courtyard was turned into a playground with a snow area and inflatable games and bounce houses. articles.title: Snow Day a huge success

pages.text: 10 Thursday, January 4, 2024 Photos by Michael Barber Rev. Scott Kail gives Evan Jahn a push on the tallest of two sledding hills fashioned from bales of hay and nearly 20 tons of snow. Madison Clopton enjoys a ride down the sledding hill. Snow Day a huge success Piedmont Community Church dazzles community with frozen fun By Matt Simons The usually dry parking lot of Piedmont Community Church was transformed on Friday afternoon, December 22 into a winter wonderland for the church’s firstever Snow Day. Using 20 tons of imported snow, the church created two sledding hills on the driveway from Craig Avenue to the back of the church and provided sleds for kids and adults. The free event was hosted by NextGen, PCC’s youth ministry. With an estimated 1,500 community members attending, it was an over-the-top success. “It wasn’t just kids playing,” said Kerry Persichitte, the church’s NextGen Director. “We had a lot of adults playing with their kids. We even saw Dottie Hutch, our liaison to our Senior community, going down the hill on a sled. And she’s 82!” “I think snow just really dives into our memories we may have as a child and creates this magical place where we can be a kid, no matter our age,” continued Persichitte. “We can put aside all of the other things in life and just have a little fun in nature.” Although the snow was the main attraction, two bounce houses were also on site, one gingerbread-themed and one snowman-themed. There was also free hot cocoa for children, a face painter, a balloon artist, opportunities to sing Christmas carols, a snow playground safe for toddlers for making snow angels, and building a snowman. , plus a Red Sauce Meatball food truck in the courtyard. Even Santa and his elves showed up to greet children and parents as they played in the snow. “I would say this is just the beginning,” said Persichitte. “Keep your eyes open for more similar events.” Children take advantage of the rare opportunity to make snowballs in Piedmont. Three-year-old Liam Li is thrilled by his time on the sledding hill. Two sledding hills were made in back of Piedmont Community Church Middle School students Lucy and Lauren double up on the snow tube. Santa paid a visit to the Snow Day event. The church courtyard was turned into a playground with a snow area and inflatable games and bounce houses. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Our annual sports recap of the year includes highlights of great accomplishments and accolades which student-athletes can reminisce upon with awe. Here are our top moments from 2023: History made on February 25 2023 began in historic fashion for Piedmont High on a day like no other: Saturday, February 25. The Highlanders won three North Coast Section banners that day as boys’ soccer, girls’ soccer, and girls’ basketball all claimed section titles. All four winter sports varsity teams reached the NCS semifinals last winter as well, including boys’ basketball, a feat that has been rarely accomplished by small enrollment public schools. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team, the No. 8 seed, started the school’s legendary day with a 1-0 victory over No. 2 University, earning their second consecutive Div. 4 championships. They allowed no goals in postseason, winning 2-0 over No. 9 St. Helena in the first round, shocking No. 1 Cardinal Newman 1-0 in the quarterfinals, beating No. 5 Healdsburg 1-0 in the semifinals, and then upending the University Red Devils at the Beach Chalet soccer fields in Golden Gate Park. William Daniel scored the game-winning goal in the 70th minute. The girls’ soccer team, seeded No. 3, then won the NCS banner with a 2-1 win in overtime against No. 1 University on an adjacent field at Beach Chalet. It marked the team’s first section title in 20 years and coach Dan Chubbock’s first championship in his third appearance in the NCS finals. The Highlanders defeated No. 14 Sacred Heart in the opening round, bashed No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals, upset No. 2 Urban 3-0 in the semifinals, and then got the job done versus the Red Devils. Hailey Marshburn scored the game-winner against University in the 86th minute, and the players and fans celebrated the double victory on the field with the boys’ team. “It was literally back-to-backto-back. The boys’ won and we heard the girls’ basketball game’s score and I had to tell the girls to focus on our game,” said coach Chubbock. “Our game was right next to the boys’ game and you could see parents turning backand-forth to watch both games. I was texting with [girls’ basketball coach] Bryan Gardere throughout the week just wishing each other luck.” “It’s crazy. I don’t think that’s happened in my time here. Three teams winning it all? I don’t think so,” said girls’ basketball coach of over 20 years, Bryan Gardere. There were no surprises for the top-ranked girls’ basketball team winning North Coast Section as a Division 4 team. They won big, 75-49, over No. 2 Branson at Pinole Valley HS that Saturday night, claiming the school’s first section banner since 2006. The 26-point finals win over the Bulls was the closest game for the Highlanders’ during the postseason. They defeated No. 9 Lick-Wilmerding 81-29 in the quarterfinals and No. 5 McKinleyville 67-29 in the semifinals. PHS earned the highest ranking in California going into the CIF State Tournament, receiving the No. 1 seed in the Open Division. Moments after the girls’ soccer team won the D4 NCS title, the boys’ soccer team met them on the field to celebrate with its own NCS plaque in-hand on February 25. Photo by Scott Stratman The boys’ soccer team following their 1-0 win over No. 2 University to capture their second consecutive D4 NCS title. Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont stands with the NCS banner and championship medals after winning its first section title in 20 years. The girls’ basketball team stands proudly after winning the Division 4 NCS title on February 25. Boys Soccer Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team’s run to its second-consecutive D4 NCS banner came with more difficult odds than in 2022. Entering as the No. 8 seed, Piedmont beat No. 9 St. Helena 2-0 in the opening round before upending No. 1 Cardinal Newman 1-0 in the quarterfinals. They also upset No. 5 Healdsburg 1-0 before defeating No. 2 University with a goal by William Daniel in the 70th minute. As the No. 8 seed, Piedmont became the lowest-seeded school to win an NCS title since De Anza in 2016. PHS was the lowest ranked D4 school to win the title since the divisions’ inception in 2018. The Highlanders went on to reach the Div. 4 CIF NorCal Semifinals as the No. 4 seed, where their Cinderella season came to a close on March 2 with a 4-0 loss to No. 1 ranked Marin Academy. Earlier Piedmont defeated No. 5 Kimball 2-0 on February 28. Enzo Bernales led the boys’ team and was named Sophomore of the Year by the Post. Girls Soccer lifts first banner in 20 years The girls’ soccer team finished with a 13-1-6 (W-T-L) record and won its first D4 banner in two decades. As the No. 3 seed, Piedmont upset No. 1 University 2-1 for the title on February 25 with a Golden Goal in the 86th minute of overtime by Hailey Marshburn to win the school’s first NCS banner since 2003. To get there, PHS shut out No. 2 Urban of San Francisco 3-0l on February 22 in the semifinals and bashed No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals on February 18. They opened the postseason with a 2-0 win over No. 15 Sacred Heart on February 15. Advancing to the Division 3 CIF NorCal Regional Tournament, No. 8 ranked Piedmont nearly upset No. 1 Sequoia in the first round on February 28, but lost 2-1 in sudden-death overtime. Soccer stars Audrey Lam and Emily Fitzgerald were named Honorable Mention by the Post as Athlete of the Year. Lam’s impact as a maestro in the midfield was easy to see—

pages.text: Thursday, January 4, 2024 13 Sports YIR Continued from page 12 Girls Basketball a double winner Piedmont’s historic girls’ basketball season saw the team finish with a 27-1 overall record and won its first WACC title in the league’s 11-year history. They won the D4 NCS title with ease over No. 2 Branson 75-49 on February 25, defeating No. 5 McKinleyville 67-29 in the semifinals and 81-29 over No. 9 Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals after receiving a first-round bye. They received the No. 1 seed in the CIF Open Division tournament for the first time since the Paris sisters led Piedmont to the school’s first two state championships. The season ended with a 48-45 loss to No. 5 Salesian on March 4. They received six All-League selections: Levingston and Martinez earned first-team honors, Perseas Gioukaris and Maddie Hill earned second-team selections, while Adrienne Blackwell and Shakila Zuberi earned honorable mentions. Of the group, Zamora and Hill graduate as four-year starters, while Levingston and Gioukaris were instrumental additions as seniors after sitting out their junior year. Hill will continue playing at Rocky Mountain University, and Staff Photo Piedmont’s Perseas Gioukaris (left), Eva Levingston, and Natalia Martinez celebrate the final moments of their D4 championship win. Staff Photo A.J. Harris became the school’s All-Time leading scorer in 2023, finishing his high school career with 1,570 points. Gioukaris will play at San Francisco State. Zamora will be at San Diego State and Levingston at Cal State Fullerton. Team leader Natalia Martinez was named Athlete of the Year by the Post. She is a senior at Piedmont this year. Trinity Zamora closed her high school career in an exclusive club with over 2,000 points and 1,400 total rebounds. She is one of the most accomplished four-year starters in PHS history. She now plays at San Diego State. A.J. Harris all-time leading scorer A.J. Harris finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s all-time leading scorer with 1,570 points. He accomplished this in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID. Harris was named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year alongside Berkeley’s Samir O’Brien. The Highlanders went 19-10 with Harris carrying the load as the team’s leading scorer and rebounder. They made it to the Division 3 NCS Semifinals as the No. 4 seed before losing to No. 1 Branson, 61-40 on February 21. Earlier PHS beat No. 5 Analy 59-38 in the quarterfinals on February 17 and beat No. 13 Rancho Cotate 65-43 in the opening round on February 14. Harris scored 28 points in the semifinals against the Bulls and 37 on Analy to eclipse the all-time mark. He scored over 30 points six times last season, including a high of 37 against Division 3 State Champions, Oakland High. He now plays at Emory University. Parker Long among best halfmilers Parker Long concluded his track career at Piedmont and was among the best to ever run the 800 meters. He graduates with the third fastest time in school history at 1:53.25, set at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. His time placed him narrowly behind some of PHS track royalty, including The Posts’ 2018 Athlete of the Year, Reece Proctor, and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson, while finishing .15 ahead of teammate from last year, Cooper Downing. PHS’ all-time top-five times in the 800 is as follows: 1. Gordon Johnson 1:51.10 (1989) 2. Reece Proctor 1:52.64 (2018) 3 Parker Long 1:53.25 (2023) 4 Cooper Downing 1:53.40 (2022) Staff Photo Parker Long achieved the third-fastest 800-meter run time in school history, coming just two seconds shy of Gordon Johnson’s 34-year-old record in 1989. 5 John Weber 1:55.26 (2010) Long won the NCS Meet of Champions’ 800 meter run with a time of 1:53.80 in a field of 12 finalists on May 20. He was also a member of Piedmont’s 4x400 relay team that qualified for the CIF State Championship, where they clocked a time of 3:23.84 in the preliminary round. He helped the team hit a season-best of 3:22.93 at the NCS Meet of Champions, the third fastest time in school history. It placed them narrowly behind last year’s record-setting time of 3:21.77, set by Parker Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Long as the second leg. Piedmont High’s second-fastest time in the 4x400 was set in 1989 by a group led by Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer Gordon Johnson. Baseball team upsets the favorites The baseball team finished with a 14-11 record last spring after bumping up to the WACC’s Foothill Division. It made most of its noise in the NCS Playoffs. As the No. 8 seed, it advanced to the semifinals on May 24 when they lost 11-10 to No. 5 Justin-Siena in Napa. They opened with a 12-inning 4-3 win over No. 9 Branson that lasted two days, May 17-18, at home. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos hit the game-winner on a single to score Peter Krumins. In the quarterfinals, Piedmont upset No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 on the road on May 20. They trailed 1-0 before going ahead 2-1 in the top-of-the-fifth, then adding three more runs in the top of the seventh inning. In the semifinals at Justin-Siena, Piedmont fell just short after trailing 11-7 entering the top of the seventh inning. PHS scored three times in the final inning, including twice with two outs. But at 11-10 with the bases loaded, a ground out ended their Cinderella story. They earned four All-League selections, including Markos Lagios with first-team honors, Michael Aikawa was second-team, while Krumins and Ryan McConathy were honorable mentions. Girls Swimming relay team Piedmont’s girls’ swimming relay team was among the most successful squad’s in the school. Their 200 medley relay and 400 freestyle relay teams finished its regular season undefeated and won the WACC title in both events on Friday, April 28. Their 200 medley team featured junior Josie Oesterer on the backstroke, freshman Abigail Jacoby on the breaststroke, junior Taylor Rolefson on butterfly and sophomore Sonja ten Grotenhuis as the final leg for the freestyle, winning the league title with a of 1:54.74. The 400 free relay team had freshman Sydney Olson replace Jacoby while ten Grotenhuis raced the second leg, winning a second league title in 3:44.42. All five swimmers earned AllLeague honors. Boys Lacrosse wins 6th consecutive league title The boys’ lacrosse team went 14-4 and won its sixth consecutive WACC Championship with a 14-6 win over Bishop O’Dowd on April 27. They went on to reach See Sports YIR on page 14 Staff Photo Piedmont’s baseball team nearly reached the D4 NCS Finals as the No. 8 seed, upsetting multiple teams on their way to the semifinals. Piedmont’s 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay team finished its season undefeated on their way to WACC titles in both events. Pictured are coach Colby Price (left), Abigail Jacoby, Josie Oesterer, Taylor Rolefson, Sonja ten Grotenhuis and Sydney Olson.

articles.text: Owen Blanford (left), Cole Carnazzo, Jonathan Dong, Asher Takazawa, Nathan Judy, Coach Stefan Bill, and Josie Oesterer Swim teams from throughout Nevada and California competed in the 2023 CA/NV Winter Speedo Sectionals on December 14-17 in Huntington Beach. “To compete at this meet swimmers must achieve qualifying times and these swimmers are on their way to being recruited to swim in college once they are in their junior and senior years in high school,” explained Piedmont Swim Team head coach Stefan Bill. Reaching this level of swimming is extremely difficult. “It takes years of dedication, focus, and hard work. Most athletes competing at Sectionals barely take any days off from swimming, swimming 1-2 times per day, and make swimming – next to academics – their number one priority in life,” he added. Bill noted that this is the youngest group from Piedmont to qualify. Meet highlights The 4x100 freestyle relay with Nathan Judy, Owen Blanford, Asher Takazawa, and Jonathan Dong was fun to watch,” said Bill. “The swimmers did well and swam above and beyond their expectations.” Owen Blandford, a junior at Piedmont High, had a superb meet. He dropped a lot of time in all of his events and improved his ranking by 50 places coming into the meet. His best event was the 200 free, where he dropped over three seconds from a time achieved one week prior. Cole Carnazzo, a freshman, had an amazing meet as well. His best event was the 200 breaststroke where he dropped over two seconds from his personal best time. He swam great in all of his races, but shined during the breaststroke events, improving his ranking by 40 places. Asher Takazawa, a freshman came into the meet injured. However, he still managed to come close to his personal best time in the 100 back and lowered his time in the 50 and 100 free. Josie Oesterer, a Piedmont High senior, had great backstroke races (100 and 200). She started the season with a heavy academic and college application work load, however, impressed everyone with her attendance. She came close to her best times at the meet. As a team captain she inspired and motivated the younger swimmers and shined in pumping up the swimmers in the 4x100 freestyle relay. “The boys can thank her for their outstanding performance during that relay,” said coach Bill. articles.text: Mackie McDonald upsets Rafael Nadal Piedmont native Mackie McDonald opened the year by making his sixth appearance in the main draw of the Aussie Open, making his way to the second round after defeating 21-year-old American Brandon Nakashima on January 15 and pulled off a stunning upset of one of the world’s greats, Rafael Nadal. Mackie went stride-for-stride with Nadal before the Spaniard suffered an injury, impressively hitting frequent long rallies against the tournament’s No. 1 seed. McDonald won the first set 6-4 after taking set-point when forcing deuce and gaining advantage, leading 4-1 at one point in the set. You could see what it meant to him, beaming a smile during a successful first set victory against one of the best players of all time. McDonald stole the first game of the second set as the returner with three break-point opportunities and then went up 2-0 as the server. He nearly took the third game of the second set as the returner by forcing deuce and briefly having advantage, but Nadal powered through. Nadal tied 2-2 as the returner and then went ahead 3-2. articles.text: Aurora Theater in Berkeley is presenting Mary Kathryn Nagle’s Manhatta, a gripping journey from the fur trade of the 1600s to the stock trade of today. Performances are scheduled from Tuesday, March 5 through March 10, with a live-streamed performance online. Directed by Shannon R. Davis, Manhatta tells the story of a young Lenape woman, Jane Snake, who returns to her ancestral homeland, “Manahatta,” with a Stanford MBA to work as a securities trader on Wall Street — the once-walled street built by enslaved Africans to keep the indigenous Lenape out. Set mainly against the backdrop of the Occupy Wall Street movement across centuries, Manahatta draws parallels between the forced removal, taxation, and the fiscal impact on Native Americans during the 2008 financial crisis and the 1626 Dutch purchase of the island of “Manahatta,” or Manhattan. Playwright Nagle, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, teases the duality in Jane as she seeks to uncover her complicity in infrastructure designed to destroy her people. Throughout the play, deemed “fascinating and provocative” by the New Haven Review, Jane’s career is thriving on “the island of many hills” (Manahatta in Lenape). Back home in Oklahoma her mother and sister are grieving the loss of family, and struggling to maintain their culture, language, and their finances to stay in their over-mortgaged home. Come join the Aurora Theatre for a discussion of its production after the show on any of four dates: Friday, February 16; Tuesday, February 20; Wednesday, February 27; and Thursday, March 7. Everyone is welcome to join Aurora Theater for Native Community Night during the Friday, February 23 production for a preshow reception at 6 p.m. and a post-show discussion following the 8 p.m. show. Showtime information and tickets ($35–$40) are available at the Box Office at 843-4822 or online at tickets.auroratheatre. org. Aurora Theater is located at 2081 Addison Street in Berkeley. Mary Kathryn Nagle’s Manhatta premieres at Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre, opening on Friday, February 9, with performances through March 10.
articles.title: Manhatta premieres at Aurora Theater Feb. 9

Performances on January 13, 14, 18, and 19 will be pay-what-you-can preview shows followed by an opening night on January 20. The show is written by Deneen Reynolds-Knott and directed by Leigh Rondon-Davis. Described by the playwright as an unabashed love story, Babes in Ho-lland is an exploration of identity, sexuality, and college life in the 1990s. In the sunless Pittsburgh winter of 1996, two co-eds connect over a shared love for R&B girl groups but quickly discover something deeper. articles.text: Catch the world premiere of Kate Attwell’s play Big Data, directed by Tony Award winner Pam MacKinnon, at San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater from Thursday, February 15 through March 10. Do our devices – tantalizingly incarnate in this funny, uncanny world premiere – really know us best? Are our digital footprints predictive of our future choices, or are they choosing for us? In the play the protagonist Sam loves Timmy, and Lucy loves Max, but the pressures of modern life leave them anxious, lonely, and susceptible to the siren song of tech. When Sam and Lucy’s parents make a shocking announcement, the family is forced to confront what’s distracted them from each other – and the legacy they’ll leave behind. ACT Artistic Director MacKinnon and playwright Attwell reunite to realize this revolutionary piece, inspired by Attwell’s experience touring Mozilla’s “Glass Room” pop-up interactive exhibit in San Francisco. Come explore questions of attention, connection, nourishment, and the dizzying possibilities of AI. “Kate Attwell has written a play so topical about how AI is rapidly and maybe forever changing how we interact and think about what we want,” said MacKinnon. “I love Kate’s voice as a playwright, her surprising humor and mischief, and all she throws into and at her characters. I feel grateful that this is our second world premiere production together at A.C.T. and hold fond memories of [our previous collaboration] Testmatch in 2019. I am also grateful that while the Bay and the world wrestle with the fundamental ethics of where we are headed, that this play is in the wrestle too.” Come to the theater on Friday, February 16 at 6:30 p.m. for a party before the show with a DJ and drinks, On Tuesday, February 27 at 7 p.m.; Sunday, March 3 at 2 p.m.; and Wednesday, March 6 at 2 p.m., stick around after the show for a lively question-and-answer session with the actors and artists behind the work. Information about showtimes, more related events and tickets ($25–$130) for the play at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theater (415 Geary St., San Francisco) are available at the ACT Theater Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf. org/bigdata. Catch the world premiere of Kate Attwell’s Big Data opening at ACT Thursday, February 15, and running through March 10.

pages.text: 16 Thursday, January 4, 2024 Arts & Entertainment Manhatta premieres at Aurora Theater Feb. 9 By Selen Ozturk Aurora Theater in Berkeley is presenting Mary Kathryn Nagle’s Manhatta, a gripping journey from the fur trade of the 1600s to the stock trade of today. Performances are scheduled from Tuesday, March 5 through March 10, with a live-streamed performance online. Directed by Shannon R. Davis, Manhatta tells the story of a young Lenape woman, Jane Snake, who returns to her ancestral homeland, “Manahatta,” with a Stanford MBA to work as a securities trader on Wall Street — the once-walled street built by enslaved Africans to keep the indigenous Lenape out. Set mainly against the backdrop of the Occupy Wall Street movement across centuries, Manahatta draws parallels between the forced removal, taxation, and the fiscal impact on Native Americans during the 2008 financial crisis and the 1626 Dutch purchase of the island of “Manahatta,” or Manhattan. Playwright Nagle, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, teases the duality in Jane as she seeks to uncover her complicity in infrastructure designed to destroy her people. Throughout the play, deemed “fascinating and provocative” by the New Haven Review, Jane’s career is thriving on “the island of many hills” (Manahatta in Lenape). Back home in Oklahoma her mother and sister are grieving the loss of family, and struggling to maintain their culture, language, and their finances to stay in their over-mortgaged home. Come join the Aurora Theatre for a discussion of its production after the show on any of four dates: Friday, February 16; Tuesday, February 20; Wednesday, February 27; and Thursday, March 7. Everyone is welcome to join Aurora Theater for Native Community Night during the Friday, February 23 production for a preshow reception at 6 p.m. and a post-show discussion following the 8 p.m. show. Showtime information and tickets ($35–$40) are available at the Box Office at 843-4822 or online at tickets.auroratheatre. org. Aurora Theater is located at 2081 Addison Street in Berkeley. Babes in Ho-lland opens at Shotgun Players Jan. 13 financial hardship, and future uncertainty threaten to destroy it. “Babes is a joyful story about first love,” said Rondon-Davis. “I saw so much of myself in this piece as a young, queer, Black femme who went to a predominantly white college where I learned blackness is not monolithic,” she said. Babes in Ho-lland, will be presented on the Ashby Stage January 13 through February 4. Shotgun Players will also livestream performances on January 25 and February 1. Tickets are available online at www.shotgunplayers.org, and may be purchased at the door on the night of the performance an hour before showtime subject to availability. By Matt Simons Shotgun Players will be performing the world premiere of Babes in Ho-lland beginning January 13. Performances on January 13, 14, 18, and 19 will be pay-what-you-can preview shows followed by an opening night on January 20. The show is written by Deneen Reynolds-Knott and directed by Leigh Rondon-Davis. Described by the playwright as an unabashed love story, Babes in Ho-lland is an exploration of identity, sexuality, and college life in the 1990s. In the sunless Pittsburgh winter of 1996, two co-eds connect over a shared love for R&B girl groups but quickly discover something deeper. While attending a predominantly white college, the two Black students create their own bubble of self-discovery, music, and sanctuary while the tensions of love, Photo by Shotgun Players Babes in Ho-lland premieres at the Ashby Stage next weekend on Saturday, Jan 13. World premiere of Big Data at ACT February 15 By Selen Ozturk Catch the world premiere of Kate Attwell’s play Big Data, directed by Tony Award winner Pam MacKinnon, at San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater from Thursday, February 15 through March 10. Do our devices – tantalizingly incarnate in this funny, uncanny world premiere – really know us best? Are our digital footprints predictive of our future choices, or are they choosing for us? In the play the protagonist Sam loves Timmy, and Lucy loves Max, but the pressures of modern life leave them anxious, lonely, and susceptible to the siren song of tech. When Sam and Lucy’s parents make a shocking announcement, the family is forced to confront what’s distracted them from each other – and the legacy they’ll leave behind. ACT Artistic Director MacKinnon and playwright Attwell reunite to realize this revolutionary piece, inspired by Attwell’s experience touring Mozilla’s “Glass Room” pop-up interactive exhibit in San Francisco. Come explore questions of attention, connection, nourishment, and the dizzying possibilities of AI. “Kate Attwell has written a play so topical about how AI is rapidly and maybe forever changing how we interact and think about what we want,” said MacKinnon. “I love Kate’s voice as a playwright, her surprising humor and mischief, and all she throws into and at her characters. I feel grateful that this is our second world premiere production together at A.C.T. and hold fond memories of [our previous collaboration] Testmatch in 2019. I am also grateful that while the Bay and the world wrestle with the fundamental ethics of where we are headed, that this play is in the wrestle too.” Come to the theater on Friday, February 16 at 6:30 p.m. for a party before the show with a DJ and drinks, On Tuesday, February 27 at 7 p.m.; Sunday, March 3 at 2 p.m.; and Wednesday, March 6 at 2 p.m., stick around after the show for a lively question-and-answer session with the actors and artists behind the work. Information about showtimes, more related events and tickets ($25–$130) for the play at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theater (415 Geary St., San Francisco) are available at the ACT Theater Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf. org/bigdata. Catch the world premiere of Kate Attwell’s Big Data opening at ACT Thursday, February 15, and running through March 10. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco is offering free admission on Monday, January 15 in honor of Martin Luther King Jr. Day. Members of the public are invited to join the museum for a day of programs centered on film, art, performance, and dance where special guests will help community members reflect on the importance of protest, creativity, and diverse communities. The museum’s program schedule will be packed with activities designed to engage community members with explorations of culture and race on what the MOAD has called its “most exciting” and “busiest” day of the year. A family art activity and gallery scavenger hunt will be held which aims to connect audiences to the museum’s current exhibitions – JoeSam: Text Messages, Spectrum: On Color and Contemporary Art, Lishan AZ: Eugene’s Cove, and the museum’s digital exhibition, The Only Door I Can Open: Women Exposing Prison Through Art and Poetry. A screening will be held for Roger Ross Williams’ groundbreaking documentary film STAMPED FROM THE BEGINNING (2023, 91 minutes) based on the book by Ibram X. Kendi, followed by a discussion about Civil Rights, the law, and reparations. Destiny Arts Junior Company will present a hip-hop dance performance and bring audiences onstage to learn their choreography with them. Additionally, Prescott Circus performers from Prescott Elementary in West Oakland will hold an interactive stilt-walking show. The Museum of African Diaspora is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. For more information contact (415) 318-7152. A photo collage by Ruby Marquez advertises the MoAD’s annual MLK Jr. Day celebration.
articles.title: Free admission at MoAD on MLK Jr. Day

articles.text: The first major West Coast exhibition of South African visual artist Zanele Muholi will be on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art from January 18 through August 11, 2024. The exhibition, titled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, brings together over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present, alongside paintings, sculpture and video, providing an opportunity for audiences to experience Muholi’s expansive artistic project to celebrate and make visible black and LGBT self-expression in post-Apartheid South Africa. A self-described visual activist using photography as a tool for resistance and social change, Muholi’s work includes issues of representation, race and the dangers of being true to one’s gender identity and culture in South Africa. Muholi’s work calls attention to the violence enacted on LGBT people while also celebrating their bravery, beauty and resilience. With a sense of profound tenderness, Muholi’s portraiture is distinguished by an intimacy that could only be established through trust. The artist sees subjects as collaborators who partake in the process of creating the images, from the selection of the location to the clothing. SFMOMA, located at 151 3rd Street in San Francisco, is open from 10 a.m. through 5 p.m. Zanele Muholi, Faniswa, Seapoint, Cape Town, 2016. Muholi’s first major West Coast exhibition will be on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art from January 18 through August 11, 2024.
