Tickets ($30 for adults, $25 ages 65+, $23 ages 19-24, free 18 and younger, free for members) are available online at sfmoma.org, or in-person at the museum counter. articles.text: In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, piano, Michael Jones, bass, and Anthony Pegram, drums – will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, January 7 at 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition is a jazz and pop piano trio dedicated to preserving the history of jazz and pop music and the traditions of the classic jazz piano trio. The jazz piano trio format of piano, bass, and drums evolved during the jazz era of the 1940s and 1950s. It flourished in Oakland and the East Bay during the 1950s with abundant local jazz piano trios. Legendary jazz pianist Dave Brubeck, an East Bay native, rose to fame at the Burma Lounge nightclub on Lakeshore Avenue in Oakland, where his Dave Brubeck Trio first performed from 1948 to 1950. Not too many decades ago, almost all the hotels and most fine restaurants and clubs in the East Bay had a pianist playing the great pop tunes of the day and the classics (standards) from the Great American songbook. In the Tradition is the last classic jazz piano trio and classic pop piano trio still active in the East Bay. Come and enjoy a relaxing couple of hours with live music in this intimate club-like environment. Snacks and complimentary wine are included. Tickets $25 at the door, or $23 in advance at the link below. Seating is limited to the first 50 patrons. The Club will feature a Sunday afternoon event each month on a specific theme, starting this Sunday with a tribute to the music of The Beatles. Music begins at 4:30 p.m.
articles.title: PCA Jazz Club concert on Sunday a tribute to music of the Beatles

articles.text: Showtime information and tickets ($29-$495) for the performance at War Memorial Opera House (301 Van Ness Avenue) are available at the SF Ballet Box Artistic Director Tamara Rojo launches the 2024 season of SF Ballet with an immersive performance of Mere Mortals from Friday, January 26 through February 1. Music and dance converge in a singular environment of mesmerizing light and video. The new ballet with music by composer Floating Points and choreography from Aszure Barton, contextualizes the ancient parable of Pandora’s Box for the current technological world. In the ancient Greek myth of Pandora’s Jar, Pandora is the first woman on earth created by the gods to serve humanity. She’s given a jar as a gift and instructed not to open it under any circumstances. When curiosity gets the better of her, she opens the jar, releasing all the evils and miseries into the world. Only hope remains trapped inside. While the ballet’s narrative dates to the first centuries of humanity, there are parallels found in contemporary society today, including unintended consequences of technology, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), and ethical dilemmas in science and technology. The work’s dramaturgist Carmen Kovacs said, “We started with the original myth, but since it has been changed and interpreted in so many ways, we thought we would do our own story and combine it with this idea of AI and how humankind has brought it upon themselves.” Ballerina Jennifer Stahl and San Francisco Ballet members rehearsing Aszure Barton’s and Sam Shepherd’s Mere Mortals, which will have its world premiere on Friday, January 26.
articles.title: Mere Mortals world premiere at SF Ballet opens Jan. 26

articles.text: There is a stillness in the air and the streets are almost devoid of traffic. The cold winter sun casts long shadows. The Christmas rush is over as the old year raced towards its inevitable close. Observations like this cause us to reflect on the year past. Generally speaking, our thoughts depend on our outlook on life. A certain overindulgence causes most of us to make New Year’s resolutions. While some of the world has gone into artistic hibernation, others have found ways to be productive. A talented musical friend of mine has written five books on violin technique. He claims that these books are his musical autobiography. There is no doubt that he has lived a full life and the books are proof of that. For some musical organizations, Spring has come early. Both San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera have a new Music Director. Oakland Symphony continues its search for a luminary to illuminate the podium. On the home front, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is planning some exciting concerts. The Piedmont Center for the Arts continues on its successful course despite some roadblocks instigated by politicians and petty bureaucrats. On a personal note, my wife and I enjoyed a New Year’s Eve feast last year at one of our favorite restaurants, Italian Colors. The festive spirit was everywhere despite the storm… um, I mean… The atmospheric river. We enjoyed superb prawns stuffed with Dungeness crab on the first official day of San Francisco’s crab season one year ago. A unique pizza topped with fragrant black truffles was not exactly Neapolitan, but it was memorable nevertheless. Adding to the evening’s enjoyment was a visit to the table by the restaurant owner Alan Carlson and his son Dylan who stopped by to give us extra slices of both black and white truffles. A lively couple at the neighboring table brought over some of their prize-winning wine and aged brandy. As the Germans say. “Das leben ist Lebenswert (literally, “life is beautiful”). As the “atmospheric river” continues on its way to the sea at the start of 2024, whether you ask the question in singular “quo vadis”, or make it more general in the plural, “quo vadimus” (where are we going?), we ask, has anything changed? Have a great year.
articles.title: Winter thoughts

pages.text: Thursday, January 4, 2024 19 Mere Mortals world premiere at SF Ballet opens Jan. 26 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Showtime information and tickets ($29-$495) for the performance at War Memorial Opera House (301 Van Ness Avenue) are available at the SF Ballet Box Office online at sfballet.org, by phone at 415-865-2000, or by email at tickets@sfballet.org. The Musical Gourmet By Selen Ozturk Artistic Director Tamara Rojo launches the 2024 season of SF Ballet with an immersive performance of Mere Mortals from Friday, January 26 through February 1. Music and dance converge in a singular environment of mesmerizing light and video. The new ballet with music by composer Floating Points and choreography from Aszure Barton, contextualizes the ancient parable of Pandora’s Box for the current technological world. In the ancient Greek myth of Pandora’s Jar, Pandora is the first woman on earth created by the gods to serve humanity. She’s given a jar as a gift and instructed not to open it under any circumstances. When curiosity gets the better of her, she opens the jar, releasing all the evils and miseries into the world. Only hope remains trapped inside. While the ballet’s narrative dates to the first centuries of humanity, there are parallels found in contemporary society today, including unintended consequences of technology, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), and ethical dilemmas in science and technology. The work’s dramaturgist Carmen Kovacs said, “We started with the original myth, but since it has been changed and interpreted in so many ways, we thought we would do our own story and combine it with this idea of AI and how humankind has brought it upon themselves.” Ballerina Jennifer Stahl and San Francisco Ballet members rehearsing Aszure Barton’s and Sam Shepherd’s Mere Mortals, which will have its world premiere on Friday, January 26. Winter thoughts By Joseph Gold There is a stillness in the air and the streets are almost devoid of traffic. The cold winter sun casts long shadows. The Christmas rush is over as the old year raced towards its inevitable close. Observations like this cause us to reflect on the year past. Generally speaking, our thoughts depend on our outlook on life. A certain overindulgence causes most of us to make New Year’s resolutions. While some of the world has gone into artistic hibernation, others have found ways to be productive. A talented musical friend of mine has written five books on violin technique. He claims that these books are his musical autobiography. There is no doubt that he has lived a full life and the books are proof of that. For some musical organizations, Spring has come early. Both San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera have a new Music Director. Oakland Symphony continues its search for a luminary to illuminate the podium. On the home front, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is planning some exciting concerts. The Piedmont Center for the Arts continues on its successful course despite some roadblocks instigated by politicians and petty bureaucrats. On a personal note, my wife and I enjoyed a New Year’s Eve feast last year at one of our favorite restaurants, Italian Colors. The festive spirit was everywhere despite the storm… um, I mean… The atmospheric river. We enjoyed superb prawns stuffed with Dungeness crab on the first official day of San Francisco’s crab season one year ago. A unique pizza topped with fragrant black truffles was not exactly Neapolitan, but it was memorable nevertheless. Adding to the evening’s enjoyment was a visit to the table by the restaurant owner Alan Carlson and his son Dylan who stopped by to give us extra slices of both black and white truffles. A lively couple at the neighboring table brought over some of their prize-winning wine and aged brandy. As the Germans say. “Das leben ist Lebenswert (literally, “life is beautiful”). As the “atmospheric river” continues on its way to the sea at the start of 2024, whether you ask the question in singular “quo vadis”, or make it more general in the plural, “quo vadimus” (where are we going?), we ask, has anything changed? Have a great year. articles.text: “We are experiencing an entertainment revolution” The 81st Golden Globes annual awards ceremony will take place on Jan. 7, 2024, at the Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills and will air live on CBS from 5-8 p.m. It will honor the Best in films and television from the past year. The list of nominees was recently posted. The Globe Awards were the creation of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association in 1944, and today is comprised of 300 international journalists who cover the American entertainment industry. In many respects its annual awards ceremony mirrors the Oscars (to include the runway glitterati, brief interviews, formal wear and haute couture) with one increasingly important difference – the unexpectedly prescient category titled Television. The Oscars, founded in 1927, continues to be Hollywood’s most prestigious artistic award ceremony in the film industry. Winners are selected by the nearly 10,000-person membership of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Science. Its list of nominations will soon be announced in anticipation of its 96th annual gala in early March 2024 and is slated to air on ABC. For decades the inclusion of television likely placed the ceremony in a tier just below the Oscars. To watch TV was, well, pedestrian. Film was something else. Since the early 1900s, there have been larger-than-life big screens. And the grainy, flickering films, silent at first, soon included sound, the photography became more vivid (recall the advent of Technicolor), dialogue more graphic, and plots more intense, some driven by special effects technology such as CGI. Movies soon took audiences to places that were and are extraordinary. To watch Top Gun for the first time was unforgettable. After almost a century the experience of going to the movies has become deeply embedded in our culture. The actors were called “stars,” and for countless fans the line between the fiction on the screen and the reality that awaited them upon leaving the theater was often blurred. Film became and remains entertainment like no other – both evocative and emotive. And then came the COVID pandemic and we found ourselves confined for long periods in our homes. As theaters closed and movie sets shut down, it quickly became evident to Hollywood that audiences regarded sitting in a dark, cavernous room with strangers to watch a movie as high risk. Lock-downs were mandated, streets eerily empty, masks and vaccines debated. As a nation, we were haunted by this invisible virus. And so we waited and turned to our televisions, watching anything that was entertaining or newsworthy. Those of us who hadn’t yet discovered Netflix and similar streaming services, learned that thousands of movies were available as well as enormous wall-mounted screens that offered state-of-the-art clarity and sound. Not only were previously released films accessible, but Netflix, Paramount+, Prime and Disney+ began making their own films and signing name actors. It became clear that many of these movies did not adhere to the standard two-hour format. What became available were lengthy series, identified by seasons and episodes. This new configuration allowed writers to develop far more complex characters, create evolving, expanding plots, increasingly diverse settings, and multiple, simultaneous story lines. A season can end (not conclude) with the promise that the story line will continue, opening later with, say, Season 2-Episode 1. If an episode is missed, it’s easy to find and watch it. If a series is newly discovered, you can start at the beginning and binge-watch. If the series proves compelling, you can wait several weeks then rinse and repeat. Meanwhile, there is always a long list of traditional movies offered on various sites such as Freevee, Hallmark, Tubi or YouTube, featuring long-ago released films now available. Which brings us back to the Golden Globes, and the “Best of“ television categories (12), derived from streaming formats, There’s “Best Television Series – Drama”; “Best Television Series – “Musical or Comedy”; “Best Television Limited Series, Anthology Series, or Motion Picture Made for Television.” Examples would be the series 1923, 1893, Yellowstone, The Crown, Jack Ryan, Bosch, or The Lincoln Lawyer. And many more, with A-list actors and superb writing. It is with these categories, many made especially for streaming on television, that the Golden Globes has become more relevant to that growing post-pandemic audience that now prefers to be entertained watching newly released series or traditional movies from the comfort of their sofas or easy chairs instead of going to a movie theater. I would suggest that we are experiencing an entertainment revolution, one that is still evolving. It is the Golden Globes that finds itself ahead of the curve, while the Academy Awards, which is focused solely on film, will either adapt or become a niche ceremony with a shrinking audience. I realize that it’s hard to imagine that movie theaters will one day be viewed with head-shaking nostalgia. Of course, I could be wrong. These places, with their giant screens and Dolby sound, will not go the way of the landline. We’ll see.

articles.text: Tianna Sansbury, Laura Monagan and Everlyn Sampi in Rabbit-Proof Fence Review by Chris Honoré Rabbit-Proof Fence is an extraordinary and surprising film, not only in its austere, Australian location, but in its focus. The story, set in 1931, is adapted from the novel Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence by Doris Pilkington, and recounts the journey of three young girls – Molly (Evelyn Sampi), Daisy (Tianna Scansbury), and Gracie (Laura Monaghan). They are, to use a softer Hawaiian word, “hapa.” One parent is white and the other is Aborigine (the indigenous people of Australia). They are referred to as “half-castes.” During this period it was Australia’s policy to take these hapa children from their parents, forcibly when necessary, and send them to Christian orphanages cum schools where they would become “civilized.” Some would be placed with families as maids, others were married off to a white male with the intention that after three generations the dark color of their skin would vanish along with all remnants of their culture. In Rabbit-Proof Fence the government official charged with reeducating the kidnapped children is called, simply, Mr. Neville (Kenneth Branagh). He is blind to the racism in his views and the cruelty inflicted not only on the defenseless children but on their parents. And therein is the essence of this film. Molly (14), Daisy (10), and Gracie (8) are taken by train to one such orphanage; however, instead of bending to the harsh rules, with Molly in charge, they plan their escape and set off into the outback, determined to return home to Jigalong, where their mothers live. What they are unaware of is that they are 1200 miles away, and uncertain how they will survive or possibly find their way. And thus begins their journey across a desiccated, unforgiving land. While they meet local ranchers/farmers along the way, they find that some are momentarily helpful, and others are hostile, carriers of attitudes born of prejudice and discrimination. The three are unaware that an Aboriginal tracker, Moodoo (David Gulpili), on horseback, has been hired by the orphanage to find the girls and bring them back. He is not far behind. Molly soon realizes that if they follow the endlessly long Rabbit-Proof Fence they will eventually come to Jigalong and there be reunited with their mothers. Meanwhile, Neville has hired his own searchers, and is certain that the girls are indeed using the Fence as a kind of compass. Studying maps of the area, he intends to intercept them before they reach home. Rabbit-Proof Fence is wonderful story of courage, defiance, and determination. The photography, the images of these three girls as they struggle find their way, are stunning and their performances, especially that of Evelyn Sampi as Molly, are touching and heartfelt. R a b b i t - P r o o f F e n c e . Directed by Phillip Noyce. Starring Evelyn Sampi, Tianna Scansbury, Laura Monaghan. Released 2002. Rated PG. 1hr 34min. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Paramount+/Apple tv

articles.text: Piedmont resident Phil Witte, a former attorney, is the cartoonist whose single panel cartoon FLIP has appeared in the Piedmont Post since 2008. His cartoons have been published in dozens of publications in the U.S. and U.K., including the Wall Street Journal, Reader’s Digest, San Francisco Chronicle, New Statesman, and Private Eye, as well as in books, calendars, and greeting cards. His humor book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and the sequel on turning 60 have sold over 170,000 copies. Phil also co-writes the Anatomy of a Cartoon blog for CartoonStock, founded by Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker. Phil’s cartoons have been exhibited in group shows in San Francisco, Minneapolis, London, and Galway, Ireland, and he had a solo show at Dominican College in San Rafael earlier this year. He has been a cartoonist-in-residence at the Charles Schulz Museum and the San Francisco Cartoon Art Museum. Phil is a member of the National Cartoonists Society. See www.philwitte.com. “The wedge was Archimedes’ idea.” “Helen?” “You’re not going anywhere until we finalize our estate plan.”

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group has a standing joke that it never rains in Piedmont on Wednesday mornings. Their lucky charm was broken on December 20 when a small group gathered in the rain with their umbrellas at the Exedra: Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kellogg, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Charlene Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Pat Keller, Priscilla Wanerus, and Dick Carter. An additional 13 walkers showed up for the group’s annual holiday luncheon at Zachary’s Pizza on Grand Avenue. That group included Christine Calliste, Aaron Katzel. Rob Smith, Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado, David Haecker, Elizabeth Richter, Chuck Oraftik, Alicia Rivera, Brenda Ferrero, Harriette Louie, Mike and Nancy Henn. As they passed the recently closed Piedmont Shell Station, its history and current status were shared. Piedmont Shell had been in Piedmont for 95 years, but it was announced in November that it would close at end of the month. The property is being sold by Shell Auto Care owner Jeff Hansen to Shell Recharge, a division of Shell Oil. The station has three 10,000-gallon gas tanks under the pumps that need to be replaced by 2025. New tanks would have enabled the station to continue to sell gas for decades, but the increased popularity of electric vehicles made the owner feel uncomfortable with the future of gasoline stations and the investment. Influencing this was California’s plans to achieve 100% new zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035, and have a 25% reduction in smog-causing pollution by 2037. Shell plans to demolish the existing station and replace it with a 14-bay electric vehicle charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. Fast charging will be provided with power up to 360kW. Pricing of charges will be on a pay-as-you-go basis with prices on an app, and varying base on the time of day. No employees will be regularly on the site. These plans need permitting and regulatory approval. Shell hopes the project will be added to the City’s public hearing January agenda, and that they will be able to start construction in the first half of 2024. The walkers planned to be at Zachary’s around 11:15 so that they could beat the lunch rush. Among those coming to the restaurant were Christine Calliste and Aaron Katzel. Christine was the day’s special guest because it was her last walk with the group for a while. She has been working with the Katzel family for over 10 years in both New York and California, and she will be retiring and returning to her native Grenada. Christine was thanked for her friendliness, kindness, and being a wonderful member of the group. Christine said how much she had enjoyed the group and being together. She promised to start a Wednesday walking group in Granada. After some warm lunch conversations and lots of hot pizza, the walkers wished each other happy holidays, and walked outside to a sunny afternoon. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Members of the Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed their annual holiday luncheon at Zachary’s Pizza on December 20.
articles.title: It’s pizza time for Walking on Wednesday group

articles.text: It is never too soon to be proactive about your health and longevity. As we ring in the New Year, many of us have considered that healthy lifestyle goals and the meals we consume are a large part of it. Gigantic Royal Corona beans are the stars of this soup. They cook up tender and, dare I say, “meaty” owing to their size and toothsomeness. They’re as fun to eat as they are impressive to those new to them. Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup Adapted from Diane Kochilas’ Fasolada – Bean Soup with Pumpkin & Corn Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 1/2 pound giant beans such as Royal Corona or Greek gigantes • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided, preferably Greek • 1-1/2 red onion, coarsely chopped, about 1-1/2 cups • 2 tablespoons fresh garlic, minced, divided • 1 tablespoon tomato paste • 1 14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes • 1 bay leaf • 1/2 teaspoon dried oregano, or 2 sprigs fresh • 1 3-inch-long strip of fresh orange peel • 1 cup corn kernels • 1 cup cubed delicata or butternut squash • 1/4 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped • 1 – 2 teaspoons honey, preferably local • 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar, scant measure to taste • 1/2 – 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • A few grinds black peppercorns, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Check the beans for debris, rinse and then soak overnight; drain and discard the soaking water. Soaking is optional but will decrease the cooking time considerably. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large soup pot over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5–10 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent scorching. Stir in 1 tablespoon of the minced garlic (set remaining 1 tablespoon aside for later), give it a quick stir; then add the tomato paste. Stir again to incorporate the tomato paste well. Add the drained beans, canned tomatoes, bay leaf, oregano, and orange peel. Top off with enough water to cover by 2 inches. Bring to a boil then reduce to a simmer until the beans are very tender, about 1-1/2 to 2 hours. When the beans are tender, scoop out about 1 cup of the soup and puree in a food processor or blender/immersion stick blender, then return to the pot. This blending step is optional but will add a bit of body to the soup. Meanwhile, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the squash and corn until lightly browned, then add the remaining garlic and sea salt. Mix well then add to the soup pot once the beans have cooked through and the pureed portion has been added back to the pot. Return the soup to a simmer and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper. Just before serving remove the orange peel and bay leaf. Stir in the chopped parsley, honey and balsamic vinegar. Serve with an additional drizzle of high-quality, extra-virgin olive oil and a few sprinkles of parsley. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok at: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.
articles.title: Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup

Shell plans to demolish the existing station and replace it with a 14-bay electric vehicle charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. Fast charging will be provided with power up to 360kW. Pricing of charges will be on a pay-as-you-go basis with prices on an app, and varying base on the time of day. No employees will be regularly on the site. These plans need permitting and regulatory approval. Shell hopes the project will be added to the City’s public hearing January agenda, and that they will be able to start construction in the first half of 2024. The walkers planned to be at Zachary’s around 11:15 so that they could beat the lunch rush. Among those coming to the restaurant were Christine Calliste and Aaron Katzel. Christine was the day’s special guest because it was her last walk with the group for a while. She has been working with the Katzel family for over 10 years in both New York and California, and she will be retiring and returning to her native Grenada. Christine was thanked for her friendliness, kindness, and being a wonderful member of the group. Christine said how much she had enjoyed the group and being together. She promised to start a Wednesday walking group in Granada. After some warm lunch conversations and lots of hot pizza, the walkers wished each other happy holidays, and walked outside to a sunny afternoon. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Photo by Deborah Quok Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup is a great dish for a cold winter day. Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup By Deborah Quok It is never too soon to be proactive about your health and longevity. As we ring in the New Year, many of us have considered that healthy lifestyle goals and the meals we consume are a large part of it. Gigantic Royal Corona beans are the stars of this soup. They cook up tender and, dare I say, “meaty” owing to their size and toothsomeness. They’re as fun to eat as they are impressive to those new to them. Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup Adapted from Diane Kochilas’ Fasolada – Bean Soup with Pumpkin & Corn Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 1/2 pound giant beans such as Royal Corona or Greek gigantes • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided, preferably Greek • 1-1/2 red onion, coarsely chopped, about 1-1/2 cups • 2 tablespoons fresh garlic, minced, divided • 1 tablespoon tomato paste • 1 14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes • 1 bay leaf • 1/2 teaspoon dried oregano, or 2 sprigs fresh • 1 3-inch-long strip of fresh orange peel • 1 cup corn kernels • 1 cup cubed delicata or butternut squash • 1/4 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped • 1 – 2 teaspoons honey, preferably local • 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar, scant measure to taste • 1/2 – 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • A few grinds black peppercorns, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Check the beans for debris, rinse and then soak overnight; drain and discard the soaking water. Soaking is optional but will decrease the cooking time considerably. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large soup pot over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5–10 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent scorching. Stir in 1 tablespoon of the minced garlic (set remaining 1 tablespoon aside for later), give it a quick stir; then add the tomato paste. Stir again to incorporate the tomato paste well. Add the drained beans, canned tomatoes, bay leaf, oregano, and orange peel. Top off with enough water to cover by 2 inches. Bring to a boil then reduce to a simmer until the beans are very tender, about 1-1/2 to 2 hours. When the beans are tender, scoop out about 1 cup of the soup and puree in a food processor or blender/immersion stick blender, then return to the pot. This blending step is optional but will add a bit of body to the soup. Meanwhile, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the squash and corn until lightly browned, then add the remaining garlic and sea salt. Mix well then add to the soup pot once the beans have cooked through and the pureed portion has been added back to the pot. Return the soup to a simmer and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper. Just before serving remove the orange peel and bay leaf. Stir in the chopped parsley, honey and balsamic vinegar. Serve with an additional drizzle of high-quality, extra-virgin olive oil and a few sprinkles of parsley. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok at: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/. articles.text: Penelope “Penny” Knowland Robb of Piedmont, a friend and colleague of many in town for many years, passed away on January 1, 2024. She was 79. Born in Seattle, Washington on March 1, 1944, she was the daughter of Joseph Russell Knowland, Jr. and Norma Diane Piva, She graduated from Piedmont High School in 1961 and in 1991 she graduated from the University of California, Berkeley with her bachelor’s degree in social sciences. Penny married Orland “Dean” Robb, Sr. on July 21, 1962, in Piedmont Community Church. They lived in Columbia, Missouri for a year before settling in Piedmont. They lived on Hillside Avenue for almost 30 years where they enjoyed countless neighborhood block parties, family celebrations, and domino tournaments. Penny and Dean had 40 wonderful years together before his death in February 2002. Penny worked as a Supervisor in the Piedmont Recreation Department for 30 years before retiring in December 2014. Many Piedmonters booked the Community Center or Veterans Hall through her. She was an active member of the Piedmont community and served as a member of the Piedmont Community Church, the Piedmont Fortnightly Book Club, the Piedmont Historical Society, and the Piedmont Seniors group. She was a life-long volunteer of the UCSF Benioff Children’s her love of baseball and travel. She was an A’s season ticket holder for over 40 years and recently worked for the A’s organization as a secretary to the owner. She enjoyed traveling and visited Italy several times throughout her life. Since her retirement, she enjoyed taking cruises and seeing the world with her friends. In November 2023, she took her family to Yosemite National Park. It was her first time going to Yosemite and it will be a fond memory for her family. Penny will be dearly missed by her children Diane Robb Logan and her husband Floyd Logan; Dean Robb Jr. and his wife Jill; and Russell Robb and his wife Mollie. Her grandchildren Kimberly Chatham, Jessica Chatham Embry, Philip, Hannah, Spencer, Allison, and Tanner Robb, and great-grandchildren Will and Addie Embry, will remember her as a kind, loving, giving, and sweet soul. She is survived by her brother Jay Knowland and his wife Cathy, extended family, and many cherished friends. She is predeceased by a sister, Patricia “Tish” Knowland Barker. A memorial service will be held on Friday, January 12, at 1 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church with a reception to follow in the church’s Guild Hall. The family asks that memorial donations be made to UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland Hill Branch at https:// www.hillbranch.org. Penny Robb passed away on January 1, 2024. She was 79. Penny’s children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren meant the world to her. She could always be seen cheering them on in the stands at their sporting events, or in the audience at their performances. articles.text: We are saddened to announce that H. Ellison Dunlap Jr., a long time member of the Piedmont Highlander Drums and Pipes band, passed away on October 24, 2023. Ellison was born on January 4, 1944 and raised in Salt Lake City, Utah. He attended classes at the University of Utah and moved to Alameda, California with his mother as a young man. He worked for Montgomery Ward as a display artist and photographer and served two years as a Mormon missionary in Wales, where he met his wife, Nancy. He and Nancy founded their printing business, West Coast Arts, in the late 1960’s. After a long career in printing, health issues forced him to retire. Ellison led a full life with numerous hobbies and businesses. He was an award-winning professional photographer, amateur historian, and also won awards as an amateur filmmaker. He headed the Social Committee for the Concord Gun Club, served as a teacher in his church, and shared his artistic talents in support of many church events. He was a member of numerous historical reenactment groups, including Roman, Medieval, Renaissance, Civil War, and WWII. He had a wide-ranging collection of militaria and loved to dress up in period outfits. He excelled in blacksmithing, ceramics, cooking, drawing, garden railroading, jewelry making, magic, mold-making, photography, sculpting, sewing, and ventriloquism. He also played the accordion and was a drummer in the Piedmont Highlander Drums and Pipes band. He was an integral part of the Piedmont Post, quietly helping with weekly circulation and distribution of the paper. Ellison is survived by his wife of 56 years, Nancy Baston Dunlap, his sons H. Ellison Dunlap III and wife Judith Hollenberger, and Anthony Marshall Dunlap, and grandchildren Herschel Ellison Ellison Dunlap, Jr., a longtime resident of Piedmont and owner of West Coast Arts, passed away on October 24, 2023 at age 79. Dunlap IV and Kayla Gray Dunlap. He is also survived by his sister Caroline Gerold Peterson. He is predeceased by his parents. Lt. Col. H. Ellison Dunlap and Doreen Brown Dunlap. Ellison is interred at the Chapel of the Chimes in Oakland. A celebration of his life will be held later this year. articles.text: Ambrose Bierce was one of the most original writers in American history. His magnum opus, The Devil’s Dictionary, reveals his pugnacious sarcasm to best effect. While there is no information about Bierce’s interest in music, I obtained a document purportedly by Bierce. This “lexicon of musical terms“ has all the earmarks of Bierce’s sharply-pointed humor. Here are a few examples: Piccolo: noun, A small instrument which causes considerable bodily injury. The bane of audiologists. Trombone: noun, the comedian of the orchestra. Given to scatological humor and flatulence. Usually played by mischievous boys who want to annoy girls. Percussion instruments: plural, tone-deaf musicians released on early parole. Some of them become conductors. Violin: noun, when played well, you think you are in heaven. When played badly you think you are in hell. Violin bow: a club made of wood resembling a slender baseball bat and strung with horse hair from the rear end of a horse. Generally used to beat a Violin black and blue. Practice: noun or a verb, an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam. Concert: noun, practicing in public. See above. Conductor: noun of questionable progeny. Literally the prince of fools. Usually an egotist from highest Valhalla who thinks he knows everything. Despised by members of the orchestra even though they aspire to the position.

November After 95 years of continuous business, the Piedmont Shell Station at the corner of Wildwood & Grand Ave. closed on November 7. Following 17 years of ownership, owner Jeff Hansen sold the property to the Shell Corporation, which intends to rebuild the station as an electric vehicle hub. Just a little over a month after the Hamas attacks on Israeli territory in early October, Piedmonters rallied to mourn the violence in the Middle East. Members of the Piedmont Jewish community installed an empty Shabbat table in the parking lot of Community Hall on November 9 as a symbolic message of solidarity with the 241 hostages in Hamas captivity. This year’s 22nd annual Turkey Trot continued to be a cherished family tradition in the city, with 2,400 people running in the 5-kilometer race on Thanksgiving morning. This year’s winner was 19-year-old Jack Stein, a recent Piedmont High School graduate who won first place with a record-breaking time of 15:30. December Holiday cheer was in the air at Lights Up Piedmont, the city’s newest iteration of the holiday tree lighting ceremony. Piedmonters gathered outside Community Hall on December 6, to drink cocoa, eat latkes, and watch the lights come on atop the city tree, along with new traditions including the simultaneous lighting of a menorah beside the city tree. The Scout Tree Lot sold out 11 days before Christmas, one of the earliest days on record. Organizers thanked Scout and parent volunteers for the return after the pandemic of their cherished tradition and its financial benefit for the Piedmont Scout Council, one of the oldest and smallest councils in the U.S. At a December 18 city council meeting, George Sanen of Griffin Structures announced that the new projected completion date for the community pool has been pushed back even further to October 2024. The original estimate was for the pool to be ready by the summer of 2024. Sports YIR Continued from page 15 The Piedmont Shell Station closed on November 7 after 95 years in business. Photo courtesy of McDonald’s official Instagram Mackie McDonald made noise in 2023 with a big upset over legend Rafael Nadal last January. went ahead 4-3 as the returner forcing deuce and taking advantage, once again. McDonald then went up 5-3, and Nadal wound up hampered by a nagging hip injury. Mackie smashed two straight aces and Nadal went to the bench with an injury. Nadal returned after a medical timeout to make it 5-4 but McDonald won as the returner, 6-4, closing out the second set. In the third set, the two sides traded games as the server until the set was at 5-5. From there, McDonald went ahead 6-5 as the returner up with two break point opportunities up 40-15. With match point, Mackie closed out the biggest match of his life up 40-15 thanks to a ball out by Nadal, two winners, and a ball into the net by Nadal to close it, 7-5 for McDonald. It marked the second time McDonald faced Nadal, last losing to him in three sets in the second round of the 2020 French Open. Unfortunately for Nadal, it seemed like the Swan Song for the aging veteran. Nadal played his very first match since his injury this week in the Brisbane International, where he defeated Dominic Thiem 7-5, 6-1 on Tuesday, January 2. This year’s Australian Open main draw starts on Saturday, January 13. Oakland A’s departs to Las Vegas In heartbreaking but expected news, the Oakland Athletics announced their official plans to depart the Bay Area to Las Vegas in April, joining the Raiders as another professional sports organization to leave for Sin City. On November 16, the Athletics’ move to Las Vegas was unanimously approved by all MLB team owners. The team announced its new stadium will not be completed until 2028, and with their lease to the Oakland Coliseum expiring after the 2024 season, this year could be the last opportunity to see the A’s play in Oakland. The team has determined it could play at the San Francisco Giants’ Oracle Park or at the A’s Triple-A affiliate, the Las Vegas Aviators’ ballpark. Re-leasing the Coliseum is also a possibility. Whatever the case may be, the A’s announcement appears to be a death-knell for MLB in the East Bay. The 80-foot holiday tree towers above Community Hall at the annual Lights Up ceremony. articles.text: in this place? What has her journey been like? The photograph’s caption reads Nipomo, Calif. And what is just outside that tent? A camp of sorts? A rest stop, if only for a night? What wave of harshness brought her to this moment? And if her gaze is lost in another place – perhaps filled with memories of where she began, or of thoughts about where this journey might end – then her emotions are clearly defined by an unrelenting uncertainty. Her moment is the Great Depression, an economic riptide that swept millions of Americans away, a time made manifest by breadlines, shanty towns, desperate men and women lost, their experiences to be etched forever in their memories, a referent voiced forever as before and after. The images from the Depression are vastly different from ours; yet, in many ways, they are the same. Our neighborhoods were silent, doors closed, drapes tightly drawn, families, friends, perhaps strangers waiting inside. Unspeaking masked shoppers walked apart, stood in hushed lines in grocery stores and pharmacies, waiting to pay, taking creased bills in change, wondering where they had been before, whose hands they had passed through. Everywhere the floors were marked with small red admonishments to keep one’s distance. How close was too close? Even the hint of a greeting smile was lost behind cloth. Is this the new normal, we grimly wondered? Or will this, the all of it, be our before and after, sometimes, always, remembered?

articles.text: After the holidays, Piedmont residents may dispose of their Christmas trees using Republic Services curbside pickup or by cutting it up and placing it in the appropriate waste cart. Christmas trees can dry out and become a fire hazard. Once you are done with your tree, you should not leave it in your home or garage or lean it against your home outdoors. Republic Services will collect natural, unflocked trees curbside from December 26 to January 6. These trees will be turned into valuable compost and mulch. Put your tree out on your regular service day. Before placing your tree on the curb, remove all lights, decorations, tinsel, ornaments, and the tree stand. If your tree is more than 6 feet tall, cut it in half. Natural trees may be cut up and placed in your organic waste cart. Flocked, or “snow covered” trees are not compostable or recyclable. To dispose of a flocked or artificial tree, cut it up so that it fits in your black waste cart with the lid closed. Republic Services will collect non-compostable trees curbside by request. Call 800-320-8077 to schedule a pickup. There is a $30.82 disposal fee for curbside collection of non-compostable trees. You can use your annual Bulky Item Clean-ups for non-compostable trees in lieu of the pickup fee. When placing non-compostable trees for curbside pickup, cut them into pieces 4-feet long or shorter. For questions about holiday tree collection, email piedmont@ repsrv.com or call (800) 320- 8077.
